#601. Obama unloads on Trump over the Iran war and mocks the president’s diplomatic strategy

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Obama bashed Trump for causing fuel prices to surge and what he saw as the unnecessary deaths of service members in a war that has raged on for nearly eight months

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Former Democratic President Barack Obama has unloaded on Donald Trump for the Iran war, mocking the Republican president’s diplomatic strategy.

“These are not serious people. They’re not serious people. And the problem is you end up having to pay the price for their lack of seriousness,” Obama said Saturday while stumping for Democrats in Ohio.

The U.S., alongside Israel, started launching strikes against Iran in late February, with Trump claiming that Americans were in imminent danger over the Middle Eastern country’s nuclear ambitions.

But Obama argued that the issue had already been dealt with under his administration — until Trump unraveled it.

“Let’s think about this Iran war. The original rationale was, we’re going to go in there and get them to give up their nuclear program, their nuclear weapons,” Obama said. “Now, the thing was, Iran didn’t have nuclear weapons, because I put a deal in place that everybody acknowledged — kept them from getting nukes. And I didn’t have to fire a missile to do it; I just had to engage in diplomacy.”

Obama was referring to the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action, commonly called the Iran Nuclear Deal, which the Middle Eastern country signed in 2015 and Trump withdrew from during his first term.

The deal restricted Iran’s nuclear program to ensure it was only using those materials for peaceful purposes in exchange for sanctions relief.

But Trump argued when withdrawing from the deal in 2018 that it “allowed Iran to continue enriching uranium and — over time — reach the brink of a nuclear breakout.”

Trump has insisted throughout the war that it would be a quick operation, but it has now dragged on for nearly eight months. Soon after the strikes began, Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz, blocking oil tankers from passing through the vital passageway and causing fuel prices to skyrocket.

A total of 21 American service members have been killed and 865 wounded in operations related to the war, according to the Pentagon.

“So seven months later, how’s that war going?” Obama asked.

“Our allies and our bases have been attacked; Americans have been killed; hundreds of Americans have been wounded; we have, we’ve run down our stock of missiles,” the former president said, though Trump has denied reports of munitions shortages. “And Iran now has veto power over the Strait of Hormuz, where oil goes through to the world market.

“This is the reason why the price of oil is up. Nobody disputes that. This is reason the price diesel is up. This is why the reason the just about everything is up.”

Trump is hosting daily rallies across the country to boost Republicans’ chances of keeping control of Congress in November’s midterm elections — all while dealing with his deeply unpopular war.

Forty-seven percent of Democrat voters and 56 percent of Republican voters think ending the war in Iran should be one of the highest priorities for the next Congress, according to a new AP/NORC Center for Public Affairs Research poll.

Obama was in Cleveland Saturday to support Amy Acton, who is running for Ohio governor against Trump ally Vivek Ramaswamy, and former Senator Sherrod Brown, who is running against Republican Senator Jon Husted.

Ramaswamy saw his betting odds plummet over a controversial ad using his opponent’s mother, whom Acton has accused of abuse, to call her a “liar” and urge Ohians not to vote for her.

Acton has an 83 percent chance of winning the race compared to Ramaswamy’s 18 percent on the prediction market Polymarket as of Saturday evening.

Ramaswamy was also trailing Acton by seven points in a traditional poll. Acton had 50 percent of support among likely Ohio voters compared to Ramaswamy’s 43 percent, according to a recent survey conducted by Marist Poll before the campaign ad was released.

In that same poll, Brown was up four points with 48 percent of voter support compared to Husted’s 44 percent.

#602. Macron accused of putting France’s right to protest at risk with ‘vandal’s law’

Making innocent protesters liable for damage would be bad for rule of law and play into far-right hands, say opponents

Emmanuel Macron has been accused by trade unions of trying to curb the fundamental French right to protest as the government fast-tracks a bill to make protesters pay for damage caused by vandalism at street demonstrations even if they did not directly cause it themselves.

The French president, who leaves office next spring, has faced more than a month of protests in which high-school students have blockaded schools demanding a response to teacher absences, repairs to decrepit buildings and changes to the university applications platform.

Trade unions and gilets jaunes (yellow vest) anti-government protesters are now joining sustained street demonstrations in a growing social crisis over schools, as well as the cost of living and public services. Authorities have increased security measures and placed restrictions on demonstrating after France saw one of its worst days of violence in years earlier this month when largely peaceful demonstrations were marred by looting, fires and vandalism of state buildings.

The senate will this week debate the government’s proposed “vandals pay” law. The legislation would mean that a person protesting could be held liable to pay up to €10,000 for damage and vandalism even if they did not directly cause it themselves, if they were continuing to demonstrate nearby or as part of the same group as perpetrators. The bill also provides for greater use of drones over protests.

The prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, said the bill, which was originally prepared in the wake of violent clashes after Paris Saint-Germain’s victory over Arsenal in the football Champions League in May, was “absolutely essential” after looting and burning during recent demonstrations across France.

The bill comes as the government struggles to contain the current crisis. Marine Le Pen, of the far-right, anti-immigration National Rally (RN), has seen her frontrunner status in next spring’s presidential election boosted as she seeks to reinforce her law-and-order credentials and back police.

Le Pen, who has lodged an appeal to France’s highest court over her conviction for embezzlement of European parliament funds, launched her presidential campaign on Sunday at a rally in Orléans, promising to “bring back order to France”.

The RN has claimed the “vandals pay” bill was originally its idea and Le Pen said she would ensure damage to property was paid for by rioters. Le Pen told a cheering crowd of more than 8,000 people at the rally: “Vandals will pay and if it takes their whole life to pay, then they will spend their whole life paying.”

She said: “We are going to restore the rule of law. Who can claim that there is rule of law when hordes come to ransack and burn our buildings?”

Éric Coquerel, from Jean-Luc Mélenchon’s radical left La France Insoumise, said on Sunday that the “vandals pay” law “would mean the end of street demonstrations” in France because people would not want to take the risk of being held responsible and made to pay up to €10,000 for vandalism they had not committed. The Communist senator Fabien Gay told the parliamentary TV channel Public Sénat: “No demonstration could take place again in our country.”

In an open letter to Le Monde, leftwing trade unions and France’s Human Rights League wrote: “This unfair law, which is a serious attack on the freedom to demonstrate, should be abandoned, or risk a major step back for the rule of law.”

At this weekend’s protests there was widespread anger at Macron for banning non-union demonstrations that his government deemed “illegitimate” and for keeping all protesters away from city centres.

Although Macron has not put in place a state of emergency, the government and local authorities have introduced limits on demonstrating, including bans on gatherings in front of schools and demonstrating in city centres, as well as curfews in some places and extended periods of police custody for the record number of people arrested.

At demonstrations this weekend, many said they had come out to defend the French right to protest in the street. Street protests in France, which are seen as a fundamental way for people to make themselves heard by a centralised state, have regularly been used to express criticism of changes to the law, from pension changes to same-sex marriage.

Serge Slama, a professor of public law at Université Grenoble Alpes, told Telerama magazine: “Although a state of emergency has been ruled out [by Emmanuel Macron] at this point, we have seen a number of decrees bringing a wide restriction on public liberties.”

He said this was “unprecedented” and would benefit the far right if they won elections next year, allowing them to put in place further crackdowns without changing the law.

Lecornu will meet representatives of protesting high-schoolers on Monday as the government comes under pressure to respond to their demands with funding and school repairs in order to avoid further school blockades.

#603. 'Day Zero' where UK reservoirs run dry could happen before Christmas, ministers are secretly warned

Published: 01:59 GMT, 26 October 2026 | Updated: 03:12 GMT, 26 October 2026

Ministers have been secretly warned that reservoirs could run dry within weeks, causing chaos for families in the run-up to Christmas.

The Government's emergency committee, Cobra, is meeting twice a week for crisis talks about water provision in the south-west of England and Sussex.

A 'reasonable worst-case scenario' drawn up in secret by officials suggested water stocks could plummet to zero per cent in weeks.

Without action, it could lead to taps running dry in homes and affect the construction of a nuclear power plant.

Wimbleball reservoir which supplies more than 400,000 people in Somerset is currently at 13 per cent capacity, while Ardingly, which serves 280,000 customers in West Sussex, is at just 17 per cent.

A summer of record-breaking heatwaves led to widespread droughts, with some parts of England still under hosepipe bans even after two autumn storms have hit the country.

Sussex and the south-west were two of the areas worst affected by the lack of rainfall, having faced their driest April to September for more than a century and are still facing critically low water supplies.

Crisis plans have been drawn up for a terrifying 'Day Zero' scenario where reservoirs run completely dry in each area.

Pictured: Wimbleball reservoir - which is at 14 per cent capacity

Ardingly in West Sussex, which supplies about 95,000 properties served by South East Water in Haywards Heath, Uckfield and the surrounding areas, is at 19 per cent capacity

Fears of winter droughts have led to requests from water companies for the government to impose non-essential use bans which would prevent businesses from being able to operate car washes, water sports fields and refill private pools.

Southern Water, South East Water and South West Water have all called on Environment Secretary Dame Angela Eagle to consider such bans.

South West Water has told the government privately it does not anticipate Wimbleball running dry, due to preventative measures it had put in place, while South East Water does not expect to run dry until next year, if situations don't improve.

However, concerns still remain for provisions in Devon's Venford reservoir and 'day zero' risk monitoring has begun for Stithians and Drift reservoirs in Cornwall.

Even if the reservoirs did run completely dry, water companies would likely be able to transfer supplies from elsewhere.

Despite wet weather returning across the country, experts warned that normal levels of rainfall will not be enough to counteract the effects of the drought.

Officials said rainfall would need to be 120 per cent higher than average in the next six months in order to provide a nationwide recovery.

Water companies have been told to conduct daily monitoring of reservoir and river levels and tougher water quality monitoring, and the Environment Agency will increase compliance checks on businesses that abstract water to check they are only taking permitted amounts.

Last week Dame Angela ordered the Environment Agency to prioritise public water supply and allow fewer releases of reservoir water into rivers to help clean them and keep ecosystems healthy to reduce 'supply interruption'.

However, this has led to fears about the effect such a move could have on salmon and other fish, which could perish due to a lack of clean water.

The government told The Times: 'Customer water supplies remain uninterrupted. We have instructed water companies to transfer water to support the lowest reservoirs, speed up leak detection and deliver daily monitoring of reservoir and river levels to help ease the pressure on public supplies.'

South West Water said it was not expecting any water restrictions in early November. It said: 'We are taking urgent action to protect drinking water supplies, repairing around 440 leaks a week and transferring three million litres of water a day to areas where it is needed most.

'We are also exploring additional water sources and working directly with households and high-using businesses to reduce consumption.'

South East Water said 'day zero' was not being considered for 2027 given the actions it had taken. Southern Water and EDF Energy, the company behind Hinkley Point C, declined to comment.

John Halsall, chief executive of South East Water, previously told The Mail, supplies in the region are now under 'severe pressure' and standpipes may appear on British streets for the first time in 50 years.

Mr Halsall also ended exemptions to a months-long hosepipe ban in Sussex – with the rules expected to be in place until next year.

However, he admitted his company's efforts to persuade customers to use less water had not been as successful as hoped – with water demand falling by about 5 per cent rather than around 10 per cent as expected.

Mr Halsall also recognised that outages in Tunbridge Wells and other towns and villages had undermined customer confidence.

Drone footage revealed 'record' low reservoir levels at Wimbleball

The Environment Agency issued this drought update on October 15, 2026

Should the government impose tough water bans or let households and businesses decide how to cope?

Environment Agency chief executive Philip Duffy previously said: 'Record-breaking summer heat and severe drought have put our water resources under immense pressure.

'Recovery depends on both rainfall and how much water we use.

'We cannot change the weather, but water companies can act now. We expect them to follow their drought plans and take the steps needed to secure public water supplies.

'We are also asking everyone to use less water. That will leave more in our rivers and the environment, helping farmers and protecting wildlife and nature.'

The Environment Agency has granted South East Water’s drought permit application to reduce the amount of water Ardingly reservoir releases each day to the River Ouse by three million litres.

Separately, it has granted a drought permit application by South West Water to reduce the amount of water sent to the River Exe each day by nine million litres.

Last week a drought declaration was made for Yorkshire, with all of England now in drought except for the North West and North East which remain in prolonged dry weather status.

#604. The affordability question Republicans can't escape

One issue is breaking through even among the most loyal Republican supporters: gas prices.

Why it matters: Republicans promised to slash gas prices. But the Iran war sent them soaring, up 37% since President Trump took office.

  • Republicans call it temporary. But there are limits to what voters will accept.
  • On recent campaign trips with House Majority Whip Tom Emmer (R-Minn.) and Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R-La.), gas prices were the most frequent concern raised at events attended by Axios.
  • These weren't rooms full of undecided voters. They were GOP donors, activists and supporters who had turned out to help Republicans win in November.

Zoom in: The first question Scalise fielded at a campaign event for Republican Marty O'Donnell in Nevada was about high gas prices.

  • "Everyone's always worried about gas prices," the attendee said, asking whether Republicans could do more to promote Trump's efforts to expand domestic energy production.
  • Another attendee pointed to the gas-price difference between California and Oregon on a recent trip, and asked whether Congress could intervene to ease state restrictions.
  • Scalise acknowledged the impact of the Iran war on gas prices — and said they'd fall once it's resolved — but blamed Democratic energy policies for making the U.S. more vulnerable to rising costs.

Zoom out: Emmer faced similar concerns during a recent campaign trip through North Carolina and Virginia.

  • "Four-dollar gas, five-dollar diesel, six-dollar diesel, totally unacceptable," Emmer told supporters at a North Carolina fundraiser. "But it ain't enough to make me vote for communists."
  • "[Democrats] are talking about affordability. That's the problem. We need to be sensitive to the fact that gas and diesel are way up. Just sensitive to it because people are struggling," he told Axios in an interview.

The big picture: Republican candidates are feeling the pressure too.

  • Texas Republican Senate nominee Ken Paxton privately blamed the Iran war and gas prices for his campaign struggles, according to audio obtained by Axios.
  • "It's the war, it's gas prices, it's diesel," Paxton told donors at a closed-door fundraiser last month, calling affordability "by far our biggest problem."

The bottom line: "I don't think gaslighting works," House GOP conference Chairwoman Lisa McClain (R-Mich.) told Axios in an interview last month. "I think if you meet voters where they're at and you have an honest conversation with them ... that's pretty refreshing to them."

#605. Your guide to Proposition TE: Exempting fire victims from the 'mansion tax'

See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred

Many changes were proposed this election cycle to Measure ULA — the so-called ‘mansion tax’ that levies a fee on property sales above $5.4 million to raise money for housing and homeless initiatives — but only one made it to the ballot. Proposition TE seeks to exempt Palisades fire victims from paying the tax if they sell their home within five years of the disaster.

California’s general election takes place on Novemer 3. Learn about L.A.’s city and county races as well races for state office.

Measure ULA, which took effect in 2023, levies a 4% transfer tax on all L.A. property sales above $5.4 million and a 5.5% tax on sales above $10.9 million. Under current rules, if a Pacific Palisades resident who lost their home in the fire sold the vacant lot for, say, $6 million, they would owe $240,000 in transfer taxes.

Proposition TE would grant a one-time exemption to that tax, offered only to homeowners in Pacific Palisades selling properties that were damaged or destroyed by the Palisades fire. The exemption would last until Jan. 6, 2030 — five years from the date of the fire — and could retroactively be applied for refunds if a resident already sold their property and paid the tax. It applies to all residential properties, whether or not their owners lived there.

Advocates argue that fire victims already have been through enough, and paying the tax as a result of selling a house that’s been destroyed is unfair.

The ballot measure was approved by 13 of the 15 L.A. City Council members. Councilmember Traci Park, who led the initiative, called it the “least we can do as the community continues to recover,” adding that many are forced to sell because of lack of insurance or rebuilding costs.

“They’re not selling to profit. They’re not selling because they want to. They’re selling because they’ve already lost everything and there’s nothing left,” Park said in a July meeting.

Critics argue that the exemption is too broad and should have included only victims whose primary residence was destroyed as opposed to landlords or investors with portfolios of properties.

Councilmember Eunisses Hernandez, the only council member who voted against putting the measure on the ballot, called it a “loophole for the ultrawealthy” and said any exemption should favor lower-income victims such as tenants who lost rentals or laborers who lost work.

“When wealthy property owners need relief, we’re willing to bend over backwards … to meet their needs and desires. But when working-class people need protections, suddenly our hands are tied,” she said at a meeting in July.

Others are hesitant to stop any funds from flowing into Measure ULA, which raises funding for housing initiatives in the midst of a housing crisis. The exemption could reduce ULA revenue by 6% per year, or $32 million annually, according to the L.A. Housing Department.

Proposition TE was spearheaded by Park, whose district includes Pacific Palisades. As fire victims navigate insurance gaps and expensive rebuilding costs, the exemption was proposed as a way to give them more flexibility should they choose to sell their homes.

#606. Ageing users and record deaths – the data behind Britain’s multibillion-pound cocaine habit

Sewage samples and crime statistics paint a picture of established users taking more cocaine, more often

Cocaine-linked crimes on the rise in Britain as consumption surges

Pubs, festivals and workplaces: how cocaine has become an everyday habit

From pub toilets and private parties to football terraces and far-right marches, cocaine has become a familiar presence across modern Britain. Deaths linked to the drug have risen to record levels, while its supply supports a multibillion-pound criminal industry.

But who is using the drug, and how has the picture changed? The figures do not necessarily show millions of new users, but highlight an established market in which some people take more cocaine, more often – and face greater harm as they grow older.

In June this year the scientists at the Home Office published a new experimental estimate of cocaine consumption. Samples taken from sewage suggested that cocaine use rose by 26% between 2021 and 2025. They estimated that people in England consumed 123,000kg of cocaine in 2024-25: the equivalent of roughly 2.5bn lines, with an estimated street value of £9.8bn.

Yet crime survey data suggests the number of people reporting cocaine use in the past year has remained flat or fallen slightly since the pandemic. One explanation is that a similar or smaller number of people are using the drug more frequently. Another is that the survey excludes people who are homeless or living in institutions, and some respondents may be reluctant to admit to illegal drug use.

Dr Josh Torrance, a specialist in drug markets, says wastewater analysis can reveal use that surveys miss. Having surveyed festivalgoers, he said: “People are often not honest about their drug use with strangers.” Although sewage estimates have substantial margins of error, and the estimated street value should be taken with a pinch of salt, the direction of travel is broadly accurate.

For several years, the market offered cocaine at falling prices. The National Crime Agency (NCA) told the Guardian that wholesale prices dropped below pre-pandemic levels in 2022 and reached “historically low levels” in 2025. However, it has seen signs that wholesale prices are rising again in 2026.

Torrance tracks advertised prices for an ounce of cocaine from a pool of vendors. He says the price fell from about £1,300 in March 2022 to about £1,000 by August 2023. When he resumed collecting data in September 2025, it was about £700. That remained steady until June this year, when it rose to roughly £800; in July it reached £1,000. By September it had eased to about £950.

“I’ve never seen such a quick increase in the price of cocaine,” he says of the summer rise. He suspects a supply disruption, but says the cause is difficult to pin down in a market with many suppliers and routes.

High purity means that cheaper supply is more dangerous. Torrance says cocaine sold as “pure” is often about 70-80% pure, and a more diluted tier (sometimes marketed as “social cocaine”) may be about 60%. The NCA says wholesale purity has remained high in recent years. In Torrance’s view, “a reduced price drives up use. With increased use and increased purity, you end up with more deaths.”

Crime survey data – while subject to caveats – shows younger people are still the most likely to use the drug, but that use is falling among the young, and rising among older age groups.

Other statistics back this up. In England, 33,612 people started treatment for cocaine problems in 2024-25 – up 57% from 2019-20 – which also suggests an increase in frequent users.

Millennials seem to be the generation with the most problematic use. People in their 30s were the largest age group seeking help. Ten years earlier, it was those in their 20s. “We’ve seen a cohort of cocaine users age and continue to use cocaine,” says Torrance.

There has been a 10% rise in recorded crime rates mentioning cocaine since 2019, according to figures collected by the Guardian from 39 police forces.

Police recorded almost 30,000 crimes mentioning the word cocaine in 2025. Most were drug offences, but 18% were violent crimes, including stalking and harassment and one murder case. About 4% were sexual offences, including 344 rapes.

A police record mentioning cocaine does not by itself demonstrate cocaine use but the figures do give an indication of the direction of travel.

Home Office figures suggest that nearly six in 10 police drug tests carried out on people arrested on suspicion of domestic abuse were positive for cocaine between July 2025 and June this year. Those tested may be more likely to have used drugs than other domestic abuse suspects, but the figures highlight cocaine’s exacerbating role.

More older people taking cocaine, increased purity on the streets, and a possible increase in frequent users have coincided with mounting harms, and not just for the victims of crime. A record number of people are now dying from taking cocaine in England and Wales. This rise has mainly been driven by older people, with more than half of cocaine deaths registered last year involving someone over 40.

Torrance says the ageing of a group that continues to use cocaine is reflected in hospital presentations and deaths. Acute overdose deaths often involve cardiac problems, he says, while the health effects of long-term use add to the risks.

An independent report last year found that the UK lacked a coordinated drug prevention strategy with dedicated funding, despite international evidence showing drug prevention programmes work.

“One reason cocaine deaths have risen so dramatically over the last five to 10 years is that we didn’t invest in upstream prevention,” Torrance says. Earlier drug education and helping people at risk engage with services would help.

“The more we can do that, the fewer of these issues we’ll see decades down the line.”

Barcelona city centre saw a night of chaos on Saturday as groups of young people clashed with police and shops were looted.

The unrest, which began late in the afternoon around the Plaça de Catalunya, led to 128 arrests, roughly a quarter of them minors, according to authorities. Fifteen police officers were also injured during the night.

The gathering, promoted on social media under the slogan "Instituts Indignats," aimed to bring the French youth movement "Lycéens Indignés" to the Catalan capital.

At its peak, the demonstration drew around 600 people, per Spanish media reports.

The disturbances started at around 6 pm, when several groups of young people, many dressed in black and wearing hoods, began vandalising street furniture. Riot police then moved in, prompting demonstrators to scatter through the adjoining streets, where clashes continued.

Protesters threw stones and other heavy objects at officers, whilst several groups erected barricades, set fire to rubbish bins and smashed shop windows. Police responded with charges to disperse participants as they worked to regain control of the area.

According to La Vanguardia, around 14 shops were looted. Clashes also caused damage to motorbikes, bicycles and bus shelters.

The violence forced numerous businesses to close and led the Guardia Urbana to restrict access to the Plaça de Catalunya. Train services stopping at Plaça Catalunya station were also temporarily halted.

The mayor of Barcelona, Jaume Collboni, condemned the incidents and announced that the city council would take part in legal proceedings to seek accountability for the damage caused.

"This will not be left as it is. We will go all the way," Collboni warned, adding that there could be consequences for the parents or legal guardians of the minors involved.

The president of the government of Catalonia, Salvador Illa, also condemned the unrest and defended the police response.

"Protesting is a democratic right," he said, although he stressed that violence cannot be justified as part of that right.

For her part, the Catalan interior minister, Núria Parlon, described the incidents as "gratuitous violence and vandalism" and insisted that those responsible were not defending any legitimate cause.

Both distanced the unrest from the housing rights encampment that has been set up in the Plaça de Catalunya for several weeks.

#608. Germany sit out FIFA Under-15 World Cup as Russia return

Germany is one a handful of FIFA's 211 nations to refuse an invitation to play at the inaugural Under-15 World Cup. The tournament will also mark Russia's return to the FIFA fold.

With nearly 1,000 matches and 189 teams, the Under-15 World Cup in Azerbaijan is bloated even by FIFA's usual standards. It marks a change in its attitude to children's international tournaments, which have not existed on anywhere near this scale before.

For Germany, it is too much too soon. The German FA (DFB) told DW that it had "consciously decided not to participate." The statement from the organization suggested the DFB — whose development of young players is under scrutiny after a run of poor performances by the men's national team — felt such a tournament was not appropriate for players so young.

"At this age level, our identification and development process is still underway, and we therefore do not believe it is appropriate to nominate a fixed squad for an international tournament at this stage," it read.

"More broadly, the DFB's approach to talent development is based on the principle of supporting young players in a long-term and age-appropriate manner. We carefully assess at which stage international competitions and development measures are beneficial for each age group.

"In our view, young talents should not be exposed too early to the accompanying aspects of professional football. These include increased expectations and pressure, public evaluation of their performances, and early interest from agents and the football market."

The refusal to play in the tournament, which began this week, is consistent with Germany's more cautious approach to youth development. While in some leagues, like the Premier League in England, there is no regulation about youths playing professionally, in Germany's top flight, the Bundesliga, players must be 16. In fact, before the 2020-21 season, players could not be granted a pro license before they were 17 years and six months old.

That change enabled Youssoufa Moukoko to make his Bundesliga debut for Borussia Dortmund a day after his 16th birthday in 2020, becoming the league's youngest player in the process.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

But, some would argue his is a cautionary tale. Hyped wildly due to his goalscoring exploits at youth level, Moukoko was fast-tracked by Dortmund and Germany, who called him up for the 2022 World Cup. Now, still just 21, he is struggling for game time and goals on loan at Corum, in the Turkish Super League, from Danish side Copenhagen.

Players under 16 are also forbidden by FIFA from having an agent. But this is poorly regulated in some regions of the world. That led Bundesliga club St. Pauli, then in the second division, to announce they would no longer work with player agents or private agencies in their youth system in 2023.

"We want to focus on partnership and dialogue with the players, their families and their relatives," explained the head of the club's youth academy, Benjamin Liedtke, as St. Pauli officially positioned themselves "against the commercialization of youth football."

Germany are one of 22 nations to refuse the invitation to compete in the tournament, 18 of whom are from UEFA, Europe's confederation. The USA are also one of the prominent refusals alongside Ukraine, whose FA told German public broadcaster Sportschau that they initially refused on sporting grounds before claiming that "other countries indicated that they would compete but did not want to play against Russia." DW contacted a number of FAs to clarify this point but is yet to receive a response.

FIFA President Gianni Infantino, who has become a notorious figure thanks to a number of scandals over the past year, told Sky in February: "We have to [look at reinstating Russia], definitely, because this ban has not achieved anything. It has just created frustration and hatred. Having girls and boys from Russia being able to play football games in other parts of Europe would help."

Eight months later, he has his wish. The ongoing tournament, billed as the "FIFA U-15 World Cup & Festival" comprises eight-a-side games with 20 minute halves, a smaller pitch and a number of other technical tweaks. FIFA say the 2027 edition will be for girls teams only.

"Young players need meaningful matches, different opponents and different football experiences in order to develop. Talent exists everywhere, but the opportunities available to young players are not always the same," said FIFA Chief of Global Football Development, Arsene Wenger, likely referencing that teams from Bhutan and Seychelles to the Bahamas and Vanuatu are present.

"This tournament gives players from across the world the chance to compete, to learn and to grow."

FIFA are yet to respond to a DW request for further comment.

The round robin stage, according to FIFA, has placed teams in "groups that provide diverse sporting and regional representation" but also appears to have, at least initially, kept apart nations in conflict with each other.

For example, Israel and Palestine or Kosovo and Serbia are not in the same groups but could, in theory, meet in the later stages of the tournament. This would not be allowed in senior football, thanks to various bans and workarounds.

FIFA are vague about how the tournament works after the round robin, saying only that it will consist of "four to five additional matches per team, determined by results and subsequent tier placement. [There will be] one winner for each of the six tiers." It also said that the winner of the top tier will be crowned champions but all teams will play matches until the tournament concludes on October 30.

But, given that they have been banned from international football since invading Ukraine in 2022, it is the presence of a Russian national team at a FIFA tournament that will likely heap the most controversy on to young shoulders. Though a Russian presence was not the reason for German refusal, not attending for sporting reasons may also turn out to be a smart piece of sport politics.

#610. Australian parliament pays tribute to Helen Haines as PM Albanese condemns increasing ‘rage and aggression’

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Helen Haines was critically injured last week in an alleged act of political violence

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Australia’s parliament resumed with increased security on Monday and paid tribute to lawmaker Helen Haines who was critically injured last week in an alleged act of political violence.

Security screening measures were enhanced at parliament house in the first session since 19 Oct when authorities allege a driver rammed an SUV into Ms Haines twice outside her electorate office.

She remained in a Melbourne hospital on Monday in a serious but stable condition after both her legs were amputated.

A 43-year-old man has been charged with offences including intentionally causing serious injury. Police have not revealed a motive.

Prime minister Anthony Albanese was the first of several lawmakers to pay tribute to Ms Haines, a respected independent.

He proposed a motion expressing parliament’s wish for her recovery and support for her family. Her husband Phil Haines looked on from parliament’s public gallery.

“While the investigations go on, we must not rush to conclusions. But nor can we shrug off the very real rise in anger that distorts and corrodes our public discourse,” Mr Albanese told parliament.

“Enabled by the anonymity and speed afforded by social media, we are seeing rage and aggression increasing, not just in politics, but toward workers in hospitality, in retail, in schools and in hospitals, toward police, paramedics and other officials,” Mr Albanese added.

Mr Albanese described a “normalisation of the language of grievance and violence”.

“We must not conflate the robustness of Australian democracy with this rising tide of rage,” Mr Albanese said. Australian Federal Police commissioner Krissy Barrett told Australian Broadcasting Corp on Sunday threats against lawmakers were evenly spread between male and female politicians. But threats against women were more “personalized.”

Ms Barrett said there was a “direct correlation” between the language political rivals use against each other and threats and abuse directed at lawmakers from the public.

Critics of Australian politics often complain that language that lawmakers sometimes use against each other would not be tolerated in any other workplace in the country.

Opposition leader Angus Taylor told parliament he disagreed with those who saw a “casual connection between robust parliamentary debate and political violence.”

“We never allow that vigorous parliamentary debate to spill over into violence,” Mr Taylor said.

Speaker Milton Dick noted that some lawmakers had suggested colleagues sign a so-called civility pledge in response to the alleged attack on Haines.

“This is a personal decision and I encourage all Members (of Parliament) to continue these discussions to decide the best way for themselves” to respond, Mr Dick told parliament.

Two months ago, Ms Haines became the first Australian lawmaker to make such a pledge, advocated by the think tank Compassion in Politics Australia. Around six federal and state lawmakers have since committed to sign.

Independent lawmaker Kate Chaney said she intended to follow Ms Haines’ example by making such a pledge.

“I think there’s something really symbolic about the fact that Helen was the only federal M.P. (Member of Parliament) to have signed this,” Chaney told the ABC.

“It is a very simple thing. It just says ‘in my political life, I pledge to act with honesty, respect and compassion.’ And that feels to me like a simple and poignant way to honour the contribution Helen’s made to the parliament,” Ms Chaney added.

Compassion in Politics Australia did not immediately respond to a request for comment Monday.

#612. Portuguese police with dogs and batons dismantle housing protest camps

More than 30 people arrested as officers clear at least 100 tents in central Lisbon and about 50 in Porto

Police in Portugal have dismantled housing protest camps in Lisbon and Porto, baton-charging campaigners in the early hours of Sunday and arresting more than 30 people.

The raids were the latest incident in days of clashes between police and campaigners who – inspired by similar camps in Spain – had sought to pitch tents in central squares to protest against the country’s deepening housing crisis.

Dozens of officers, some with dogs, moved shortly after 2am on Sunday to clear out the more than 100 tents that had sprung up in Lisbon’s Rossio Square. Police said they had also taken down a smaller camp of about 50 tents in Porto’s Dom João I Square.

The camp in the heart of Lisbon had been set up after thousands of people marched along one of the Portuguese capital’s main thoroughfares to rail against housing prices that have soared past average incomes in the country.

Police described their actions on Sunday as proportionate and said they had earlier urged people to leave the camps of their own accord. The operations in the two cities led to the arrests of 31 people for disobedience and 171 structures were removed, police said on social media. Eleven people were injured, including three police officers.

Reuters reported that 25 people detained in Lisbon had been released with orders to appear in court on Monday.

The group Casa Para Viver (A Home to Live In) contested the police figures, saying the raids had left more than 20 people injured as police moved into the camps with batons, dogs and rubber bullets.

“Choosing the early morning to deploy police dogs and fire rubber bullets at people who were sleeping or peacefully protesting is a political decision,” the group said in a statement as it called for further protests on Wednesday. “It shows that this government would rather crack down on those who speak out against the housing crisis than solve the crisis itself.”

Fabian Figueiredo, an MP with the Left Bloc, described the police action as a “wound that had been inflicted” on the country’s democracy. “Fighting for a home is a right. So is peaceful protest. The constitution guarantees both,” he said on social media. “Let’s keep going – for the sake of our future.”

The housing protest camps in Portugal trace back to early October when campaigners began pitching tents in Porto, prompting police to clear them out. Similar actions soon began sprouting up in Lisbon, leading to dozens of arrests and reports of injuries as police repeatedly clashed with campaigners.

As European cities grapple with a wave of discontent, much of the focus in Spain and Portugal has been on housing costs that have priced many local people out of the market.

The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment

House prices in Portugal have more than doubled since 2017, while those seeking to rent have struggled with prices that have nearly doubled, fuelling one of Europe’s most acute home affordability crises.

Residents have long told of bearing the brunt of a market that has surged as a result of liberalisation, the issuing of so-called golden visas, digital nomad schemes and the proliferation of short-term rentals.

Campaigners have called on the centre-right government to scrap proposed legislation that would make evictions easier and end rent caps on new leases. The legislation recently passed a first parliamentary reading.

In Spain, the sprawling housing camp in the centre of Madrid marked its fourth week on Saturday, becoming one of the most tangible symbols of a widespread protest movement that has led to early general elections on 29 November.

With contributions from Reuters and Agence France-Presse

#613. Inside the GOP's fight to avoid a House wipeout

House Majority Leader Steve Scalise won't talk about defeat, even as his outside GOP allies are pulling money anyway.

Why it matters: Republicans face brutal political headwinds, but Scalise (R-La.) stands out from his fellow leaders for refusing to even contemplate losing the House.

Zoom in: At an event for Republican Marty O'Donnell, who's challenging Rep. Susie Lee (D-Nev.), Scalise argued that his presence in the district was evidence Republicans are still on offense.

  • "If it's some horrible cycle for Republicans, then why am I here?" Scalise told supporters at a Las Vegas country club Thursday.
  • "This is a winnable race," he said. But MAGA Inc., a super PAC allied with President Trump, pulled nearly $1 million in advertising from the race last week.

The big picture: House Democrats lead the generic ballot by eight points in new Washington Post-ABC polling. Trump's approval is at a record low of 31% (Reuters/Ipsos) and 72% say the country is on the wrong track (Post/ABC).

  • He's making 56 campaign stops between August and Election Day as part of what he's dubbed the "Save America Tour," complete with T-shirts featuring a map of his travels.
  • "This is like better than a rock band," Scalise told Axios during an in-flight interview while campaigning in Arizona and Nevada last week.

Scalise identified 35 competitive districts, including 15 Democratic-held seats Republicans believe they have a chance to flip.

  • He pointed to Reps. Mike Lawler (R-N.Y.), Juan Ciscomani (R-Ariz.), Rob Bresnahan (R-Pa.) and Ryan Mackenzie (R-Pa.) as races he'll watch closely as bellwethers for how the night could unfold.
  • The pro-Scalise super PAC Save American Freedom is also launching a $3.5 million get-out-the-vote and digital advertising blitz to help 52 House Republicans, Axios' Alex Isenstadt reports.
  • Among the Republicans benefiting are Reps. Brad Finstad (R-Minn.), Mike Carey (R-Ohio) and Rob Wittman (R-Va.), along with GOP candidates Ralph Alvarado (KY-6), Alex Mealer (TX-9) and Jenny Costa Honeycutt (S.C.-1).

The intrigue: The GOP's pullback in some districts has fueled speculation that Republicans are giving up on the House to save the Senate. But Scalise argued it will still benefit his members.

  • He pointed to Iowa, where the Congressional Leadership Fund, a super PAC allied with House Republicans, pulled financial support from Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks' district. Senate Republicans subsequently bought the airtime for Ashley Hinson.
  • "You actually get a three for one," Scalise said, arguing that shifting the ad time to Hinson will benefit Miller-Meeks, Rep. Zach Nunn and the Republican running to succeed Hinson in her House district.
  • "You're going to probably see that in some other areas too," Scalise said. He pointed to Senate races in North Carolina and Texas, where he acknowledged "challenges" at the top of the ticket.

The bottom line: Scalise isn't ready to look beyond Election Day, even as Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) publicly weighed in on that very scenario last week.

  • Johnson said he intends to remain the top House Republican even if Democrats win the majority. The race for the top job could become a three-way fight among Johnson, Scalise and Rep. Jim Jordan (R-Ohio).
  • Scalise repeatedly declined to say whether he would endorse Johnson for minority leader or consider running himself.
  • "Anybody who's thinking about planning for us losing is in the wrong business," Scalise told Axios.

In a major intervention, the Prime Minister signalled he is ready to suspend Labour's Brexit 'red lines' to secure a closer deal with Brussels.

Angela Rayner suggested that Labour could even take Britain back into the EU's single market without holding a referendum.

Andy Burnham opened the door to reviving free movement with the EU without a referendum

Despite the fact that more than four million citizens were granted settled status in the UK when Britain left the EU, the PM claimed that free movement was a 'revolving door' where 'people would come and then go back'.

#615. Allegations against Thomas Markle Sr challenge media’s Meghan narrative

Duchess of Sussex’s decision to cut ties with elderly father cast in new light as he faces sexual abuse image claims

Meghan ‘deeply distressed’ by allegations against father

The depiction of the Duchess of Sussex by certain sections of the media has often been one of a fame-hungry daughter casting off an elderly father in his declining years and keeping him from his grandchildren as she embraces the international celebrity stage.

Their estrangement has been the subject of countless headlines since her marriage to Prince Harry. But her statement today, released after child sexual abuse image allegations made against Thomas Markle Sr, 82, suggests deeper, darker fears as the cause.

“I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications’ distortion over the years, any distance from my father and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children, was for one reason: to protect them,” she said.

It has been speculated that the source of the estrangement between Meghan and Markle Sr, an award-winning TV lighting director, was over his decision to collude with a photographer and be paid for setting up shots of him preparing to attend the Sussexes’ wedding at Windsor Castle where he was due to walk her down the aisle.

In the end, Markle Sr pulled out of the wedding due to health issues, and it was Harry’s father, now King Charles, who lent the bride his arm on her final steps to the altar of St George’s chapel after she walked the first part of the aisle alone.

Since that day in May 2018, the relationship between daughter and father has never recovered. Now it appears the reasons why are contained in a letter from the same year, sent to the Metropolitan police and containing “troubling and disturbing allegations” against Markle Sr and shared with Meghan in the summer after her wedding.

The precise nature of those allegations has not been clarified, though they were enough for Meghan to want to keep her own family at a distance from him, her statement makes clear.

The fact she says that “the breadth of what has now been uncovered is more sickening than one could ever imagine”, suggests the 2018 letter did not go as far as what has now been alleged.

Markle Sr has vigorously denied the latest allegations, which are made by his son Thomas Markle Jr, 60. First published by the Sun newspaper, they claim Markle Sr downloaded child sexual abuse images to computers and mobile phones found at his former home in the Philippines.

He has called the accusations “sick lies” from a son with whom he has a troubled relationship, and claims to have had no access to the computers and phones in question in the two years since he left Mexico, where he was previously living, for the Philippines, according to the Daily Mail.

Our US morning briefing breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters

Meghan clearly hopes to reframe the narrative of her estrangement from her father, which has often been shaped by his loquacious tendencies in many media interviews.

When speaking to journalists, Markle Sr has frequently lamented the breakdown of his relationship with his youngest daughter (he has two other children, Samantha Markle and Thomas Jr, from an earlier marriage). He has spoken of how he has been unable to reach Meghan, and of how he has never been allowed to meet his grandchildren, Prince Archie, seven, and Princess Lilibet, five.

The media depiction has often leaned towards that of an uncaring daughter, whose father paid for her education, helped her to cultivate her interest in acting through his television work, and found himself abandoned in his time of need.

For the most part, Meghan has not publicly acknowledged his many health woes – he has suffered a series of strokes and recently had a leg amputated due to complications with a blood clot – and she clearly believes this has been weaponised against her.

However, in 2025, Meghan’s spokesperson confirmed that the duchess had “reached out” privately to her father when he was hospitalised and very unwell. He is now understood to be in a rehabilitation centre in Florida undergoing physiotherapy after the amputation of his leg.

Whatever the outcome of this latest development, it adds a new dimension to the complicated, fractured relationship between Meghan and her family.

#616. Your guide to L.A. City Charter Amendment LA: Restructuring public works administration

See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred

The aptly named Measure LA, appearing on the Nov. 3 ballot for Los Angeles voters, is intended to restructure how the city administers public works and remove restrictions on using existing city resources to raise money.

California’s general election takes place on Novemer 3. Learn about L.A.’s city and county races as well races for state office.

Measure LA would change the way public works are administered in Los Angeles, allow the city to lease its underused land to tenants and open the door to greater city involvement in business enterprises. It also would ease some competitive bidding rules.

The proposed changes to the Los Angeles City Charter are intended to more efficiently deliver basic city services and speed repairs to deteriorating infrastructure such as streets in need of repaving, unsafe sidewalks and busted streetlights.

Councilman Bob Blumenfield, Councilwoman Katy Yaroslavsky, City Controller Kenneth Mejia, former City Controller Ron Galperin, Streets for All Chief Executive Michael Schneider and LA Forward Institute Chief Executive David Levitus are backing the measure.

Councilwoman Monica Rodriguez provided an argument against the measure.

Proponents of the measure say Los Angeles is falling short in providing basic services, including street and sidewalk maintenance, upkeep of streetlights and trees and other services administered by the Department of Public Works.

The measure is intended to streamline public works decision-making to improve city services and add new sources of revenue by leveraging existing resources such as underutilized city land.

Measure LA’s perhaps most controversial element is the proposal to increase the power of the director of public works while reducing the sway of the Board of Public Works or potentially eliminating it.

The director would be able to manage public works projects, including construction, buying or leasing property, exercising eminent domain with City Council approval, granting street permits, regulating parking and recommending budgets for the department.

An opponent of the measure, Rodriguez said the Board of Public Works was established to provide independent review of city contracting, with commissioners’ decisions made in public meetings.

“Removing this important check and balance would reduce public scrutiny and weaken accountability over billions of taxpayer dollars for public projects,” Rodriguez said in her ballot argument against the measure.

Commissioners are appointed by the mayor. They work full-time on the board for five-year terms administering the Public Works Department while assisted by several bureau heads and the director of public works.

Proponents of the measure say the current system of overseeing public works is ineffective because responsibility is spread among multiple officials, commissions, agencies and bureaus.

“Angelenos see the results in crumbling streets, buckled sidewalks and streetlights that stay dark,” proponents said in their ballot argument.

Another key element of the measure is establishing a two-year budget cycle for the city, which currently adopts its budget annually. Under Measure LA, the mayor would be required to submit a proposed two-year budget to the City Council by April 1. A two-year budget would enhance planning for infrastructure improvements under another new requirement that the city adopt a Capital Infrastructure Plan.

Most major U.S. cities rely on multiyear capital improvement plans to schedule spending on roads, bridges, parks and buildings.

A long-term infrastructure plan administered with two-year budgeting “sets clear priorities, identifies the projects that need to get done, and plans how to fund them over time,” proponents said.

Currently, the charter prohibits the city from mortgaging city-owned property and prevents it from operating purely commercial or industrial businesses. The measure would remove these restrictions to raise new revenue.

Easing restrictions on operating a business also would allow the city to use its intellectual property to sell merchandise with city logos, as is done in other cities including New York, Yaroslavsky said.

Serbia is going to the polls on Sunday 25 October for snap parliamentary elections that could represent one of the most important political turning points in the country in more than a decade.

Voters will elect 250 members of the National Assembly, with more than 6.45 million people eligible to vote. Eighteen electoral lists, featuring a total of 2,418 candidates, are taking part in the election. The elections were called after President Aleksandar Vučić dissolved parliament on September 9, following a proposal by the Serbian government.

However, the political reasons for the early election go much deeper than the constitutional procedure itself. Serbia has been going through a period of intense political and social polarisation for almost two years, beginning after the tragedy at the railway station in Novi Sad on November 1, 2024.

The collapse of a concrete canopy at the station killed 16 people. Student protests that followed initially focused on demands for accountability and the publication of documents related to the station’s reconstruction but gradually developed into a broader movement against, as they claim, corruption, political responsibility and the way that state institutions function.

During 2025, students organised mass protests, university blockades, blockades of institutions and roads, as well as rallies across Serbia. The movement gradually expanded beyond student issues and became the strongest yet challenge to Aleksandar Vučić’s government, whose rule had not been seriously challenged for a full 14 years. In May 2025, students called for snap parliamentary elections, and during 2026 they decided to participate in the elections with their own list.

This fundamentally changed the character of the election. What was supposed to be another parliamentary contest has become, in many ways, a referendum on Vučić’s political dominance and the political system that has been in place in Serbia for more than a decade.

The largest political bloc is built around the Serbian Progressive Party, running under the electoral list “Aleksandar Vučić – United Serbia.” Although Vučić is no longer president of Serbia, he remains the central figure of the campaign. In late September, he resigned from the presidency in order to lead the SNS (Serbian Progresive Party) campaign and run for the position of prime minister, the position he had already held before becoming President of the Republic. This has further turned the election into a direct vote on his political future.

The list “Ivica Dačić – Stability Factor” is also taking part, bringing together the Socialist Party of Serbia and smaller parties. An important part of the political spectrum consists of right-wing and nationalist-oriented lists, including “Authentic Right – Miloš Jovanović – Boldly Serbian,” and the pro-European opposition centre is represented by the list “European Serbia". Participants in the election include the minorities Alliance of Vojvodina Hungarians, the SDA of Sandžak, Usama Zukorlić’s list, the Albanian Coalition and several smaller parties and movements, which, in the event of a close result, could play an important role in forming the new government.

The most distinctive participant is the Student List – “Students Win.” It is not a conventional political party and does not have a traditional party leader. Candidates were selected through student plenums, and the list includes professors, doctors, artists, activists and other people who have generally not held senior political positions. The list has 250 candidates and represents an attempt to transform the protest movement into a parliamentary political force.

The fundamental problem is no longer simply the relationship between the government and the opposition. At the centre of the conflict is the question of trust in institutions.

For a large part of the protesters, the Novi Sad tragedy became a symbol of a much broader problem: corruption, political accountability, public procurement, institutional control and the relationship between the government and its critics. The authorities, on the other hand, describe the protests as an attempt to destabilise the country and bring to power a movement without sufficient political experience. Moreover, government officials claim that “foreign actors” are actually behind the student movement, while President Vučić has repeatedly stated that foreign intelligence services are financing a “colour revolution” in Serbia.

As a result, two fundamentally different narratives have emerged. The government emphasises stability, economic development, national interests and the danger of foreign interference. The student movement focuses on accountability, the fight against corruption, the rule of law and the independence of institutions from political influence.

The biggest change is the disappearance of the traditional opposition as the main challenger to the ruling party. In the 2023 election, opposition parties grouped around the “Serbia Against Violence” coalition won around 24% of the vote and 65 parliamentary seats. However, subsequent fragmentation and internal disputes weakened their position. In the meantime, the student movement has taken over much of the political energy and voter support that previously belonged to the traditional opposition.

As a result, the main political dividing line is now much simpler: the ruling SNS and Vučić versus the Student List, while the other parties are fighting to enter parliament and secure the role of potential coalition partners. Here, voter turnout becomes a particularly interesting factor, as does which parties will clear the 3% electoral threshold. The election outcome could ultimately hinge on these seemingly minor technicalities.

The most important trend is that Serbia’s political system is undergoing a major transformation. The student movement is the first major social movement in many years to successfully move beyond traditional opposition parties and attract large numbers of people who had previously been politically inactive.

At the same time, the SNS still has a very strong party infrastructure, a large network of local organizations and a stable core of voters. This means that the outcome is far from predetermined. Opinion polls have produced different forecasts, and because of the changing political landscape and the large number of undecided voters, the result is difficult to predict with precision.

Another important trend is the continued polarization of Serbian society. The country is divided not only over the government and the opposition, but also over identity, Serbia’s relationship with the European Union, Russia and the West, national issues and the country’s future foreign-policy orientation.

A third trend concerns European integration. Serbia remains a candidate for EU membership, but its European path has been slowed by problems involving the rule of law, its relations with Russia and its limited alignment with parts of the EU’s common foreign policy, as well as the stalled normalisation process with Kosovo. At the same time, Belgrade continues to maintain close relations with both Russia and China.

If the SNS wins, Vučić will seek to form a new government and stabilise the political system after almost two years of protests. If the Student List wins enough seats to form a government alone or with its allies, Serbia could enter an entirely new political era. And if the result is close or disputed, there is a real possibility that the political crisis will continue even after the polls close.

For all these reasons, this election is not simply an election for a new parliament. It is a test of the survival of the political model that has dominated Serbia for more than a decade — and a test of whether a new, non-party movement can change that model.

#618. Anne Carson’s Best Books

“I came to think of translating as a room,” Anne Carson wrote, in her illustrated book of poems “Nox,” “where one gropes for the light switch.” When the Swedish Academy awarded Carson the Nobel Prize in Literature this month, they continued a long tradition of recognizing the superior art of poet-translators, from Rabindranath Tagore to Pablo Neruda, Czesław Miłosz, Seamus Heaney, and Jon Fosse. In her essays and poems—as in her translations of Sappho, Euripides, and Sophocles—Carson lays down each word as if it were arrived at after a suspended period of searching and testing, of slowly gathering a language to illuminate half-sensed, mysterious thoughts and feelings. As I noted earlier this month, her great theme is eros, and her truly exceptional books let us inhabit the longing and loneliness of desire. Below are my favorites.

The six pieces in Carson’s second collection are clear, sharp, splintered, and luminous. It includes her single most arresting poem, “The Glass Essay,” a chilly, desolate account of the end of a love affair, told by a speaker who believes that she is “turning into Emily Brontë / my lonely life around me like a moor, / my ungainly body stumping over the mud flats with a look of transformation / that dies when I come in the kitchen door.” The poem’s anguished meditations on love’s savagery and isolation are designed to draw blood.

“The Beauty of the Husband: A Fictional Essay in 29 Tangos”

“Shall we sharpen our eyes and circle closer to the beauty of the husband,” the twenty-fifth section of this furious book-length poem begins. Its swerving, combative style is inspired by the tango, “the forbidden dance”—a stunningly physical encounter between two people who should never have touched but are now violently intertwined. Also intertwined are ancient myths of warring city-states, the raw, moody poetry of John Keats, and the modern battle between a faithless husband and his wife, the poem’s raging speaker. The book was awarded the T. S. Eliot Prize in 2001, making Carson the first woman ever to win it.

The “Geryoneis,” a poem by the blind Greek poet Stesichoros, shows us glimpses of Geryon, a winged red monster with three heads, who is brutally killed by Herakles. Carson loosely, haltingly translates Stesichoros’ verses—“Arrow means kill It parted Geryon’s skull like a comb”—then tells the story of Geryon and Herakles as a gay romance. They first see each other at a bus depot: “There it was one of those moments / that is the opposite of the blindness. / The world poured back and forth between their eyes.” The cosmic tenderness of their hungry young love turns into pain and flight, and the poem into “a cry—upcast to that custom, the human custom of wrong love.”

This brilliantly irregular book begins with Carson’s translations of fragments by the Greek elegiac poet Mimnermos (“Half moon through the pines at dawn / sharp as a girl’s ribcage”) and ends with “The Anthropology of Water,” my favorite of Carson’s essays. A woman on the pilgrimage road of Santiago de Compostela meets a man whom she calls “my Cid” and who becomes her lover. In the rain, they walk and talk from Saint-Jean-Pied-de-Port to Finisterre, for a little more than a month. “There is no question I covet that conversation,” the woman thinks. “There is no question I am someone starving. There is no question I am making this journey to find out what that appetite is.” We read to find out if her “tawdry, staggering, irresistible” need can ever be sated, or if this is a lonely journey with no end.

#619. Embarrassing name? How we live with names we don't like

Names are central to our identity, so what happens when that name is a source of ridicule? Research points to negative life outcomes, but some people learn to embrace unfortunate names.

As a child growing up in Australia, Louise Pain hated her surname.

"People used to tease me; I was called things like 'Pain in the a*s,'" she told DW. "I remember actively hating my surname when I was a child and wanting to change it."

The jokes have followed her throughout her life, even after she moved to Germany. But one thing did eventually change: Pain's feelings about her own name.

Names are not only a fundamental part of how we identify ourselves — they can, beyond teasing, also influence how other people treat us. So, what happens if we dislike our own name, or if it is perceived negatively by those around us?

"A person's name is vital to their sense of identity," psychoanalyst Mikita Brottman told DW. "When someone has an embarrassing name, that embarrassment can be incorporated into their identity."

Research on name bias has linked negatively perceived names with romantic rejection,as well as lower educational outcomes, lower self-esteem and more frequent smoking.

This suggests that names could influence our life trajectory, namely through self-esteem and opportunity.

But a person's relationship with their name is not necessarily fixed. Pain's lived experience, and that of another woman with the first name Tiny, shows how people can find ways to reclaim, and even come to value, names that once triggered ridicule and rejection.

Names can act as "signals" when you first meet someone, personality psychologist Jochen Gebauer told DW. Those signals may lose importance as people get to know each other, but Gebauer said their effects could also accumulate over a lifetime, potentially contributing to "real measurable advantages and disadvantages."

Research led by sociologist Anthony Lee found that a name can evoke inaccurate assumptions about intelligence, competence, trustworthiness, sociability and attractiveness. For Pain, other people's reactions have extended beyond jokes. In high school, a teacher refused to believe that 'Pain' was her real surname and reprimanded her in front of the class.

"Your name couldn't possibly be Pain. Write your real name!" she recalled the teacher saying.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In Lee's UK-based research, less familiar names tended to fall along a dimension partly characterized as "weirdness," which may help explain why difficult-to-pronounce or culturally unfamiliar names receive more negative evaluations.

Tiny, now 54, encountered the same questions about her unfamiliar name growing up in Greece.

Her parents had adapted "Tiny" to "Tinie" to make it sound more Greek, but people would repeatedly ask what her real or baptismal name was.

Even relatives have refused to accept it. Recently, two elderly aunts introduced her to someone as "Haritini," a conventional Greek name.

"I didn't even bother correcting them at this point," Tiny told DW.

Tiny's relationship with her name has also evolved.

"The jokes [from others] got repetitive and boring pretty fast, so at least I was left with the sense that I have something unique with my name going on."

Pain, now 41, discovered how much cultural context could change the reaction to her surname when she began learning her father's native French as a teenager. In French, 'pain' means bread.

"People started calling me 'Bread! Louise Bread.'"

Later, after moving to Germany, the jokes became mostly bread-related rather than the more scathing ones she had experienced in Australia. "That helped me to feel better about my name," she said.

As they got older, both Pain and Tiny developed coping strategies to pre-empt people's reactions to their names.

Tiny sometimes introduces herself with: "Hi, I'm Tiny. It's my name and not a statement," or, "I'm Tiny. Not a difficult name to live up to."

"This usually stops people from asking awkward questions."

Pain also began to embrace the humor surrounding her name.

"I was convinced that I should become either a doctor or a dominatrix, or perhaps both, to become either 'Doctor Pain,' or 'Mistress Pain.'"

"Names can conjure that whole spectrum of shame and pride," psychoanalyst Melissa Daum told DW.

Pain now finds that people tend to see her surname as "funny and endearing… it's become something that is more of a funny talking point."

But the childhood discomfort has not entirely disappeared. When Pain thinks about having children, her feelings about the name become more complicated.

"I don't really want to pass on my surname ... so there is a deeper wound there."

But Pain also believes her father would be deeply hurt if future children had a different name. The surname she once hated connects her to him and to her French heritage.

"Something that once feels like an inconvenience or a source of self-consciousness can become a marker of distinctiveness, history, or belonging," Daum said.

"My parents seemingly made an unfortunate choice, but by now I have embraced both the name and the sense of uniqueness that comes with it."

That does not mean she uses Tiny everywhere. She avoids it on dating apps because "Tiny might give off the wrong message," and does not use it in her email address when she wants to appear professional.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Pain, meanwhile, uses a Germanized version of the French word for bread as her social media surname.

Online, people have more control over what name they present to others. As Daum put it: "Choosing one's own name can feel like an act of mastery, even a refusal of that original passivity: I will decide what I am called and how I am encountered."

But accepting a name does not necessarily mean embracing it in every situation.

Pain once wanted to change her surname. Tiny considered using her middle name in her thirties. Neither ultimately abandoned the names that had caused them difficulties.

For Tiny, at least, a name that once made her feel awkward has become something she can imagine carrying for the rest of her life.

"It might be cute to eventually be a granny called Tiny." Edited by: Richard Connor

#621. Volkswagen to build $4bn Audi SUV factory in US despite job cuts at home

VW investment, creating 4,500 jobs in Georgia, comes amid Trump’s damaging tariffs, intense Chinese competition and costly shift towards EVs

Audi has said it will spend $4bn (£3bn) to build its first factory in the US, as its parent company, Volkswagen, struggles with the impact of steep tariffs imposed by Donald Trump.

The German brand’s chief executive, Gernot Döllner, joined Trump on stage at a campaign rally on Saturday night to announce the factory in Macon, Georgia, in an unusual move by a big European brand just days before the US midterm elections.

The Republican party under Trump is trying to retain control of both houses of Congress, but it is polling poorly as it struggles with higher fuel prices caused by Trump’s war on Iran, as well as his trade war against some of the US’s biggest trading partners.

Trump has long tried to convince voters that his tariffs are helping to increase the number of manufacturing jobs in the US, and has seized on any new factory investments. However, US vehicle and parts employment has fallen since Trump took office last year.

Audi, Volkswagen’s most important premium brand, has suffered from Trump’s 15% tariffs on imports from the EU as well as the president’s efforts to cut sales of battery electric vehicles in favour of petrol cars.

It said it aims to build 200,000 SUVs at the new US factory, creating 4,500 jobs. The factory will build the Q7, Q8 and Q9 SUVs, shifting some production from Bratislava in Slovakia.

Volkswagen has said Trump’s tariffs cost it up to €5bn(£4.2bn)a year, before the impact of lower sales. The German manufacturer this month said it was still struggling with “continued high pressure from import tariffs”. The carmaker was also forced to shift some production of its cheapest cars, such as the Jetta saloon and Taos SUV, from Mexico to the US.

The new factory may add to tensions in Germany, where Volkswagen has started to cut as many as 100,000 jobs and close factories. It has blamed the job losses on intense competition from Chinese carmakers, as well as the tariffs and a need to invest heavily in the shift to EVs for markets other than the US.

Döllner said he accepted the invitation to speak at Trump’s rally out of respect for the US.

Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning

“We are planning to bring our ⁠biggest and most premium SUVs, and produce them here in Macon, Georgia,” he said at the event. “This is a long-term investment because we believe in the American market.”

Volkswagen’s chief executive, Oliver Blume, told investors in July that “US tariffs create a significant burden and restrict international trade”.

However, the group has said there is still demand in the US for Audi’s large petrol SUVs, and it is planning its largest-ever SUV, the Q9, with the American market in mind. Large petrol-powered SUVs have played a big role in global carbon emissions.
