#639. Baby orangutans in India expose illegal wildlife trade as experts question a billionaire’s zoo

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

The villagers who first spotted the five baby orangutans in a casuarina forest in India in early September were puzzled by their reddish hair and unfamiliar faces.

The three males and two females, aged six to eight months — were left on a plantation in eastern India’s Odisha, over 2,700 kilometers (1,700 miles) from their native rainforests in Borneo and Sumatra, evidence of a growing illicit trade of apes being trafficked into India.

They're now at an Indian zoo, where keepers reportedly have been playing classical music to soothe them.

Wild orangutans are native only to the islands of Borneo and Sumatra, where they sustain rainforests by spreading seeds across vast areas, allowing trees to regenerate and store carbon that would otherwise contribute to global warming. The species is critically endangered, threatened by severe habitat loss. There are about 119,500 orangutans left in the wild, according to conservation organization World Wildlife Fund.

The global illegal wildlife trade is estimated to be worth $34 billion annually, according to a 2026 study by National University of Singapore researchers, and India is emerging as an important market. Experts say seizures reflect a fraction of a booming trade in exotic or non-native animals sold to wealthy Indian collectors.

India’s wildlife laws were mainly designed to protect native species such as elephants, rhinoceroses and tigers from being trafficked overseas. Gaps in controls on imported animals complicate efforts to trace the origins of exotic wildlife.

In 2022, two juvenile Sumatran orangutans were found in boxes at a checkpoint between the northeastern states of Assam and Mizoram. Another was rescued in Mizoram in 2023, and a young orangutan was found in an apartment near Mumbai in November 2024. At least 23 gibbons were seized at Indian airports in 2025, according to an analysis by nonprofit Wildlife Trust of India. In May 2026, Egyptian authorities seized three India-bound, sedated baby chimpanzees.

“India has become the number one destination for the live trade of primates,” said Sinan Serhadli, a wildlife trafficking expert at the Orangutan Information Centre in Indonesia’s North Sumatra province.

India’s exotic wildlife trade and Southeast Asian trafficking routes

Wealthy collectors who prize rare animals as “status symbols” are driving the trade in trafficked animals from Southeast Asia, a regional hub for trade in species from elsewhere, said Uttara Mendiratta, a wildlife trafficking researcher in India.

Expanding tourism has led to more direct flights to India through cities like Bangkok and Kuala Lumpur, giving traffickers routes that are faster, albeit riskier, than overland border crossings.

“The profit margins are so high that they can afford to lose a few (animals) and still make a profit,” Mendiratta said.

Questions also surround legal trade. Most commercial trade in orangutans is banned, but exceptions exist for captive-bred animals. India imported 41 orangutans between 2021 and 2024, according to CITES, the global treaty regulating trade in endangered wildlife.

Sinan Serhadli, a wildlife trafficking expert at Indonesia’s Orangutan Information Centre, questioned whether the animals were legitimately bred in captivity.

“It just shows the loopholes. And ... corruption as well,” he said.

The CITES Secretariat declined to comment, saying the matter was under review

Loopholes in India’s wildlife laws enable wildlife trafficking

Concerned about diseases spreading from animals to people during the COVID-19 pandemic, India allowed people to register their exotic animals in 2020 without proving their origins.

They can report births, deaths and breeding of non-native species through an online portal. But the government lacks enough staff and expertise to adequately inspect collections and identify global species. The system also leaves room for trafficked animals to be misrepresented as registered ones, Mendiratta said.

India tightened its wildlife laws in 2022, giving authorities clearer powers to seize illegally traded exotic animals and prosecute traffickers. But by then, it already had “opened the floodgates,” she said.

India’s exotic pet trade “sits at the crossroads of biodiversity loss, unbridled community demand, and organized criminal activity,” said a 2026 report by Humane World for Animals India.

India's forest ministry didn't respond to AP's request for comment.

Indonesia renews push to repatriate orangutans from India

Indonesia’s Ministry of Forestry said it was taking “active steps” to bring home the five baby orangutans found in Odisha, sending experts to verify their origins and assess their health.

Their mothers were likely killed, traumatizing infants that normally would depend on them for up to nine years.

Conservationists have successfully returned orangutans to Indonesia from Thailand, but so far only one has been repatriated from India.

When one orangutan was transferred last year to a private wildlife facility known as Vantara, run by billionaire Mukesh Ambani’s family, India’s federal wildlife officials and India’s CITES authority were not informed, a federal wildlife official to New Delhi wrote in a report.

Officials concerned over the orangutan's care at a local public zoo ordered it transferred to Vantara, which describes itself as a wildlife rescue and rehabilitation center. The orangutan was treated for a respiratory infection and pneumonia before it was returned to Indonesia on Oct. 19 after 19 months at the private facility.

India’s CITES authority didn’t respond to AP’s request for comment.

Questions over the world’s rarest great ape in Indian zoo

Vantara, a 3,500-acre wildlife facility in western India, has over 150,000 animals and over 2,000 different species.

It has faced international scrutiny over its animal acquisitions. In November 2025, CITES questioned shipments to Vantara that included snow leopards from Germany, a bonobo said to have been bred in Iraq and a gorilla reportedly from Haiti. The primates are not native to those countries.

India’s Supreme Court cleared Vantara of wildlife trafficking and animal mistreatment allegations in 2025.

In September, 27 wildlife conservation and animal welfare organizations issued a letter urging the facility to end imports of wild animals, raising concerns about endangered species and animal welfare.

The groups said they had “never encountered anything comparable to the scale and diversity” of Vantara’s imports, citing more than 60,000 animals acquired in a short period.

One controversial acquisition, according to Vantara's 2024-25 inventory, is a Tapanuli orangutan, the world’s rarest great ape. Recognized as a distinct species only in 2017, it's only found in a small area of Indonesia’s Sumatra island, where 716 remain in the wild.

“The Tapanuli orangutan is hovering just above extinction,” said Serhadli, whose organization is one of the few that works with the species. The one at Vantara would be the only Tapanuli orangutan in captivity.

CITES trade data shows that the animal left Indonesia in 2024 and arrived in India via the United Arab Emirates.

“That can’t happen legally,” Serhadli said.

Indonesia’s Ministry of Forestry said it was taking “seriously” reports that a Tapanuli orangutan might be outside the country. It said it couldn't confirm the animal’s species, origins or how it got to India. An investigation would require checking permits and transfer records, along with scientific testing, the ministry said.

Neither Vantara nor Indonesia’s CITES authority responded to requests for comment from AP.

Milko reported from Islamabad, Pakistan. Associated Press journalist Edna Tarigan contributed from Jakarta, Indonesia.

#640. Lula’s Last Dance

In the final days of his final campaign, supporters of the Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva turned to a British classic. David Bowie and Queen’s 1981 hit, “Under Pressure,” became the soundtrack of a viral video showing scenes from the eighty-year-old Lula’s half century in politics. Here was the humble trade unionist, born into extreme poverty, standing up as a fiery-eyed tribune of the workers. “Can’t we give ourselves one more chance?” the song implores, over clips of a younger, scraggly-bearded Lula rallying the people, casting his vote in the ballot box, and winning elections. “Why can’t we give love that one more chance?” we hear as the song crescendoes, amid footage of Lula mobbed by ecstatic crowds, kissing the Brazilian flag, and embracing a kaleidoscope of his countrymen, from red-shirted throngs in São Paulo to Indigenous leaders from the Amazon. Then there’s an older Lula, back on the streets after being freed from prison for what his allies always believed were unjust corruption charges, and mobilizing opposition to Brazil’s far right in defense of the country’s democracy. The song subsides: “This is our last dance.”

The music could stop this weekend, as Brazilians vote in the second round of their Presidential election. Lula faces a career-ending defeat, with the odds favoring Flavio Bolsonaro, a hard-right challenger who, like his jailed father, the former President Jair Bolsonaro, is bent on unravelling Lula’s legacy. The first round, which took place on October 4th, was grim for Lula. In a surprise result, the incumbent placed two points behind Bolsonaro, who is currently a senator, while right-wing parties and candidates surged in congressional and state elections across the country. Brazil is now poised to become the most important entry on a long list of Latin American states that have swung to the right in the past two years, a shift that runs in concert with the Trump Administration’s ideological vision for the hemisphere. (If Lula loses, only Mexico, Guatemala, and Uruguay will remain as countries with elected left-leaning governments.) Even if Lula pulls out a narrow victory, he could spend his next term significantly constrained by a federal structure dominated by the right. He’s also going up against history: the first-round winner in Brazil’s Presidential race has won the second-round vote in every election stretching back to 1989, the first direct Presidential election held in the country after it was redemocratized following years of military dictatorship.

Lula ran in that 1989 election, too, and lost in the runoff. But he went on to become the most consequential figure in Brazil’s modern democratic era, and his Workers’ Party one of the leading political forces in South America. He was finally elected to the Presidency in 2002 and served two terms, until the end of 2010, harnessing a commodity boom to invest in major social spending, including welfare programs, that lifted tens of millions out of poverty. He positioned Brazil as a world leader in climate action, helping slow the deforestation of the Amazon. And he led Brazil into the vanguard of the Global South, charting an independent line in foreign policy that placed his country as one of the new pillars of an aspirational reconfigured global order. Constitutional rules prohibiting more than two consecutive terms in office led to his being succeeded in 2011 by his close political ally Dilma Rousseff, whose tenure suffered tougher economic headwinds and was brought to an end by a sprawling corruption scandal that implicated a swath of Brazil’s political and business establishments. The investigations led to Lula himself being convicted of corruption and money laundering in 2018, and being given a twelve-year sentence; five hundred and eighty days later, he was released, after a court ruled that he had been denied adequate due process, an outcome that confirmed for many of his supporters the belief that his incarceration had been engineered to keep him out of an election cycle that he would have won. (The charges were completely annulled in 2021.)

Instead, Jair Bolsonaro, a hard-right former Army man who looked approvingly on the days of military rule, was elected. As President, he slashed Lula’s protections for the environment, cut funding to universities and to urban-housing programs, and badly mismanaged the pandemic. In 2022, Lula summoned his old populist magnetism, built a coalition large enough to defeat Bolsonaro, and won a third term. But Bolsonaro, styled in international media as the Trump of the Tropics, did not accept losing. On January 8, 2023, thousands of his supporters stormed the heart of Brasilia, the federal capital, vandalizing the buildings of the Supreme Court, Congress, and the Presidential Palace.

Brazilian authorities later determined that Bolsonaro was part of a coup plot to oust Lula; he’s currently serving a twenty-seven-year sentence under house arrest. The insurrection drew immediate and obvious parallels to the United States, which, during much of the past decade, has lurched alongside Brazil through a strange hall of mirrors. In some ways, the two largest democracies of the Western Hemisphere are experiencing a shared reality on different time lines: Jair Bolsonaro and Trump both ran as anti-establishment demagogues, peddling a divisive nationalism that tapped into widespread voter apathy and disillusionment, and won a base among devoted evangelical Christians. (They also both came with a soap-opera-worthy cast of scions and hangers-on, a number of whom appear enmeshed in a range of suspect, self-dealing enterprises.) Lula and Joe Biden, well-known veterans of an older, more liberal status quo, seemed the right sorts of politicians to thwart the reëlection of Bolsonaro and Trump, respectively, but they failed to defeat Trumpism or Bolsonarismo as movements. Like Biden, in this cycle Lula found that a disconcerting number of his compatriots were unmoved by his calls to save democracy from those who would seek to undermine it—or didn’t buy into his rhetoric in the first place.

Though no one can accuse Lula, as they did Biden, of lacking the mental and physical acuity for the job—his social media includes various videos of him working out—his politics, rooted in unions and labor movements from the nineteen-seventies and eighties, don’t register as much in a Brazil now reshaped by the more atomized gig economies of the twenty-first century. Lula can tout some strong macroeconomic indicators—unemployment is at its lowest rate since 2012—but most Brazilians feel the crunch of a cost-of-living crisis, persistent concerns about law and order, and a growing pessimism about the direction of their country. Those dynamics hobbled the Democrats in 2024; meanwhile, anger over inflation in the U.S. has only intensified in the past two years under Trump.

There are more than echoes ricocheting between the United States and Brazil. Trump has slapped tariffs on the Brazilian economy and punitive sanctions on Alexandre de Moraes, the chief justice most heavily involved in the prosecution of Jair Bolsonaro. (The sanctions were dropped, though the White House has recently weighed reimposing them.) Lula seized on these acts as meddling in the campaign, and as an assault on Brazilian sovereignty encouraged by the Bolsonaro family. But such is the scale of Brazil’s polarization that many Brazilians are insensible to Lula’s entreaties and want the left defeated. If elected, the younger Bolsonaro, who comports himself as a more moderate version of his father, has been clear on his plans not only to secure his father’s freedom but to punish the top figures in the judiciary who pushed for his prosecution. His brother, Eduardo, who has spent Lula’s term in self-imposed exile in the United States, wants to purge the country’s foreign ministry. A year ago, Brazil’s decision to investigate and punish Bolsonaro, Sr., was hailed by many observers as a courageous example of how to deal with assaults on the peaceful transfer of power. But a return of the Bolsonaros, Oliver Stuenkel, a German Brazilian political scientist and writer, told me, “would force us to reassess that conviction among democracy scholars around the world that Brazil led the way in showing how to protect democracy against authoritarianism.”

On Sunday, the two candidates took part in an acrimonious, largely unedifying televised debate, where they paced around each other onstage and hurled insults. Bolsonaro cast Lula as a thief, suggesting that it was best to keep his physical distance, “because my wallet could be stolen.” Lula called Bolsonaro a “thug,” an apparent allusion to alleged ties to a host of paramilitary organizations in Rio de Janeiro. (Bolsonaro has previously denied any such connections and dismissed the allegations as “smears.”) In the vein of El Salvador’s President, Nayib Bukele, Bolsonaro has promised a ruthless crackdown on crime, with expanded maximum-security prisons to detain more suspected cartel members and chemical castration for convicted rapists. Some in Bolsonaro’s camp want him to follow the lead of the Argentinian President, Javier Milei, a radical libertarian who has hacked away at public spending and shut down whole government ministries. But most Brazilians don’t have much of an appetite for such shock therapy. “If I were a Flavio supporter or an adviser, I would be worried about overinterpreting my mandate and going too far,” Andre Pagliarini, a historian of Brazil at Louisiana State University, told me. “The election may be a repudiation of Lula, but it’s not a sign of deep support for the kind of reactionary overreach that Flavio is promising.”

In the event of Lula’s defeat, Brazil may cut a very different pose on the world stage. Lula is a champion of the Palestinian cause; Bolsonaro, like his father, has made a point of befriending the Israeli right. He may also seek to weaken Brazil’s commitments to the U.N.’s climate treaty and to non-Western blocs such as the BRICS. A senior Brazilian diplomat, speaking to me on condition of anonymity, suggested that a Flavio victory would see “Brazil having to resign from being one of the protagonists of the Global South to becoming a pawn on Trump’s chessboard.” That may be an exaggeration, given Brazil’s clout and heft, and also its extensive ties with China, its biggest trade partner. Brazil’s lucrative agrobusinesses, whose owners mostly back Bolsonaro, need the Chinese market and often compete with U.S. exporters. “You’ve seen versions of this all over Latin America, with leaders on the new right who have very quickly pivoted to a more neutral or nonaligned posture when it comes to the China-versus-U.S. competition,” Brian Winter, editor-in-chief of Americas Quarterly, told me. “But it’s especially true of Brazil.” After next month’s midterms, Trump’s brand could be weaker than it has ever been, and his signature policy for the region—an anti-cartel security pact called the Shield of the Americas which he unveiled this March, in Florida—could be short-lived. “It’s mostly an anti-incumbent wave that we’re seeing,” Chris Sabatini, the director for Latin America at Chatham House, told me. “And so, what this will mean is a lot of these initiatives that Trump has started, like the Shield of the Americas, will not live past the Trump government.”

Lula is hoping that millions of disaffected Brazilians who didn’t vote in the first round may yet come out to cast a ballot for him. He has had time to take stock of the global scene and has contemplated his place within it. In an interview with The New Yorker’s Jon Lee Anderson last year, he described his uneasiness watching Trump, who looms over the hemispheric right. As Lula put it, “I saw a speech of his in the U.S. Congress recently, and it was absurd—those Republicans clapping at whatever nonsense he said. “It was almost the same kind of speech that anarchists used to make in Italy and Brazil at the beginning of the century, calling for a society without institutions, a society where the empire of capital rules.” He lamented the waning of the international order, which the United States helped author after the Second World War. “We thought we were creating a more civilized, more solidarity-based, more humane society,” he said. ♦

#642. Your guide to L.A. City Charter Amendment PRK: More money for parks

See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred

Let’s get one thing out of the way from the start: L.A.’s Charter Amendment PRK isn’t a tax hike.

The Nov. 3 ballot measure is a tool for voters to rework the parameters of the city budget, by increasing the amount of money that must go to the Department of Recreation and Parks.

Charter Amendment PRK would accomplish that by doubling the minimum budget allocation set aside for the department, which oversees the upkeep of green spaces, playing fields and even senior centers.

Park advocates have long argued that the existing city allocation is inadequate, leaving neighborhoods with decaying recreation centers, deteriorating swimming pools and filthy park bathrooms. This year, they convinced city leaders to send voters a proposal to boost the parks budget gradually over a decade.

Supporters say that change finally will allow the city to give Angelenos the park and recreation services they deserve.

Critics contend it will tie the hands of the city’s elected officials, forcing them to cut other services to make room for additional park funding.

California’s general election takes place on Novemer 3. Learn about L.A.’s city and county races as well races for state office.

The City Charter, which serves as L.A.’s governing document, requires that the parks department receive .0325% of the total assessed value of taxable properties in Los Angeles.

That translated into $303 million for the park system this year. If the formula were left unchanged, the minimum allocation gradually would grow to $493 million over the next 10 years, according to a city analysis.

If voters approve Charter Amendment PRK, the minimum allocation would double that amount — to $986 million — by 2036, the analysis said.

“This forces a ramp-up in the expenditures that are dedicated to care for our parks,” said City Councilmember Monica Rodriguez, who spearheaded the proposal.

Rodriguez pointed to a December 2025 report that found that the city needs nearly $2.7 billion to address the deferred maintenance facing its park and recreation resources, which include not just natural spaces but also dog parks, skate parks, senior centers and even community gardens.

If voters approve the measure, it will be up to future mayors and council members to figure out how to pay for it — whether by siphoning money away from other city agencies or coming up with new funding.

Councilmember Katy Yaroslavsky also voiced support for the measure, saying the gradual ramp-up will give city leaders time to find the money.

“A 10-year runway gives us the space and grace we need to figure out how to double the allocation in a way that doesn’t result in short-changing other departments,” she said.

Dozens of groups have lined up behind the proposal, including the Trust for Public Land, TreePeople, Friends of the Los Angeles River and many others. At City Hall, the measure is backed by Rodriguez and several other council members as well as City Controller Kenneth Mejia.

Rodriguez and Mejia signed the ballot argument in favor of Charter Amendment PRK, as did Rev. Gregory Boyle, founder of Homeboy Industries, Nicole Chase, president and chief executive of the Boys & Girls Club of the San Fernando Valley, and several others.

Backers of the measure say the parks department provides an essential safety net for the city’s low-income residents, offering summer camps, sports activities and senior programs for free or at reduced prices.

When temperatures soar, the city’s recreation centers welcome residents who lack air conditioning. During emergencies, those facilities are converted into places of refuge from fires, floods or other disasters.

Despite those varied responsibilities, the department has been underfunded for years, said Tori Kjer, executive director of the Los Angeles Neighborhood Land Trust, who pushed for the measure to reach the ballot.

“If you talk to many Angelenos, they are unhappy with their local park, and that is because we have not funded it with the resources it needs,” she said.

Kjer said the department never recovered from the 2008 recession, when city leaders cut staffing by more than 25%, leaving it with about 1,500 workers last year. The city also began charging the department for the cost of water, electricity, trash pickup and other city services.

The Los Angeles Police Protective League, which represents 8,500 rank-and-file officers, opposes Charter Amendment PRK, calling it an egregious example of “ballot box budgeting.”

The more the City Charter puts restrictions on city spending, the fewer choices the city’s elected officials will have in the middle of a budget crisis, said Tom Saggau, a spokesperson for the union.

“We love our parks. We want to make sure there are enough police officers to keep them safe,” he said. “And when you start budgeting through the ballot box, it sets a dangerous precedent, especially in a city with so many competing priorities.”

Councilmember Bob Blumenfield, who represents the southwest San Fernando Valley, was the only council member to vote against drafting the measure.

In June, he told his colleagues — and a booing audience — that he had a long history of supporting park spaces. But he also said that as a former state lawmaker, he had been “traumatized” by the budget process in Sacramento, where many programs could not be touched because of spending requirements.

“The more things we wall off, the more difficult that [budget] process is going to be,” he said.

Backers have downplayed such warnings, saying the measure gives the City Council the power to reduce the park funding allotment by 30% during fiscal emergencies.

Park advocates originally planned to ask L.A. voters to approve a sales tax hike, going so far as to submit the initial paperwork to the city clerk. That effort failed to draw sufficient political support, spurring those groups to change course.

Last spring, advocates persuaded council members to pursue a ballot measure that would double the parks allocation over four years.

But that idea drew red flags from the city’s policy advisers, who warned it would significantly increase the city’s structural deficit — the gap between how much money the city takes in and how much it spends.

In a memo, City Administrative Officer Matt Szabo said that locking in spending for certain city departments would reduce the options available to future councils. The idea also runs counter to the city’s fiscal policies, he said.

Council members crafted a compromise, stretching out the increases over 10 years instead of four.

Forget pricey haunted houses and tourist-packed ghost tours. Some of the most atmospheric places to spend Halloween are historic cemeteries, where crumbling mausoleums, elaborate sculptures and famous names provide all the spooky scenery you need – and entry is often free.

A new ranking of 30 cities has revealed the best places to explore Europe’s most fascinating burial grounds, from Paris to Oslo.

The "Tombstone Tourism Index", by travel eSIM app Saily, took into account five separate factors when looking at cemeteries: famous “residents”, visual merit, heritage status, crowd-free experience, and transit access from the city centre.

Each category was given an individual percentage of importance to reveal the most tourism-worthy cemeteries.

"Every October, people queue for hours at haunted attractions while walking straight past the real thing – some of the most atmospheric, story-filled places in any city," said Matas Cenys, head of product at Saily.

"Historic cemeteries are open-air museums with sculpture and incredible stories, and they don't charge entry. Halloween is a good excuse to discover them, but they're worth visiting any day of the year."

While the legendary Parisian cemetery has some 70,000 graves across 44 hectares, a staggering 1,445 notable people are buried here, many of whom attract visitors year-round.

Père Lachaise is the eternal resting place of the likes of Chopin, Édith Piaf, Oscar Wilde, Jim Morrison, Marcel Proust, Gertrude Stein, Molière, Balzac, and Sarah Bernhardt, to name just a few.

The grave of The Doors singer Jim Morrison is especially popular, while Oscar Wilde's lipstick-covered tomb has needed a glass barrier.

More than 4,500 photos have been shared on Wikimedia Commons, making it the most documented cemetery on earth. It’s also free to visit, and just 15 minutes from Paris’ centre.

Make sure you download the official app to help navigate this huge space and avoid getting lost, especially in spooky season.

Think of Norway’s capital and cemeteries don’t necessarily come to mind. That’s likely because the Vår Frelsers Gravlund has only 123 Google reviews, making it the index’s best-kept secret.

Despite that, the cemetery is just 10 minutes from the centre of Oslo, and is home to the father of modern drama Henrik Ibsen, ‘The Scream’ artist Edvard Munch, painter Christian Krohg and polar explorer Fridtjof Nansen.

These four figures who define Norway’s history are all buried within walking distance of each other in a striking cemetery, landscaped in the Victorian era. It’s well worth adding a visit to your Scandinavian bucket list.

This Edinburgh cemetery is even less known than Vår Frelsers Gravlund, with just 90 Google reviews, despite the fact that it sits just steps from the city's busiest street.

The Dean Cemetery, a Category A listed site, lies between Queensferry Road and the Water of Leith, and is filled with elaborate Victorian monuments.

The people buried here are among those who built modern Edinburgh, including architect William Playfair, philosopher Dugald Stewart, and portrait painter Henry Raeburn.

The Olšany Cemetery in Prague is a veritable maze of crumbling Baroque tombs, elaborate Art Nouveau monuments and overgrown pathways, making it an especially good spot for a wander during spooky season.

Franz Kafka, one of Prague’s most famous literary figures, is buried here, adding another reason to seek out this historic burial ground.

Pair a visit with nearby Vyšehrad Cemetery, where Czech cultural icons including composers Antonín Dvořák and Bedřich Smetana, artist Alfons Mucha and writer Karel Čapek are laid to rest.

Arguably the most atmospheric cemetery in the UK, Highgate Cemetery in London is actually a little controversial as it’s not free to enter, unless you’re a grave owner or hold a grave owner's pass.

Nevertheless, it remains very popular and for good reason.

Karl Marx was laid to rest here, alongside George Eliot, Christina Rossetti, and Michael Faraday.

The Victorian Gothic architecture is particularly impressive – think overgrown mausoleums, ivy-draped angels, and an Egyptian Avenue.

The whole cemetery is Grade I listed, has some 950 notable burials, and is hugely photogenic, meaning it’s well worth the visit if graveyards are your thing.

#645. Are the French police the most violent in the EU?

As protests continue in France, the French police are under scrutiny after new allegations of police brutality. The force has a bigger arsenal than most in Europe.

Videos of alleged police violence are going viral on French social media as a wave of protests grips France. One video shows the police beating a man to the floor then dragging him away unconscious. Another shows an officer grabbing a young man from behind, seemingly unprovoked, and dragging him by the neck. Another shows a young woman being hauled off with a twisted arm, screaming in pain. These videos could not be independently verified.

The French police have drawn renewed criticism from rights groups, not only because of their methods but also because of their use of stun grenades and rubber bullets. France has one of the most heavily armed police forces in Europe. During the student protests of the past weeks, several teenagers sustained life-changing injuries as a result: One had a hand blown off, one was blinded in one eye, another had his jaw broken.

More than half a million people took to the streets in France on Saturday, most of whom protested peacefully, criticizing public sector cuts, the cost-of-living crisis and supporting students' demands for better conditions in classrooms.

Rioters took advantage, burning buildings, looting stores and lobbing projectiles at the police, creating a difficult situation for the officers and other emergency services.

The protests over the weekend followed a series of protests by high-school students, who barricaded school buildings to denounce a shortage of teachers and demand repairs to crumbling infrastructure.

More protests will be happening this weekend, with the French government saying it will even deploy military forces.

The French police have a bigger arsenal than most European countries. For instance, officers use the so-called LBD-40, a type of gun used to fire rubber bullets.

Many countries, like the UK and Germany, mostly do not allow the use of rubber bullets in protests.  In some European countries, like Spain, they are sometimes used but cause fewer injuries than in France.

"It is not a French specificity. But there are guidelines. There must be a certain distance," Anastassia Tsoukala, an associate professor of criminology at the University of Paris-Sud, told DW. "Even if you try to respect the guidelines, people may move and then all of a sudden they may lose one eye. So it's extremely dangerous."

Police in France routinely use tear gas, as do police in many other countries in Europe. In warfare, its use is actually forbidden under agreements like the Chemical Weapons Convention.

What makes the French police stand out from other forces is its use of stun grenades.

"These grenades contain a high level of explosive substances. So from this point of view, France is unique," said Tsoukala.

Minister of the Interior Laurent Nunez insists that weapons used by the police are "non-lethal." However, some of the equipment used by the force is classified by France's own internal security code as "war material."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The police's use of these weapons has received renewed criticism after it resulted in injuries during the protests. The teenager who lost use of an eye is suspected of being hit at close range with a rubber bullet from an LBD-40.

"When we look at crowd control, it is clear that if we measure police brutality by the number of deaths amongst demonstrators or members of the crowd, and if we also measure it by the number of cases of maiming, the French police are the most brutal in the whole of the European Union," says Sebastian Roche, a researcher at France's National Centre for Scientific Research who specializes in comparing police forces across Europe.

He points to the political context to understand the French police's equipment and how it is used today.

"The political authorities are free to decide on the police's equipment," the police expert says. "When LBDs were introduced into the [French] police force, they were intended for units like anti-organized crime units. This is the same weapon that is today used for crowd control. It gives an idea of how the way in which politicians in France think we can or should deal with political protest has evolved."

Another difference between the French police and forces elsewhere is the methods. German police, for example, are supposed to try to avoid escalation.

Roche compares how protestors were moved in Lützerath, Germany, in 2023 to the more aggressive methods in Sainte-Soline, France, in 2023. Both places saw environmental protests.

"In Lützerath, dogs were used, there were some injuries but far fewer seriously injured people on both sides. In Sainte-Soline, the military police was sent in and used LBDs and grenades intensively. There were serious injuries amongst both police officers and demonstrators. Two protestors were left in a coma."

According to international standards set by the United Nations, use of force by officers of the law "should be exceptional," in the case of "prevention of crime" or "lawful arrest." Any use of force should follow a principle of "proportionality," which means no more than necessary to achieve its objective.

French Interior Minister Nunez has insisted in radio interviews that officers have largely respected this principle, which is also enshrined in French law, during the current protests.

However, rights group Amnesty International describes the police response to the current protests as "disproportionate" and calls upon French authorities to "act upon their human rights obligations."

The French branch of the League of Human Rights condemns the "violent repression" of the high school protest movement.

DW contacted two police unions and the French Interior Ministry for comment, but none responded before time of publication.

"It was very complicated to contain all the different groups," Interior Minister Nunez said in Marseille on Tuesday. "The police did a great job and there were a great number of crimes that were prevented thanks to their commitment."

Experts are critical of the police's actions.

"Public order is subordinated to human life and safety," Tsoukala said. "As a jurist I should say that this is a non-negotiable value."

The French police have no independent watchdog, only an internal division called the IGPN (General Inspectorate of the National Police) that can investigate when problems occur. The IGPN says it has opened at least 40 cases since the beginning of the latest protests.

Countries like the UK and Denmark investigate incidents differently, with independent watchdogs. However, Tsoukala criticizes leniency and a lack of transparency across Europe when incidents with the police occur.

"They are acquitted or they receive extremely light penalties," she said. "And I'm afraid this is the standard method to deal with police brutality cases across Europe."

#646. ‘Gaza’s suffering has become campaign fodder’: Palestinians fear the worst from Israel election

Humanitarian catastrophe largely ignored as rivals Gadi Eisenkot and Benjamin Netanyahu vow to end Hamas rule

As Israel prepares to go to the polls, Palestinians in Gaza are bracing for an outcome that could shape their future, knowing their fate rests with the country that has reduced much of the territory to rubble and killed nearly 75,000 people.

Gaza, where nearly a million displaced Palestinians face dire sanitary conditions, water shortages and the constant threat of Israeli strikes, has been largely absent from the election campaign.

Both Benjamin Netanyahu’s far-right coalition and Gadi Eisenkot’s opposition Yashar party have focused instead on the goal of destroying Hamas in the wake of the 7 October attacks and the trauma inflicted on Israeli society. The humanitarian catastrophe unfolding just across the border has received little, if any, attention.

“We hope a government will come to power that is less inclined towards killing, displacement and our extermination,” said Sami Abu Rumi, 47, from Rafah, who is now displaced in al-Mawasi, Khan Younis. “But, ultimately, we see the thinking of Israeli governments as largely similar.”

Neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot has set out a clear plan for Gaza’s future. Both have vowed to end Hamas rule and both support Donald Trump’s controversial peace plan.

Eisenkot, the former military chief whose party is leading Netanyahu’s Likud in the polls, has pledged to restore Israel’s international standing after three years of war. Yet he is no dove.

A senior commander during Israel’s 2006 war with Hezbollah, Eisenkot, whose son and two nephews were killed fighting in Gaza, later championed the “Dahiya doctrine”, which advocated overwhelming force against civilian areas where militants operated. Critics say the strategy has since been employed in Gaza, causing widespread destruction that, they argue, amounts to war crimes.

“Eisenkot talks of defeating Hamas, while Netanyahu boasts about military operations and the killing of Palestinians,” said Abu Rumi. ‘‘Gaza’s suffering has become campaign fodder. Meanwhile, families here struggle to feed their children, keep them in school and access medical care. With homes and infrastructure destroyed, simply surviving has become a daily struggle.”

Earlier this week, the Arab-led Joint List party in Israel aired a 48-second election video showing drone footage of Gaza’s ruins. “[We] behave as if everything that has happened here is completely normal,” the voiceover says. “As if tens of thousands of people weren’t killed here … as if entire cities were not destroyed and turned into wastelands.”

The party vows it “will not be silent”, adding: “[The other parties] want more destruction. We offer life.”

The chances of Arab parties joining an Eisenkot-led coalition are slim to none, although they could offer support from outside government. Yet among Palestinians in Gaza, pessimism runs deep: whoever wins, little is expected to change.

“I do not believe anyone genuinely cares about Gaza or has its people’s interests at heart,’’ said Haneen Hamdouna, 45, from Beit Lahia, who has also been displaced to al-Mawasi. ‘‘Whether it is Netanyahu, Eisenkot or someone else, attacking Gaza seems to have become part of Israeli election campaigning.

“For years, we have said that the incoming government might be better than the one before it, only to be shocked when it turns out to be worse. Perhaps 200 trucks would be allowed into Gaza instead of 100, but that would not mean any real change in our lives.”

In Gaza, most people are too preoccupied by the struggle to find food and water to follow the election campaign. Fears of renewed hunger are mounting as markets run short of fresh produce and other essentials.

Residents say commercial deliveries have been suspended for about a week, driving up prices. Flour now costs more than three times its previous price, while dwindling humanitarian aid has left families increasingly vulnerable to another food crisis.

Yet, some people in Gaza are following the Israeli elections closely, driven less by hope of change than fear of what the outcome could mean for their future.

They fear that Palestinian suffering has become a recurring feature of Israeli election campaigns, with candidates competing over who can take the toughest stance towards Gaza rather than offering any prospect of a better future.

“A friend was supposed to hold his son’s wedding in the coming days,” said Karim Mareesh, 43. “But he decided to postpone it until after the Israeli elections. He feared that the far-right government might secure another term, prompting the war to resume and forcing him to flee again. He could lose his tent and the wedding supplies he had struggled to save up for.”

Hope is hard to find in Gaza, where three years of war have reduced entire neighbourhoods to wastelands of shattered concrete and bomb craters. It is harder still to imagine a future when Israeli restrictions on food and humanitarian aid have turned hunger into a weapon of war. And almost impossible to see any light at the end of the tunnel when more than 20,000 Palestinian children have been killed since 7 October 2023.

“I feel that everything said about addressing our suffering is nothing more than an attempt to soothe our pain, or simply words and promises that we no longer believe,” says Noor AlMoghanni, 20, from Gaza City.

“Whether Netanyahu wins or loses, the reality here will not change. As I see it, their goal is to destroy Gaza and the foundations of life here.”

#647. Exclusive: Secret pay-for-play text rocks Trump White House

Top Trump adviser Ric Grenell allegedly outlined a stunning pay-for-influence offer to a Turkish billionaire last year: access to "POTUS," "VIP events" and administration officials, according to a text message, reviewed by Axios, that the White House counsel is investigating.

  • "Once the money comes to the company here, I will arrange the donation to Kennedy Centre [sic], and you'll be joining the VIP events and get close with the administration, even with POTUS," the May 3, 2025, text says.
  • Grenell has called the accusations "lies" and denied sending the text message.

Why it matters: Administration officials say the text is a key piece of evidence in the White House's investigation — ordered by President Trump — into whether Grenell abused the president's trust and misappropriated a potential multimillion-dollar donation to the Kennedy Center, which Grenell led at the time.

  • Grenell also served in another Trump-appointed capacity: as special envoy to Venezuela, where Turkish businessman Turhan Mildon also had contracts.
  • "We need to make you the 'American face' down in V," Grenell allegedly wrote in the same 2025 text message to Mildon, whose attorneys sent the text, at least one financial document and other correspondence to the White House counsel's office, according to sources familiar with the investigation.
  • Mildon is married to another Trump adviser: former U.S. attorney for New Jersey Alina Habba, who stormed into the Oval Office on Oct. 9 and accused Grenell of hoodwinking her husband into making a Kennedy Center donation that never arrived, Axios first reported.

Zoom in: At the heart of the alleged scheme is a financial transaction involving a private Houston-based defense company's software and the Democratic Republic of Congo, Habba and Mildon's attorneys have told the White House.

  • Mildon alleges that at Grenell's direction, Mildon wired $17.6 million to Texas Armament & Technology. He says the money was to be split in roughly two parts: one for the Congo deal and nearly $6 million for the Kennedy Center.
  • To back up his claims, Mildon provided the 2025 text that discussed the Kennedy Center donation and Congo "software." In the text to Mildon, the sender also says, "There is an e-mail that was sent to you, can you please take a look at it for me ?"
  • That email also was furnished to the White House, as was a May 29, 2025, financial record showing $17.6 million was wired to the company, known by its initials TXAT, sources said.

It would be 17 months before Mildon learned that the Kennedy Center never received the money that he thought was included in the wire he sent at Grenell's direction, Habba told the president.

The intrigue: Here's where the story gets mysterious and murky. It's unclear what the Congo contract was for, how it related to the Kennedy Center or what the financial specifics were.

  • The text doesn't mention any financial numbers, either for TXAT or the Kennedy Center. But a source familiar with the situation said that other correspondence furnished to the White House does have financial specifics.
  • The financial transaction sent to TXAT didn't appear to come from Mildon's bank account, as Habba initially indicated to Trump.

Instead, the $17.6 million was wired to TXAT from Congo's "Ministère des Finances" in Kinshasa, the capital city, where Mildon has business and access to finances, a White House official said.

  • A spokesman for Mildon would not comment. Spokespeople for TXAT and Congo's government couldn't be reached.
  • "We're trying to find out whose money this is," the official said.

Complicating the matter further: Habba's numbers kept changing after she first alerted Trump to the alleged theft of the Kennedy Center money.

  • At first she said the Kennedy Center contribution was for $17 million.
  • Then she said it was about $6 million after talking to Mildon. The exact figure seems to be $5.6 million.

The other side: Grenell, who declined to comment for this article, previously told Axios that the claims against him are "absurd."

  • "I've never asked for one cent to be sent somewhere else pretending it was for the Kennedy Center, and I've never received any payment from him at all," he said. "Make him give proof to what he is saying, not make these absurd allegations."
  • When told of the text message's exact wording, Grenell hotly denied he sent it because "center" was spelled in British English as "centre," a source briefed on his thinking said.
  • Grenell's allies also have questioned everything from Mildon's background as a businessman to his associates, his age (he's 29 but some records indicate he's 25) and his $10 million wedding last month to Habba, 42, whom he began dating last year.

Friction point: As the New York Times examined Mildon's activities in Venezuela, he had a falling out with Grenell, with whom he had been friendly since 2024.

  • Mildon met Habba in 2025 at the Kennedy Center.
  • The Times previously reported aspects of the text message concerning Venezuela and the money from Congo.

Inside the room: On Oct. 9, when Habba arrived at the White House, she was "pretty animated," said one administration official, and exclaimed at one point, "Ric stole the money!"

  • The problem, however, was that Habba "didn't have all her stuff in order. She went in there half-cocked without all the facts yelling about Grenell stealing. And the facts keep changing," the source said. "That doesn't mean Ric is out of the woods. This looks really shady."
  • After Habba leveled her accusations, Trump called White House Counsel Will Scharf into Oval Office and asked him to look into her claims, sources said.

Trump and Scharf then phoned Grenell, who denied everything and said he would have instantly alerted everyone to the idea of a $17 million contribution.

  • "There's no way this is true. This is crazy," Grenell told Trump at one point, according to a source briefed on the discussion.

Behind the scenes: Scharf grew skeptical of Habba's claims early last week because she and Mildon's attorneys were initially slow to furnish any records to help his inquiry, said a source. They submitted the documents on Friday.

  • Scharf is still gathering evidence and plans to verify the digital footprint of the 2025 text, the source said, noting that a printout of the message has the same image of Grenell that appears on his smartphone contact card display.
  • Kennedy Center insiders also have contacted the White House and said they frequently saw Mildon at exclusive events at the facility, indicating he was a big donor. That includes appearances in the vice president's box, next to the president's, a source said.
  • "Here's where Alina might be telling the truth: Mildon did get access. So why did he get access? Was he doing business in Congo with Ric? Why so much access if the contribution was never paid?" one of the administration officials asked.
  • "There's a lot of questions. And POTUS wants answers."

#649. What to Stream: 'Minions & Monsters,' Matthew Perry, Daddy Yankee and 'The Gilded Age'

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

A docuseries about Matthew Perry and the latest “Minions” movie are some of the new television, films, music and games headed to a device near you.

Also among the streaming offerings worth your time this week, as selected by The Associated Press’ entertainment journalists: Daddy Yankee's new album, the fourth season of “The Gilded Age” and the video game “Phantom Blade Zero.”

— “Minions & Monsters ” (Wednesday on Peacock) is the third “Minions” movie and the seventh in the overall “Despicable Me” franchise. But the film, directed by Pierre Coffin, the voice of the Minions, is one of the yellow guys’ most charming. In the 1920s-set film, the Minions come to Hollywood as silent movie stars who embark on making a monster movie. In his review, AP’s Mark Kennedy wrote: “The movie has playful references to old screen gods … but the kids in the audience won’t get them and their parents are just too tired.”

— In “Hanging by a Wire” (Wednesday on Paramount+), director Mohammed Ali Naqvi chronicles a 2023 rescue in Pakistan. Eight people (two adults and six teenage boys) were suspended in a cable car over a chasm after a wire broke. With archival footage and firsthand accounts, the film chronicles the drama from every angle, on the ground and above.

— Back in 2022, the reggaeton icon Daddy Yankee announced his retirement. It was short-lived. Songs — written and released after revealing he had converted to Christianity — followed. And on Friday, he will release a new album, “La Postal,” a 15-track concept album where each track is a love letter to, well, love: romantic love, familial love, self-love and so on. The first taste arrived in the form of “BOTZ (Kiss Me Again),” high-energy, mainstream-friendly romantic reggaeton from the man who knows it best.

— The Canadian rock band Nickelback will release their 11th studio album, “Everything Under the Sun,” also on Friday. Expect their familiar recipe of glossy hooks, post-grunge rock riffs and gravelly vocals, from energetic opener “Rattle The Cage” to power ballads like “Make Me Love You.” There are also a few surprises: Guest appearances range from Sammy Hagar to actor Ryan Reynolds.

— Country star Dustin Lynch will release his seventh studio album, “Clean Slate,” also on Friday. Across 12 tracks, Lynch sharpens his tools; these are radio-ready stompers in the making. “There’s a lot of life on this record,” Lynch said in a press release. “Falling for somebody, missing somebody, looking back at things you might do differently now, going out and having a damn good time, and figuring out what matters when everything else gets quiet.”

— Parker Posey hosts “The Mob,” a Hulu competition series from the team behind “The Traitors.” Twelve celebrities — including Aida Turturro, Bruno Tonioli, Debi Mazar and Joe Gorga — live in an Italian villa and complete tasks drawn from mob movies, all for a shot at up to $250,000. The group picks one member as the don, who decides who gets paid and who goes home. It debuts Monday with new episodes weekly.

— A three-part Netflix docuseries, “The One About Matthew Perry,” revisits the life of the late “Friends” star, best known as Chandler Bing. Emmy-winning director Mary Robertson draws on interviews with Perry's sister, Mia Perry Bowick, along with friends and collaborators, plus photos and videos not seen before. It premieres Tuesday, just before the third anniversary of the actor’s death.

— In “Nocturne,” on Apple TV, Liev Schreiber plays a former soldier and homicide detective who leaves Philadelphia for a small Pennsylvania town, only to see a serial killer, played by Stephen Graham, target his community and family. Zazie Beetz co-stars as an FBI agent. The 10-episode series, adapted from Lars Kepler’s novels “Lazarus” and “The Sandman,” premieres Friday, Oct. 30, with two episodes.

— Michael C. Hall returns as Dexter Morgan when “Dexter: Resurrection” begins its second season Friday, Oct. 30, on Paramount+. This time he’s up against two killers in New York, one with a long history and one new, and he’s also dealing with middle age. Dan Stevens and Brian Cox join the cast, and Uma Thurman returns.

— Julian Fellowes’ period drama “The Gilded Age” returns for a fourth season Sunday, Nov. 1, on HBO Max. Carrie Coon’s Bertha Russell deals with the fallout of her social rise, while Christine Baranski’s Agnes van Rhijn looks for a way back to the top. Jim Gaffigan appears as President Grover Cleveland.

New video games to play from Oct. 26-Nov. 1

— “Phantom Blade Zero” aims to create an entirely new genre: “Kungfupunk.” Beijing-based developer S-Game describes it as a mix of martial arts, steampunk machinery, the occult and “elements that do not fit a single category.” It’s the tale of an elite assassin named Soul who’s framed for his master’s murder and has just 66 days to live. Can he survive long enough to unravel the conspiracy? If not, at least he can wreak vengeance with a wicked assortment of swords and a few less pointy secondary weapons. Start carving your path Thursday, Oct. 29, on PlayStation 5 or PC.

— Dalton’s Dinos is one of those weird roadside attractions that make cross-country drives so fun. Sure, it looks like it’s been abandoned, but you’ll soon discover there are “Terrible Lizards” underground. In this debut release from North Carolina’s WDR Studios, you have no weapons to fight the monstrous beasts. Instead, you’ll need all the running, jumping and climbing skills you can muster to explore a sprawling subterranean environment and escape with all your limbs intact. Dig in Thursday, Oct. 29, PlayStation 5, Xbox X/S or PC.

#650. “Fatherland” Cleans Up the Rough Edges of History

Paweł Pawlikowski’s “Fatherland” offers an amiable eighty-two minutes of condensed history, centered on the septuagenarian novelist Thomas Mann’s trip, in the summer of 1949, to Germany—West and East—in order to receive each country’s Goethe Prize on the occasion of that great predecessor’s bicentenary. If Pawlikowski’s aim was to portray Mann (played by Hanns Zischler) as a terminal bore and a pompous ass, he succeeded brilliantly, even if he failed to suggest the reasons for his own animosity. Mann, who has been living in Los Angeles since 1941, is accompanied on the journey by his daughter Erika (Sandra Hüller), who serves as his assistant, even editing his speeches. And he does gives speeches. He gives an impromptu one at a press conference at their first stop, Goethe’s native Frankfurt; he gives a carefully crafted one at the formal prize ceremony there, and he gives another at the East German ceremony in Weimar, Goethe’s longtime home, overtly under Soviet dominion. What’s more, he gives speeches, terse but fusty, in private, to Erika.

For the most part, Mann struts around looking iconic, bearing an air of absurd vanity in his belief that, as an eminent anti-Nazi exile and a Nobel Prize winner who left Germany, in 1933, soon after Hitler came to power, his supra-ideological presence in both Germanies, at a time of Cold War tension, could indeed matter. But Mann most of all strikes an air of formality even in private, even when, in Frankfurt, he gets the grim news of the death of his son Klaus (August Diehl)—Erika’s brother and confidant, who is also a noted author—from a drug overdose. (His death was ruled a suicide.) Most pompous of all are the silences; the most conspicuous of them hollows out one of the major early scenes, when father and daughter, newly arrived in West Germany and travelling by car to Frankfurt, pass through streets of destruction, a country ravaged by war—and remain silent. Yes, awestruck and horrified, no doubt; still, I wondered throughout why silence served Pawlikowski as an optimal mode of expression.

Throughout my viewing, something felt off—in style and in substance—and the first concrete diagnosis came through in my colleague Anthony Lane’s recent New Yorker Profile of Pawlikowski, which I had deliberately delayed reading until after seeing the movie. (History may have no spoilers, but drama does.) That in-depth portrait mentions a fundamental change the filmmaker wrought upon Mann’s real-life 1949 journey: the author was, in fact, accompanied by his wife, Katia, who, in “Fatherland,” is said to be too weak to travel. The character of Erika, a writer and intellectual with her own range of uneasy connections to Germany—she’ll encounter an ex-husband and an ex-lover there—is a screenwriter’s convenience, a walking plot-production machine. Behind closed doors, however, the switch from a spouse to a child, from Mann the husband to Mann the father, is the switch from the intimate to the casual, from uninhibited speech to guardedness.

It took no more than minutes of curiosity to find that the fulcrum of “Fatherland,” the death of Klaus —the first character seen in the movie—occurred not during the Germany trip but some months before it. As for the trip itself, it was far more tumultuous, far more infuriating to Mann, and far more unflattering toward West Germany than the movie lets on. Upon his return to the United States, Mann wrote, for the Times, that, in West Germany, “they live by the slogan: ‘Everything was better under Hitler!’ By virtue of the experiences they claim to have had, they declare triumphantly that democracy has been tried and found wanting. Democracy to them means the Occupation Powers and all who ‘collaborate’ with them.” This isn’t the elegant stuffiness of “Fatherland”; it conjures a Fassbinder-esque film—outspoken, insolent, crude, loud, and brazen. Mann may not have shared his testimony, his vision, his voice with Erika during the tour, but he might have with Katia.

To share that voice in “Fatherland,” Pawlikowski would have to imagine it. But his economy of expression also suggests that the film, which is never at risk of spilling out beyond the confines of its scripted pointedness, depends on an economy of imagination. Its contrivances are less like conveniences or abridgments than like deceptions: the facts and the tone are in service to a style that itself has little room for variety or range. “Fatherland” is a muted, muffled quiet-box of understatement, twisting history less for dramatic effect than for affectlessness. Pawlikowski has developed a felt-lined aesthetic—of black-and-white images, in the traditional nearly square screen dimensions, that leave space around the characters—that bespeaks observational detachment and comes off as culture personified. This forced reserve and mannered dignity create a hermetic atmosphere of refinement (from behind the camera) and of elimination (in front of it). It is a cinema of prefabricated meaning and predetermined moods, in which images limit the very kinds of events that can be depicted.

Here, Pawlikowski further rarefies the style that he developed in “Ida” (2013) and advanced in “Cold War” (2018), but not to advantage. I found myself thinking of other filmmakers who rarefy: Christopher Munch, whose 1991 feature, “The Hours and Times,” about the 1963 Barcelona jaunt of John Lennon and Brian Epstein, has the decency to stick to these characters and not replace Epstein with, say, George Martin; or Hong Sangsoo, whose radical reduction of space and span in his new movie, “The Day She Returns,” creates great cinematic leeway for the uninhibited voice of its actress-protagonist; or Robert Bresson, whose severe restraint served artistically as both microscope and microphone, to experience infinitesimal gestures on a cosmic scale of moment and morality.

In “Fatherland,” such microscopy is reversed. Pawlikowski’s camera reduces the figures and voices, in order to fit them into his own rigidly molded spaces. The characters are petrified like specimens, expressing and embodying only what fits into the film’s design, with no potential for inconvenient loose ends for viewers to follow outside the frame’s borders. It’s a sieve too fine for anything as inconvenient as bodies or as coarse as discourse to get through—an aesthetic of purification, disincarnation, signification, as if the mere fact of keeping voices down and holding thoughts in were itself a mark of urbanity, conferring that cultural virtue upon a dignified audience. The movie sanitizes the past and removes its tang, its pungency, leaving a craving for contact with nature, with raw experience, with incongruities and accidents and anything but what fits, in lieu of such synthetic sophistication. ♦

#651. Your guide to L.A. City Charter Amendment PRT: Greater public insight into airport, harbor departments

See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred

Charter Amendment PRT would affect the city’s departments of airports, harbor and water and power, which operate as self-funding businesses that report to three different boards.

California’s general election takes place on Novemer 3. Learn about L.A.’s city and county races as well races for state office.

The amendment would change the composition of Los Angeles World Airport’s board of commissioners, which oversee Van Nuys and Los Angeles International airports. It would require that two of the seven board members live in Van Nuys and three live around LAX — a footprint that the amendment does not define.

The Port of Los Angeles, one of the busiest in the nation, serves as a landlord to operators at its terminals. The amendment would require the Los Angeles Board of Harbor Commissioners to annually allocate a portion of the harbor’s operating income to investments in waterfront public access projects. It also would broaden public insight into how lease agreements with the port affect the local workforce by requiring any leaseholder extending a lease or lease applicant to disclose overview on its employment.

The amendment also offers greater flexibility for how the airport and water and power departments lease space to long-term investments.

Supporters include Councilmembers Tim McOsker, Imelda Padilla and Traci Park, community activists near the Port of Los Angeles in Wilmington and San Pedro and near Van Nuys Airport, and neighborhood council members near LAX in Westchester.

There was initial pushback among some terminal leaseholders at the Port of Los Angeles.

Following a series of scandals that shook public trust in local government, Los Angeles City Council launched a massive charter reform to boost accountability across city departments. Charter PRT emerged from that reform.

McOsker, who co-sponsored the amendment, said it would offer greater public access and participation into government processes. He believes it is important that those overseeing LAX and Van Nuys understand how neighboring communities are affected by airport decisions.

“The folks that live and work and drive around and experience the impacts of the airport operations should have some say in the future of airport operations,” McOsker said. “They know the best of what the impacts are on the tens of thousands of folks that live around each of those facilities.”

McOsker stressed that the port is on public land and another space that residents should have greater insight into by offering transparency into how leaseholder agreements affect the local economy.

#653. Ukraine: Life near the front line in Sloviansk

As Russian continues to attack Sloviansk in eastern Ukraine, thousands of residents refuse to leave or struggle to find a way out. For many, poverty, family ties and beloved pets make evacuation painfully difficult.

A few days ago, three Russian aerial bombs struck a residential neighborhood on the outskirts of Sloviansk. One hit a five-story apartment building, injuring seven people. Along with neighboring Kramatorsk, Sloviansk is one of the last major towns in the eastern Ukrainian region of Donetsk still under Ukrainian control. Since summer, the city has been a combat zone.

In a courtyard surrounded by damaged apartment blocks, a dusty carpet hangs over the metal frame of a swing set. Tetjana, a pensioner who lives in the building across the street, has brought it out of her rubble-strewn apartment to clean it. She was in her kitchen when the bombs struck.

"The bomb hit the second floor, and a woman who lived on the fourth floor was screaming," she tells DW. "They managed to rescue her before that entire section of the building collapsed," she adds.

Despite being offered the opportunity to evacuate, Tetjana has yet to leave Sloviansk. "I don't know where I would go," she says. Rent can cost up to €400 ($449) a month. Tetjana's pension is the equivalent of just €67 ($75) a month. Even with monthly relocation assistance of about €40 ($45), she could not make ends meet. "I couldn't live on that. Nowhere!"

Meanwhile, electricity and water are still available in her neighborhood, but the gas supply has been cut off. "We'll get through this," Tetjana says hopefully. "Everything will be OK. That's what I tell everyone. I want that so much."

Days after the attack, the few residents remaining in the damaged buildings were still clearing out their apartments. But another attack hit as they worked. This time, the bombs struck a building housing a state-run emergency assistance center and the Red Cross. While firefighters put out the blaze, rescue workers and volunteers retrieved belongings left inside and cleared away broken glass. Eight people were injured in the attack.

"I was on the balcony when there was a deafening bang. It felt as if someone had hit me over the head," says Natalja, describing one of the recent attacks. The pensioner comes to this part of the city to care for her twin sister. "She can no longer get around. Today, I couldn't bring her bread, only crispbread," she tells DW. Although shops and a few stalls remain at the burned-out market, bread is not available every day.

"I tried to persuade my sister to leave. I would go to a nursing home and she would go to a hospital. But her dog is sick, and I have one, too," Natalja says, noting that pets are not allowed during evacuations. "I can't leave my sister behind. She is worried and angry with me, as if everything were my fault. I have no strength left."

Natalja slowly sets off for home, "so I can get there before dark." The city center is nearly 4 kilometers (2.5 miles) away. Public transportation has been suspended since 30 people were killed in an attack on two buses in neighboring Kramatorsk.

The center of Sloviansk is heavily damaged. Few people are out on the streets, though a handful of shops remain open. Of the city's 100,000 residents, about 20,000 remain, most of them elderly people who are unable to leave.

Vasyl, a pensioner, is from the village of Mayaky, north of Sloviansk. A neighbor drove him into the city center, where he sat down for lunch in a cafe. "We're used to living under fire by now," he says. "But it's a bad habit. We should have broken it long ago."

Vasyl wants peace for his homeland. But he rejects Russian President Vladimir Putin's demand that the part of the Donetsk region under Ukrainian control be handed over to Moscow.

Two elderly women talk on a street covered with nets to protect against drones. "I can't remember the last time I slept through the night," says Iryna, a pensioner. "It's terrible, but I have nowhere to go. I'm supposed to leave my two cats behind, but I love them so much. They're all I have."

"We can only hide, trembling, and pray to God that everything will be all right," Iryna continues. "When I have to go to the market, I don't know if I'll make it there alive."

Russian drones attacked the central market several weeks ago, injuring at least three people. Since then, fewer vendors and customers have been coming to the market.

Valeriya sells women's underwear. With kindergartens closed, she has to bring her 5-year-old daughter Sofia to work. Their neighborhood in Sloviansk is not yet subject to the mandatory evacuation of families with children.

"We're used to this life by now. We were evacuated in 2022, but later returned. Now we're waiting to be evacuated again," Valeriya says.

Sofia races through the market aisles with her friend Anya, who is a year older. Anya's mother is a soldier defending her hometown. Her grandmother, Tetjana, sits nearby selling men's clothing. She, too, has to look after her granddaughter while working.

Tetjana has started shipping her belongings to the Dnipropetrovsk region, where she hopes to start a new life. She is sending them while the post office is still open. "It hurts to see our Ukraine being destroyed," she says, fighting back tears. "Who will rebuild our cities?"

She hopes to return one day. But the fate of Bakhmut weighs on her mind. "Look at Bakhmut. There are no houses left. I'm counting on our boys to hold our cities, even though it's very difficult." Bakhmut, about 50 kilometers (31 miles) from Sloviansk, fell to Russian forces in 2023 after months of heavy fighting.

The women see little hope for a ceasefire. "Putin won't want one. And our younger generation will ask us what we fought for in the first place," Tetjana says. She believes Russia must withdraw from Ukrainian territory.

Drones buzz overhead as gunfire echoes across the market. "It's hard for our boys to shoot them down," Tetjana says. "But they're doing their best."

#655. Nine killed and 40 injured after gunmen open fire at church funeral in Jordan

Footage broadcast on state TV shows three attackers approaching Greek Orthodox church and firing shots

Nine people have been killed after gunmen opened fire at a funeral at a church in Jordan in a rare attack ⁠on the country’s Christian minority.

Authorities described the attack on Friday as a terrorist act by extremists.

Maj gen Abdallah al-Maaytah, the head of Jordan’s ⁠Public Security Directorate, said most of those injured in the shooting at St George’s Greek Orthodox church in Hamoud, in Karak governorate, were receiving treatment, and that the ⁠hunt for the attackers was continuing. Jordan’s health minister said 40 people were injured.

The interior minister, Mazin Al Farrayeh, said the attack had been carried out by “extremists”, but it was too early to tell whether they had any links to known groups ⁠inside or outside Jordan.

Such attacks are rare in Jordan, which is relatively stable, though authorities in the US say in recent years they have repeatedly ​foiled attempted attacks by Islamist militants.

There was no immediate claim of responsibility.

A ‌video, aired on Jordan’s state-owned Al-Mamlaka television station ‌that appeared to be from a security camera on the church, showed three people firing at it from a pavement and hiding behind trees and a ‌low wall. It then showed the attackers running towards the church’s entrance. Reuters was able to verify the video from the entry path and wall surrounding the church, as well as other details.

In a post on X, Jordan’s prime minister, Jafar Hassan, said: “This is a result of a terrorist ideology and blind extremism and we will not allow society to go down this path.”

A priest described how he and ‌others ordered people to ‌get to the ground at the church. “A sense of panic took hold among those present,” Theodoros Soueiss said. “The gunfire was indiscriminate, and you never knew where a bullet might land.”

Khaled Burqan, who was at the funeral, told Al-Mamlaka that dozens of people were present and the gunmen opened fire on them for several minutes.

Ihab Ammareen, another witness, told the station he saw bloodied people collapse ‌on the floor after the attack. “People were crying, wailing, screaming – it’s hard to describe,” he said.

Jordan’s King Abdullah, a leading US partner in the fight against militant Islamist groups, visited Karak hours after the attack and said the perpetrators would ​be punished “with an iron fist”.

“The terrorist attack against Karak will be met with the harshest retaliation. Those who delude themselves into thinking they can divide Jordanians with their bullets have no chance in the face of our unity,” he said in a statement.

Reuters footage from the church after the attack showed blood smeared on the floor near its entrance, where security forces were deployed.

Security has been ⁠stepped up at malls, ⁠foreign embassies ​and other locations across Jordan, the US embassy in Amman said on Saturday.

In a post on X, the UN secretary general, António Guterres, condemned the violence and said attacks against civilians and places of ⁠worship were unacceptable.

People who gathered at a Karak government hospital to support the injured expressed shock. “What happened today has ​left people unable to speak or raise our voices. ​But our only reproach to the state is that ​it must investigate these dark ideas – where they come from and how they enter the minds of our children,” said Hani Al-Mbaydeen, who was outside the hospital.

Christians make up ‌a minority of Jordan’s population. ​The country is home to several ​biblical sites that attract Christian pilgrims from around the world. The US ambassador to the UN, Mike Waltz, described it on X as a “depraved and brutal attack on a house of worship”. Jordan was among the US allies in the region to be hit by Iranian attacks this year after the US and Israel launched strikes against Iran in February.

#657. Supreme Court won't revive accused 9/11 mastermind's plea deal

The Supreme Court denied on Monday a bid by Khalid Sheikh Mohammed, the accused mastermind behind the 9/11 terror attacks, to reinstate plea agreements that would have spared him and two co-defendants the death penalty.

Why it matters: The denial keeps the death penalty on the table for the accused 9/11 plotters as they move closer to their June 2028 military trial date, when the government hopes to finally secure convictions more than 25 years after one of America's deadliest terrorist attacks.

Driving the news: The Supreme Court released an order list Monday identifying the cases it intends to hear and denying those it won't, like the petition in Khalid Shaikh Mohammad, et al. v. United States.

  • The order doesn't explain why the appeal was rejected.
  • Justice Brett Kavanaugh recused himself from the decision. He served as associate counsel to President George W. Bush, where he reportedly assisted with legal and policy discussions following 9/11.

Catch up quick: The government and the three men entered into plea agreements in 2024 that would have spared them the death penalty.

  • The decision was met with outrage and pushback from some 9/11 victims' families.
  • Then-Defense Secretary Lloyd Austin withdrew the agreements days later, declaring that "responsibility for such a decision should rest with me."
  • Mohammed and his co-defendants, Walid bin 'Attash and Mustafa al-Hawsawi, appealed that decision. While a military court initially sided with the defendants, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit sided with Austin, prompting their final appeal to the Supreme Court .

Zoom out: Mohammed and his co-defendants were first arraigned in 2008 for their alleged roles in the attacks involving four hijacked planes that struck the Twin Towers in New York City and the Pentagon, with a fourth crashing in Pennsylvania.

  • Mohammed and his fellow defendants have been held at the U.S. military prison at Guantánamo Bay, Cuba, since 2006.
  • Prosecutors had sought a January 2027 trial date, but a judge determined that timeline would leave too little time to resolve outstanding pretrial issues.

What we're watching: The new tentative trial date is for June 5, 2028. Go deeper: Khalid Sheikh Mohammed to stand trial in 2028 over 9/11 attacks
