#659. Is the Military Low-T?

Last week, a research letter published in the Journal of the American Medical Association—using data from a sample of nearly five hundred military members—reported that approximately twenty-five per cent of participants had at least one measured testosterone level that could qualify them as deficient. The letter is something of a Rorschach test, offering new information that could either bolster or undermine Pete Hegseth’s effort to establish a “high-T Department of War.” Universal screening for testosterone deficiency among men thirty and older has become one of Hegseth’s signature policies: “No fatties, no trannies, no beardos, no weirdos,” he crankily told a crowd of mid-level military members last month, during his “State of the Force” speech. “The patriotic cowboys are in—with testosterone testing on top.”

Every relevant medical society recommends against screening asymptomatic men for testosterone deficiency, because it is akin to scouring a hotel room with a black light: you’re going to find a lot of stuff of indeterminate significance that you wish you hadn’t seen. The data in the JAMA letter, collected across five U.S. military sites between August, 2024, and January, 2026, suggest that more than a hundred thousand men in current service could qualify for testosterone-replacement therapy (TRT) if their screening results are treated as diagnostic. Other military data collected between 2018 and 2025 had estimated the prevalence of diagnosed testosterone deficiency in male military members at less than one per cent.

This variation reflects that a diagnosis of testosterone deficiency can be made rigorously, with a desire to rule out, or capaciously, with a desire to rule in. Decreased testosterone is often cited as an explanation for an array of nonspecific symptoms, including depressed mood, poor libido, fatigue, and spotty memory. Serum testosterone levels vary with stress, sleep, body shape, and time of day; borderline low levels are common and are hard to interpret outside the context of a careful clinical evaluation. Different organizations even use different thresholds to determine what a “low” value is: the Centers for Disease Control uses two hundred and sixty-four nanograms per decilitre, whereas the American Urological Association and the military use three hundred.

These ambiguities make the condition a perfect container for all manner of dysphoria and shame, and set patients and doctors up for conflict. Before prescribing TRT, evidence-based doctors will require multiple confirmatory tests, disregard symptoms that are vague and easily attributed to other causes, and recommend other interventions to boost testosterone production. Patients who are intent on starting injections may then flee to wellness influencers and direct-to-consumer prescribers. “I’ve been experiencing lack of energy, motivation, and 0 sex drive,” an aspiring T user lamented on Reddit’s r/Testosterone forum, dismayed that his physician would not offer him a prescription because his blood work looked fine.

TRT might restore a man’s sex drive, build lean muscle, and boost energy, but it can also accelerate hair loss and lead to abnormal blood counts and clotting. (It also carries a risk of infertility; wanton TRT use among America’s soldiers risks doubling as an inadvertent sterilization effort.) Nonetheless, testosterone prescriptions have accelerated wildly in recent years, both from licensed sources and on the gray market. The fastest growth has been among young people, who sometimes inject doses intended to push testosterone levels far beyond the usual physiologic range.

In the MAHA/MAGA manosphere, the epithet “Low T” stands in for a failure to meet increasingly punitive standards of maleness. “It’s about restoring and optimizing your natural capabilities, protecting your longevity, and insuring you have the biological foundation required to sustain the fight,” Hegseth said when he announced the policy in July, emphasizing that America’s soldiers should remain on “the leading edge of lethality.” But optimization is a goal with no clear threshold for success: one can always look better, feel better, or, I suppose, be something closer to a killing machine. Hegseth is promoting gender-affirming care for cis men, encouraging them to better align their bodies with his idea of what they should be.

When I learned about testosterone deficiency during medical school, twenty years ago, the term referred to a circumscribed diagnosis requiring the presence of specific signs and symptoms: absent libido, infrequent erections, scant body hair, and blood work demonstrating low morning testosterone levels on multiple occasions. It was considered uncommon, especially in young men, yet under-recognized in many instances. (The most common genetic cause of primary testosterone deficiency is the presence of an extra X chromosome; it’s a disorder called Klinefelter syndrome, which goes undiagnosed in upward of fifty per cent of cases.) I’ve never diagnosed low T, although I’ve had patients request an evaluation. This means I’ve probably missed it, but not in the patients who thought they had it.

Separately, doctors have long prescribed TRT to older men for quality-of-life reasons. Men’s testosterone production decreases with age, and older men might experience its lack in much the same way that menopausal women experience decreased estrogen production: fatigue, loss of libido, increased frailty. In both of these cases, hormone prescriptions are not recreational, but they are elective; the drug is being used to supplement rather than restore, and “the real question is benefit” rather than diagnosis, Brad Anawalt, an endocrinologist and men’s-health expert at University of Washington School of Medicine, told me.

Over the past decade, however, several factors have shifted the norms around who seeks a testosterone prescription and who gets one. “Hormones have become magical,” Anawalt said, and testosterone is “the most magical of all. It’s genuinely hard to have a candid conversation about the science of testosterone with almost anybody, because there’s so much emotion in it.” In part, this is because low testosterone, which was previously treated as a source of individual suffering, has been cast as a social crisis. Testosterone levels have dropped worldwide by as much as fifty per cent since the nineteen-seventies—a decrease associated with the rising prevalence of obesity, because excess fat tissue decreases the production of testosterone and its binding proteins.

Low T due to obesity is best treated through weight loss and life-style modifications, but because testosterone supplementation can help shed pounds, many men would rather start there. Members of online testosterone forums often introduce themselves by sharing their age, their weight, and, sometimes, a photo. After a period on testosterone, they’ll post an “after” shot—washboard abs, straining traps, bulging pecs. “You look superb, man” is a typical encouraging response; “kind words, bro, thank you” a customarily humble reply.

In addition to obesity, some researchers posit that hormone-disrupting chemicals, such as the phthalates and bisphenol A (BPA) found in certain plastics, may have a role. This is a favorite preoccupation of Robert F. Kennedy, Jr., and who himself has copped to taking testosterone supplements to maintain his ropey physique, and who calls the global testosterone drop an “existential problem.”

A worldwide decrease in testosterone is notable, and might be a problem, but its public-health significance isn’t yet clear. Testosterone has been measured differently over time and across studies, often without controlling for relevant concerns such as participant B.M.I. or presence of symptoms. Kennedy told a Fox News host that “a teen-ager today, an American teen-ager, has less testosterone than a sixty-eight-year-old man,” which is a dramatic overread of current trends: with the data we have, we can say with confidence only that average testosterone levels have decreased over time, but not much about in whom, why, or what it means. Lower testosterone on average across a cohort doesn’t equate to meaningful clinical deficiency in an individual, since a fifty-per-cent drop might still land someone comfortably within the normal range. Still, some researchers—and many men seeking testosterone prescriptions—argue that “normal” should be an age-adjusted variable. “To optimize your overall physical (sexual/athletic/aesthetic) performance, a man 40s and 50s needs to be in the 700-1000 range,” one r/Testosterone regular advised his comrades.

Low testosterone is often diagnosed without any measured testosterone recorded for the patient at all. Data from 2018 suggest as many as one quarter of men are prescribed testosterone without recent blood work. That’s what we know from the doctor-to-pharmacy world; we have much less insight into the prescribing habits of direct-to-consumer (D.T.C.) platforms, and even less clarity on how much testosterone is being purchased on the gray market with no prescription at all. In one study, D.T.C. providers were happy to prescribe testosterone to a secret shopper with a level of 675 ng/dl. Whatever we might think the rate of testosterone use is, it’s almost certainly an undercount.

The Trump Administration draws a sharp distinction in legitimacy between the use of hormone therapy in the case of transgender-affirming care versus in cisgender-affirming care. I asked Anawalt to help me puzzle over why I consider these interventions discontinuous with one another, rather than variations on a theme. “The trans population I take care of—a fair number of them aren’t looking to become something different than the gender they feel they are,” Anawalt told me. “They’re not looking to become supermen or superwomen.” This was a provocative suggestion: that transgender care, by offering harmony between a body and an identity, is, in a sense, naturalizing, whereas TRT used to compensate for insecurity and enhance masculinity might be the more unnatural intervention.

Testosterone’s current cultural ubiquity “reduces masculinity to a single number,” Anawalt said, even as that number fluctuates and means little out of context. Hormones work via exquisitely calibrated feedback systems, sensitive to all sorts of stresses and rhythms, acting as messengers across our internal ecologies to keep things in balance—a balance that can easily be disrupted by circumstance. In 2020, a group of researchers led by Christopher Frueh, a clinical psychologist at the University of Hawaii at Hilo, published a description of Operator syndrome, a cluster of symptoms—including sleep disturbances, psychiatric illness, chronic pain, and hormone disruptions, and symptoms of traumatic brain injuries—observed in some special-operations personnel after prolonged periods of physical and emotional stress. Testosterone deficiency is a feature of Operator syndrome, and Hegseth has cited the condition as a rationale for his screening program.

Yet it seems reductionist to think of the individuals who fit this profile as primarily “testosterone deficient.” Rather, testosterone production is suppressed in men living under stressful conditions as “an adaptation to energy scarcity, not a disease, and it typically resolves within days of restored sleep and intake,” as the military’s own document on testosterone screening acknowledges. Evidence that TRT helps men with Operator syndrome is mostly hypothetical, and no prospective study has been conducted. In one small case series comparing a handful of special-operations personnel who were on testosterone with those who weren’t, there were no observed benefits in terms of mood, sleep, or sexual function in the men taking TRT. Instead, men on testosterone reported higher pain scores, and researchers noted anecdotal reports of increased irritability and aggression. Several study participants also apparently expressed a belief that, as special forces, they ought to have testosterone levels well above those of a civilian.

There are approximately seventy thousand troops classified as special ops in the United States military, out of a force that contains some two million people. Nonetheless, in twenty-first-century pop culture, depictions of Navy SEALS and other élite fighters in the diffuse and secretive war on terror have come to stand in for the American military as a whole. Hegseth has advocated for operators accused or convicted of war crimes to be pardoned, and routinely references special ops as the embodiment of the “warrior ethos” he strives for. “When the broader force has strayed from the path, has strayed from sanity, has strayed from standards, you have been keepers of the flame,” he told a room of special-ops members in 2025.

Operators are supposed to look a certain way that is decidedly high-T—“You don’t have to be six-foot-three, two hundred and twenty-five pounds, and be able to bench four hundred pounds, but it helps,” the Montana congressman Ryan Zinke, a former SEAL, told Politico. But the American military as a whole looks much more like the country it serves. In 2022, two-thirds of active-duty American service members were overweight or obese, and twenty-one per cent qualified as obese. Given this context, JAMA’s finding that a similar proportion of men might be found to have borderline low testosterone comes as no surprise.

“I think there’s a decent amount of this which is related to just a kind of feeling of humiliation,” the writer Phil Klay, a former marine, told me. “We’re in the wake of failed wars, right? And in the wake of failed wars, there’s always some asshole who is gonna want to say that the reason that we bailed is because we weren’t hard enough, we weren’t cool enough,” he said. Recurrent failures in the Middle East, of course, are low-T; “no fatties” is a plank in Hegseth’s response to those failures.

To live in a state of high T, conversely, is to project a kind of indestructibility. Kennedy once reported that Mehmet Oz had told him that President Trump has “the highest testosterone levels that he’s ever seen for an individual over seventy years old,” and remarked that the President has “the constitution of a deity.” Recently, a young man named Gabe Poirot was interviewed on Fox News about the eighteen days he spent in a coma, in 2021, during which he claims to have met Jesus. “Talk about testosterone!” he marvelled to Kayleigh McEnany. The Jesus he met wasn’t a “soft or passive Jesus,” Poirot recounted, but a man who was huge, strong, and more rageful than anyone imagines, a “lion angry for me. He’s a mustang on my behalf.” In a 2024 survey, nearly eighty per cent of Republican men reported that they thought America had become “too soft and feminine.” Rising anxiety that the future feels suspiciously female may be precipitating the demand for T prescriptions. But the desire also reflects an increasing faith that medicine can ameliorate more ancient types of dread.

In 2012, Stephen Colbert joked that “low T” was “previously known as getting older.” Indeed, in the past decade, death itself began to seem like the ultimate low-T activity. Lower testosterone levels have been associated with higher age-adjusted mortality in some studies, though no trial has demonstrated that higher testosterone leads to a longer life. Still, the idea has stuck. “People are, like, ‘Well, you’re not a younger man anymore’—well, duh? Like, people just want you to wither away and die,” the podcaster and testosterone evangelist Joe Rogan once said. It’s hard to picture how a guy like Rogan, Hegseth, or Kennedy eventually decides to stop juicing. One imagines them as forever brawny, neck veins popping, even as the mortal coil snakes tighter around their chests. ♦

#660. Adultery review – The chemistry in this steamy ITV drama is electric

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Romola Garai and Dominic Cooper add star power to this familiar tale of infidelity

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

“There’s a psychological equation. It says that attraction, plus an obstacle, equals excitement. But what happens if the attraction is too strong; the obstacles are too great?”

If the name alone hadn’t tipped you off, this question, posed by a northern-accented Romola Garai in the opening of ITV’s new sexy six-part drama, Adultery, gives a pretty good idea of what’s to come.

Garai plays Beth, a harried, married mum of two and part-time zumba teacher who’s going through a rocky patch after the death of a friend. Minutes into episode one, her world literally collides with Tom (Dominic Cooper), a charmed, middle-class GP who’s also married with kids, when she knocks him off his bike with her car. One thing, as they say, leads to another…

Infidelity is hardly unfamiliar telly terrain. This series follows in the multitude of footsteps that went before it: The Affair, Scandal, Doctor Foster, The Good Wife, The Betrayal, to skim just a few off the top of the considerable iceberg. Any drama worth its salt these days will likely throw in an affair at some point, even if it’s a B-plot device helping chivvy the story along rather than being dished up as the main event.

Perhaps it’s indicative of the fact that we’re a sex-obsessed species of dreadful gossips. Whatever the reason behind the fascination, this kind of show, covering nothing in the way of new ground, lives and dies by the chemistry of its leads. Fortunately, here the casting team absolutely understood the assignment.

Garai and Cooper bring far more than simply good looks and star power to illicit proceedings (though these certainly help); they manage to create an instant, natural warmth that’s both believable and familiar to anyone who’s ever felt that punch-to-the-solar-plexus connection with another person within seconds of meeting.

This palpable, mutual attraction has more substance than merely sexual, with an innate understanding and easy affection behind all that tortured yearning. It’s this depth of feeling that makes the speed at which both parties decide to press the f***-it button and risk blowing up their entire lives somewhat plausible.

To be honest, I would happily watch Garai do just about anything – there’s something so inherently lovely about her, isn’t there? – but she’s in her element when pining, those big, doe eyes following Tom around like a lovestruck mooncalf. Cooper, meanwhile, hits Aidan Turner-levels of smouldering intensity, barely able to rip his eyes away from Beth whenever they’re in the same room.

ADVERTISEMENT. If you sign up to this service we will earn commission. This revenue helps to fund journalism across The Independent.

The attraction, then, is clear – and so are the obstacles. Namely, the fact that Tom and Beth are married to other people, with the added complication that their teenage kids are in a romantic relationship themselves.

The show is more sophisticated and nuanced than many that have gone before it in terms of presenting the humanity of everyone involved, thanks to smart writing from Bafta winner Danny Brocklehurst and a stellar ensemble cast. (Mercifully, the former has eschewed the “jump the shark” style of his many Harlan Coben adaptations here in favour of a more naturalistic style.)

Neither Tom nor Beth are in loveless marriages, per se, just ones that have hit their own respective tricky patches; neither his wife, Hannah (Shelley Conn), nor her husband, Neil (Matthew McNulty), are cartoon villains, cardboard cut-out collateral damage or blameless saints, but rather complex, flawed, living, breathing human beings.

It makes the pathos feel all the more real as the drama unfolds, holding the tension of the uncomfortable truth that cheating doesn’t automatically make someone a monster without shying away from its potentially devastating consequences.

“We’re all one moment away from our lives disintegrating,” says Hannah to her therapist at one point, in what could either be viewed as a self-fulfilling prophecy, given the extreme anxiety and intrusive thoughts that have strained her marriage in recent years, or a burst of pure prescience.

Like with all tales of forbidden love, it seems inevitable that Tom and Beth will, at some point, get found out. The only question is when and how the wheels will come off. But safe to say, attraction, plus an obstacle, is unlikely to equal happily ever after...

#661. Your guide to L.A. City Charter Amendment SC: Board of education campaign finance rules

See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred

Los Angeles voters are being asked to change the city charter in several ways this November. Among them is Charter Amendment SC, which deals with campaign finance rules for the Los Angeles Unified School District Board of Education.

Eligible voters are those who reside in the city of Los Angeles, as well as voters who live outside the city but within LAUSD districts.

California’s general election takes place on Novemer 3. Learn about L.A.’s city and county races as well races for state office.

The amendment aims to clarify campaign finance rules for candidates running for a seat on the board of education, which overseas LAUSD and its approximately 350,000 students.

Repetitive language in the Los Angeles City Charter would be deleted and would make clear the same campaign finance rules apply to both mayoral candidates and board of education candidates, except in certain instances, the measure says.

Among those requirements are rules governing campaign contribution limits, filing deadlines, public disclosures and fundraising windows.

Diego Andrades, a former member of the city’s Charter Reform Commission, said Amendment SC won’t substantially change any requirements for board of education candidates. Rather, he said by deleting duplicated language in the charter, the rules will be easier to understand.

It also will better ensure LAUSD board candidates and mayoral candidates continue to be held to the same campaign finance rules in the future, Andrades said.

There was no argument submitted in opposition to the amendment.

#663. The fallout from Trump's Russia energy moves

President Trump's moves to avoid new penalties on Russian energy sent shockwaves through Washington, sparking diplomatic tensions and political turmoil.

Why it matters: Trump's push to lower energy prices ahead of the midterms could provide Russia an economic lifeline and is exposing divisions within his own party.

  • Oil, gas and petroleum product exports help finance Russia's war on Ukraine.

Catch up quick: Late Friday, Trump waived new sanctions against Russia and tariffs on top buyers of Russian energy that would have taken effect under the bipartisan Graham Act he signed last month.

  • That came just days after the administration waived certain sanctions as part of a deal aimed at enabling higher exports of Russian diesel after high prices have become a political millstone for Republicans.

Here's what's on our radar:

A new rationale. Energy Secretary Chris Wright, in CNN and ABC appearances yesterday, called the diesel deal a "carrot" to get Russia to ease its assault on Ukraine.

  • It's an "incentive to Russia, that if they can reduce the conflict with Ukraine, they can get an energy ceasefire or reduce the conflict such that they have diesel to export, we'll allow it to flow to world markets," Wright told ABC's "This Week."
  • Ukrainian drone strikes have lowered Russia's refining capacity. Trump, in a Truth Social post yesterday, also cast his recent decisions as a way to get a peace deal with Russia.

A new clock. Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters Saturday that Trump wants to take 60 days to review implementing the Graham Act in order to gauge its impact on the global and U.S. economies.

A deteriorating relationship. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has sharply and publicly criticized both the diesel deal and Trump's decision to waive, for now, the Graham Act penalties.

  • Trump's post, meanwhile, bashed Zelensky for hitting Russian refineries, "knowing that these attacks are seriously hurting the world diesel markets, including those in the United States."

Republican rifts. Many GOP lawmakers and candidates, to varying degrees, have joined Democrats in criticizing Trump's Friday night sanctions waivers and the diesel deal days earlier.

  • Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.) told the AP that she disagrees with Trump's decision not to implement, for now, the bipartisan law named after her late brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.).
  • She's running for a full term after being appointed to replace her brother. Former Rep. Mike Rogers — the GOP candidate in Michigan's tight Senate race — also expressed concern with the decision but avoided directly criticizing Trump on CNN yesterday.
  • Other Republicans were far harsher, including retiring Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.), who called Friday night's move "beyond irresponsible."

Lame duck rumblings. "A growing chorus of House Republicans is warning President Trump that they're ready to block additional Pentagon funding unless the administration gets tougher on Russia," The Hill reports.

What we're watching: With the midterms just weeks away, more Republicans are openly breaking with Trump.

#664. Myanmar’s Aung San Suu Kyi ‘sounds strong’ but is isolated, son says

Kim Aris tells the Guardian chance to speak with detained Nobel laureate was ‘public relations’ move from military leaders

Myanmar’s former democratic leader Aung San Suu Kyi appears to be in good physical and mental health but is living in near-complete isolation, her son has said after the first call with his 81-year-old mother in more than five years.

“She still sounds certainly all there mentally, and physically she sounds strong,” Kim Aris said. “I don’t think she has anybody outside of the military or the police around her, so essentially she’s been held in solitary confinement from what I gather.”

After being deposed in a 2021 military coup, the Nobel Peace prize laureate has been moved to an unspecified location in the capital. “I’m still not entirely sure where she is,” said Aris. “I think it’s a residence in Naypyidaw, which is fenced off and it has a scrubby bit of land around it.”

Aris, who has lived in the UK most of his life and whose late father was a British historian, was allowed to speak to his mother on Thursday at the Myanmar embassy in London. While he welcomed the chance to talk, he said the invitation was part of a “public relations” campaign by the country’s military leaders.

The former junta chief Min Aung Hlaing has sought to rebuild international diplomatic ties, and in April switched his military fatigues for civilian clothes after elections that were widely condemned as a sham.

Activists have long demanded “proof of life” for Aung San Suu Kyi, as well as scores of other political prisoners. In August, she was finally photographed during a Red Cross visit. Last week, a government spokesperson published images of her smiling in a wood-panelled room as officials delivered two gardening books given to her as gifts by Britain’s King Charles. A paper calendar on the wall behind her showed the date.

Aris said these photo-ops were well-known stunts that the regime had used before to pretend his mother, a national icon, was being treated fairly. The daughter of the assassinated national independence hero Gen Aung San has spent much of her life since the late 1980s in and out of house arrest for leading pro-democracy movements.

“She remains completely shut off from the rest of the world. I think she’s unaware of what’s happening outside of where she is because she’s not allowed any newspapers or radio or television,” Aris said. “She’s been locked up for five years on trumped-up, politically motivated charges and she should be free.”

Ruled for decades by generals and suffering from western sanctions, Myanmar experienced a brief democratic moment after Aung San Suu Kyi was allowed to run in a 2015 election that her party overwhelmingly won. She took up the role of “state counsellor” under a civilian-military power-sharing agreement.

Her international reputation was soon tarnished after the 2016-2017 mass killings and expulsions of Rohingya Muslims. Aung San Suu Kyi flew to the international court of justice in The Hague, where she said she acknowledged military units might have used “disproportionate force”, but defended the government against accusations of genocide.

Aris said that his mother was never “silent” on the Rohingya crisis and what she said on the issue “could fill volumes”. Under her leadership, Myanmar launched a domestic inquiry and appointed the former UN chief Kofi Annan to head a commission.

He added that as state counsellor, Aung San Suu Kyi was “always walking on a tightrope”, knowing the military could strip her of her fragile power at any moment.

“The very hard-won nascent democracy that she was trying to lead was holding on to things by a thread,” he said. “The military could have taken over at any point, and they were doing their best to make my mother’s situation a lot more difficult and to undermine her position. And I think in that respect they did a pretty good job.”

The 2021 power grab by the military triggered a civil war that has killed more than 100,000 people, according to conflict monitors.

Aris said the level of public global support for his mother had “dwindled incredibly” since the Rohingya crisis and that the whole country was now suffering from a lack of international attention. While many governments have called for Aung San Suu Kyi’s release, she is not treated as the beloved international figure that she once was.

“Never mind my mother, the fact that people ignore what’s happening in Burma shouldn’t be down to what was being done to the Rohingya,” he said, using the country’s former name. “And that seems to be the case sometimes, that people say: ‘Oh, well, look how the Rohingya were treated. We can ignore what’s happening in Burma.’”

Russia has been selling off gold throughout this year. September brought a further reduction in its reserves of the precious metal of around 6.2 tonnes, bringing the total reduction since January to about 62 tonnes.

Only once in its modern history has Russia disposed of gold at a similarly rapid pace, when in 1998 it sold 118 tonnes from its reserves in just three months.

According to Adam Stroniawski, managing director of Polish precious metals dealer Mennica Skarbowa, "Russia has a serious budget shortfall because of its war in Ukraine and wants to inject more funds into the defence sector". He tells Euronews that Russia is selling gold outside the London bullion market, saying that "the sell-off of reserves will take place in Hong Kong, and the main buyer is China's central bank".

Stroniawski concludes that the impact of these transactions on the global gold price would therefore be negligible.

According to Hong Kong trade data, from January to July around 100 tonnes of Russian gold reached Hong Kong – nearly three times as much as in the same period last year.

The expert does not rule out Russia returning to the group of countries buying gold and rebuilding its reserves, just as it did after its 1998 sell-off.

A few days before the Russian central bank published its data, investors learned that Kazakhstan also plans to sell part of its gold reserves.

The country, which straddles two continents, was among the world's biggest buyers of gold in the first eight months of 2026. It has now announced that by the end of the year it intends to reduce its gold holdings so that gold accounts for 75% of its total reserves.

"The liquidation of part of Kazakhstan's gold-denominated foreign reserves may seem surprising, because for years the country was one of the biggest buyers of bullion," says Stroniawski.

He says the shift may be temporary, driven by the need to plug a budget deficit or take profits.

"Kazakhstan has been buying gold for a long time, so it will now be selling at a significant profit," he adds.

The expert stresses that both the scale of the planned reduction – from around 78% to 75% of total reserves – and the spreading of sales over time mean that these transactions, too, will not have a major impact on global gold markets.

The change in approach by Russia and Kazakhstan raises questions about whether this is the beginning of a new trend among central banks, and whether Poland might follow in their footsteps. In recent years Poland has significantly increased its gold reserves and could take profits while gold prices remain high. In Stroniawski's view, however, this scenario is highly unlikely.

"This stems from internal factors, with government policy and central bank policy moving in different directions. In this parliamentary term it is unlikely that reserves will be liquidated," says Stroniawski.

Indeed, the National Bank of Poland has been actively buying gold for several years, and Poland's current reserves are already close to the target of 700 tonnes. According to the expert, this does not have to mean the end of gold purchases by the central bank. He says large gold reserves improve the country's credit standing and help to stabilise the currency.

"At present, with its level of gold reserves, Poland ranks 10th in the world. In my opinion, reaching 700 tonnes will only be one stage. It does not mean the end of purchases or the start of a sell-off," says Stroniawski.

"At the moment, many investors who bought gold a few years ago may be thinking about taking profits," the expert says. He adds that the precious metal saw significant price increases in recent years, although its price has weakened in 2026.

Gold prices rose 25.5% in 2024 and 67.4% in 2025 in US dollar terms, according to the World Gold Council. However, they fell 4.4% in the first nine months of 2026.

Stroniawski sees temporary corrections in the price of gold as not affecting its long-term upward trend. He believes buying by central banks and investors who treat gold as a safe haven and a reserve asset will support further price rises.

"When it comes to gold, I wouldn't assume it will ever be cheaper. However, buying it delivers reliable profits only over the long term," Stroniawski emphasises.

#666. Can Germany revive its economy before the AfD gains ground?

Conflicts, rising costs and Chinese competition are testing Germany's economic model like never before. Can new growth sectors create jobs and ease voters' economic fears, thereby helping contain the far-right AfD?

Germany's export-led economic model faces unprecedented strain just as support for the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party reaches a new peak.

Chinese rivals are steadily eroding the market share of major German industrial players, while persistently high energy prices, elevated labor costs and excessive red tape are adding to the structural crisis.

After two years of contraction, real GDP edged up only 0.2% last year, according to the Federal Statistical Office, Destatis. Exports to China fell 9.7% in 2025, withGerman vehicle and part shipments plunging by a third.

While there are signs the German economy is turning the corner, the government's latest forecast of 1.3% growth in 2026 is still modest compared with the pre-COVID boom years.

The AfD is currently polling ahead of all other political parties in Germany. The country's many economic challenges have been a major factor in the right-wing populists' rise.

Germany's domestic intelligence agency sees reliable indications that the AfD is right-wing extremist in its entirety.

The party has vowed to put Germany back on a growth path by ending the transition to renewable energies, lowering taxes and renegotiating European Union treaties, while also reforming welfare and sharply restricting immigration.

As Chancellor Friedrich Merz's coalition searches for a fresh growth strategy to fend off the rise in populist politics, the government has set out its high-tech agenda focusing on six priority sectors.

These are artificial intelligence (AI), quantum computing, microelectronics, biotechnology, clean energy (including nuclear fusion) and climate-neutral mobility.

Irene Bertschek, head of the Digital Economy research unit at the Leibniz Center for European Economic Research (ZEW), argues that Germany's research in these "key enabling technologies is very strong, particularly in the area of climate-neutral technologies."

Yet, the results are often commercialized abroad, Bertschek told DW, with the United States leading in AI and China closing the gap quickly.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

A report published Monday by the Made for Germany initiative — a group of 147 companies and investors — builds on the government's plan, estimating that these and other new technologies could attract up to €4.1 trillion ($4.6 trillion) in investment by 2035.

Realizing that potential, however, will depend less on today's industrial giants, like Volkswagen, Siemens and BASF.

"It will not primarily be the established companies that conquer these new fields, but innovative newcomers — startups," Oliver Falck, director of the ifo Center for the Economics of Innovation and Digital Transformation, told DW.

The task, Falck said, is to create the right conditions for startups to emerge, including proximity to top universities, access to private capital and enough freedom to experiment.

He argues for state financing during the early-stage "valley of death" — the risky phase between research and commercial viability when private financing is often scarce.

There are clear signs this shift is already happening. Data from Deutsche Bank and startupdetector, a German startup database and market intelligence platform, show more than 3,000 startups were founded in Germany in the first half of 2026, up 88% from the same period last year. One-third of the new ventures have an AI focus.

Venture-capital investment soared 44% to €5.8 billion in the first half of 2026, with firms such as Neura Robotics and drone manufacturers Stark and Quantum Systems benefiting.

US investors, meanwhile, are increasingly buying up Germany's famed Mittelstand — its traditional small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) — with an eye on their specialized technology.

"The German Mittelstand is highly innovative. Now it is essential to invest in key technologies such as artificial intelligence and to tap into the potential that arises at the intersection with established technologies," Bertschek stressed.

The expert, who is also chair of the German government's Commission of Experts for Research and Innovation (EFI), thinks SMEs should make better use of their huge amounts of production data and collaborate with AI startups to help those young firms grow.

Another idea for accelerating the shift to new high-tech sectors comes from Sven Gabor Janszky, chairman of the Leipzig-based futures-research institute 2b AHEAD. He argues that Germany needs special economic zones to help catch the next wave of economic growth.

"For a few specific technologies, you lower the regulations, you recruit ambitious workers and pump money into these zones," Janszky told DW.

This, he added, would follow the examples of Silicon Valley and Chinese mega-cities Shenzhen and Shanghai's Pudong district, and echoes the conditions that helped rebuild the German economy after World War II.

In Janszky's view, these zones would help Germany position itself as a first mover in emerging fields rather than remaining tied to older industrial strengths.

"EU regulations may try to prohibit this move, but Germany will have to overcome them so we can grow the economy again," he added.

The sharp rise in Germany's defense spending will also help several of the high-tech sectors now being prioritized.

According to the International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS), the defense budget is expected to reach around €120 billion in 2026 — roughly 2.6% of GDP. The government wants this figure to hit 3.5% by 2029.

The resulting procurement will provide a major boost to the production of drones, sensors, communications systems and other dual-use technologies that have both civilian and military applications.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Yet, with major rival China benefiting from much lower energy and worker costs, along with huge government subsidies, Germany will continue to face similar price disadvantages when exporting its new high-end tech. But that doesn't have to spell failure, said Falck, the ifo expert.

"Take the semiconductor industry as an example. It is probably unrealistic to aim for leadership along the entire value chain. But it is enough to lead at individual choke points," he pointed out.

"And that is exactly where Germany is strong: as a supplier of equipment for state-of-the-art chip fabs and as a supplier to the world's AI gigafactories, with power semiconductors."

In other words, with a first-mover advantage, decades of high-quality production data and a focus on specialized niches, Germany can remain a major force in advanced industrial and engineering technologies.

#670. ‘Why would I leave?’: Middlesbrough pushes back against ‘hardest place to grow up’ label

Teesside town has come out worst in children’s commissioner’s report, but residents say such rankings are demoralising and counterproductive

“It’s disappointing, it’s just another kicking,” said a youth worker after the town in which they work was labelled as the hardest place in which to be a child in England.

“It suggests our children are living unhappy lives,” said a teacher, who described her pupils as joyful.

A clearly riled Chris Cooke, the mayor of Middlesbrough, said: “We get told a lot by people outside this place what we are. We know what we are. There is another side.”

They were all reacting to a report published this week by the children’s commissioner, Rachel de Souza, titled The Childhood Lottery, in which she declared childhood to be in “a state of emergency”.

The report drew on a “landmark dataset” that “brings together 162 measures of children’s lives to build a comprehensive picture of the areas in England where it is the hardest to grow up”. The metrics included everything from child poverty to exclusion rates to poor air quality. And at the bottom was Middlesbrough.

The Guardian visited the town this week and spoke to children and professionals about growing up there. No one denied there were many challenges, but equally no one thought the label was helpful.

At a busy, buzzy youth club in the residential suburb of Coulby Newham, children aged 10 and up were making papier-mache Halloween decorations, cooking, playing table tennis and, outside on a strikingly mild October evening, getting ready to play dodge ball. “You’d think they were playing professionally,” said one volunteer.

Hannah*, 15, said her life was good but she knew it was not the same for others. “I love living in Middlesbrough. I love Albert Park and the Dorman Museum. I love going to the football. I love coming to youth club and making friends,” she said.

A boy looked confused when asked if it was hard being a child in Middlesbrough. “I’m going to be here the rest of my life,” he said. “Why would I leave?”

His friend let the side down by declaring: “I’m going to a hot country when I’m older … Hawaii. Or Zanzibar. Middlesbrough is too cold and scruffy.”

Wayne Mason, a former soldier who is chief executive of Linx Youth Project, which runs the club, said of the report: “We are disappointed. What it’s doing is attaching yet another label to Middlesbrough and its young people, and we already have many, many labels. It’s disappointing … all this negativity attached to the town.”

He and the project’s deputy, Eilís Sexton, were at the club but could not stay long as the local Rotary club was about to give them a much-needed and much-appreciated cheque.

Sexton was worried about the message the report sent out. “I’ve been thinking about young people who want to start their own families and how it’s going to make them feel, knowing that their child is going to have the ‘most difficult upbringing’ in the country? It is quite demoralising for them,” she said.

She was born and raised in the area and studied at Teesside University. “I did move out of Middlesbrough for six months and I hated it,” she said.

Neither of them disputed the statistics but they said there was another side. “Pride is the overriding thing that we see with the young people,” Mason said. “We know youngsters living in some of the most deprived areas of Middlesbrough, of which there are many, who don’t want to leave. They don’t want to leave because this is their home.

“We always talk about deprivation and poverty and crime, but we don’t talk about community.”

The report comes weeks after a collision on the A66 in which a car with five young people inside crashed into a police car carrying two police constables, killing the occupants of both vehicles.

Some subsequent media portrayals painted a picture of an urban dystopia where gangs were in charge, but residents said the reality was different.

It would have been hard for children to avoid media coverage about the deaths. Hannah said she had been past where it happened and burst into tears.

Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters

In Middlesbrough town centre there is a huge open square and the contemporary art gallery Mima, currently hosting the Turner prize. Next door is the town’s oppressive 1970s-built magistrates court building. Opposite is the grand Victorian town hall where Cooke, the elected Labour mayor, has his office.

When it comes to the subject of it being hard to grow up in Middlesbrough, Cooke is better equipped than most to talk about it. He grew up in a violent family. His father took his own life when he was a teenager, and his mother’s mental health spiralled. He said that as a young boy he felt he had to be in charge of everything because he was terrified of being separated from his sister.

Cooke had periods of not going to school and ended up in care. “I bounced around the system. People struggled to take me because I was quite difficult. I think that’s the polite version. What wouldn’t have helped me during any of that time is someone telling me that my life was difficult or that my life would get harder or that this place wouldn’t let me achieve the things I wanted to.”

He said he remembered applying for jobs as an apprentice and being told not to include his TS6 postcode for fear of being judged. He not only included it, he made it bigger, he said. “This is why I’m angry. I don’t need people characterising Middlesbrough when we already know the challenges.”

The fact that Cooke came out the other side was, he said, because of “beautiful” foster carers and other people around him. Middlesbrough is one of 16 councils in England that spend more than 80% of their core funding on social care. Cooke said he was passionate about spending on youth services, reeling off a list of initiatives that included a fund to ensure there were youth clubs in every Middlesbrough postcode.

A 15-minute walk from the town hall is Newport primary school, where the headteacher, Patricia Maxwell, showed the Guardian around. It has a particularly well-stocked, well-used library – Middlesbrough’s reading for pleasure stats are way over the national average.

Maxwell had read the commissioner’s report. “It wasn’t telling me anything anything I didn’t already know,” she said. “But also it wasn’t telling people about all the positives that our children grow up with in Middlesbrough.”

Stacey Carlisle, the school’s deputy head, agreed. “It just suggests that those children are living really quite unhappy lives, and that is not the case for our children,” she said. “They’re joyous and joyful, our children. Yes, there might be challenges at home for some, but it’s the same in affluent areas as well.”

Both teachers said they would not want to work anywhere but Middlesbrough. “We’d like to do more,” Maxwell said. “We want our children to reach their full potential and to thrive and flourish and become the doctors or whatever it is that they want to be in the future.

“But what we don’t want is them to feel labelled and told that they can’t go on and achieve those things. Just because you’re living in a challenging environment does not mean that that defines you.”

By ELEANOR HARDING and CAROLINE GRAHAM, US EDITOR THE MAIL ON SUNDAY and GETHIN HICKS, REPORTER

#672. India slashes cost of cancer drugs after court rules mark-ups are ‘extortion’

Case filed in 2022 by patient unable to afford medicine leads to cap on drug prices for millions who face ruin if diagnosed

The Indian government has moved to reduce the price of cancer drugs after a retired bank clerk took her case to the supreme court.

From next month, 137 cancer drugs in India will be cheaper as the government tries to tackle the tragedy of poorer patients either forgoing treatment, selling land or falling into debt to meet the high cost of some medicines, which are making large profits for hospitals and pharmacists.

Sarojam Radhakrishnan, a former bank employee in Kerala, was diagnosed with breast cancer in 2021. Doctors prescribed life-saving targeted treatments but the monthly cost, of more than 63,000 rupees (£500), was far beyond her family’s means.

Realising that thousands of families were being ruined by the cost of such drugs, Radhakrishnan filed a petition to the Kerala high court in 2022 demanding government intervention to lower the costs.

When the case reached the supreme court, the judges looked at hospitals’ and retailers’ mark-ups on cancer drugs and called the situation “carnage” and “extortion”.

During a hearing on 29 September, justices Vikram Nath and Sandeep Mehta noted how a life-saving cancer drug supplied to hospitals at 2,700 rupees carried a vastly marked-up price of 27,000 rupees.

The judges found that hospitals, distributors and chemists enjoyed large margins on medicines. Analysis by the National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority revealed a trade mark-up on some cancer drugs averaging 170%, with some extreme examples stretching to more than 700%.

A 30% trade margin cap on the price of 42 drugs has been in place for some years but many others remained off this list. Now, prodded by the supreme court’s findings, the government has imposed the cap on 137 other drugs.

“The measure is expected to reduce medicine prices by up to 70% and help cancer patients save 2,500 crore rupees [£199m] annually, significantly reducing the amount they pay from their own pockets,” a statement from the Department of Pharmaceuticals said.

People on low incomes in India dread illness, as the cost of treatment can mean financial ruin, particularly for cancer patients.

Whenever the Indian Cancer Society holds a free diagnosis camp in Gurgaon where he lives, Krishan Kalra urges local drivers, maids, cooks and tailors to turn up because tests they cannot afford are offered free.

As a former member of the council of the Rajiv Gandhi Cancer Institute and Research Centre, Kalra knows the importance of early diagnosis, but he said very few people attended. “When I ask why, they say they’re too scared – if something serious like cancer is detected, they haven’t got the money to pay for the treatment so they prefer to remain in the dark,” he said.

With the cost of cancer drugs ranging in price from 38,000 to 380,000 rupees, many families quietly walk out of the doctor’s consulting room upon hearing the estimated cost of treatment.

Studies by the Public Health Foundation of India show that spending on healthcare pushes about 55 million Indians a year below the poverty line.

Few Indians can afford the premiums for comprehensive health insurance. The government’s nationwide insurance scheme, Ayushman Bharat, covers treatment for some cancers but it provides only 500,000 rupees’ worth of annual cover for a family – the cost of just one dose of Kadcyla (ado-trastuzumab emtansine), a drug used to treat breast cancer. Patients may need up to 14 doses.

Dr Ravi Kannan is a surgical oncologist and director of Cachar cancer hospital and research centre in Silchar, Assam. He has worked in hospitals elsewhere in India and is familiar with doctors’ trauma of seeing patients walk out to go home and die.

“Some families start the treatment, hoping against hope to manage the cost. They start but they don’t come back for chemotherapy or radiation. They can’t sustain the cost,” he said. “The decision is a welcome step if the outcome is that more patients can access the drugs they need.”

India records about 1.56m new cancer cases annually – up from 1.39m cases in 2020 – making it a significant public health challenge.

As the supreme court delves deeper into the subject, what was clear, said Jyotsna Singh, co-convener of the Working Group on Access to Medicines and Treatments, a civil society network, was that a “total overhaul” of the healthcare system was needed.

“Right from the cost of manufacturing a drug to the point of sale, we need to make the system transparent and regulate the entire supply chain. Only then will these drugs become available to those who need them,” she said.

Singh said companies and hospitals were likely to try to find legal loopholes to wriggle out of the 30% cap, suggesting that hospitals may offset the lower price charged for a drug by raising charges on other items.

The supreme court judges have also asked the government’s lawyers why the cap should apply only to cancer drugs and not the entire range of non-patented drugs. The court has given the government until 27 October to respond.

Unfortunately, the court’s ruling came too late for Radhakrishnan, who died in September 2022 while her case was still pending in Kerala.

#673. Your guide to the L.A. County sheriff's race: A rematch between Luna and Villanueva

See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred

Four years ago, the race for Los Angeles County sheriff was one of the most closely watched local elections. Challenger Robert Luna ultimately beat the combative sitting sheriff, Alex Villanueva, by more than 20 percentage points.

Now, in a bit of political deja vu, the two lawmen are facing off again for the job of leading the largest sheriff’s department in the country.

This cycle, the race has drawn a lot less attention. But it again presents voters with a decision between two experienced leaders with distinct visions for how best to improve the sheriff’s department and keep Angelenos safe.

California’s general election takes place on Novemer 3. Learn about L.A.’s city and county races as well races for state office.

Former Long Beach Police chief Robert Luna came out of retirement to run for sheriff in 2022, promising to turn around a department that had veered off course.

As someone who didn’t have the wide name recognition or countywide political experience of some of his challengers, Luna’s second-place finish to Villanueva in the primary was far from guaranteed, but he ultimately cleared the rest of the field by a wide margin.

Fast-forward four years to June, and Luna received 44.2% of the vote in this primary — less than six points short of winning the race outright — versus Villanueva’s 21.7%. And Luna’s been a more effective fundraiser, bringing in $366,000 since Jan. 1, more than three times the nearly $109,000 Villanueva had raised by June 30, according to their most recent campaign filings. Luna had $352,000 in the war chest as of June 30, and Villanueva had about $56,000.

But Villanueva has wide name recognition in L.A. County. And he pulled off a historic political upset of his own in 2018 when he beat Sheriff Jim McDonnell, who is now the Los Angeles police chief. It was the first time an incumbent L.A. County sheriff lost a reelection campaign in more than a century. It was also the first time in 100 years that a Democrat had been elected to the nonpartisan sheriff’s job.

After running on a progressive platform and pitching himself as a criminal justice reformer, Villanueva tacked hard to the right. Within two years he was a favorite of conservative media, including Fox News, where he appeared repeatedly to vilify “woke” culture and criticize Democrats. He ultimately switched his party registration to Republican in a move that solidified a new base of law-and-order supporters while alienating many who supported him in 2018.

Villanueva’s tenure was marked by controversy and scandal. He launched, then walked back a criminal leak investigation of a Los Angeles Times reporter and was ordered to testify after sheriff’s deputies took and shared pictures at the site of Kobe Bryant’s helicopter crash. Villanueva defied subpoenas over so-called deputy gangs.

Now, Luna is the one defending his record as sheriff over the last four years. He’s presided over declines in homicides and violent crime and established a period of relative calm after the stormy Villanueva years. But Luna’s department has come under scrutiny in the wake of a July 2025 incident in which a grenade exploded accidentally in a department parking lot, killing three deputies. The state has fined the department more than $350,000 after identifying a series of safety violations leading up to the blast.

And the Civilian Oversight Commission filed suit against the department in June for declining to provide certain records related to three cases of use of force the commission issued subpoenas for in February 2025. Luna has said the county’s attorneys maintain that the unredacted records can’t be released until it completes a “meet and confer” process with the Sheriff’s Department union, a claim that watchdogs have disputed.

Fundraising data will be updated regularly until the election.

The Sheriff’s Department provides law enforcement services to all unincorporated areas in Los Angeles County. It also has contracts with 42 of the county’s 88 municipalities, including Malibu, West Hollywood and Santa Clarita.

Villanueva asserts that recruitment and retention have suffered under Luna. The former sheriff said he keeps up with the department he once ran, and that deputies frequently complain to him about understaffing and low morale.

“They’re being asked to do too much and there’s no support at all,” Villanueva said. “The fact is there are just no people left, there are no deputies left to respond to emergent situations.”

Villanueva added that the number of unfilled sworn positions at the department has risen since he was sheriff. County and Sheriff’s Department records confirm that while sworn vacancies more than doubled during Villanueva’s term from about 477 in December 2018 to 1,069 by Nov. 9, 2022, Luna has presided over a further increase in sworn vacancies to 1,452 three years later.

Luna disputed Villanueva’s claims that there aren’t enough deputies to maintain an effective department. “He’s factually incorrect,” the sheriff said. “He’s just pulling numbers out of thin air.”

The department has reported that the number of new deputies who graduated in academy classes rose by nearly a third between 2024 and 2025, to more than 400 last year. Data also show that retention rates have risen under Luna after falling precipitously toward the end of Villanueva’s tenure.

“We’re doing so much better, and remember, I inherited a lot of the challenges with staffing from my predecessor,” Luna said, “because of his horrible, fractured relationships.”

Luna points out that violent crime has fallen every year since he took office. Between 2023, his first full year in office, and 2025, homicides fell by more than 25%. That’s one reason why he says voters should send him back to the Hall of Justice for another four years.

“I definitely want to continue the progress that’s been made in crime reduction,” he said. “What I’m also excited about is at the same time I’ve been reducing crime, I’ve been reducing uses of force. We’ve been reducing deputy-involved shootings.”

Department statistics confirm those assertions and also show that last year, property crimes were broadly down from 2022.

Villanueva said he and many of the deputies he talks to feel that crime has run rampant since he left office. Contributing to that assessment, he claimed, is a perceived inability or unwillingness to effectively fight certain types of crime. Deputies have told him some sheriff’s stations don’t have the resources or people they need, he said.

“It’s popping up right now every day. We have the street takeovers, we have the looting that’s going down left and right,” Villanueva said, adding that as sheriff, he’d restore order and be “focused on making sure the community stays safe.”

With millions of people expected to travel to Southern California for the 2028 Summer Olympics, whoever is voted in as sheriff in November will spend many hours working with the Los Angeles Police Department and other law enforcement agencies to prepare for the Games and ensure fans and athletes are safe.

Villanueva said he’s concerned that the “combination of incompetence and ideology” that he believes Luna has brought to the Sheriff’s Department leave him ill-prepared to handle the next four years.

“We’re under the deadline of getting ready for the Olympics, and there’s no way that Luna is going to be in position to assist with the Olympics,” Villanueva said.

Luna rebutted the claim by highlighting the key role his department played in the multiagency law enforcement effort to keep people safe at the World Cup this year.

“We had a very successful World Cup,” Luna said. “That builds a foundation for all the events coming up, including the Super Bowl, the 2028 Olympics and Paralympics, as we have been continuously preparing for that.”

#675. Bob Woodward reveals "dream source" in memoir, "Secrets," out next month

Bob Woodward — in an eye-opening excerpt from his forthcoming memoir, "Secrets," that's previewed in the new issue of The New Yorker — reveals that one of his best friends, the late Richard Darman, was also one of his best sources during the Ronald Reagan and George H.W. Bush administrations.

  • "Darman was willing, even eager at times, to talk about the most sensitive intelligence matters, including N.S.A. intercepts and covert C.I.A. operations," Woodward writes in his book, out Nov. 15. "He was always careful not to talk about matters that would harm national security, I believed, but he would go right up to the edge — a reporter's dream source."

Why it matters: Woodward, 83 — who followed the blockbuster Watergate reporting of his youth with a shelf of revelatory books about American presidents — gives a searingly honest account of the collapse of his friendship with Darman after a Post series that was damaging to Bush. Woodward details a disappointment in his Washington Post career and, in the case of a story where he was the responsible editor, a "moral failing."

  • The New Yorker calls the Darman excerpt "A Dangerous Friendship," revealing the danger of "getting too close to a source." Woodward and Darman never reconciled, although "Secrets" describes their deathbed encounter.

Woodward writes in his New Yorker debut that he and Darman, who controlled the paper flow to Reagan as staff secretary and was budget director for Bush 41, "had countless long lunches together — Saturday or Sunday — at the Madison Hotel, across the street from the Post, discussing government, journalism, and ourselves":

"I felt like I was getting a master class in how government really operated. Plus, many scoops. In later years, Darman would drive out on weekends to our country house near Annapolis, Maryland, to spend large parts of the day with me and my wife, the journalist Elsa Walsh, who was particularly fond of him. Some people found him arrogant, but I loved his comfortable confidence as a friend and a source. It was part of what made him so extraordinary and valuable. He knew how to turn on the charm, and he did for both Elsa and me."

Behind the scenes: "From critical national-security information to the colorful office tales he shared, Darman provided me with a gold mine of information," Woodward recalls. "I interviewed him in at least fifty-eight meetings or phone conversations. I have boxes filled with hundreds of pages of notes on our discussions. After our most important conversations, as is my practice, I typed a memo of one to six pages, laying out in detail what he'd said."

  • Detailing Darman's "hatchet man" role, Woodward reveals that the "hardest of Darman's targets to dislodge was the First Lady, Nancy Reagan. While Darman poured scorn on her in private, describing her to me as a 'mean bitch,' he could not find a way to drive a stake into her heart."

After a hard-won legislative victory, Darman told Woodward, Reagan said: "Whew! Ever feel like you shit a pineapple?"

#676. Bulgaria: Concerns about security in the Black Sea dominate presidential election campaign

Bulgaria's presidential election campaign has been shaped by recent drone attacks on ships in the Black Sea and the government's reduced support for Ukraine, making foreign policy a key factor in the first round.

Six months after Bulgaria's parliamentary election, the country is gearing up to choose its next president.

Although the role of president in Bulgaria is largely ceremonial, the election on October 25 — with a potential runoff on November 1 — will serve as a test for the government of former President Rumen Radev, whose party won a landslide victory in April, securing an unprecedented majority — the first in Bulgaria in almost three decades.

Although there are 27 candidates on the ballot, the race has narrowed to a duel between the incumbent president, Iliana Yotova, who served two terms as Radev's vice president and is backed by the prime minister, and former caretaker Prime Minister Andrey Gyurov, who is supported by opposition parties.

According to the Bulgarian Constitution, the Bulgarian president embodies national unity. He or she represents the country at international level (with a few exceptions), is the commander-in-chief of its armed forces, appoints members of the Supreme Judicial Council and various regulatory bodies, including caretaker governments, and has the power to veto legislation.

Hristo Panchugov, a political scientist at the New Bulgarian University in Sofia, argued that although the president's powers are formally limited, the office is particularly significant in the current context.

"For the first time in Bulgaria's modern democratic history, we have an absolutely uncontested majority that is not held together by any coalition, but rather by a single political party that faces an opposition that is completely falling apart," he told DW.

Panchugov went on to say that it would have been better if the campaign had focused more on "whether the president could serve as a counterbalance."

Opposition candidate Andrey Gyurov reiterated this point in an interview with DW: "We are seeing a concentration of power that always bears the marks of a slide toward autocracy... A president should know how to say no."

Iliana Yotova declined DW's request for an interview.

Initially, the presidential race was characterized by small rallies, a lack of televised debates and numerous personal attacks on the two leading candidates.

In recent weeks, however, following drone attacks on ships in the Black Sea, the two frontrunners' diverging positions on support for Ukraine have come to the fore.

Bulgaria's government initially declined invitations to join the Coalition of the Willing and NATO's anti-drone initiative but changed its position on the latter after the recent drone attacks.

Yotova has advocated for the establishment of a "Coalition of Peace," in which she believes Bulgaria would have a stronger diplomatic voice in the process to endRussia's war in Ukraine.

"There are many warmongers in our country; I am not one of them," she said at a campaign rally this month. "As long as I am president — and if you place your trust in me — not a single Bulgarian soldier will go to Ukraine."

Yotova has sought to reassure voters that no Bulgarian troops will be sent to Ukraine, even though this has not featured in public debate, and has been ruled out by a 2025 parliamentary declaration that reaffirmed that the Bulgarian Armed Forces would not participate in hostilities there.

Nevertheless, the recent drone attacks on commercial ships in the Black Sea have put new pressure on both the president and Rumen Radev's Progressive Bulgaria party.

"The drone strikes in the Black Sea brought the otherwise abstract geopolitical situation right into the daily lives of every Bulgarian," Boriana Dimitrova, managing partner of the Alpha Research market and social research agency, told DW.

Many in Europe, including Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, have laid the blame for the attacks squarely at Russia's door. The fact that Bulgaria's leaders did not clearly attribute blame for the attacks fueled frustration across the country.

After the first drone attack, President Yotova convened the country's Consultative Council on National Security. Its subsequent declaration did not name the source of the threat in the Black Sea.

A week later, after the second attack, Prime Minister Radev said, "We lack solid, clear evidence to level accusations against any specific party; however logic suggests the outcome works to the advantage of Russia." He then summoned the Russian ambassador for talks.

The stance of the government and president is having an impact on the race.

"We're seeing a slight decline in support for Iliana Yotova, which is not threatening her first-place position by any means in the first round, but there has been a decline given the ambiguity of some of the positions she has taken," said Boriana Dimitrova.

As the issue of security entered the public debate, some Bulgarians took to the streets in Sofia to protest against what they saw as the government's ambiguous foreign policy stance on this matter.

"I think the drone attacks in the Black Sea and the utterly spineless stance of the president, the prime minister, and everyone acting in unison were the last straw, and I believe that, on the eve of the presidential election, this should serve as a catalyst," Vlada Tzenova, one of the protesters, told DW.

All this is reflected in the preliminary results of the latest opinion poll conducted by Alpha Research. While expected voter turnout is up, the gap between the two frontrunners has narrowed: Yotova is still ahead, leading Gyurov by about 12 percentage points in the first round, but the margin is smaller than it was.

Nevertheless, these recent dynamics do not necessarily mean a shift in the balance of power.

Panchugov said that Gyurov's campaign has been hampered by his hesitancy to declare his candidacy, a lack of "passion" in his campaign, and the fact that he made few comments on current affairs before he joined the race.

Moreover, supporters of the candidate of the pro-Russian nationalist Vazrazhdane (Revival) party, which ranked third in the Alpha Research poll, would be most likely to support Yotova in a second round.

What could decide the outcome of the election is the fact that both GERB and DPS, two of the established parties that attracted the support of more than 660,000 voters in April, did not field a presidential candidate.

According to Alpha Research, half of GERB's supporters do not intend to vote in the first round. The party dominated Bulgaria's political landscape for 17 years but lost power in December following mass anti-corruption protests backed by opposition parties supporting Andrey Gyurov.

Most of the remaining GERB supporters are expected to back Gyurov, as the party has historically opposed Iliana Yotova's political home, the Bulgarian Socialist Party.

At the same time, both Gyurov's campaign and nationalist parties are seeing increased mobilization, with the latter drawing support from voters disappointed by the government's cautious response to the drone attacks.

"We can view these elections as the first test of confidence in the party that recently won the election," Boriana Dimitrova said. "In peaceful times, the center attracts the most attention; in turbulent times, those candidates who take a clearer stance — regardless of the direction — gain greater visibility."

#678. Dogs That Weren’t Rescued

People love talking about the tragic fates from which their rescue dogs were spared. Kill shelters, international conflicts, New Jersey—pups are rescued from all kinds of precarious situations.

Yet a brief look back through dog history shows that most canines weren’t rescued. Far from it. Instead, they hurtled through life just like the rest of us—working, succumbing to temptation, and then dying atrocious deaths.

For example, Lassie was beloved, but her owners were poor, so they sold her to a finance bro. Famously, Lassie escaped and crossed hill, dale, and stream to return to poverty and the family she adored. Unfortunately, one of the waterways she forded was full of vibrio vulnificus, colloquially known as flesh-eating bacteria. Lassie died.
