#679. ‘It should never be forgotten’: families recount care home victims’ experiences in wake of Covid findings

Relatives recount distress and loneliness their loved ones went through in pandemic as a result of isolation policy

“At the time it felt like a devil’s bargain – it was horrible, but it was what [we thought] we had to do to keep people safe,” says Amy of the “devastating” and “terrifying” restrictions that led to her maternal grandparents being locked down in separate care homes during the early days of the Covid-19 pandemic.

Eva and Eric had been married for more than 60 years when her dementia and his increased frailty meant they needed separate residential support. When the first lockdown was announced in March 2020, however, it in effect cut them off from each other and their granddaughter, to whom they had been especially close after the early death of Amy’s mother.

“I spoke to Grandad on the phone when it was possible – it often wasn’t possible due to staff not being able to take him a phone – and he was desperately lonely, isolated in his room, unable to talk to anyone because they were worried about [the spread of Covid],” says Amy, 39, who lives in Milton Keynes and works for a large software company. “I consoled myself that they were keeping him safe. That all the isolation was necessary.”

Instead, she says, he was depressed and very afraid until he finally caught the virus in 2022. Amy saw him for the first time on a Covid ward, “when I had to beg and beg and beg the hospital staff to let me visit him”. Eric died shortly afterwards.

Six years after Covid struck, the latest report from the public inquiry into the pandemic, published this week, has convinced Amy that the policy of isolating residents was “cruel and pointless”, she says. “I want to smash something. I can never get that time with them back.

“The impression I had at the time was that [the government] were doing their best in the face of an unstoppable tidal wave, but it sounds like they put out a hand and expected it to stop the ocean.”

The inquiry concluded that the entire care sector had been an “afterthought” to government planners, and that a claim by the then health secretary, Matt Hancock, to have put a “protective ring” around residents was entirely unfounded. Instead, the decision to discharge untested patients from hospitals into care homes led to the virus spreading “like wildfire”, while blanket restrictions on outside contact led to “immense emotional harm” and “profound isolation” for vulnerable residents.

The findings are no surprise to the family members of care home residents, many of whom have told the Guardian of the immense distress their loved ones went through. Roger Dennison’s father, Lucius, was a sprightly 90-year-old care home resident when the first reports of the coronavirus emerged; they watched the news together in Lucius’s room and wondered how quickly it would peter out.

Weeks later, Lucius’s care home had firmly locked down, and the only way Dennison could talk to his dad was through a window that had been opened a few inches at the top. “You’re standing on tiptoe, trying to shout in and then be heard on the other side,” he says. “It was very confusing. It wasn’t very happy as an experience.” They tried it just once but stopped because it was too distressing for Lucius.

After that, Dennison, who had previously visited every other day, was reliant on passing messages through staff, while Lucius was “in his room, largely on his own”. The disease “became a growing apprehension for me once it became clear people were coming into the home and bringing it with them”, says his son. “I think there was a sense of inevitability.” Lucius caught Covid in the first wave and died in hospital in April 2020.

To care workers, too, the situation was terrifying and immensely distressing, says Nick (not his real name), who was a senior worker at a home in West Yorkshire. “The situation from the very start was frightening because we all thought that if you got Covid, you died or were going to be seriously unwell. I remember having to strip naked at the back door of my house because we had a resident return from hospital who had shared a ward with Covid patients. As a care home, we tried to refuse their return based on the risk of infection but were told [by the hospital] that we couldn’t.”

From that point, he says, “all hell broke loose”. “Our first case of Covid was about a week later.” They had already run out of personal protective equipment, he says.

“The mental health impact on all staff was huge. Watching people die at such a high rate in such a small space of time; having to say goodbye to so many people we came to know and love; putting our own health on the line every day and then quite possibly carrying that home to your family. Mentally, we were all spent.”

Like many, Catherine Bennett, a retired teacher from Lewes in East Sussex, says she was not shocked by the inquiry’s findings: “We knew what was happening. I am, however, very angry.” Her father, who had been in a care home since 2018, “felt a terrible sense of abandonment” that no one was able to visit and became paralysingly afraid of catching the virus.

“For a long time he didn’t go down for meals; he stopped doing all his activities so he wouldn’t meet anybody.” After some months, she says, the care home built a room where residents could talk to relatives through a glass panel and speakers. It was, she says, “very distressing for a man of his age to be separated from his loved ones in that way, to be able to see us through the glass but not be able to touch us or have any meaningful contact”. Her father died in the home in 2022.

Diana, a retired social worker from Derby, feels a similar lasting anger about the experience of her sister, Helen, whose mental health needs meant she was living in a care home in Carlisle when the pandemic struck, and who experienced a similar bewilderment at her sudden isolation. The first time Diana was able to sit with her was after a year of lockdown when Helen was very unwell; she died the same day.

“I just think they threw care homes under a bus while they partied in Downing Street, and I do feel rather cross about that,” says Diana. “I think it is a major trauma for this country and I think it should never be forgotten.”

The son of Myanmar’s Aung San Suu Kyi has been allowed to speak to the detained former democratic leader for the first time in more than five years.

“Today, I was finally able to speak with my mother, Daw Aung San Suu Kyi, after more than five years. Hearing her voice again means more than words can express,” Kim Aris said in a post on Facebook on Thursday.

Aung San Suu Kyi is under house arrest in the capital, Naypyidaw, according to Myanmar authorities, where she has been sequestered since being unseated in a 2021 military coup.

Images accompanying his Facebook post appeared to show Aris, who lives in the UK, standing outside the Myanmar embassy in London.

“I am deeply grateful to everyone who has stood by my mother and me. I believe your voices helped make this moment possible,” he said in the post. “But my mother is 81 and remains unjustly detained. One conversation is not regular family access.”

Myanmar’s military has held the Nobel peace prize laureate in almost total seclusion since the February 2021 coup, which ended a tentative decade-long experiment with democracy. But in recent months authorities have increasingly advertised the loosening of her detention and published photographs of her taking private meetings, as supporters have demanded “proof of life”.

On Monday, authorities said she received a package from Britain’s King Charles, including two books about soil and a “sealed diplomatic communication” from the monarch. Buckingham Palace did not comment on the contents of the communication.

Myanmar authorities said Aung San Suu Kyi was moved from a prison in Naypyidaw to house arrest in April, and in August they published images of her meeting the nation’s Red Cross representative.

After ruling Myanmar as military chief since the coup, Min Aung Hlaing was installed as civilian president this year.

Analysts described the election that put him in office as a charade, and said he could be loosening restrictions on Aung San Suu Kyi in an attempt to court international legitimacy.

#681. Your guide to L.A. County Charter Amendment A: Binding arbitration

See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred

Los Angeles County voters will be asked to approve a change that could impact how tumultuous labor negotiations for key public safety personnel are conducted — and potentially concluded.

Measure A is a charter amendment that would require binding arbitration between county government and negotiators representing sheriff’s deputies, firefighters, lifeguards and other public safety workers if contract talks reach an impasse and no compromise can be reached.

It would alter the current last step, in which county supervisors can impose a final offer that these employees must accept — by law, public safety personnel cannot strike.

California’s general election takes place on Novemer 3. Learn about L.A.’s city and county races as well races for state office.

Historically, when the time comes to execute a new contract for public-employee unions, there is an often protracted, sometimes bitter push-pull process. Labor negotiators generally seek pay increases and improved benefits. Their government counterparts often aim for a deal that protects county coffers.

Reaching the stage at which supervisors mandate terms is rare. A February Times story noted that the county said it has imposed contract terms only twice in the last quarter-century.

In addition to firefighters and sheriff’s deputies, the new system would apply to bargaining units for district attorney investigators, deputy medical examiners and county lifeguards. The new structure, as Supervisor Lindsey Horvath stated at a February board meeting, would impact 14 units representing about 16,500 employees.

L.A. County Chief Executive Joseph Nicchitta has said mandatory arbitration would amount to a “seismic change” in how the county conducts labor negotiations.

The initial phase of contract talks still would have union and county representatives seeking to hammer out a mutually beneficial deal, with a presumption that both sides would negotiate in good faith. But if a gap remains and an impasse ultimately is declared, the supervisors no longer would dictate the final offer.

Instead, a three-member arbitration panel would be formed. The county and union each would select one member, with the sides together choosing the third person, who would serve as chair. If they can’t agree on the final panelist, a state entity could provide a list of qualified arbitrators to choose from.

The arbitrators would focus on key employment elements such as wages and hours and would hold hearings and receive evidence from the parties. At the end of the process, a binding result would be issued and made public.

The measure is backed by four of the five supervisors. During the February meeting, Horvath, who authored the initial motion, said that binding arbitration would promote transparency and push the sides to reach a deal. She said that 21 California jurisdictions, including Sacramento and San Francisco counties, have implemented binding arbitration.

Supervisor Hilda Solis called this “another tool in the toolbox.”

A battery of labor unions representing county workers are on board, including the International Assn. of Firefighters Local 1014, the Assn. for Los Angeles Deputy Sheriffs and the Los Angeles County Lifeguard Assn.

Dave Gillotte, president of IAFF Local 1014, which represents more than 3,000 L.A. County Fire Department employees, said contract negotiations with the county generally are intense and lengthy. He said the goal is never having to resort to binding arbitration, but that if required, this would allow a “neutral third party” to make the final decision.

“Binding arbitration really brings about leverage to move both parties to work hard to get a contract done, where we don’t have that now,” Gillotte told the Times.

No formal opposition arguments have been submitted to the registrar-recorder/county clerk. However, during the February board meeting, Supervisor Holly Mitchell raised financial concerns about changing course.

“The board has a responsibility to fully understand the long-term consequence of permanently shifting compensation authority away from the board,” she said. Mitchell referenced a county report that detailed financial difficulties in some municipalities that utilized binding arbitration. She asked whether an arbitrator would be required to consider the county’s overall fiscal status when making a ruling.

During that meeting, Mitchell abstained from a vote to put the item on the ballot. In a follow-up March 17 meeting, she was the only vote against adopting the ballot language. Even so, Mitchell hasn’t formally come out in opposition to Measure A.

Lula da Silva has been declared the winner of the Brazilian election, in a result that will send shockwaves throughout South America.

The left-wing candidate defeated Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the eldest son of former President Jair Bolsonaro. The senator had finished first in the election's first round and hoped to revive his father's far-right movement.

At times, Lula's reelection looked like a long shot, as voters soured on him and his Workers' Party after years of corruption scandals and rising prices, while sweeping societal changes left the former metalworker and union leader looking out of touch with an increasingly app-based economy and its growing ranks of informal workers.

Lula's victory marks another comeback in a career full of them. The 80-year-old was jailed from 2018 to 2019 on corruption charges that were later overturned, paving the way for him to beat Jair Bolsonaro in the 2022 election.

"He is a statesman, a giant," leftist federal lawmaker Erika Hilton, who was with Lula in Sao Paulo during the vote count, told Reuters

Pollsters said better-than-expected turnout had powered Lula to victory. Leonardo Barreto, the co-founder of consultancy Think Policy, said voters had chosen Lula's familiar embrace over Bolsonaro's novelty.

"People today are choosing between change, with some apprehension, and a known path, which guarantees certain rights," he said.

During the campaign, Lula pointed to a track record of falling poverty and inequality, while unemployment, illiteracy and deforestation hit record lows during his third term.

He warned Bolsonaro would cut welfare spending, backslide on social advances and hand over Brazil's sovereignty to US President Donald Trump, whose State Department led a campaign to get the Bolsonaros back to power.

Lula's win deprives Trump of a major addition to what has been a growing bloc of friendly right-wing Latin American governments that have embraced Washington's agenda on security and migration.

Celso Amorim, a former Lula foreign minister, told Reuters the leftist "would be very important for establishing a point of balance in Latin America. Lula is that balance."

#683. Musk pledges 1 SpaceX share for every child in America

Elon Musk said Monday he'd give one of his shares in SpaceX to every "kid" in America next year.

Why it matters: It'd be a roughly $11 billion giveaway at current stock prices, nearly double Michael Dell's record-breaking Trump accounts gift.

What they're saying: "Next year, I will give one of my SpaceX shares to every kid in America. This will be the first of many," Musk said in a post to X just before 4 a.m. ET Monday.

  • He did not specify if "kid" meant all minors under 18 or some other status, nor did he elaborate on what "first of many" meant.
  • He also did not reply to X accounts asking if he meant all kids present in the U.S., or just citizens.

By the numbers: Per the Census Bureau, there are just over 72 million people under 18 in the U.S.

  • If each got one SpaceX share, at Friday's closing price of $146.03, that'd be a market value of a little over $10.5 billion.
  • Musk owns billions of SpaceX shares, so the giveaway would make only a small dent in his holdings.

Zoom in: Musk's pledge isn't the first from SpaceX.

  • In July the company's COO Gwynne Shotwell said she'd gift a share of the stock to each of 2 million Trump accounts, a gift now worth nearly $300 million.

Zoom out: Musk's announcement comes one day after Anthropic said it was setting up a new public benefit fund with 5% of the company's equity, an entity potentially worth $100 billion or more.

  • Musk responded to Anthropic's news by saying "I recommend giving the shares directly to the public," later adding "This is what I will be doing."

Published: 21:52 GMT, 25 October 2026 | Updated: 02:41 GMT, 26 October 2026

A Jewish documentary maker has reportedly been awarded a £400,000 payout from the BBC following allegations she was bullied out of the broadcaster and the victim of anti-Semitism.

Oscar-winning filmmaker Lucie Kon said she was mistreated by BBC colleagues who said Zionists like her were 'evil' in the wake of the October 7 Hamas terrorist attacks on Israel.

Ms Kon – who has family living in Israel – alleges she was instructed by coworkers to consider 'what drove Hamas to do what they did,' and told she should 'call Israel terrorists, too' if she wished to label Hamas as such.

She also said her colleagues told her a documentary about the Nova music festival massacre should 'contextualise' the terrorist attack, and it was 'disgusting' that former Prime Minister Rishi Sunak visited a Jewish school.

After making a formal complaint about her treatment, Ms Kon claimed the BBC asked her to stay at home for months before isolating her and eventually ousting her from the workplace.

It was then she began unfair dismissal proceedings against the broadcaster, who without any admission of liability, paid her compensation which was funded in part by the licence fee.

Oscar-winning filmmaker Lucie Kon has been awarded a £400,000 payout from the BBC following allegations she was bullied out of the broadcaster and the victim of anti-Semitism

Ms Kon claimed she was mistreated by BBC colleagues who said Zionists like her were 'evil'. Mc Kon (left) is pictured in February at the BAFTA Film Awards

The broadcaster has not issued a formal apology to Ms Kon - who worked on shows such as Panorama and BBC Breakfast - and refused to acknowledge she was the victim of anti-Semitism while in their employment.

Ms Kon, who told the Telegraph the BBC attempted to 'stop' her doing her job because of her religion, is the first person the broadcaster is known to have paid a settlement to as a consequence of anti-Semitism.

'It was like having Jew stamped on my forehead,' Ms Kon described feeling in the wake of the October 7th terrorist attacks.

'I think I made too much noise about being a Jew inside the BBC,' she said. 'I stood up for my community. I was open about being a Zionist. The BBC says, bring your authentic self to work. And I did. And I lost my job as a result.'

Her payout comes just one year following the resignation of the BBC's director-general, Tim Davie, whose premiership saw the broadcaster being accused of institutional bias, including claims of anti-Semitism.

Under his tenure, more than 200 Jewish staff accused the corporation's Board of 'ignoring' their pleas for an investigation into alleged anti-Semitism at the broadcaster.

In July 2024, more than 200 Jewish staff, contractors, suppliers and contributors wrote to BBC chairman Samir Shah asking for an urgent formal investigation by the BBC Board into 'systemic problems of anti-Semitism and bias at the BBC, alongside senior management's demonstrable failure to properly address the issue'.

The premiership of former BBC director general Tim Davie (pictured) saw the broadcaster being accused of institutional bias, including claims of anti-Semitism

The BBC has not issued a formal apology to Ms Kon and has refused to acknowledge she was the victim of anti-Semitism while in their employment (Pictured: BBC Broadcasting House in London)

Attached to the letter was a report titled 'Being Jewish and working at the BBC' which included testimony from staff who argued the corporation was no longer 'a safe space to be Jewish'.

The same staff members wrote again to the BBC Board last December, accusing it of ignoring their pleas and offering 'words not action' after a gap of more than a year.

Matt Brittin - Mr Davie's successor – has since pledged to eradicate anti-Semitism at the company, however, Ms Kon said she informed him that she and fellow Jewish BBC employees continue to be bullied and abused.

She alleged other Jewish employees have left the broadcaster because of how they were treated, adding she has friends who are 'still struggling' and 'still suffering' because they are a Zionist or Jew.

A BBC spokesman said: 'While we do not comment on individual staffing matters, anti-Semitism in any form is not tolerated at the BBC.

#687. “An Unprecedented Case of Child Abuse”

One morning earlier this month, deputies with the Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department arrested Guojun Xuan and Silvia Zhang, the couple at the center of a nationwide surrogacy scandal. Officers had staked out the pair’s ten-thousand-square-foot mansion, in the city of Arcadia, long before dawn. At 8:45 A.M., one of them took a battering ram to the gate. Within minutes, Guojun and Silvia were led outside in handcuffs.

At a press conference a few hours later, the L.A. district attorney, Nathan Hochman, warned that he was about to share details from an “incredibly disturbing” and “unprecedented case of child abuse.” For years, he explained, Guojun and Silvia had recruited surrogate mothers from across the country to carry babies for them. The couple had even set up their own agency, Mark Surrogacy, to lend a patina of legitimacy to their family-making operation. They eventually ended up having twenty-seven children, most of them still infants and toddlers. Many of those children, Hochman said, had been living in “a house of horrors.”

Listen to a five-part audio series based on this story.

The couple’s mansion had been outfitted with thirty-two surveillance cameras, which captured nannies beating the kids with hands, sticks, and shoes. Although the parents claimed to be unaware of these acts, videos also showed them in their home office, laughing at CCTV footage of the beatings. Prosecutors were now charging them with conspiracy to commit child abuse, and Guojun with participating in the abuse himself. During one incident, Hochman said, Guojun lifted one of his sons into the air while hitting his head so hard “that the child’s body lurched in alternating directions with the blows.”

This wasn’t the first time the couple had been arrested. In May, 2025, Silvia and Guojun were jailed after one of their children, a two-month-old, was hospitalized with bleeding inside his brain. Social workers removed the baby’s siblings from the house and placed them in foster care, where they remain. After four days in custody, the parents were released. The D.A.’s office declined to file a case, requesting more investigation from the Arcadia police. At Hochman’s press conference, I asked about the timing of the charges, given that officers had seized the home videos more than a year ago. “We do it methodically,” he replied, noting that the footage required translation, as both the parents and the nannies spoke Mandarin.

After that first arrest, Silvia and Guojun kept at it. Even while under scrutiny from police and the child-welfare system, the couple went on to have six more babies through surrogates. They launched custody battles in Virginia, Pennsylvania, and Georgia, in an attempt to bring those infants to California. And, when some of the surrogates resisted that idea, the parents sued them for breach of contract and demanded a million dollars in damages. All the while, Silvia and Guojun maintained that their arrest was simply a misunderstanding, and that their vast family would soon be reunited.

Earlier this year, I published an investigation into the couple for the magazine; last month, In the Dark released a podcast series in which we expanded on that reporting. A source with knowledge of the case told me that The New Yorker’s findings—and the public scrutiny that followed—played a role in the county’s decision to press charges. According to court records, investigators observed thousands of acts of alleged abuse in the home footage, and the extent of the violence “cannot be fully conveyed through written description alone.” If convicted as charged, both parents face over a decade in prison.

News of the arrest spread quickly. Kayla Elliott, a surrogate for the couple who’d first exposed their scheme on TikTok, immediately texted a group chat composed of some of the couple’s other surrogates. “Everyone was, like, ‘What the hell?’ ” she told me. Elliott watched a live stream of the press conference from her home, in Corpus Christi, Texas; her husband watched from work. “We talked about it so many times, like, ‘What’s taking so long?’ ” she said. “ You have to try to be patient and trust the process, but it was difficult when the lives of these kids are on the line.”

That afternoon, I drove to a courthouse in Pasadena, where the couple was being arraigned. Silvia entered the courtroom wearing an oversized white T-shirt and black pants. Her right eye was puffy and red, but she otherwise looked the same as when I’d seen her in the spring. Guojun, though, was barely recognizable. The last time I’d tried to interview him, he had been energetically strolling around a parking lot with a full head of black hair. Now he was in a wheelchair, completely bald. According to his lawyer, Guojun had a rare form of leukemia and was recovering from a bone-marrow transplant. A medical port stuck out from his chest, its catheters dangling.

Both Silvia and Guojun pleaded not guilty. The judge then turned his attention to the question of bail. MacKenzie Teymouri, a deputy district attorney, was requesting that it be set at a hundred million dollars for each defendant. It was an extraordinary sum, she acknowledged, but the couple had extraordinary resources.

I’d known that Guojun was wealthy; he and Silvia ran a real-estate investment firm, routinely purchasing properties in cash, and it had likely cost them more than two million dollars to have so many children. But their actual finances were fuzzy. Now Teymouri was telling the court that the couple’s assets exceeded a hundred million dollars. Sheriff’s deputies and the F.B.I. were still searching the mansion, she said, but already they’d discovered antique sculptures, along with reserves of expensive alcohol. These included crates and crates of Moutai, a pungent Chinese liquor that Guojun’s former employees told me he liked to drink straight from the bottle. According to a law-enforcement source, the F.B.I. is looking into whether Guojun engaged in money laundering. (An F.B.I spokesperson confirmed that agents had searched the house, but declined to comment further; one of Guojun’s lawyers denied his client’s involvement in illicit financial transactions.)

At the arraignment, Guojun’s criminal-defense attorney, Mitchell Krems, protested that a nine-figure bail was “absurd.” He said that Guojun could die at any moment, and asked for five million dollars instead. After some back and forth, the judge decided on twenty million dollars for each defendant, with the additional conditions that the couple wear electronic monitoring devices, leave home only for court or medical emergencies, and surrender all their passports. (Authorities had found several hidden in a safe, including a Mexican one in which Guojun’s last name was given as “Xuan Lozano.”) The judge also granted Teymouri’s request for a protective order that would forbid the parents, who were both charged with multiple counts of dissuading witnesses, from interacting with the children. According to court records, cameras captured the couple coaching some of their kids to deny that they had been hit.

Outside the courthouse, Krems held an impromptu press conference. He blamed any abuse on the couple’s nannies and denounced the charges as biased. “We wouldn’t be in front of this court,” he said, “if my client was white and was Elon Musk.” Silvia and Guojun, he went on, were being unfairly targeted because they were Chinese immigrants from “a Communist country,” trying to “exercise their liberties to have as many children as they want.”

Surrogacy is banned in China and most of western Europe. Yet in the U.S., where there are thousands of surrogacies each year, no federal regulations govern the industry. While some agencies, clinics, and attorneys ask intended parents to undergo background checks, screenings aren’t mandatory. In fact, no state laws require parents to disclose the number of children they have, or, for that matter, the number of surrogates they’ve hired.

Reporting and commentary on what you need to know today.

In recent weeks, fertility experts have claimed that Silvia and Guojun would have been unable to carry out their plans had they worked with industry professionals. This is not quite true. I discovered that, in addition to the ersatz firm they operated out of their house, the couple made occasional use of independent agencies. They also enlisted the services of blue-chip fertility clinics and pricey fertility lawyers.

One reason there are so few rules around surrogacy is that the practice is viewed primarily as a fertility treatment, and such treatments tend to be tailored to the parents’ desires. The laws regulating adoption, by contrast, are designed around protecting a child who has already been conceived. In the wake of the Arcadia case, several efforts have emerged to redress this asymmetry. In May, a group of fertility lawyers launched SurroStudy, a screening service that employs licensed social workers who can perform home studies and background checks on all of the parties in a surrogacy arrangement, including the intended parents. “None of us wants to be caught up in a scandal because we find out, ‘Oh, God, it’s their twenty-fifth kid,’ ” Rich Geisler, a fertility lawyer and the co-founder of SurroStudy, told me.

Around the same time, a group of surrogates, not connected to Silvia and Guojun, launched an advocacy organization called the National Surrogate Alliance. Kayde Mason, a two-time surrogate, told me that she’d created the group after noticing there were professional organizations representing the interests of fertility doctors, lawyers, and agency owners, but none for the women putting their bodies on the line. “Who were the surrogates in your story supposed to reach out to?” Mason asked me. “There should’ve been someone ready to step in and provide support and there wasn’t. There has to be somewhere for surrogates to go that’s bigger than just the agency they signed up with.”

The women who had carried for Silvia and Guojun told me that they would have never agreed to work for the parents if they’d been informed of the scale of their family. In fact, in August, five of them sued the couple for fraud and sexual battery, among other claims. Jamie Majerus, their lawyer, told me that she hadn’t been able to find any precedent for the complaint’s unusual legal argument about reproductive exploitation. “You can’t have consent when you sign a contract based on misrepresentations,” Majerus said. “Each plaintiff in this case surrendered her body to the couple’s enterprise, and she did so only because they deceived her into believing she was helping a single loving family conceive this one child.”

Last Friday, Silvia and Guojun again appeared in court, where their lawyers argued that both defendants should be released on their own recognizance—that is, without posting bail. Mitchell Krems said that Guojun’s grave medical issues—which included a “hole in his chest,” mucus coming out of the back of his head, and diabetes—were not being adequately addressed in jail. Guojun had shuffled out of the house the morning of his arrest (bragging, according to one law-enforcement source, about his unproven connections to President Donald Trump), but Krems said that his client was now unable to walk. He added that Guojun would have difficulty accessing his bank accounts because he didn’t remember his passwords.

Matt Koohanim, Silvia’s defense attorney, took a more puzzling tack. He contended that Silvia was merely Guojun’s assistant and had no legal claim to the children. “This is more of an employer-employee arrangement,” he said. It was true the couple had never married—but Silvia had described herself as Guojun’s partner and the children’s legal mother on the couple’s surrogacy contracts, and throughout their child-welfare proceedings. Koohanim knew this firsthand, since, for the past year, he has been representing Silvia in her effort to regain shared custody of the couple’s twenty-plus children.

Koohanim went on to say that Silvia never interacted with the surrogates, despite hundreds of exchanges, including voice memos, texts, and recorded phone calls, that show she was their direct point of contact. As for the alleged abuse, Koohanim wanted the court to know that the children lived in a giant house and had their own beds. “There were no cigarette-burn marks,” he said, lowering the bar. “There were no cages. There were no dog collars.”

Felony child-abuse cases tend to focus on a discrete, visible assault—what the law terms “great bodily harm.” This type of injury was not experienced by most of the children in the Arcadia case—Silvia and Guojun had even allegedly instructed their nannies not to leave marks when hitting the children—but Teymouri laid out the aggregate physical and psychological harms. She talked about how the Arcadia children didn’t go to school, didn’t get taken to playgrounds or restaurants. Instead, they were beaten “from sunup to sundown” in nearly every room of the house. The violence was so unrelenting, Teymouri said, that she’d had to mute the videos she watched because of the “constant screaming.” In one of the tapes that she described, Guojun walks into a bedroom, patrolling its rows of sleeping children with a flashlight, “like a warden.” When one of the kids sits up, he allegedly smacks the kid down. During their search of the house, Teymouri added, the authorities had found four cattle prods.

At the end of the hearing, which lasted over an hour, the judge declined to reduce the bail from twenty million dollars. Elliott was one of several surrogates who told me that, though she was relieved that the parents would remain in custody for now, she longed to know how the babies were doing. “They’re not our genetics, but we still gave birth to them, and we still carry a little part of their DNA inside of us,” she said. Maria Castellanos, a surrogate who’d had two children for the couple, told me that she celebrated both of their birthdays every year. She was hoping that their foster parents might get in touch and send her a picture. “That’s all I want,” she said. “I just want to make sure the kids are O.K.” ♦

The doxing of Jane Doe and the fallout from the “Cornell Seven” rape case.

“She Made Me Do It”: a famed equestrian instructor shot his most annoying student.

Parents disagreed on whether to vaccinate their children. Then the kids got sick.

#688. Germany news: AfD's Weidel calls for major EU reforms

Far-right Alternative for Germany co-leader Alice Weidel reveals the party's plan to reform the EU. Meanwhile, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was in Berlin to talk to developers and investors. DW has more.

One of Weidel's reforms is for European parliamentarians to no longer be directly elected

Nvidia's Jensen Huang had words of encouragement for Europe's growing AI economy during a conference in Berlin

Germany's Finance Ministry has erroneously introduced an approved tax hike on tobacco products months before it was scheduled to come into effect

Germany's Bundesbank has forecast growth for the fourth quarter after a dip in the third quarter

This blog is now closed. Below is a round-up of top stories from and about Germany on Wednesday, October 21, 2026.

We'll be back with the latest headlines out of the country on Thursday. Tschüss!

Alice Weidel, the co-leader of the Alternative for Germany (AfD) party, has presented her party's proposals for a European Union that she said was "in severe need of reform" during a visit to the European Parliament in Strasbourg, saying they rested on three core pillars.

"We would like to rebuild and reform the European Union," she said. "We would like to found the European Union on three major principles: the first one is subsidiarity, the second one is responsibility, and the third one is sovereignty."

On subsidiarity — the idea that power should reside as close to the grassroots level as possible as much as possible — she said it was important to put the "competences" on the "lowest level of decision-making," saying "we don't want the state, or the [European] Commission — that is not elected — to intrude and disturb your private life in decision-making."

"I'm an economist, and for me, the European Union is not a group of sovereign states any more," Weidel said. She said that in sovereign states' parliaments, leaders were elected, "and so the decision-making on the sovereign level should be made in the national parliaments and not here, to be very clear."

This is already the case in the vast majority of core EU public policy areas. National governments decide foreign and defense issues, finance and health policy, education policy and much more. The notable exceptions Weidel objects to are fiscal policy and the primacy of EU law, but only after sovereign member states agree to them.

She said the European Commission was not elected but had a "legislative right of initiative," saying this was a "huge disturbance of checks and balances" and of a "democratic decision-making process."

Weidel accused the EU of failing to follow its own rules, for instance on sovereign debt and whether the European Central Bank should or can guarantee it, citing issues like this as questions of responsibility.

Finally, she reiterated her desire for "sovereign states to protect their borders," saying that "if the European Union is not capable of protecting our borders, the outer borders ... then it is a decision of the sovereign states to protect our national borders."

"If Schengen is over, if Schengen doesn't work, then we need to get out of Schengen and protect our borders," she said of the open-border zone within much of the EU.

She said that if the EU fails to protect the bloc's external borders, "we should have a veto right to opt out of this chaos."

While the EU maintains a border management agency, Frontex, national authorities are responsible for the external borders of the Schengen zone and the EU.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz criticized China for "unfair practices" in trade, and said he wants EU member states to balance out their trade deficits.

That elicited a bold comparison from a journalist who said, "You sound very much like Donald Trump."

A massive stage, all in black. A colorful laser light show. Upbeat music. AI-generated videos on a gigantic screen. On stage, just one man in a black leather jacket: Jensen Huang, the 63-year-old CEO of Nvidia, which manufactures superfast computer chips needed for AI data centers and happens to be the world's most valuable company.

The relaxed Nvidia boss set out his vision of the upcoming AI revolution and, of course, the products Nvidia has developed for the "second wave" of AI. The 4,000 attendees at Berlin's Tempodrom arena were thrilled by what Jensen Huang had to say (see entry below).

Huang said Germany and Europe could be part of the next industrial revolution — not as developers of AI language models or computer chips, but as producers of robots, machines, tools, and entire factories controlled by AI applications.

"You have to transfer AI into the real world of production," he said. Europe could use its data to train AI and develop customized models for automakers, pharmaceutical companies, and many small and medium-sized businesses.

Unsurprisingly, Nvidia offers all the AI software and hardware needed to get in on the action. A new addition to the Nvidia universe is a "Giga-Factory," which is housed in modular shipping containers and can be set up in just a few days or weeks anywhere with a suitable power grid.

There was also something for consumers: a high-performance laptop with a built-in AI agent that acts as a "friend and helper," capable of taking over tasks and programming new agents. Huang went on to demonstrate four small robot ducks that had been trained by this AI agent to perform cute tricks, which were met with laughter and applause.

But it wasn't all cheers. A woman in the audience interrupted a product demo to point out that AI is also used to control Russian drones. She was escorted out by security guards, but Huang assured the audience that he would speak with her later. He was keen to add that Nvidia has also developed a security system designed to keep AI agents in check and prevent misuse.

Nvidia is now valued at €5 trillion ($5.6 trillion) on the stock market. That is roughly equivalent to the total economic output of all of Germany in 2025.

The German military, known as the Bundeswehr, has rated the threat of sabotage against it as "significant," according to a reports by the Süddeutsche Zeitung (SZ) and public broadcaster WDR.

A spokesperson for the Defense Ministry pointed to several recent cases, including the discovery of a drone close to an airbase in Wunstorf and acts of sabotage against Navy ships.

The military is looking to increase security to counter the threat, with the ministry spokesperson naming increased surveillance at airports and military docks by soldiers or infrared cameras.

"The incidents highlight the ability that Russia has almost certainly had for a while now, as well as very likely the increased intention, to act against Bundeswehr forces and facilities, as well as partners such as Ukraine in Germany," SZ reported based on internal military analysis.

The aim is therefore "very likely an intention to degrade the current political and society-wide German support for Ukraine."

The ministry spokesperson also pointed out that the incidents did not mark a major change, with the military facing similar challenges over the past decades.

He said "automatic defense concepts" are in place for acute terror threats, but "we are not at that point."

German trade with Russia collapsed following the 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine, especially due to the decision to cut all imports of Russian gas. However, some trade has continued.

According to the German Federal Statistical Office (Destatis), German imports of Russian goods were down by 96.4% in the first half of 2026 compared with the same period in 2021.

This amounted to €500 million ($561 million) in 2026, down from €15 billion. German exports to Russia were also down, but still significant, reaching €3.4 billion in the first six months of 2026. However, this was about a quarter of the exports in the same period in 2021.

Pharmaceutical products made up more than 40% of German exports to Russia, with machinery, food and animal feed also being exported in smaller quantities.

Jensen Huang, the head of chip manufacturing giant Nvidia, was speaking at a company conference for developers and investors in Berlin's Tempodrom auditorium on Wednesday.

He was seeking to encourage Europe to build out its data center infrastructure and touted Nvidia's modular tools to help speed up that process.

"Europe's AI economy is starting, and it's accelerating, and it's great to see," Huang said.

He promoted a new design for a ready-made modular computing center that comes in a box akin to a shipping container and that could make it possible to construct a data center in a matter of days. Huang said it "will change the way people build AI centers."

Nvidia has invested $10 billion (€8.9 billion) in European startups over the past year, the Nvidia boss said.

Europe has fallen behind the US and China in terms of building up data centers and is currently home to around 5% of the world's AI computing capacity in comparison to 75% in the US. This capacity is required to train AI models and its lack is seen as a major obstacle for European developers.

Most current data centers are reliant on Nvidia GPUs to run.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

A spokesperson for Germany's Federal Financial Ministry on Wednesday addressed confusion surrounding the implementation of a new tobacco tax saying, "The tax increase in the law's wording was approved to go into effect on January 1, 2027, that remains the case."

The spokesperson confirmed that the mix-up over when the new law would take effect resulted from a technical error that put the law on the books immediately rather than January 1 as intended.

The issue stemmed from a mistake in the government's original writing of the law.

Customs officials have reportedly been informed and the Financial Ministry's website makes clear that the price increase will not be charged until the beginning of the new year.

"Gen Z regelt" — or Gen Z's Got It — a youth initiative, has called for mass protests in 21 cities across Germany on Saturday, October 31; including Berlin, Cologne, Hamburg and Munich.

Thousands are expected to participate in demonstrations protesting "broken schools and austerity," as well as the cost of living, social injustice, military conscription and climate change.

French protests that exploded in violence and rampant destruction of private and public property this weekend also grew out of student frustration over the national school system and soon included numerous unions, groups and individuals voicing anger over a number of issues.

Gen Z regelt's website clearly states that the initiative is "against all violence," whether directed at people or property.

Police say they are "vigilant and relaxed," adding that they intend to protect people's right to congregate and express their opinions.

Still, images of massive damage and public violence from France, Italy and Spain have raised concerns among domestic policymakers and police, who have warned against allowing the protests to be hijacked by left-wing extremists.

Andreas Roßkopf, head of the German Federal Police's GdP union, made clear that officers would deal harshly with riots and rioters, telling the Rheinische Post newspaper on Wednesday, "State, but also federal police, will offer a firm and decisive response" to any trouble.

Roßkopf also warned that radicals and extremists could insert themselves among demonstrators in order to "attack police" or "simply be destructive."

The Bundesbank, Germany's central bank, has said it is expecting to see an uptick in growth for Europe's biggest economy in the fourth quarter.

"German economic output is likely to improve again markedly in the fourth quarter," the bank said in its monthly report on Wednesday. "However, the future economic recovery depends, not least, on the development of the war in the Middle East."

The optimistic outlook follows a dip in the third quarter, which the bank chalked up largely to this summer's drought that caused such low water levels in the Rhine River, an artery in western Germany for industry, that most ships could not travel.

"The low water levels are also likely to continue to have a negative impact on foreign trade via European ports as a result of restrictions on inland water transport," the bank wrote.

The forecast will be welcomed by the Merz government as it has struggled to boost the economy after two consecutive years of recession followed by weak growth in 2025.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has said he does not think Europe is on course for a trade war with China while acknowledging what he called "unfair practice" on the part of Beijing.

Speaking at a business conference in Berlin, Merz said the imbalance did not mean "the beginning of a war, of a trade war with China. We are looking for peaceful solutions, but the level for that is fair trade."

The German chancellor has been pushing for the EU to be better prepared for trade disputes with China, including calling for a means to quickly exclude non-EU countries from the EU's single market if they flood it with cheap goods.

Merz said the EU needs to be able "to protect our markets and defend ourselves against those who don't play by the rules."

"Anyone who disrupts the functioning of the markets through unfair subsidies, overcapacities, aggressive pricing, or artificially undervalued currencies must expect a response," he said.

That includes tools that "enable us to respond swiftly and vigorously to targeted attacks on our industry and supply chain, with the idea being that in the best case we will not have to use it."

Germany has a rather generous parental allowance system in comparison to many countries, with parents being able to take off 14 months, if each parent takes at least two months off, with the government paying up to €1,800 (just over $2,000) a month during that period.

However, this system has become the subject of a planned reform under the government of Chancellor Friedrich Merz.

The plan is to reduce the maximum amount of full-time paid parental leave to 12 months. With three months each reserved for both parents and the remaining six months free to be divided up however the parents choose. It also raises the minimum payment from €300 to €330 and the maximum from €1,800 to €1,900.

The government's aim is to make cuts to help the Ministry for Family Affairs reach its savings target of €1.6 billion, while also encouraging more fathers to take parental leave. Currently, fewer than half of fathers in Germany take parental leave.

Now the Ifo Institute for Economic Research has cast doubts on the government's savings plan.

"The savings target and the goal of increasing fathers’ participation in the planned parental allowance reform are at odds with each other. The higher the number of fathers who are motivated to participate by the reform, the less the government saves," Ifo researcher Kyra Puteanus said.

The institute estimates savings of around €880 million from November 2027, when the reform comes into effect. However, if more fathers, who generally earn more and thus are able to request the highest payment, do take up the parental leave, this will quickly reduce the savings, with Ifo predicting that even if the uptake by fathers only increases by 1%, savings will fall to €597 million. An increase of 3.1% would undo any savings from the reform, according to the institute.

"Since 2010, however, the share of fathers receiving parental allowance has almost doubled. A rapid increase can therefore not be ruled out, especially if months are otherwise forfeited," Ifo researcher Franziska Nuernbergk said.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The Israel Defense Forces (IFD) said in a post on X that they have killed Tamer Mohammad Ibrahim Al-Zabaq, a member of the Hamas terror group who was involved in the October 7 attacks.

The post said that al-Zabaq had been one of the men responsible for the abduction of Shani Louk, a dual German-Israeli national.

Louk was initially thought to have been taken hostage following the Hamas-led attacks but it was later confirmed that she had been killed.

In the immediate aftermath of the terror attacks, pictures and videos shared online showed a young woman, believed to be Shani, lying face down in a pick-up truck driven by militants. It was unclear from the footage whether she was alive.

The IDF also accused Al-Zabaq of operating to "restore Hamas' military capabilities, in systematic violation of the ceasefire."

"The terrorist was eliminated in order to remove the threat he posed," the IDF said.

The claims in the X post could not be independently verified.

Israel has carried out numerous deadly strikes on Gaza since the ceasefire came into effect just over a year ago.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, addressing the Business Global Dialogue summit in Berlin on Wednesday, renewed calls for US President Donald Trump to invite South Africa (a G20 member) to the upcoming G20 summit that he will host in Miami this December.

"Whoever talks about the future of the global economy must include all important partners. Of course Africa belongs at the table," he said, adding: "The African Union is a G20 member, as is South Africa. That is why I urgently insist that South Africa be represented at the G20 summit."

Merz made a similar plea last year, when Trump angrily insisted that he would not invite South Africa to the annual summit of the 20 leading industrial and emerging economies.

Trump has accused South Africa of committing genocide on white farmers and dismissed South African pushback against his repeated claim. The anti-immigrant president also took the unusual step of offering South Africans political asylum in the US — as long as they are white.

The US President is apparently less bothered by wars of aggression, extending an invitation to President Vladimir Putin to come to Miami, despite Russia being thrown out of the G8 — now G7 — over its 2014 invasion and annexation of Ukraine's Crimea.

Beyond his plea for South Africa's inclusion, Merz said he would travel to the US with what he called a "Miami Growth Agenda" aimed at slashing bureaucracy, pushing structural reforms and making investment easier.

"Those" he said, "are the prerequisites for new economic growth and prosperity, not only in Germany, but globally."

Russian FSB agents have arrested a German national, accusing him of being a mercenary under contract with the Ukrainian army.

"The Federal Security Service of the Russian Federation has detained a German citizen who is a serving member of the Armed Forces of Ukraine," said a statement cited by Russian news agencies.

The FSB says the man, whom they described as a sniper, previously fought in Afghanistan and Syria as well as in Ukraine between 2016 and 2018.

They say he arrived in Ukraine last November and signed a three-year contract with the Ukrainian army before deserting over unpaid wages.

Last week, the FSB arrested a Swedish national whom Russian authorities also accused of fighting on Kyiv's behalf.

Russia has arrested hundreds of foreign nationals that it accuses of "espionage," "sabotage" or "treason" to long prison sentences since it began its invasion of neighboring Ukraine.

A number of foreign nationals have also been jailed over supposed "mercenary activity."

#689. ‘Too big to not fail’: Google outage exposes UK reliance on a handful of cloud providers

Our dependence on internet services of a few key tech companies leaves us vulnerable to cloud failures, bugs and more, experts say

It happened again. A power outage hit a datacentre in London, and things cascaded from there: multiple banking services faltered, court hearings were put on hold and patients reported temporary glitches on the NHS app.

The datacentre in question was in Google’s europe-west2-b zone, one of more than a dozen “zones” that the US search giant maintains in Europe to service its clients.

The outages – which have affected, according to the website Downdetector, Royal Mail, Revolut, HSBC and Lloyds bank, among others, are so far not of the scale of a similar cascade this time last year, when Amazon Web Services went down for nearly half a day.

That outage hit a far bigger node – Amazon’s us-east-1 – in a concentrated region of Virginia, which hosts the greatest density of datacentres on Earth. It saw cascading effects worldwide: taking out the Roblox game and Signal messaging app and causing smart mattresses worldwide to suddenly heat overnight and toast their occupants.

Today’s problems appeared to peak at about 9am, and by mid-afternoon were somewhat resolved, according to reports submitted to Downdetector. Because Google Cloud stores data and runs operations for a number of businesses, there were widespread knock-on effects – mostly confined to UK businesses.

Revolut confirmed “a service disruption affecting multiple services”, but added that “all our customers’ money and data are safe”. Lloyd’s said its app was working, but “we understand some [people] are having issues with certain online services this morning”.

HM Courts and Tribunal Service, which handles remote video hearings in courts across England and Wales, said it was “aware of an issue affecting Cloud Video Platform,” and was “working with our technology partners to restore service”.

Like the far bigger outage last year, it’s a reminder of the physical infrastructure – often creaking and provisional – that underpins most of the virtual world.

Michał “rysiek” Woźniak, an internet infrastructure expert, said the outages were a reminder of the increasing concentration of the internet and vital services on the infrastructure of a few key companies – the “hyperscalers”.

“Hyperscalers have become too big to not fail. But worse, they’ve become so deeply ingrained into the very fabric of our digital lives that switching away from them seems unimaginable.”

The Guardian has reported that British police keep vital data on Microsoft’s Azure cloud, despite being apparently aware that this exposes sensitive information to US government insiders, hostile foreign actors and outages like today’s. Up to 60% of the UK government’s infrastructure is hosted on cloud services – mostly Amazon, Microsoft and Google.

“I am sure Google’s engineers are doing everything they can to mitigate them, but it is unreasonable to have a handful of gigantic companies whose outages time and again cause public institutions or large swaths of the digital economy to stop working en masse,” said Woźniak.

Last year’s AWS outage was later revealed to have been caused not by a power outage, but by a bug in automation software. A separate outage was caused by an AI tool that Amazon had adopted after laying off tens of thousands of staff last autumn.

Woźniak pointed at an announcement this year from Google indicating that it was also embracing AI, with 75% of all new code “now AI-generated and approved by engineers”.

“One can only wonder how that affects the reliability and quality of Google’s services. Multiple large outages at another hyperscaler, AWS, a year ago have been linked to internal AI tooling.”

A Google spokesperson said: “We have resolved a disruption to Google Cloud services at a third-party facility in our europe-west2 cloud region due to a power event. Services have been restored. We will update our public status dashboard with an analysis of the incident.”

#690. Indian court orders release of two leaders of Cockroach movement

Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka spent a week in jail after defying restrictions on protests in Delhi amid government crackdown

An Indian court has ordered the release of two leaders of India’s Cockroach movement who were jailed last week amid a mounting state crackdown on youth-led protests.

The two leaders of the Cockroach Janta party (CJP) movement, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka, had spent a week in Delhi’s Tihar jail after being arrested by Delhi police last week.

On Wednesday, a special magistrate ordered that Das and Ranka be released, despite efforts by police to keep them in prison. They were made to sign a bond pledging no further breach of peace.

Their arrest came after a draconian police crackdown on a CJP march held in the capital two weeks ago to protest alleged manipulation of the country’s electoral roll, which led to the barricading of central Delhi and thousands of young people being detained.

Das and Ranka were taken into custody for a second time days later after they jumped police barricades and held up an Indian flag at a site in central Delhi that police had cordoned off.

The pair were charged with trespass and violating the peace and sent to jail for five days, which was then extended by two further days. Their detention had provoked outrage among leaders and supporters of the youth movement, who accused the government of “cowardice” for jailing CJP leaders for holding a peaceful protest.

After the magistrate’s ruling on Wednesday evening, Das said that “truth has triumphed”.

The release of the two leaders is likely to come as a blow to the ruling Narendra Modi government, which has implemented an unforgiving crackdown on recent protests that have erupted across India.

He had said that, once his fellow Cockroach leaders were released, they would “gather, re-strategise, and determine how to move forward”.

#692. How AI giants will reshape global philanthropy

The AI boom is about to rewrite the rules of global philanthropy, shifting its center of gravity to Silicon Valley, where the IPOs of AI giants Anthropic and OpenAI will create the world's largest charitable organizations.

Why it matters: Rather than massive donations earmarked for renaming hospital wings or university graduate programs, expect the new wave of giving to mirror startup culture: flexible capital, ambitious bets and a search for measurable impact.

Driving the news: Anthropic announced Sunday that it plans to launch a massive benefit fund with 5% of its shares.

Zoom in: The company's pledge — which would amount to $100 billion if it reaches a value of $2 trillion in its IPO — will go to a public benefit fund and is set to grow as its valuation rises.

  • Anthropic says the fund will be a wholly owned LLC, giving it flexibility to make large donations to nonprofits or distribute money directly to specific populations.
  • The commitment builds on the pledges of co-founders to give away 80% of their equity. A program available to early Anthropic hires and used by a large number of company staffers matched donations at a 3:1 ratio. The company says roughly half its employees participate in donation matching.
  • The company says the fund's shares will not be used for lobbying or political giving in the U.S. or abroad.

The big picture: Anthropic is joining OpenAI, which is controlled by a nonprofit foundation that holds a 26% equity stake in the company, worth about $130 billion based on the company's current valuation. The foundation has the power to appoint OpenAI's board.

What they're saying: Anthropic says much of its public-benefit work — including AI safety and interpretability research, applied biomedical research and discounts for nonprofits and scientific institutions — will continue inside the company.

  • The new fund is intended to make other kinds of giving possible at greater scale, the company says.
  • Anthropic cited AI's effects on the labor market as one potential use and said it has already committed $200 million to studying and addressing that issue, but that "bolder approaches may be needed."
  • Anthropic has not specified what those approaches would be, or whether the fund would make direct payments to workers affected by AI.

Between the lines: Anthropic's founders and some employees have close ties to effective altruism, a movement ostensibly dedicated to directing resources toward causes where they may do the most good.

  • Effective altruism has come under sharp criticism from the Trump White House, which has emphasized aspects of the movement that are far from the philanthropic mainstream.
  • Those include an acute interest in animal welfare, as well as seemingly abstract ponderings about the value of life, including comparing that of an infant to an adult, or future people to present people.
  • In an X post, Taylor Budowich, a former White House official, highlighted one such comment from Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei in 2010, when he said in a blog post that an adult death is "perhaps 2 or 3 times worse than an infant's death."
  • Budowich also shared a few other "insane beliefs of those who make up Anthropic and how they think about prioritizing charitable giving."

The bottom line: Anthropic's fund — and the charitable giving of a massive new cadre of millionaires and deca-millionaires — could become one of the largest vehicles for new giving.

  • The bigger change may come with a new generation of Silicon Valley donors aiming to reset the agenda of modern philanthropy.

#693. Your guide to L.A. County Charter Amendment E: Jail alternatives

See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred

Los Angeles County voters may feel like they’re going back to the future. With a single ballot measure, they are being asked to do two things: fill in gaps necessary to institute previously approved ethics reforms, and fix a major misstep that invalidated a previously approved jail alternatives funding proposal.

California’s general election takes place on Novemer 3. Learn about L.A.’s city and county races as well races for state office.

Some history is in order, and we’ll start with the second half of the ballot measure, as it will have a greater impact on county finances. In November 2020, 57% of county voters approved Measure J. This mandated that at least 10% of locally generated, unrestricted revenue be allocated to incarceration alternatives, advancing what was called the county’s Care First, Jails Last vision. In fiscal year 2025, this directed $288 million to mental health treatment, housing support and other services.

The problem? When voters approved the county reform effort Measure G (more on that below) in November 2024, some ballot language had the unintended effect of repealing Measure J. The administrative error was discovered only in July 2025, eight months after the measure passed, by a member of the county’s governance reform task force.

So this part of Measure E would ensure that Measure J remains in effect. A July motion from county supervisors Lindsey Horvath and Holly Mitchell carries the heading, “Restoring the Will of Los Angeles County Voters at the Ballot Box.”

Measure G, propelled by Horvath, will result in expanding the Board of Supervisors from five to nine members in 2032 and create a new county chief executive position, with an election in 2028. It passed narrowly, with 51.6%.

It also called for creating a county ethics commission and an ethics compliance office. Other branches of government already have this, including the city of Los Angeles, where the commission’s duties include overseeing campaign finance, such as the matching funds program for political candidates. The commission also regulates lobbying and can issue penalties for fundraising and other infractions.

The Measure G governance reform task force is setting everything up, but officials realized that for true independence, the seven-member commission and the compliance office must be permanently enshrined in the county charter. That requires the approval of voters.

Establishing the commission and the compliance office, Horvath said in a statement in May, “delivers on the will of the voters and marks a monumental step toward greater transparency and accountability in County government.”

Horvath and some other supervisors are backing this. So are the League of Women Voters of L.A. County, good governance group California Common Cause and the AAPI Equity Alliance.

The League of Women Voters of L.A. County described its long-standing support of the county starting an ethics commission and compliance office and ensuring that it comes with true independence, transparency, sufficient funding and the authority to conduct investigations.

“An ethics watchdog cannot be dependent on the officials it may someday have to investigate,” the league said in a statement.

The league initially was neutral on Measure J, but “we do not believe a decision voters made at the ballot box should be undone because of an administrative or drafting error,” its statement said.

No opposition for the measure was submitted to the registrar-recorder/county clerk. The Los Angeles Daily News has editorialized against Measure E, asserting that “fine” ethics reforms are bundled with ballot-box budgeting that amounts to “really bad policy.”

Shops across Brussels were boarded up on Saturday as businesses took precautions against a repeat of the looting and violence that hit the Belgian capital a week earlier. Though some clashes did eventually take place, they were limited in comparison.

Along the city’s shopping streets, wooden panels covered display windows and entrances, turning stretches of retail frontage into blank walls.

Luxury brands including Tiffany & Co., Prada, Versace and Ferragamo were among those taking protective measures. Lacoste, Nike and Nespresso stores were also boarded up, alongside smaller businesses, including an optician and a phone repair shop.

The precautions extended beyond retailers, with a Quick restaurant covering its windows and entrance with wooden panels.

Some businesses remained open despite the barriers. At Nike, customers could enter through an uncovered doorway, while Quick displayed a small notice reading “open” on its boarded frontage. Pedestrians continued walking past the shops, with traffic moving through the surrounding streets.

The measures come amid fears of further disorder following calls on social media for a fresh gathering in Brussels on Saturday. Shops around Avenue Louise, Porte de Namur and Rue Neuve have reinforced their premises against possible damage and theft.

Several stores on Rue Neuve were looted during unrest on 17 October. Police used tear gas and water cannon as rioters clashed with officers in central Brussels.

For businesses trading on Saturday, the boards offered a way to protect their windows while keeping at least some doors open to shoppers.

#696. Gifts for Cats (and Their Owners) That Are Worth Knocking Off the Table

Cats: what would we do without them? To the cat agnostics, not to mention the cat haters, I say: don’t answer that! (Also, what’s wrong with you?) But to the cat lovers, my intended interlocutors here, I say: no need to answer, either. We both know. A catless world is a terrible thing to contemplate. No lap snuggles? No headbutts? No slow blinks? No raising of the rump to welcome a wealth of scritches? No occasional, inexplicable biting? We’d truly be lost without our fuzzy, innocent but knowing friends.

A catless world would also be devoid of a whole slew of objects and accoutrements, gadgets and doodads—some meant for cats and some for the humans obsessed with them—that turn a house into a home, or, in some cases, a living room into a giant obstacle course. There are two things I can’t resist: any item that might improve or enrich my two cats’ lives in some way (even if that perceived improvement is a pathetic fallacy that exists purely in my own mind); and any item that captures, for me, the half-sweet, half-tart character of the feline species. If there’s a special cat fanatic in your life (or a special cat!), why not treat them, this holiday season, to one of the below?

It’s never too early for the cat-loving parent to Stockholm syndrome their kids into becoming cat lovers, too, a process that might begin with stuffing the proverbial stocking with a nice cat-centric book. My daughter is now past the age of picture books, but one of her favorites, and mine, used to be “Rich Cat, Poor Cat” ($29), by the magnificent Bernard Waber (best known for his Lyle the Crocodile series), in which a scraggly street cat named Scat finds a home. Other picture books we never tired of were Jenni Desmond’s “Red Cat, Blue Cat” ($14), about two feline frenemies; “No Kiss for Mother” ($21), by Tomi Ungerer, in which a young kit refuses to play nice; and Judith Kerr’s Mog the Cat series ($36 for eight of the books). For the slightly older child, I’d suggest either Esther Averill’s fantastic “Jenny and the Cat Club” collection ($22), about the shy black cat Jenny Linsky and her community of cat friends in nineteen-forties Greenwich Village, or Ursula K. Le Guin’s “Catwings” series ($28), about a litter of flying cats. Finally, a book for adults that kids will also enjoy leafing through is “The Encyclopedia of Movie Cats” ($50), from A24.

The best gift for an actual cat is almost undoubtedly the gift of play. I love watching my cats go nuts for catnip, and these knitted cigarette-shaped catnip toys ($15 for three), for the bad-boy feline about town, are super cute. (For a healthier-looking playtime option, these felted vegetable toys, for $6, are also terrific.) Feather wands ($9) can help the rotund cat get her jumps in, but if she prefers a more brainteasing kind of exercise this tri-tier ball tower ($12) will keep her occupied. Finally, a clicker toy ($13) is my own cats’ personal favorite. Hours of fun following that little red dot . . . if only all of us were so easily amused.

Let’s face it, neither a cat tree nor a scratcher is likely to stop your cat from shedding on your furniture, or destroying it (and I have the totally clawed-down Design Within Reach sofa to prove it). Still, it’s nice to make them feel like they have their own little domain, and if this domain is aesthetically pleasing, so much the better. This rustic pearwood-and-sisal cat tree-cum-scratcher (£90) will make one’s cat look like Robinson Crusoe sleeping in a tree; this fun cherry-shaped cat tree ($136) is very Claes Oldenburg; and this mid-century-modern scratching chair ($48) will class up any joint. A plush window perch ($23) will allow a bored house cat a view of the outdoors. (I always think of this kind of contraption as a public service, since there’s nothing that makes my heart beat faster than spotting an indoor cat lounging on one while walking down the street.) And, perhaps most useful, this techy litter robot ($599) will keep one’s home odor-free.

I know, I know. Feline-themed clothing and paraphernalia can easily veer corny or “crazy cat lady,” but there’s some cool stuff out there that avoids these pitfalls. I, for one, always enjoy a good vintage Kliban shirt ($48). This nineteen-seventies Danish cat tapestry ($408) is giving Ingmar Bergman’s “Scenes from a Marriage” décor (in a good way), and drinking coffee out of this William Steig New Yorker-cover cat mug ($24) could turn a terrible morning into a good one. The cat bus from Miyazaki’s “My Neighbor Totoro” always gives me a warm, happy feeling, so falling asleep in a room illuminated by this night light ($57) seems very soothing. Another famous cartoon cat that I’m obsessed with is, of course, Garfield, and this vintage ceramic figurine ($35) takes me straight back to 1981.

There’s never enough support for the people and organizations that are helping to save cats from the mean streets of America’s cities. I live in Brooklyn, and I adopted my extremely soft black-and-white cat, Gully, from Bushwick Street Cats, a nonprofit doing fantastic work with stray cats in the area. (They also helped neuter my other cat, the grumpy but loving Gingy.) Two other great organizations near me are Flatbush Cats and Brooklyn Animal Action. I can’t imagine a nicer gift than making a donation in someone’s name to one of these charities, or the cat charity of your choice, wherever you live.

Believe it or not, I love dogs, too (though maybe not as passionately as I love cats), so I was delighted to take my editor’s note and add a few choice finds for our canine friends. Since my knowledge of dogs is much less intimate, however, I solicited the assistance of two friends. Susan Korn, who owns both an accessories brand called Susan Alexandra and a gentle senior chihuahua named Pigeon, makes fabulous hand-beaded leashes ($155) and collars ($98). Pigeon, meanwhile, recommends this dog shampoo ($98) and this human-grade dog food (a basic plan starts at roughly $1 per meal). My friend Claire Jarvis has recently found herself the owner of a large, Marmaduke-like setter named Frankie, who’s been enjoying this wand toy ($32) and this harness ($40). He’ll also “walk on water” for these freeze-dried elk treats ($30). ♦

#697. Billionaire Mukesh Ambani launches India’s biggest-ever IPO

Low-cost broadband provider Jio Platforms aims for £81bn valuation when it floats on the stock market on Wednesday

India’s second-richest man, Mukesh Ambani, is launching what could be the country’s biggest-ever initial public offering (IPO), despite a stock market downturn.

Mumbai-based Jio Platforms, a telecoms company backed by Meta Platforms and Google, is hoping to raise up to 302bn rupees (£2.4bn) and is targeting a 10.3tn rupees valuation when it floats on the stock market from Wednesday.

Set up a decade ago as a subsidiary of Ambani’s conglomerate Reliance Industries, and led by Akash Ambani, the oldest son of patriarch Mukesh, Jio offers low-cost broadband to millions of Indians.

Jio secured 212 anchor investors on Monday before its blockbuster IPO. They include some of the world’s largest fund managers, such as: BlackRock; Singapore’s sovereign wealth fund; the Abu Dhabi Investment Authority; Fidelity Investments; Schroders; JP Morgan Asset Management; Franklin Templeton; Invesco; and Prudential.

On Wednesday, shares will be offered to retail investors, and the IPO is set to close on Friday.

Reliance Industries said in a stock exchange filing last week that Jio had set a price range of 1,065 rupees to 1,119 rupees a share for its maiden share sale, offering up to 270m new shares.

The family-owned conglomerate has been encouraging its 400,000-plus employees to buy shares, offering them a discount of 54 rupees a share.

At the top end of the price range, Jio would be worth 10.3tn rupees, which would make it India’s fourth-largest company, behind its parent Reliance Industries, Bharti Airtel and HDFC Bank. It would be more than twice as much as the 4.9tn-rupee valuation in 2020, when Meta and Google invested in the company.

However, the top valuation is far below initial expectations of more than £110bn when the telecoms group posted a draft prospectus in the summer.

It comes amid a broader stock market slowdown in India, with the blue chip Nifty 5o index down more than 12% this year.

Niha Masih takes a look at the stories, ideas and news makers of modern India

Isha Ambani, who sits on Jio’s board as a director, told investors last week that the business idea was spawned by the poor connectivity she and her brother Akash faced when they returned to India on a break from studying in the US in about 2009-10. She struggled to submit a college assignment online because the internet was not working.

“What followed was a conversation about why should India be left behind,” she said. “Akash firmly believed that the answer and solution to this was creating a digital technology platform company.”
