#728. Your guide to the L.A. County Superior Court judge elections: Every competitive race

See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred

Fifteen seats on the Los Angeles County Superior Court are up for election June 2, but only 11 of the contests are competitive with two or more candidates.

Binh Q. Dang (Office 39), Ann M. Maurer (Office 60), Mariela Torres (Office 141) and Candice J. Henry (Office 196) are running unopposed for seats on the bench.

Three of the competitive seats are held by incumbents, while eight races are wide open. Candidates who earn more than 50% of the vote in the primary win the seat outright. If no candidate receives a majority, the top two vote-getters move onto the November ballot.

Of the competitive races, two are unusually contentious.

In one, a judge is seeking reelection even though he has been removed from hearing cases because of what a presiding judge deemed deteriorating mental and physical health. The candidate, however, argues that he suffers from Parkinson’s disease, which has not affected his mental fitness.

Follow live updates, analysis and highlights from 2026 election day’s key races, such as California governor, Los Angeles mayor, L.A. City Council and more.

In the other race, a longtime judge is under fire from his challenger over courtroom comments an outside commission found inappropriate, prompting admonishment. The judge says he believes the commissioners — who found no ethical or moral wrongdoing — took issue with the way he criticized litigants rather than the substance of what he actually said.

The county court system, which hears criminal cases as well as a multitude of civil matters, is vast with locations as far north as Lancaster and as far south as Catalina Island.

The Judicial Elections Evaluation Committee of the Los Angeles County Bar Assn. has rated the 28 candidates in contested races in this election. The committee’s evaluations — “exceptionally well qualified,” “well qualified,” “qualified” or “not qualified” — are included in this guide. The committee’s full report, including details about its process, is available online.

Here is our look at the candidates for each office.

California’s primary election takes place on June 2. Learn about L.A.’s city and county races and others for state offices.

Robert S. Draper, Superior Court judge Bar rating: Not qualified

Draper joined powerhouse firm O’Melveny and Myers in 1968 and made partner in 1976. He represented major national and international clients and focused on complex civil litigation, including antitrust, business disputes and other matters. He started his own firm in 2005.

In 2012, then-Gov. Jerry Brown appointed Draper to the Los Angeles County Superior Court, where he now presides over high-value business disputes and complex civil matters. Previous assignments include juvenile dependency and civil litigation.

Priorities in his courtroom include fairness and efficiency.

“That means keeping cases moving, requiring preparation from counsel, and making timely decisions so litigants are not left waiting,” he said in an email.

The election arrives as Draper, 84, faces professional scrutiny. In January, the Commission on Judicial Performance issued a 56-page inquiry, launching a proceeding that will examine whether he committed willful misconduct in office, exhibited a persistent failure or inability to perform duties, or acted with prejudicial conduct.

The seven counts include an appeals court decision invalidating a $10-million judgment reached in his courtroom. The appellate court noted that Draper made “extreme and bizarre comments” at a post-trial motions hearing and, during the trial, issued “arbitrary and capricious evidentiary rulings.”

Draper said he intended to fight the charges.

“The charges rely on statements that have been taken out of context and do not accurately reflect the record,” he told The Times, adding that the pending litigation limits his ability to respond. “I welcome a public proceeding where the facts can be fully examined and understood.

Draper, who has been working in the world of law for about six decades, is on leave from the bench. A presiding judge determined he was unfit to hear cases, mainly because of his health. Draper told The Times he has Parkinson’s disease, which does not affect his intellectual capacity to hear cases.

“Serving on the Superior Court has been the greatest honor of my professional life. I have taken that responsibility seriously every day, and I intend to defend my record and continue serving,” he said.

The Los Angeles County Bar Assn. rated him as unqualified for office, one of only three candidates across all races to receive the designation.

Tal K. Valbuena, deputy district attorney, Los Angeles County Bar rating: Qualified

Valbuena immigrated to the United States from Karachi, Pakistan in 2000. He began a career as a financial auditor but changed paths after he served as a juror and, he says on his campaign website, “I witnessed a Black man targeted because of his race and charged with murder.”

He passed the bar in 2014, worked on civil litigation at a law firm and in 2016 became an L.A. County prosecutor. After handling general felonies and misdemeanors in the adult criminal and juvenile courts, he was assigned in 2022 to the Mental Health Division.

“I have worked extensively with issues of competency, insanity and mentally disordered offenders, requiring close collaboration with medical experts and careful application of nuanced legal standards,” he said in an email.

Priorities include ensuring access to justice within the courtroom, partly by “being attentive to language and cultural barriers.”

Valbuena is the treasurer of the Southern California chapter of the South Asian Bar Assn., sits on the L.A. County LGBTQ+ Commission and teaches a college course on legal rights.

Angie Christides, L.A. County deputy district attorney Bar rating: Qualified

Christides has more than two decades of experience as a deputy district attorney, according to her campaign website. She spent eight years — five in the Hardcore Gang Investigation Unit — conducting serious felony trials, primarily in Compton. Her case log includes more than 25 murder trials and two death penalty cases.

Christides previously served in the Long Beach Superior Court, where she ran the veterans court program, reviewing requests for alternative sentencing and mental health diversion petitions.

“I have seen firsthand how the justice system affects everyone involved — victims, defendants and families alike — and that perspective informs my approach to every case,” she said in an email.

Priorities include bridging a trust gap between the public and the legal system. She aims to improve “access to justice,” partly by reducing “unnecessary delays.”

To illustrate her point, she recalled being assigned murder cases a decade old before reaching trial.

Outside of work, Christides teaches yoga and surfing to underprivileged youth.

Irene Lee, L.A. County deputy district attorney Bar rating: Well qualified

Lee launched her legal career in 2007 as a clerk in the district attorney’s Organized Crime Division, primarily prosecuting hate crimes.

The following year, she became a deputy district attorney, focused on domestic violence and child abuse cases.

In 2021, she joined the county counsel, assigned to Juvenile Dependency Court.

She served as a legal adviser to the county Sheriff’s Department and last year became a special assistant to Dist. Atty. Nathan Hochman. Her duties include recruiting, a new hires diversity panel and a fentanyl awareness campaign.

Lee’s priorities include expanding civic engagement and language accessibility, with an aim to demystify legal proceedings for students and nonnative English speakers. She hopes to bolster collaboration between the criminal and juvenile dependency systems, writing, “I have seen how families often navigate these systems simultaneously, yet the systems rarely communicate with one another.”

She volunteers in a fifth-grade classroom through the Project LEAD legal education program and is president of the Korean Prosecutors Assn.

Francisco ‘Frank’ Amador, attorney Bar rating: Not qualified

Amador, a bankruptcy attorney, did not respond to interview requests. He won admission to the bar in 2001 and, according to his campaign website, served as a U.S. Marine and police officer.

“I promise to do a good job and serve the community in a neutral and unbiased manner,” he states on his site.

Under the name Frank Amador, he ran for and lost a Los Angeles County Superior Court judicial seat in 2022. As Francisco Amador, he failed in a 2024 run for a judgeship in Imperial County.

Maria Ghobadi, L.A. County deputy district attorney Bar rating: Well qualified

As a child, Ghobadi and her family fled Iran during the Islamic Revolution, settling in Southern California.

In 2007, she joined the San Joaquin County district attorney’s office, where she prosecuted misdemeanors and felonies and later served in the Domestic Violence and Child Abduction units.

In 2015, she joined the Los Angeles County district attorney’s office, where she handles complex murder and other cases in the Gang Homicide Division.

Last year, she prosecuted a man accused of killing a 13-year-old boy who was waiting for his mother to finish work at a Pico Rivera gas station.

Ghobadi has completed 21 homicide trials, 85 jury trials and more than 1,500 preliminary hearings.

Her priorities are ensuring dignity and respect in the courtroom and effective time management.

“Unnecessary delays or cases that languish in the system can undermine both due process and access to justice,” she said.

She has served as a board member at Saddleback Community College in Mission Viejo and the Waymakers Foundation and volunteered in a fifth-grade classroom through Project LEAD. She volunteered in free health clinics in college.

Rhonda A. Haymon, L.A. County deputy public defender Bar rating: Qualified

Most of Haymon’s 26-year legal career has been in the public defender’s office, handling juvenile and adult cases that range from petty theft to homicide.

“I have tried over 100 jury trials and have lost only four,” she said, adding that one loss was later overturned.

The Southern California native also has been assigned to the restorative justice drug court and the Law Enforcement Accountability and Integrity Unit, where she consulted on police misconduct cases.

She taught for six years as an adjunct professor at Southwestern Law School and serves on its Women in Leadership board.

Haymon ran for a judicial seat in 2024, losing to incumbent Judge Lynn Diane Olson. The electoral challenge followed a courtroom conflict in which Olson held Haymon in contempt. Haymon contends the judge misused her power and that the State Bar imposed no corrective measures following a review.

“Their decision to take no action speaks volumes,” Haymon told The Times.

The experience taught her “what it feels like to not have equal access to justice.” Ensuring such courtroom access would be a priority for her.

Justin Allen Clayton, L.A. County public defender Bar rating: Qualified

A Los Angeles native who attended public schools, Clayton earned his law license in 2012. In a decade as a public defender, he’s handled more than 1,000 adult and hundreds of juvenile cases.

He has served as deputy in charge of the Inglewood branch since 2023, he says, functioning as a “working supervisor” who conducts arraignments, appears on behalf of defendants at hearings and oversees and trains attorneys on case preparation, trial strategy and a client’s competency to stand trial.

He would improve court efficiency with clear calendaring practices and firm and fair deadline enforcement.

“By encouraging meaningful settlement discussions where appropriate and ensuring that all parties are prepared, I would reduce unnecessary delays while protecting each litigant’s right to be heard,” he said.

Chellei G. Jimenez, attorney Bar rating: Qualified

Jimenez opened a family law practice in Palmdale more than two decades ago, handling divorce, custody, spousal and child support, workers’ compensation, personal injury and other civil matters. Clients range from technology professionals and stay-at-home parents to military families and the LGBTQ+ community, she said.

“I have represented thousands of clients in complex family law cases that dealt with domestic violence and child custody,” she said in an email.

A priority is enhancing court efficiency with Zoom and other remote capabilities. She aims to expand access to justice “by supporting funding that allows more self-represented litigants to utilize Los Angeles County’s Self-Help Centers.”

In addition to her career, Jimenez has served as a mentor in a State Bar program that provides oversight and guidance to provisionally licensed lawyers. She’s scored high school mock trial competitions since 2015.

Samuel Wolloch Krause, attorney/legal author Bar rating: Qualified

A partner at Hall Benefits Law, Krause specializes in the federal Employee Retirement Income Security Act, executive compensation, employee benefits, fiduciary and tax matters.

He has worked for an international law firm and, according to his campaign website, served as chief legal officer and general counsel for California Schools VEBA, a public employee benefits organization. Krause has contributed to three books on law and volunteered as a temporary Superior Court judge.

His decision to run for office was propelled by a 2023 spinal cord injury and two-year recovery.

“Learning to live with a disability has helped me to better understand, on a personal level, some of the issues faced by marginalized communities with respect to access to the justice system,” he said in an email. “I want to take this and everything I have learned over my career and put it to work helping make the system better.”

His priorities would be improving accessibility and efficiency and ensuring that everyone “is treated fairly, respectfully and without bias.”

Anna Slotky Reitano, deputy county counsel Bar rating: Qualified

Reitano won admission to the bar in 2009 and worked for over 10 years in the public defender’s office. She spent three years representing juvenile clients, primarily felonies as well as some drug cases, followed by five years working on adult felony trials, serving mostly indigent defendants.

When representing those without means, she focused on “mental health diversion and treatment to support rehabilitation in cases where the client was amenable,” she said in an email.

In May 2024, she joined the Justice and Safety Division of the county counsel’s office, where she supervises civil litigation and advises county departments.

She would prioritize maintaining trust in the legal system, tapping into her experience in defense, prosecution and civil litigation. She aims to enhance “access to justice” by ensuring clear communication and the consistent availability of interpreters.

Reitano said her approach is informed by having a brother with schizophrenia.

“This has given me a deeper understanding of both the challenges individuals and families face and the ways in which the system can fall short in addressing those needs,” she said.

She lost a run for a judicial seat in 2022.

Ben ‘Benny’ Forer, deputy district attorney Bar rating: Well qualified

Forer has spent most of two decades in the Cyber Crime Division, according to his campaign website, where he is lead prosecutor. He’s worked in the felony trials and mental health units. And he teaches a cyber law and privacy class at USC’s engineering school, writes legal textbooks and gives lectures to law enforcement agencies, including the Secret Service, nationwide.

His priorities are a fair, patient and accessible courtroom and utilizing his expertise in technology, cyber law and the 4th (unreasonable searches) and 5th (due process) amendments.

“I would use that background to handle digital‑evidence questions thoughtfully and consistently, so that cases involving phones, apps and online activity are resolved on the actual facts and law, not confusion about the technology,” he said.

Forer is an ordained rabbi who mentors clerks and others entering the legal field. His website details working with psychologists and psychiatrists to craft diversion programs and treatment plans for “justice-involved people with mental illness.”

Cheryl C. Turner, attorney Bar rating: Qualified

Turner passed the bar in 1987, clerked as an extern for a U.S. District Court judge and worked at a firm on class-action lawsuits.

She later established her own practice, where she mostly handles civil litigation, including real estate, land use, zoning and development. In addition, she takes wrongful termination and other employment cases, banking and finance litigation, and criminal defense. Turner also serves as a temporary Superior Court judge.

Fairness and accountability are her campaign priorities.

“I will ensure that all parties, regardless of their background or status, fully understand the legal process and what they are facing,” she said.

In 2021, she became board chair of the Apartment Assn. of Greater Los Angeles.

She previously ran unsuccessfully for the state Senate and Assembly.

Dan Kapelovitz, attorney/experimental filmmaker Bar rating: Qualified

A former features editor at Hustler magazine, Kapelovitz became a lawyer in 2009. He joined a corporate law firm, clerked for a federal judge and worked for the city attorney before founding his criminal defense practice in 2013.

Kapelovitz focuses on felony defense, though he handles “everything from disturbing the peace to murder” for a client base that is 90% indigent. He provides pro bono representation in animal-rights cases.

Ending a “two-tiered system” in which affluent and poor clients often have different results, especially when it comes to attaining bail, and eliminating courtroom bias are among his campaign priorities.

“Most judges are good, but too many of them are biased either toward the prosecution or the defense,” he said.

Kapelovitz’s ballot designation references his experimental films, which include 2012’s “Triple Fisher: The Lethal Lolitas of Long Island.”

This is at least Kapelovitz’s fourth try for office, following failed runs for L.A. County district attorney in 2024, state attorney general in 2022 and governor in the 2021 recall campaign.

David Walgren, Superior Court judge Bar rating: Exceptionally well qualified

Los Angeles native Walgren earned his law degree in 1995 and began work as a deputy district attorney.

Over 17 years, he rose through specialized units, including the Hardcore Gang and Major Crimes divisions, where, in 2011, he won the involuntary manslaughter conviction of Dr. Conrad Murray, who prescribed the propofol that led to Michael Jackson‘s overdose death.

The Los Angeles County Bar Assn. named Walgren prosecutor of the year in 2012, the same year then-Gov. Jerry Brown appointed him to serve on the Superior Court.

Walgren said his top courtroom priority is ensuring that cases are handled fairly and efficiently, with timely decisions.

“I run a disciplined courtroom and focus on applying the law consistently so that outcomes are based on the facts, not delay or confusion,” he said in an email.

A related aim is maintaining confidence in the system with respect.

“When the court is fair, efficient and respectful, the system works the way it is supposed to,” he said.

Anthony ‘A.J.’ Bayne, L.A. County deputy public defender Bar rating: Well qualified

Bayne’s three-decade career has been dominated by 25 years as a deputy public defender. He started with misdemeanors and moved up the ranks to “special circumstances” cases in which defendants face enhanced sentences, including the death penalty.

He spent 19 years in the Compton Courthouse, including supervising misdemeanor trial deputies as deputy in charge.

Bayne is an inventor, with patent-pending applications for artificial intelligence tools designed to aid attorneys with workflow automation. That work feeds into one of his campaign priorities: leveraging AI and technology to address heavy caseloads.

“I would actively engage with court administration and the judicial council to identify where technology can reduce friction, and I would be a vocal advocate for modernizing court infrastructure,” he said in an email.

Easing case backlogs, which can result in extended pretrial detention for defendants, is another priority. He would identify and address “systemic bottlenecks that delay resolution.”

Outside of work, he practices jiujitsu and is trained in the self-defense techniques of Krav Maga.

David DeJute, law professor/attorney Bar rating: Qualified

DeJute started as a litigator with law firms 35 years ago, followed by nearly a decade as vice president of litigation at Sony Pictures Entertainment.

In 2005, he became an assistant U.S. attorney, serving for 11 years and handling 10 trials. He successfully defended President Obama against “birther” lawsuits challenging his eligibility to hold office.

DeJute joined Michelman and Robinson in 2017, working in the complex litigation group.

His priorities on the bench would be to uphold the rule of law and ensure due process.

“I have experienced discrimination, which I abhor when directed to me or to anyone else,” said DeJute, who is gay. “Every person deserves to be heard and treated with dignity and respect.”

The son of a judge, DeJute teaches as an adjunct law professor at Pepperdine University, where he and others provide free legal services to victims of the Palisades and Eaton fires.

Sharee Sanders Gordon, L.A. deputy city attorney Bar rating: Qualified

A onetime elementary school teacher in Watts, Gordon entered law school after seeing how violence impacted her students. She has been a deputy city attorney for more than a quarter-century. In 2002, she helped launch the Neighborhood Prosecutor Program, working with the L.A. Police Department’s 77th Street station.

After an assignment directing the city attorney’s prostitution diversion project, she spent 10 years leading the Neighborhood School Safety Program, which works with police and community groups to protect L.A. Unified campuses.

She started in the city attorney’s filing division, where she files an array of misdemeanor cases and trains police on filing guidelines, in 2023. Gordon has served as a temporary judge in the Superior Court and has been a mock trial judge for student competitions.

Her priorities are ensuring fair and impartial justice and enhancing trust.

“My career has been grounded in service,” Gordon said in an email. “I understand that trust in the judicial system is developed when communities feel seen, heard and protected.”

Pat Connolly, Superior Court judge Bar rating: Well qualified

Connolly, the son of a police chief, started as a prosecutor working on homicides and gang-related matters, which he termed “the most serious cases in the system.” That includes the 2008 conviction of a man who killed an off-duty sheriff’s deputy.

Later that year, Connolly won a Superior Court seat in what he calls a “high volume” courtroom. His duties include running a program that offers treatment to qualified individuals as an alternative to incarceration.

“The court system only works if cases move,” he said. “That requires a judge who is willing to take responsibility, keep things on track and apply the law without hesitation.”

Connolly has been admonished three times by the California Commission on Judicial Performance, most recently in 2021, for two incidents. In one, the commission found that he “displayed improper demeanor” to two attorneys early in the pandemic. In the other, he was faulted for an “inappropriate remark” when he told an acquitted defendant the verdict was “a gift from God because there’s no question in my mind that you’re guilty of this crime.”

In an interview with The Times, Connolly defended his comments. In the former instance, he rejected an assertion that he had spoken sarcastically to the attorneys and said they asked him to release defendants facing serious charges “without providing the paperwork to back up their claims.”

In the latter, he said he did not impugn the jurors — who were not present — but was advising the just-acquitted defendant to stay out of trouble.

“At no point in time did I mean, or was it my intent, to disparage a jury,” Connolly said. “It was to try and make a difference. Perhaps I should have said it differently, but what I said I meant, and I mean it today.”

Outside the courtroom, he coaches youth flag football.

Thompson is now assigned to the Major Crimes Division, where he focuses on prosecuting murder and cold cases.

He said in an email he is running “because I believe that judges should serve humbly and follow the laws, not fight them, particularly more recent laws dealing with reducing prison overcrowding and granting diversion.”

He has also been highly critical of his opponent, alleging Connolly’s supporters applied undue pressure to a judge who endorsed him. Connolly was not accused of having anything to do with the matter and declined to discuss it with The Times. However, Thompson alleged that his supporter received career-related threats from those in support of his opponent.

Dammeier began in law enforcement, working for a decade as a dispatcher, jailer and police officer. He went to law school and, for a quarter-century, represented police and other public-sector unions, “handling employee rights cases at every level from administrative hearings to the U.S. Supreme Court,” he said in an email.

In 2013, The Times reported, a law firm in which he was a named partner dissolved after two Costa Mesa City Council members sued one of his clients, the city police union, over legal and political tactics the politicians asserted were overly aggressive.

Dammeier recently said his team was the focus of “antiunion attacks by political forces” and said that after multiple investigations, none of the firm’s attorneys faced charges or disciplinary action.

#729. Russia frees jailed American Stephen Hubbard during Witkoff talks

During talks between Vladimir Putin and Steve Witkoff, Putin announced that jailed American Stephen Hubbard had been released. The Kremlin also said Russia was "in principle" ready to resume trilateral talks next month.

Russian President Vladimir Putin announced the release of US captive Stephen Hubbard during talks with US special envoy Steve Witkoff in St. Petersburg on Wednesday.

Hubbard had been taken captive by Russian forces on charges of being a mercenary, which he denies. He was sentenced to seven years in prison at a closed trial in 2024.

Putin said Hubbard was at the airport and Witkoff said he was now "going home to his family."

US President Donald Trump later said he had made the request directly to Putin during a phone call last week.

"The United States, out of respect for President Trump, was not required to give anything in return — an unprecedented situation for Russia," Trump claimed in a post on his Truth Social platform. "There was no 'swap' necessary for this release."

However, in a follow-up post, Trump also claimed that "numerous people" had called him to apologize after they criticized him for suspending a new round of sanctions, which he said was a necessary concession.

"If sanctions would have been placed, certainly those negotiations would have come to a complete and total halt," Trump's post said.

The release of Hubbard was seen as a goodwill gesture to the Trump administration as the two sides discuss a deal for peace between Russia and Ukraine.

"We've brought some papers. It's really some ideas, some sort of peace deal between Russia and Ukraine, and you'll read that at your leisure," Witkoff told Putin.

After the talks, the Kremlin said Witkoff's proposals "lacked substance" and would not be of real use for a potential peace settlement.

However, Putin agreed "in principle" to resume peace talks with Russian, Ukrainian and US delegates after November 10.

Such talks should focus on "building a security system for Russia and Ukraine after the conflict ends," Putin's foreign affairs adviser Yuri Ushakov said.

Putin also proposed that Witkoff discuss the restoration of bilateral ties between Washington and Moscow.

Meanwhile, Putin appeared open to a potential trilateral meeting with Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Beijing.

"A possible first-ever meeting of the leaders of China, Russia and the United States... is being prepared," Ushakov said.

The meeting — the ninth such talks between Witkoff and Putin — came a day after Witkoff met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Norway.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz also said on Wednesday that Berlin was supporting Ukraine to end the war as quickly as possible, adding that any capitulation by Ukraine would be "a capitulation by all of us."

The Ukrainian leader remained in Oslo on Wednesday where met with lawmakers in the Norwegian parliament.

#731. Trump tells Axios why he endorsed Netanyahu's reelection

President Trump endorsed Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Sunday, just nine days before Israel's Oct. 27 elections.

Why it matters: Trump's decision to weigh in nine days ahead of the election could give Netanyahu a boost at a critical moment in the Israeli leader's fight for political survival, with most polls showing his coalition falling short of the 61 seats needed to form a government.

  • This is the first time in the history of the U.S.–Israel relations that a U.S. president explicitly and publicly endorsed a candidate in the Israeli elections.

What he is saying: In a Sunday post on Truth Social, Trump called Netanyahu "a Great Warrior Prime Minister" and a "great partner" in the war against Iran.

  • "If Israel has the wrong Leader, which would be anyone other than Bibi, America will have to do this work [in Iran] ourselves, and I am not inclined to do so," Trump wrote.
  • Trump called Netanyahu "the kind of Partner that the United States of America is demanding of Israel" and gave him his "Complete and Total Endorsement."

Behind the scenes: Trump began planning his endorsement earlier this week.

  • "I was always going to do that. I just didn't want to do it too soon," Trump told Axios in a short phone interview on Sunday.
  • Trump said he endorsed Netanyahu because they have a "good relationship" and would "continue to do well" together if Netanyahu is reelected.
  • "It is important that Israel has a person they can count on," Trump said.
  • Asked if he could work with another Israeli leader, Trump said: "Maybe I will, maybe I won't. Who wants to take the chance?"

The other side: Netanyahu thanked Trump for his endorsement in an X post.

  • "Together we will complete the mission," Netanyahu wrote.
  • Netanyahu's main rival, Gadi Eisenkot, told Israel's Channel 12 that he respects the U.S. president and appreciates what he has done for Israel.
  • "But the elections are a domestic Israeli issue. The only ones who will decide are the citizens of Israel, and I will stand firm on this," Eisenkot said.

The big picture: Trump had repeatedly declined to endorse Netanyahu in recent months amid growing tensions between the two leaders over Iran and Gaza.

  • ⁠Some of Netanyahu's rivals urged Trump to remain neutral, Axios previously reported.
  • Some of Trump's closest advisers believed his Middle East agenda would fare better if Netanyahu lost and a different government formed.
  • Trump himself has been very frustrated with Netanyahu, including in recent weeks.
  • In private conversations, Trump blamed Netanyahu for Israel's failures to prevent the Oct. 7 Hamas attacks. Trump called the prime minister "his own worst enemy" and questioned whether Netanyahu was damaging Israel's international reputation, according to two people who have discussed the matter directly with the president.
  • However, Trump decided to stick with Netanyahu.

Driving the news: Netanyahu and Trump discussed two weeks ago the possibility of launching a major new operation against Iran before the Israeli and U.S. elections, Axios reported.

  • Trump initially seemed to be leaning toward accepting Netanyahu's proposal and resuming attacks, but he grew more hesitant and decided to wait until after the elections.
  • In his endorsement, Trump seemed to suggest he would let Netanyahu strike Iran after the midterm elections, saying "we will soon finish the job."

Peltola and her family sustained minor injuries after a driver struck the car transporting group to campaign stop

Mary Peltola, a Democrat who is running for Alaska’s lone US Senate seat, and her family suffered minor injuries in a car crash while driving to a campaign stop on Saturday, her campaign said.

The family was on its way to the Alaska Federation of Natives annual banquet when another vehicle crashed into the one transporting Peltola and her family, her campaign said in a statement on Sunday. Peltola required medical attention after the collision.

“Mary and her family sustained minor injuries but are in good spirits,” Cheryl Bruce, Peltola’s campaign manager, said in a statement. “Unfortunately, per the advice of medical professionals, Mary’s upcoming events in Fairbanks and Bethel will be rescheduled for later in the week as she takes time to recover.”

Bruce added: “Mary is disappointed that the accident is delaying the start of her Alaska Always tour, and she is eager to get back on the campaign trail to speak directly with Alaskans about her plan to take on the rigged system and lower costs for working families.”

Police responded to a “multi-vehicle collision” at about 6.55pm on Saturday, according to the Anchorage police department. Peltola’s family and the occupant of a second vehicle were taken to a local hospital “with non-life-threatening injuries”, according to the authorities, while the occupant of a third vehicle refused medical transport.

“The circumstances of the collision are under investigation,” reads a statement from the police department.

Peltola, an Alaska Native and former congresswoman, is challenging Republican incumbent senator Dan Sullivan, hoping to become the first Democrat in nearly two decades to represent the state in the Senate. Both candidates have tried to rally support from Alaska Native voters, a key constituency in the high-stakes race that has become one of the most watched in the nation.

On Friday, Donald Trump ordered the justice department to block the certification of the Senate election in Alaska if Sullivan loses. The lawsuit cites potential confusion with another Republican candidate who is listed on the ranked-choice ballot as Daniel J Sullivan Jr, who is a retired schoolteacher.

#733. Bill Irwin Is the O.G. Clown

Seldom does the theatre adequately address the topic of enemas. But Molière’s “The Imaginary Invalid,” which Bill Irwin has adapted and is starring in on Broadway, will serve all your peristaltic needs: Irwin’s hypochondriacal title character encounters a syringe the size of a submachine gun. “Molière pushes the envelope,” Irwin said the other day, on a park bench in Union Square, where he and his wife, Martha, and their Ridgeback mix, Zelda, had just dropped off their compost. “I worry that we might have too many enema references, though.”

Irwin typically skews self-deprecatory in conversation. He first came on most people’s radars through his baggy-pants clowning on Broadway and, later, on “Sesame Street,” as Mr. Noodle, radiating a kind of doomed naïveté. “In clowning, there’s a paradigm,” he said. “Chaplin and Keaton and Harold Lloyd—the young guy who’s going to make it in life, or who’s going to impress his mother or girlfriend.” He went on, “But you get a little older, and you realize, I don’t do that anymore. I’m no use to that genre anymore.” Irwin, who is seventy-six, had on sneakers and a loose blue jacket. As his recent roles suggest, he is better served performing the catalyst or the antagonist. In “The Imaginary Invalid,” his character is trying to marry his daughter off to a doctor against her will. In this summer’s “The Odyssey,” as the Cyclops, he prays to his father, Poseidon, to curse Odysseus and his men after they’ve broken into his cave, blinded him, and, as Irwin put it, “fucked with my cheese.”

When Irwin first met with the film’s director, Christopher Nolan, to discuss playing the Cyclops, he asked if he’d be wearing a mask. “Chris said, ‘Probably.’ He didn’t know yet. He often doesn’t know.” In Nolan’s 2014 film, “Interstellar,” Irwin voiced and did much of the puppetry behind TARS, the robot that resembles an enormous metallic KitKat bar. For “The Odyssey,” Irwin, wearing full-body makeup and prosthetics, shot with a thirty-six-foot-tall puppet in a cave in Greece and in a miniature mockup of the cave in Culver City. “Tom Holland said Chris was the most meticulously prepared shoot-from-the-hip director he’d ever worked with,” he recalled.

Irwin initially told Nolan that he might be too old to play the Cyclops. (“You need a guy who doesn’t need kneepads.”) He had no such anxieties with “The Imaginary Invalid”: Molière, who played the title role himself in 1673, wrote the play while he was in a tubercular decline, creating a part in which he could cough a lot while staying in character. Irwin was not rattled by the fact that Molière died after his fourth performance. Asked how his own health is, Irwin replied, “It is a daily question. But good, I think.” He added, “Martha and I ride Citi Bikes, and I’m a more law-abiding cyclist than I normally would be.”

He was pleased to hear, from his “Imaginary Invalid” co-star Rachel Bloom, the co-creator and star of TV’s “Crazy Ex-Girlfriend,” that clowning is huge in L.A. these days. “She said that the same young guys who, eighteen months ago, would have used a different label—‘improv’ or something—are now all ‘I’m hard-core clown,’ ” he noted. His years in the trenches have fostered compassion: “I have great sympathy for anyone who has signed on to be Ronald McDonald. He’s the least tuned-in-to-clown-history example of clowning. I learned at the Ringling school that the lower lip is the expressive lip. Like, tonight, when I do the show, I’ll go”—he twisted his lower lip—“because that’s the one that defines the expression. Ronald McDonald’s makeup is all upper lip, and that’s why he’s kind of frozen-looking.”

He talked about losing himself in a role. “When I watch myself, there’s usually more of me than I’d like there to be,” he said. Many of his roles feature an element of absence—from his early work as a silent clown to the strangled emotion he brought to assorted Beckett projects to his Tony-winning turn as George in “Who’s Afraid of Virginia Woolf?” What he holds back is what defines him. When a passerby in the park—a former colleague—called out, “Bill! I saw you!,” Irwin replied, “Hey, man! Did you come? You dog, you.”

Confused, the man asked, “What do you mean?”

“No, I mean, I saw you just now. I haven’t seen you in decades.”

#735. Child health in England at risk from sharp rise in NHS waiting times, report says

CQC research finds long delays are making conditions harder to treat and highlights regional disparities in care

Thousands of children in England are experiencing some of the sharpest rises in waiting times for healthcare in the history of the NHS, a report has revealed.

While some adult waiting times have improved, children and young people are being “hit hardest” amid soaring demand and falling numbers of staff, according to the annual state of care report by the Care Quality Commission.

In community health services alone, 80,000 children and young people have been waiting more than a year for an appointment – almost 11 times the number of adults, the report said. Experts said that was “wholly unacceptable”. Children’s health conditions were getting worse and becoming harder to treat as a result, they added.

More broadly across health and social care services in England there were signs of improvement, including more GP appointments, increased use of digital solutions and shorter waits for elective care. The report also highlighted examples of local innovation, including neighbourhood models and integrated care teams.

But improvements were struggling to keep pace with rapidly rising demand for health and social care. In many areas, including mental health services, patients’ needs are also becoming more complex.

Persistent inequalities across the entire health and care system mean people’s experience of care is fractured and heavily dependent on where they live and who they are, according to the report.

Across all areas of the country and every part of the health and social care system, there was “unwarranted variation” in access to services, quality of care and outcomes, the CQC said.

Some adults with cancer were waiting far too long to begin treatment after being diagnosed, while there remained “sustained pressure” in urgent and emergency care.

But the report highlighted how children in particular were bearing the brunt of long waiting times. And, despite growing demand, health visitor and school nurse numbers were “continuing to decline”, the CQC said.

It also raised concerns about regional variations in rates of children being admitted to hospital for diabetes and asthma, and sounded the alarm over particularly high rates of rotten teeth among children in some areas.

Dr Ronny Cheung, of the Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health, said community health services existed to support some of the country’s most vulnerable children outside hospital, including those with complex conditions, developmental disorders and safeguarding needs.

“Yet these children face some of the longest waits in the NHS, while waiting times for adult community services have improved. It is wholly unacceptable that more than one in four children still wait over a year for treatment, and without urgent action, too many more will be left to suffer unnecessarily.

“As a paediatrician, I am sick of seeing children wait so long for support that they miss crucial opportunities to improve their health and development.”

Behind the figures were children struggling at school, families pushed to breaking point and conditions becoming more complex while they wait, Cheung added.

The CQC chair, Julia Neuberger, said that while some health and social care services were “working well”, improvements were not keeping pace with demand. “To repair a fracturing system, there must be a collective response,” she added.

The Department of Health and Social Care said the report showed “the scale of the challenge this government inherited” when it was elected in 2024. “While the CQC recognises signs of progress on waiting lists, cancer care and general practice, patients and families rightly expect faster improvements – which is why the secretary of state has committed to go further to end corridor care, transform support for mothers and children, and deliver a new national care service,” a spokesperson added.

“We are very close,” the 20-year-old Italian, who would become the sport’s youngest-ever champion, said after his win in Austin. “We try to finish on a high and hopefully we can clinch it very soon,” Antonelli said.

#739. Behind Elon Musk's plans for a mega-merger of SpaceX and Tesla

This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here.

See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred

One company makes electric cars that are inherently terrestrial, ferrying millions of drivers on roads around the world. The other shoots rockets into space and has aspirations to make it to Mars. At first glance, they would seem like an odd pairing.

Yet, this week Elon Musk said that aerospace firm SpaceX and EV carmaker Tesla — two trailblazing companies he built and serves over as chief executive — were considering a tie-up, confirming speculation that what would be the biggest corporate merger ever is a real possibility.

And like much else on Wall Street, the driving force apparently is artificial intelligence, including demands for massive infrastructure spending to support its vast computing power.

Although Tesla’s best-selling Model Y and Model 3 require drivers to get behind the wheel, the company has developed an autonomous ride-hailing vehicle called a Cybercab with no human controls that has just begun pilot testing. Musk sees it and a robot called Optimus as keys to the future of Tesla, which will rely on vast cloud computing power that it and SpaceX already are developing together.

“This is a strategic no brainer for Musk and the SpaceX ecosystem to merge with Tesla,” analyst Dan Ives, a partner Yorkville Ives & Co., said in a statement.

But even if the deal makes strategic sense, there are myriad practical challenges in combining two trillion-dollar companies with vastly different operations — as well as regulatory concerns that are not just domestic, but also probably will include China and Europe. Shareholders of both companies would have to approve the deal.

After years of delays, Elon Musk demonstrated the new Tesla Roadster in Texas on Thursday. Production won’t actually begin until 2028.

SpaceX, which was founded in 2002 in El Segundo and moved its headquarters from Hawthorne to Texas in 2024, is a rocketry pioneer that has become the world’s dominant launch provider though it has limited domestic operations in a handful of states.

By contrast, Tesla, which still operates its original factory in Fremont, Calif., assembled 1.65 million cars, as well as some trucks, in the U.S., China and Germany last year, employing more than 100,000 workers.

Musk disclosed the proposed merger during a call with analysts Tuesday while discussing SpaceX’s third-quarter financial results, which surpassed Wall Street estimates for all its business lines, including rocket launches, its Starlink internet satellite business and AI, which includes renting computer power to other AI companies.

“There’s a lot to be gained from cooperating on developing superintelligence software,” Musk said.

The tech mogul stressed that it was far from a done deal, noting that each company’s board formed a special committee to consider the matter. He is not participating due to his conflicts of interest, owning shares of both companies.

“I think some people out there assume that a SpaceX and Tesla merger is a certainty, and I think that would be overstating it,” Musk said. “Do I think it would be a good idea? Yes, but at the end of the day, the shareholders have to be supportive of this.”

Shares of SpaceX closed up 3% on Wednesday to $386.47, while Tesla shares rose even more, up nearly 8% to $159.31.

The gains added $64 billion to Musk’s net worth, which ended the day at $989 billion. He was the world’s first trillionaire for a time this year, after SpaceX’s June 12 initial offering, before the stock slumped.

Merging SpaceX, with its $2.15-trillion market cap, with Tesla, valued at $1.53 trillion, would almost certainly result in the largest ever corporate merger , exceeding Vodafone’s roughly $200-billion buyout of German conglomerate Mannesmann in 2000.

The stage for the possible marriage was set this year when SpaceX acquired Musk’s privately held xAI company in a $1.25-trillion deal that brought the AI company’s assets to the rocket maker.

Ever the showman, Musk also seemed to presage the merger last week with the unveiling of Tesla’s new superfast Roadster, which has yet to be released but was specially outfitted with SpaceX booster rockets to perform flips in midair on a livestream.

Dan Levy, a Barclays analyst, said the rationale for the merger clearly lies in what he calls an “AI vertical integration play” in which Tesla’s vehicles, robotaxis and robots would benefit from SpaceX’s now formidable AI infrastructure, including its Grok large language model AI platform.

Elon Musk’s announcement that he’s moving SpaceX headquarters to Texas could present a blow to Hawthorne and the Southern California space economy that it helped to revive.

Tesla’s vehicles also could use SpaceX’s Starlink satellite network for connectivity and its robotaxis would benefit from xAI’s fleet management software while SpaceX’s data centers could potentially benefit from Tesla’s solar products business, among some synergies. Also noteworthy is that the two companies are jointly developing a $17-billion AI chip plant in Texas.

“While we suspect there would be some financial synergies, the true value would be in vertical integration,” Levy said in an Oct. 14 note.

Eric Talley, a corporate law, governance and finance expert at Columbia Law School, said other practical considerations may be at play, including the challenges Musk faces running both companies separately while developing joint strategic initiatives.

“Mr. Musk has been trying simultaneously to run two fairly significant, actually enormous companies that were moving closer and closer to one another,” he said. “There has always been this kind of apprehension … how many of the new exciting things were going to be done inside SpaceX versus how many of Mr. Musk’s new exciting things were going to be done inside Tesla.”

Another impetus for the merger plans might be the sales struggles Tesla has been experiencing and the vast technological challenges from robotaxi competitors such as Waymo.

Tesla’s electric vehicle business is slowing, weighed down by competition from China, the loss of federal EV tax credits last year and declining support for green vehicles under the Trump administration — even as the recent surge in gas prices is renewing interest for the vehicles among consumers.

Tesla’s vehicle deliveries increased slightly from the second quarter, with just over 486,000 new vehicles delivered in the third quarter. Still, that’s down from 497,000 in the third quarter a year earlier, with EVs making up only around 6% of new vehicle sales in the U.S.

“Elon needs something that is forward indicating for Tesla, and selling more electric cars isn’t it,” said Karl Brauer, an auto analyst at iSeeCars.com. “He was obviously trying to tie the two companies together with the quote-unquote flying car last week.”

The merger would give Tesla more breathing room as it spends billions on developing its robotaxis and autonomous driving technology, while positioning the company as a technological leader working on cutting-edge technologies that would shape the future.

“I think self-driving tech is the most important thing for Tesla to solve in its current form,” Brauer said. “If it’s tied to SpaceX ... they can share expenses and they become one big company.”

Although it’s unclear what form a merger would take, analysts see SpaceX, with its larger market capitalization, acquiring Tesla at some sort of premium to satisfy shareholders in the automaker, whose share of the combined mega company would be diluted.

Musk might also personally favor that scenario because he owns 48% of SpaceX’s stock, but has 82% of the voting power through a dual-class structure. If SpaceX acquired Tesla, the class structure would remain in place, with Musk owning 37% of the shares of the combined company while retaining 56% of the voting power, according to Levy’s calculations.

SpaceX is seeking to sell 555 million shares at $135 each, raising $75 billion and valuing the rocket maker at $1.77 trillion — making it one of the largest public companies.

“It would result in a much higher voting share of the combined company for Musk,” he wrote.

However, even if Tesla’s shareholders were to approve the merger, there are potentially regulatory hurdles abroad.

In Europe, where governments are worried about the threat posed by Russia after its invasion of Ukraine, officials may view an even larger SpaceX with trepidation. That concern has been heightened after reports that the military grade version of Starlink, called Starshield, that Ukraine relies upon for its operations, was temporarily slowed down last week, Talley said.

Musk has denied any involvement, but the Wall Street Journal has reported he might have ordered the slowdown after political tension between the White House and Ukranian President Volodymyr Zelensky.

“Europe is simultaneously dealing with their own security concerns about an increasingly aggressive Russia and whether a larger version of SpaceX and Tesla could be even more threatening,” Talley said.

Similarly, Chinese authorities might be concerned that a full integration of Tesla into SpaceX might lead to the EVs cars conducting surveillance, he said. There were media reports this year that Tesla was weighing a spinoff of its China business due to the potential merger, but Musk called one report “fake news.”

Given the record of the Trump administration, Talley doesn’t believe that U.S. regulators would block the merger, but state attorneys general could file a lawsuit to oppose it, just like they did this year over Paramount’s $111-billion merger with Warner Bros., though a deal was later reached and the litigation was dropped.

Whatever the outcome of the potential merger, Musk probably will remain focused on his ambitions to send humans to Mars on SpaceX’s massive Starship rocket under development — even as he has consistently missed self-imposed target dates.

“I think he’s been perhaps a little bit more conservative in his outlook, and realizes this is probably going to take a lot longer than even he thought,” said Marco Caceres, an aerospace analyst with Teal Group.

Jordan Bardella has been overwhelmingly re-elected leader of France's National Rally (RN), securing 98.98% of the vote in an uncontested leadership election.

The result was announced on Saturday, the opening day of the party's two-day congress in Orléans, as the RN seeks to consolidate its position ahead of the 2027 presidential election.

Bardella received 75,497 votes, with 779 blank ballots cast, according to RN lawmaker Yoann Gillet, who oversaw the election. Turnout among party members reached nearly 68%, with electronic voting taking place between 21 September and 22 October.

Ahead of the official announcement, Bardella thanked party activists and urged them to rally behind Marine Le Pen's presidential ambitions.

"Once again, I am going to need you (...) to lead Marine Le Pen to the Élysée," he told supporters.

His re-election reinforces the division of roles between the RN's two leading figures, who have presented themselves as a "winning ticket" for the 2027 elections.

Under that strategy, Le Pen is expected to seek the presidency, while Bardella is positioning himself as a potential prime minister should the party secure a parliamentary majority.

Le Pen is due to address thousands of supporters on Sunday, when she is expected to set out the next phase of her presidential campaign.

The congress was accompanied by a large counter-demonstration, with thousands of protesters taking to the streets of Orléans on Saturday to voice their opposition to the RN.

Authorities estimated the turnout at around 11,000, while organisers put the figure at 26,000. The march, which began around midday, remained peaceful.

Officials had previously said they expected up to 30,000 demonstrators.

Several prominent left-wing politicians and trade union leaders joined the protest, including Bally Bagayoko, mayor of Saint-Denis and a leading figure in La France insoumise.

Socialist Party leader Olivier Faure accused the RN of contributing to what he described as a "poisonous, racist and xenophobic climate".

CGT trade union leader Sophie Binet also criticised the party, declaring that "there is no worse enemy of working men and women than the far right".

The demonstration comes amid heightened political and social tensions in France, following a renewed wave of protests and serious violence a week earlier.

Saturday's turnout was lower than the more than 50,000 people who demonstrated against a National Front congress in Strasbourg in March 1997, one of the largest protests against the party in its history.

Beyond Bardella's re-election, the Orléans congress is intended to showcase the RN's unity and political programme, six months before the presidential election.

Marine Le Pen is now preparing to lay out her vision for France at a major National Rally gathering in Orléans on Sunday ahead of the 2027 presidential election.

According to her entourage, the address will be a "high-calibre" speech centred on the theme of "rebirth".

The party has already begun presenting its economic and social priorities ahead of the election.

Earlier this month, the RN unveiled its alternative budget, challenging the government's fiscal proposals.

Le Pen also placed housing and the cost of living at the centre of her political agenda during a speech in Hénin-Beaumont on 14 September.

Sunday's address is expected to offer further details of the RN's strategy as it seeks to turn its electoral support into a victory in the 2027 presidential race.

#741. Suspect in shooting death of Missouri teen on highway charged in second road incident

Man accused of shooting teen who was driving to a party is also linked to shooting of a vehicle days earlier, police say

A man accused in the shooting death of a Missouri teen has been charged in a second shooting incident – both of which involve firing into cars on the highway.

Alyssa Wilson, 17, was shot and killed as she drove down Interstate 170 in Overland, Missouri, on 14 October. The teen was on her way to a Halloween party at St Louis Zoo, called Boo at the Zoo, when a suspect fired a single shot into the back of Wilson’s Buick Encore.

The shot struck Wilson in the back, incapacitated her, and sent her crashing into a concrete highway median, according to prosecutors. She was pronounced dead at Barnes-Jewish Hospital.

The suspected shooter, Willie James Herndon, 43, of Texas, had no known relationship to the teen.

“Alyssa was 17, excited about her life, excited about her future,” her father Robert Hickman said, as state charges were announced. “She had 60 days until she turned 18, and we were getting ready to take our first family vacation together to go to Disney for her to see her favorite person in the world, Princess Tiana, and unfortunately, she’s not going to get to do that any more. This was a senseless act.”

Now, federal court documents show that Herndon has been charged in a second shooting incident, this one just a few days earlier.

On 11 October, St Louis metropolitan police received a report that a vehicle was shot just after exiting Interstate 55 in Missouri. Surveillance footage captured a white SUV fleeing the scene – a vehicle that matched the appearance of Herndon’s Buick Enclave.

A shell casing was also recovered from the scene. Prosecutors said they were conducting ballistics tests to determine if it was fired from the same weapon that killed Wilson.

In a federal criminal complaint, prosecutors lay out how they tracked what appeared to be Herndon’s Buick Enclave from the first shooting incident on 11 October, then the scene of Wilson’s death on 14 October, to a Days Inn in Caseyville, Illinois 16 October.

There, prosecutors approached Herndon’s wife Taiya Herndon, 45, and were speaking to her when Herndon “emerged” from the hotel room and began to flee. As he was arrested, he was “screaming words about a shooting”, prosecutors said.

Inside the Days Inn hotel room, prosecutors said they found a ABC-15 rifle “in plain view”, ammunition that matched the kind used in Wilson’s shooting, a receipt from a gas station near the scene of Wilson’s death on Interstate 170, two license plates and handwritten notes describing police vehicles Herndon believed were tracking him.

Federal prosecutors in Illinois have charged Herndon with being a felon in possession of a firearm. He has separately been charged with first-degree murder and armed criminal action in St Louis county, Missouri. His federal public defender did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

#742. US sanctions target Iran's rail sector as Tehran shifts cargo from sea routes to overland corridors

As US sanctions expand to Iran's rail sector, Tehran is relying more heavily on overland links with China and Central Asia. But capacity constraints, delays and costs limit rail's ability to replace maritime trade.

The United States has opened another front in its economic pressure campaign against Iran, this time targeting the railways Tehran increasingly relies on as maritime trade becomes more difficult.

On October 1, the US Treasury sanctioned three Iranian railway companies alongside seven automakers and five foreign suppliers of automotive parts as part of its Operation Economic Outcast.

Washington says Iran's rail and automotive industries provide revenue and logistical capacity to the state and are connected to networks involving the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).

The timing of the move is significant. Since the US maritime blockade sharply restricted Iran's southern trade routes, Tehran has tried to move more goods through its land borders and railway connections with China, Central Asia, Russia and Turkey.

Rail transport has become more important just as Washington decided to target it.

Shahriar Naghizadeh, director general for foreign trade at Iran's railway authority, was quoted by the semi-official Mehr news agency as saying that the country has around 15,000 kilometers (9,300 miles) of main and secondary railway lines, more than 35,000 wagons and nearly 500 diesel locomotives.

The network carried around 44 million tons of freight in the Iranian year ending in March 2026, up from about 40 million tons the previous year, according to Naghizadeh. And authorities are targeting 54 million tons this year.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Iran is linked to neighboring markets through 13 rail crossings, providing overland access to Turkey, Azerbaijan, Afghanistan, Pakistan and onward routes to Central Asia and China via Turkmenistan.

The new US sanctions raise questions about how foreign railway operators, freight forwarders, banks and insurers will continue dealing with Iranian rail companies.

Bloomberg reported in May that freight trains traveling from the Chinese city of Xi'an to Tehran had increased from around one per week before the US blockade to roughly one every three or four days.

In September, a train left China carrying automotive parts, consumer goods and other cargo. It ran through Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Turkmenistan before entering Iran at Sarakhs with an expected transit time of 14 to 16 days.

For Iran, such services offer a route to Chinese suppliers that avoids the area around the Strait of Hormuz. But advertised transit times do not necessarily reflect what an importer experiences.

A Chinese freight company told DW that actual delivery times can stretch far beyond advertised schedules because of border inspections, customs procedures and train availability.

It estimated that rail transit along the main route from western China to Tehran would take 50-60 days under current conditions. Road transport along a similar route is around 22 to 25 days.

The gap between a scheduled 14-day transit time and commercial estimates of up to 60 days highlights one of the central challenges facing Iran.

Customs inspections, gauge changes, payment problems and sanctions can all be another potential point of delay.

Increasing the number of trains also requires more locomotives, wagons and cooperation from several transit countries.

Alireza Salavati, managing director of London-based Middle East Analytica, said rail is increasingly useful for Iran but should not be mistaken as a replacement for maritime trade.

"A workable overland route now links China and Iran, but I would not call it a replacement for sea freight," he told DW.

Under normal conditions, ships can move far larger quantities at lower unit costs. Rail becomes more attractive for goods where speed and continuity matter more than the cheapest transport.

That includes automotive components, machinery, electronics and industrial inputs, whose absence can stop an entire production line.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Salavati argues that the effect on companies cannot be measured only in freight charges.

For a manufacturer importing $1 million (€890,000) worth of inputs every 30 days, a 30-day journey means roughly a million dollars of inventory may be tied up in transit.

Cutting the journey to 15 days could reduce that amount significantly, depending on payment arrangements. The reverse can be much more damaging.

If input costs rise while delivery times stretch from 30 to 45 days, companies need more working capital simply to maintain the same production flow, the expert explained, pointing out that a factory can have customers and orders but still have to reduce production because too much cash is trapped in goods that have not arrived.

"Reliability matters as much as speed," Salavati said. "A 15-day train is little use if the container waits a week to depart, or if the bank or insurer will not touch it."

The new US sanctions add another source of uncertainty to that calculation.

Optimizing its railway use would give Iran more options than having to rely on southern ports alone, but the overall scale remains limited.

Washington's sanction strategy is designed to isolate Iran by closing maritime, financial, aviation and now railway channels.

Still, Salavati argues that the same pressure may accelerate Iran's integration with alternative networks.

"Washington's efforts to isolate Iran may also be pushing it deeper than at any point in recent years into China's economic orbit and closer to Russia's wartime strategic system," he said.

That does not mean China or Russia can make up for the economic cost of US pressure, since Iranian importers still need insurers, banks and customers able to absorb higher prices.

Container trains can only carry a fraction of what a large cargo vessel can transport, so for now, rail provides Iran with a limited alternative trade channel.

Its wider success depends on better financing and becoming more reliable — but even then it is not a wholesale substitute for sea freight.

#743. Bust companies revived in ‘phoenix’ deals more likely to fail again, study finds

Exclusive: research for the Guardian shows ‘pre-pack’ deals with former management also pay far less to creditors

The boss whose twice-bust business appears to be back

Insolvent businesses reacquired by their previous management in “pre-pack” administrations are much more likely to fail again and tend to repay far less to creditors, research for the Guardian suggests.

The study is the latest to raise questions about the practice of “phoenixism” – accounting’s controversial art of liquidating companies to allow directors to return with a new entity, free of debts.

The process tends to involve pre-pack administrations, where a supposed corporate rescue is agreed before commencing insolvency proceedings. These orchestrated deals often leave unsecured creditors nursing large losses. HM Revenue and Customs estimates that phoenixisms cost taxpayers hundreds of millions of pounds a year.

Cases have included owners extracting millions of pounds in dividends and loans from businesses they subsequently arrange to buy back from administrators.

The study was commissioned by the Guardian from Turnstone Intelligence, which used AI agents to read official documents relating to more than 1,700 administrations during 2019. The research company noted much poorer outcomes when a business’s assets were reacquired by “connected parties”, such as former directors and shareholders.

It found that 44% of pre-packs had resulted in a second insolvency by July 2026 when assets were bought by a connected party. Just 26% of pre-packs produced a subsequent insolvency when the acquirer was unconnected to the failed company.

Ben Sims, managing director of Turnstone Intelligence, said: “I was surprised how big the gap remains. These results support what many in the industry have long suspected and will feed the continuing debate as to whether saving these businesses is worth the impact on taxpayers and creditors.”

The data showed that connected parties appeared far more likely to be permitted to defer payments in pre-packs. A total of 198 out of 303 connected-party administrations – 65% – allowed former owners and directors to reacquire the assets via future instalments. For unconnected pre-packs, 28% of buyers used deferred payments.

Unsecured creditors, who typically include HMRC, received a return in only 23% of pre-packs involving a connected party deferring payments, with those deals paying out just 1.58p in the pound. When the buyer was unconnected, 36% of pre-pack administrations resulted in repayments to those creditors, at a rate of 7.86p in the pound.

“What was interesting to us was the sheer scale of losses,” Sims said. “You would hope these deals would provide better outcomes to creditors, but we see them getting almost nothing. Of course, the biggest loser is often the taxpayer.”

The findings appear to closely mirror results from two well-known reports in the field: research by the University of Wolverhampton for the government in 2014 (Graham review) and a European Union-funded 2018 study. Both pointed to poorer outcomes in connected pre-pack administrations. Those issues were compounded when the assets were reacquired by connected parties through deferred payments.

Riz Mokal, an honorary law professor at University College London who co-authored the EU study, said: “These are striking findings and are consistent with our earlier work. They reinforce a wider concern that connected-party pre-packs can allow non-viable ‘zombie’ businesses to shed their unsecured liabilities and continue trading, harming not only their creditors, including HMRC, but also competitors that continue to pay their way.”

The methodology used by the latest researchers was broadly consistent with the earlier, EU-funded study. They used AI agents to read filings submitted over the past seven years for administrations commenced in England and Wales in 2019 – which Turnstone said was “long enough for creditor returns to settle and buyer failures to show”.

Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning

The sweep of insolvency filings identified 544 pre-pack sales in 1,738 administrations during 2019, with the study’s numbers checked by other computer models and verified by humans.

Phoenixism is legal and its defenders say the practice can deliver better returns for creditors, with experienced directors sometimes better-placed than newcomers to salvage a failed company.

R3, an insolvency industry body, said the research looked only at cases that predated 2021 rules that “increased scrutiny of connected-party pre-pack sales and introduced additional safeguards and transparency requirements”. These included requiring independent evaluators to clear sales to connected parties.

Caroline Sumner, chief executive of R3, said: “A connected-party pre-pack administration sale is a legitimate and regulated insolvency process overseen by licensed insolvency practitioners and subject to extensive professional and statutory requirements. The duties of an administrator in a pre-pack administration sale are to achieve the best outcome for creditors of the company overall.

“It’s important to distinguish between phoenix activity and connected-party pre-pack administrations. Concerns about phoenixism generally relate to businesses seeking to avoid liabilities while continuing to trade through a new entity.”

#744. Decades-old GOP winning streaks are suddenly at risk

Democrats are running surprisingly competitive races in traditionally Republican territory across the country this midterm election cycle, and it's putting GOP winning streaks at risk that stretch as far back as the 1930s.

Why it matters: Democrats hope ending political droughts in states such as Kansas, Texas and South Carolina will help make inroads in what has long been off-limits territory.

Kansas - 1932

  • Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kansas) is facing a surprisingly tough challenge from Democrat Adam Hamilton, a Methodist pastor who has significantly outraised the incumbent GOP senator.
  • The two are neck-and-neck in the polls, and Cook Political Report rates the race a tossup.
  • A Democrat hasn't won a U.S. Senate seat in Kansas since George McGill was reelected in 1932.

Texas - 1988

  • Democratic state Rep. James Talarico is giving Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton (R) a real run for his money in the Senate race. Talarico generally leads in polls by low single digits. Cook rates it a tossup.
  • Texas has been a consistent heartbreaker for Democrats in recent cycles. They last won a Senate seat in the state with Lloyd Bentsen in 1988.

South Carolina - 1998

  • Polls have routinely shown Republican Sen. Darline Graham, who was appointed to replace her late brother Lindsey Graham following his death in July, leading Democrat Annie Andrews by just a few percentage points.
  • Andrews, like other Democratic Senate candidates, has raised colossal sums, while Graham has struggled as a political neophyte. Still, Cook rates the race as "likely Republican."
  • The state has gone Republican in every U.S. Senate election since longtime Democrat Fritz Hollings was last reelected in 1998.

Between the lines: Democrat Troy Jackson, if he defeats Republican Sen. Susan Collins of Maine next month, would be the first registered Democrat to win a U.S. Senate seat in Maine since 1988.

  • That's a bit of a technicality: Independent Sen. Angus King has caucused with Democrats since he was first elected in 2012.

Gubernatorial races

  • Texas hasn't elected a Democratic governor since Ann Richards in 1990, but Democrat Gina Hinojosa is in a tight race with Republican incumbent Greg Abbott that Cook rates as "leans Republican."
  • Democrat David Jolly is also hoping for an upset against GOP Rep. Byron Donalds in a race Cook also rates as "leans Republican." Democrats narrowly won the Florida governorship in 1994 and have lost ever since.
  • Georgia's Keisha Lance Bottoms and Alaska's Jonathan Kreiss-Tompkins are both vying to be the first Democrats elected governor in their states since 1998. Cook rates Georgia as a tossup and Alaska as "leans Democratic."

House races

  • Democrats have never won Nevada's 2nd District, which was created in 1983. It has changed shape over time but has always been anchored in the rural north half of the state.
  • Democrats feel they have a strong candidate in former state Assembly Majority Leader Teresa Benitez-Thompson and a weak opponent in former Air Force lieutenant colonel Dave Flippo.
  • The party is also bullish about Montana's 1st District, where they hope the populist appeal of former smokejumper Sam Forstag will help him prevail over the GOP nominee Aaron Flint, a veteran and radio host. Democrats haven't won a U.S. House seat in Montana since 1994.

Cook rates Nevada's 2nd Distric as "likely Republican" and Montana's 1st District as a tossup.

The other side: Republicans are also competitive in a handful of races where they haven't won in quite a while.

  • Republican former Rep. Mike Rogers is locked in a tight U.S. Senate race in Michigan with Democrat Abdul El-Sayed. He would be the first Republican elected to the Senate from the state since the 1994 GOP wave.
  • Democratic Oregon Gov. Tina Kotek faces a close race with Republican Christine Drazan, who would be the first Republican elected governor of the state since 1982.
  • Oregon is essentially the GOP's version of Texas: Republicans have lost by single digits in gubernatorial elections since 2002.
