#745. Thomas Markle's alcoholic ex-wife, the wayward son he 'cut off financially' - and how the grubbiest royal scandal in history unfolded: GUY ADAMS

Published: 01:55 GMT, 26 October 2026 | Updated: 02:26 GMT, 26 October 2026

Shortly after his daughter Meghan married Prince Harry, Thomas Markle was the subject of a cover story on America's most notorious supermarket tabloid, The National Enquirer.

Published in October 2018, it gave a compelling insight into why his absence from that summer's royal wedding might, in the great scheme of things, turn out to have been a blessing in disguise.

The article was based on a tape recording of the retired TV lighting director discussing his time in Hollywood, where he'd won three Emmy awards.

Two excerpts stood out. In one, Markle brazenly talked about having dabbled in Class A drugs, confessing: 'In the industry I worked in back in the 70s and 80s there was cocaine around a lot. And I'm sure that I had an occasional sniff of cocaine.'

In the second, he gave a bizarrely equivocal answer when asked if he'd ever consorted with prostitutes in South-East Asia, where he'd holidayed on a number of occasions.

'Have I ever paid for a sex worker? Uh, there was a Playboy Club in the top floor of a hotel in the Philippines [but] I never paid for sex. I would go upstairs and enjoy myself in the Playboy Club, but… not for sex. I didn't get sex out of it,' Markle said.

But at the weekend he admitted to the Mail on Sunday that he had paid for sex in the Philippines.

The tape recording turned out to have been secretly made by Markle's son, Thomas Jr.

The Duchess of Sussex has been estranged from her father, Thomas Markle Sr, 82, since 2018. Pictured: The couple together on the day of Meghan's marriage to film producer Trevor Engelson in 2011

Roslyn Loveless, the first wife of Meghan Markle's estranged father Thomas, pictured outside her home in Albuquerque, New Mexico

Meghan Markle's half-brother Thomas Markle Jnr pictured hand-in-hand with a woman outside the apartment building where he lived with his father in the Philippines on May 10, 2025

In a separate interview, around the same time, he discussed his father's love life, claiming that in between divorcing his mother, Roslyn Loveless, in 1975, and marrying Meghan's mother, Doria Ragland, in 1979, he'd enjoyed a lengthy relationship with a lady from the Philippines named Marty.

'There's a certain type of woman he likes. He likes Asian women a lot,' said Thomas Jr, before adding enigmatically: 'He likes to go on vacation to Thailand, Vietnam. He likes their culture a lot.'

Fast-forward eight years and Meghan's father, now 82, is once more the subject of a toe-curling sex scandal. The principal setting is, again, the Philippines.

And the most explosive details are, as previously, being made public by Thomas Jr, one of two children from whom he appears to be irreparably estranged.

The whole thing kicked off at exactly 10.04pm on Thursday, when it emerged that Filipino police were investigating Thomas Sr over a huge stash of child sex images that had allegedly been found at his home in Cebu, a tourist island some 350 miles south-east of the capital Manila.

It had purportedly been discovered by Thomas Jr, who told The Sun newspaper that he'd found 'hundreds if not thousands' of images in four cardboard boxes that had been shipped there from Rosarito in Mexico, where father and son had lived before moving out to the Philippines for a 'fresh start' in January 2025. 'When I found this material, I was horrified and I had no option but to report my dad,' he said.

'I have supported, cared for him and helped him for years – but that stops now. I won't speak to my father ever again unless I'm called to give evidence against him.'

Thomas Jr, 60, claims to have come across the material in July, while searching for a mobile phone handset he could give to the father of his fiancee, a 28-year-old Filipino woman named Rose.

Mr Markle faces child sex allegations which he denies and told The Mail on Sunday he was 'not buying' the idea that his first wife, who died two years ago, wrote the letter to the Met Police in early 2019

He says he charged up an old LG device, which had previously belonged to his Dad, only for explicit video of 'naked young girls' to flash up on the screen.

Other images, of what The Sun described as 'victims appearing to be aged no older than ten or 11,' were discovered on a Lenovo ThinkPad laptop.

There were also alleged to be explicit DVDs and photographs, some of them secreted in the pages of a couple of coffee table books that belonged to Thomas Sr. One was called Lewis Carroll Photographs Of Children: Four Nude Studies, the other Hollywood Lolitas: The Nymphet Syndrome In The Movies.

According to Thomas Jr, he promptly reported the discovery of the material to the FBI, hoping they would launch an investigation into his father.

Thomas Sr had moved back to the US in May after suffering serious health difficulties, including a stroke and a blood clot, which resulted in the amputation of his left leg below the knee.

Yet three months passed, without an FBI probe ensuing. So Thomas Jr instead decided to report the matter to police in the Philippines.

On Friday morning, he transported the four cardboard boxes to the police headquarters in Cebu City in a Toyota HiAce people-carrier under the watchful eyes of a Sun reporter.

Thomas Jr, who had until now sided with his father in various public spats with Meghan, then used the newspaper to issue a mea culpa to his estranged half-sister, saying yesterday: 'I'm so, so sorry… I now know I have been protecting the wrong person for the past nine years.'

The Duchess of Sussex had by then set a second hare running. On Friday, she issued a statement declaring herself 'deeply distressed at the news that has come to light in the last 24 hours'.

Thomas Sr recovering in a hospital bed after surgery in the Philippines last December

Meghan added that in 2018, the Metropolitan Police had shared with her details of a letter which 'made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father'.

She was 'given assurances that these were being investigated', and subsequently decided to prevent her children from having contact with their grandfather, in order 'to protect them'.

It later emerged, the letter had in fact been sent in early 2019, shortly after The National Enquirer's revelations about Thomas Sr's previous exploits in an 'X-rated jiggle joint' in the Philippines. The letter's author was Thomas Sr's alcoholic ex-wife Roslyn Loveless, who died in 2024.

She alleged that he had admitted going to the Philippines and Thailand to abuse children, according to sources who have seen the letter's contents.

The Met is now 'reviewing its handling of the matter' and may yet refer itself to the police watchdog.

One odd wrinkle is that the letter seems to have ended up not with officers specialising in child sex abuse but with the Force's 'Fixated Threat Assessment Centre', a unit frequently referred to as its 'stalker and obsessive unit', which deals with people who threaten royals, celebrities and other public figures.

It's unclear whether this means officers concluded that claims made by Ms Loveless suggested she was a potential threat to Meghan, or whether they were instead concerned about Thomas Sr. Either way, an informed source said last night that the Met would almost certainly have had no jurisdiction to carry out further inquiries since Mr Markle was not in the UK and neither was his alleged offending nor the purported victims.

Another tricky factor for the law enforcement agencies might be the fact that the age of consent in the Philippines was only upgraded to 16 in 2022. Prior to that point it was just 12.

Quite how seriously the Duchess of Sussex took the 2019 letter from Ms Loveless is, at this stage, unclear. In February 2019, shortly after it arrived, Meghan authorised five friends to brief her favourite outlet, People magazine, about her estrangement from Thomas Sr. The resulting article suggested the Duchess wished to repair the relationship.

Later, in a 2022 Netflix documentary, Meghan declared that she had been 'a daddy's girl my whole life'. She only appears to have categorically cut him off in late 2025, when Thomas Sr was gravely ill in hospital in the Philippines.

At that point, a representative was dispatched to hand-deliver a letter in a scene witnessed by the Mail's Caroline Graham.

Prince Harry and Meghan Markle at The Community Recording Studio in Nottingham earlier this month, their first official engagement since returning to the UK

None of which is, of course, to suggest that the Duchess is anything but a victim of this week's appalling developments. One might argue, in fact, she is the only member of her troubled American family who emerges from recent developments with her reputation enhanced.

Thomas Jr's motives are, to this end, very much open to question.

A twice-divorced window-fitter, with two grown-up sons (one is a marijuana farmer in Oregon, where the activity is legal), his chaotic personal CV includes an arrest for allegedly putting a gun to a girlfriend's head during a drunken row (charges were filed in 2017 but later dismissed after they reconciled) and a court appearance for drink-driving.

He also appeared on Australia's version of Celebrity Big Brother in 2022, alleging that he and Meghan had once been close, but that 'money changed her' after she achieved fame.

In recent years, the 60-year-old has been almost entirely financially supported by his father. The duo moved out to the Philippines together in January 2025, and Thomas Jr remains there.

Thomas Sr, for his part, returned to the US in May to recuperate from the health crisis that saw his leg amputated.

He left behind his most recent girlfriend Rio Canedo, a local nurse who he'd met when she treated him in hospital.

At 46, she is three and a half decades his junior.

Meghan's father initially spent time in Pennsylvania but has lately been in a nursing home in Lakeland, Florida, where he is being supported by Samantha Markle, the Duchess's somewhat outspoken second half‑sibling, who is the eldest child of Ms Loveless.

Samantha, a former actress and model who has given a number of unflattering interviews about Meghan over the years, remains very much in her father's camp.

She told the Daily Mail at the weekend that her brother's allegations about their father are 'disgusting', saying they have 'no merit in them whatsoever'.

She described Thomas Jr as a 'liar' who is fabricating the claims to make cash.

Furthermore, she has alleged that his original complaint to the FBI in July followed a family row over money: shortly after returning to the US in May, Thomas Sr changed passwords to a bank account his son had access to.

'My brother first came out with these lies days after the cash from my Dad was cut off. He has used Dad as a cash cow for years, and once the money stopped he made up the most outrageous lies he could to make money from the media,' was how Samantha put it.

She further described her brother as a 'delusional alcoholic' and said the devices said to contain illicit material had been untouched by her father since he'd arrived in the Philippines, where they had been kept in storage.

'Dad had no access to those computers for two years. Who knows who could have had access to them? Anyone could have set Dad up. There is no merit in these disgusting allegations whatsoever and my brother is disgusting for making them up.'

In remarks which may do little to improve her father's reputation in the court of public opinion, Samantha added that one of the photographs at the centre of the investigation, which purportedly shows her father on a bed with a young-looking Asian woman, 'may be one of his girlfriends'.

She went on: 'Dad dated a wonderful Japanese woman called Carolyn who I loved. She was in her 30s but she looked like a teenager. Asian women have great skin and are small and petite. They look much younger than they are.

'Dad had another girlfriend called Gail. She was Asian and gorgeous but looked very young.'

And what of Thomas Sr? He is purportedly in severe ill health, but has declared himself prepared to do 'whatever it takes' to clear his name, saying that the computers and phones at the centre of this week's events haven't been in his possession for more than two years so: 'If there is anything bad on there it was put there by someone else.'

As we have seen in an interview with the Mail on Sunday, he admitted that when he was single he travelled to the Philippines at least twice and 'slept with prostitutes', adding, perhaps ill-advisedly, that: 'I like Asian women but that is not a crime'.

#747. On one Altadena block destroyed by Eaton fire, a return, an exit and lessons in resilience

This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here.

See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred

At 8 o’clock Wednesday morning, with rain clouds gathering in the distance, a work crew applied the finishing touches to a new Altadena home with giant picture windows that frame the grandeur of the San Gabriel Mountains.

Jonni Miller and Anthony Ruffin expect to be home for Thanksgiving.

“We can’t wait to get back,” said Miller.

Their good friends Lily Knight and Steve Hofvendahl, who lived two doors away for a quarter of a century, are beginning a new chapter of their own. They’ve sold their property and will be moving to the Pacific Northwest, a decision made with heavy hearts but a sense of reinvention.

“This is going to sound really woo-woo,” Knight said, but in the aftermath of the fire, she saw a “network of lights” that represented, for her, the hearts of the people in her life. “That’s where I live,” she said, rather than in a structure. “And so that makes leaving easier, because I feel like the bonds that are true bonds will hold.”

This is the Altadena story at the moment — some people are returning, some are leaving, some haven’t yet decided. A place that had a distinctive and cherished identity before the fire, mixed race and mixed income, still doesn’t know what its new identity will be.

“I think we’ll have a clearer picture at the end of year three, and we have not even come upon the second anniversary of the fire,” said Victoria Knapp, an Eaton fire survivor and former chair of the town council.

To date, 233 new homes have been completed, 3,851 building permits have been issued and 2,396 residences are under construction. It’s not clear what will come of 2,000 or so properties, Knapp said. So far, 515 lots have been sold, with 44% going to developers, foreign interests and private equity investors.

Michele Zack’s updated history of Altadena dwells on the past, peeks into the future.

Almost all the homes on West Palm Street between Olive and Glen were wiped out in January 2025. I met many of the residents within weeks of the disaster, and most were committed to rebuilding. Ruffin and Miller, whom I’ve known for years through their work helping and housing homeless people, will likely be the first to return to West Palm.

Knight and her husband, who couldn’t join us Wednesday, just closed the sale of their property to a nonprofit housing developer whose mission is to address the racial wealth gap. As much as they loved their life on West Palm, selling made sense in more ways than one. They’re both actors, and given their ages and Hollywood‘s transformation, opportunities for work were limited.

They had turned their double lot into a robust orchard, with more than 100 fruit trees, and the front porch of their yellow farm house was a neighborhood gathering place. There was no way to replace what had been lost, and having been underinsured stacked the odds against a return. For its climate, natural beauty and less outrageous real estate prices, the Pacific Northwest appealed.

“We would be building a tiny house on a big piece of property, which, for resale, whenever that needed to happen, wasn’t a good choice,” Knight said.

As we spoke, a symphony of power tools could be heard.

“Some of it had to do with not wanting to be in the crucible of rebuilding,” Knight said of the decision to sell.

Miller and Ruffin never considered moving, except when it appeared they might not be able to afford to rebuild. The house they lost was Ruffin’s home from the time he was a young boy. His father had purchased it in 1972, when Altadena was one of the few suburban areas where Black buyers were welcomed, and Ruffin bought the house from him about 25 years ago.

The new house has a modern contemporary design, and in the living room, those big windows show off the mountains. In the kitchen, large accordion windows open to a patio, giving the back of the house an airy, indoor-outdoor feel. The building materials are fire-resistant, as are the windows, and the eaves are fire-hardened as well.

As thrilled as Miller and Ruffin are about moving back, they’re wiped out physically and emotionally. Miller still struggles with the loss of family heirlooms. The letter her grandmother wrote her on the day she was born. The silverware that had been in the family for generations.

“I’m ready to be home,” Miller said. “I can’t even explain how tough this is. People keep trying to say, you know, at least you’re getting this beautiful new home. And it’s just kind of like, yeah but … we didn’t make this choice. Yes, I’m happy. Yes, I’m grateful. But it was a huge cost.”

“We’re grateful because there’s people with kids, and working,” whose lives are still unsettled, said Ruffin, who had told me immediately after the fire that for all his woes, he felt fortunate compared with his clients on skid row.

“And people are still living in their cars,”Miller said Wednesday in reference to fire victims who are still a long way from home.

Miller and Ruffin have made frequent trips to West Palm to check on the rebuild.

“It’s been really hard, working on skid row, seeing what’s going on there, and coming here to see this devastation, too,” Ruffin said. “You’re trying to navigate a natural disaster and you’re trying to navigate a man-made disaster. You’re always in a disaster, and there’s no break.”

Before the fire, Ruffin enjoyed a morning meditation. He’d sit in his front yard and take in the mountains as the sun rose and the birds greeted the day.

“There are rabbits again,” Miller said. “We saw a bobcat in our backyard. The ravens are amazing.”

“We saw some deer one time,” Ruffin said.

A neighbor’s flowers are blooming, and on Knight’s property, survivor trees include pomegranate, sapote, finger lime, orange and banana. Miller is going to take some of those banana pups for her yard, and out front, she’ll plant a pollinator garden.

As we began our goodbyes, Miller conceded that her friend’s planned departure has been a blow.

“It was hard for me to talk to Lily for a little bit there, because she was leaving and it’s such a big loss, because you are like a part of my heart,” Miller said.

“I’m sorry,” Knight said as they embraced.

“Don’t be sorry,” Miller said. “I’m so happy for you.”

Knight reminded Miller that she’ll be returning often to visit an uncle.

Through loss, displacement, uncertainty and the sometimes unbearable weight of impermanence, people have endured.

“All of us,” Knight said, “have found our own resilience in one way or another.”

She had told me last December at a block reunion that despite their loss, as she and her husband approached their 70s, “it’s really kind of exciting to think of a whole new life.”

West Palm Street had a vibe more priceless than the real estate, and residents vow to return.

We walked over to King’s yard, where she and Hofvendahl hosted a reception years ago when Miller and Ruffin got married.

Hofvendahl’s garden was his pride and joy, even though the work was never-ending. In some ways, Knight said, the decision to leave might have been harder for him. But maybe that was akin to the way people hesitate before jumping into cool water, Knight said. You resist at first, but when you let go of your fear, it feels pretty good.

A truck backed into a dirt driveway with a load of lumber.

A fence has gone up around the property owned by Aimin Li and Shigang Xiong, signaling the start of their rebuild.

Monica Koskey’s house is nearing completion. Not long ago, she and Peter Koskey got married, with the unfinished house as their wedding chapel.

But West Palm, and Altadena, are coming back.

The most important California stories and recommendations in your inbox every morning.

Steve Lopez is a California native who has been a Los Angeles Times columnist since 2001. He has won more than a dozen national journalism awards and is a four-time Pulitzer finalist. Lopez is the author most recently of “Independence Day: What I Learned About Retirement, From Some Who’ve Done It and Some Who Never Will.” His book “The Soloist,” inspired by his columns on his relationship with a Juilliard-trained homeless person, was a Los Angeles Times and New York Times best-seller, winner of the PEN USA Literary Award for Non-Fiction, and the subject of a Dream Works movie by the same name. He has also written three novels and two column collections.

Climate scientist Dr. Daniel Swain joins host Beth Ruyak to explain why this winter’s El Niño sharply raises California’s risk of heavy rain, flooding and coastal erosion this winter.

#748. Anti-party, anti-politician candidates surge in midterms

In red states and blue, unconventional candidates are downplaying — or even disowning — party labels to tap into voters' deep disdain for Washington.

Why it matters: They might not all win, but the sheer number of political outsiders connecting with voters tells us something about the electorate: It's angry and willing to take risks.

  • The candidates — whether they come from the pulpit or the NFL sidelines — are making the same bet: Voters are tired of career politicians.

Zoom in: Consider three unorthodox Democrats leading in Senate contests in three red states: a Presbyterian seminarian in Texas (state Rep. James Talarico), a megachurch pastor in Kansas (Adam Hamilton), and an Alaska Native in that state (former Rep. Mary Peltola, who once skipped a week of House votes to go fishing when Chinook salmon were running).

  • Deep-blue Minnesota's Senate race features Michele Tafoya — a former NFL sideline reporter who's endorsed by President Trump but calls herself an independent Republican. She's mounting a serious challenge to Democrat Peggy Flanagan, the lieutenant governor.
  • In House races, on the Democratic side there's a smokejumper in Montana (Sam Forstag), a 29-year-old barista in Colorado (Melat Kiros) and a Tejano singer in Texas (Bobby Pulido).

Four independent Senate candidates are courting Democratic voters without running with a (D) next to their names — and sometimes without a Democrat officially in the race.

  • In Nebraska, Dan Osborn, a union steamfitter and former factory mechanic, is mounting a serious independent challenge to Sen. Pete Ricketts, a former two-term governor whose family owns the Chicago Cubs.
  • In Montana, Seth Bodnar, a former Army Green Beret and University of Montana president, is running as an independent for an open Senate seat. Democrats tried to persuade their nominee to drop out, but she stayed in the race.
  • In South Dakota, Brian Bengs, a onetime park ranger, is challenging Republican Sen. Mike Rounds as an independent. Four years ago, Bengs ran against Sen. John Thune as a Democrat.
  • In Idaho, former Army tank commander and tech executive Todd Achilles is running as an independent against Republican Sen. Jim Risch. (Achilles previously served in the Idaho House as a Democrat. The official Democratic Senate nominee dropped out of the race in July.)

For many Republicans, quasi-Democrats running as independents amount to foul play — an attempt to deceive voters by discarding an unpopular brand.

Between the lines: Even candidates with more conventional backgrounds are shading their biographies to meet the populist moment.

  • In the Maine Senate race, Democrat Troy Jackson — who spent two decades in the state House and Senate before being term-limited out in 2024 — introduces himself as a fifth-generation Maine logger.

Zoom out: The populist path to Washington is at least as old as President Andrew Jackson, who first took office in 1829. It's as fresh as President Trump.

  • In recent years, there have been unorthodox candidates on both sides. Some succeeded; others didn't.
  • Al Franken, famous for being a writer and actor on "Saturday Night Live," won a U.S. Senate seat in Minnesota in 2008 and served more than eight years before resigning.
  • Herschel Walker, a celebrated college and NFL running back, couldn't find the end zone in his 2022 Senate race in Georgia.

Say what you want about the 45th and 47th president: The New York developer with a penchant for gold leaf has connected with disaffected working-class voters.

  • Democrats have struggled to match Trump's appeal to non-college-educated voters, but Trump has made their task easier this cycle with an unpopular war and tariffs that voters blame for high prices.

The bottom line: A version of the insurgent-vs.-establishment battle played out in Democratic primaries earlier this year, when seven House incumbents went down — tying a 21st-century high.

  • That included Kiros, the 29-year-old Colorado barista and democratic socialist who defeated a 15-term incumbent in the primary and is on a glide path to victory next month.

#750. ‘I feel so happy!’: Ecstasy, relief among Brazil’s Lula supporters

Sign up now: Get ST's newsletters delivered to your inbox

Thousands of supporters spilled onto the streets celebrating President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva’s victory.

SAO PAULO – Joyful cheers of “Let’s go, Lula!” rose from the jubilant crowd again and again as Brazilians paraded down Sao Paulo’s Paulista Avenue on Oct 25, celebrating the leftist leader’s improbable election win.

Thousands of people spilled onto the streets following President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva’s victory over his right-wing rival Flavio Bolsonaro.

Lula, who turns 81 on Oct 27, joined the parade, leaning out of the sunroof of his car with a megaphone in his hand and his trademark rasp more hoarse than ever.

“I just had to tell you that I love you. Tomorrow, the fight continues,” he said.

He received 51.8% of the votes compared to 48.2% for former president Jair Bolsonaro’s son, who has refused to acknowledge the result.

“I feel so happy!” 43-year-old Anna Zanatta told AFP before bursting into tears of joy.

“Lula’s victory represents many things for us: freedom, our democracy, our history,” she said, waving a flag bearing the message “Antifascist Action”.

Zanatta viewed a hypothetical Bolsonaro victory as a “threat” to Latin America’s largest democracy.

“I was born under a dictatorship, and I promised my granddaughter that we Brazilians would never go through that again,” she said, referring to the military regime which ruled from 1964 to 1985.

Doorman Alfonso dos Reis, 64, carried a sign reading “Lula again with the strength of the people” alongside a photo of the president.

“We’re going to build a much better country,” he beamed.

Fireworks boomed and cars honked their horns as the crowd marched down Sao Paulo’s main avenue, which turned into a sea of yellow and green as the Brazilian flag covered every square inch of the place.

Lula appeared alongside lawmaker Andre Janones, who created the “Lula’s Army” WhatsApp channel which surged to 10.8 million followers during the second-round campaign.

Lula’s supporters attribute his comeback in part to the lawmaker’s digital battle.

“I owe this victory to the rebellious youth who rose up to defend democracy,” Lula said.

Mateus Freitas, a 33-year-old theatre actor, waved a flare that sent red smoke into the air, the color associated with Lula’s Workers’ Party.

“No amnesty! No amnesty!” Freitas yelled at the top of his lungs.

He was referring to attempts to free Jair Bolsonaro, who governed from 2019 to 2022 and is serving a 27-year sentence for attempting a coup following his own electoral loss to Lula in 2022.

His son Flavio had promised to liberate him if elected.

“We stopped a government that would have been a fascist government, led by militias, criminals, racists, homophobes,” Freitas told AFP.

“This is a victory for minorities, for the people, for Brazilian workers...Lula’s government is inclusive,” he said.

The leftist victory has swerved Brazil away from a rightward turn, unlike a recent string of wins championed by US President Donald Trump across Latin America.

#751. US south-west braces for more storms after enduring days of rain and flooding

More inclement weather forecast in rain-soaked Four Corners region after evacuations and rescues last week

Another round of heavy showers and thunderstorms were expected to hit the south-west US on Sunday after the region endured days of rain that forced evacuations, water rescues and multi-million-dollar damage.

The National Weather Service issued a flood watch for much of the Four Corners – the meeting point of Arizona, Colorado, New Mexico and Utah – even as local officials forecast further receding of swollen rivers that surged since rains picked up on Wednesday.

About 4ft (1 meter) of water flooded the home of Shane Ferrari, the sheriff of San Juan county, New Mexico. He said the area’s situation was stable on Sunday, but he and other residents were trying to clean up and deal with damage.

The New Mexico governor, Michelle Lujan Grisham, said in a statement on Saturday that law enforcement had reported hundreds of water rescues between the cities of Farmington and Bloomfield.

“Families in Bloomfield and Farmington spent the night on rooftops watching the river flood their homes, and our national guard and state police crews have been bringing them to safety,” said Lujan Grisham. “Right now, our focus is saving lives. If you’re told to evacuate, go. Once the water recedes, the state will do everything in its power to help San Juan county families rebuild.”

“No deaths have been reported,” she added.

The San Juan River in Farmington on Friday ran 2 ft above its previous record set in 1909.

San Juan county spokesperson Devin Neeley said the county did not have official numbers on damage to homes or the number of people evacuated, but he was not aware of any loss of life.

Neeley said the flood waters were receding but left mud and silt, much of which has been contaminated with sewage because of failures at waste plants. There were still power outages affecting multiple areas, and it would probably be a few days until residents got their power back on.

“It’s a pretty active disaster zone,” he said. “We’re not on the downswing by any means.”

The flooding is just the latest from two months of on-and-off heavy rain caused by tropical moisture coming ashore from the Pacific. After months of drought, other recent deadly flooding struck the Grand Canyon and areas of New Mexico.

New Mexico has been hit with back-to-back weather events this weekend. A tornado struck Santa Fe on Saturday, damaging at least eight houses, including to roof collapses, according to a statement by the city of Santa Fe. No injuries were reported.

#752. ‘You can’t bring in robots’: the leather firm handmaking everything from wallets to cigar cases

In the third article in a series on high-end British manufacturing, we visit the Ettinger factory in Walsall

‘Our town is making jeans again’: reviving jobs and skills in Wales

From feathers to pet portraits, Rolls-Royce rides high on custom craze

“It is all down to attention to detail and everything we do is based around that.”

Gary Billingham is demonstrating how the 28 pieces which make up an Ettinger wallet are cut from leather using a hydraulic press by the small team at one of Walsall’s last remaining leather goods factories. The edges of the pieces are thinned down so they are ready to be turned, glued and stitched together by hand.

Billingham has been at the factory near Birmingham since the 1980s, when “there were three pages in the Yellow Pages” business directory listing leather factories in the West Midlands town. “They were everywhere. It has gone from that to about five factories. It is more like a cottage industry.”

About 20 people, mostly women, work carefully and precisely in Ettinger’s factory – a site of leather goods production since the 1890s – with a handful more doing work from home.

Robert Ettinger, the company’s chief executive, says the vast majority of its manufacturing process has to be done by hand. “You can’t bring in robots.”

He still owns the British brand founded in 1934 by his father, who turned to selling and manufacturing leather goods in the UK after fleeing Nazi Germany via Paris and a stint in the film industry.

Ettinger began making wallets and sourcing leather items, and today the company supplies a range of luxury goods to wealthy customers, including King Charles and Queen Camilla whose royal warrants they hold.

The company’s bestseller is still a wallet, but they also sell leather pill containers, cigar cases, picture frames and various accoutrements for dog owners, from treat cases to dog-waste bag holders, all of which can be personalised with initials.

The brand sits in a niche between the big label luxury and high street with a British hand-crafted leather tote bag for just under £800 compared with more than £2,000 charged by a big swinger such as Louis Vuitton.

An array of machines resembling pastry-cutters are used to punch out leather shapes that are then glued by hand with a brush to build up each item with trims and linings.

The tiny seams around the leather edges are thinned down with a shaving machine, known as a skiver, and turned inward before being stitched with a sewing machine. Each piece is then carefully checked and trimmed using a scalpel and sharp scissors before being polished and wrapped in tissue paper.

Gerry Ettinger, the founder, began by using an array of manufacturers before buying his original factory at the heart of London’s leather-working trade in Clerkenwell near the Smithfield meat market in the 1950s.

Robert Ettinger says: “When I was a kid, there were dozens and dozens of small factories, making leather goods, and they all specialised. One made suitcases, and one made handbags, and one made wallets.”

As the area gentrified in the 1990s, the Ettingers decided to move and bought out one of their suppliers, James Homer in Walsall, established in 1890. It was then mostly making corporate promotional leather goods. Staff were trained up and new machinery brought in to make the high standard of goods expected by Ettinger’s new international clientele led by the Japanese.

Walsall has been a centre of leather-working from the middle ages. It was focused on saddle-making with more than 100 firms operating in the town by the end of the 19th century.

As the use of horses in everyday life declined, the factories began expanding into making other leather goods, ranging from bicycle saddles, car upholstery and furnishings to bags, gloves and purses.

The industry thrived during the first world war when there was high demand for military saddle wear but began to suffer in the 1950s as it faced competition from abroad and from human-made alternatives to leather.

Still, by 1970 there were about 50 leather goods manufacturers in Walsall, and the town produced around half of the British-made fancy leather goods, according to the Wolverhampton Heritage and History Society.

Tracy, expertly glueing and building Ettinger’s elaborate cigar cases before they are sewn, has been at the company for 15 years and working in the leather industry since she left school 40 years ago.

“When we were that age it was all leather work. You could walk out of one job and into another on the same day,” she says.

That history is recognised in street names and the local Saddlers Centre shopping mall and there is a leather skills training centre which offers courses in bridle making.

Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning

Launer, whose customers included the late Queen Elizabeth II, J&E Sedgwick, the bridle maker, and small leather goods firm E Hulme, founded in the 1920s, continue to make leather goods near Ettinger’s factory. However, all employ only small numbers of people and the local industry is a shadow of its former self.

Even Walsall’s leather museum, housed in a former factory that dates back to the 1880s, is now closed amid disputed plans to move it to a modern city centre site.

That reflects a rapid decline in the leather goods manufacturing industry across the UK with just 7,000 people employed in it today compared with 37,000 30 years ago.

Ettinger itself had to cut its staff numbers by about seven after the Covid pandemic hit trade.

Robert Ettinger says he never really considered shifting production overseas, despite most of his customers coming from outside the UK.

“We might have made more profit, but then we would also have much more competition because when you’ve got 50 companies bringing in a purse from the far east, then it’s all about price.”

He says the gambit is now paying off as a younger generation increasingly appreciates British craft, with online sales up 30% on last year and UK sales up by a fifth, with shoppers aged from their early 20s.

“A lot of younger people are now thinking that they want something that will last, that won’t go out of fashion in three months’ time. Yes, it costs more, but it lasts for 15 or 20 years, and can be repaired. I’ve just repaired my wallet which is 17 years old.

“Our products are affordable luxury. A purse or wallet for £200 or £300, it’s the price of some trainers and they’re not made in the UK. So it’s not out of reach of most people.”

Still, expanding production in the UK might be tricky. Billingham says it is hard to find and train new staff. Even those who attend Walsall’s Leather Skills Centre are more likely to go into making car upholstery or saddles.

“We are all getting old now, that’s a problem, we are from 40s to 60s. If you find someone working for somebody else you take them,” says Billingham.

“To take five to 10 people on would be great but the reality is they are not there.”

Robert Ettinger says the UK should look at how young people are trained into the trade in mainland Europe, where he was sent by his father to serve an apprenticeship.

“They spend a few years really learning a trade, everything from making leather goods, to being a chimney sweep, or a butcher, or baker. When you pass all the apprenticeship exams, you then go on to do more and become a master, a Meister. We don’t have that here. So, it’s harder for us to take on younger people.”

He is optimistic things could change. “People might go into jobs which they don’t really enjoy or get bored of doing, and then they join us, and, you know, it’s like a family in our factory.”

A nurse was killed and a health worker severely injured after being attacked while responding to an Ebola alert in Congo, according to the World Health Organization.

It was the latest in a series of attacks on health workers and responders that authorities say is hampering efforts to slow the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in the world.

The attack took place Saturday in the town of Bafwasende in the country's eastern Tshopo province, WHO Director General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said in a post on X on Sunday.

“Everyone working to protect communities from this deadly disease must be able to work in dignity and safety. Healthcare must always be protected,” he said.

WHO regional director for Africa, Dr. Mohamed Yakub Janabi, also condemned the attack on X. “Misinformation and fear must never fuel violence,” he said.

Local authorities have not yet commented on the attack or the suspects.

The country’s health ministry’s most recent data indicates more than 9,800 cases including more than 4,700 deaths have been recorded since the start of the outbreak in May, making it the deadliest Ebola outbreak in Congo’s history.

Last month, a Congolese politician was beaten to death in North Kivu after publicly defending the government’s response to Ebola. He had been calling on the public to obey response measures, particularly social distancing and handwashing, on a radio show.

It came after authorities launched a village-centered approach to fight the outbreak which faced resistance from some residents who dismiss Ebola as a hoax. There is widespread distrust of the country’s government because of how it has managed past Ebola outbreaks as well as chronic corruption.

Responders say skepticism about the disease among communities has complicated efforts to work with residents, including in remote areas and emerging hot spots that already face shortages of medical supplies and healthcare workers.

Back in May at the start of the outbreak, two tents at health centers were set alight in two separate attacks in just one week by angry residents.

Those on the front line of the response to the outbreak have previously said some members of various response teams have been held captive in some health zones, and some teams responsible for safe and dignified burials have been threatened.

#754. Football: German coach Hürzeler flying high in Premier League

Fabian Hürzeler is younger than his star player, a fellow Premier League German. But, contrary to his reputation in his homeland, Hürzeler has become a popular figure both on and off the pitch in England.

"We are absolutely in love with him. He's been an incredible manager. The results are extraordinary and we're flying."

Those words from Ben Parker will be familiar to fans of any club who have been on the kind of winning run Brighton and Hove Albion are currently on.

But all the signs on and off the pitch suggest that the man in question — Brighton's German coach Fabian Hürzeler — is more than just a flash in the Premier League pan.

Hürzeler has never coached in Germany's Bundesliga. After winning promotion to Germany's top flight with St. Pauli in 2024, he left to become the youngest man ever to take charge in England's Premier League at 31. His team currently sit third, having won six games in a row including a 5-0 thrashing of bitter rivals Crystal Palace last weekend.

It was the repeat of a fixture last season that marked Hürzeler's lowest Brighton ebb, with a 1-0 home loss making it one win in 12. "There are only two options," the German coach said at the time. "Give up or keep pushing harder, and that's always the option I choose in my life."

Parker, the co-editor of Brighton and Hove Albion fanzine, Dogma, admitted to DW that there were plenty who weren't sure if persisting was the answer. "There was some disquiet at the end of that game, there were people shouting: 'You're getting sacked in the morning.'"

While such sentiment may be difficult to swallow for many coaches, Parker said that Hürzeler told him in an interview soon after joining the club that he welcomed it when needed.

"He talked about wanting a fan relationship that had a two-way aspect. The club and him are really ambitious, so if the performances aren't up to scratch, we should be telling him that. And that's what happened on that day. I see the whole thing as being quite healthy."

Hürzeler never played at the top level. He represented Germany's youth teams and turned out for Bayern Munich's reserves but soon grew frustrated with second-team football. He then accepted a player-coach role at German fifth-tier side Pipinsried at the age of 23. From 2018, he was also an assistant coach for Germany's U20s.

He performed this alongside a job at an art dealership in the German state of Bavaria, where he moved with his family at the age of two having been born in the United States. After starting as an assistant coach at St. Pauli in 2020, he took over after head coach Timo Schultz was fired in late 2022. Since then, he hasn't looked back.

That unusual path to top-flight management and some innovative tactics at St. Pauli led to a perception in Germany that Hürzeler was a little aloof and something of a 'laptop manager' in the vein of former Bayern Munich and Germany boss, Julian Nagelsmann who had a similarly nondescript playing career. This, so the charge goes, meant Hürzeler wasn't able to forge the relationships and togetherness needed to make a team more than the sum of its parts.

That was rarely what was reported by his players and staff at St. Pauli, nor is it Hürzeler's belief. "I want to be myself, I don't want to play a role, and my age definitely helps regarding understanding the players," he said.

"I always say I speak their language and I understand their thoughts, because it wasn't that long ago when I played."

His antics on the sideline also earned him a reputation as a bit of a hothead. Hürzeler was booked seven times during St. Pauli's promotion push and since joining Brighton, the German has been booked nine times and been sent off once. When asked about this, he said: "Emotions are part of the game."

Parker said this authenticity has also been reflected in his relationship with Brighton and Hove, on the south coast of England.

"For most Brighton fans he comes across as quite a quirky, interesting, left-field figure. The mantra he set out when he first arrived was quite counter-culturalist, to challenge the establishment, and that fits well here," Parker said.

"You will see him walking along on the seafront, going up for coffees around town, and he travels back and forth on an ebike, not in a chauffer-driven car as a lot of managers might. He's also hosted fan events in pubs, which I believe he paid for. So I'd say he's very approachable."

But Hürzeler isn't the only 30-something German beloved in Brighton.

Pascal Gross, who rejoined the club from Borussia Dortmund in January, is also a firm favorite. The midfielder, who retired from Germany duty after the World Cup earlier this year, has scored three and made four in the club's opening seven league games. The 35-year-old's connection with Hürzeler is also key, with Groß admitting he stayed in touch with Hürzeler even before he resigned. The return is proving to look a great decision for both sides.

"I was here for seven years, got married here and both my kids were born in England. The most important milestones in my life happened here. I missed my friends and the feeling of being deeply connected to the club."

The feeling is mutual, said Parker. "Pascal Gross is everybody's favorite player. He's Brighton's first best signing, from Ingolstadt, and second-best signing, from Dortmund. He's a sensational player, and it's probably true to say there is a lot of warmth towards German football and Germany because of these hugely important characters at the football club."

The Premier League club's success has been built on a smart coach and player recruitment strategy guided by local owner, Tony Bloom. Part of the model is that those who shine brightest will often be snatched by the bigger fish.

"I think he's said he's a supporter of Bayern Munich, and he uses them as an example of the standards he wants," said Parker of Hürzeler. "I can see that he could be a good fit in a couple of years time. He won't go to a Liverpool or a Chelsea, I think there's a strong pull to Bayern in particular."

Bayern's current boss, Vincent Kompany, is in little danger at the moment, though Bayern coaches are only ever a few losses from crisis. For the meantime, Hürzeler is also happy where he is, having extended his contract to 2029. Again, the feeling is mutual.

Next up in the Premier League is a trip to Liverpool, where Jürgen Klopp became the first German coach to make a real mark on the Premier League. But before that, Hürzeler's team have an assignment in the Europa Conference League, a competition Brighton are among the favorites to win. Parker hopes a first major trophy is in sight.

"If he can be the person that wins us that first trophy, then he will go down as the greatest."

Bookmakers have suspended betting on Michael Carrick being sacked by Manchester United.

His United future is hanging by a thread and almost all major betting companies are no longer offering a market on Carrick being dismissed.

Attention inevitably then turns to who might replace Carrick if indeed the axe does fall, with United languishing in 16th in the Premier League table.

Currently, former Newcastle manager Eddie Howe (4/5) is the bookies' favourite, while Julian Nagelsmann and Antonio Conte are also in the running.

Nagelsmann (5/2) has been out of work since leaving his post as Germany boss after their disappointing World Cup campaign.

#757. The overlooked geography of American poverty

Data: U.S. Census; Map: Erin Davis/Axios

California and Louisiana have something surprising in common: Both have among the nation's highest poverty rates when the cost of living is factored in, according to Census Bureau data.

Why it matters: Southern states dominate America's traditional poverty rankings. But that familiar geographic divide starts to disappear when more of a family's financial realities are taken into account.

  • Axios analyzed 2023-2025 state poverty estimates from the Census Bureau to see what happens when housing, taxes, medical expenses and government benefits enter the picture.

What we found: Under the Census' traditional-style official measure, Louisiana had a 19.6% poverty rate and California was at 10.7%. New Hampshire was the lowest at 5.4%.

  • The South is home to 10 of the 11 states where the traditional poverty rate significantly outpaced the national average.
  • California's poverty rate jumped by nearly two-thirds to 17.8% under the broader Supplemental Poverty Measure, or SPM. Louisiana remained near the top at 19%.
  • Maine posted the nation's lowest SPM rate at 6.4%, followed by Nebraska at 7.5% and Minnesota at 7.9%.

How it works: The traditional measure compares pretax cash income with a family-size threshold that doesn't change by geography.

  • The SPM adds benefits such as SNAP and housing assistance, factors in taxes and tax credits, subtracts work and medical expenses, and adjusts for geographic differences in housing costs.

Zoom out: The official poverty rate fell for a third straight year to 10.2%, while child poverty reached a record-low 13.4%.

  • Yet the SPM remained statistically unchanged at 13.1% — nearly three percentage points above the official rate.
  • Real median household income hit a record $87,460 in 2025.

Yes, but: The SPM doesn't replace the official poverty rate.

  • Census designed it as another lens — one that captures resources and unavoidable expenses the traditional measure misses.
  • The state figures also aren't single-year 2025 estimates. Census recommends three-year averages because state samples in the Current Population Survey are smaller.

The bottom line: Income alone doesn't tell you whether a family can make ends meet.

Israeli forces carried out a major security operation in the West Bank city of Hebron on Saturday, a day after two Palestinian gunmen killed two Israeli soldiers and wounded three others at a military checkpoint near the city.

The Israeli military said the operation was aimed at locating militants and weapons in the area where the attackers had operated. Both gunmen were killed during Friday's exchange of fire.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu announced a large-scale military response following the attack, saying Israeli forces would conduct an extensive operation in Hebron.

The military said its forces were conducting "precise, targeted and thorough searches" and that the operation was expected to continue for several days.

According to the Israeli military, the operation is focused on the area from which the attackers came. Residents leaving the affected neighbourhoods are being directed through designated exit points, where security checks are being conducted.

The military operation has also resulted in the displacement of hundreds of Palestinian residents.

Hebron Mayor Youssef al-Jaabari and local activist Issa Amro estimated that approximately 250 families had been forced to leave their homes, while Hebron Governor Khaled Dudin put the figure at 150 families.

In the Ein Dir Baha neighbourhood, Israeli troops marked buildings with X symbols after clearing them of residents. Streets were largely deserted, with military vehicles patrolling the area.

Local Palestinian officials said the operation had affected approximately one-third of the city, although the Israeli military described its actions as focused on the neighbourhoods linked to Friday's attack.

Governor Dudin criticised the scale of the operation, arguing that civilians who had no involvement in the shooting were being affected.

"This amounts to collective punishment being imposed on civilians who have nothing at all to do with this," he told AFP.

The mayor said local authorities were working to provide assistance and temporary accommodation to displaced residents.

"We will find them shelter and provide these people with all the help they need," he said.

Israeli forces also restricted vehicle access to Hebron, with gates at entrances to the city closed to traffic. Palestinians were seen crossing checkpoints on foot.

The operation comes just days before Israel's general election on Tuesday, with Netanyahu facing a closely contested race against an opposition bloc led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot.

Netanyahu has pledged a strong response to the killing of the soldiers, signalling that additional military measures could follow.

Israeli National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir has called for the dismantling of the Palestinian Authority, which administers parts of the West Bank under agreements reached with Israel in the 1990s.

Netanyahu has also reiterated his opposition to the establishment of a Palestinian state, saying he had resisted pressure from successive US administrations on the issue.

The Israeli government's security policies in the West Bank remain a major issue in the election campaign, alongside concerns over attacks against Israeli civilians and military personnel.

Meanwhile, tensions across the occupied West Bank remain high amid continuing Israeli military operations and reports of violence involving Israeli settlers and Palestinian residents.

Israeli human rights organisation Yesh Din reported 672 incidents of settler violence over a 26-day period, nearly half of them linked to the olive harvest.

The latest operation in Hebron is expected to continue for several days, with Israeli authorities maintaining that their immediate objective is to address security threats following Friday's deadly attack.

Nine people were killed and 40 others wounded on Oct 23 in an attack on a church in the village of Hamoud in the Karak governorate.

Jordanian security forces have arrested three suspects in connection with an attack on a church in the US-allied country that killed nine people, state television reported on Oct 26.

The Oct 23 attack during a funeral at a Greek Orthodox church in the village of Hamoud in Karak governorate, about 120km south-west of the capital Amman, also wounded 40 others. Witnesses said the shooting lasted several minutes.

Jordan’s Public Security Directorate said the suspects were located while hiding in an abandoned house in Karak.

They refused to surrender and attacked security forces, who returned fire and arrested all three after wounding them, the directorate said in a statement published on state media.

No security personnel were injured, and a number of firearms and ammunition were found in the suspects’ possession after their arrest.

“Terrorism has no place among us,” the directorate said, adding that the suspects had met their “just fate”.

Jordanian authorities have said the attack was carried out by “extremist terrorists”, but it was too early to determine whether they had links to known groups inside or outside Jordan. No group has claimed responsibility.

King Abdullah, a US partner in the fight against Islamist militant groups, has ordered security forces to respond with an “iron fist” to the rare attack on Jordan’s Christian minority.

Such violence is highly unusual in Jordan, a relatively stable state in the Middle East, though authorities say they have foiled several Islamist militant plots over the years.

The Public Security Directorate did not name the suspects or publicly identify possible affiliations with any Islamist militant groups.

Interior Minister Mazen al-Faraya said on Oct 26 the authorities were reviewing the circumstances that led young people towards extremism and would hold accountable anyone found to have participated in the attack. REUTERS

Joshua Loudermilk, one of two men apparently discredited by the new Ali G movie Ali G: Who Iz I?, has said that he was in on the joke, but that the film-makers didn’t realise this.

Loudermilk, a 54-year-old aspiring actor from North Carolina, has told the Guardian he recognised star Sacha Baron Cohen early in the shoot but continued pretending to be a hard-right Maga sympathiser prepared to defend the US border at all costs.

The movie involves Loudermilk being recruited by another Cohen character, the ex-Mossad terrorist expert Col Erran Morad, to help form a citizens’ warrior force to protect US borders, making use of his top-secret new weapon: a gun disguised as buttocks.

Along with fellow recruit Michael Aboud, the chair of the El Paso county Republican party, Loudermilk joins Morad on a mission to stop the birth on US soil of the baby of a fictional South American drugs kinpin. This involves abducting a woman apparently in labour, abandoning her in a deserted medical facility, kidnapping her newborn child (a lifelike prosthetic) and driving it in a zipped bag to the border in order to deliver it by drone to Mexico.

Aboud is shown taking the decision to drop the child from a great height into Mexico rather than have it touch US soil. He has since called Cohen a “liar” and a “pervert” and expressed his intention to sue. The film repeatedly stresses that both men were “not in on it”.

Loudermilk has told the Guardian he was surprised the production company did not notice social media updates he posted shortly after the shoot in which he named Cohen and expressed his excitement about the project.

But rather than being upset about his involvement, Loudermilk – who recently appeared as Squire Dap in the North Carolina Town of Hudson Fall Dinner Theatre’s production of Camelot – says he welcomes the publicity boost.

“I want to use this to my benefit,” he says. “I would hope Sacha would read this and laugh, like: ‘Hey, you got me!’ I had so much fun creating that character. I was trying to see if I was any good at acting in comedy. And I realised: ‘Oh, I think I’m good at this.’ And that’s what I wanna do for the rest of my life.”

His experience began in September 2025 when Loudermilk spotted a post on Craigslist by a body called the American Citizen Initiative (whose website is no longer active) recruiting “patriotic legal Americans” “concerned about the border crisis” who “believe that illegal immigration is out of control”.

The ad, one of dozens posted across US states simultaneously, invited “real American citizens” to “attend an exclusive, hands-on event experience where you’ll learn the truth about what’s happening on the border and how you can make a difference”. Attendees were promised $300 as well as travel expenses.

“I was like: this seems kind of weird,” says Loudermilk, who describes himself as broadly apolitical. “I don’t really care much about our borders. My mom’s from Ireland.”

Recently made redundant, his motivation for responding was primarily financial. “I know rightwing and leftwing organisations have money and will pay people to just hold a sign up. I remember thinking: I wanna get on that gravy train. I want some George Soros money. I’ll pretend to be whatever. Just let me feed my family. It could have been save the whales and I would have done it.”

In his application, Loudermilk fabricated hard-right views, mentioned that he had been a preacher and neglected to declare his ambitions to become a comedy actor – in part, he says, out of embarrassment. He then filled in a “silly questionnaire – very obvious, very slanted to the right”.

Loudermilk was then called for a video interview, which involved the identification of left-leaning celebrities, as well as figures including Borat, Cohen’s bumbling Kazakh reporter, who Loudermilk duly named.

He was also asked if he was a Trump supporter. “The funny thing is: not really. He’s just a leader. But I was like: I’m going to be an improv actor so I said: ‘Yeah, I support Trump!’ Next thing I know they’re like, ‘We want you to come out to be a part of this.’

The company flew him to Ontario, California, with an initial offer of $1,000, plus food and expenses, on top of which Loudermilk received a further $700. “It was all real secretive. They frisked me down and I got in a truck to go to a karate studio.”

Once he arrived, Loudermilk was greeted by security and informed an Israeli commander wanted to meet him. “That was a red flag. Why would Israeli commander be in America? I go in there and immediately I see this really tall guy with this horrible plastic surgery. My first thought was: that looks like Sacha Cohen. But I was like: nah, that can’t be him.”

Loudermilk’s suspicions were further raised, he says, when he met his fellow recruits. “They were old, old, old white guys who were really out of shape. Everyone’s wearing these Trump shirts. They didn’t seem like warriors. I thought: they could probably get better people for this.”

Morad then produced the top-secret new gun in the shape of large, strap-on bottom, out of which bullets are fired from the anus. Initially, Loudermilk was baffled by its logistics. “I kept thinking: no-one’s gonna wear that thing because your butt’s gonna be abnormally large. No one has a butt like that. Are you gonna put a butt on top of a butt? You can’t run in that. And you’d have to wear some really big khaki pants.”

He volunteered to be first to try the weapon out, whereupon Morad demonstrated the trigger system, which involves the pumping of an attached rubber penis. “And he kept calling it ‘shmeckel’. I’m like: that’s Sacha Cohen. At that moment I knew it.

“And I was like: oh no, I can’t break character. I’ve got to go along with it. So what I decided [was] that whatever he did, I was going to take it another step further. He’s not going to punk me; I’m going to trick him. So I decided to get into character and just have a good time because they’re paying me.”

As the plot became more “ridiculous”, says Loudermilk, so his enjoyment increased. During a scene in which he, Morad and Aboud help deliver the (prosthetic) baby, the three men become covered with fake excrement. “This big blast of pooping pap,” recalls Loudermilk – but he was reassured after inadvertently sampling some of the fluids. “I thought: ‘This doesn’t taste bad.’ So I just kind of hung in there. It was disgusting, but I was having fun.”

At the climax at the Mexican border, says Loudermilk, he handed the remote control to the drone to Aboud, “because that was boring. It was ridiculous – they’re not flying a real baby”. Instead, he “wanted to have fun with Sacha,” so he grabbed the “butt-gun”, yelling about the need to defend themselves, and eventually discharged fire, aided by Morad, who helps pump the penis trigger.

Loudermilk declines to defend Aboud’s decision to then endanger the life of the baby by dropping it from the drone, but expresses some sympathy for his unwitting co-star.

“I felt sorry for the poor fella. Because I’m all-in and he’s just kind of following me around like in a daze, like: what’s happening? He was scared to death, and obviously very uncomfortable, bless his heart.

“I’d never met the guy before, but [at times] it felt he was totally freaking out on me. So I had to make him believe that I believed all this. So I would tell him, ‘You’re being a wimp, man. Our freedom is on the line.’ I kept trying to keep him from quitting.

“But I’m surprised he didn’t figure it out. Like, come on, Michael – why would they recruit you to defend our border? Think about it.”

Loudermilk concedes his decision to maintain the pretence of being far-right once he had worked out the true nature of the project was in part because he “was a little offended. Like: really? You’re picking on these Americans that aren’t the brightest. You’re gonna make fun of them and they’re not gonna know any better. So I decided I needed to be their ally, even though I’m not that way.”

At the end of filming, Loudermilk signed a non-disclosure agreement at the request of the production company, which he says he was not given a copy of, and which mostly related to the top-secret weapons. “They came up to me after I was done and said, ‘Oh, you did so well!’ I said, ‘You get what you need? Can I talk about it?’ They said, ‘Oh no, not yet. Especially the butt-gun.’”

Loudermilk considers any such terms breached now the film is out and mentions him by name: “It’s fair game.” He adds that, after shooting, he had some qualms about not coming clean to them that he had twigged. “I felt a little bad. And that’s why I thought: I should make a little post.”

In December last year, Loudermilk posted three times on his public Facebook page about “eight hours of intense filming one on one with Sasha [sic] Cohen”, as well as twice on his Instagram, which is also public.

“But they never saw it. And the fact they missed that makes it even better to me. So I guess it’s on them.”

Last week, representatives for the film confirmed again to the Guardian that Loudermilk was not in on the joke. They have not yet responded to a further followup question on this.

The film was released nationwide in the UK on Friday, as well as in a limited run in the US. Loudermilk, who has not yet watched it, says he is unconcerned about the prospect of recriminations from anyone upset by his apparent actions.

“That people would be disgusted is a compliment. Oh, I really did a good job, huh! I pulled it off and I was so proud of myself.”

#761. More than third of post offices in TG Jones stores to shut by early 2027

Closures within chain formerly under the WH Smith brand raise fears of high streets becoming ‘postal deserts’

Towns and even city centres face being left as “postal deserts” after it emerged that more than a third of post offices within the troubled TG Jones chain are closing.

So far this year 36 branches within the high street chain formerly known as WH Smith have closed and a further 34 are set to close by early 2027, according to Post Office records analysed by the Guardian.

TG Jones was bought and renamed by Modella last year. Before the private equity group’s restructure won approval from creditors in July, the chain operated 180 post offices and it had been feared that as many as 60 could be closed under the shake-up.

Up to 150 of the 450 stores acquired by Modella are expected to shut, about 65 of which have already closed and at least another 46 are to cease operating early next year. This total of 110 announced closures include the 70 containing post offices.

The larger-than-expected wave of TG Jones branch closures follows an announcement in the summer that 52 post offices will close within Morrisons Daily convenience stores this year, some of which are close to the TG Jones sites. The move forms part of a wider plan by Morrisons to close 100 loss-making small stores.

The raft of closures means that towns such as Stevenage in Hertfordshire, Bracknell in Berkshire and Orpington in Greater London, and some smaller cities including Hull and York are each losing two post offices in a matter of months. Telford’s last one is due to close in January.

The majority of these lost sites replaced former crown post offices, the now almost entirely closed network of more than 100 directly operated large branches, which offered a full suite of services such as identity and passport checks, driving licence and banking operations.

Some regions such as Essex, the West Midlands, Wales, Suffolk and Hertfordshire have been particularly hard hit. Six post offices in TG Jones stores in Essex are going, with Clacton-on-Sea and Brentwood shutting in January after the closure of ones in Basildon, Southend-on-Sea, Harlow and East Ham. Five are closing in the West Midlands and four in Wales.

The Post Office is trying to find new operators in these locations but so far only Stirling has reopened after a TG Jones closure, and a permanent replacement for Ipswich is set to open in November. Temporary branches are to operate after TG Jones closures in Maidenhead and Uxbridge.

Such losses can be devastating to the health of local economies. As the Post Office itself pointed out to a parliamentary inquiry into revitalising high streets, almost a third of small- and medium-sized businesses use their local branch at least once a week and more than half use the network at least once a month. Many small businesses report that losing this access would threaten their viability within months.

After the closure of more than 6,800 bank branches across the UK, the Post Office “plays a critical role in protecting this essential service”, according to thetstate-owned company’s evidence to the inquiry. Post office operators already run 250 banking hubs, which combine services for several banking brands, across the UK.

Mole Meade, a senior member at the CWU, the largest union for postal workers, said the closures would leave some areas as “postal deserts”.

Meade added: “What we are seeing with the TG Jones closures is the continuation of a long-term strategy of cutting costs and chasing profit, with little regard for the communities that depend on post office services.

Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning

“The CWU believes the Post Office should be focused on protecting and expanding access to services, not presiding over a continued reduction of the network.”

The Post Office said: “We fully recognise the challenging trading conditions that TG Jones and many other high street retailers are facing at the moment. We proactively sought expressions of interest from our postmasters and partners to take on post offices within TG Jones stores that may close as a result of their restructuring plan or any decisions taken by landlords.

“There is interest in taking on every location where it has been confirmed that a post office within a TG Jones store will close. In some locations there are over 40 applications from our postmasters who recognise the significant footfall operating a post office brings to their store … We’re committed to replacing every branch within a TG Jones store that closes and are working to progress applications as quickly as possible.”

The state-owned Post Office – which is still reeling from the Horizon IT scandal – announced the closure of more than 100 branches in late 2024.

WH Smith travel stores in railway stations, hospitals and airports were not part of the Modella deal and remain owned by its original stock market-listed parent company.

#762. Could I pull off a red bikini at 55? My husband's deep love helped me love myself

This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here.

See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred

I have a trick ankle. When it gives way, I can go from standing upright to lying flat on my back in a heartbeat.

This usually happens at the most inopportune moments.

As a college student, I fell down the stairs in broad daylight at a UCLA fraternity house, my skirt hiked over my head. The guy I was crushing on helped me to my feet and became my college sweetheart.

After my partner of 30 years’ shocking death, I went on my first date in decades. Unfortunately, it just didn’t go well.

As a young professional, my trick ankle gave out and I collapsed in front of my boyfriend, Drew, in the parking lot of a TV studio in Hollywood. I got back up unscathed and proceeded to surprise him with an on-air Valentine’s Day marriage proposal on “KTLA 5 Morning News.” When we got back in the car, Drew was officially my fiancé.

Recently, my ankle gave way while hiking in the Santa Monica Mountains. I slid down that trail with my leg dragging behind me and injured my right knee. This time, I needed surgery.

Although I had already consulted with three orthopedic surgeons, Drew, who married me despite my nosedive in the parking lot, wanted me to see Dr. Bert Mandelbaum at Cedars-Sinai.

“He only does young, virile Olympic athletes and FIFA soccer players,” I protested. As a woman in her 50s living in youth-obsessed Los Angeles, I was well aware of my age.

Drew persisted. A week later, I limped into Mandelbaum’s exam room.

“Diana, this MRI shows your medial meniscus is torn and that your ACL is severed,” Mandelbaum said.

“It’s my trick ankle,” I moaned, adding that I’d had this surgery before, after a snow skiing accident in my late 20s.

“I swim, hike, do yoga and paddle board.”

“Well, none of those require an ACL,” Mandelbaum pointed out. “I recommend a debridement of your meniscus only. It’s a less invasive surgery and a much easier recovery.”

I was surprised by his meniscus-only recommendation, especially because the other three surgeons had breezily recommended the full reconstruction.

It felt weird taking my husband and his girlfriend to the Rose Café in Venice. But Alzheimer’s had changed our marriage. Meanwhile, I was also having my own dates at the same cafe and exploring dating apps.

As I drove back to my newly remediated home in the fire-ravaged Palisades, I considered how differently these two knee surgeries were. In my late 20s, I’d wanted a full reconstruction, hard stop. I’d been a gymnast and cheerleader in my youth, and I still wanted to be able to do cartwheels. (That surgeon had looked at me quizzically, “Cartwheels? Really? I haven’t heard that one before.”)

As soft sunlight slanted in through my car window, I realized I’d already passed the performance baton onto my teenage daughter Dayna. My enjoyment now came from sitting back and watching her shine. Her cartwheels, in the form of her singing and acting in Pali High musical productions, were now my cartwheels. As age acceptance pulsed through me, I made my decision: I would go with the meniscus-only option.

Two weeks post-op, I started physical therapy, and as the weeks passed, I felt more and more like myself. A will of steel rose within me to get into the best possible shape. My next birthday was fast approaching, and I was headed toward the legal speed limit in California: 55.

“You’re looking good, Di,” Drew said, coming up from behind me, and encircling my waist with his hands.

“Let’s have a party for my birthday,” I said.

I told him I was planning to be more like my spirited grandmother, who had never apologized for her age and lived to be 94. I vividly remember, when I was about 8, and seated next to her at the family dinner table, how I’d run my index finger along her forearm. Curious, I’d asked, “Grandma, why do you have all these brown spots?”

Popcorn, a movie and some final kisses? It was a breakup date I’d never forget. But are we really over?

She’d turned to face me head-on, eyes widened in feigned shock, her right hand over her heart. “Today me, tomorrow you,” she’d said, wagging her crooked, arthritic finger in my face.

Her prophetic words had scared me. With the arrogance of youth, I’d never considered that growing older could be anything but positive.

To further aid me in my age acceptance campaign, I started to affectionately refer to my birthday as my “Double Nickels.” With my husband onboard, we chose a venue: the Penthouse, a swanky restaurant atop Santa Monica’s Huntley Hotel. On the appointed evening, Drew and I watched the sun set over the Pacific with an intimate coterie of dear friends, imbibing cocktails, mocktails and my favorite Schramsberg sparkling wine. (When I die, I want to be buried at their vineyard in Napa Valley.)

When we sat for dinner, speeches — or rather, roasts — broke out around the table, with our shared peals of laughter making the air ring with life and its sweetness. Tipsy, I stood up to address the table, having no idea what I was going to say. I started with thank you, and then, upon hearing Gloria Estefan in the background singing about the rhythm and the beat, I called to my friends to join me in a conga line around our table. (Note: I kicked off my heels before dancing, because, again, the trick ankle.)

Waving my white dinner napkin aloft, I thought of my grandmother: loud and proud. It was a smashing evening, and I fell asleep that night deeply grateful for my 55 years.

Lying in bed the next morning, Drew and I reviewed the highlights of the previous evening. Soon we were howling, bordering on hysterical. So much so, that I could no longer look directly into my husband’s face. It was when I was looking away, in that barely-breathable moment, that I had another idea.

L.A. Affairs is a first-person column in the Los Angeles Times chronicling romance and relationships. We are looking for original essays. Here’s how to send us yours.

As our marital negotiation ensued, I agreed to toss my one-piece for a new bikini if he made the travel arrangements to the tropical destination of his choice.

About six weeks later, I laid my red bikini-clad body atop the white, powdered sugar sand of Cancún, Mexico. I was certainly not cutting the svelte figure I had in my 20s. But I was alive, healthy and with my favorite person in the world. The fact that Drew still gazed upon my more than half-a-century-old, decidedly not-hot physique with love and desire was a marvel and a gift.

Trick ankle aside, it’s love that we need to age gracefully.

The author is a writer and literary/entertainment publicist. She is at work on a memoir. She’s on Instagram: @dianadanielepr.
