#763. New Respect Orders could ban repeat antisocial behaviour offenders from public centres

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood says antisocial behaviour is ‘a blight on our communities’

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

I would like to be emailed about offers, events and updates from The Independent. Read our Privacy notice

Repeated antisocial behaviour offenders may be restricted from town centres under new, tougher police powers being brought into force.

The Home Office said the new Respect Orders filled a gap in existing anti-social behaviour powers, and would give police and councils the ability to take stronger enforcement action.

As well as police and local councils, housing associations and transport networks will also be able to apply for a Respect Order under the new rules.

The Anti-social Behaviour, Crime and Policing Act 2014 classifies antisocial behaviour as “behaviour by a person which causes, or is likely to cause, harassment, alarm or distress to persons not of the same household as the person”.

The Metropolitan Police distinguish between 15 types of antisocial behaviour, including disruptive unlicensed drinking in public spaces, littering and “general nuisance behaviour”.

Frequent offenders could be hit with curfew bans, or be ordered to cease drinking in public centres, including high streets and local parks.

From Monday, breaching a Respect Order will be a criminal offence, punishable by up to two years’ jail, the Home Office said.

The orders will only apply to adults, but under-18s can still receive an existing Youth Injunction which includes both prohibitions and requirements.

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said: “Unchecked, anti-social behaviour blights our communities. But it is not inevitable and I won’t accept it.

“For too long, we have lacked the powers we need to deal with this problem properly. From today, that changes: authorities will be able to take tough action against these offenders.

“This delivers on a commitment we made to the British people in our manifesto. And, most importantly, those who make life a misery for others will now face the consequences of their actions.”

Catherine Akehurst, the National Police Chiefs’ Council lead for anti-social behaviour, said: “We welcome the new legislation to introduce Respect Orders, which will provide police and partner agencies additional tools to tackle anti-social behaviour, which we know can so often undermine a sense of safety in communities, erode pride in neighbourhoods, and diminish overall quality of life.

“This new tool will enable swift enforcement against prolific offenders, while prioritising rehabilitation and support to break cycles of criminal and anti-social behaviour.”

#765. Rising emissions and temperatures: The cost of Trump's climate retreat is now clear

The world is set to breach the critical 1.5-degree temperature limit, with Donald Trump's US withdrawal from climate action worsening the outlook, according to a UN report. But there is a small silver lining.

For over a decade, scientists have warned the world must limit global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 Fahrenheit) to avoid the most severe consequences of climate change.

Decades of "insufficient" action on cutting the fossil fuel emissions heating the planet means overshooting 1.5-degree temperature threshold is now "imminent and unavoidable," according to the United Nations Environment Program's (UNEP) annual Emissions Gap Report.

If current climate policies continue, temperatures will rise by an average of 2.8 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels within this century. But even if countries meet their new climate pledges, global warming is still projected to reach 2.6 degrees Celsius. Both scenarios would tip the world into a period of catastrophic weather extremes.

The projections reflect a gap between what governments promise to do and the action they are taking to curb emissions. Some 167 countries have submitted climate action plans to the UN, covering 83% of global greenhouse gas emissions. But those pledges to cut emissions fall far short of what is needed to limit warming.

Among the world's largest emitters, Indonesia, China and the United States saw emissions rise in 2025, according to preliminary estimates. The increase in the US "far exceeded that of all other countries," driven by a resurgence of coal — the dirtiest fossil fuel source — and rising electricity demand, partly linked to massive AI data center expansion.

The outlook has worsened in part because of US President Donald Trump's withdrawal of the United States from the historic Paris climate accord in which the world came together in 2015 to agree to halt climate change. The US is the second-largest annual emitter of climate-warping greenhouse gases.

Since Trump entered the Oval Office for a second time, his administration has taken a sledgehammer to climate policy, gutting environmental regulations and expanding oil and gas production.

"The main takeaway is simple — governments need to get on with enacting policies that cut fossil fuel use as soon as possible," said Bill Hare, CEO of the global science and policy institute Climate Analytics, of the report.

Exceeding 1.5 degrees Celsius even temporarily sets humanity on a dangerous course, as it increases the risk of triggering potentially irreversible or difficult-to-undo "tipping points," like the loss of coral reefs, long-term retreat of ice sheets, and the Amazon Rainforest turning into a grassland.

As ecosystems disappear and sea levels rise, these changes could trigger a deadly chain reaction, releasing more greenhouse gases and accelerating warming, dramatically increasing the likelihood of deadly extreme weather.

This summer alone, Europe recorded more than 32,000 excess deaths related to heat and nearly 1,500 people died in a flash floods in Nepal and Tibet, after climate change laid the groundwork for a glacier to collapse.

But scientists maintain 1.5 degrees Celsius is not a magic number, and that every fraction of a degree of warming brings escalating risks. To reduce the risk of future damage, countries should still focus on rapidly transitioning away from fossil fuels, the largest contributor to global climate change, and toward renewable energy like solar and wind.

Now the best-case scenario is overshooting 1.5 degrees Celsius for a short time before bringing temperatures back down quickly.

"Overshoot is not surrender," UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said in a press statement. "We can still keep it as small and as short as possible — and bring temperatures back below 1.5 degrees before the end of the century."

UNEP lays out a scenario in which the world sees warming peak at 1.7 to 1.8 degrees Celsius around mid-century, before falling back to 1.5 Celsius by 2100. Getting there would require steep emissions cuts of 69% by 2040, relative to 2025 levels.

It would also require removing 330 billion metric tons of carbon dioxide from the atmosphere and storing it in the ground. But recent studies have cast doubt on the feasibility and costs of the technology, as well as the nascent carbon removal industry's ability to scale as quickly as required to meet climate goals.

The UN warns any delays will make the challenge harder, saying that every five years that emissions remain at current levels adds about 0.1 Celsius to projected peak warming.

"We must pull out all the stops to minimize peak warming and return to 1.5 Celsius by the end of the century," Inger Andersen, Executive Director of UNEP, said in a press release. "This is possible."

Still, climate policies have proven effective in reducing emissions. The UNEP report draws on more than 200 studies that analyze how measures like carbon taxes, government climate targets, building codes and subsidies for low-carbon technologies are working.

Carbon-pricing schemes have been the most widely studied so far. China's pilot schemes reduced emissions by about 11%, while the European Union's emissions trading system saw an 8% cut, compared with projected levels without these policies.

"There are more opportunities than ever to accelerate action," according to the report, pointing to the boom in renewable energy since the adoption of the Paris Agreement a decade ago.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Global renewable electricity capacity has grown three times faster than anticipated, and solar build-out grew seven times faster. In 2024, more than 90% of renewable projects were cheaper than fossil fuel alternatives.

While total energy supply from coal, oil and gas has continued to rise, that's happened at a slower rate than was projected in 2015. And coal use is likely to peak and decline by the end of the decade.

"We have a wealth of success stories showing that emissions can be cut quickly," Andersen said. "It is now up to nations to urgently put in place policies that spark fast, deep and sustained emissions reductions, and put the world on track for a more stable climate and more stable economies and societies."

#766. Wanted: Chief small talk officers. Awkward applicants welcome

Some people don't like to make small talk. Others — especially younger Americans— say they simply don't know how to do it.

Why it matters: A communication-skills app is betting that a baptism by fire in small talk can help rebuild social confidence — and it's hiring people to approach strangers to put that theory to the test.

Driving the news: RiseGuide is hiring Chief Small Talk Officers — recently rebranded from Head of Hanging Out to stress the seriousness of the assignment.

  • The monthlong gig pays each of up to three hires $2,000, plus a budget for outings to parks, bookstores and fitness classes, where they'll strike up conversations with strangers.
  • Officers will rate their small talk skills before and after the assignment, with regular check-ins to assess their interactions. They'll also track conversation lengths and strangers' receptiveness, Anastasia Sliusarenko, RiseGuide's brand and reputation manager, tells Axios.
  • "I'm personally rooting for applicants who kind of feel socially awkward," she says, because their improvement could be more noticeable. She acknowledges the irony of using an app to combat screen time, but says the ultimate goal is for users to "get off the app" and practice their skills in real life.

What they're saying: "We actually know from research that something like social confidence can actually be trained... it's not a personality trait," Laura Berssenbrugge, a therapist who specializes in working with Gen Z and Gen Alpha, tells Axios.

  • Social confidence doesn't have to look like the loudest extrovert in the room, Berssenbrugge adds. "That can be social confidence for them. Ours might look a little bit different, and that is absolutely okay."

The big picture: Smartphones and personalized digital feeds may be changing how Americans find common ground and navigate conversations with strangers.

  • Earlier generations often shared cultural reference points, from limited TV channels to major sporting events, that offered easy conversation starters. Today's algorithms instead feed people niche interests, reducing opportunities for common ground.
  • Phones also offer an easy escape from awkward interactions, potentially reducing opportunities to practice face-to-face conversation.

Zoom in: Even bars, once natural gathering places for spontaneous conversations, aren't immune to the shift, D.C.-area bartender Matty Pivec tells Axios.

  • "If you're sitting at a bar, you kind of naturally fall into place of talking to the person next to you... If you have your phone while you're waiting for the bartender, it's much easier to avoid that."
  • "It's become more of a chore than kind of a pleasant surprise to be able to hold a conversation with a stranger," he says, adding, "I think it's kind of a dying thing to go out and meet strangers."
  • John Lemay, a 14-year veteran bartender at D.C.-area bar Spider Kelly's, partly blames dating apps: "Why would you engage in conversation with somebody [at a bar] if you can just check those boxes and wham, your perfect date pops up," he says.

Between the lines: Avoiding strangers might spare people the anxiety of appearing awkward or "cringe," but it also cuts them off from the psychological benefits of casual interactions.

  • Psychologist Ellen Hendriksen points to a study of Chicago rush hour commuters that found those who interacted with strangers reported more positive experiences than those who kept to themselves.
  • Many "underestimated how much they were going to enjoy that," she says.

The bottom line: The goal isn't to become an extrovert. It's to get comfortable with the discomfort of striking up conversations with strangers.

#768. Top officials from Mecca Pact countries to meet Iranian officials in Tehran: Sources

Sign up now: Get ST's newsletters delivered to your inbox

Ministers from the Mecca Pact countries met up in Riyadh earlier in October, following an escalation of attack on Saudi Arabia by the Iran-aligned Houthis in Yemen.

Top officials from the Mecca Pact countries Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan are set to meet Iranian officials in Tehran on Oct 26 to discuss regional coordination, two people with knowledge of the matter said.

Saudi Arabia will be represented by Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman, and Pakistan by army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir, the people said on condition of anonymity.

The Turkish head of intelligence will also join, one of the people said.

The Saudi government media office, Pakistan’s military media wing, and Turkey’s foreign ministry did not immediately respond to Reuters’ requests for comment.

The planned talks would be the first high-level contact between Iran and all members of the three-nation bloc since Saudi Arabia has come under escalating attacks from Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis.

Munir visited Tehran last week, where he met Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and other senior officials. During the visit, Iranian officials told him there would be no talks with Washington until Tehran’s demands were met, according to Iranian media.

Pakistan has been a key intermediary between the United States and Iran. Earlier mediation efforts helped produce an interim peace agreement in June, but the deal quickly unravelled as fighting between Iran and the United States resumed weeks later.

Saudi Arabia intercepted another wave of missiles and drones on Oct 25 as fighting with the militant group continued unabated.

Ministers from the Mecca Pact countries held an emergency meeting in Riyadh earlier in October and agreed to ensure the “rapid deployment” of military forces and capabilities in Saudi Arabia.

The conflict has become an increasingly destabilising element in the US-Israeli offensive against Iran, turning US ally Saudi Arabia into a pressure point ⁠in the wider war.

Turkey, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement in August, under which an armed attack on one member is considered an attack on all.

The agreement’s first article says the parties shall use “all necessary means” to eliminate threats to one another’s territorial integrity, sovereignty or internationally recognised borders, according to a text seen by Reuters.

Efforts by Turkey’s Parliament to ratify the agreement began last week and are still underway, while Pakistan approved the pact last week. REUTERS

#769. First look: Disneyland's Indiana Jones ride reopens with more capacity — and more spiders

See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred

Theme parks attractions are never really finished, especially those intended to be built to last. And so it is with Disneyland’s Indiana Jones Adventure, which officially reopens Friday after a six-week refurbishment. The ride is looking as fresh as it has in years. There were minor changes — more large spiders and other creepy critters were added to one foreboding tunnel — but also some substantial ones designed to increase the attraction’s capacity and reliability.

Todd Martens' newsletter delivers news and commentary on the past, present and future of theme parks, right from the theme park capital of the world — Southern California.

While some ride refurbishment closures result in very noticeable changes to the guest — for instance, the recent addition of a face-shifting buccaneer on Pirates of the Caribbean, or the temple-shattering projections that were added to Indiana Jones Adventure back in 2023 — other updates are less visible yet enhance the experience, such as helping to eliminate downtime.

That is the case for Indiana Jones Adventure. Behind-the-scenes engineering modifications over the last year have boosted not only the attraction’s reliability, but allowed its capacity to increase by about 125 people per hour. Ultimately, that allows for about 1,000 more guests per day, says Nicholas DiBernardo, an area manager for Attractions Engineering Services and eight-year veteran of the resort.

A yearly rehab of the ride is required, says DiBernardo, in part because it is one of the resort’s most complex, with many moving show elements. To ensure that it continues to meet the theatrical and safety standards required, it may appear to Disneyland regulars that Indiana Jones Adventure receives tune-ups with more regularity than other rides at the resort.

When asked whether that’s the reality, DiBernardo answers: “Yes and no.”

“Every attraction is different,” he says. “Indiana Jones typically has a refurbishment every year just because of the size of the attraction and the amount of work that goes into keeping this attraction up. It all depends on the needs for improving show quality or maintenance reliability.”

Two key changes were made to the attraction in 2026. The most recent — and the reason for the ride’s downtime this fall — was something of a wishlist item, and that was changing the machinations that drive its first major show scene, the doors that lead guests face-to-face with Mara, the deity within the Temple of the Forbidden Eye that drives the ride’s action. Prior to the refurbishment, the doors were controlled by hydraulic actuators. Now they’re fully electric. In simple terms, DiBernardo says the doors are now easier to maintain, there’s no longer a risk of a hydraulic spill, and they should properly open and close with significantly more dependability.

That may not sound like a sexy ride enhancement, but it’s one that DiBernardo says will ensure Indiana Jones Adventure runs more efficiently. “In the past, when the old actuators would fail, the doors would have to remain open, ruining the guest’s show experience,” he explains. Not just that, but it slowed down the ride, as fewer cars could be dispatched so riders weren’t seeing the vehicle in front of them.

Elsewhere, DiBernardo says capacity was able to be increased by improving the loading and unloading process, again a change that will be invisible to guests. Essentially, the vehicles park more accurately.

DiBernardo, who works Disneyland’s third shift from 2 a.m. to 11 a.m., says this adjustment, a mix of hardware and software changes, was made over the course of the past year. The problem, oversimplified: Vehicles did not always park in their precise loading and unloading position. Because a theme park attraction needs to operate with extreme exactness to ensure guest safety, DiBernardo says that before this fix, operators would have to send vehicles through the temple sans guests to reset them.

“That was a major win for us,” says the lifelong San Pedro resident. The parking issue was completed in May, and it’s changed the ride’s capacity.

Of course, a huge cause of downtime for a Disneyland attraction is often largely out of the park’s control. It’s us, the guests, who are the problem.

“Our No. 1 downtime driver is guest items,” DiBernardo says. “Guests will be on the attraction, and they’ll have a large water bottle or a backpack. All the vehicles have a pouch for them to store everything, but if they don’t do that, there’s many twists and turns throughout the ride, and those articles can fly out. We’ll have to stop the ride. Not only are we working on ways we can improve maintenance reliability, we’re also working with our operations to help notify guests to store their items.”

To that end, each Indiana Jones Adventure vehicle has been outfitted with new, bigger pouches that should make it easier for riders to dump in their items. All of that should ensure more guests throughout the day can enjoy the attraction, and right now they’ll want to, as all the figures have been dusted, blacklight paint has been reapplied, and the Indiana Jones audio-animatronics have been disassembled and rebuilt.

Walking through the attraction on Thursday, DiBernardo pointed out how all the figures are currently moving with full mobility. The first time we see Indy he’s attempting to force shut a door, one that moves with the figure in front of vibrant animations. Later, he’s hanging over a guest in one of the ride’s grandest illusions, one designed to trick guests into believing the vehicle is reversing (it doesn’t move backward, but rather the walls shift) as a crater of a ball closes in on us.

Walking the track, I noticed many a detail I hadn’t seen on my hundreds of rides on the attraction over the decades. As Indy hovers above us, for instance, his legs and hips subtly shift. Elsewhere in the ride, when a vehicle dips down a hill, it’s actually going down steps. The latter are painted on the track, but DiBernardo notes that over time the cars eventually strip away the paint. I had never seen the stairs. Of course, it’s easy to be distracted by the skull in front of us hovering over a pit of lava, where many of the lights have now been refreshed.

Indiana Jones Adventure has changed over the years. Some opening day effects are long gone, such as the illusion created by actual shifting doors at the start of the attraction, or visions of tumbling rubble near its beginning. But Indiana Jones Adventure remains one of the park’s most detailed attractions, one in which I’m still discovering artistic minutiae more than 30 years after it opened in 1995. And as the recent refurbishment proves, it’s an attraction that remains an ever-evolving work of art.

“The sky is the limit on what we can also add to this attraction,” DiBernardo teases. But for now, it looks good as new.

Mr. Todd’s Wild Ride comes out every Tuesday, but we occasionally publish special editions (like this one!) when we have breaking theme park news. Make sure you’ve signed up to be the first to know.

Martens joined the Los Angeles Times in 2007 and has covered a mix of interactive entertainment as its game critic and pop music as a reporter and editor. #770. UK government to make unprecedented intervention in setting of water bills

Exclusive: Angela Eagle tells utility bosses next price review ‘must focus on value for money for customers’

Ministers will make an unprecedented intervention in water bills and how companies prioritise investment, directing bosses to bring down costs and stop leaks and sewage overflows.

Angela Eagle, the environment secretary, has told suppliers in England and Wales she plans to intervene in the next price review – conducted by the water regulator, Ofwat.

Sources at the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) said Andy Burnham’s 10-year plan, which will follow next week’s budget, would hand the government more robust powers to keep bills affordable and direct local investment. But sources close to Eagle said there also needed to be immediate action as companies began to make decisions before the next price-setting process, expected to conclude in 2029.

There has never been government intervention in the five-year review process. It is run by Ofwat, which analyses companies’ business plans and determines how much can be charged to customers in their bills to fund investment and running costs.

Eagle has written to regulators and water company chief executives, saying that the process must meet specific government priorities, including offering bill payers much better value for money – though stopping short of demanding bill cuts.

The letter to companies and regulators says they must be focused on investment in new technology to save money, and early intervention on leaks and sewage. It also called for far better communication and decision-making power handed to local communities and leaders.

The first priority must be affordable bills, the letter says, adding: “Affordability means a laser focus on value for money for customers.”

The letter says the public is clear about what the objectives for the industry should be. “They want clean rivers. They want reliable water services. They want to know that their money is being spent wisely, and that bills are kept affordable. And they want confidence that the system is working in their interests.”

The letter warns company bosses that it will “not be a business-as-usual price review … it is the beginning of a long-term transition to a different model for the water sector”.

Defra sources said Eagle intended it to be the first in a series of changes that will be announced in the coming months on the water industry, calling it “one of the clearest symbols of public frustration with Britain’s infrastructure”.

A Defra source said the intervention by Eagle was a down payment on bigger changes that would come in the 10-year plan. The source said: “Angela will take a much more bullish approach to telling water companies and regulators what is expected from them. This is the start of a journey to a very different water system and one that delivers for the public.

“There are also things we want regulators and companies to be doing now and so Angela is using the levers she’s got to influence their investment decisions at an early stage and make sure they’ve got no excuses. As well as looking at ownership structures, there are other ways we can go further than what came before.”

The new intervention from Eagle comes as the government continues to explore more radical options for the stricken company Thames Water. The Guardian reported earlier this week that Burnham had told officials to contemplate options that were not previously considered feasible, even if that meant spending taxpayer money and going to court.

Burnham previously said he would nationalise Thames Water – which is running out of cash and recently asked its creditors for an additional £2.4bn – but is struggling to find a way to do so without spending billions of pounds, getting tied up in a lengthy court battle, or both.

The outcome of the last price review process in 2024 led to highly controversial bill rises, after Ofwat authorised a £104bn modernisation programme, funded in large part through progressive annual rate increases that will see average water bills surge by 36% over the second half of the decade. The biggest increase was allowed for Southern Water, whose customers will pay 53% more by 2030, at an average of £642 per year.

Over the summer, several major suppliers requested permission to charge billions more to cover mounting capital costs and debt obligations, sparking fury from campaigners and from politicians, including Burnham.

The prime minister criticised the decision, warning that bill payers must no longer be treated as a “blank cheque” or a “bottomless source of funding for other people’s failures”, saying ordinary households were being forced to plug massive corporate balance-sheet deficits.

However, campaigners for public ownership have warned the move will do little in practice to reduce bills or the environmental impact of sewage or leaks. Sophie Conquest, the lead campaigner at We Own It, said: “These proposals are yet more reshuffling of the deckchairs on the Titanic, and fall far short of Burnham’s promise to end 40 years of neoliberalism.

“This government should be intervening on behalf of households to stop bill hikes. If water companies can’t function without siphoning more and more money out of our pockets, then this government should let them go bust.

“From there, we can bring water affordably into public hands. ⁠Under public ownership, we can put people and the environment ahead of the interests of faraway shareholders and hedge funds.”

#771. Khan hails traffic-free Oxford St as ‘truly momentous occasion for the capital’

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

London Mayor Lord Sadiq Khan of Tooting has hailed the pedestrianisation of Oxford Street as “a truly momentous occasion for the capital”.

From Monday, almost a kilometre of the busy central London shopping street, between Orchard Street and Great Portland Street, will be traffic-free with vehicles being diverted onto nearby roads.

Oxford Street, which produces an annual spend of around £3.1 billion, is one of the world’s busiest shopping areas, with around half a million visitors each day and the overhaul comes in time for the run-up to Christmas.

Buses, taxis, private hire vehicles, private motorised vehicles, cycles, scooters and pedicabs can no longer enter while deliveries can be made from midnight to 7am.

Emergency services will have access to the street at all times.

The area has become increasingly popular as an office location thanks to the Elizabeth line and Lord Khan believes the scheme will help revitalise the site, boost economic growth and attract visitors.

Describing it as “a new vibrant destination”, he said: “I’m hugely excited to see my bold vision for Oxford Street coming to life from today. It is a truly momentous occasion for the capital.”

He added: “For centuries, Oxford Street has reinvented itself, adapting to changing times and helping shape British culture along the way.

“There has been talk of pedestrianising Oxford Street for decades. After so many false dawns, and now working with a Government who share the scale of my ambition, I’m proud that we’re finally unlocking a new era for the street.”

He hopes the changes will open up the chance to bring new experiences to the street, from sport to fashion and cultural events.

He said: “Revitalising Oxford Street will boost jobs and economic growth in the capital, unlock the full potential of this key part of the West End and help build a better, greener and more prosperous London for everyone.”

The move marks the first phase of a pedestrianisation and wider regeneration project aimed at putting Oxford Street among top global shopping destinations including Times Square, the Champs-Élysées and La Rambla.

Critics have said the scheme is too rushed and fears have been raised about diverted traffic increasing congestion.

New bus stops are sited along Wigmore Street, Henrietta Place and Cavendish Place approximately 200 metres from the traffic-free area.

The deputy leader of Westminster City Council believes Lord Khan is “rushing preparations”.

Councillor Tim Barnes has previously said: “If this is going to be the ‘greener, better and more prosperous’ success that the mayor has promised, then issues around access, air pollution, street cleaning and public safety need answers urgently.

“Right now there’s a danger that we will have all of the downsides and too little upside.

“Traffic will be pushed to the small streets nearby causing economic and environmental harm.”

London transport commissioner Andy Lord suggested the scheme is creating a safer space for people to enjoy the retail and leisure.

He added that “we will be closely monitoring these changes to make sure they are working for everyone and supporting the continued economic growth London needs”.

Housing, Communities and Local Government Secretary Angela Rayner said: “This marks an exciting new chapter for Oxford Street, creating a greener, more vibrant place that will attract visitors and investment, support businesses and jobs, and drive growth in the heart of our capital.”

The scheme has the backing of businesses including John Lewis and Selfridges, who both described it as “exciting”, along with Under Armour and Grosvenor Property plus organisations such as UK Hospitality and the New West End Company.

Savills co-head of global retail Sam Foyle said: “Alongside significant investment, it sends a powerful signal about the street’s future, further strengthening Oxford Street’s position as a world-class retail destination for leading global brands.”

Minimal construction will take place in the immediate weeks to reduce disruption in the busy Christmas period.

By the end of spring 2027, visitors to Oxford Street should see more than 50 new trees, two new public squares and better signage.

More than 100 new seats, dining tables and new lighting are also to be installed.

Oxford Street Development Corporation (OSDC) chief executive Nabeel Khan said: “The transition phase is a vital opportunity for us at OSDC to test ideas, learn from people’s experiences and work closely with local communities, businesses and accessibility groups to ensure the future street is as welcoming and inclusive as possible.”

#772. Zelensky says Musk-owned satellite system still restricted in Ukraine

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Ukraine's use of the Elon Musk-owned SpaceX satellite system remains partially restricted, despite earlier signs this week that it had been fully restored.

Why it matters: The current restrictions limit the Ukrainian military from using drones to intercept Russian attack drones and from using its drones to send supplies to soldiers on the front lines, Zelensky said.

The intrigue: Ukrainian officials say they are still scrambling to determine whether the restrictions result from a political decision by the Trump administration or Musk.

  • Ukrainian officials have heard different versions of what happened, with the Trump administration and SpaceX executives accusing each other.
  • "SpaceX as a company tells us it is a technical problem. But our contacts in the company say it is coming from the White House. When we ask the White House, they say it is Elon," a Ukrainian official told Axios.

Musk said in a Wednesday X post that the U.S. government was involved in disrupting Starshield.

  • "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS," he wrote.
  • President Trump said on Friday that the White House was not involved in restricting Ukraine's use of the system.

Behind the scenes: The Telegraph reported Friday that Musk proposed to Trump throttling the Starlink and Starshield satellite networks used by the Ukrainian military.

  • A source familiar with the discussion told Axios that Trump didn't push back on Elon's idea.
  • A White House official denied the Telegraph's account. "This is totally false. As President Trump said, we didn't slow down Starlink at all, and the service is currently operational," the official said.

State of play: But the service is not fully operational. Before the restrictions, the Starlink and Starshield network operated even on drones that reached 400 kilometers per hour. Now it is restricted to 161 kilometers per hour, Ukrainian officials say.

  • Zelensky told reporters on Saturday that the Ukrainian military tested the system on Friday in cars in European Union countries.
  • The cars drove 180 kilometers per hour, and the satellite systems continued working. But once the cars crossed into Ukraine, the system disconnected at 161 kilometers per hour.
  • "The conclusion is that the restrictions apply inside Ukraine but do not apply in European Union countries. In other words, this is a planned operation," Zelensky said.
  • Zelensky also expressed skepticism about SpaceX's claim that the speed limit results from technical problems.

The other side: Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Saturday evening before leaving on a trip to India that he is "not sure Zelensky knows what he is talking about."

  • Rubio said nobody in the U.S. government ordered Starlink to be slowed down. "It sort of happened," Rubio said, adding the system "is back up and running."

Catch up quick: The Ukrainian military uses SpaceX's Starlink satellite communications system to control and operate its reconnaissance and intercept drones. When Starlink doesn't operate at full capacity, Ukraine's ability to gather intelligence, use interceptor drones and conduct long-range strikes against Russia is impeded.

  • Ukraine relies on two satellite systems: One is SpaceX's Starlink, which it uses for communications, ground forces, logistics and defensive drones — ones that shoot down incoming drones.
  • The other is Starshield, which is controlled by the U.S. government and used for offensive military purposes.
  • Ukraine said both systems were restricted.

What to watch: On Friday, Ukraine's chief negotiator, Rustem Umerov, spoke with Trump's adviser and envoy, Jared Kushner, to discuss the Starlink issue, Zelensky said.

  • They also spoke about holding a meeting between U.S. and Ukrainian teams next week to continue the discussions on the latest Trump administration proposal for a deal with Russia on ending the war.

Editor's note: This story has been updated with comments from Secretary Rubio.

#774. From affordability to AI, the Issues driving the US Midterms

Sign up now: Get ST's newsletters delivered to your inbox

With US President Donald Trump in the White House, his party is likely to bear the brunt of voter anger.

Ahead of the US midterm elections on Nov 3, national polls show that most Americans are deeply dissatisfied with the direction of the country.

Economic anxiety is at the fore of voters’ frustration. Many Americans say they are struggling to afford basic living expenses.

Also weighing on voters is an unpopular war with Iran that has disrupted global oil supplies and driven up the cost of petrol, home heating and diesel.

Other top concerns include healthcare costs, data centres, immigration and government corruption.

The midterms, held halfway through a president’s four-year term, determine control of Congress.

All 435 seats in the House of Representatives and about a third of Senate seats are up for election.

Republicans currently hold narrow majorities in both chambers.

With President Donald Trump in the White House, his party has unified control of the federal government, which means it is likely to bear the brunt of voter anger.

This election cycle, spending on political advertising is projected to reach a record US$11.6 billion (S$14.8 billion), surpassing even the 2024 presidential election.

Republicans are outspending Democrats. Still, polls suggest Democrats are favoured to win control of the House and have a meaningful shot at the Senate.

Here’s a look at some of the top issues that are animating the elections.

The economy is almost always the dominant issue in US elections.

About 84% of registered voters say the economy is “very important” to their midterm election vote, according to a Pew Research Center survey conducted from Sept 28 to Oct 4.

By a 51%-45% margin, voters say they trust Democrats more than Republicans to do a good job handling the economy, according to a New York Times/Siena poll conducted in mid-September.

“Affordability” is a major buzzword of the 2026 election, and voters overwhelmingly view the national economy through the prism of household expenses.

Average petrol prices were US$4.29 a gallon on Oct 24, up from about US$3.06 in 2025; mortgage rates in September crossed 7% for the first time in almost two years and have largely continued to climb higher. Those costs are increasingly straining people’s budgets.

Democratic candidates blame Trump’s tariffs and the Iran war for rising prices and are campaigning to end both.

Republican candidates tout Trump’s 2025 tax-cut law, which granted tax breaks for tipped employees, overtime work and Social Security retirement income.

About 65% of Americans disapprove of Trump’s handling of US military action in Iran, compared with 33% who approve, according to Pew, and Democratic candidates have blasted the war as unpopular, costly and open-ended.

The war has also created fissures within the Republican Party. Some Republican candidates have privately or publicly broken with Trump, who disappointed some supporters after campaigning for president on an “America First” platform and promising to avoid new military conflicts.

Texas Attorney-General Ken Paxton, the Republican nominee in one of the most consequential Senate races, said in a leaked audio recording that the war and high prices were a drag on his campaign.

Other Republican candidates have called for the war to be brought to an immediate end.

“I have been one of the leading and deciding votes against the continuation of the war in Iran because I take that seriously,” Representative Tom Barrett of Michigan, who is in one of the most competitive House elections in the nation, said in a campaign debate on Oct 6.

A deep distrust of government courses through the electorate.

A record-high 89% of US adults view government corruption as widespread, according to a Gallup poll released in early September.

The surge was particularly pronounced among Democratic voters: 91% said government corruption was widespread in 2026, up from 57% in 2024, when Trump’s predecessor Joe Biden, a Democrat, was in the White House.

Democratic candidates and some Republicans have linked government corruption to high costs, arguing that federal lawmakers and officials are elites enriching themselves at the expense of ordinary Americans struggling to make ends meet.

There are growing bipartisan calls to ban stock trading by members of Congress.

Other government accountability proposals offered by candidates include term limits for members of Congress and Supreme Court justices and limitations on members of Congress becoming lobbyists when they leave office.

Democrats have pointed to Trump’s stock trading and earnings from cryptocurrency-related ventures while in office as examples of the president using his position for personal financial gain.

Democrats and some Republicans condemned his Justice Department’s now-abandoned plan to create a US$1.8 billion “anti-weaponisation” fund to compensate victims who claim they were targeted by the Biden administration for political or personal reasons.

The Justice Department’s handling of files related to the late sex offender and financier Jeffrey Epstein angered victim advocates and sparked allegations that the Trump administration is protecting powerful individuals.

In a Pew survey conducted from Sept 28 to Oct 4, 85% of Democratic voters and 69% of Republican voters said the future of democracy was very important to their vote in the midterms.

Democratic leaders have repeatedly characterised Trump as an existential threat to democracy.

They have pointed to his repeated false claims that his 2020 presidential election loss to Biden was “rigged” and that voting by mail is riddled with fraud.

Party leaders accuse Trump of employing authoritarian-like tactics in intimidating political opponents and minority groups with hostile language on social media and at political events.

Individuals who leak government information to the media “should be shot”, Trump said on Oct 14 at a campaign rally in Arizona.

“Our President is shredding our democracy” and “Republicans in Congress simply sit idly by, and don’t stop the chaos”, California Democratic state Senator Mike McGuire, who is favoured to win a House seat on Nov 3, said at a campaign debate on Oct 6.

However, Democratic candidates in the most competitive elections have publicly downplayed a potential third impeachment of Trump and centred their campaign platforms on lowering costs.

“Any sort of corruption has to be rooted out,” Representative Chris Pappas, a New Hampshire Democrat running for the Senate, said on CBS’ “Face the Nation” programme on Oct 11. “But we have to focus like a laser on the economic challenges that people are living right now.”

About six in ten voters are worried about healthcare costs, and about half say it is “extremely important” for candidates in the midterm elections to talk about that issue, according to a KFF Health Tracking Poll released on Oct 6.

That survey also found that voters, by a 42% to 22% margin, trust the Democratic Party to do a better job handling healthcare costs than the Republican Party.

That 20-point advantage for Democrats is a wider gap for the party than in a survey from KFF released in April.

Many progressive Democratic candidates have campaigned for a government-run, universal health insurance system that would replace private health insurance.

Some Democratic centrists seeking politically competitive seats, such as Representative Marie Gluesenkamp Perez of Washington state and former Representative Elaine Luria of Virginia, say that sweeping proposal is unrealistic.

They say the party should focus instead on incremental improvements to the Affordable Care Act, Democrats’ healthcare overhaul signed into law by then-President Barack Obama in 2010.

Democrats have campaigned against the Republican-led 2025 tax law’s reductions in spending on Medicaid, a joint federal and state programme that serves low-income and disabled Americans.

Republican candidates have focused more on targeting healthcare fraud. They describe a universal government-run system as tantamount to a government takeover of healthcare that would hike taxes.

A surge in migrant crossings into the US from Mexico during Biden’s presidency helped power Trump’s 2024 election victory over Biden’s vice-president, Kamala Harris.

But a sweeping federal immigration crackdown, including ramped-up deportations, in Trump’s second term triggered a public backlash and calls to abolish or scale back the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency – including in states and districts that favoured Trump in 2024.

In some of those districts, Hispanic voters, who shifted sharply towards Trump in 2024 but have since moved back toward Democrats, can swing election outcomes.

They overwhelmingly disapprove of Trump’s handling of immigration (by 69% to 30%) and border security (by 58% to 39%), according to an NBC News/Telemundo poll conducted from Sept 21 to 28.

Most Republican candidates have defended Trump’s immigration policies and warned voters that Democrats would return to Biden-era “open borders”.

Some Democratic candidates running in Republican-leaning districts have charted a moderate path on the issue, mixing support for strict limits on illegal entry with proposals to expand legal pathways for undocumented immigrants to achieve citizenship.

Adam Hamilton, a Kansas Democratic pastor vying to unseat Republican Senator Roger Marshall in an agricultural state that relies heavily on immigrant labour, called Biden’s border-security policies a “disaster”.

Representative Don Davis, a North Carolina Democrat seeking re-election in a district that favoured Trump by 12 percentage points in 2024, praised the President’s border enforcement policy but said the government needs to do more to increase screenings at ports of entry to detect fentanyl and other contraband.

AI data centres, the warehouse-like computing facilities that support artificial intelligence systems, have aroused intense opposition and become a bipartisan flashpoint in the 2026 election.

Many Americans express concerns about data centres’ energy, water and land consumption impacts.

Additionally, the broader public unease and pushback against AI often manifests as opposition to data centres.

Democrats are more likely than Republicans to be concerned about the role of AI in daily life and its potential to take jobs, according to Pew.

Trump supports the expansion of data centres and AI, arguing that the US needs to outpace China in an emerging technology that is reshaping society.

Many candidates for Congress from both major parties have emphasised their opposition to the construction of new data centres in campaign advertising.

They include former senator Sherrod Brown of Ohio, the Democratic nominee in a Senate election that could sway control of the chamber.

Brown attacked incumbent Republican Jon Husted for helping lure data centres to the state with tax incentives when he was Ohio’s lieutenant governor.

Transgender rights is a prominent wedge issue in the 2026 campaign, just as it was in 2024, when Trump’s presidential campaign benefited from targeting Harris’ support for transgender inmates having access to gender reassignment surgery.

“Kamala is for they/them. President Trump is for you,” was the tagline in a Trump TV ad that Democratic and Republican campaign officials said was effective.

Republican ads in the midterm elections emphasise opposition to transgender athletes’ participation in women and girls’ sports.

According to a Sept 18-24 survey from The 19th/YouGov, 45% of US adults are more likely to vote for a candidate who supports banning transgender athletes from women’s and girls’ sports teams, compared with 20% who favour candidates opposing bans.

Some Democratic candidates in culturally conservative areas have aired campaign ads stating their opposition to transgender athletes competing in women’s sports.

Older Americans vote in disproportionate numbers in midterm elections, and many of them are concerned about the stability of the Social Security social insurance programme, which provides monthly income to retired workers, surviving family members of deceased workers, and disabled individuals.

The main fund that pays for retirement and survivor benefits is projected to exhaust its accumulated reserves in 2032, and incoming tax revenue will only be able to pay 78% of benefits if Congress does not intervene.

Social Security is funded primarily by a compulsory payroll tax that applies to the first US$184,500 of workers’ earnings in 2026, and surveys show widespread public support for raising or eliminating that cap to shore up the programme’s finances. BLOOMBERG

#775. New EU plan for Arctic warily eyes influence of Russia, US

The EU unveiled its priorities in the Arctic as it vies with Russia, China and the US for influence. EU foreign affairs chief Kaja Kallas said drone incursions, GPS jamming and cable sabotage undermine Arctic security.

The EU on Tuesday presented a new Arctic Strategy that outlines the bloc's priorities in the key region amid challenges such as security threats, climate change and mining.

Russia is building up its military power in the Arctic, and US President Donald Trump has threatened Greenland, saying the Danish territory is needed for American security interests but later signed a deal with Denmark over US military access to the territory. China is also investing in the region and has shipping ambitions there.

The northern parts of Finland and Sweden, along with Greenland are located within the Arctic, meaning part of the region is in the European neighborhood.  Iceland and Norway, two other Arctic states, are also involved in the European single market.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"The Arctic is one place where the tectonic plates of geopolitics are colliding," European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said.

"When we see that sovereignty, territorial integrity and the rules that have underpinned security in the region can no longer be taken for granted, we have to act and change our strategic posture," she added.

EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Kaja Kallas said Russia "has reopened Soviet-era bases and is testing new weapons" in the Arctic.

"Drone incursions, GPS jamming and the sabotage of undersea cables undermine Arctic security," Kallas continued. Russia's shadow fleet, which is an attempt to circumvent Western sanctions, is active in the Arctic.

On Arctic security, the EU plans to develop a maritime security hub in the region "to facilitate information sharing form seabed to space." The bloc also intends to expand European icebreaker capacity and extend its satellite surveillance program in the region.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

However, the EU does not intend to compete with NATO in the region, EU Commissioner for International Partnerships Jozef Sikela told DW. Twenty-three EU countries are members of NATO.

"NATO will remain basically the center of defense and the center of deterrence, but NATO doesn't have a budget, the member state has," Sikela said. "This is first about the proper focus and the proper use of resources of the NATO member states and about better coordination."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In regard to the climate, the Arctic is warming about four times faster than the global average. The melting of ice and glaciers in the Arctic pose risks to Europe such as prolonged heatwaves, drought and flooding.

Sikela said, "Collaboration among the Arctic is very difficult," adding, "We're not getting information about the permafrost from the biggest part of the Arctic territory."

Sikela accused Russia of "unprecedented" actions in the Arctic and said the "catastrophic level of drilling and opening new mines" in the region is contributing to its rapid warming. The Arctic is rich in critical minerals and rare earth elements such as nickel.

As part of the EU Arctic Strategy, the bloc intends "to strengthen climate research, observation and monitoring" and launch flagship projects utilizing AI to "anticipate extreme weather and cascading disasters such as coastal flooding."

Although Russia and other non-EU countries such as Norway drill in the Arctic, the EU does not want to expand new drilling in the region. European Commissioner for Energy and Housing Dan Jorgensen said the EU's view "on drilling in the Arctic remains the same and it's very clear: oil, coal and gas must stay in the ground."

Regarding economic interests in the Arctic, the bloc may take further steps to bypass the US. The strategy calls for "resilient submarine cable connectivity linking Greenland directly to Europe, with potential future extensions towards Canada and Japan."

The EU also outlined new plans regarding the residents of the Arctic region. The bloc wants to strengthen dialogue with Indigenous people along with expanding Erasmus+ opportunities for Arctic youth.

#778. After dark, San Diego becomes electric. Here are 9 nightlife spots to hit up immediately

It stopped me mid-scroll. In an Instagram reel, one DJ was mixing an upbeat track in a dark, packed room while another danced on a stage behind her, twerking perfectly on beat. Above them, a message flashed on a massive screen: “Love. Dance. And F— Ice.”

The crowd went wild, matching the energy of the two Los Angeles-based DJs who go by Mango and Ginger. The night looked so electric that I could feel the FOMO traveling through my body.

Featuring artists like Soulja Boy, E-40, Too $hort and Ashanti, SeaWorld’s Summer Spectacular has everyone talking.

When I tapped the location tag, I assumed I was looking at an underground warehouse party in downtown L.A. or a venue in Hollywood. Instead, the party — known as If You See Me You See Me — was happening 120 miles south in San Diego. As a DJ and music lover, I knew I needed to get down there ASAP.

For many Angelenos, San Diego is the place to go for a peaceful weekend getaway — think scenic cliffs, serene beaches, fresh fish tacos and visits to Balboa Park and the San Diego Zoo. But it’s easy to sleep on its vibrant nightlife scene — and I don’t just mean the bars crowding the Gaslamp Quarter. The city is home to some of the most exciting late-night spaces, from hi-fi listening lounges to a cinematic Middle Eastern restaurant that feels straight out of Disneyland.

Skip the usual stops like the San Diego Zoo and Legoland. Instead, check out these independent shops in lively shopping districts for your next weekend getaway to San Diego.

“People just aren’t aware,” says San Diego native Mo Perez, who as DJ Dopemo regularly packs out parties at North Park’s Bluefoot Bar and Lounge. “Then they come here and they’re like, ‘Wow, San Diego is really fun.’”

This is part of the reason why Sasha Marie, a longtime DJ and former member of the Soulection music collective, decided to continue hosting her event If You See Me You See Me, in partnership with Future Is Color, in her hometown of San Diego, even amid invitations to bring it to other cities. She invites DJs from around the globe, many of whom wouldn’t typically play in San Diego, to spin at the party.

“I feel like it’s important to show that something can be successful here,” she says.

Consider this your wake-up call to tap into San Diego’s nightlife scene, whether you want to go dancing or vibe to diverse sounds or have a cocktail in a one-of-a-kind atmosphere. These nine great spots are a sampling of how the city comes alive after dark.

#779. Storm Boelo: Travel disrupted and events cancelled as UK hit by wind and rain

Fresh deluge of wet weather comes after Storm Austen brought strong winds to many regions on Friday

Amber weather warnings have come into force as the worst of Storm Boelo could be set to hit parts of the UK.

Storm Boelo’s winds will peak from Saturday evening, leaving areas in the warning zone, including Scotland, parts of Northern Ireland and the far north of England, braced for gusts of 60-70mph and even 80mph in exposed coastal spots, the Met Office said.

The forecaster’s amber warnings came into force on Saturday at 9pm.

Maximum gust speeds of 75mph have already hit South Uist Range, Western Isles, Highland and Eilean Siar, Scotland on Saturday, according to the Met Office, which has also issued several yellow warnings for rain.

Storm Boelo follows Storm Austen, the first named storm of the season, which brought strong winds to parts of the UK on Friday.

Gusts of 76mph were recorded at St Mary’s airport in the Isles of Scilly, with 74mph at Aberporth in south-west Wales and 71mph at Culdrose in Cornwall.

Heavy downpours since 8am on Saturday have already seen rainfall totals of 72mm in White Barrow, Wiltshire, along with 43mm in both Cwm Dyli, just south of the Snowdon range in North Wales, and Inveruglas on the west shore of Loch Lomond, Scotland.

Hundreds of homes were still without power in south-west England after Storm Austen hit the region on Friday where the National Grid said power had been restored to 131,225 properties by Saturday at 7pm.

An amber wind warning, the Met Office’s second most severe, is active across Scotland, the north of England down to Carlisle from 9pm on Saturday to the same time on Sunday.

A further amber warning runs from 9pm on Saturday to 10am on Sunday in the north-east of Northern Ireland.

Storm Boelo, the second named storm of the season, will bring a danger to life from flying debris and crashing waves and people should stay indoors as much as possible, the forecaster said.

The amber warning sits within wider yellow wind warnings which extend south into parts of England and North Wales and cover the whole of Northern Ireland.

The Environment Agency had issued 58 alerts for spots across England where flooding is possible by 8pm on Saturday, as well as 12 warnings stating that flooding is expected.

Met Office chief forecaster Jason Kelly said: “Storm Boelo will be felt across the UK this weekend, with the strongest winds and greatest potential for disruption in the north.

“Amber warnings are in place across mainland Scotland, parts of Northern Ireland and the far north of England, where gusts of 60-70mph are expected widely, with the potential for 80mph in exposed coastal locations.

“Strong winds will also affect other parts of the UK, with gusts of 50-60mph possible in places. Heavy rain will provide an additional hazard, particularly in the north, bringing the potential for further impacts.

“People should prepare for the potential for disruption, particularly to travel and power supplies.”

People should secure loose items outside, plan ahead if they are travelling and keep an eye on the latest forecast and warnings, he advised.

Storm Boelo has already caused widespread disruption.

Boelo’s strong winds disrupted flights at Dublin airport, where as of 4pm on Saturday, nine outbound and 10 inbound flights had been cancelled by airlines because of weather issues.

It also reported that six inbound flights performed go-arounds – five of which landed on the second attempt, with the other diverting to another airport before returning a short time later.

Network Rail shared images of a trampoline beneath a train and a shed by the tracks, in a call for those living near rail lines to secure their garden furniture firmly.

Visit Liverpool announced that the region’s River of Light event, featuring illuminated artwork, had been cancelled “in the interests of safety”.

London’s annual Diwali on the Square celebrations this Sunday were also cancelled on independent health and safety experts’ recommendations in light of the storm.

Other attractions closed on Sunday include Edinburgh Castle and the Fountains Abbey estate in North Yorkshire, which was due to host its Fountains by Floodlight event.

#781. Serbia's long-standing Putin-supporting leader concedes defeat to student-led protest movement

By TOM MIDLANE and JAKE HOLDEN, UK NEWS REPORTER

Published: 21:26 GMT, 25 October 2026 | Updated: 02:04 GMT, 26 October 2026

Serbia's strongman leader Aleksandar Vucic urged his supporters to avoid 'killings' after he conceded defeat to a student-led movement in a result that represents a seismic political shift in the Balkans nation.

High turnout and gathering tensions marked a highly contested parliamentary election on Sunday.

Although there were 18 parties hoping to enter the 250-member Parliament, the contest ultimately boiled down to a referendum between Mr Vucic's Right-wing Serbian Progressive Party and the Students' List.

The latter is a group of 250 academics, professionals and public figures selected by university students who have led protests against Mr Vucic for almost two years – headed by cardiologist Ilija Srdanovic.

The youth-backed Students' List emerged triumphant among Serbia's 6.4 million voters as Mr Vucic conceded defeat on Sunday.

Mr Vucic, who had been endorsed by Russian President Vladimir Putin and who denounced the student movement as a foreign-led attempt to unseat him, led with virtually absolute power for 14 years.

'The Students' List has won,' Mr Vucic told supporters at his party's election night event, though he blamed Serbia's independent media as well as alleged interference by unnamed European countries and an 'American deep state' for the loss.

He continued: 'I do not want unrest, I do not want killings, I do not want anything like that on the streets.

Supporters of the 'Student List' bloc celebrate following the first results of the parliamentary election, in downtown Belgrade, Serbia, October 25, 2026

Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) prime ministerial candidate Aleksandar Vucic concedes defeat during a press conference at the party headquarters in Belgrade, Serbia, on October 25 2026

A Students' List supporter waves a Serbian flag from the window of a car on October 25, 2026

'We never wanted that, unlike them. They destroyed two years of life in this country; they will succeed in destroying more.'

Mr Vucic said that his SNS party won around 1.7 million votes compared to the Students' List, which he said took around 2.2 million.

Supporters of the Students' List immediately flooded onto the streets of Belgrade and other cities around the country, honking horns, shouting and chanting 'Aleksandar is gone', referring to Mr Vucic.

Ivo Petrovic, 31, a software developer and Students' List supporter, said: 'It's unbelievable, I mean most people don't even realise yet what a victory we've won today.

'I haven't cried yet, which tells me that I haven't processed it. It's going to take a while.

'Everyone is ecstatic, everywhere you go people are blaring their horns and putting up three fingers.'

The three fingers is a holy gesture in Serbia, representing the Holy Trinity and has become a symbol of protection among the student protesters. It gained added resonance as Students' List was listed third on the election ballot paper.

Marta Kos, European Commissioner for Enlargement, said: 'Serbia has raised its voice. After nearly two years of protests for democracy, the rule of law and the fight against corruption, the citizens of Serbia turned out to vote in historic numbers.'

Ursula von der Leyen, President of the European Commission, said: 'Today, the people of Serbia turned out in record numbers to shape their country’s future.

'Congratulations to the Student List on its victory in the parliamentary elections. We stand ready to support reforms on the rule of law, media freedom, the fight against corruption and strong democratic institutions, and to work together to advance Serbia’s future in the European Union.'

The outcome, which Mr Vucic announced only around an hour and a half after polls closed, came after tensions had built as voting progressed during the day.

Police in anti-riot gear cordoned off an area in central Belgrade around the election commission headquarters.

Special police vehicles could be seen near a Belgrade park where Mr Vucic's loyalists have been camping for over a year, and large groups of black-clad men had congregated at various points throughout the city.

Ilija Srdanovic (centre), the main candidate on the student-backed electoral list, celebrates the Students' List's victory in the Serbian parliamentary elections on October 25, 2026

A Students' List supporter throws a three-fingers sign after Aleksandar Vucic's defeat in the parliamentary election in Serbia on Sunday - the gesture has become a symbol of protection among student protesters

People celebrate in the Serbian capital Belgrade after Aleksandar Vucic, leader of the Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) conceded defeat in the parliamentary election on October 25, 2026

Mr Vucic was seeking to become Serbia's prime minister after serving two near-full terms as president. He resigned the presidency last month to lead the campaign.

Support for the populist had eroded since 16 people were killed in 2024 when a concrete canopy collapsed at a train station in Novi Sad. That set off a wave of youth protests that blamed the collapse on high-level corruption, cronyism and rampant graft during renovation work at the station.

Despite the protests, Vucic retained considerable support among many of Serbia's voters. Admirers viewed him as a capable leader who can steer the nation through global uncertainties – the image that was carefully crafted by the mainstream media.

While the increasingly authoritarian Mr Vucic has routinely outplayed Serbia's fractured opposition in the past, the leaderless youth movement proved to be a tough opponent that rattled his firm grip on power in Serbia like no one else in the 14 years since his party took office.

The newly formed Students' List movement was shaped by university students but none actually appeared on the election list. Instead, its candidates are little-known experts, athletes, farmers and artists.

This approach was meant to counter Mr Vucic's one-man rule and restore a sense of community and solidarity. The students' message during the campaign focused on a non-partisan effort to rebuild Serbia's economy and restore its democracy.

The students have used youthful energy to attract voters who are disillusioned with local politicians. Vilified by pro-government media, they cycled and walked through the country to reach voters in rural areas – Mr Vucic's traditional strongholds.

The student victory echoed the recent electoral defeat of a Vucic ally in Hungary, where youth participation helped oust the autocratic Viktor Orbán after 16 years and bring in a new pro-European government. It was likely to resonate beyond Serbia as countries across Europe have faced angry youth and student protests.

Ilija Srdanović (pictured) blows kisses to supporters following the results of the parliamentary election. He tops the Student List's 250 candidates but will not necessarily become prime minister after their victory

Aleksandar Vucic (far left), leader of the right-wing Serbian Progressive Party (SNS), concedes defeat in the parliamentary election in Serbia on October 25, 2026

Supporters of the Student List wave Serbian flags and set off coloured flares in celebration after victory in Sunday's parliamentary election

Supporters of the electoral list 'Student List - Students Win' celebrate following the results of the parliamentary election in Belgrade, Serbia on October 25, 2026

Monitors predicted that total turnout in the election could reach around 70 per cent, unseen in Serbia since 2000.

During the day, long queues formed at polling stations in Serbia and in cities around the world. Some in the Serbian diaspora were made to vote in the middle of the night after authorities tied voting hours to local Serbian time.

Recent Serbian elections had been marred by irregularities and the EU was closely watching the conduct of Sunday's vote in a candidate nation for the bloc's membership.

Independent election monitors reported dozens of cases of irregularities on Sunday such as photographing of ballots that suggested pressure on voters and attempted vote buying.

Mr Petrovic accused Vucic loyalists of 'attacking the closest polling station to the parliament earlier in the day' and said teams of students were deployed around the city to try and defuse any potential flare-ups or intimidation.

Both international and local election monitors had expressed concern about the safety and fairness of an election campaign marked by detentions, near-total government control over the media and reports of surveillance and cyberattacks against activists.

Local elections earlier this year in ten municipalities in Serbia saw violent attacks on journalists and activists. The previous parliamentary vote in 2023 was followed by opposition protests alleging fraud.

#782. Trump's Russia waiver draws instant bipartisan backlash

Top Republicans and Democrats alike lined up Saturday to condemn President Trump's decision to waive recent sanctions on Russia, calling it "irresponsible" and "a deal with the devil." Why it matters: Trump already faces a bipartisan effort to overturn his Russian diesel deal when Congress returns after the election.

  • Now he may have to deal with even broader outrage over sanctions Congress approved just a month ago.

Driving the news: Late Friday night, Trump issued an executive order waiving implementation of the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, which he signed in September.

  • The act would have imposed broad sanctions not only on Russia, but on other countries buying its oil.

What they're saying: Democrats forcefully criticized Trump's decision.

  • "By giving the Russian economy life support, Trump's deal with the devil keeps getting dirtier," Senate minority leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) wrote.
  • "Trump's latest surrender to Putin again betrays our Ukrainian partners and defies clear congressional intent of legislation designed to punish Russia for its illegal war of aggression," Rep. Don Beyer (D-Va.) posted on X.
  • "These waivers have nothing to do with our national security, & everything to do with sucking up to Vladimir Putin. I hope my Republican colleagues will join me in condemning this craven, cowardly action," Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) said on X.

Republicans were equally unsparing.

  • "We should be increasing economic pressure on Russia, not easing up. We need to use every tool at our disposal, including fully implementing the Graham sanctions and my REPO Act, to squeeze Putin until he ends his illegal and barbaric war in Ukraine," Rep. French Hill (R-Ark.) wrote. "I have requested a classified briefing on the rationale for this decision."
  • "Beyond irresponsible. What part of enforcing a law passed 86-11 by the Senate does the President and his advisors not understand?" Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) posted on X. "It's unconscionable that this administration is capitulating to a Russian dictator who illegally invaded Ukraine and butchers innocent civilians every single day."
  • Sen. John Cornyn (R-Tex.) posted simply: "Lindsey would be appalled."

Graham's sister, Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.) told the AP that she disagrees with Trump's decision.

  • "The president and I share the same goal to end the war, get gas and diesel prices down, and the [Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act] bill is one of the tools he can use to do that," she said, adding that it was up to Trump if he uses it or not.
  • "Personally, I would choose to keep the pressure on Russia ... because I don't trust Putin."

One soon-to-depart congressman, Rep. Don Bacon (R-Neb.), hinted at the trouble Trump may face when Congress returns.

  • "Congress has a lame-duck session. The President has an agenda: supplemental, reconciliation, Ballroom, etc… I think the agenda is dead. Many of us won't fund these things knowing he is propping up a dictator's invasion and throwing an ally under the bus," Bacon wrote.

For the record: The White House defended Trump's decision.

  • "President Trump has been clear that he wants to see this brutal war come to an end. As talks continue, this Act provides the President with additional authorities to pursue a peaceful resolution," spokeswoman Taylor Rogers said in a statement.
  • "Enforcing the sanctions provisions now would impede ongoing U.S. efforts to negotiate a durable and comprehensive peace agreement between Ukraine and Russia. The President retains the ability to exercise these authorities at any time if he determines that doing so would advance national interests."

What to watch: The question now is just how hard Congress will push back when it returns in a few weeks.

The UK is bracing for a second storm this weekend, as strong winds and heavy rain are expected to disrupt travel and cause further power cuts in the north.

Storm Boelo, the second named storm of the season, is expected to bring heavy, frequent showers and winds potentially exceeding 80mph to northern parts of the UK.

Thousands of homes in the south-west of England have already been left without power after Storm Austen hit the region on Friday.

The Met Office has advised people to stay indoors as much as possible and said the storm will bring danger to life from flying debris and crashing waves.

The forecaster has issued an amber alert, its second most severe weather warning, covering Scotland, the north of England down to Carlisle from 9pm Saturday to the same time on Sunday. Another amber warning is also in place for the north-east of Northern Ireland from 9pm Saturday to 10am Sunday.

A large yellow warning for very wet and windy weather will cover the whole of the UK’s north from midday Saturday to 9pm on Sunday. Another warning for heavy rain covers Wales and parts of western and southern England from 11am to 11pm Saturday.

Widespread travel disruption is expected on ferries and trains. TransPennine Express has warned against making all but essential train journeys on Saturday and Sunday, while Avanti West Coast has strongly advised users not to travel north of Preston on Sunday.

The Met Office has also warned that power cuts across the south-west of England could be replicated across amber areas in the north this weekend.

In the south-west of England, 31,000 homes were without power at one stage on Friday. More than 3,700 were still without electricity on Saturday morning, according to the National Grid map.

Human-driven climate change has continued to reshape rainfall patterns and weather conditions globally. The UK experienced its hottest summer on record this year, with five heatwaves and a record-breaking 40 days of temperatures above 30C.

Storm Boelo’s winds are expected to peak from Saturday evening. The wet weather will clear overnight in many areas, while more rain continues to hit Scotland and northern Ireland.
