#808. Brazil election: Lula, Brazil’s political titan, defies the passage of time

Sign up now: Get ST's newsletters delivered to your inbox

Brazil's President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva celebrates after winning the presidential run-off in Sao Paulo.

RIO DE JANEIRO – Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, Brazil’s president granted an unprecedented fourth term in office, once likened the events of his life to a miracle.

The titan of the political left made history by becoming the first person to win a presidential run-off after losing the first round in Brazil.

His shock win follows a long and storied political career, beginning in the bowels of a metalworkers’ trade union and even including stints behind bars.

He charted a rocky road to his fourth election victory.

Questions about his ability to do the job at almost 81 encouraged Lula to do squats and jog along the campaign trail to prove that he was fitter than ever.

Initially startled by his second-place finish to Flavio Bolsonaro earlier in October, Lula dusted himself off and launched into an energetic run-off campaign.

He upped his social media game at the eleventh hour, posting selfie videos and buying a cellphone for the first time.

The shift highlighted a certain disconnect with his country’s extremely online, deeply polarised population, 14 years after he was first elected.

His victory preserves Latin America’s largest country as a leftist stronghold amid a regional lurch to the right championed by US President Donald Trump.

Lula, a defining figure in Brazilian politics over four decades, rose from poverty to the presidency, fell into disgrace and was jailed, before once again rising from the political ashes when he returned to power almost four years ago.

His first-round campaign focused heavily on his life story and legacy, which critics said was a misreading of what weary Brazilians wanted to hear.

The president grew up in deep poverty, the seventh of eight children in a family of illiterate farmers in the arid north-eastern state of Pernambuco.

He worked as a shoeshine boy and peanut vendor before becoming a metalworker and trade unionist. In the 1960s, he lost a finger in a workplace accident.

After losing three presidential bids, Lula finally entered the presidential palace in Brasilia in 2003 and was re-elected in 2006.

He left office in 2010 as a blue-collar hero who presided over a commodity-based economic boom that helped lift 30 million people out of poverty.

Massive corruption scandals haunted Lula and his party, fuelling a wave of disgust that propelled Jair Bolsonaro into the presidency in 2018.

Lula was jailed before the election until the charges were annulled on procedural grounds and the lead judge on the case was found to be biased.

However, Lula was not exonerated and the scandal contributed to enduring polarisation in Brazil.

Bolsonaro’s presidency brought more division, and by the 2022 election, Lula pulled off a dramatic comeback by a razor-thin margin.

In his third term, Lula is credited with restoring social programmes eroded by his predecessor, curbing the destruction of the Amazon rainforest, and putting Brazil’s democracy back on a more secure footing.

But the father of five still triggers fierce rejection among voters frustrated by crime and corruption.

He has also faced criticism over Brazil’s mounting public debt, which, with high interest rates, costs the government around US$18 billion (S$23 billion) a month in interest alone.

Lula came under fire for an election-season spending push, including an increase to the Bolsa Familia social welfare benefits which, launched 20 years ago, remains his most significant legacy.

“He has that love for the poor. That’s all it is,” fisherman Antonio Carlos Lima Ferreira told AFP at his home in the interior of Maranhao state, recalling times when he had to send his son to bed hungry.

“Today, at my table, I can choose what I want to eat.”

Lula said recently he did not want to be remembered as “just the Bolsa Familia president”.

Lula, who has not cultivated a potential successor, campaigned on a pledge to stop the far right from returning to “destroy” the country.

His improbable victory on Oct 25 awed his supporters, many of whom feared an erosion of rights under a theoretical Flavio Bolsonaro presidency.

Lula “will always remain a symbol of the defence of democracy”, civil servant Gustavo Monteiro, 58, told AFP at a leftist rally.

“He represents the fight against political repression.”

The leftist veteran has already spent more time in office than any other democratically elected leader in Latin America’s biggest country.

“There is no one in this country with more experience as president than me,” Lula told foreign media, including AFP, in an interview. AFP

#811. In the funny and sexy 'Wicker,' the perfect man is society's worst nightmare

This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here.

See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred

Reason No. 1 to watch “Wicker” is the natural intrigue of seeing Alexander Skarsgård molded out of twigs: face, arms, pecs and abs — and yes, there’s also a shot of that.

Reason No. 2 is that the married filmmaking team of Alex Huston Fischer and Eleanor Wilson have made a mischievous, crowd-pleasing folktale with several sweet beats of romance. Their wicker man isn’t an object of punishment, like the one that made Nicolas Cage flail around screaming about bees. His creator, an unnamed basket-weaver (Peter Dinklage), braided him as a mate for a lonely virgin, a fisherwoman (Olivia Colman) who stomps around her rustic village smelling like sushi and tossing her head back in an Eliza Doolittle guffaw.

In public, the fisherwoman acts tough. But alone in her candlelit cottage, she’s visibly weary of her joyless routine. The liveliest noise in her spinster hovel is the sound she makes using the chamber pot. Once married, however, she wakes up the whole town screaming with delight; her wicker spouse is the handy type who breaks the bed at night and fixes it in the morning. His competence is a major turn-on.

Fischer and Wilson’s bawdy fable is predominately about how this flammable hunk makes the rest of the villagers burn up with jealousy. He’s not like the other men — he’s better. The time period is vaguely medieval and the accents British, save for Skarsgård, who speaks in a flat, neutral exhale, the sound of breeze riffling through straw. Meanwhile, Dinklage’s pizzicato mutterings always sound like he’s about to burst into song.

Based on “The Wicker Husband,” a 10-page short story by Ursula Wills-Jones, “Wicker” is pitching itself as kooky smut, which it is, for about 15 worthwhile minutes. Romantasy is a hot-selling genre. Forget Fabio: People are reading bodice-rippers about sexy dinosaurs, gargoyles, aliens, orcs and even trees. (Those curious to explore beyond mammalian biology should check out Chuck Tingle, the author of “I’m Gay for My Living Billionaire Jet Plane.”)

That audience will want more scenes than they get of Skarsgård swooping Colman to bed as the sound design adds an array of naughty creaks. “Wicker’s” louder point is societal. It’s “Frankenstein” if the rabble wanted to be (or be with) the monster — and a parable with plenty to say about today.

Representing petty humanity are several couples each named for the husbands’ jobs: the Tailors, the Bakers, the Innkeepers and the Bottlewashers. Elizabeth Debicki plays the queen bee, a bully born into high status as the doctor’s daughter, whose icy lavender gowns contrast crisply against Colman’s hand-knitted rags. Clever and ambitious, Debicki’s snob is itching for an excuse to leave this hamlet for the city. Being stuck, she instead bends the residents to her will. As Hedda Gabler warned, bored women are time bombs whose agitation puts everyone at risk.

“Wicker” is brisk, visual storytelling boosted by Sofi Marshall’s clever editing and Lol Crawley’s assured camerawork. Smartly, Fischer and Wilson build out this community with its own strange customs, big and small, each executed without explanation, question or complaint. At weddings, brides proudly wear a heavy matrimonial collar, an accessory more often associated with the stockade, while grooms strap carrots to their crotches and waggle them at goats.

Nearly all of their rituals are rooted in female submission, expressed without words to keep the film from feeling like a lecture. The script prefers to show horrors without dwelling on them. When the perverted old butcher claims a beautiful young bride, the poor girl barely makes a peep. But we glimpse despair under her smile — and one of the next times we see her, she’s chained up in a cellar.

Our three Sundance correspondents, Amy Nicholson, Mark Olsen and Joshua Rothkopf, pick their favorites from this year’s lineup and reflect on memories of Park City.

Our hearts go out to the wives, even when their actions don’t deserve it. “Wicker” also spends a fair amount of time with the husbands to show how much pressure they feel at home too, light as their burdens often seem. The innkeeper is annoyed that his wife wants more conversation. The newlywed bottlewasher is alarmed that his bride wants him to fix the roof. The wicker man’s superiority makes all the villagers feel ashamed. “Wicker” is empathetic to their insecurities, yet it has no tolerance for how moral hypocrites ignore the opportunity for self-improvement in favor of scorching everything to the ground.

An orphan and an outcast, Colman’s fisherwoman wasn’t raised to fit in. Note how she dances, ignoring the regimented steps to nuzzle sweetly into her husband’s rib cage. On her character’s wedding day, Colman traipses into the church like it’s a prank, then nervously straightens up as she realizes this ceremony is serious. The most touching beats in the film are simply scenes of a woman who’s always fended for herself experiencing kindness. Love changes her, not all at once but gradually, like a rescue dog. And it makes her feel vulnerable too.

Colman nimbly balances right on the line between humor and pathos. Still, even she can’t leap over the fact that the second half of the film skips several emotional beats. The fisherwoman’s love story is “Wicker’s” pulse, but the movie is really about the town and it sidelines her character to skewer the place. Frustratingly, by the end, we’re barely inside her head or heart at all.

Skarsgård’s wicker man is tall, blond and handsome on the outside, but hollow by design. He rarely shares what he’s thinking, although there’s one lovely image of him gazing at the sun through his woven hand, perhaps quietly contemplating his own existence. Lately, Skarsgård seems to be doing the same, gravitating toward roles that, at their core, interrogate the impact his looks have on other people. (See also the marvelous “Pillion,” in which his silent biker dominates a cowed lover.)

The special effects team has done terrific work re-creating his body down to the creature’s fringed lashes. More importantly, they’ve kept Skarsgård’s sad blue eyes and the actor puts more soul into them than the script gives his character. “I was made for you,” he says simply. The theater swoons.

Demonstrators are demanding pensions that guarantee a decent standard of living for both current retirees and future generations.

Their key demands include linking pension increases to actual inflation, raising the minimum pension to match the minimum wage, closing the gender pension gap and protecting the public pension system from privatisation.

The CGT is also calling for easier access to early retirement without financial penalties for workers who have contributed for at least 35 years, as well as the repeal of several pension reforms introduced since 2011.

The Madrid demonstration comes as several European countries face a weekend of protests over a range of political and economic grievances.

In France, authorities are deploying 70,000 police officers and gendarmes amid heightened tensions, including demonstrations against Marine Le Pen's National Rally congress in Orléans.

Italy is also stepping up security, with 1,500 officers deployed in Rome and 1,800 in Milan as demonstrators mobilise against the rising cost of living and government policies.

Italian authorities fear renewed clashes following violent unrest on 17 and 18 October, which has prompted tighter security measures in several major cities.

Although the demonstrations have different demands, they reflect mounting political and economic tensions across Europe, with governments facing growing pressure over living standards, public spending and social policies.

#813. Two children’s laureates to give royalties to Sally Rooney after her UK sales halted

Irish and Welsh authors Chris Haughton and Nicola Davies show solidarity after Rooney’s support for Palestine Action

The children’s laureates for Ireland and Wales are donating royalties from their works to Sally Rooney in a show of solidarity after she was forced to stop selling books in the UK because of her support for Palestine Action.

Chris Haughton, Ireland’s children’s literature laureate, said he also wanted to demonstrate the “absurdity” of the bestselling author being unable to receive royalties from her own UK sales because of her public support for the direct action group.

Haughton, whose books have sold millions worldwide, said: “I really want to express my full support for Sally Rooney. As someone who is in the UK a lot of the time, I can’t do what she has done, but I can support her instead of supporting Palestine Action.

“As authors, we need to be focused on freedom of expression, this is everything we’re about, and this is just showing solidarity with an author who has bravely spoken out.

“The entire situation is just a farce. Sending Sally Rooney the money adds another level of absurdity to this absurd situation, it’s making a mockery of the law.”

Haughton said he has twice been arrested for holding placards allegedly supporting Palestine Action, which became the first direct action group to be proscribed under the UK Terrorism Act in July last year, placing it in the same category as the likes of al-Qaida and Boko Haram. His alleged offence carries a maximum sentence of six months in prison.

After the ban was introduced, Rooney, whose books include Normal People and Conversations with Friends, said she would use proceeds from her sales to support Palestine Action. Providing money one knows or has reasonable cause to suspect will or may be used for terrorism carries a maximum jail term of 14 years.

Nicola Davies, the children’s laureate for Wales and author of The Day War Came, about a child refugee from war, said: “I can’t say that I am standing up for the children of Wales if I allow the children of Gaza to be murdered and mutilated without comment.

“Gaza is smaller than the Welsh county of Flintshire, and it’s as if all Wales’s children were concentrated there and being bombed. So I support Sally Rooney in the stand she’s taken, and when my half-year royalties arrive shortly, I will donate to her the royalties from my book The Day War Came, whose sales have been boosted by the conflicts in Ukraine and Palestine.”

Haughton, who will be donating royalties from his UK book sales, said: “Palestine Action are the only organisation – or the most effective organisation – in the UK that that has had some success in stopping arms going to a genocide. I’m very sure that I will be on the right side of history.”

Asked at prime minister’s questions on Wednesday whether he would review the ban on Palestine Action in light of Rooney’s situation, Andy Burnham said proscription “followed a rigorous and evidence-based process that came before this house, endorsed by parliament”.

He said he would not comment further given that the supreme court is due to hear a legal challenge to the ban on 4 and 5 November. The challenge is on the basis that the ban interferes disproportionately with the rights to freedom of expression and protest.

#819. Why US investors are snapping up Germany's famed Mittelstand

Increasing amounts of US capital are flowing into Germany's traditional industrial firms and family-owned businesses. As many business owners struggle to find successors, more companies are becoming acquisition targets.

What do the long-established German companies Birkenstock, Viessmann, Linde and ebm-papst have in common? All have fallen into American hands.

Traditional German family-owned businesses and small-to-medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) have become increasingly attractive to US companies and investors.

Last year, US investors were involved in 76 acquisitions and investments in German industrial and manufacturing companies, according to an analysis by financial data provider PitchBook. The transactions were valued at about $29.5 billion (€26.3 billion) in 2025, nearly double the 2022 total. As of August 19, 2026, the figure stood at $23.9 billion.

"From what we are seeing in the market, the interest from US investors in German companies is definitely still there," said Samar-Ahmad Albrecht-Mahmood of Veracity Capital Investments, which advises companies looking to invest in Germany.

German companies, particularly those in the industrial and manufacturing sector, remain attractive, "because many of them are highly specialized, have strong customer relationships and very good technical know-how," he told DW. "In many cases, these are businesses that have built up a strong position in their niche over decades."

At the same time, many German business owners are reaching an age where they are thinking about selling their business, Albrecht-Mahmood underscored, pointing out that "there is often no successor within the family."

"This brings companies onto the market that might not have been available for sale a few years ago," he said.

Notable takeovers this year include ebm-papst, the Mulfingen-based manufacturer of electric motors and fans, which was bought by US company Madison Air for $5.4 billion in August.

In June, the long-established Augsburg-based company Everllence, formerly MAN Energy Solutions, was sold to Bain Capital, with the US investment firm acquiring a 51% stake in the company.

According to Die Deutsche Wirtschaft (DDW), a German business information network focused on the Mittelstand (medium-sized and family-owned companies), no country owns more German firms than the United States. Of the total 7,861 companies identified in the database "German Companies Under Foreign Ownership," 1,750 are currently held by US investors.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

PricewaterhouseCoopers (PwC), one of the world's leading auditing and consultancy organizations, also underscored the growing US investor interest in acquiring German companies. In a report, titled Destination Germany, PwC said that while the number of acquisitions and equity investments has not increased, the financial volume of the deals has jumped.

The report highlighted, in particular, the acquisition of BASF Coatings by the US investment firm Carlyle, in partnership with the Qatar Investment Authority (QIA), for around €7.7 billion.

The deal was struck on October 26, 2025, and closed on June 30 of this year.

According to a recent survey by the American Chamber of Commerce in Germany, about 62% of the US companies active in the country are expecting business conditions to improve over the next three to four years.

Meanwhile, some 52% of them are planning to expand their operations in Germany, up from 49% in 2024.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

At first glance, however, the increase in US acquisitions and equity investments does not seem to align with the decline in US investment flows to Germany last year.

According to the Bundesbank, significantly less investment capital flowed from the US to Germany in 2025 than in the previous year.

While foreign direct investment in Germany has risen overall — from €57.4 billion in 2024 to a total of €86.1 billion last year — investment from the US amounted to only €11.8 billion, nearly 44% less than in 2024.

In contrast, investment from the United Kingdom rose to around €26 billion.

"I would say the trend is continuing, although perhaps not simply in terms of higher deal numbers every year," Albrecht-Mahmood said. "The general interest in good German industrial companies, especially strong Mittelstand businesses, remains high."

Relatively low valuations also play a role, the expert argued. "Compared to the US, we still see situations where German companies are valued more moderately, particularly in the SME segment. This can make acquisitions quite attractive for international buyers."

This article was originally written in German.

#823. Zadie Smith tells Dua Lipa inequality has made culture clashes feel ‘existential’

Novelist says demise of Britain’s ‘incredible’ welfare system and housing struggles have led to deeper divisions

The novelist Zadie Smith has said that inequality has made culture clashes feel “existential”, adding that it has become “natural to look to your left and think ‘who the fuck are you?’”

In an interview with Dua Lipa as part of the Southbank Centre’s London literature festival, Smith argued that the demise of Britain’s “incredible, historic” welfare system has led to greater divisions.

The pair discussed Smith’s debut novel, White Teeth, which was published in 2000 and primarily set in the last three decades of the 20th century.

Asked by Lipa about how attitudes towards multiculturalism have changed since the 80s and 90s, and the current “dividing line” on immigration in UK politics, Smith pointed to increased inequality and unemployment.

“When you’re living in basically decent housing, when you hurt yourself you know you can go to hospital and be treated just like the rich kid down the road – then the differences [with others] become interesting, sometimes annoying, but not existential,” said the novelist.

“Now, they’re existential. When you can’t get a job, when there’s no housing, when your schools are falling apart, when the hospitals are falling apart – now it feels existential.”

White Teeth traces the stories of three families – the Joneses, the Iqbals and the Chalfens – and is set in Kilburn and Willesden in north-west London, where Smith grew up. The writer praised her state education, saying it has stood her “in incredibly good stead” throughout her life. “I can talk to anyone. The posh kids up the hill? Not so much.

“Now, when you look at my neighbourhood, the same schools, the same situations – everything is harder, everybody is poorer, everybody is struggling more,” she continued. “It becomes very, very natural to look to your left and think ‘who the fuck are you?’ That is an economic and structural question.”

Smith encouraged developing “a nostalgia for the left”. While “you don’t want the LGBTQ+ politics of the 80s, you don’t want the racial prejudice” depicted in White Teeth, “do you want the healthcare and the schools and the education? I think you do. So it’s about looking back and seeing what was of value – and what was [of] value to me was a social democracy that basically functioned, and might function again if people cared about it, wanted it, believed it could happen again.”

On the writing process for White Teeth – which she began when she was 21 and was published when she was 24 – Smith said that she finished the acclaimed novel in the aftermath of being broken up with and moving back in with her mum.

“Everybody else was out clubbing, I was like, ‘I’m fucking stuck in this room, finishing a novel,’” she said. But Valentine’s Day was approaching, and “all my girlfriends were like ‘we gotta go out, go on the pull’.” She ended up finishing it on 14 February and then “literally ran straight out to the club” – so the ending of the novel is “a chaos”, she said, adding that this is “why young people shouldn’t write novels”.

Since White Teeth, Smith has written five novels – The Autograph Man, On Beauty, NW, Swing Time and The Fraud – along with short stories and nonfiction. Her most recent book was the essay collection Dead and Alive.

Lipa and Smith also discussed facing criticism for their works, with Lipa saying that “learning to live with reviews – bad reviews, good reviews” was “one of the hardest things for me to learn to deal with”. Smith said that literary criticism is “absolutely essential” because it “helps develop taste”.

“I’m very interested in criticism,” added Smith. “Even if it’s a bad review of me, if it’s well written, if it’s intelligent … I quite love ‘takedowns’.”

#828. If LAUSD must consolidate schools, it should also integrate them

This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here.

See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred

Los Angeles Unified has seen enrollment decline by hundreds of thousands of students since its school populations peaked more than two decades ago. Now the district is preparing to make consequential decisions about which schools will remain open, which will consolidate and where students will go. Those choices could deepen long-standing inequities — or become a rare opportunity to build a more integrated school system.

The pressures are real: falling birthrates, lack of affordable housing, migration, immigration enforcement and competition from private and charter schools have all contributed to the declining enrollment. LAUSD has managed the leadership transition from Alberto Carvalho to Andrés Chait with relative ease, while reporting gains in student test scores across the last five years. But shrinking enrollment will probably bring school closures, consolidations and layoffs. The question is: Can the district continue to improve while it’s shrinking?

LAUSD has started to host regular listening sessions and solicit community input. These forums are necessary, but listening alone will not ensure that equitable decisions are made. As district officials navigate difficult conversations with teachers, staff, parents and community members, they should keep in mind that the most common solutions to declining enrollment are not always the most effective. School closures must produce genuine savings, minimize disruptions, and reduce racial and economic isolation.

Decades of research show why these guardrails matter. School closures are politically unpopular and have provoked fierce community resistance, including hunger strikes. School closures are also not neutral: In many cities, closures disproportionately affect Black and Latino students and can exacerbate geographic inequality in educational access. Students lose connections with teachers and peers at an age when they need stability the most.

The damage can extend beyond enrolled students. Schools are embedded in neighborhood ecosystems. Their loss affects families, alumni and former staff, producing what scholars call “institutional mourning.” People grieve the loss of schools the way they do people, and school closures can lead to neighborhood blight.

For an equity-focused district, the first question should therefore be whether closure is truly necessary. The second question should ask how to prevent consolidations from inflicting harms. And the third should explore how to seize the opportunity to rethink school attendance zones in ways that further equity goals.

The standard argument for school closures is financial: Fewer campuses should mean lower costs. Yet research shows that, at least in California, school closures do not necessarily improve district finances. Savings can be offset by the costs of receiving more students, providing transition support and transporting children farther from home.

California law requires districts to consider operating costs and savings, yet closure plans often focus only on the immediate savings while overlooking longer-term costs. Before closing a school, LAUSD must consider both the short- and medium-term costs and benefits, and ensure that closures or consolidations do, in fact, lead to savings.

Some consolidation may be unavoidable. In these cases, LAUSD should treat attendance boundaries and assignments as tools for integration. Racist housing and mortgage-lending practices helped produce today’s segregated neighborhoods and schools. In Los Angeles, attendance zones have helped reserve some of the best-resourced schools for affluent children, while segregation perpetuates disparities in academic outcomes. There is strong evidence that desegregation improves student outcomes at a scale few other policies match.

Every consolidation proposal should include a racial and socioeconomic impact analysis comparing alternative scenarios. The board should then favor mergers and boundary changes that increase integration, guarantee displaced students access to well-resourced schools and provide transportation. Such plans may face resistance, particularly from families accustomed to privileged access, but examples in Brooklyn District 13 in New York and the Charlotte-Mecklenburg School District in North Carolina show that school mergers can boost integration, and research consistently documents the broad benefits of desegregation.

In Brooklyn, leaders merged an underenrolled elementary school serving mostly Black and low-income students with a more affluent and racially diverse school that needed additional space. A working group with equal representation from both communities developed a shared vision for the new school, including a temporary co-principalship.

In Charlotte-Mecklenburg, overcrowded majority-white schools were paired with nearby underenrolled majority-Black schools. The campuses stayed open but were split between lower and upper grades to foster integration. These efforts also require ongoing oversight to ensure that bringing students together leads to true integration within classrooms and programming.

Back in California, LAUSD at the very least should revise its Choices application, the unified application process for public schools, magnet schools, multilingual schools and affiliated charter schools, so that displaced low-income students receive priority in subsequent enrollment cycles. A child should not lose a neighborhood school only to be shut out of L.A.’s most desirable and best-resourced campuses.

LAUSD has a chance to model equity-centered “rightsizing”: decisions that weigh real savings against human costs, honor the histories of affected communities and expand opportunity for students long denied it. LAUSD can leverage this extraordinarily difficult moment to right past wrongs and create a stronger, more integrated school system.

Huriya Jabbar is a professor of education at the University of Southern California and Alvin Makori is a PhD candidate in education at the University of Southern California.

Protesters demonstrated over the high cost of living in France, rising fuel prices and a lack of funding for education. They come after a series of protests which started in the capital's high schools last month, with students demanding more funding for education, more teachers in schools and better facilities.

Those protests then went nationwide before expanding to include wider society.

Riot squads fired tear gas at protesters in the capital as well as in Marseille, Lyon, Bordeaux, Lille, Toulouse, Montpellier and Nantes.

Two people were "seriously" injured, Nunez said: one man in Toulouse, who reportedly had fingers blown off, and another person in Clermont-Ferrand. He did not give details of either case.

Authorities had deployed 70,000 security forces across the country for the new marches.

The violence came a week after rioting that saw public buildings vandalised, hundreds of shops looted and 2,700 people arrested, casting a pall over a country that goes to the polls in six months to choose a successor to President Emmanuel Macron after 10 years.

Nunez said Saturday's outcome was more "positive" than a week ago, with more police on the streets acting more rapidly, conducting more pre-demonstration checks and better protecting businesses.

There was nevertheless widespread anger at the government over a protest crackdown viewed as repressive and as an assault on the right to protest.

Protests also took place in Italy, Belgium, Spain and Portugal over different issues, yet with some overlap on inflation and education problems.

Mass protests last Saturday saw widespread violence and clashes with police in several cities, with buildings and vehicles set alight and masked individuals smashing shop windows and looting stores. Unrest continued in Paris last Sunday, as masked youths erected flaming barricades and police charged crowds.

The French government ramped up security operations this weekend, and many businesses took matters into their own hands and boarded up windows or closed for the day.

A last-minute route change to a planned Paris protest prompted pushback from unions and politicians on the left in France, who argued that the move could scatter demonstrators and fuel further chaos.

Police had initially approved a march between Bastille and Nation squares in the east of the capital but overturned the decision on Friday, instead proposing a route between Porte d’Italie and Porte de Vincennes along the city's southeastern edge.

To the south of the capital, authorities also kept a close watch over the hard-right National Rally party's congress in Orléans.

The weekend event, which both Marine Le Pen and Jordan Bardella are attending, drew both supporters and counterprotesters on Saturday.

Police said at around midday Saturday that they had seized multiple items "intended for use in acts of violence or to create a hostile atmosphere," in locations including Orléans, Pau, Rennes, Marseille, and Tours.

Wild boar hunting, which uses rope snares, is legal and common in parts of Indonesia as a pest control measure to protect crops, but illegal inside protected forests or national parks.

Officials have repeatedly cautioned that careless placement of snares near wildlife areas could instead trap endangered sun bears or orangutans.

Orangutans - native to the rainforests of Indonesia and Malaysia - are considered critically endangered, with declines in their population resulting human activities.

Only about 120,000 remain in the wild in Borneo and Sumatra - about half the number from a century ago, according to conservation group WWF.

#833. Brutal, revolutionary empire builder: Genghis Khan's legacy

Berlin is host to a major exhibition on the founder of the Mongol Empire and his successors. Here's how Genghis Khan disrupted the course of history.

Genghis Khan is one of history's most radical figures. A blood-thirsty invader whose conquests caused the deaths of an estimated 40 million people, he was also a visionary political thinker who established the largest contiguous land empire in history.

The founder of the Mongolian Empire died in 1227. Ahead of the 800th anniversary of his death, Berlin's James-Simon-Galerie explores his legacy and the "Mongol Century" (1250–1350) in the exhibition "Genghis Khan and the World of the Mongols."

The ruler remains "incredibly relevant" to this day, says Matthias Wemhoff, the director of the exhibition project.

"What the era of Genghis Khan — the 'Mongol century,' if you will — vividly demonstrates is how quickly established structures can collapse, how rapidly vast empires can vanish from the map and how swiftly the entire landscape can be utterly transformed," the archaeologist tells DW.

The charismatic leader's unprecedented impact on the world also evokes present-day disruptive individuals who are triggering sudden, unpredictable societal shifts, says Wemhoff: "There's always been this question: Are world politics shaped by individuals or rather by groups and sociological processes?"

In this case, the answer is clear, says the museum director, who also co-wrote a 2026 book on the nomadic leader.

"If Genghis Khan hadn't existed, the course of world history would truly have been entirely different — so much of it is inextricably linked to his person," Wemhoff says.

Genghis Khan was born as Temujin around the year 1162. His father, a Mongol chieftain called Yesugei, died when he was still a child. His family was abandoned by its tribe. To secure his familial position, Temujin killed his older half-brother, Bekter, when he was still a young teenager.

Thanks to his charismatic personality, he built alliances and found followers who helped him become the sole ruler on the Mongolian steppe. He formally adopted the title of Genghis Khan in 1206.

At its peak, the Mongol Empire covered approximately 24 million square kilometers (about 9.3 million square miles), stretching from China and Korea to parts of Eastern Europe and the Middle East, and accounting for over 16% of the Earth's total land area.

Wemhoff lists various innovations under his rule: For one, Genghis Khan transformed warfare. Commanders were promoted for skill, discipline and loyalty rather than based on aristocratic rank or tribal loyalties. Soldiers were organized into decimal units of 10, 100, 1,000 and 10,000.

Despite being illiterate by modern standards, he also pushed for the introduction of the first written script for the Mongolian language, which allowed to build a state bureaucracy, track population and tax registers, record decrees, issue legal decisions and handle diplomacy.

A set of laws were established that replaced fragmented tribal customs with a unified legal system.

Trade was simplified through his adoption of a paper currency.

A policy of religious freedom was also established across the Mongol Empire, allowing all individuals to practice their chosen faith without state coercion.

Before the Mongol Empire, the Silk Road was fragmented by local conflicts and heavy taxes. Mongol rule placed the entire route under a single authority, making long-distance travel vastly safer.

The Mongol Empire is known as a period of relative political stability, economic growth and cultural exchange, an era historians call the "Pax Mongolica."

But "it all came with incredible levels of cruelty. The millions of people who fell victim to the Mongols — the mass executions, the abuse of women — this happened on a scale previously unheard of," notes Wemhoff.

The exhibition opens with a raid that happened after Genghis Khan's death, but took place just 260 kilometers (around 160 miles) away from Berlin: the 1241 Battle of Legnica, in Silesia, Poland.

It embodies the brutality and intensity of the Mongols' methods.

There came the "highly mobile, agile Mongols on small horses — lightly armored in lamellar gear, wearing helmets that left the face exposed, and wielding bows capable of firing 20 or more arrows in a single minute," points out Wemhoff.

European knights, heavily armored and mounted on large, massive warhorses, didn't stand a chance against their enemies.

"When a hail of arrows rained down on them, the horses eventually went down, and the knights ended up lying on the ground, stuck on their back, much like a June bug," he adds. "The two styles of combat were simply mismatched."

The Mongols' western campaigns shifted historic power centers in a way that still impacts world politics today.

For example, after the Mongol invasion of Kievan Rus', which was the first East Slavic state, its thriving capital Kyiv was reduced to a depopulated ruin. Moscow became a key regional power, partly because it chose to cooperate with the Mongols rather than pursue resistance.

"In our Western European collective memory, the Mongol invasion plays hardly any role. It's something of an anecdote," says Wemhoff, noting that the era of Genghis Khan and his immediate successors is barely mentioned in standard Western European school curricula.

Germans are mainly familiar with the name of the empire's founder through the 1979 Euro-disco pop band Dschingis Khan, which represented West Germany at the Eurovision Song Contest with a campy song of the same name that reduced complex history to extreme tropes.

But in eastern Europe, the Mongol invasions "changed everything fundamentally," says Wemhoff. "And so fundamentally that we still feel the consequences of it today."

The exhibition "Genghis Khan and the World of the Mongols" runs from October 21, 2026, to April 18, 2027.

#834. Brazil election: Five economic challenges facing Brazil’s re-elected President Lula

Sign up now: Get ST's newsletters delivered to your inbox

Leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva’s (right) won Brazil’s run-off election on Oct 25 and is set to begin his fourth term in January.

BRASILIA – Brazil’s economy has beaten expectations in recent years, but mounting debt and entrenched structural problems could complicate leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva’s fourth term, which begins in January.

Here are the five main economic challenges he faces.

Brazil’s public debt has surged more than 10 percentage points during Lula’s current term to over 82% of gross domestic product, driving up borrowing costs.

The root cause is years of rising mandatory spending, leaving under 8% of the federal budget adjustable.

Lula has sent mixed fiscal signals, at times dismissing debt worries as “nonsense”, while arguing strong economic growth would resolve the problem.

His team has pledged to keep the government’s current budget rules, which cap spending growth and set primary balance targets – revenues minus expenditures, excluding interest payments on public debt – and hinted at tightening them.

Hitting those targets will be harder, given Lula’s promise to raise the minimum wage faster than inflation, which also lifts pension costs, after already raising welfare benefits and promising new spending.

Even with interest rates at 13.75%, Brazil’s annual inflation of 4.6% remains above the central bank’s tolerance range of 1.5% to 4.5%.

The central bank delivered its fifth straight rate cut in September on growing signs of an economic slowdown, but markets expect inflation to remain above the official 3% target until as late as 2029.

Lula’s platform promises lower interest rates through fiscal discipline that spares social programmes, but most economists say rates will only fall faster if Brazil cuts spending, and it is unclear how he will square the two.

A record nearly 84 million Brazilians and 9.3 million businesses are behind on debt payments, according to credit bureau Serasa, as high interest rates bite.

That has fuelled public dissatisfaction despite strong indicators such as record-low unemployment and wage growth outpacing inflation.

Lula plans a new round of debt relief, this time through discounted purchases of distressed household loans from banks, plus tax debt forgiveness for some small business owners. Analysts say such measures offer only temporary relief.

The government has also discussed with the central bank ways to rein in heavy use of easy but expensive credit, such as credit cards and unsecured consumer loans, though it has not detailed any proposals.

Lula will likely struggle to push his economic agenda through Congress after voters elected the most conservative legislature since Brazil’s return to democracy in the 1980s.

Although he defeated right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro in the run-off on Oct 25, Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party and its allies are set to control both chambers.

Lula’s aides have signalled he will keep pushing to curtail tax breaks, but lawmakers have repeatedly resisted measures that raise the effective tax burden.

During his current term, Lula has struggled to name nominees and win Senate approval for them at key institutions, including the Supreme Court, central bank, securities regulator and antitrust watchdog, and that is likely to be even more difficult ahead with the rightward shift of Congress.

Lula won congressional approval in 2023 for a sweeping overhaul of Brazil’s consumption taxes, and a new value-added tax is set to take effect in January.

With under three months to go, the government has still not disclosed the effective rate, which independent analysts estimate will be around 28%.

Fearing a backlash during the campaign, the administration has also held off on sending Congress a Bill to regulate a new tax on products considered harmful to health or the environment, such as cigarettes and alcohol.

That delay could push back revenue from the tax and has fuelled criticism of the government’s handling of tax policy. REUTERS

#838. If you zoom out, Trump's utter failure is even more embarrassing

This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here.

See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred

Being far from the United States for a couple weeks, scanning news from home for just minutes daily over morning coffee, gave me a new appreciation for the metaphors about the clarifying view from 38,000 feet or seeing the forest and not just trees.

President Trump is perhaps best viewed at such distance. If anything, the big picture is less flattering still, ugly even.

At home, with the 24/7 daily drubbing of news alerts on phone, laptops and TV, each Trump outrage, controversy or scandal is soon forgotten amid attention to the next. We’re inured to our reality-show president, who sees each day as a new episode for him to be both showrunner and star. But seen from afar, all at once, somehow the threads come together in the patterns that show just how dangerously flawed, flailing and, yes, failing this unprecedented presidency is.

Over the first half of this month, as early voters began passing judgment in midterm elections, the broader patterns of the crazy quilt that is Trump 2.0 were clear. More in chronological order than of outrageousness and national or global consequence, those patterns included:

“Hello, New America, formerly known as New Mexico,” Trump greeted residents on Oct. 3 in his video endorsement of a Republican candidate there. (He spoke from the Resolute Desk in the Oval Office, once more ignoring historical norms against using the trappings of office to partisan ends.) Days later, he proposed to rename either the Pacific or Atlantic as “Trump Ocean” and declared that anyone who referred to “Artificial Intelligence” instead of his preferred “Super Intelligence” is “THE ENEMY!” (Of course, Elon Musk and other ever-capitulating tech titans fell in line, again. No command is too dumb, as Trump knows: At a rally in Kentucky last week, he boasted that tech moguls “kiss my ass.”)

He regularly attacks, penalizes and now, it seems, wishes the worst on states and cities that didn’t vote for him. At MAGA rallies in Nebraska on Oct. 5 and Texas on Oct. 7, the president of the United States defended the costs of his war against Iran, adding to the crowd’s cheers: “Let ’em take out Los Angeles, let ’em take out San Diego. This is a very small price to pay.” Yet again excuse-makers said he was just joking. That’s no defense. Sick joke, sick mind.

Trump’s Louis XIV-like attitude of “L’État, c’est moi” (“The state, it is me”) was rarely as plain as on Oct. 6 and for days afterward when the government ran taxpayer-financed ads extolling Trump, one with the song “Love Me” as the backdrop. A federal judge finally ordered them to cease airing. Trump justified the ads as “patriotic” but reluctantly said he’d bankroll them from the hundreds of millions in political funds he sits on. Over the same period, the Nobel Committee’s series of announcements of its annual awards triggered days of Trump tirades at being passed over again, but those rants kept him in contention as a global joke.

On Oct. 10 came reports that Trump’s ever-compliant “Justice” Department had opened an antitrust investigation of five broadcast outlets – ABC, CBS, CNN, Fox and NBC — for jointly ceasing pooled coverage of the White House last month in protest of Trump’s banning CNN, MS NOW and Politico because he didn’t like their reporting on him. A federal judge has twice ruled for the banned outlets, though Trump has continued to ban CNN from Air Force One.

Trump’s long-ago promise — that he’d hire “only the best” — continues as a punch line. He named a new press secretary while I was gone and, as I suspected after seeing video of Katie Zacharia’s hapless inaugural White House briefing, she was fired before I’d returned. Last week, Kimberly Guilfoyle was sacked as ambassador to Greece, where the former fiance of Donald Trump Jr. had been exiled after they split, amid evidence that she’d asked a Republican donor to pay off $100,000 of credit card debt. (What’s the big deal? Don Jr. and his new wife got several times that amount from a Russian oligarch for their recent multiday wedding celebration.) Next, Axios had a juicy scoop that former Trump lawyer Alina Habba Mildon recently went to Trump in the Oval Office to complain that Trump envoy Ric Grenell misallocated money that she and her billionaire husband — who sought Grenell’s help in getting some of the spoils in U.S.-controlled Venezuela — had intended for Trump’s Kennedy Center makeover. (Grenell denied her claims.)

After years of ambiguous signals, Trump this month unequivocally took sides between invader Russia and ally Ukraine: Vladimir Putin’s. On Oct. 9 he announced purchases of diesel fuel from Russia, thus helping it to finance its war. On Friday he waived sanctions against Russia that he’d signed into law just weeks ago. And in between, Reuters reported that an order hindering Ukraine’s defensive access to the Starshield satellite system came from “inside the White House.”

Trump does all this even as Russia aids Iran against the United States, sabotages other European allies and commits war crimes in Ukraine. On Monday, he grotesquely claimed that Russia “has been fine on Ukraine,” as the world saw photos of a year-old baby in a stroller and her mother among the dead in a Ukrainian park hit by Russia.

Returning to Washington on Sunday, I read a Wall Street Journal editorial that called for “a bipartisan reckoning for Mr. Trump’s budding alliance with the Kremlin against Ukraine, Europe and American interests.”

Thousands of demonstrators gathered in the French city of Orléans on Saturday to protest against the National Rally, which is holding its national congress ahead of Marine Le Pen's presidential campaign launch.

Bally Bagayoko, the La France insoumise (LFI) mayor of Saint-Denis, joined the demonstration alongside Socialist Party leader Olivier Faure and CGT trade union chief Sophie Binet.

Around 50 political parties, trade unions and associations called for the protest against what they described as "racism, fascism and imperialism." Authorities had expected between 20,000 and 30,000 demonstrators.

"We have come to tell the far right, looking them straight in the eye, that we are not afraid," Bagayoko said upon arriving in Orléans.

The mayor rejected suggestions that demonstrators were seeking to provoke violence, insisting that they were defending freedom and democratic values.

Bagayoko also accused the National Rally of spreading hateful rhetoric and criticised President Emmanuel Macron for failing to do enough to curb the party’s growing influence.

The demonstration comes amid heightened tensions across France following a deadly attack in Trappes, west of Paris, on Friday, which left one person dead and five others injured.

Bagayoko drew a connection between the spread of hateful rhetoric, particularly on social media, and the attack. The alleged racist motivation behind the shooting is being investigated by authorities.

Nearly 3,000 police officers and gendarmes were deployed across Orléans amid fears of clashes between protesters and far-right supporters.

Authorities also mobilised armoured vehicles, helicopters and drones, while several businesses boarded up their windows and public transport services were suspended.

The city's mayor, Serge Grouard, introduced a nighttime curfew for children under 15 during the weekend.

The National Rally expects thousands of supporters at its two-day congress, where party president Jordan Bardella is expected to secure another term as leader.

The gathering will culminate on Sunday with a major rally marking the launch of Marine Le Pen's campaign for the 2027 presidential election.

The event is intended to demonstrate the strength of the party as Le Pen seeks to consolidate her position ahead of next year's vote.

Marylou Magal, a journalist for L'Express, said entry checks at the event included a "quick body search," with security putting "a hand around women’s backs ‘to check whether they are wearing a bra’. If they are not, they are not allowed in, ‘because of FEMEN.'"

Rapporteur's Elisa Braun reported having the same experience.

"Security staff checked whether some female journalists, myself included, were wearing bras, apparently to make sure we weren’t Femen activists in disguise," she wrote in a post on social media.

The rival gatherings come during another weekend of nationwide protests over living costs, public services and government policies, with security forces on heightened alert following recent unrest.

#845. Brazil election: Lula, iconic working class president, wins historic fourth term in dramatic comeback

Sign up now: Get ST's newsletters delivered to your inbox

Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva won by more than four million votes.

SAO PAULO – Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva won an unprecedented fourth term on Oct 25, the country’s electoral court said, in a shock result that defied polls, precedent and global anti-incumbent sentiment to put the brakes on a wave of right-wing election victories across Latin America.

Lula, an icon of the global left and the most dominant force in Brazilian politics in this century, defeated Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the eldest son of former president Jair Bolsonaro.

The senator had finished first in the election’s first round but lost in the runoff by over four million votes, said he would ask for the result to be annulled due to a Supreme Court ruling on Oct 25 that extended voting for two hours.

Bolsonaro’s refusal to concede defeat has echoes of his father’s reaction after losing to Lula in 2022. Former president Jair Bolsonaro never accepted his loss and was later given a 27-year sentence for plotting a coup to remain in power.

The scale of Flavio Bolsonaro’s loss to Lula – by more than twice his father’s losing margin – and the fact his campaign also asked for an extension due to rains in the south, make any annulment unlikely, analysts said.

Mario Braga, a Latin America analyst at the risk consultancy RANE, said there could be right-wing protests in coming days, but “it’s very improbable that it will lead to the reversal of the result”.

For Lula, his victory marks another comeback in a career full of them. The 80-year-old was jailed from 2018 to 2019 on corruption charges that were later overturned, paving the way for him to beat Jair Bolsonaro in the 2022 election.

“He is a statesman, a giant,” leftist federal lawmaker Erika Hilton, who was with Lula in Sao Paulo during the vote count, told Reuters.

At times, Lula’s re-election looked like a long shot, as voters soured on him and his Workers’ Party after years of corruption scandals and rising prices.

Sweeping societal changes also left the former metalworker and union leader looking out of touch with an increasingly app-based economy and its growing ranks of informal workers.

A Tokyo-listed exchange-traded fund tracking Brazil’s Bovespa index fell nearly 15% in Asia trade on news of Lula’s victory.

Pollsters said better-than-expected turnout had powered Lula to victory. Leonardo Barreto, the co-founder of consultancy Think Policy, said voters had chosen Lula’s familiar embrace over Bolsonaro’s novelty.

“People today are choosing between change, with some apprehension, and a known path, which guarantees certain rights,” he said.

During the campaign, Lula pointed to a track record of falling poverty and inequality, while unemployment, illiteracy and deforestation hit record lows during his third term.

He warned that Bolsonaro would cut welfare spending, backslide on social advances and hand over Brazil’s sovereignty to US President Donald Trump, whose State Department led a campaign to get the Bolsonaros back to power.

Lula’s win deprives Trump of a major addition to what has been a growing bloc of friendly right-wing Latin American governments that have embraced Washington’s agenda on security and migration.

Celso Amorim, a former Lula foreign minister, told Reuters the leftist “would be very important for establishing a point of balance in Latin America. Lula is that balance”.

Lula becomes the first candidate since Brazil’s return to democracy in the 1980s to be elected after finishing second in the first round.

Lula, who was president between 2003 and 2011, campaigned on a potent mix of pragmatism and populism that has shaped his career in national politics for half a century, rolling out a slew of reforms aimed at improving the lives of workers and poor Brazilians.

These gained steam with late-campaign pledges that ranged from free nationwide weekend public ​transport, which has to be formally submitted to Congress, to a ‌15% increase in his trademark welfare programme that is already being implemented.

Lula also championed a constitutional amendment that became Brazil’s biggest labour reform in decades, which passed with wide support in Congress.

Still, Lula’s fourth term could be his most difficult yet, after Brazil elected its most conservative Congress since returning to democracy in the 1980s.

Combined, Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party (PL) and allied parties could control over 280 seats in the Lower House and up to 50 seats in the Senate, enough for comfortable opposition majorities in both chambers.

That may deepen recent trends of presidents ceding power to Congress on the budget, major legislation and key nominations.

Lula faces an economy that his government forecasts will grow a meager 2.3% in 2027, adding to fiscal concerns tied to high interest rates and public debt that has risen past 82% of GDP, the highest since the pandemic.

The President’s critics blame spending, though borrowing costs have driven most of the increase in debt.

Goldman Sachs said it expects Lula to make modest progress at most to contain spending in a fourth term, as he stays committed to a state-led growth model.

Surging household debt also concerns economists. Trying to address the issue, Lula rolled out a provisional ban on online betting and unveiled a new debt relief program during the campaign.

The incoming right-wing Congress will try to pass structural reforms that favor businesses, experts say, prompting spending cuts that could trigger popular backlash.

#846. Bulgaria seeks suspects in Germany after Starlink sabotage

A Bulgarian court has issued arrest warrants for two young German nationals suspected of setting fire to Starlink antennas. The case is reminiscent of another in Poland, which Warsaw says was orchestrated by Russia.

Bulgaria on Monday issued European arrest warrants against two 19-year-old German nationals, saying it suspected their involvement in the sabotage of a series of Starlink antennas near the capital Sofia.

"The evidence gathered makes it possible to conclude that there are reasonable grounds to suspect the involvement of the two defendants," the court in Sofia rules, granting a request from prosecutors.

Ukraine's military uses Starlink's military-grade satellite internet service Starshield for battlefield communications amid Russia's invasion.

Bulgaria does not directly border Ukraine, but it is on the Black Sea, one of the flashpoints of the conflict. A similar case in Poland, which does directly border Ukraine, led to a total of four arrests last week, also in Germany.

The two teenage suspects are accused of deliberately setting fire to the antennas on the evening of October 9.

Of 18 in a mountainous region south of Sofia, three were destroyed entirely, two were partially burned and three more were damaged, according to prosecutors.

Prosecutors say the suspects entered from Serbia in a car with German license plates, claiming to be tourists, staying just a few hours around the time of the alleged crime.

Plamen Tonchev, the head of Bulgaria's domestic intelligence agency DANS, said he was working on the assumption that it was deliberate sabotage and said other such acts could not be ruled out in future.

News of the arrests follow just a week after a total of four people were arrested in Germany, accused of sabotaging a Starlink satellite communications station in central Poland in late September.

German police detained three resident men and a woman, two of them Turkish nationals, early last week.

Polish officials said they believed that Russia was behind the sabotage attempt, with Prime Minister Donald Tusk calling it an act of "hybrid warfare."

The domestic intelligence agency also claimed that Russia had cooperated with organized crime elements in Germany on the alleged operation.

Meanwhile, in the Baltic, Lithuania's prime minister on Sunday said that Russia was likely behind an attempted arson attack on a company hosting communication hardware for Starlink satellites.

#847. No magic words will cure the racism that festers in America

This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here.

See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred

Martin Luther King III and his wife, Andrea Waters King, were in Georgia when they learned about the July death of Nolan Wells, who authorities in Mississippi said drowned even though no water was found in his throat, lungs or stomach.

“We were getting our daughter prepared for college when he died,” Waters King said about Wells. “The news just hit in the pit of your stomach.” Wells graduated from high school in 2025 and had just finished his freshman year at a community college about an hour south of Jackson, the state’s capital. “For me, the mother … just really reflecting on her tears, her anguish. It just really struck a chord for me, given the history of Mississippi.”

King, the son of the civil rights icon Martin Luther King Jr., said the appearance of a laissez faire attitude from authorities regarding the recent deaths of children is chilling — not only Wells but also year-old Kohen Wiley, who was killed in a police shooting in June in Mississippi. Authorities there recently deemed the use of force justified, although the context was an accusation that someone in the car with him had stolen diapers.

“We see these incidents where Black people are being hung from trees — and we know Black people don’t hang themselves — and then, Mississippi. It makes you wonder what in the heck is wrong with our society? This is not only about Black people, Black children — these are all our children.”

He was echoing the words of James Baldwin, who in the days leading up to the 1980 general election wrote in the Nation: “The children are always ours, every single one of them, all over the globe; and I am beginning to suspect that whoever is incapable of recognizing this may be incapable of morality.”

King and Baldwin are, of course, right about that.

“The community needs answers, and this is true no matter the child,” King said. “Where is our humanity if Nolan’s death goes unanswered? Who are you if the death of a 1-year-old did not strike some type of blow to your heart? That brings us to the next question: If it keeps happening like this, particularly in the South, what do you say to the children?”

In many ways it doesn’t matter what we, as a society, say.

The reason the racism that began the story of America continues to be written into its passages is that children follow what we do, not what we say.

Not what we read on Sundays or write into legislation at the Capitol. Children do what they see the adults in their ecosystem do. If we want a more perfect union, we must push for that, individually, in our everyday actions. It’s not rocket science. It’s just compassion — though at times it feels as if it would be easier to learn rocket science.

“I think back to the fact that Martin Luther King Jr.’s mother had to pull him aside and tell him that you are just as good as anyone else,” Waters King said. “Unfortunately, the conversations in 2026 that we were having with our children are the ones Black parents had in 1926.

“But I also would remind families, and particularly children of the South, that the civil rights movement came out of the South. Black children need to know and understand their history and understand as brutal as that history has been, it has also been beautiful. We are very strong, magnificent, noble people. We are the cradle and the backbone of democracy. The children of the South need to see more from adults in the South.”

The title of the 1962 book “The Other America: Poverty in the United States” doesn’t scream best seller, but it reached the desk of President Kennedy and was part of the scaffolding President Johnson used to build his “Great Society” policies. It became one of the most influential books in recent American history.

It also shared a thesis with one of Martin Luther King Jr.’s final speeches.

“There are literally two Americas,” he said at Stanford University in 1967, less than a year before his assassination. “One America is beautiful … overflowing with the milk of prosperity … but tragically and unfortunately there is another America, and this other America has a daily ugliness about it that constantly transforms the buoyancy of hope into the fatigue of despair. In a sense the greatest tragedy of this other America is what it does to little children.”

Of course, everyone knew we weren’t an egalitarian society before that book. What “The Other America” did was provide a vocabulary to understand and discuss the race-driven disparity, so that the bourgeoisie would have a more comfortable way to talk about racism. Much in the way I just used the word “bourgeoisie” to make white people comfortable. Translating stark talk of racism into generalities might have made policy-making more achievable, but it also ensured the solutions would be inadequate to the real problems that remained unnamed. Generally speaking, I don’t have a problem with euphemisms, but far too often softening of words leads to softening of actions.

And children don’t always follow what we say, but they almost always follow what we do.

#848. STEPHEN GLOVER: Burnham is ducking all the big decisions while wasting time on the trivial and ridiculous. He has no idea how to save a country heading for bankruptcy

Published: 01:00 GMT, 26 October 2026 | Updated: 01:25 GMT, 26 October 2026

Defence Secretary Wes Streeting tells us we must be ready for war in 1,000 days. He’s thinking of a Russian attack. Scary stuff.

His warning comes days after he launched a ‘national resilience conversation,’ when he asked us to prepare for disruption caused by natural disasters or cyber attacks by hostile states. He said we should all have three days of emergency supplies.

The Government is trying to make the hairs stand up on the back of our necks. War with Russia in less than three years! That isn’t just serious. It is apocalyptic.

Why, then, doesn’t the Government prepare for the life-or-death struggles it claims lie ahead? Why does it concentrate on the trivial or the ridiculous – or both – instead of rearming our depleted Armed Forces so that we can defend ourselves?

Ministers’ reactions to Streeting’s alarums make my point. When asked a few weeks ago how she would react to the Government’s ‘Be Ready’ campaign, Housing Secretary Angela Rayner said her disaster box would include mascara, concealer, baked beans and a bottle of Sauvignon Blanc.

I very much doubt that a single bottle of white wine would last Ms Rayner three whole days. She also forgot to mention an adequate supply of vapes.

Andy Burnham’s response to a similar question last week was even more absurd. He said he would stock up on baked beans, as well as soup. He then recommended Twiglets, without which he wasn’t sure he could survive for long.

I happen to share the Prime Minister’s fondness for Twiglets, but they are hardly vital for survival. No one asked Wes Streeting to invoke societal breakdown but, given that he has done so in such a heavy-handed manner, Burnham’s answer was inexcusably frivolous.

'The PM immerses himself in gimmicks', writes Stephen Glover, as the Government announces plans to clamp down on 'headphone dodgers' and fill in potholes

Since the ‘King of the North’ came down from Manchester to run the Government, it has seemed to me that his approach is similar to a guest at the tail end of a long dinner party who has drunk too much.

He loves to muse aloud. Wouldn’t it be nice if we did this? Or that? His latest thought is that it might be a good idea to have open borders again, though he isn’t categoric. Let’s have a conversation about it. Another glass, Andy? Oh, all right, just the one.

We have the highest taxes in peacetime history and a welfare budget spiralling out of control, with 1,000 new people signing on for disability benefits every day. And, as I’ve said, we have tragically weakened Armed Forces, even though Wes Streeting thinks we could be at war in 1,000 days.

These are huge problems, which would be challenging for the most determined and coherent of governments. But Andy Burnham and his crew have no intention of tackling them.

Instead, the PM immerses himself in gimmicks. In the past week or so, he has pledged to clamp down on ‘headphone dodgers’ who make a racket on public transport, bear down on private car park fines, and fill in potholes on 7,000 miles of roads.

Of course it would be wonderful if Andy dealt with these irritations. But we all know that louts won’t stop playing loud music on trains. Rogues will still slap tickets on our windscreens in car parks. Councils will probably go on spending money on things other than filling potholes.

The Prime Minister may realise deep down that he won’t deal with these issues. He’s trying to convey that he cares about the daily frustrations that drive us mad. He wants us to think he is on our wavelength. That he’s one of us – which is why he appeared last week on Channel 4’s Celebrity Gogglebox.

This is a dangerous policy. People will soon see that he has failed to solve the nuisances he identified. As prime minister, John Major introduced the ‘cones hotline’ in 1992. Thousands of calls were made but little or nothing was done, and unsightly traffic cones continued to litter our roads.

The big decisions are being ducked while Andy Burnham talks about Twiglets and appears on Gogglebox. I suppose he’s planning an early election

There’s an even more apposite comparison. In 1974, Labour prime minister Harold Wilson faced problems comparable in seriousness with those confronting Andy Burnham. Inflation was running at 26 per cent and the trade unions were doing their utmost to destroy British industry.

Wilson – who had just become prime minister for the second time, and was to last only until April 1976 – devoted much energy to a programme he described as ‘Little Things Mean a Lot’.

He had innumerable bees in his bonnet, which were doubtless shared by many people. He wanted to preserve local breweries. He disliked empty office blocks and juggernauts (which have grown much larger since 1974). He championed protection for caravan owners.

Not all of his causes were hopeless or cranky. Despite metrification, he defended the British pint of beer. We should thank him for that.

But most of what he did was fiddling while Rome burnt. He couldn’t solve the big problems that were literally ruining Britain, so he turned his attention to smaller matters, which occupied a great deal of his time and that of ministers.

So it is with Andy Burnham who, unlike Wilson in 1974, may – I stress ‘may’ – be at the beginning of his prime ministership rather than towards the end. He shirks the big challenges.

On Wednesday John Healey will deliver his first Budget. Since its contents have been widely leaked, it’s a reasonable bet that it will be a ‘steady as you go’ Budget that won’t tackle the terrifying problems threatening to bring the country down.

Despite largely sharing Wes Streeting’s fear of war when he was himself Defence Secretary, Healey is unlikely to increase front-line defence spending on Wednesday.

According to yesterday’s Sunday Times, the Chancellor will announce new investment in producing armaments such as drones. That is welcome, but it won’t address the critical shortage of Royal Navy ships, the smallest British Army for 200 years, and a much reduced RAF.

Both Burnham and Healey have already said there won’t be a decision to increase defence expenditure to 3 per cent of GDP until the completion of yet another spending review, which probably won’t happen until next autumn. By that time, a third of Streeting’s 1,000 days will have passed.

Difficult decisions are also being kicked into the long grass over welfare reform. This awaits the outcome of a report, in this case from former Labour Cabinet minister Alan Milburn, into young people not in education, employment or training. Will Burnham ever dare to cut welfare?

Nor is there any prospect of public spending – which stands at 45 per cent of GDP, compared with 39 per cent just before the pandemic – being reduced in the Budget. Our gargantuan debt will go on rising, whatever assurances Healey may give.

The big decisions are being ducked while Andy Burnham talks about Twiglets and appears on Gogglebox. I suppose he’s planning an early election, and hopes that being seen to care about everyday things will endear him to a cynical electorate.

God help us if this ploy works. Our essentially trivial Prime Minister may understand what irritates ordinary people, but he has no idea how to save a country heading for bankruptcy, or any plan to defend it from the Russian threat.

#851. Algeria to send troops to Niger in first foreign deployment in over 50 years

Algeria’s parliament approved a resolution Sunday to send troops to Niger, making it the first time Algerian soldiers will be deployed abroad since 1973, when they were sent to support Egypt during the Arab-Israeli war.

Authorities have not released any information about when and where exactly the Algerian army detachment will be deployed, or how many soldiers will be involved.

Algerian Sen. Belkacem Boulghiti said troops would be sent “to protect Algeria’s economic and strategic interests, particularly its oil facilities in Niger.”

“We are not sending our soldiers to wage war in Niger, but for a mission to secure economic infrastructure," he told reporters as he left the chamber after the vote. "It is simply an adaptation of our doctrine to evolving circumstances so we can rise to the new challenges imposed by the situation in the Sahel region.”

Algeria’s state-owned energy giant and the largest company in Africa, Sonatrach, has been working with the Sahelian country on the Trans-Saharan Gas Pipeline, which is designed to transport natural gas from Nigeria, through Niger to Algeria for export to European markets.

The western Sahel region comprising Niger, Mali and Burkina Faso, has been shaken by violent extremism due to deadly attacks by armed groups linked to al-Qaida and the Islamic State group and the governments fighting them. All three countries have seen coups in recent years and struggled with overstretched security forces.

The move on Sunday emphasizes the thawing relations between Algeria and Niger.

In August, Algeria was the first country to express support for Niger after aggrieved soldiers staged a mutiny against the military junta under Gen. Abdourahmane Tchiani, which was repelled by loyalist forces aided by Russian troops.

After its foreign ministry assured Niger of its “full solidarity and firm support," Algeria then sent a delegation to Niger's capital, Niamey, with four combat fighter jets and a military transport aircraft in what Niger’s ruling council described as “the demonstration of the strategic support.”

The diplomatic rift between the two countries plunged to a historic low last year.

Last April, the countries of the Alliance of Sahel States — Niger, Mali and Burkina Faso — recalled their ambassadors from Algeria following an incident in which a Malian drone was shot down by Algeria's army near the border.

Algeria's foreign ministry also condemned the 2023 coup which brought Niger’s junta leader Tchiani to power.
