#852. Aleksandar Vucic: Serbia’s veteran ruler felled by student-led movement

Sign up now: Get ST's newsletters delivered to your inbox

Aleksandar Vucic rose to prominence in the 1990s as an ultra-nationalist ally of strongman Slobodan Milosevic, serving as his information minister in 1998.

Belgrade - The dominant force in Serbian politics for over 14 years, Aleksandar Vucic, who conceded defeat in a snap parliamentary poll on Oct 25, rose from the wreckage of strongman Slobodan Milosevic’s cabinet to the centre of power using his brand of populist nationalism.

For supporters, the 56-year-old represented stability, development and patriotism in a country scarred by the bloody wars of the 1990s and ensuing international isolation.

But opponents saw him as an increasingly authoritarian figure, twisting between the Kremlin and Brussels and leading a government accused of endemic corruption.

Vucic conceded his party had lost after voters cast ballots in record numbers in the vote on Oct 25, defeated by a new political force that emerged from a years-long protest movement.

“Based on a stratified sample, it is clear that we lost these elections,” Vucic told supporters at his party headquarters in Belgrade.

Vucic rose to prominence in the 1990s as an ultra-nationalist ally of Milosevic, serving as his information minister in 1998.

After protests ousted the Yugoslav strongman in 2000, Vucic became a senior figure in the far-right Serbian Radical Party.

He was then a vocal supporter of Bosnian Serb political and military leaders Radovan Karadzic and Ratko Mladic, both later sentenced to life for genocide and other crimes committed during the Bosnian war.

But Vucic underwent a dramatic rebrand in 2008, co-founding the conservative, pro-European Serbian Progressive Party (SNS), which won parliamentary elections in 2012 and has dominated Serbian politics since.

He served as deputy prime minister, defence minister and prime minister before becoming president in 2017.

Even after polishing his image, Vucic has been reluctant to distance himself from nationalist leanings and far-right associates.

He has stopped short of condemning Serbs convicted of atrocities during the 1990s conflicts and looked the other way as pro-government media and political allies openly praised war criminals.

Despite trying to deny state involvement in a large funeral gathering for Mladic in the Serbian capital in September, several of his ministers attended, drawing sharp criticism from Brussels.

A relentless campaigner, he maintained a near-constant presence on pro-government television channels, embracing locals in tiny rural villages and chastising critics during lengthy news conferences.

He has cultivated the image of a tireless leader criss-crossing Serbia, attracting investment and creating jobs.

At the same time, he has juggled the competing interests of European Union aspirations and Serbia’s close ties to Russia.

Supporters praised him as a brave defender of Serbian sovereignty, spending billions of euros on defence – as he warned of foreign influence and pressure from NATO-member neighbours.

He often cited Serbia’s infrastructure and improved living standards as proof of his success, once pledging to make the country a “land of cranes”.

From the gleaming waterfront district to the numerous projects unfolding in preparation for Expo 2027, his party’s slogan “United Serbia” is plastered on billboards across the capital.

But when a concrete canopy collapsed at a newly renovated train station in 2024 killing 16 people, the accusations of corruption which had dogged many of his signature projects caused an outpouring of anger.

Student-led demonstrations calling for transparent investigations drew hundreds of thousands to the streets in the largest protests since the Milosevic era.

As demands grew into calls for snap elections, Vucic and his supporters pushed back.

Students manning university blockades were labelled tools of foreign powers.

In September, nearly two years into the protests, Vucic finally called snap elections for October, citing “major turbulence on the domestic political scene”, thus meeting a key student demand.

“All of this will end on Oct 25,” Vucic said, referring to the protests, at a major pre-election rally in Novi Sad, the city where the canopy had collapsed. AFP

#856. Abandoning capitalism won't save France. The U.S. should pay attention

This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here.

See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred

On Monday, France’s Interior Minister, Laurent Nuñez, admitted that police have “lost control” as some cities continue to see massive waves of looting and mayhem. Social media brims with images of stores being ransacked, cars burning and mask-wearing goons running wild. In Limoges, the beautiful Hotel de Ville was burned to the ground.

But the chaos, as is so often the case, began peacefully. And many supporters and leaders of the protests have condemned the violence. I think that violence has more to do with France’s miserable record of assimilating immigrants from North Africa and the Middle East than with budget cuts. Call me cynical, but I don’t believe the goons pillaging Louis Vuitton stores are planning to resell the handbags to buy better school supplies or to bolster their teachers’ salaries.

The initial protests were about budget cuts, primarily in education. As allied groups joined in — socialist and communist parties, labor unions, etc. — the argument expanded to generalized complaints about France’s “austerity” policies. In short they argued, as they have for generations, that the government should spend more on pensions and other entitlements.

The problem is that France can’t afford it. It’s borrowed money to pay for its lavish government sector for a very long time. It has run consecutive budget deficits — i.e., took in less than it spent — for more than half a century. In 1974, public debt was around 15% of its gross domestic product. Today it’s at 116%. Government spending now makes up 57% of the GDP and France spends three times as much on “social protection” — including pensions and family benefits — as does the United States, and more than any other country in Europe and the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development.

Naturally, the blame for this sorry state of affairs, according to some supporters of the protests, is on capitalism. French economist Thomas Piketty says the country’s woes are the result of the state pursuing the “capitalist logic” of not investing enough in the public sector and not taxing the wealthy quite enough. In terms of personal income taxes alone — France has massive payroll and consumption taxes as well — the top 10% of French taxpayers provide 74% of the revenue. The top 1% provide a third. France also has the highest corporate tax rates of any OECD country.

I’m hard-pressed to see how just a bit more taxing and spending will solve France’s problems.

I have real sympathy for the nonviolent French youth. Their economy is moribund in large part because retirees have a stranglehold on the state’s finances, consuming 14% of GDP. One reason education spending is so tight: A third of the education budget goes toward Education Ministry pensions.

I don’t think retirees should be thrown to the wolves, but such a system is objectively unsustainable. Yet, in 2023, when French President Emmanuel Macron introduced reforms to bump up the retirement age to 64 from 62, the resulting protests paralyzed the country (that modest reform was suspended last month). France is now caught in what economists call the “dependency trap,” producing too few workers to pay for the lifestyles of its older generations.

When protesters talk about feeling “hopeless,” what they often mean is that the gravy train will run out before they get to partake in it. I don’t blame them for being resentful, but it’s difficult to see how this is a failure of capitalism or “neo-liberalism.” As Margaret Thatcher famously said, “The problem with socialism is that you eventually run out of other people’s money.”

The most obvious answer to France’s problems is economic growth — much easier said than done, of course. The reason that’s so hard for France isn’t because the government is “unresponsive” to the people and their concerns, it’s because it’s too responsive. For decades, the French have demanded the economic policies that got them into this mess, and the government appeased them.

France is an outlier in its poor economic performance and lavish social spending, but its problems are recognizable across the West, including in America. The U.S. economy has grown twice as fast as France’s over the last quarter of a century, but the demands for less “capitalism” from young Americans echo those protesting in Paris.

France has the sort of universal health insurance many insist would solve everyone’s problems here. It hasn’t spared France from political turmoil. Our own Social Security and Medicare aren’t far from insolvency, but demands for higher benefits and “Medicare for All” only grow louder.

The French canary in the coal mine is a good reminder that the best solution to some crises is to avoid them in the first place.

#858. Arrested for attempted fleecing: Moment sheep that farmer said had been stolen three times are spotted in his field as he is held over £100,000 insurance fraud

Published: 00:00 GMT, 26 October 2026 | Updated: 01:22 GMT, 26 October 2026

Police officers stumbled across a field of confused-looking sheep while investigating a farmer's claim that his sheep had been 'stolen'.

City of London police officers discovered the flock - which the farmer had claimed were rustled from his fields three times - last Tuesday while they were carrying out a search warrant.

The allegedly 'stolen' sheep were, in fact, found alive and grazing in the farmer's own rented fields in South Molton, Devon.

Officers from the City of London's Insurance Fraud Enforcement Department (IFED), the national lead force for fraud and cyber crime in England and Wales, arrived at the Devon farm and counted up eight sheep.

But they quickly discovered there were far more safe and well in the next field.

The farmer had claimed nearly £100,000 in insurance over the alleged theft of more than 650 of his livestock - including two dead sheep - in 12 months.

Bodycam footage shows the moment officers discovered the 'stolen' sheep in the farmer's rented fields

The farmer had claimed more than 650 sheep had been stolen and two had died - but the flock were found alive and well last Tuesday

A total of £28,220 was paid out from an insurer for two of the claims, while his third claim for a staggering £64,800 was not paid after the IFED and insurance industry intervened.

Police said a 24-year-old man was arrested on suspicion of fraud by false representation and making or supplying articles for use in fraud later that day, on October 13.

The man has since been released under investigation.

IFED officers attended two residential addresses, a garage and two vehicles alongside the local neighbourhood policing team, the local authority and the Rural Crime Agency.

Officers seized further documentation relevant to the investigation, along with a mobile phone.

They also discovered two shotguns, which breached licensing conditions.

Officers also discovered two shotguns which breached licensing conditions at a residential address

Police found the goods while carrying out a search warrant in South Molton, Devon

Officers and veterinary professionals also carried out checks on the welfare of the animals and the number of sheep present against records held by the Rural Payments Agency.

Fortunately, the sheep were all found well and alive.

Carley Parodi, Detective Constable from IFED at City of London Police, said: 'Rural insurance fraud may be less common, but it can have a significant impact on insurers and genuine customers.

'Fraudulent claims distort the true picture of risk and can contribute to higher premiums for honest policyholders.

'We will continue to investigate these offences and take action against those who seek to profit through fraud.'

Tim Passmore, Chair of the National Rural Crime Network, also said: 'Livestock insurance fraud harms rural businesses, increases costs for honest policyholders and undermines efforts to understand and tackle rural crime.

'The National Rural Crime Network welcomes the partnership between the insurer, the Rural Crime Agency and the City of London Police in investigating these suspected offences.

'Sharing intelligence and working together is vital to protecting rural communities and ensuring suspected fraud is properly investigated.'

#860. ‘Tonight we celebrate’: Serbia’s students jubilant after poll win

Sign up now: Get ST's newsletters delivered to your inbox

Supporters of the Students’ List wave a giant Serbian flag as they celebrate their victory in the Serbian parliamentary elections on Oct 25.

BELGRADE – Celebrations erupted across several Serbian cities late on Oct 25 as people hailed the student-backed movement deposing veteran leader Aleksandar Vucic’s party in a snap election.

Cars flying Serbian flags honked horns in Belgrade as fireworks lit up the skyline and people massed in public squares and near parliament.

“I feel as though I am finally living in a free country,” student Mila Martic told AFP.

The parliamentary election was the culmination of nearly two years of student-led protests after the 2024 collapse of a canopy at Novi Sad railway station that killed 16 people.

The disaster has been widely blamed on corruption and triggered some of Serbia’s largest protests since the fall of strongman Slobodan Milosevic in 2000.

Within moments of Vucic conceding defeat, people poured into the streets to join crowds that had already begun gathering shortly after polls closed; within hours, thousands were on the streets in several cities.

Many passersby held three fingers aloft, the student-backed election list’s ballot number and a traditional Serbian greeting, and some lit flares.

Meanwhile, at the Students’ List headquarters, supporters applauded, cried, and hugged each other, chanting “Victory, victory!”

“I am experiencing emotions I’ve never felt before. I am so happy for my family,” she added, holding back tears.

“Serbia has won as we promised. Never again a tyrant in this country!” Radomir Saicic, a university professor and candidate on the Students’ List, told the supporters in the List’s headquarters.

He urged people to celebrate the victory peacefully and with dignity.

“Tonight we celebrate the best way Serbia knows, with song, dance, hugs and tears of joy.

“Tomorrow the work starts, serious, responsible hard work to build Serbia in which the law applies equally to everyone.”

Meanwhile, groups of hooded men dressed in black hurried out of a pro-government encampment that had occupied a local city park across from parliament for months.

Crowds poured into the park and dismantled the remaining tents; one tent was set on fire, but there were no reports of clashes.

Trucks carrying riot police were seen leaving the city centre as crowds cheered and waved at them.

An AFP journalist saw the students’ supporters starting a folk dance, while Mirjana Nikolic, a candidate on the Students’ List and rector of the University of Arts, paid tribute to “all these young people, without whom none of this would have been possible”.

Local broadcasters also showed jubilant scenes in other Serbian cities, including a gathering of thousands in Novi Sad where the protest movement began. AFP

#863. The homeless man living in front of a London mega-mansion

Anders Fernstedt lives in London without any money. The Swedish native has built a most unusual home under the porch of a house worth over €200 million. How did that happen?

There's a lot of stopping and staring in Knightsbridge. This part of central London is within a stone's throw of Buckingham Palace, Hyde Park and Harrods, bringing inquisitive tourists in droves.

While it may not divert quite as many eyeballs as the seat of the British monarchy, a curious collection of plants, garden umbrellas, shopping bags and children's toys filling a building's entrance causes many a curious glance.

The peculiar arrangement on a grand portico is what Anders Fernstedt, a man from Sweden who fell on hard times, has been calling home for more than three years already.

That building hosting his makeshift setup was, just a few years ago, London's most expensive house.

The mega-mansion at 2-8A Rutland Gate sold in 2020 for a then-record £210 million (€244 million, $278 million) to Hui Ka Yan, the founder of China's Evergrande group, who was sentenced to life in prison last month.

Hui never moved in and the house was registered under his wife's name. The freezing of her assets means it can't be seized by liquidators and the house is in a state of limbo.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

So too was Fernstedt when he first stumbled across it. "I just thought, it would be a shelter for the night. I'm an avid camper, like an amateur botanist. I'm not afraid of nature," he told DW.

Fernstedt has never been inside the property, which appears to be in a state of disrepair. Instead, he gradually built his home in the portico, where grand columns guard the 45 rooms, indoor swimming pool and 116 windows. Year round he sleeps under the portico roof and a large umbrella which provides a hidden nook in which he's placed mattresses and bedding.

"I haven't had a bad night's sleep for as long as I can remember. And that goes for four seasons. It's not cold in the winter, and because I don't have walls, I get the breeze in the heat," he said.

"My conceit when I started was that sort of fake dream. Oh, I'm just a boy, my parents are in the house, everything's normal, I just asked them for permission to camp on the balcony."

Fernstedt was raised by his mother in Sweden before embarking on a range of careers at home and in the US, building a name for himself in the tech world.

In 2016, he moved to England where he worked as a journalist and fact checker at publications including The Economist, before work dried up around the time of the COVID pandemic.

A share in a tech company from his days in the US gave Anders a nest egg he relied on. But it couldn't last forever and he found himself living in a tent and then temporary accommodation, where he experienced violence and brushed up against people with severe addictions.

"Perhaps in this contemporary world, the biggest curiosity about my lifestyle is I'm completely off money," he said.

Fernstedt has built relationships with bakeries, cafes and florists in which he gets unused food, flowers for his home and use of power. He also makes use of a homeless charity in nearby Victoria for showers, clothing donations and socializing. But he's also made himself a broadly accepted part of one of London's most affluent neighborhoods.

"This is a very sophisticated neighborhood. I'd stayed for a few weeks and I knew everybody knew that I was here. And I thought, how can I sort of convey my presence without being present? And I thought, my constituency has to be the neighbors' children and grandchildren. Because if they plead my case at the kitchen table, my prospects improve," he said, by way of explaining the toys that line his abode.

"It is, in a way, a squirrel's nut collection," he added, when asked if he's worried about leaving his possessions out in the open. "I have so many nuts that I won't notice when something disappears."

There are some neighbors who do object to his presence, but Anders does his best to keep his home neat and his life quiet. Indeed, many others feel his presence prevents the house being a target for thieves or vandals. Overall though, he's found the community welcoming.

"Sometimes they introduce themselves asking what might I want or need. And my stock answer being: 'well, what you just gave me, a little bit of normal time, right? And neighborly banter'," he said. "Sometimes I'll be given food and very elegant Italian dinner jackets and clothes have arrived on a few occasions."

Not all homeless people in London have found such a stable lifestyle. Homeless charity Crisis estimates that there are over 200,000 people classified as homeless in England's capital, where "4,392 people were recorded sleeping rough in London between April and June, up from 4% on the same time last year. This is up 58% compared to 10 years ago."

According to government figures, there were 105,138 empty homes in London in 2025, or 1 in every 37 homes. Andy Burnham, who became British Prime Minister in July, has since vowed to offer "every rough sleeper in England a route off the streets by Christmas."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

With such an enormous price tag, even after six years of being abandoned, Fernstedt knows that the house he lives at could potentially become untenable at virtually any moment.

But over the last few years, it's given him something he craved when pitching up his tent or being moved from one scary temporary residence to the next.

"I'm no longer really worried that I'll cycle around the corner and everything will be gone. Because I've been here so long, I'm free of worrying now, and if we worry too much, we won't be happy."

#866. Joining a social club is good for your health. Here are 7 quirky ones in L.A. to get you started

Lerew’s rampant club joining was research for an exhibit he curated at the Los Angeles Public Library on L.A.’s rich history of clubs and societies. Titled “Something in Common,” it was billed as an exploration of “the ideas, interests and beliefs that bring us together.” It closed in the fall of 2022, but two years later Lerew remains something of an expert on L.A.’s social offerings and how to get involved with a community.

Stay up to date on the best things to do, see and eat in L.A.

Joining a club or society where you might meet like-minded people has a wide range of health benefits. It wards off loneliness, which is associated with increased risk of heart disease, high blood pressure and stroke, and which has reached epidemic proportions in the United States. Above all else, it brings meaning to our lives.

“Many of us find that once we join a group we get more responsibility and we feel we are needed, and that gives us a sense of purpose,” said Sam Pressler, a fellow at the University of Virginia’s Karsh Institute of Democracy, where he studies community and social connection. “That’s a critical piece.”

Joining a club also can increase your support network, which might come in handy the next time you’re looking for a job, experiencing a health crisis or need someone to watch your kid.

The yoga scene in Los Angeles is unparalleled. Whether you’re just starting out, on a budget or seeking something different, these studios have an option for everyone.

“It’s good to be seen and known,” Pressler said.

Fortunately, the club offerings in L.A. are extensive.

“Think of something you’re into, a fan of, enjoy doing or identify by and there’s almost guaranteed a group already that’s doing that,” Lerew said. Maybe you love making kaleidoscopes, or feminist literature, or the history of the circus — in Los Angeles, there’s a club for that.

If you do decide to join one, Lerew suggests keeping a few things in mind: You may feel uncomfortable at first, or members may be wary of newcomers, but if you’re genuinely interested in it, you should stick with it regardless.

“Get out there, and you’ll find people,” Lerew said. “And if they’re not your people, that’s OK. Your people are somewhere else.”

#868. Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado, who pipped Donald Trump to win 2025 Nobel Peace Prize, returns home after a year in exile

Published: 18:12 GMT, 25 October 2026 | Updated: 01:08 GMT, 26 October 2026

Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado, who pipped Donald Trump to the 2025 Nobel Peace Prize, has returned home after nearly a year abroad.

Ms Machado, 59, has been in exile since covertly leaving her South American homeland late last year to receive the award.

'I'm here. With you all,' she wrote on social media early on Sunday, addressing her fellow countrymen.

She appeared on Sunday at a church in the city of Barquisimeto in northwestern Venezuela, surrounded by cheering supporters. Her Vente Venezuela party said she had previously made several unsuccessful attempts to return, each of which had been blocked.

However, her return risks straining ties with the Trump administration. In January the US captured the country's then-incumbent president Nicolás Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores in a raid, before flying them to New York to face criminal charges.

Ms Machado has heaped praise on Mr Trump for launching the controversial operation, and even gave him her Nobel Prize medal.

She has been in exile for ten months since secretly travelling to Norway in late 2025 to receive the Nobel Peace Prize for what judges called 'her efforts to advance democracy in Venezuela'. Machado was initially barred by Mr Maduro's government from exiting the country after spending more than a year living mostly in hiding.

Since Mr Maduro was overthrown, Washington has allowed his deputy, Delcy Rodriguez, to rule as interim president. Rodriguez went on to sign a favourable oil deal with the US in August.

Opposition leader Maria Corina Machado gestures upon arriving at a church in Lara, Venezuela on October 25, 2026 after returning to the country following a year in exile

Supporters greet and take photographs of Ms Machado inside the church on October 25, 2026

Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado greets supporters after returning to the country following nearly a year abroad, in Maracay, Venezuela on October 25, 2026

It is not clear what Ms Machado's plans are now she is back on Venezuelan soil, or how she made it back into the country, but she has said in the past she would run for president again if new elections were held.

Her return was celebrated by her ally Edmundo González Urrutia, who ran as opposition presidential candidate in 2024 in her stead. He called her the country's 'sovereign voice'.

He wrote on social media: 'Venezuela! I am thrilled to announce to you that our leader, my dear Maria Corina, is on Venezuelan soil.

'Today is a very important day for Venezuelans. Our sovereign voice returns to lead and guide this process!

'Very soon I will be with you and with her so that our country truly advances toward freedom.'

In 2023 Ms Machado announced her intention to run for president, winning an independent presidential primary to decide the opposition's candidate with more than 90 per cent of the vote.

However, she was barred from running for office by the Maduro administration, who accused her of fraud and tax violations.

Ms Machado has consistently said the allegations against her were ideologically motivated. She went into hiding after the 2024 vote, which the opposition and much of the international community accused Mr Maduro of stealing.

Her desire to return had also caused friction in Washington, with US officials asking her to delay her trip, it was reported in June.

In a sign of her awkward position, Ms Machado has been sidelined from US-sponsored talks toward a democratic transition between the interim government and opposition representatives.

But an alliance of Venezuelan opposition parties earlier this month reaffirmed Ms Machado as its leader.

Ms Machado, 59, has been in exile since leaving her South American homeland late last year to receive the Nobel Peace Prize. Pictured: Greeting supporters in Maracay, Venezuela

Ms Machado cradles a little girl as she greets supporters from the roof of a vehicle in Maracay, Venezuela

Demonstrators hold up a sign reading 'Elections now!' during a protest in Caracas, Venezuela on October 22, 2026

Should Maria Corina Machado’s return shape Venezuela’s path to true democracy or deepen its crisis?

'We are at the beginning of a new era. We will finally make the liberal democratic republic a reality - Venezuela will be free,' Ms Machado told the alliance.

'I have always been grateful to the president of the United States for opening a door to progress toward freedom, democracy and true sovereignty,' she added.

This week, thousands demonstrated in Caracas and other cities, demanding her return from exile in Panama.

In Caracas, protesters carried signs that read 'Elections NOW and this time they're not going to steal from us' and 'Brave MCM', referring to Ms Machado's initials.

However, Donald Trump has repeatedly expressed support for interim President Delcy Rodriguez and hailed deals on oil production and other business ventures by US companies in the South American country.

The US President said in September that it was too soon to consider democratic elections in Venezuela.

International energy firms committed last month to expanding projects in the country in a signing ceremony overseen by Ms Rodriguez and US Energy Secretary Chris Wright.

Ms Machado has said only a 'serious, democratic government' can provide the stability needed by investors.

In June, she said she would do whatever it took to come home and help the survivors of devastating twin earthquakes that month, which killed at least 6,500 people and left thousands missing.

A faction of the opposition and the interim government held their latest session of talks this month, which aim to remake the top court and electoral council, among other goals, ahead of eventual elections. They do not include Ms Machado's political movement.

In 1992, Ms Machado established the Atenea Foundation (Fundación Atenea) which cares for orphaned and delinquent street children in Caracas. A decade later she was a co-founder of Súmate, an election monitoring NGO.

She was elected to the National Assembly in 2010 with a record number of votes, but expelled from office in 2014 by speaker Diosdado Cabello – a decision later upheld by the Supreme Court of Venezuela.

Ms Machado has led the Vente Venezuela opposition party since 2011 and in 2017 helped found the Soy Venezuela alliance, which aims to unite bipartisan pro-democracy forces in the country.

#872. Kimi Antonelli aiming to complete his F1 title march in style in Mexico City

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Kimi Antonelli will aim to finish his march to the Formula One title in style as he heads to Mexico City next weekend on the brink of the championship.

The 20-year-old will become the sport’s youngest champion if he finishes ninth or higher next Sunday, after securing a resounding victory at the United States Grand Prix in a blistering demonstration of why he will be this season’s deserving title winner.

Antonelli roared home from pole ahead of Charles Leclerc by a dominant 13.0 seconds, delivering everything he needed to in his first shot at clinching the crown.

But to be celebrating the title in Texas, the Italian needed slip-ups from his rivals. Lewis Hamilton extended the championship race by finishing fourth and George Russell just about did his bit despite only managing a disappointing eighth.

Antonelli now holds a whopping 123-point lead over Russell, 125 left to play for, with Hamilton a point further back.

“We are very close. We try to finish on a high and hopefully we can clinch it very soon,” Antonelli said.

“I am going to approach with the same mindset – to have fun and fight for another win. Would be best to finish well, that’s the goal but just going to try and enjoy the rest of the season.”

Antonelli leapt from his Mercedes and launched himself into the arms of his mechanics for the ninth time in this dominant season.

His joy at another brilliant win was evident in his radio messages, roaring: “Yes! Let’s go! That’s how we do it! Let’s go!”

His ever-calm race engineer Pete Bonnington praised his charge for avoiding his usual penchant for pushing track limits, saying: “You’re a good lad!”

“I am very happy because I have a very good group of people around me in the team and my father who always comes,” Antonelli added.

“A great group of people that help me to be more relaxed and not worry about these kind of things, help me to block out the noise and allow me to enjoy the weekend and perform.

“On Thursday a lot of talk about championship and stuff and I just try to not worry about that and deliver the best result I could. Today was very important for me and the team.”

Antonelli roared away from the line to see off Max Verstappen and executed a one-stop strategy to complete a comfortable win. Leclerc passed the Dutchman in the closing stages to seal second for successive races.

Hamilton was on the cusp of opening the door to Antonelli’s celebrations, but reeled in Isack Hadjar and Lando Norris late on to secure fourth.

Russell started sixth but was hit by a five-second penalty and trudged home eighth having failed to match his Mercedes team-mate’s exploits.

Mercedes boss Toto Wolff, whose belief in Antonelli never wavered despite a difficult debut season last year, described the win as “another small step”.

If that felt like an understatement, the 54-year-old was far more effusive after the race as he hailed the Italian’s best victory of his dominant season – better even than his Monza win from the back of the grid.

“The race of a champion who isn’t the champion yet,” Wolff said.

“I’ve said that this is probably the best race I’ve seen, but my problem is that I don’t remember past races. Monza was actually also pretty good, obviously with the advantage of the home crowd.

“But the headline is this is the best we can keep.”

#876. 65 of our favorite places to eat in the San Fernando Valley

Los Angeles has many valleys, but only one is the Valley. You know it as soon as you crest over the 101, 405, 170 or 5 freeways, its bordering hills verdant or golden depending on the time of year. Pull off almost any exit and you’ll immediately be greeted by shopping centers, strip malls, mom-and-pop markets and fine-dining dens serving up some of the city’s most ambitious and heartfelt meals.

Bounded by mountains on all sides, the San Fernando Valley spans 260 square miles and is home to nearly half of L.A.’s population, around 1.8 million people. Across its expanse, it assumes many identities.

Our favorite places to eat and drink in the 818. From high-end sushi to burger shacks, tiki bars, dives and more.

Long before its peaks and basins were crisscrossed with highways and miles-long boulevards, the Tongva people lived along the water-rich and wooded areas of the Valley for more than 7,000 years. In the late 18th century, Spanish settlers by way of Mexico traversed over the Santa Monica Mountains into what is now known as Encino.

More than a century ago, the citrus orchards began to give way as Warner Bros., Walt Disney and Universal studios built out their filming lots. A tinge of Tinseltown and tourism followed, while room to grow brought a midcentury housing boom to the region. Themed restaurants and tiki haunts popped up to keep diners entertained. Now, it’s difficult to find a Valley establishment that hasn’t made a TV or film appearance.

As Valley dwellers began settling in — immigrants, suburban families, celebrities — its food scene flourished in step.

On Ventura Boulevard in Sherman Oaks, you’ll find Casa Vega, its dim interior practically untouched since Rafael “Ray” Vega first founded it in 1956. The son of Tijuana-born immigrants who ran popular Cafe Caliente on Olvera Street beginning in the 1930s, Vega introduced many Valley diners — including a flock of silver screen regulars — to Mexican-American staples such as fajitas and enchiladas.

The Valley is home to the state’s first materia, a Middle Eastern cafe brewing sand coffee and a dedicated margarita bar from an award-winning beverage team, with plenty of neighborhood dives in between.

Farther south in Studio City, take your pick from a parade of Japanese restaurants along Sushi Row. The stretch of Ventura Boulevard became a hub for high-end Japanese cuisine after pioneering chef Kazunori Nozawa opened his Edo-style sushi restaurant Nozawa in 1987. Though that location has since closed, Nozawa has spawned a global restaurant empire with his KazuNori, Nozawa Bar and Sugarfish chains.

Pull off the main drag and you’ll find hidden gem burger shacks, taquerias, hot dog joints, kebab shops and neighborhood delis. Meanwhile, Valley residents are spearheading new concepts.

“We’re born and bred Valley kids, so we had to do it in the Valley,” said Marissa Shammas on opening Yala Coffee, a Middle Eastern-inspired cafe, with her husband Zain Shammas in Studio City. “[People] commonly think [the Valley] is where things go to die — and we think that that’s where things go to be more.”

There’s more to discover than ever when it comes to dining in the 818 (or 747). Eight Times food writers spent months exploring the Valley in search of the best for this guide, reconnecting with old favorites and finding new surprises.

For me, it was also an exercise in nostalgia. Old shortcuts returned like muscle memory as I reacquainted myself with the Woodland Hills blocks where I navigated young adulthood. In North Hollywood, my home for several years into my early 30s, former standbys suddenly returned to the forefront of my mind: The tiki bar across the street from my old apartment, a hole-in-the-wall Puerto Rican restaurant where salsa music draws you in, a vibrant Jamaican bistro that now sits in Sherman Oaks. I found myself wishing I could linger in the Valley longer.

Here are our favorites, spanning Filipino-Mexican fusion in a Northridge car wash-turned-restaurant, a DMV-adjacent street-stand for lamb barbacoa in Arleta and a fast-growing mini chain of Sephardic pastries. It’s time to dig into the Valley.— Danielle Dorsey

We’re gathering feedback on how our guides can better serve you and help you find the next great restaurant, hike or activity in Los Angeles.

#877. What Earth's sixth mass extinction event means for humans

Human activity is driving plants and animals to extinction at an unprecedented rate. As countries meet in Armenia to discuss ways to reverse nature loss, DW reveals how declining biodiversity is already harming people.

From the tiniest microbes in the human gut to giant whales in the ocean, biodiversity is the sum of all life on the planet. It's another word for nature. And because nature is like a team, every player has a job.

When various species from trees to animals work together, they regulate weather, maintain soil health, purify water and support food production. These benefits are known as ecosystem services and they underpin human well-being.

"It is really an abstract concept, but we experience it absolutely every day," said Rebecca Shaw, chief scientist at conservation group WWF. "And we almost never think about it when nature is functioning."

But as biodiversity declines, Shaw and other scientists are calling on the world to really think about it. Because biodiversity is struggling as humans push ecosystems to the brink through intensive farming, burning fossil fuels and pollution from sources like plastic and chemicals.

Over the past 52 years, monitored vertebrate populations have collapsed by an average of 73%, while freshwater ecosystems are faring worse with a drop of 85%, according to WWF's recent Living Planet report.

It tallies with other studies that show a million animal and plant species face extinction unless humanity reduces its pressure on nature.

"It is a really steep decline," said Shaw. "What it's telling us is that nature is in trouble, and it's an early warning indicator that the fabric of life that we depend on for freshwater and food and for clean air is unraveling."

Some 200 countries are gathering in Yerevan, Armenia over the next two weeks for COP17, the latest UN biodiversity summit, to advance commitments to reverse nature's unraveling by 2030. But progress toward those targets remains insufficient, with funding and implementation among the biggest challenges.

Take wetlands as an example. Some 85% of these vital ecosystems disappeared between 1700 and 2000. One study from Canada's University of Waterloo found that habitats like marshes and swamps in southern Ontario provide C$4.2 billion (€2.63 billion) worth of water filtration services each year, removing nutrients like phosphorus and keeping drinking water sources clean.

The study found that as they disappear, water quality worsens, which massively increases the cost of treating it.

Another example is the decline in pollinators like bees and bats. More than 75% of global food crop types rely in part on animal pollination.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

At the same time, soil and ecosystem degradation coupled with storms and heat waves linked to climate change are already damaging harvests. A recent UK government report stated that every critical ecosystem is on a "pathway to collapse," warning that nature's decline posed a grave threat to global food supply and geopolitical stability.

"The UK, like many other countries, relies on imports for much of the food and so is reliant on ecosystems around the world," said Louise McRae, a research fellow at the Zoological Society of London, who also contributed to WWF's Living Planet report. "This is why we need to care about global biodiversity."

Nature also provides the basis for many modern human medicines, with some 50% coming from natural compounds.

Penicillin, the first antibiotic, is produced by a mold and is estimated to have saved over 500 million lives. Before its discovery, a person could die from a simple cut. Around 70% of cancer drugs come from natural products or synthetic compounds "inspired by nature," according to the World Health Organization.

As biodiversity disappears, humans risk losing access to undiscovered treatments.

To return to the "nature as a team" metaphor, if a player disappears, sometimes a species with similar functions in the ecosystem can jump in as a substitute.

But not always, particularly if it's a "keystone species." They play a disproportionately large role in their environments, and their disappearance has significant knock-on effects.

The oyster is one such species. Wild oyster populations are facing massive declines, while 85% of their reefs have been lost worldwide. An adult oyster filters up to 50 gallons of water a day.

"No one would ever think they did anything but sit in a shell and be slimy," said Shaw. "But you lose oysters, you can lose water filtration and clean water, you can lose the habitat for many other species that we interact with or sometimes consume."

And, said Shaw, the humble oyster protects coastal communities from storm surges. If you lose it "you lose the coastal protection."

The loss of a single species can also lead to more disease. One study suggests a decline in red foxes in North America is linked to the spread of Lyme disease, a tick-borne illness that also affects humans.

Extinction is a natural process. But the planet has experienced five mass extinctions, when a large proportion of species globally disappeared over a short geological period. The rate at which species are disappearing today suggests Earth is experiencing a sixth event driven largely by human activity, according to scientists.

Both McRae and Shaw called the declines extremely worrying, but said they shouldn't provoke despair.

Though she acknowledges that the underlying global trend is moving in the wrong direction and cannot be ignored, McRae said "the statistics are there to just motivate us to action rather than to cause alarm."

And the Living Planet report also highlights conservation successes, showing that nature can recover.

The number of green sea turtles, for example, had fallen significantly, but has now bounced back. This is thanks to a massive worldwide effort to protect nesting beaches and changes to fishing practices that reduce accidental capture.

Sea otters are another example. Prized for their fur, in the 1800s they were hunted to near extinction on the US Pacific Coast. When they disappeared, it meant sea urchins had no predators, leaving them free to decimate kelp forests.

That matters because as well as providing habitat for other species, these giant underwater groves protect coastlines from storm surges and absorb carbon, making them important for climate protection.

Following a ban on commercial hunting, sea otters have also rebounded, helping kelp forests recover.

"You can see that ripple effect that really had an obvious and a measurable impact. But critically, it can be reversed," said McRae, adding that biodiversity loss and climate change are intertwined and exacerbate each other but have joint solutions.

"We're learning how to turn things around at very small scales," said Shaw. "Now the real challenge is to turn things around at very big scale so we can see it in the global indicators."

Ukraine has re-established a "stable" connection to Elon Musk's Starlink network, Kyiv announced on Saturday, following rising tensions with the US over the service.

"Monitoring systems are recording a recovery in the speed of Starlink/Starshield. We are registering a speed of more than 400 km/h, the connection is stable," Ukrainian Defence Minister Yevhenii Khmara said in a statement.

"This result is above all important for our front, for our soldiers, for the operation of drones, for logistics and for communications," he added.

Starlink, and its military version Starshield, have proved crucial to the Ukrainian military's operations as it has continued to battle Russian President Vladimir Putin's invading forces, providing resilient internet and communications over the battlefield.

But the service has been at the centre of a dispute between Washington and Kyiv in recent weeks after Ukrainian forces reported restrictions on the military use of the network.

Serhiy Beskrestnov, an adviser to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on military technology, said last week that SpaceX had introduced a speed limit overnight without warning.

"Our defence forces did not receive a warning about this limitation and this led to the disruption of several missions," Beskrestnov wrote in a post on Telegram.

Trump told reporters this week that he would speak to Musk if access to Starlink had not been restored.

On Tuesday, Zelenskyy also addressed reported restrictions on US intelligence sharing during a press conference with Nordic leaders, saying he was "thankful" that "intelligence works now."

"I'm speaking about early warning, what is very important for our people, for children, adults, civilians, because we can hear when ballistic is coming," he said.

It comes as Ukrainian authorities announced that two people had been killed and 18 were injured in Russian strikes on the Donetsk region.

"On 23 October, the Russians killed two residents of Donetsk Oblast: in Sloviansk and Kramatorsk," regional governor Vadym Filashkin said on Saturday morning. "A further 18 people in the region were injured over the past 24 hours."

Ukrainian forces hit back on Friday and overnight with strikes on the Tolyattikauchuk chemical plant, a Proton-Electrotex building in Oryol, and an aircraft at the Yeysk air base in Krasnodar Krai, according to the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine.

The General staff said the strikes on the chemical plant and Proton-Electrotex building would disrupt supply chains and production processes for Russian missiles.

#879. At 42, I finally got pregnant via an egg donor. Then my husband told me he didn't want the baby. What he did next cut even deeper

Earlier this year I fulfilled a lifetime ambition, owning my very own campervan. Forgive me if I sound like a cliche, as a single, childless woman aged 51, with two sausage dogs for company. I’ll often tie my paddleboard to the roof and take off at the weekend.

And why shouldn’t I? This is not the life necessarily I planned for myself, but I’m making the most of it.

A decade ago I spent over a year trying to conceive naturally, suffering a devastating miscarriage in the process. When I then became pregnant via donor egg IVF, my husband freaked out at the idea of a child that wasn’t all ‘ours’, forcing me to undergo a termination. And, even after all that, he still dumped me, later settling down with a young, fertile woman who could have his child ‘as nature intended’.

I like to think I’m over it and embracing the second part of my life, but there are times when I think of my ex and the howling injustice. He can keep on reproducing until his final breath and yet women have a fertility window of 20 years (if we’re lucky). In that time, if we’re sensible, we try to ensure we’re in a loving relationship and in decent enough financial circumstances to raise a child.

I spent my 20s and 30s working in the antiques industry. Fluent in Spanish and Italian, my job took me all over Europe and I embraced every aspect of it, working all hours with no intention of settling down. I was far too busy enjoying life and all it had to offer.

Before I knew it I was 40 and still single. While I had enjoyed three semi-serious relationships, I knew I’d never met The One. On a whim I bought a holiday home in the Dolomites, a part of northern Italy I’d come to know well. It was there in 2015 that I met Mateo, who, like me, was in the antiques business.

What started as a fling grew serious pretty quickly. We fell in love. Within a year I found myself regarded as part of his family and the community, so I left my home in West Sussex to move lock, stock and barrel to Italy.

I was ten years older than Mateo, but to look at us as a couple you’d never know – I’ve always looked after myself (with a bit of tweakment help) and we shared the same zest for life and sense of humour. The age difference simply never seemed to bother him. So when Mateo asked me to marry him, I didn’t hesitate in saying yes. I knew he wanted to become a father and I wanted to become a mum.

'There are times when I think of my ex and the howling injustice. He can keep on reproducing until his final breath', writes Carrie Darbyshire

I was 42 and two months pregnant when we got married in 2017, three months after he’d proposed. A fortnight after exchanging vows, I miscarried. We hadn’t told anyone about the pregnancy and so we faced the grief alone. My gynaecologist assured me there was no reason to worry, now my body knew what to do, we should try again.

Mateo rallied around, looking after me and we had lots of fun trying. Every weekend we’d have lunch with his huge family or drinks with his wide circle of friends.

Occasionally I’d be asked if there was any ‘news’; I’d assure people we were trying and close down the conversation.

A year passed without a positive pregnancy test. By then I was about to celebrate my 43rd birthday so I booked another visit to the gynaecologist. When hormone tests showed my eggs weren’t viable, she mentioned that we should think about assisted fertility treatment with a donor egg.

While this option is common in many countries, it is less so in Italy and so she suggested we research clinics in Spain, where the procedure was widely available. When I explained this to Mateo, he was unsure at first but, after sleeping on it, assured me he was on board.

Within days I’d found a clinic with a glowing reputation. All of the private Facebook groups I was in said it was expensive – yes – but would guarantee results. It was €7,000 (£5,800) for each attempt. Fortunately, I had a small inheritance from my grandmother. Throughout it all, Mateo assured me that he was committed to the treatment we were signing up for.

The private Spanish clinic redefined the meaning of luxury. It was set in a renovated farmhouse, and the walls in the lobby were covered with testimonials to the clinic’s success and beautifully framed, handwritten thank-you notes. Our gynaecologist rattled off the patter about Spanish law, anonymity and the checks involved. We’d never know the identity of our donor and neither would our child. We went through the characteristics of the sort of donor we wanted – ideally someone who matched my hair colour, eye colour, height. Before we left, Mateo gave a sperm sample and we were told to wait to hear about a match.

The matching process happened very quickly. While the donor started to take drugs to stimulate her egg production, I was on medication to ensure my body would be ready to accept the fertilised embryos once her eggs had been removed and fertilised using my husband’s sperm.

All went to plan, resulting in four embryos of sufficient quality. The plan was to transfer two in our first round, and freeze two for use later. I’d been sent images of the embryos – admittedly at that point just round blobs – and I spent hours looking at the pictures. Whether fertilised in a Petri dish or in my womb, they were my babies. I’d secretly given them names (Sofia and Valentina) and talked to them every day. I was going to become a mum. I just knew it.

We travelled to Spain for the transfer, which went seamlessly and I left feeling certain that one day we’d be back for the other two.

During the two-week wait to see if the transfer had been successful, I’d sing to the embryos in my womb, gently willing them to implant and grow. Mateo wasn’t as excited as me, but I put that down to him being preoccupied with his work, running his family’s busy antiques restoration company.

'When I became pregnant via donor egg IVF, my husband freaked out at the idea of a child that wasn’t all "ours", forcing me to undergo a termination'

Even before we got the positive pregnancy test, I’d had an inkling we were expecting. My breasts felt heavier and I developed a metallic taste in my mouth. The first eight weeks were tough, I felt nauseous for most of the time but I stayed focused on me and not me and Mateo. Is that where I went wrong? I do wonder.

We paid for a private eight-week scan, and I burst into tears on hearing the sound of a heartbeat – I just knew it was Sofia who had implanted and taken. Mateo looked bewildered. Mentally I dismissed his reaction as the enormity of fatherhood hitting him.

Back at home I circled the date when we were going to announce the news to everyone.

A few days after the scan I asked Mateo if, when we broke our big news to family and friends, he wanted to also explain we had conceived via a donor egg. It was then that my world fell apart. He got very upset telling me we shouldn’t have gone about it this way. He was, I suspect, frightened of how his family would react. He said that I’d tricked him into going down this route.

His arguments were totally unfair. I’d never lied to him and believed this was the only option left for us. Seeing his obvious distress made me painfully aware of our age gap. He might have been in his mid-30s but he was acting like a schoolboy. He simply wasn’t prepared for the grown-up conversations we needed to have around how we created our family and how we would navigate this together.

My default mode was one of frustration and anger. At the time I had no idea how to process these emotions. I was so tired from the pregnancy and trying to pull my marriage back from the brink. Mateo’s way of dealing with all of it was to avoid me. He’d leave for work first thing and come back late. This behaviour went on for a week, until he told me he didn’t want to be a father this way.

And then, nervous, he suggested perhaps we should make this (pointing to my stomach) go away and start again and see if we could do it naturally. When I asked if he meant undergoing a termination, he nodded. I was speechless, aghast he could suggest such a thing.

I asked him how he’d feel about his precious village knowing we had done that. It was then he burst into tears. Throughout the rest of the evening, he went on and on about how we shouldn’t have conceived this way and how it wasn’t right.

We slept in separate bedrooms that night, and my mind went into survival mode: should I move back to the UK, have our child and tell him where to go?

I realised this just wasn’t an option for me. I didn’t want to be a single parent. I had no long-term financial cushion. I’d read the scary headlines about the six-figure sums required to raise a child.

My parents had died and I didn’t have a vast network of supportive mum friends I could rely on back in the UK.

Despite everything, I still loved Mateo, our life together and his family and friends who had always supported me. I convinced myself we could start over and try again to conceive naturally.

I flew to London where I had a termination, away from the prying eyes of Mateo’s family. I went to the clinic on my own, although I was staying with a friend who was appalled by my predicament. As cowardly as it sounds, I dissociated from my body and the procedure. That was the only way I could get through it without breaking down. While in London, Mateo messaged me continually, checking I was OK, reassuring me how much he loved me.

Even though I’d had the termination because of him, I still wanted to get home, to my place of security and love.

However, from the moment I put the key in our front door, I found myself repulsed by him, I didn’t want him near me. On the first night, feigning sickness, I slept in a separate bedroom.

We struggled along for a few months, neither quite ready to sit down and work out what our future looked like, whether we even had one. I seethed with resentment towards Mateo and what he’d made me do and threw myself into work as a means of coping.

After returning from a week-long work trip, I discovered Mateo had moved in with his mum, a temporary arrangement, apparently. After I’d got over the shock, I realised how relieved I felt to have space.

A couple of days later I heard the familiar sound of his car on the drive. Mateo came in and explained that for his mental health he needed a break. Then, a month later, we had the conversation: he wasn’t coming back.

While a part of me, deep down, knew this was coming, I was still floored. I’d lost everything. My husband, my in-laws, our group of friends... and my chance of having children. As soon as everyone knew, the shutters went down, my in-laws would say hello to me on market days and if I bumped into them, but it was swift. I’m not sure what Mateo had told them about why our relationship had broken down and I didn’t want to know.

That winter passed by in a work-focused blur. When spring arrived with what would have been our due date, I recognised for my own emotional wellbeing, I needed to close this chapter of my life and move away.

Within weeks our house was on the market and a buyer snapped it up. Before I left, I asked Mateo what he wanted us to do with the remaining embryos. As I’d guessed he would, he said they should be destroyed. The same day I emailed the clinic to tell them of our decision, I sank into a black hole. I finally accepted that I needed antidepressants and took a low dose for the next two years.

Nine months after we split, in 2019, I returned to the UK, bought a cottage on the south coast, and have slowly rebuilt my life and myself.

Three years ago, Mateo called with the news he was married and going to be a father. Even though firmly back in the UK, the news still crushed me. I’d done so well in healing and yet I couldn’t stop crying. He deserves to be happy. But more importantly, I deserve happiness too.

I’ve been on a couple of dates in the last few years but it took me an awfully long time to grieve over the child I aborted, the husband I lost and the end of a life I thought I’d have forever.

Have I come to terms with never being a mum? No – and I’m sure every childless woman who wanted children, if they’re being honest with themselves, will know that you never ever do.

Carrie Darbyshire is a pseudonym. All names and identifying details have been changed.

#881. Vance no longer a hurricane but as a tropical storm still threatens Mexico's Pacific coast

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

A gradually weakening Tropical Storm Vance churned Sunday off Mexico's southwest Pacific coast but still threatened heavy rains and flash flooding in several western states of the country.

Vance, a former Category 2 hurricane as of Friday, was losing strength but still was expected to dump heavy rain on the Mexican states of Colima, Nayarit and Sinaloa, as well as parts of Michoacan, Jalisco and Durango, the U.S. National Hurricane Center in Miami said.

The cyclone was located about 315 miles (510 kilometers) west-southwest of Acapulco, or about 285 miles (455 kilometers) south of Manzanillo, with maximum sustained winds of 70 mph (110 kph), the center said. Vance was moving to the northwest and expected to turn northward in coming days.

Rainfall totals of 2 to 4 inches (5 to 10 centimeters) could produce flooding and mudslides, especially over steep terrain, according to the hurricane center. It said isolated totals of 7 inches (17 centimeters) of rain were possible in some spots.

Meanwhile, Tropical Storm Olana formed far out in the central Pacific, where it posed no threat to land. Olana had top sustained winds of 45 mph (65 kph) and was located about 580 miles (935 kilometers) west-southwest of Johnston Island, a central Pacific atoll, the hurricane center said.

It’s been an intense hurricane season in the Pacific Ocean, with storms spawning in assembly-line fashion near Hawaii and Mexico as El Niño conditions worsened by global warming create unusual weather, like this week's severe flooding and tornadoes hitting the southwestern United States and the prolonged drought in Central America's Dry Corridor.

Sign up now: Get ST's newsletters delivered to your inbox

BELGRADE, Oct 25 - Trams and traffic halted by crowds. Tens of thousands of people choking the city's main boulevards; the air thick with smoke; a man on a car waving a flare.

Familiar-sounding scenes after a month of sometimes violent protests across European cities as students take to the streets calling for better education standards and better prospects.

Except, on Sunday night in Serbia's capital Belgrade, students were not protesting but celebrating an election victory after long-time ruler Aleksandar Vucic conceded defeat to a student-backed list of candidates in parliamentary elections.

It was the culmination of a two-year, peaceful protest movement that called for Vucic to step down and an end to what they said is rampant corruption in the Balkan country - a charge Vucic denies.

The students' win marks a profound political shift in the country of some 6 million people and shows what power younger generation have when they are able to harness widespread discontent.

"That is the best thing that happened in my life. We will now breathe freely," said Milica, a law student.

Vucic had ruled as prime minister or president since 2014, and oversaw a period of strong economic growth, but he faced growing opposition from student-led protests after the collapse of a railway station awning killed 16 people in November 2024.

Tomorrow, the disparate group of 250 student-backed candidates will have to turn towards ruling, but Sunday evening was a time to party.

At their headquarters, the unknown candidates, many of them lawyers, professors, actors or farmers, hugged and cheered in near disbelief at what they had achieved.

"The people have won! The people defeated a dictator! The people will lead Serbia!" said Nebojsa Cosic while waving a flag on the street. REUTERS

#889. Uganda imposes 21-day quarantine on citizens returning from Congo

Sign up now: Get ST's newsletters delivered to your inbox

KAMPALA, Oct 25 - Ugandan citizens returning to the country with a history of travel to Democratic Republic of Congo will be quarantined for 21 days, Health Minister Chris Baryomunsi said on Sunday as Uganda tightened Ebola precautions.

Uganda says it is Ebola-free after declaring an end to its latest outbreak in July, but there has been concern among health experts after two people who had recently passed through the country later tested positive in Kenya and Nigeria.

Uganda says it is investigating the Nigerian case, which involves the wife of a Swiss diplomat. The woman, 42, returned from Uganda through Addis Ababa to Abuja on Oct. 3, according to Nigeria's Centre for Disease Control, which said she is in isolation and has improved remarkably.

The agency said 53 contacts had been traced.

Ugandan officials are reviewing genomic sequencing, travel information, interactions and movements in coordination with Nigerian authorities and international partners.

Swiss authorities had said the woman is believed to have contracted the virus in Uganda. Baryomunsi pushed back, saying Switzerland was "speaking prematurely". He said the woman's relatives from West Nile visited her in Kansanga, a suburb of Kampala, and that those relatives had visited Congo.

"What evidence do they have that she never travelled there?" he said. "We should speak science, not politics."

Kenya's first Ebola patient had travelled from Congo to Uganda and taken a flight from Entebbe airport to Nairobi on Oct. 3. The patient died two days later.

Both the Kenyan and the Nigerian cases travelled through the same Ugandan airport on the same day but there was no physical interaction between the two, Diana Atwine, the health ministry's permanent secretary, told the press conference, citing a review of the airport's CCTV system.

Baryomunsi said all 60 contacts linked to a Kenyan Ebola case had completed their 21-day monitoring period and been discharged.

"The ministry has intensified traveller screening at Entebbe International Airport and all land border crossings. All travellers intending to enter Uganda by air, land or water must complete the passenger locator form," he said.

Genomic analysis of Nigeria's only confirmed Ebola case showed the virus was closely related to the strain detected in Kenya's index case, though Nigerian authorities said there was no evidence that the Kenya case travelled to Nigeria or had a direct connection.

Uganda borders Congo, where the outbreak began, and has previously battled Ebola outbreaks.

Late on Sunday, World Health Organization Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said a nurse was killed and a health worker severely injured when they were attacked while responding to an Ebola alert in the northern Congolese town of Bafwasende.

"Everyone working to protect communities from this deadly disease must be able to work in dignity and safety," he wrote on X, saying the attack occurred on Saturday. REUTERS

#890. Trump focuses on Nicki Minaj’s ‘beautiful’ rear, AOC and owning Greenland in marathon rally speech

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

‘I looked at one hell of a beautiful ass before – Nicki Minaj,’ Trump said as a crowd of his supporters in Michigan roared

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

President Donald Trump spent nearly two hours Sunday afternoon talking about rapper Nicki Minaj’s “beautiful” rear, his indifference to Congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and owning Greenland.

Trump stopped in Port Huron, Michigan, to campaign for Senate candidate Mike Rogers and other Republicans in November’s midterm elections during his month-long rally blitz.

He spent the beginning of his speech attacking Roger’s Democratic opponent, Abdul El-Sayed, calling him a “Jihadist Muslim Brotherhood member” and demanding he go through metal detectors at the U.S. Capitol building if her were to get elected. El-Sayed, who is muslim, has vehemently denied any ties to the Islamist organization.

But in typical Trump fashion, the president went off-script, making for some bizarre moments. Here are the highlights:

Trump made headlines last week for oddly gushing over Republican Senator Jon Husted’s butt at a rally in Ohio. Instead of letting the story die down, Trump brings it up whenever he can.

At Sunday’s rally, Trump defended himself, saying, “I had just found out he’s a great athlete. A brutal tackler…I’m looking at him up and down and I’m studying him and then I made the mistake — I told, in fun, I said, ‘I looked at his ass,’ and I’ve never done that with a man before, it’s true.”

Then he quipped, “Off the record — women, yes, men, no, okay? By the way, I looked at one hell of a beautiful ass before – Nicki Minaj.”

The president pointed at Minaj, a vocal supporter who traveled with him to Michigan on Air Force One, and then said, “That’s hard to miss! Stand up! That’s hard to miss!”

Minaji stood from her seat as the crowd cheered, and she gave them a thumbs-up.

Despite Ocasio-Cortez constantly bashing the Trump administration, Trump suggested he was indifferent to the New York Democrat.

“Somehow, I don’t mind AOC that much. I don’t know why,” the president said. “She doesn’t bug me too much.”

The same could not be said for another member of the progressive House group AOC is part of, called “The Squad.”

The president continued his attacks against Representative Ilhan Omar from Minnesota Sunday, calling her a “little troublemaker.”

“She comes from Somalia — probably, maybe the worst country in the world,” Trump said.

Trump claimed during his speech that the U.S. owns Greenland, a semi-autonomous territory of Denmark in the Arctic.

“We own Greenland — we work it with Denmark. We signed a very good agreement with great lawyers,” the president said. “Infinite period of time. No limits. No nothing.”

Last month, Trump announced an agreement with Greenland that would “give the U.S. permanent access to the island and permission to build military bases there without Danish approval.”

The deal must still be passed by the Danish parliament to be ratified.

Trump admitted that Americans are “taking a hit” with high gas prices brought on by his war in Iran.

“Short term, you’re taking a hit. It's not a big hit. I thought gasoline would go up much more,” the president said. “The nastiest, the meanest, the No. 1 state sponsor of terror is Iran, by far. And you had to make sure they didn’t have a nuclear weapon.”

“Honestly, I thought they were gonna go up much more,” Trump said.

The national average cost for a gallon of gas was nearly $4.30 on Sunday, according to the motor club AAA. A year ago, the average cost was just above $3 per gallon.

Trump also took time to complain about not winning a Nobel Peace Prize, while he’s in an active war with Iran.

He said this year’s winner, Navi Pillay, a South African-born jurist and former United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights, was “a woman that nobody ever heard of.”

“So, I’m not in love with Norway. Frankly, Norway sucks,” Trump said in a rebuke to the Norwegian Nobel Committee, which picks the winner. “Norway has become a shithouse country, actually.”

#893. These 10 buildings tell the story of L.A.'s Roaring 1920s, year by year

Los Angeles may be notorious for ignoring history and reinventing itself at breakneck speed, but there are exceptions. And some of them take up entire city blocks.

A startling number of L.A. County’s most inspiring and entertaining structures went up in 1920s.

L.A. City Hall, the downtown Central Library and the (much-amended) Hollywood Bowl are three of that era’s most famous buildings, and the Hollywood sign (1923) and Watts Towers (begun in 1921) date to the same decade.

Stay up to date on the best things to do, see and eat in L.A.

But beyond those familiar favorites, there are dozens of other remarkable buildings that went up between 1919 and 1930, as Los Angeles was passing San Francisco as the West’s biggest city.

How busy were builders? The county’s population jumped from 936,000 to 2.2 million in that decade.

This year-by-year tour covers 10 of the most admired and emblematic among those buildings. They’re not all works of cutting-edge architecture, but they are enduring parts of the region’s character. They’re also a reminder that despite the many elements that made the Roaring ‘20s unique, there are always rhymes in history.

A century ago, the influenza epidemic of 1919 was a fresh memory. Movies and radio were disrupting pop culture. And plenty of people were nervous about the coming ’32 Olympics.

And now? Here we are, struggling to climb out of a pandemic, reckoning with the advent of artificial intelligence and nervous about the coming ’28 Olympics.

And where will those Olympics be held? The 1923 L.A. Memorial Coliseum, of course.

Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado returned to Caracas in a surprise move that could pose the biggest test yet to acting President Delcy Rodriguez’s political opening and the Trump administration’s strategy for post-Maduro Venezuela.

“I’m here, with you,” Machado posted on X on Oct 25, confirming her return after months abroad. She gave no details on how she entered Venezuela, but her party shared photos and videos of her arriving at a church in Lara state, where emotional supporters embraced her and said, “She will be the next president of Venezuela.”

Machado’s team earlier thanked President Donald Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio for their support, signaling an effort to underscore her ties with Washington even as her return risks complicating the administration’s Venezuela strategy.

Trump, speaking to reporters as he left the White House, said he didn’t know about Machado’s return. Other US officials, including her longtime ally, Representative Maria Elvira Salazar of Florida, celebrated the move, with Salazar calling it “the beginning of a new chapter.”

France is bracing for another day of nationwide protests on Saturday, with tensions mounting after authorities in Paris reversed their approval of a major demonstration route, prompting a legal challenge from trade unions.

The march was due to follow an agreed path between the symbolic place de la Bastille and Nation. But on Friday evening, the police prefecture imposed an alternative route along the outer boulevards of southeastern Paris, citing the risk of renewed violence.

Warning that the new route would be more difficult to secure and could create disorder, organisers said they intended to continue with their original plans.

The dispute comes a week after widespread violence and looting overwhelmed police in several French cities.

According to authorities, more than 3,000 shops were damaged or looted across the country on 17 October, when 60,000 police officers and gendarmes were deployed.

Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez has announced that 70,000 officers would be mobilised this Saturday, supported by specialist intervention units, armoured vehicles and water cannons.

Despite its scale, the deployment is not unprecedented.

It is comparable to a security operation mounted on 14 July this year, when France's national celebrations coincided with a World Cup semi-final against Spain.

During the largest mobilisation of the Bloquons tout movement in September 2025, some 80,000 officers were deployed, while at the height of the Yellow Vest protests, on 8 December 2018, the government mobilised 89,000 police officers and gendarmes across the country.

In Paris, a police intelligence assessment obtained by Le Monde estimates that between 60,000 and 120,000 people could take to the streets on Saturday.

According to Le Monde, police have also identified between 300 and 600 potentially violent activists.

The Interior Ministry has instructed prefects to reinforce checks at railway stations and major transport routes to detect equipment that could be used in violence and to consider restricting movement of individuals deemed a serious threat to public order, potentially including the suspension of some public transport services.

Alongside the strengthened security response, the government has also made a series of promises to engage in dialogue over demands.

On a visit to Limoges following the destruction of its historic town hall during last weekend's unrest, French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu promised government proposals on education, as well as state support for reconstruction efforts.

President Emmanuel Macron also met secondary-school representatives on Friday, promising a major overhaul of the Parcoursup university admissions system, according to participants.

But student organisations, demanding a €10-billion plan to revamp the education system, said they would continue demonstrations until concrete reforms were announced.

In Lyon, France’s third largest city, authorities are also preparing for further unrest after seeing some of last weekend's most serious destruction.

Around 150 to 200 businesses were targeted by looters, according to authorities, most of them in the Presqu’île, the city’s main shopping district.

The metropolitan authority and the local chamber of commerce and industry have arranged for 40 private security guards, divided into two teams of 20, to patrol vulnerable shopping areas on Saturday.

The prefecture has also prohibited demonstrations across large areas of central Lyon amid concerns of renewed attacks on businesses and public buildings, as well as confrontations between rival political groups.

Despite the ban, student organisations in Lyon have said they intend to demonstrate on Saturday as calls for gatherings continue to circulate on social media.

The Solidaires trade union and the Human Rights League had legally challenged the restrictions, but their appeals were rejected by Lyon's administrative court on Friday evening.

Restrictions were also imposed in other cities across France.

In Bordeaux, trade unions are challenging a ban on their planned city-centre demonstration.

In Marseille, a trade union march is scheduled to take place along a modified route avoiding major shopping streets.

Curfews and restrictions on gatherings have also been introduced in Toulouse, Limoges and Saint-Étienne.

In Orléans, between 20,000 and 30,000 opponents of the far-right National Rally are also expected to demonstrate as the party holds its congress.

Around 3,000 police officers and gendarmes are being mobilised in the area, with the authorised counter-demonstration route to be diverted away from the historic centre.
