Sunderland and Leeds were forced to share the spoils in a goalless stalemate at the Stadium of Light.

A scrappy first half saw Brian Brobbey have two promising opportunities to put the Black Cats ahead but he was denied both times by James Trafford.

Both sides threatened after the break and Nilson Angulo enjoyed the better chances for Sunderland before Ao Tanaka came close for the visitors.

A point snaps the Wearsiders’ four-game losing run in the Premier League but they remain bottom of the standings, while Leeds stay in the top half of the table, sat seventh.

Brobbey made his return from injury with a place in the starting line-up as one of six changes from Sunderland’s midweek Europa League draw against Lech Poznan and Daniel Farke made three switches to the side who drew 1-1 with Manchester United last weekend.

Leeds sniffed around the Sunderland box in the early stages as Jayden Bogle skewed wide and Harry Wilson’s free-kick was met by Jaka Bijol, but his flicked header was easily held by Robin Roefs.

The Black Cats had an excellent opportunity to take the lead when Brobbey fired towards the bottom left corner, forcing Trafford into a low save.

Brobbey was in the thick of the action again, pouncing on the ball following a tame exchange of passes between the Leeds defence, and Trafford was quick off his line to block the striker’s shot.

The chance spurred Sunderland on as they enjoyed a bright spell around the Leeds box, but neither side was able to put a shot away as the half petered out.

A bizarre incident at the start of the second half saw Nordi Mukiele caught around the throat by team-mate Luke O’Nien and the defender was forced off, with Omar Alderete replacing him seven minutes after the restart.

The centre-half was immediately called into action to clear a dangerous Leeds delivery into the area and Sunderland were forced to scramble away an overhead kick attempt from Brenden Aaronson.

Tarik Muharemovic’s header from a corner was held by Roefs as Leeds continued to pile on the pressure.

Angulo had a fierce effort pushed away by Trafford and minutes later the winger was again denied by a diving save from the Leeds goalkeeper.

An inswinging corner from Granit Xhaka was cleared as far as Angulo, who had another effort blocked for the Black Cats.

Leeds broke through substitute Anton Stach down the middle and a cross from Bogle on the right was hooked away at the back post by Noah Sadiki.

Tanaka’s shot was stopped by Roefs and O’Nien and Dominic Calvert-Lewin raced for the loose ball, which was eventually cleared.

A mistake at the back nearly allowed Chemsdine Talbi through, but the substitute’s strike was blocked by Bijol.

In the final minutes, Sean Longstaff was denied by a low stop from Roefs and the midfielder had a strike blocked by bodies in front of the goal line as the points were shared.

#901. France: Young voters blase about Glucksmann's Socialists

Raphael Glucksmann wants to lead France's Socialists to power without working with the left-populist Jean-Luc Melenchon, who is particularly popular with young voters. How can the center-left candidate win them over?

The historically working-class Parisian neighborhood of Belleville has gentrified in recent years. It was here that Raphael Glucksmann, a member of the European Parliament for France's center-left Socialists, celebrated his victory in the party's presidential primary on October 11.

Two rounds of voting had been anticipated, but the 46-year-old son of philosopher and essayist Andre Glucksmann triumphed in the first round with a convincing 66% of the vote and will be the Socialist candidate in France's 2027 presidential election.

As he left the Cantine de Belleville restaurant, Glucksmann was flour-bombed by an unidentified assailant. The following morning, he called on his rival, the left-wing French populist Jean-Luc Melenchon, to condemn attacks carried out by his supporters, though it is not clear that the attacker was indeed a supporter of Melenchon's La France Insoumise (LFI).

The incident has highlighted the issue set to dog Glucksmann's presidential candidacy over the coming weeks: How can he win over Melenchon's supporters if he refuses to work with their candidate?

"Where do you stand on Melenchon?" That was the question that dominated much of the Socialists' primary campaign. Party leader Olivier Faure spoke in favor of leaving the door open for cooperation with the LFI, but Glucksmann called for a clear break with the far left. His decisive victory is therefore also seen as a vote in favor of a clear demarcation.

The other primary candidates questioned Glucksmann's political experience. Segolene Royal, a previous presidential candidate, compared his bid for the Elysee with that of an "intern" wanting to take charge of a company. She said Glucksmann had no experience in government or even running a local authority.

Despite Glucksmann's victory in the primary, his starting position is a difficult one. A poll by Toluna Harris Interactive, published the day after his win, projects that he would win 10–11% of the vote. The same poll put Melenchon on 18%, meaning the far-left man would be much more likely to reach the runoff. But the survey was conducted before Glucksmann won the primary, and so does not take into account any potential boost the nomination may give him. Still, 10% would be an improvement on the Socialists' performance in the last presidential election in 2022, when their candidate Anne Hidalgo won just 1.75% of the national vote.

There is also the complication that the Socialists are banking on a man who is not even a party member to lead them from irrelevance. Raphael Glucksmann actually belongs to a small center-left party called Place Publique.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Glucksmann has his work cut out for him — especially with young people. In an Ipsos survey in September, which posited Glucksmann as the social-democratic candidate and Edouard Philippe as the only candidate from the political center, Melenchon scored 41% among the under-25s. Meanwhile, 20% of this age group supported the far-right nationalist Marine Le Pen. France's young electorate is politically divided, but Melenchon still dominates on the left.

The 75-year-old is currently rallying alongside the students whose protests have drawn international attention. At a rally near Clermont-Ferrand in central France, he expressed solidarity with their movement and reiterated his calls for lowering the voting age to 16 and abolishing Parcoursup, France's national admissions procedure for higher education.

In an analysis for the Fondation Jean-Jaures, a Socialist-aligned think tank, the political scientist Antoine Bristielle distinguishes between a core group of committed LFI voters and the broader left. Melenchon's most loyal supporters, he says, are often young, educated city-dwellers, and many are under financial pressure. Four in 10 households in this group live on a net monthly income of less than €2,000 ($2,200).

Bristielle estimates that just under a third of the left-wing electorate in his study care more about a left-wing victory than their allegiance to any particular party. Almost half of the people in this group are younger than 35 and would consider voting for the Socialists, the Greens or LFI. Redistribution and an active government are important to them, but most would prefer politicians who are willing to compromise.

The pattern recently observed in Germany, where young women are more likely to vote for the left and young men for the right, does not apply in France. Political scientists Anja Durovic, Nonna Mayer and Noemie Piolat found that in the 2024 European and parliamentary elections, young French women were not significantly more likely to vote for the left, or less likely to vote for the far right, than men of the same age. It remains to be seen whether this pattern will be replicated in the 2027 presidential election.

Glucksmann says he would ease the burden on earned income by reducing France's CSG social security tax while increasing taxes on inheritances worth more than €2 million. He also presents himself as a committed supporter of European integration, while Melenchon has called the EU a neoliberal institution. Glucksmann's political profile combines social policy demands with foreign policy positions that could also appeal to voters from the camp of the current president, Emmanuel Macron.

France's Ukraine policy is one such issue. Glucksmann favors decisive support for Kyiv. Manon Aubry, a member of the European Parliament for Melenchon's LFI, says her party supports military assistance only under certain conditions, namely: The provision of aid to Ukraine must first be subject to democratic debate; it must not enable attacks deep inside Russian territory; and it must not weaken France's own defense capabilities. In 2024, LFI MPs voted against the French–Ukrainian security agreement.

The tension between the parties of the left was once again apparent in the aftermath of the flour attack in Belleville. The LFI MP Sebastien Delogu posted a declaration of support on X for the taxi driver who was going to have to clean his car.

Glucksmann must win over a lot of voters from Melenchon's camp if he is to have a chance of winning the presidency. This is likely to prove a much more difficult task than simply distancing himself from Melenchon.

This article was originally written in German.

#905. Serbia’s Aleksandar Vucic concedes defeat in historic election win for student protest movement

Sign up now: Get ST's newsletters delivered to your inbox

Serbian Progressive Party prime ministerial candidate Aleksandar Vucic reacts after conceding defeat during a press conference on Oct 25 at the party headquarters in Belgrade, Serbia.

BELGRADE – Serbia’s Aleksandar Vucic conceded defeat to a student-led protest movement in a historic election on Oct 25 that ends his long grip on power and heralds a new political era in the Balkan country.

Vucic, a populist and nationalist, has dominated Serbian politics as prime minister or president since 2014.

But he called snap elections in September after almost two years of student-led demonstrations against perceived corruption and creeping authoritarianism triggered by the deaths of 16 people when a train station canopy collapsed in the city of Novi Sad in 2024.

“It is clear that we have lost these elections, the Student List has won,” Vucic said in a televised speech.

Within moments of his announcement, the streets of Belgrade erupted in celebration. Tens of thousands of people thronged along the city’s main boulevards, with cars honking, people dancing and students shouting “victory” and “he’s done”.

The students’ win marks a profound political shift in the country of some six million people and is reminiscent of the defeat of Hungary’s Viktor Orban in April.

It may also offer a blueprint for other student movements across Europe, which have taken to the streets in recent weeks to protest, in some cases violently, against poor education standards and a lack of prospects.

Vucic said the students would have between 135 and 140 seats in the 250-seat Parliament and that his Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) would have 105, based on preliminary results.

“Dear Serbia, tonight the voice of the people is being heard,” said Radomir Sajcic, a professor at Belgrade University, speaking on behalf of the students at their headquarters.

“Tonight we celebrate victory, tomorrow we build the future.”

European leaders and officials congratulated the Student List on its victory, among them President of the European Commission Ursula von der Leyen and European Commissioner for Enlargement Marta Kos.

“We stand ready to... work together to advance Serbia’s future in the European Union,” von der Leyen wrote on X.

Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar assured the students of his country’s support.

Lines snaked from polling stations in cities and towns across the country earlier in the day, and even Vucic waited for nearly two hours to vote in Belgrade. Pollsters and the election commission put turnout close to 70%, the highest since the break-up of Yugoslavia in 1992.

“(The turnout) did not surprise me because there was a large and strong mass that has formed throughout the past two years,” said voter Katarina Petrovic.

Vucic, who resigned from his second term as president to run again for prime minister, was a strong incumbent and few in the student protest movement dared believe he would concede so fast.

Supporters credit him with modernising Serbia’s economy and building new highways, railways, schools and hospitals.

“Some businessmen, some people will leave us but our structure is firm, we are very united, very strong, we are used to being in the opposition,” Vucic said.

Much remains unclear about how the student-backed candidates will fare.

Their list of 250 largely unknown candidates includes university professors, actors and farmers, and is led by cardiologist Ilija Srdanovic, who was in tears after Vucic’s announcement.

However, it is unclear who will be prime minister and enact the students’ domestic agenda, which aims to root out graft and improve schooling.

Political analysts predict some kind of purge of Vucic allies in the police, security services and ministries. But the students have been quieter on their international ambitions.

As Vucic did for years, they will have to juggle relations with China, a major investor, Russia, Serbia’s traditional ally and principal supplier of natural gas, and the European Union, Serbia’s largest trading partner.

“The biggest uncertainty is... who is going to lead the government, who will be the key ministers, and how they will operate based on the promises they made to fight corruption, to reintroduce the rule of law, but also to re-establish Serbia’s position in foreign policy,” said Radivoje Grujic, a Warsaw-based election consultant.

The student-led street protests sparked by the station disaster started small but quickly became the biggest in a generation, calling for Vucic to step down. Rights groups and activists say repression worsened in the period since.

Vucic and the SNS repeatedly denied accusations of repression, corruption and spying on their opponents. He has said the students are funded by foreign agents in Croatia and Montenegro, a charge the students dismiss.

Meanwhile, on the streets of Belgrade, a traditional brass band struck up, and a group including a man in a “students are champions” jumper floated balloons in the shape of the number three, representing the number of the students’ list of candidates.

“We will drink a beer to celebrate, we will get drunk, we are so happy, I have no words to describe how much,” said Andjela, a student who was with a group of friends.

Dejan Soskic, a former central bank governor and a candidate of the Student List, called on people to maintain order and peace, and thanked voters for their civilised conduct during the electoral process. REUTERS

Student List supporters celebrate the outcome of Serbia’s parliamentary election in Belgrade, Serbia, on Oct 25.

#911. Is Germany's eight-hour workday under threat?

Would you work 12 hours straight? The CDU/CSU and SPD are locked in a dispute over reforms to the Working Hours Act. Workplace flexibility, collective bargaining agreements and worker protection rules are at stake.

The town of Leuna, in the eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt, is one of the country's largest chemical industry hub, where more than 100 companies have established operations. Among them is the Finnish biotechnology group UPM, which has recently built a biorefinery for wood-based chemicals in Leuna. It's now hiring.

One of the job listings is for a chemical technician to oversee the rollout of new facilities. But to qualify, candidates must be willing to work 12-hour shifts. Is that legal? According to German law, standard working hours are limited to eight hours per day. It is permissible to extend this to ten hours, provided that workers receive compensatory time off for the overtime, and there must be at least 11 hours of rest between two shifts.

Business associations and the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) and Christian Social Union (CSU) parties have long called for these rules to be made more flexible.

Rainer Dulger, president of the Confederation of German Employers' Associations (BDA), points to the European Working Time Directive, which allows for a maximum weekly working time of 48 hours. "The allowance is being taken advantage of almost everywhere else — except here," Dulger told the dpa news agency in August.

Companies say they often find the existing rules too rigid, particularly in industries with seasonal fluctuations — such as tourism — or in project-based work, or during irregular peaks in workload, such as in the restaurant industry. They could deploy their staff more efficiently, says Dulger: "The Working Hours Act dates back to the era of fax machines and rotary-dial phones. It knows nothing of laptops or daycare hours."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In their 2025 coalition agreement, the CDU/CSU and the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) agreed to reform the Working Hours Act. "In keeping with the European Working Time Directive, we want to allow for a maximum weekly rather than daily working time — also and especially to promote a better work-life balance," the agreement said.

The SPD would have preferred to leave the law unchanged, but had to accept the conservative parties' plans. The Social Democrats pointed out that longer working hours are already permitted in exceptional cases, such as in emergency services, the health care sector and security services. Workers in power plants, refineries and the chemical industry are also allowed to work up to 12 hours at a time.

Even Chancellor Friedrich Merz himself seemed unaware of this exception until quite recently. After visiting the UPM refinery in Leuna in September, he recounted to business leaders at the German Employers' Day in Berlin that he was "completely surprised" to learn that the facilities operate on a continuous 12-hour shift schedule, thanks to the approval of the works council.

Merz recounted the shift supervisor describing the work schedule as "really great" — with three-day work weeks. "He said we have plenty of time for our families — it's a great way to organize things." Merz went on to conclude that this demonstrates the benefits of relaxing the Working Hours Act.

"Working more than eight hours is not exploitation. Rather, it can be a good opportunity to organize working hours more flexibly — both for businesses and for the people working there," the chancellor said. "We should do it."

But there is resistance from within the SPD and from trade unions opposed to amending the Working Hours Act. The trade union Verdi argues that significantly longer workdays would have negative consequences for employees' health and would disadvantage people with family and caregiving responsibilities. In certain industries, employees could also be put under pressure to accept longer shifts.

An initial reform draft was drawn up in June 2026 by the Labor and Social Affairs Ministry, headed at the time by Bärbel Bas, an SPD politician who has since resigned for personal reasons.

The draft includes some conditions, including a collective bargaining agreement between employers and unions if any schedule changes were made, as well as health and safety regulations, and working hours to be tracked electronically.

Annika Klose, spokesperson for labor and social policy for the SPD parliamentary group, explained the thinking behind the idea. Flexibility, she said, is "not a one-way street." The coalition agreement explicitly aims to promote a better balance between family and work. "So that it's sometimes possible to take your child to football practice in the afternoon and then continue working afterward — but not that my boss tells me against my will: 'You're working the shift from 9 a.m. to 10 p.m. tomorrow.'"

The CDU/CSU immediately rejected the draft. Businesses were also up in arms. "This draft must be withdrawn and completely revised," demanded Dulger in a statement, saying it was "steeped in mistrust." The German Confederation of Skilled Crafts (ZDH) spoke of a "breach of the commitments agreed to in the coalition agreement." The reform has been on hold ever since.

At the Employers' Day event, Merz held out the prospect of progress. "This is indeed long overdue. I believe we can accomplish this relatively quickly and create flexibility in the labor market."

It remains to be seen, however, whether the new SPD Labor Minister, Alexander Schweitzer, shares this view. In early October, his party released a paper on reforming working hours that read like a declaration of war against the CDU. "Self-determination, Not Deregulation" is the title of the seven-page document that was signed by the SPD working group on labor, the youth organization Jusos, the "60plus" working group and the women's wing of the SPD.

In the paper, the Social Democrats not only reiterate the points that already appeared in Bas' draft back in June. They also demand that, in the future, employers and employees should decide on working hours "jointly and by mutual agreement." They argued that it is not "in the spirit of a modern reform of working time law" if only employers can determine when employees finish work.

From a political perspective, the dispute over reforming work hours has long become more than just a debate over legal provisions. It is a fundamental dispute over how much flexibility workers should be expected to tolerate in the future and to what extent the state should protect them. And it is yet another stumbling block for the already beleaguered government in Berlin.

Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky said SpaceX’s Starshield satellite internet had been working at speeds of up to 420kph since early Oct 24.

KYIV - Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said US warnings about imminent Russian ballistic missile strikes, critical to Ukraine's air defences, had been fully restored after recent issues.

Speaking to Ukraine's TSN television channel, he said SpaceX's Starshield satellite internet had been working at speeds of up to 420kmh since early Oct 24, after it had been throttled earlier in October amid diplomatic pressure on Kyiv from Washington.

Zelensky said he discussed both issues in a meeting with US special envoy Steve Witkoff in Oslo, casting the changes as results of that meeting.

The US has pressed Ukraine to suspend strikes on Russian oil refineries, which it argues added to high energy prices, a sensitive issue for the Trump administration amid its war on Iran and US midterm elections next month.

Zelenskiy said that in order for Kyiv to halt the strikes, Moscow must stop hitting Ukraine’s power infrastructure, or the US should allow the use of Starshield over Russia to detect launch places of its ballistic missiles, or supply Ukraine with Patriot missiles.

Speaking about the upcoming technical talks between Kyiv, Moscow and Washington in November, Zelensky said Ukraine would not discuss limits to its armed forces, or enforced post-war neutrality. Kyiv has long sought entry into the NATO alliance despite the reticence of some members.

Zelensky also renewed his push for a trilateral US-brokered meeting between him and Vladimir Putin.

The Ukrainian leader has long argued Putin is the only person in Russia who can make major decisions to end the war or meaningfully discuss core issues, such as the fate of the nearly 20% of Ukraine that Russia occupies.

#914. This must be West Adams

With Victorian mansions and Craftsman bungalows tucked off its boulevard, driving down West Adams can feel like you’re traveling back in time. Many of the core structures were built between the 1880s and 1910s, making the South L.A. neighborhood one of the oldest in the city. But pops of vibrant street art bring you back to the present, like David Flores’ pensive portrait of Bob Marley set against crimson poppies or the mural of a little girl in a backward cap who holds her hand up in a “W” sign, a nod to the West Coast.

Get to know Los Angeles through the places that bring it to life. From restaurants to shops to outdoor spaces, here’s what to discover now.

“It’s both a historic neighborhood and one that is in transition,” said Ryan Wilson, co-founder of West Adams’ private co-working club the Gathering Spot. “There are a lot of things that are emerging.”

Founded by wealthy Pasadena industrialists Henry E. Huntington and Hulett C. Merritt, West Adams’ first denizens were of similar economic stature. But as Beverly Hills and other Westside neighborhoods were developed, well-to-do white residents were persuaded to resettle in those areas.

Affluent Black Angelenos took their place, including architect Paul R. Williams, who designed the nearby headquarters of the Golden State Mutual Life Insurance Co. — once the largest Black-owned insurance company in the West — as well as more than 2,000 private homes, with celebrity clients like Frank Sinatra and Lucille Ball. Oscar-winning actor Hattie McDaniels, blues musician Ray Charles and attorney Johnnie Cochran also had homes in the neighborhood that was then known as Sugar Hill.

In the 1950s, the expansion of the 10 freeway fractured a core section of West Adams, leading to the demolition of numerous homes through eminent domain. A second exodus left the area somewhat neglected.

More recently, the neighborhood’s relative affordability has made it a target for developers. In response, longtime residents are stepping up to protect the legacy of the majority Black and Latino neighborhood.

In 2020, siblings Jasmine and Giovanni Maldonado, who grew up in West Adams, began hosting the monthly pop-up Midcity Mercado as a way to remain in the neighborhood and combat ongoing gentrification and displacement. Taking place in the parking lot that Jasmine’s retail store Persona shares with her mother’s long-running restaurant Mariscos Marias, the family-friendly market features more than 30 rotating BIPOC vendors.

“Midcity Mercado is a celebration of survival,” Maldonado said. “It’s a really beautiful way to share our perspectives and our stories. It unites us in a way where we can appreciate the change and at the same time celebrate what once was.”

And even though the neighborhood is changing, there’s still plenty of history to explore. You can visit one of 70 sites recognized as cultural landmarks, such as UCLA’s William Andrews Clark Memorial Library, or meditate in the verdant gardens of an Italian Renaissance mansion. The neighborhood also has long-standing favorites for Oaxacan food and Creole cuisine; a community-oriented bookstore; a cannabis-friendly ceramics studio; special-occasion-worthy Japanese dining and more.

If you think you know West Adams, it’s worth taking another look.

Anyone who’s lived in a major metropolis can tell you that neighborhoods are a tricky thing. They’re eternally malleable and evoke sociological questions around how we place our homes, our neighbors and our communities within a wider tapestry. In the name of neighborly generosity, we may include gems that linger outside of technical parameters. Instead of leaning into stark definitions, we hope to celebrate all of the places that make us love where we live.Our journalists independently visited every spot recommended in this guide. #920. How reliant is Ukraine on the US-controlled Starlink internet service?

Kyiv keeps issuing warnings that the satellite internet system Starlink is being restricted in Ukraine. How dependent is the country on the system, and what would happen if it went down?

Few technological systems have played such an important role in the war in Ukraine as Starlink, central to the communications, reconnaissance and drone operations of the Ukrainian armed forces. There are currently widespread concerns that Elon Musk's satellite internet service in Ukraine may be restricted or even switched off. In recent days, Kyiv has repeatedly reported disruptions and restrictions affecting its use.

Since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, Ukraine has made extensive use of the satellite internet service, which is operated by the US company SpaceX. With it, military personell can continue to communicate and exchange data, even when infrastructure has been destroyed or cellphone networks are down.

According to the Center for Security Studies (CSS) at ETH Zurich, around 50,000 Starlink terminals were in use in Ukraine in 2025. These are the system's specialised receiving and transmitting devices, which enable communications on the battlefield. They are also used to relay orders between command levels and receive drone footage.

The importance of the Starlink network can in part be explained by events at the beginning of the war. According to a CSS analysis, the KA-SAT satellite system previously favored by Ukraine was targeted in a cyberattack just hours before Russia's invasion. Starlink quickly became a vital alternative.

When discussing current affairs, the terms "Starlink" and "Starshield" are often used interchangeably.

However, Starlink is SpaceX's commercial satellite internet service, whereas Starshield is specifically designed for governmental and military use. While based on the same technological infrastructure, it is designed for security and defense applications.

This distinction matters, because the latest reports of restrictions seem to primarily concern systems used for military purposes. Elon Musk recently stated that Starshield systems are controlled by the US government, whereas Starlink is a commercial service operated by SpaceX.

Alongside communications, Starlink is mainly used for drone operations. The system provides an internet connection for ground, naval and aerial drones.

This connection means video footage can be transmitted almost in real time, while drones can be controlled over long distances. Ukraine uses these systems for reconnaissance and attacks deep behind enemy lines.

According to ETH Zurich, images and GPS coordinates of Russian positions are also transmitted via these communication channels. The data is sent to artillery units and used to coordinate operations.

According to Ukrainian media reports, on Tuesday night, SpaceX temporarily introduced a speed restriction for Starlink terminals in Ukraine, limiting terminals in motion to a speed of about 160 kilometers per hour (100 mph).

Such a restriction has direct consequences for fast-moving Ukrainian drones, some of which travel at speeds of up to 300 kilometers per hour (186 mph). If the connection to the drone is lost, live video footage can no longer be transmitted, and the systems can no longer be controlled in real time. The drones effectively have to continue their mission while flying blind.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Restricting or even shutting down a Starlink network would therefore not only make communication more difficult. It would also affect Ukrainian drone operations, and other military activities.

However, Starlink and its military counterpart, Starshield, are only one essential component of Ukraine's defense system. Ukraine also receives reconnaissance data from western partners, including information about Russian air attacks, missile launches, troop movements and anti-aircraft positions, as well as potential routes to avoid them.

This information helps with air defense and offensive operations. Without this intelligence, it would be significantly harder for Ukraine to carry out long-range drone operations against targets in Russian territory.

The two elements are particularly effective when combined. Reconnaissance data provides information about potential targets and routes, while Starlink ensures that this data can be quickly relayed to units.

This is why reports that the US is limiting access to its reconnaissance data are as worrying as the possibility that Starlink might be throttled. Other NATO countries, such as the United Kingdom and France, can also provide reconnaissance data, but not to the extent as the United States.

Europe has several alternatives to Starlink, including Eutelsat/OneWeb. However, their ability to match Starlink's performance in wartime conditions has not yet been tested on a large scale.

The recurrent concern about possible restrictions makes clear that satellite communications have become a central component of Ukrainian defense. And while relying on a single provider simplifies operations, it also shows how dependent modern armed forces have become on private technology companies. Experts say this marks a fundamental change in warfare.

Meanwhile, Ukraine's successful use of Starlink has helped the system to achieve global recognition.

#931. My Ring Doorbell is sabotaging my relationship. The video description feature reported his infuriating habit - and my secrets have been caught out too. But our Ring keeps making false accusations, and I'm worried what neighbours will say

The other night, while I was out on the razzle, a neighbourhood spy caught my partner – a reformed smoker – brazenly having a ciggie in front of our house.

The cheek of the man, waiting until I left to secretly indulge his vice.

Who was this co-conspirator? My Ring doorbell. Thanks to its new AI-enhanced ‘Video Descriptions’ service, which summarises the action on your doorstep as a line of text, my partner got stitched up like a kipper when Ring told me: ‘There is a man on the driveway smoking a cigarette.’

It pinged in alongside a thumbnail of the incriminating video featuring his easily identifiable hulk with the offending item in his mouth.

Enraged, and perhaps fuelled by one too many glasses of lady petrol, I fired off several accusatory texts. His defence? ‘I was just doing the recycling.’ Pah.

Then I actually bothered to watch the video, rather than just lazily depending on the description. He was right. One hundred per cent, humiliatingly right.

His arms juggling a green box overflowing with drained wine bottles and empty jars of overpriced chickpeas, he’d had no choice but to hold the front door key in his mouth.

A key that Ring’s AI, in all its wisdom, had decided was a ciggie.

Helen Down says her Ring doorbell's new feature, which summarises action on your doorstep as a line of text, has been causing domestic drama in her house

Helen's Ring doorbell thought someone was smoking outside the house, when in reality it was her partner, sorting the recycling, with his front door key in his mouth

An embarrassed apology ensued, followed by cursing at Ring’s new feature.

It’s not the first time Video Descriptions has caused domestic drama chez nous.

My 17-year-old, all six-foot three-inches of him, was distinctly miffed when Ring described him as a child (‘A child is walking on the path’).

And I can no longer do a secret Co Op snack dash without being busted (‘A woman is approaching the front door carrying a snack’).

What’s galling is, I never even signed up for Video Descriptions. Like many Ring users, I had a month’s free trial foisted on me in the hope that I’d cough up for another hefty subscription. I didn’t.

Ring, which is owned by Amazon, often sells the doorbell itself for next to nothing.

On Prime Day you can grab one for as little as £39.99, a 75 per cent discount. Bargain! Until you realise the real spend is in the add-ons.

I bought my first Ring four years ago, after my urchin of a teen tried turning the house into a nightclub while I was on holiday. What I didn’t know was that, without a subscription, Ring is just a good old-fashioned doorbell with a camera stuck on it.

You can snoop in real time, but if you want to check retrospectively on whether that vital parcel has arrived, or if your teen was lying about getting home at midnight, you need, for £49.99 a year, a Ring Protect subscription.

In the last four years, I’ve handed over nearly £200 for the privilege of watching my own doorstep. I’m not alone. At least one in five Brits now own a smart doorbell, with Ring the dominant brand.

And in 2024, when Ring hiked its Protect subscription prices by 43 per cent, increasing the yearly fee from £34.99 to £49.99, most of us sucked it up.

At least one in five Brits now own a smart doorbell, with Ring the dominant brand

Not just because it’s handy for tracking deliveries but also because they create a sense of security. Albeit a false one given that Ring doorbells, as a sign of affluence, can make houses more attractive to burglars.

The biggest problem, however, is that some people – you know who you are – use smart doorbells for digital curtain twitching.

There’s a fine line between monitoring your parcels and snooping on the folks next door. If I wanted to, I could set my camera zone wide enough to spy on my neighbours’ doorstep as my own.

This potential for invading privacy is about to get more problematic. Last week Ring launched a feature called ‘Neighbours’ in the UK.

Billed as a ‘free, community-powered space’, Neighbours will be part of the Ring app that acts like a public forum and message board.

And since it will be open to every busybody in town, not just Ring owners as anyone can download the app for free, it will pose a threat to social media platforms such as Next Door and street-based WhatsApp groups. Which would be a shame because I love my local WhatsApp thread.

It’s a gem that’s helped find new homes for battered sofas and supplied no end of plumber recommendations.

And in the past month alone, we’ve had an update on a local fire, a plea for toiletries for a refugee charity, requests to check sheds for an AWOL moggie, a ‘Thank you’ for the glorious sunflower display outside Number 12 and, most bafflingly, a request to borrow a garter.

But it really comes into its own when public spats begin. Watching from the sidelines as fights break out over the Low Traffic Neighbourhood scheme, peskily parked Lime bikes and the controversial building development two streets away; it’s as juicy as an episode of The Traitors.

The neighbourhood WhatsApp group is a wondrous microcosm of British politeness, passive-aggression and eccentricity. Let Big Tech take over and we’ll lose something precious.

Worse still, Neighbours will allow anonymous posting. And this is where things could go horribly wrong.

Our WhatsApp group already goes into overdrive when unidentified ‘yoofs’ in hoodies walk the street after 9pm, despite the fact that, more often than not, it’s only a couple of innocent teenagers heading home after a ‘motive’ (meet-up) in the park.

On WhatsApp, the poster is a known and named neighbour who has to look you in the eye as you nod ‘Hello’ the next morning.

Strip away that accountability, add someone who’s got nothing else to do, some blurry camera footage and AI that can’t distinguish a key from a ciggie – and you have a recipe for all hell breaking loose. So no, Ring. We don’t need another platform for local trivia, and we don’t like crisp snitches either.

#937. How big is Russia's threat against Germany?

Experts believe that, so far, Germany has been ill-prepared — both militarily and mentally — for Russian provocations. They also warn against the idea that ending support for Ukraine would make Germany safer.

Warnings keep mounting about Russia's threat to Germany. On October 12, Sinan Selen, president of Germany's domestic intelligence agency, the BfV, said that Russia's covert attacks and destabilization efforts against Germany and other European countries are "not a temporary development but a long-term hybrid attack."

Even if the war in Ukraine were to end, said Selen, the Russian threat would not disappear. "For Russia, this is about completely redrawing the map of Europe and redefining its own role within Europe and in global politics."

He added that Russia's aggression would continue to be felt not only in Ukraine, but also in the Baltic states, in Poland and in Germany.

German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt has described the threat situation as one in which "our country is not at war, but we are the daily target of hybrid warfare." Russia's goal, he said, is not to defeat Germany militarily "but to subdue us politically and socially."

Security experts, however, are not so sure that Russia is only interested in exercising political and social influence. Last year, political scientist Carlo Masala told the political talk show Maischberger that "Russia is preparing for a major war." And he didn't mean just a cyberwar. Inspector General Carsten Breuer, the Bundeswehr's highest-ranking officer, agreed.

For now, though, Russia remains tied up in its war against Ukraine. According to NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte, there is no immediate military threat to NATO territory. But according to military experts, European intelligence agencies, and the German Defense Ministry, Russia will have the personnel and equipment to wage a conventional war against NATO by 2029. The Russian defense industry is running at full speed, and Moscow plans to expand its armed forces to 1.5 million soldiers.

At the moment, Russia has other objectives, believes Stefan Meister, an expert on Eastern Europe at the German Council on Foreign Relations (DGAP): "I don't think Russia has any interest in a direct military conflict with NATO right now. It wants to test NATO and also display its capabilities," he tells DW.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

An example of Russia's hybrid war might be the failed attack with an explosive-laden drone against a Ukrainian transport aircraft at Leipzig-Halle Airport in August. Soon after, the German government stated that it was certain Russia was behind the attack.

Security expert Nico Lange told DW at the time that Germany was very lucky the explosives did not detonate: "Honestly, it was pure coincidence and not the result of German defensive measures."

As for why Germany was targeted specifically, Lange said: "I believe that Germany has always been a primary target of Russian influence and hybrid warfare. Russia believes that Germany is the key to European decision-making. Germany is now leading the way in supporting Ukraine."

Moscow swiftly responded to the German government's accusation with an angry denial. Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said it was "the beginning of a real war," though there was no immediate further escalation.

Nevertheless, there is always the risk that things could spiral out of control following a Russian provocation and subsequent response, according to Stefan Meister: "Accidentally shooting down an aircraft that they were trying to intimidate would trigger a counter-reaction. But I don't believe that Russia is currently aiming for a direct war but rather for provocations, polarization, and sowing uncertainty among the population."

Not everyone shares the assessment that Russia poses a threat to Germany — some believe that the threat can be averted.

Despite the war in Ukraine, politicians from the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) and the populist left-wing Alliance for Social Justice and Economic Reason (BSW) want to improve relations with Russia, resume Russian energy supplies and end support for Ukraine.

AfD co-leader Tino Chrupalla said in early September, "People are fed up with this escalation against Russia, with the billions being squandered there on a system that is actually funded by German taxpayers' money."

The message appears to have resonated among the population, especially in eastern Germany. The AfD saw strong gains in all three state elections in September. In Saxony-Anhalt, it became the strongest party by far and may even run the government there soon, which would be the first time that a far-right party has held power in Germany since the end of WWII.

The CDU's security policy expert Roderich Kiesewetter disputed the claim made by the AfD and BSW that ending aid to Ukraine would mean greater security and more money for German schools and infrastructure: "Spending on education, social policy, and infrastructure is only possible if we live in freedom and democracy — and, above all, in peace and security. Anyone who believes that we'll have more money for social programs if we stop supporting Ukraine and let Russia have its way is either gravely mistaken or is making themselves a tool of Russian propaganda."

The perceived security threat has led the German military, the Bundeswehr, to fast-track significant modernization through substantial investment. But it is struggling to find enough recruits for its planned expansion. Many young Germans have taken to the streets to protest against plans to reintroduce conscription. Defense Minister Boris Pistorius faced criticism from inside his own party, the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD), for saying that Germany must become "capable of waging war." Many found the statement to be too militaristic.

Is Germany prepared for a military threat? "Not at all. Germany is not well prepared militarily or in the civilian sector, and the population isn't mentally prepared for it either," said Meister. "Just look at the demonstrations against conscription and the military that continue to take place, even though Germany needs a draft. For decades, we've grown up in this culture of pacifism, in a comfort zone. I believe there is very limited societal resilience, but above all, we are not at all mentally prepared for war."

Chancellor Friedrich Merz and his conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) are under increasing political pressure — especially from the far right — to scale back support for Ukraine. But Merz never tires of emphasizing that Ukraine will continue to receive support under his chancellorship, calling it a matter of Germany's security. He recently visited Kyiv once again and, together with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, surveyed the destruction caused by Russia.

But this also means that the threat from Russia will continue and even intensify, says Stefan Meister: "I believe we will see a massive increase in attacks such as the one in Leipzig, of provocations involving drones. We will see attacks on infrastructures and possibly also on specific individuals within the military-industrial complex. I believe this is the real, concrete danger facing Germany in the coming months."

#939. Algeria to send troops to Niger in first foreign deployment since 1973

Sign up now: Get ST's newsletters delivered to your inbox

ALGIERS, Oct 25 - Algeria's parliament approved a resolution on Sunday authorising the deployment of army units to Niger, a parliamentary statement said, in what would mark Algeria's first foreign troop deployment since it sent forces to support Egypt in the 1973 war.

Lawmakers unanimously backed the deployment of National Army units to Madama in northern Niger, near the Libyan border, at the site of a former French base used during Operation Barkhane, the statement said.

No troops have been officially deployed yet, according to a Niger security source. But Niger presidential chief of staff General Bacharou Ibro Amadou has been visiting the Kawar area in the Bilma department of Agadez region since October 19. He travelled to Madama for talks with local military commanders before returning to Dirkou to meet military and traditional authorities on plans for the base.

The move highlights a rapid improvement in ties between Algiers and Niamey after a period of strain.

Algeria opposed the 2023 coup that brought Niger's current military leaders to power. Relations worsened last year, when Niger recalled its ambassador from Algiers after Algeria shot down a Malian drone near their border.

Niger, Mali and Burkina Faso are all ruled by military leaders who seized power in coups and later formed the Alliance of Sahel States.

Niger, like other countries in West Africa's Sahel region, is battling insurgents linked to al Qaeda and Islamic State. Algeria, which shares a border with Niger, has traditionally regarded stability in the Sahel-Sahara as a key regional security priority.

Ties have improved this year. Niger President Abdourahamane Tiani visited Algiers in February, and Niger Defence Minister Salifou Mody travelled there on October 20 with a delegation of defence experts for talks on security cooperation.

Algeria has also deepened its economic interests in Niger. State energy company Sonatrach is working with Niger and Nigeria on the Trans-Saharan Gas Pipeline, which is intended to create a new export corridor for African gas to international markets, particularly Europe.

Sonatrach said in 2022 that it had signed a production-sharing agreement with Niger's petroleum ministry for the Kafra region, where two exploration wells held proven reserves of 168 million barrels and 100 million barrels, respectively. REUTERS

#945. Government commits extra £432m to get rough sleepers off streets by Christmas

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

The money will double the funding pot for tackling the problem of homelessness in England

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Chancellor John Healey will use his Budget statement on Wednesday to confirm an additional £432m aimed at addressing rough sleeping.

The money will double the funding pot for tackling the problem, according to an announcement made ahead of the statement.

Andy Burnham pledged in August to offer every rough sleeper in England a pathway off the streets by Christmas.

The prime minister will bring private firms, charities and local leaders together at a rough sleeping summit at Downing Street on Monday to consider ways of tackling the issue.

Mr Burnham said that “every part of society” needs to contribute to ending rough sleeping.

“Rough sleeping isn’t a fact of life. It’s a thing governments either choose to accept or don’t,” he said.

“Well, I don’t accept it. That’s why we’re doubling funding so that people aren’t just offered a safe route off the streets this winter but have that same support right through the rest of this parliament, too.

“But we can’t do it alone. If we’re going to end rough sleeping, we need every part of society behind us on this.”

The most up-to-date annual national statistics estimated there were 4,793 people sleeping rough on a single night in autumn 2025 in England.

The new Budget funding comes on top of £442m committed earlier this year.

It will allow the rough sleeping programme to continue until the end of the current parliament in 2029.

Organisations attending the summit include the National Housing Federation, which will work with housing associations to identify at least 2,000 potential homes and bed spaces.

Beauty firm L’Oréal Group will launch a social salon partnership with St Mungo’s and Haircuts4Homeless, while Virgin Media O2 will provide digital support to organisations working with the homeless.

Other attendees at the summit include the Salvation Army, Ikea, the Morrisons Foundation and Comic Relief.

Housing secretary Angela Rayner said: “This is a big ambition – we know that. But we will not back down from making sure everyone has the offer of a route off the streets this Christmas.

“This summit is about bringing every part of society together behind that mission.”

Thierry Cheval, the boss of L’Oreal Group UK and Ireland, said: “Beauty plays an essential role in restoring dignity and a positive sense of self.

“For people rebuilding their lives, this simple act of care provides a crucial boost in confidence and wellbeing as they re-engage with the world and take their next steps towards social integration.”

Mairi MacRae, acting chief executive at homelessness charity Shelter, said: “Matching the money with new commitments from businesses, local leaders and charities demonstrates that we can choose to end rough sleeping as a society.

“Helping people off the streets is the first step, the next is ensuring everyone has a long-term settled home with the right wraparound support, for which this extra injection of cash is vital.

“To keep people from returning to the streets and eradicate homelessness in all its forms, the government must not waver from its promise to deliver a council housing revolution.”

Mr Burnham pledged as his “first instruction” on day one in No 10 in July to “finally end long-term, rough sleeping across the UK at the earliest opportunity”.

But he has faced criticism from the Conservatives over his record as mayor of Greater Manchester on the issue.

Shadow housing secretary Katie Lam said: “Burnham is throwing another £432m at a problem he failed to solve in Greater Manchester. Under Labour, rough sleeping has hit record highs – yet their answer is always more taxpayers’ money and more empty promises.

“Healey must use his Budget this week to cut taxes for working people, get the ballooning benefits bill under control, and stop pushing up energy prices.

“Instead of piling more costs onto hard-working people, Healey must focus on easing the cost of living and delivering real value for taxpayers’ money.”

The £432m will be confirmed in the chancellor’s statement on Wednesday, on top of the £442m already committed.

#947. Trump has no designs on taking over state elections, says US attorney-general

Sign up now: Get ST's newsletters delivered to your inbox

US Attorney-General Todd Blanche (right) has defended a preemptive lawsuit blocking the results of Alaska’s Senate race from being certified.

NEW YORK - The Justice Department’s bid to preemptively block the results of Alaska’s Senate race is not an attempt to give US President Donald Trump control of state elections, US Attorney-General Todd Blanche said on Oct 25.

Blanche’s agency on Oct 23 sued to stop Alaska from certifying the results of its US Senate race if the Republican incumbent candidate loses narrowly. But the Justice Department is not setting the stage for overturning an election result if it’s unfavourable to Trump, Blanche said.

“President Trump is not trying to take over a state election in any way, shape, or form,” Blanche told CNN’s State of the Union programme. “We’re not laying any groundwork for the president to do that.”

Election officials around the country have told Reuters they are preparing ​for potential federal interference in the Nov 3 midterm elections that will decide control of the US Congress, including legal challenges and disputes over voting that could disrupt certification of the results.

In addition to the Alaska lawsuit, the Trump administration has taken other vote-related actions against states, including a lawsuit to stop California from counting certain mail-in ballots and a mostly unsuccessful attempt to force 30 states and the District of Columbia to provide complete voter rolls.

The Alaska action is specific to that state, Blanche said, reiterating the Trump administration’s contention that voters will be “confused” because two Republicans on the ballot have almost identical names: incumbent US Senator Dan S. Sullivan and challenger Dan J. Sullivan Jr The latter Sullivan is only running “to confuse voters,” Blanche said.

“Never before have opponents gone to such lengths to try to thwart and cheat an election as they’re doing in this case,” Blanche told CNN.

Dan J. Sullivan has denied in interviews with US ​news outlets that his aim is to cause confusion or divert votes from Dan S. Sullivan. His campaign did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The lawsuit was filed to give officials “the ability to determine whether there was confusion that violates the law,” Blanche said.

He declined to comment on whether Trump ordered him to file the lawsuit, although the president himself has said he did so. Trump briefly spoke about Alaska again on Oct 25, accusing Democrats of orchestrating Dan J. Sullivan’s campaign.

“They’ve made it very unclear and I think it’s very unfair,” Trump told reporters before boarding a flight to Michigan. “I think it’s illegal because it’s unfair. You want fairness in voting.”

But critics, including Democratic and some Republican election officials, view the move as part of a pattern of federal overreach in election oversight.

“The fact that Todd Blanche and the Justice Department are willing to go along with it, they’re willing to put their name on it, is an indication of how far they will go after this election is over to try to challenge the results,” US Senator Adam Schiff, a California Democrat, told NBC’s Meet the Press on Oct 25. REUTERS

#950. China's influence in the gaming industry is growing

Home to more than 700 million gamers, China is the world's largest gaming market — but it's also one of the most tightly regulated. The effects reach far beyond China, impacting players around the world.

In a dark underground hideout, dim light spills from a handful of oil lamps. A comrade fiddles with a rifle. A red flag hangs on one of the roughly hewn stone walls, bearing a hammer and sickle on a white star — the symbol of the ChineseWorkers' and Peasants' Red Army. Weapons are scattered on the ground. One is picked up, and soon the action moves into the snowy forest, where gunfire erupts among the trees.

Such a scene could fit in a new installment of "Call of Duty," the popular first-person shooter game that transports players to battlefields past, present, and future. But it is actually from "The Defiant." The game is currently being developed by the Chinese studio Hoothanes Technology in Hangzhou. It tells the story of Chinese forces fending off the Japanese army in the 1930s and 1940s.

Developer Connor Xu tells DW the weapons featured in the game are unique. They were used only in Asia and are therefore unfamiliar to many Western players, he says. The same goes for the story, which Xu says has never before been told in a video game.

"The Defiant" is also designed to appeal to an international audience. In just a few years, China has emerged as a major player in the global gaming industry despite strict regulations, censorship and a former ban on video game consoles.

More than 700 million people in China regularly play video games. According to market research company Newzoo, most consider gaming an important part of their lives. Many use games to stay in touch with friends.

"Games make life more interesting," developer Xu says. "I can try different roles, different stories, different characters, because we only have one life to live, but we can play a role in another story. That's really attractive, I think, to Chinese users."

People in China primarily play games on PCs and smartphones, while consoles are much less common. There are historical reasons for that: While gamers in Europe and North America debated whether PlayStation or Xbox was the better console in the early 2000s, the devices were not officially sold in China between 2000 and 2014. Chinese authorities said the restrictions were intended to protect children and teenagers from becoming addicted to gaming.

Minors in China are currently allowed to play online games for no more than three hours a week. There are no such limits for adults, but gaming is subject to strict controls. Anyone who wants to play must register using their real name and a personal identification number. That effectively allows the state to track who plays what and when, as well as whom they communicate with.

There is also a gray area that the Chinese government appears to tolerate. Some players log in using VPNs, giving them access to games that are not officially available in China. Some younger players use their parents' accounts to get around the limits on gaming time.

Despite its strict controls on underage gamers, China has become increasingly receptive to video games in general, having recognized the industry's enormous economic potential. Early on, games released for Chinese players often appeared to be copies of Western titles. At the same time, Chinese tech companies such as Tencent and NetEase invested in numerous Western gaming companies.

One distinctive feature of the Chinese market is its licensing system. "Unlike a lot of the other big video games markets in the world, China has a tightly regulated and licensed official video games market," George E. Osborn tells DW. The journalist advises NGOs and governments on video games and spoke at the Gamescom congress. In his book "Power Play," he describes how authoritarian states use video games to pursue political objectives.

The rule for all games in China is simple: No license, no sales. "That system essentially forces developers who want to release their video games to go through multiple layers of approval from China's Ministry of Propaganda, Ministry of Culture," Osborn says.

Games are prohibited from containing material that threatens China's unity, sovereignty or territorial integrity, among other restrictions. Pornographic content and gambling are also banned. Games may not incite crimes that threaten national security or spread information authorities believe could disrupt public order.

"The whole point around this criteria is that it's deliberately designed to be pretty vague," Osborn says. Whether a game violates the rules is a matter of interpretation. Sometimes games are altered even after release. In the 2025 action role-playing game "Wuchang: Fallen Feathers," for example, enemies based on famous Chinese figures from the Ming Dynasty suddenly could no longer be killed. Instead, they would collapse from exhaustion.

The Chinese action role-playing game "Black Myth: Wukong" became an unexpected international hit in 2024. By then, it was clear Chinese developers could do more than cater to the domestic market — they could create successful games for a global audience as well. The game was inspired by the 16th-century Chinese literary classic "Journey to the West."

Osborn sees nothing wrong with bringing Chinese culture to audiences around the world. The question, he says, is how much the state actually intervenes in the games themselves. "I think in general, video game players are actually quite deeply skeptical of these kinds of things. They are generally very good at spotting when someone might be selling to them or someone might be propagandizing. And so I think if it's too obvious, it won't work," he says.

Because of the licensing system, Western developers also have to comply with government requirements if they want to sell their games in China. And they do want to, Osborn says, because the market is too big to ignore. "But I think when you start thinking about the potential impact this has on creative standards around the world, I think it's really important that developers ask themselves the question of what will we or won't we compromise on here?"

He fears the real danger lies in self-censorship. That could lead developers, for example, to leave queer characters out of their games. That would represent a major step backward, he says, because games help many people explore their identities.

China is not the only country where games are modified to comply with national regulations. In Germany, for example, symbols that violate the country's constitution, such as the swastika, may not be shown in games unless the game in question explicitly contributes to the country's culture of remembrance. Depictions of extreme violence also have to be removed from German versions.

Glorifying violence is prohibited in China, too, yet Xu's team is still allowed to develop a war game. How does this add up? Xu explains it this way: "I think in this game, the most important thing is not violence. The most important thing is to tell history."

Xu says the team is committed to delivering a historically accurate product. Whether it succeeds will be for historians to judge.

This article was translated from German and edited by Sarah Hucal.

Published: 00:01 GMT, 26 October 2026 | Updated: 00:16 GMT, 26 October 2026

The owner of a family bakery that faced a ban from Borough Market for 'being too successful' has criticised the way businesses are being penalised in Labour's Britain.

Bread Ahead founder Matthew Jones claimed his bakery had been told to leave the food market because his firm was expanding so rapidly.

But market bosses and Mr Jones have now agreed to extend the bakery's lease up until 2028.

Mr Jones lamented the process to keep his stall where it is and the pressures put on him running a business in Labour's 'doom and gloom' Britain – despite the bakery's popularity.

He said he had found it easier to open and run his bakery abroad, with new ventures in New York and Malaysia.

British businesses have been hit by successive tax hikes by the Labour government.

Former chancellor Rachel Reeves increased the employer National Insurance contribution rate from 13.8 per cent to 15 per cent and reduced the secondary threshold to £5,000.

The punitive policies sparked fury among hospitality firms because it dragged many part-time and lower-paid staff into tax for the first time.

Bread Ahead founder Matthew Jones (pictured) has insisted he would still leave Borough Market because he no longer feels welcome there

Mr Jones said: 'What's happened to our country? Why are we doing this? Why are we penalising businesses?

'Why can't we just have a break and just leave people alone? Just let them run their businesses, employ their staff, pay their taxes, do what they need to do. Because that's what we're doing.'

The bakery has served doughnuts, sourdough, pastries and coffee to its customers in Borough Market since 2013.

Last month, after entering a renewal process for its lease, the bakery was told that it had been 'too successful' and was told to leave, according to Mr Jones.

He alleged that Borough Market told him opening new chains abroad went against its policy. Representatives of the market also told him that they do not have the space to house such a popular stall – because it attracts so many customers.

Bread Ahead is preparing to open a bakery in New York in November, which will be its first location in the US.

The company also has a number of sites across Asia and the Middle East – including in Bangkok, Dubai and Saudi Arabia.

He told the Daily Mail: 'The whole process was infuriating. It is really frustrating and we just want to get on with running the business.

'We still get the sense that we are not really going to be welcome [at Borough Market] in the long run.

'We've got an 18-month extension now, but even so, why 18 months? At the end of the day we probably will leave in 18 months. We're not entirely sure yet but the reality is in that time there will probably be new management in place who will have a different set of ideas.'

The market clarified to the Mail that the lease was always set to end in March 2028, but that no agreement had been reached beyond this.

The bakery has become an online sensation thanks to visitors' glowing reviews of their products

Mr Jones said: 'It's so much easier opening up and running a business abroad. The speed of things, there's just no blockages in the way and everyone wants you to do it. It's just not like that in Britain anymore.'

Mr Jones founded Bread Ahead in 2013 after leaving school at 15 and going on to work as a chef.

He said the business environment when he was growing up was much more conducive to budding entrepreneurs.

'We had a wonderful run here but now it just feels like banging my head against a brick wall,' he added.

The company has become an online sensation thanks to visitors' glowing reviews of its baked goods.

But the bakery owner told the Mail that it could cost up to £1,000,000 to move the shop out of Borough Market and into another London location.

He previously said that it could put the jobs of its 83 employees at risk.

He told the Mail today: 'We're not a big business. We're not Greggs. We're not Gail's. You know, we're not SpaceX. We're a family business and we started with nothing.

'Ultimately we'll just have to find another location locally and move into it because we want to be there for our customers. We don't want to disappoint people, and it's great trade. We've built up a local reputation.

Bread Ahead is set to open a bakery in New York in November, which will be its first location in the US

Shane Holland, Chair of the Borough Market Trust, said: 'Our position on Bread Ahead’s lease expiry is unchanged, and it is important to clarify that the extension agreed does not secure a long-term future for the business at the Market.

'This extension was first discussed in July and has remained on the table throughout our recent negotiations. We're pleased that Bread Ahead has now accepted, providing additional time to plan for the end of its current tenancy. No agreement has been reached for the period beyond March 2028.

'As with all traders approaching the end of their lease, we will continue to work constructively with Bread Ahead throughout the remainder of its lease.'

Hospitality owners have been beset with challenges in recent years with rising bills as well as the impact of Labour's previous policies, including tax hikes and sharp increases in the minimum wage.

#954. Kimi Antonelli moves to brink of F1 title with supreme United States GP triumph

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Mercedes driver Antonelli, 20, will head to Mexico City next week with a whopping 123-point lead over George Russell, with Lewis Hamilton a point further back - a finish of ninth or higher for the Italian will seal the title

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Kimi Antonelli demonstrated his title-winning prowess with a thumping victory at the United States Grand Prix but his coronation as champion was put on ice.

The 20-year-old delivered everything he needed to in his first shot at becoming the youngest Formula One champion in history by converting his pole position into a resounding win in Austin – crossing the line 13.0 seconds ahead of Charles Leclerc.

For the title to be wrapped up, the Italian needed major slip ups from his rivals. Lewis Hamilton extended the championship race by finishing fourth and George Russell just about did his bit despite only managing a disappointing eighth.

Antonelli will head to Mexico City next week with a whopping 123-point lead over Russell, with Hamilton a point further back. A finish of ninth or higher will seal the title, no matter where his rivals finish.

He leapt from his Mercedes and launched himself into the arms of his mechanics for the ninth time in this dominant season.

Leclerc claimed second for successive weeks after an impressive race for Ferrari, making a late move on Max Verstappen who completed the podium.

Lando Norris made a one-stop strategy work to claim fifth for McLaren.

Antonelli believed it would take something “catastrophic” from his rivals for him to clinch the crown in Texas, but knew winning the race was required for his end of the bargain.

He then needed Russell, whose faint title challenge has evaporated over recent races, to finish ninth or lower and Hamilton to be fifth or lower.

Part one of Antonelli’s job was done on Saturday as he soared to a magnificent pole as the sun began to drop on the Circuit of the Americas. With Hamilton only fifth and Russell sixth, his chances of getting over the line increased.

If the Italian was feeling any nerves as he sat on the grid waiting for his shot at history, he certainly did not show them as he blasted off the line and left Verstappen in his wake.

The Dutchman was swallowed up by the fast-starting Leclerc, who also jumped Isack Hadjar, while Verstappen then had to fend off Hamilton who rose to fourth. The Ferrari pair went wheel-to-wheel before Leclerc’s magnificent move on Verstappen.

The four-time world champion was soon up to speed and rocketed up the inside of Leclerc to reclaim second but Antonelli had already checked out – 2.4 seconds ahead at the end of the opening lap.

Russell’s role in the celebration-delaying picture was hampered as he was investigated for leaving the track and staying ahead of Oscar Piastri – with whom he banged wheels as he rejoined.

A five-second penalty was dished out to the Mercedes man. In a race fraught with jeopardy, Russell and Hamilton were now both on the cusp of handing Antonelli his crowning moment.

Verstappen was the first to pull the trigger on a pit stop on lap 14, swiftly followed by Hamilton and Leclerc but Antonelli – who started on the more durable medium tyres – and Mercedes chose not to respond.

Russell pitted and served his penalty on lap 24, rejoining a net eighth before Antonelli pitted a lap later and was now a net third – on much fresher tyres than those ahead.

New race leader Verstappen was showing strong pace, while Hamilton was promoted to fourth when Hadjar boxed.

The Dutchman pitted for a second time with 25 laps remaining, as Antonelli charged through on Leclerc to lead once more.

Leclerc and Hamilton stopped again in the final 16 laps, rejoining fourth and sixth – with the British driver needing to make up two places to ensure he kept Antonelli from the trophy.

He dispatched Hadjar swiftly but Norris had done a magnificent job on a one-stop strategy. The reigning champion – about to yield his crown – was reeled in on lap 47 by Verstappen and Leclerc, and Hamilton rose to fourth the following lap.

All the action was taking place behind Antonelli, who marched on serenely out front.

Antonelli has been the standout performer of the 2026 season and will be crowned a worthy champion over the coming weeks, fittingly shining brightest once again in the Lone Star State.

#961. Russia wants blackout in Ukraine as winter comes — Zelenskyy

Ukrainian President Zelenskyy says Russia is trying to cut electricity and heating to civilians ahead of winter. He also called the US president's waiver of new sanctions on Moscow a boost for Vladimir Putin.

Russia is stepping up its attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure in a bid to cut electricity and heating in the country as winter approaches, Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Saturday.

His remarks come as Moscow intensifies its attacks on civilian targets in the capital, Kyiv, and elsewhere, with key observers saying its objective is to render the country virtually unlivable.

In a post on social media platform X, Zelenskyy said Russia had just carried out one of its biggest attacks on Ukraine's energy sector since it began its full-scale invasion of its neighbor in February 2022.

"More than 15 critical power generation and transmission facilities were targeted across different regions of Ukraine," he wrote.

"Restoration work is ongoing, with all necessary services and all available resources of Ukrainian energy companies involved," he added.

Zelenskyy said that Russia was planning to leave Ukrainian citizens in the cold this winter.

"Russia is trying to cause a blackout in Ukraine — right before winter. Russia is trying to leave millions of our people without electricity and heating," he wrote, calling on allies to put pressure on Moscow to stop this happening.

He said Russia had "expanded ‌its campaign ​against the energy system" and was trying "to stretch ⁠Ukraine's ​reserves ​and repair ​capacity as ‌thinly as possible." ​

The Russian Defense Ministry, for its part, said on Saturday that its forces had attacked several infrastructure targets in Ukraine overnight.

Among those named was an electricity substation in the northwestern city of Zhytomyr.

However, it also said Ukraine's largest steelworks, in the city of Kryvyi Rih, had been hit, saying the facility supplied steel products to the Ukrainian military-industrial complex.

It said another steel plant in ​Zaporizhzhia, a city near the front ​line, had also been struck.

Ukrainian authorities have also said that one person — an ambulance driver — was killed ​and ‌19 others injured, including a child, in a Russian airstrike on Kherson in southern Ukraine.

Russian state news ​agency TASS has also reported the death of one woman as a result of Ukrainian drone strikes in Russia's Belgorod region that also injured a man.

Meanwhile, Zelenskyy also reacted to US President Donald Trump's decision to waive a package of new sanctions on Moscow, saying the move would only encourage Russian leader Vladimir Putin.

"A US sanctions blackout, easing pressure on the aggressor, financial rewards for Putin — all of this only encourages him to keep attacking," Zelenskyy said.

On Friday, Trump signed an executive order that waived sweeping US sanctions and tariffs targeting Russia's energy revenues, two days before they were due to take effect.

The waiver has been hailed by a Russian presidential envoy as a "historic moment."

"The Trump administration's suspension of the [Lindsey] Graham Act is an important and truly historic moment," Kirill Dmitriev said on social media.

Dmitriev said the act, named for the late US senator who sponsored the bill, "would have caused "serious damage first and foremost to the US economy and global markets."

Trump's move came as he increasingly criticizes Zelenskyy, fueling speculation that the US leader is siding with Moscow in the conflict.
