#963. Epstein haunts GOP in US midterms as Democrats vow fresh probes

Sign up now: Get ST's newsletters delivered to your inbox

President Donald Trump on stage at a rally, where protester Blake Miley revealed a T-shirt with the message, “Release the Epstein Files,” on Oct 12 in Youngstown, Ohio.

WASHINGTON – President Donald Trump can’t shake the furore over Jeffrey Epstein.

Democrats are preparing to launch congressional investigations into the administration’s handling of files related to the late, disgraced sex offender if they regain power after the Nov 3 midterm elections. They say the administration botched the release of documents and are using the issue to hammer Trump and GOP lawmakers in key races.

“The Epstein investigation is going to be one of our top priorities,” Representative Robert Garcia, the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, said in an interview, alongside probes into the Trump family’s business dealings, allegations of corporate corruption and the president’s immigration crackdown.

“The country wants disclosure, they want release of the files and they want justice for the survivors,” Garcia said.

For Trump, it’s a full-circle moment. The president in 2024 indicated a willingness to release files pertaining to investigations into Epstein. But in office, after releasing several tranches that failed to satisfy lawmakers and many Epstein victims, Trump urged the public and Congress to move on from what he called a “hoax.”

The midterms in 2026 have made clear that many are not ready to move on. With Trump and his party fighting an uphill battle to keep control of Congress, the lingering tumult over Epstein’s crimes has added to the GOP’s electoral woes and underscored how difficult it has been for the president to put the issue to rest.

Polls show Democrats poised to obtain a majority in the House and they have made it clear they intend to open fresh investigations into Epstein’s actions, Trump’s ties to him and the government’s handling of the files.

Any probe would ripple well beyond Washington, with Wall Street and corporate America already bracing for a wave of Democratic investigations. Garcia said major banks that had ties to Epstein’s financial dealings are among those who could be called to testify.

A White House official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said the administration was focused on the upcoming midterms and declined to detail any preparations for potential House probes. The administration has nothing to hide on the Epstein case, the official said.

White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis said Trump had “been totally exonerated on anything related to Epstein” and through disclosures of files “done more for Epstein’s victims than anyone before him.”

Democrats are not waiting until they regain power to put the spotlight back on Epstein.

In Texas, Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico sought to counter September’s Republican midterm convention by holding an event with an Epstein survivor and demanding that all of the files be released. In Georgia, Senator Jon Ossoff has criticised how Republicans handled the release of the documents.

And it’s not just the candidates who have kept Epstein hovering over the midterms. At a Trump rally in October, a woman wearing a T-shirt that read “Release the Epstein Files” was physically accosted by supporters of the president and removed from the arena by security. Vice-President J.D. Vance was interrupted by a protester calling for the release of the files at a North Carolina rally on Oct 26.

The Epstein files have long been the centre of speculation over the late financier’s wealthy and powerful contacts and any connections they may have had to his conduct.

“The Epstein issue blows up into a larger narrative of how Republicans were helping their donors, the billionaires, the wealthiest and most well-connected people at the expense of working-class people,” said Neera Tanden, a longtime Democratic operative who leads the Center for American Progress.

Epstein and allegations of child sexual abuse have been a particular lightning rod for elements of Trump’s own base. Some of his supporters helped stoke the so-called Pizzagate conspiracy that sought to link Hillary Clinton to a fictitious cabal of child sex traffickers.

Following his campaign pledge, Trump’s administration released some of the Epstein files a month into his presidency to cheers from right-wing supporters, but many of those documents had been previously released. Subsequent releases were messy, including efforts to redact Trump’s own name from files.

As the controversy dragged on Trump bristled at continued questions from reporters about Epstein.

Trump, who shared a friendship with Epstein in the 1990s and early 2000s, has repeatedly said he cut ties with him almost two decades ago before his crimes came to attention. Epstein was arrested in 2019 on federal charges that he engaged in sex trafficking of minors. He died in jail by suicide, according to the authorities.

US financier Jeffrey Epstein, who was arrested in 2019 on federal charges of sex trafficking minors, was found dead in jail.

Garcia said Democrats have a two-pronged goal of releasing more files and investigating some of those named in previously disclosed documents.

“There has to be real accountability there. And there has to be real investigation,” he said. “This is one of the most bipartisan issues in the country. People are interested in this topic, people ask about it all the time.”

While current House Oversight Chairman James Comer, a Republican, has investigated the Epstein case to a degree, including through subpoenas and depositions, Democrats say he hasn’t done enough to obtain testimony under oath from key figures.

“People are angry,” Garcia said. “The president made promises, and he went back on them.”

A House Oversight Committee spokeswoman said every witness in the panel’s investigation was required to “verbally acknowledge that they understand their obligation to tell the truth.”

In a statement, the spokeswoman touted the committee’s work, which she said included 19 witness interviews and depositions, releasing approximately 65,000 pages of documents and uncovering allegations of sexual misconduct that were referred to the Department of Justice.

Garcia has called previously for Attorney-General Todd Blanche to testify. When asked about a potential subpoena, Garcia said all options were on the table.

Blanche, who previously served as Trump’s personal attorney, handled the initial release of files and met with Ghislaine Maxwell, who was convicted for helping Epstein traffic women and girls for sex. Democrats strongly opposed his confirmation, citing among other matters his handling of the Epstein matter.

A Justice Department spokesperson referred inquiries to Blanche’s previous remarks and said the attorney-general will follow the law.

Blanche acknowledged “we made mistakes and I’ve owned up to those mistakes,” such as failing to properly redact documents, in a recent interview with the “Pod Force One” podcast. But he said those actions had been corrected, and defended Trump.

“I can tell you that President Trump, from Day One, said ‘Release as many of the files, I want everything released’,” Blanche said. BLOOMBERG

#968. What happened to the cast of Once Upon A Time? From a real-life fairytale romance to a scandalous affair and a tragic death; a look back at the stars 15 years after the show first aired

Published: 00:01 GMT, 26 October 2026 | Updated: 00:15 GMT, 26 October 2026

It's hard to believe it's been 15 years since fairy tale fantasy drama Once Upon A Time first hit screens back in October 2011.

Spanning across seven seasons, the ABC series centered around two alternate worlds, featuring characters who lived in the real-world town of Storybrooke, Maine and their fairy tale counterparts who resided in the Enchanted Forest.

The main premise saw The Evil Queen aka Mayor Regina Mills (Lara Parrilla) cast a dark curse which results in the fairy tale characters losing their memories of who they really are and becoming trapped as their alter-egos in Storybrooke.

Their saviour comes in the form of bail bonds collector Emma Swan (Jennifer Morrison), who is actually the long-lost daughter of Snow White (Ginnifer Goodwin) and Prince Charming (Josh Dallas), who was sent away as a baby before the curse took hold so that she could one day return and break it.

Blending a mix of fantasy, drama, adventure and romance, the age-old conflict between good and evil and a huge helping of nostalgia thanks to the plethora of classic Disney, fairy tale and folklore characters; Once Upon A Time was a major hit when it first premiered, attracting a whopping 12.93 million viewers for its pilot episode.

It's hard to believe it's been 15 years since fairy tale fantasy drama Once Upon A Time first hit screens back in October 2011

The ABC series centered around two alternate worlds, featuring characters who lived in the real-world town of Storybrooke, Maine and their fairy tale counterparts who resided in the Enchanted Forest

While much of the cast were already established actors, the show undoubtedly significantly boosted their popularity, with the stars building a solid fanbase who have continued to support them throughout their careers.

However as the years went on, the show suffered a mass decline in viewership, going on to be cancelled following the seventh season, with the last episode airing in May 2018.

Despite no longer producing new episodes, the fantasy series has gained a whole new following as teens who watched the original run are now watching the show with their own children, while the series continues to spark debate amid its online fandom.

And as Once Upon a Time marks 15 years since it first aired, we take a look back at the varied fates of the show's main cast....

Lana Parrilla (Regina Mills / The Evil Queen)

Lana excelled in her standout role as the villainous Evil Queen / Storybrooke Mayor Regina, garnering a massive fans base and numerous awards and nominations.

Since leaving the show, she went on to make appearances in 2021's The Tax Collector, anthology series Why Women Kill (pictured) and 2023's The Lincoln Lawyer

Lana embarked on a romance with The Gentlemen star Benjamin Clementine, following the collapse of his marriage earlier this year

Lana, now 49, excelled in her standout role as the villainous Evil Queen / Storybrooke Mayor Regina, garnering a massive fan base and numerous awards and nominations.

Since leaving the show, she went on to make appearances in 2021's The Tax Collector, anthology series Why Women Kill (which also featured co-star Ginnifer Goodwin) and 2023's The Lincoln Lawyer.

As well as TV and film, Lana also branched into music, releasing a house song called It's Over Now in 2021 alongside Italian DJ Glovibes.

She once again teamed up with Glovibes, along with singer Luciana, for the 2024 dance track, You.

But while she was successful on screen, Lana has faced bad luck in her life, with the star seeing her LA home targeted by trespassers back in August 2024.

TMZ reported that when security approached the person, he ventured further onto the property grounds, leaving them to call the Los Angeles Police Department.

After law enforcement surveyed the property, the suspect – a 40-year-old homeless man – emerged from the house and surrendered.

Lana, who herself had suffered homelessness in her early career, was out of town when the incident took place.

In her personal life, Lana secretly married fiancé Fred Di Blasio in 2014, however, five years later she announced on her Instagram that she was 'no longer married' and was instead starting a 'new life path'.

This new path has since led to a romance with The Gentlemen star Benjamin Clementine, following the collapse of his marriage to 'City Superwoman' Dame Helena Morrissey's musician daughter Flo earlier this year.

The couple made their red-carpet debut last month at the series two premiere of The Gentlemen, in which Benjamin plays a former soldier called Nanny.

Ginnifer Goodwin (Mary Margaret Blanchard / Snow White)

Ginnifer, now 48, had a major career breakthrough with her lead role as Snow White and Mary, the school teacher of young Henry and the mother of long-lost daughter Emma Swan

She went on to make television appearances in anthology series The Twilight Zone and Heartstring, before landing the lead role of Beth Ann Stanton in dark comedy series Why Women Kill [pictured]

Meanwhile, during her time on the ABC show, Ginnifer met and fell in love with co-star Josh Dallas, who plays Prince Charming

Ginnifer, now 48, had a major career breakthrough with her lead role as Snow White and Mary; the schoolteacher of young Henry and the mother of long-lost daughter Emma Swan.

Following her success in the series, which she left at the end of season six, Ginnifer went on to have big triumphs with her voiceover work, including starring as Judy Hopps in Disney's Zootopia franchise – of which she won a selection of awards for.

She went on to make television appearances in anthology series The Twilight Zone and Heartstrings, before landing the lead role of Beth Ann Stanton in dark comedy series Why Women Kill.

Meanwhile, during her time on the ABC show, Ginnifer met and fell in love with co-star Josh Dallas, who plays Prince Charming.

Their fairytale ending saw them tie the knot in California in 2014, with the couple going on to welcome two sons; Oliver, 12, and Hugo, 10.

During an appearance on the Today show in 2020, Josh revealed that he fell in love with Ginnifer at first sight.

'I knew right away. I knew right away, it was that thing,' he said. 'It was that thing - I turned around and I saw her and I knew I was in trouble.'

Josh shared that 'understanding' has helped their relationship as well as 'willing to be flexible, and just love. You gotta love and be willing to grow with that person, or let that person grow too and give them space.'

Josh Dallas (David Nolan / Prince Charming)

Josh, 47, left thanks swooning thanks to his role as the handsome Prince Charming and alter-ego David Nolan

Following his years on the show, Josh jumped into another long-term TV project, starring as Ben Stone in the NBC/Netflix supernatural mystery drama Manifest, which he appeared on from 2018 to 2023

Like his wife, Josh also briefly reprised his Once Upon A Time role to appear in the series finale in 2018. Back in 2023, Josh said he has 'nothing but gratitude' for 'Once Upon a Time'

Josh, 47, left fans swooning thanks to his role as the handsome Prince Charming and alter-ego David Nolan.

Following his years on the show, Josh jumped into another long-term TV project, starring as Ben Stone in the NBC/Netflix supernatural mystery drama Manifest, which he appeared on from 2018 to 2023.

Josh also reunited with his love Ginnifer Goodwin for his voice role as Frantic Pig in 2016's Zootopia, later reprising his part in 2025 for the sequel.

Like his wife, Josh also briefly reprised his Once Upon A Time role to appear in the series finale in 2018.

Back in 2023, Josh said he has 'nothing but gratitude' for Once Upon a Time.

He told how after years since the series finale, it is 'humbling' to know that the fantasy drama still has an audience.

He told People: 'It's still finding an audience. People come up to me all the time talking about 'Once' and saying they just started watching it and they're loving it.

'Or I've had people come up to me — which makes me feel old, but that's okay — they'll say, 'You were my childhood. You got me through college, all through high school' and that show changed their life and it's super humbling.

'It's just nothing but gratitude to be part of a show that was such a big part of some people's fabric of their lives.'

Elsewhere, in 2026, Josh made minor appearances in TV series The Hunting Party and We Were Liars, while he's set to lend his voice for animated film Hexed, which is due for release in November.

Jennifer portrayed Emma Swan, a Boston bail-bond agent who discovers she's Snow White and Prince Charming's daughter

Jennifer's directing career also saw her direct feature film Sun Dogs, an episode of Euphoria and the first four episodes of the second season of Peacock anthology series Dr. Death

Jennifer portrayed Emma Swan, a Boston bail-bond agent who discovers she's Snow White and Prince Charming's daughter and is lured back to Storybrooke by the son she had adopted, as he vows to break the curse.

Already an established actress thanks to roles in How I Met Your Mother, after her run in Once Upon A Time, Jennifer, now 47, went on to appear in other shows including This Is Us, Will Trent and All's Fair.

In 2016, Jennifer launched her own film production company, Apartment 3C (37F) Productions, going on to direct her first feature film, Sun Dogs, later that year, with the film going on to bag numerous accolades.

Jennifer's directing career also saw her direct an episode of Euphoria and the first four episodes of the eight-episode second season of Peacock anthology series Dr Death.

Her personal life has also seen her enjoy relationships with former Once Upon A Time co-star Sebastian Stan, Australian actor Jesse Spencer and Puerto Rican actor Amaury Nolasco.

Jennifer has been with Salvadoran-American actor Gerardo Celasco since 2019. They went on to marry in April 2022, before welcoming a daughter two years later.

Emilie, now 44, already had a flourishing television career, thanks to roles in Roswell and Lost. She went on to further boost her profile as Rumplestiltskin's true love Belle in the hit series

Prior to Once Upon A Time, Emilie, now 44, already had a flourishing television career, thanks to roles in Roswell and Lost.

Following her stint on Once Upon A Time, Emilie continued to focus on her TV career, with appearances in A Lover Scorned in 2019, True Colours in 2022 and The Reluctant Royal in 2025.

Emilie's love life went on to improve, with the actress becoming engaged to American writer-director Eric Bilitch in 2016. The couple have welcomed three children together.

Robert Carlyle (Mr Gold / Rumplestiltskin)

#970. France: Protesters clash with police in nationwide protests, amid rising social polarization

Unrest broke out in parts of France as students, trade unionists and Yellow Vest activists took to the streets to protest high prices and inequality. Police arrested over 1,000 people amid chaotic scenes.

Police and protesters clashed amid mass rallies across France on Saturday, over high prices and social inequalities and the state of the education system.

France's Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said some 1,200 people had been arrested across the country and that 150 police officers had been injured.

"It's a miracle the toll wasn't higher," Lecornu said while visiting officers deployed in Paris on Saturday evening.

Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said 110,000 people took part in the demonstrations in Paris alone, while 110 marches had taken place across the country.

The Interior Ministry said some 550,000 people turned out for the nationwide demonstrations.

The ministry said the arrests were made following violent incidents in Paris, Marseilles, Rennes, Toulouse, Angers and other cities across the country.

"Such actions include attempted looting, confrontations with law enforcement, the setting of fires to street furniture and the targeting of seats of power and media outlets," the ministry said, blaming the unrest on what it described ​as the "hard-left."

In Paris and Marseille, police fired tear gas at protesters as violent clashes took place.

AFP reported that dozens of shops were looted in Paris, Marseille, Nice, Bordeaux and Lille.

The windows of the offices of French broadcasters CNews and Europe 1 in western Paris were also broken by protesters, and AFP journalists reported seeing several parked cars torched.

French President Emmanuel Macron condemned the violence in a post on X and warned: "Those who have broken, attacked the prefectures as well as businesses, looted even our town halls, will be prosecuted and punished."

In Lyon, situated in central France, the city's tourism office was set alight with flames and black smoke seen billowing from the building.

In the city of Limoges, the town hall was set alight as unrest broke out. The blaze spread from a wing of the building and eventually reached the roof, where it continued burning as crowds stood watching.

The historic building was largely destroyed by the blaze, despite attempts by firefighters to douse the flames.

Meanwhile, in the northern city of Lille, protesters smashed their way into the city hall and vandalized the premises before leaving, according to an AFP photographer.

Riot police within minutes confirmed that all the protesters had left.

The protests come on the heels of an initial wave of demonstrations that began last month over the situation at schools in the country, with pupils complaining about teacher absences and run-down facilities.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In the French capital, police had banned rallies around the Elysee presidential palace, the prime minister's office and the Champs-Elysees avenue, along with other key locations.

A march through the center of the city was also banned.

Reports began emerging late on Saturday morning of riot police clashing with protesters in the Saint-Denis area on the outskirts of the capital, as well as near the Gare du Nord train station, among other areas.

In Paris, DW correspondent Jack Parrock said unrest was playing out in small pockets of the city.

"The videos circulating on social media of the violence in France don’t paint the full picture," Parrock said.

"The significant percentage of the people we met out on the streets of Paris were teachers, nurses, students, and workers, who want no part in the unrest, but do also seem to understand why the outbreaks are happening," Parrock explained.

"Amongst those people, we did still witness a collective rage against a government they don’t feel is listening to them," said Parrock.

On the matter of how police were responding, Parrock said they had seen police "seemingly try to show some restraint — clearly intending to de-escalate some of the recent tension."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Students have been joined by trade unionists and remnants of the Yellow Vests ("Gilets jaunes") movement, which staged mass weekly protests from November 2018 to June 2020, initially against rising fuel prices. They later morphed into protests against the high cost of living and economic inequality in general.

The student protests over the past weeks have been backed by Jean-Luc Melenchon, the leader of the hard-left France Unbowed ("La France insoumise", or LFI), who marched in one demonstration on Tuesday.

The government has blamed the LFI for pouring fuel on the fire of widespread public discontent, an allegation the party has denied.

#971. Can you convert an RMD to a Roth IRA?

This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here.

See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred

Dear Liz: I’m supposed to start required minimum distributions soon. Can I deposit my annual distribution into a Roth IRA? I understand that I have to pay taxes on the RMD, but if I can put it in a Roth, I would guess I don’t have to pay future capital gains taxes. I am retired and not working, so I wasn’t sure whether I can contribute to a Roth IRA.

Answer: You can’t. Contributions to IRAs, including traditional and Roth versions, require you to have earned income at least equal to the amount you’re contributing. Contributions are also limited to a certain dollar amount. In 2026, the limit is $7,500, plus $1,100 for people 50 and older.

There may be another way to get the tax-free growth you want. You can convert traditional retirement funds to a Roth IRA without earned income. Qualified Roth withdrawals are tax-free, and there are no RMDs during the original owner’s lifetime.

But late-in-life conversions can be tricky. Not only are conversions typically taxable, but they can temporarily raise Medicare premiums, subject more of your Social Security benefits to tax and push you into a higher bracket. You should consult a tax pro before converting.

Keep in mind that you can’t convert the RMD itself. You must take your required distribution for the year before converting additional money.

Dear Liz: Why do you seem to discourage older people living in homes that have appreciated over the years from selling because of the tax consequence? Recently, someone complained they could not move out of their family home because they would owe $400,000 in taxes. Why don’t you show the math: If they owe $400,000, even at the maximum (20% capital gains), that means they received $2,000,000. So even after taxes, they net $1,600,000. People who are asking the question you answered today need to either recognize they are swimming in money after taxes, or that they incorrectly think their net profit is taxed 100%.

Answer: If you’re referring to the couple who wanted to use their home sale proceeds to give down payments to their children, your math is a bit wonky.

The couple said selling their paid-off home would generate more than $1 million in proceeds. Proceeds aren’t the same as taxable gains, and the tax bill depends on the home’s original cost, qualifying improvements, selling expenses and the $500,000 home-sale exclusion for eligible married couples.

Taxable home sale gains can have the same impact as Roth conversions, in that they can raise Medicare premiums, make more Social Security benefits taxable and push other income into higher tax brackets. Some taxpayers also face the 3.8% net investment income tax.

Furthermore, the couple weren’t complaining that they couldn’t sell their home — they wanted to. My response was to remind them that their generosity could have big financial consequences.

Your ultimate point is a good one, though. Taxes matter, but they should never be the only consideration in a major financial decision.

Dear Liz: I know from personal experience after selling a longtime residence that tax return information is shared with the Social Security Administration. If the two-year look-back shows high enough modified adjusted gross income, Medicare premiums can increase significantly. There are appeal options, but a one-time home sale doesn’t necessarily qualify.

Should the couple consider a home equity line of credit to generate funds without triggering taxes?

Answer: That’s one option a financial planner might suggest, although HELOCs typically have variable interest rates and require monthly payments, which can burden retirees.

Another possibility is a reverse mortgage, which generally costs more but doesn’t require monthly loan payments. Interest and fees increase the loan balance, reducing equity available for future needs. Borrowers must continue paying property taxes, insurance and maintenance, and the loan generally comes due when they sell or permanently leave the home.

But again, taxes are just one factor. The planner can help them sort through all their options to find one that best fits their goals and needs.

#972. France’s far-right leader Marine Le Pen launches presidential bid as protests rattle the nation

Sign up now: Get ST's newsletters delivered to your inbox

French far-right leader Marine Le Pen delivers a speech during a political rally to launch her presidential campaign, after the party's congress on Oct 25 in Orleans, France.

ORLEANS, France - Far-right leader Marine Le Pen, the frontrunner in the 2027 French presidential election, formally launched her campaign on Oct 25 with a promise to restore order and national confidence.

As France faces one of its most turbulent periods in years, Le Pen cast herself as the best placed to navigate what she described as mounting economic, social and security crises.

“We are not living through the end of the world but the end of a world, their world,” she said of her political opponents.

Le Pen chose to make her first campaign address in Orleans, home to Joan of Arc, the 15th-century warrior heroine revered by nationalists as a symbol of patriotism and sovereignty.

Addressing a crowd of cheering supporters, she promised “zero tolerance” policing and said restoring security was the state’s first duty.

Mass protests over living costs and inequality last weekend descended into looting and vandalism.

The street turmoil has given Le Pen a boost and an opinion poll published on Oct 25 put her on 32% to 33.5%, well ahead of her nearest rival, hard-left leader Jean-Luc Melenchon on 17%, as voters desert mainstream parties for the political extremes.

Surveys suggest she would easily defeat Melenchon in a run-off ballot, expected to be held in early May.

Seeking to project optimism, Le Pen built her speech around the theme of a national “Renaissance”. She said France was living through a period of upheaval but would emerge stronger if it embraced her vision of security, prosperity and renewal.

“We say: ‘Things were good before, they will be better tomorrow!’,” she said.

Le Pen promised a hard line on immigration, pledging to restore border controls, automatically expel foreign criminals and crack down on gangs and drug traffickers.

Le Pen herself could have to campaign wearing an ankle tag after she was convicted of embezzling European Parliament funds. She is appealing the court verdict.

Marine Le Pen (centre), an MP from France’s far-right National Rally party, reacts on stage alongside party president Jordan Bardella and other delegates at the rally.

On the economy, Le Pen pledged spending restraint, lower business taxes, reduced bureaucracy and support for industry, innovation and artificial intelligence. She rejected further increases in the retirement age.

The congress was designed to showcase unity at the top of the National Rally party, with Jordan Bardella re-elected party president and presented as Le Pen’s choice for prime minister.

Bardella’s speech was interrupted by activists from a Jewish student union, drawing attention to recent accusations he made antisemitic comments in his youth, which he denies.

Le Pen has spent more than a decade trying to transform the party she inherited from her father, Jean-Marie Le Pen, in 2011, softening its image and broadening its appeal beyond its traditional anti-immigration base.

On Europe, Le Pen stopped short of advocating a French exit from the European Union, but said she would roll back Brussels’ influence, restore national control over borders and laws, and put French interests first, including avoiding foreign wars.

“The future belongs to us,” she said, before leading the flag-waving crowd in singing the national anthem. REUTERS

#975. Jaguar Land Rover cyber-attack was ‘state-sponsored’, former minister suggests

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Former armed forces minister Al Carns said that it would be ‘highly unlikely’ for Russia to not know about Jaguar Land Rover cyber-attack

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

A cyber-attack which caused up to £2.1bn of damage to Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) last year was state-sponsored, a former armed forces minister has suggested.

Estimated at £1.9bn (ranging from £1.6bn to £2.1bn by the Cyber Monitoring Centre), the cyber-attack was the most economically damaging in UK history. In June, a New York Times investigation linked the attack to a Russian hacking group.

Al Carns, former armed forces minister, made the comments in July at an event at the Chatham House think tank. He was asked about how the UK could deter “threats in the absence of political leadership”, according to a report in The Telegraph.

Mr Carns reportedly replied: “We have all the detail. We know all of the information, we know all of the threats. Sometimes it comes out sporadically, but it’s not a centrally coherent national conversation between government and society.

“We know there is £15bn of cyber-attacks, we know there’s espionage going on, we know there’s 35,000 casualties a month-ish in Ukraine. We know the Jaguar Land Rover attack was state-sponsored, etc, etc.”

Mr Carns told The Telegraph that his comments were not based on an official Ministry of Defence assessment, adding: “It would be highly unlikely for an attack of that scale to emanate from anywhere without the host state knowing about it”.

Jaguar Land Rover had to halt production for five weeks last September after the cyber attack. They were forced to shut down their computer networks, leaving them unable to operate their production lines.

They arranged a war room to fight the hackers comprising of cybersecurity investigators, and representatives from the National Crime Agency, the National Cyber Security Centre, Google and the FBI, according to The New York Times.

Microsoft, who had reportedly been tracking the Russian group responsible, apparently alerted Jaguar to who had breached their systems. The encryption used by the group was described as “really, really complicated”.

MPs have been pushing the UK government to be more transparent about who they believe to be behind the damaging hack. Labour MP Graeme Downie said this Summer that ministers should be more open about the incident “so the British people can see we are already in a conflict with Russia”.

This weekend, defence secretary Wes Streeting warned that Britain must be ready for war in 1,000 days.

Writing in The Telegraph, Mr Streeting warns Britain’s adversaries could be ready to attack the UK in 2030.

He wrote: “Our adversaries’ willingness to harm us is not new. What has changed is their capacity. By 2030 their force strength and war economy could put them in a position to attack.

“That gives us a little over 1,000 days to complete our mission: to be ready with our allies to fight and win.”

#979. After federal subpoenas, Mark Walter tapped a Magic Johnson-linked firm for billions in loans

In February, after getting served with subpoenas in a federal criminal investigation, the billionaire sports mogul Mark Walter’s insurance companies abruptly stopped lending to him.

But within weeks, new loans started rolling in from a different source: a financial firm whose owners include his business protege, basketball legend Earvin “Magic” Johnson.

Amistad Financial Group, a holding company that counts Johnson as a board member and minority shareholder, lent about $1.26 billion to Walter’s companies between March and June of this year, according to a Bloomberg News review of business records and a person with knowledge of the activity who asked not to be identified discussing sensitive matters. Another $1.06 billion went to intermediaries that routinely serve as conduits for loans to Walter.

The combined $2.31 billion of lending, which hasn’t been reported previously, highlights the way Walter relies on debt to fund his business empire, and Amistad’s role. Even before this year, the firm’s insurance units had provided billions of dollars of loans to Walter affiliates, filings show. It also acted as an intermediary to help him tap loans from his own insurers, Bloomberg reported previously — transactions that are now part of the federal investigation.

Walter himself owns a single-digit voting stake in Amistad but doesn’t control it, participate in its management or sit on its board, according to a person familiar with its operations.

Representatives for Walter’s TWG Global holding company and for Johnson did not respond to messages seeking comment.

A former point guard who led the Lakers to five National Basketball Assn. championships, Johnson has described Walter as a business mentor. They have done deals with each other for more than a decade, including Johnson’s participation in the Walter-led purchase of the Dodgers baseball team. Johnson doesn’t serve on Amistad’s three-person executive committee, and it’s unclear whether he was involved in or aware of the lending decisions. Some of Amistad’s insurance units are led by Eric Holoman, Johnson’s former business manager.

The federal investigation, being pursued in parallel by the U.S. Department of Justice and the Securities and Exchange Commission, focuses on Walter’s insurance companies’ failure to disclose that more than $20 billion of loans on their books went to his other businesses.

The recent lending came from two Amistad subsidiaries, Equitrust Life Insurance Co. and Heritage Life Insurance Co. It’s unclear whether Amistad executives were aware of the investigation when the loans were made. Walter’s insurers disclosed the subpoena in a regulatory filing on June 26, but the filing did not get much attention until Bloomberg News reported on it in July. Information about lending activity after June 30 won’t be disclosed until next month.

Walter is now scrambling to reduce debts to his own insurance companies, Delaware Life Insurance Co. and Clear Spring Life and Annuity Co., in part to assuage concerns from ratings agencies about the scale of affiliated lending. He has agreed to sell the Lakers at a $12.5-billion valuation to free up cash and proposed a $6.5-billion debt swap with Delaware Life. This week, the insurer said it had regulatory approval to proceed with part of that, swapping $3.8 billion.

Because he doesn’t legally control Amistad, Walter is under no such pressure to reduce his reliance on its money.

His ties to Amistad are deep. Its official corporate address is the Chicago office suite that houses Walter’s family office. Walter’s financial firm, Guggenheim Partners, serves as an investment manager for both Equitrust and Heritage Life.

Walter’s brother-in-law serves as president of Heritage Life. Walter used to control Equitrust when it was owned by Guggenheim. He sold it to Johnson in 2015, and Johnson sold it to Amistad last year.

Recipients of the new Amistad loans include a company through which Walter holds his stake in used-car seller Carvana Co., and another containing his interest in the Billie Jean King Cup, the women’s tennis competition that he has backed since 2023. The destination for most of the money wasn’t clear from regulatory filings.

The federal investigations revolve around how Walter’s insurers came to lend so much money to his other businesses without disclosing the arrangement to their regulator, the Delaware Department of Insurance, as required. As of the end of last year, the amount of money they had invested in affiliates was $24 billion, or about 45% of the companies’ total invested assets.

Much of the money was routed to loans for newly created limited liability companies with no public profile. These LLCs were created by Amistad and other intermediaries, which in turn sent the money back to Walter.

In January and early February of this year, that lending arrangement continued, with Delaware Life loaning $730 million to newly formed LLCs that then sent the money to Walter’s other businesses, regulatory filings show. That stopped after the U.S. Attorney’s Office in Manhattan sent the grand jury subpoenas.

But in March, Amistad’s Equitrust sent $500 million to 10 LLCs. These borrowers had been formed days earlier by Federico Hermida, a Miami-based executive at ABS Capital Co., a longtime business partner of Walter’s that has often served as an intermediary in deals between Walter and his insurers. In June, Amistad’s Heritage Life sent $303 million to a subset of the Hermida borrowers. A representative of ABS declined to comment.

Heritage Life also sent about $253 million to LLCs set up by two other intermediaries that Walter has used for loans in the past: the real estate firm Bradford Allen and Hudson Trading, both based in Chicago. Representatives of Bradford Allen didn’t respond to requests for comment, and Hudson Trading declined to comment.

The remaining $1.3 billion of loans were made to companies that are known to be part of Walter’s business empire, or that were formed by a Walter employee, or were confirmed by the person with knowledge of the matter.

Most of the loans carried interest rates of 8% or more, and were due to mature in September or earlier. The insurers won’t have to disclose whether those loans were repaid, extended or replaced with new debt until they file their next quarterly financial reports next month.

Despite the borrowing from Amistad, Walter had not significantly reduced his debt to his own insurance companies by June 30, the date of the most recent regulatory filings. After climbing from $24 billion to $25 billion through March, the amount of affiliated investments dropped to about $24 billion as of June.

#980. Ukrainian President Zelenskyy speaks at EU summit amid spat with Donald Trump

EU leaders reaffirmed support for Ukraine at the Brussels summit. But souring relations with the US over Russia and Starlink and a big hole in the budget will make for a difficult winter for Ukraine.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy was applauded by EU leaders when he appeared at this week's summit in Brussels. But getting what he needs from Europe will be tough, and a public dispute with US President Donald Trump has put him in a very difficult position.

Speaking to press at the summit, he said that "Putin wants to destroy us" and that Ukraine must prepare for a hard winter.

Experts view the upcoming cold season as a rough one for Ukraine as well.

"Ukraine is arguably entering the most difficult winter since [Russia's] full scale invasion," Olena Prokopenko, a senior fellow at the German Marshall Fund of the United States, a nonpartisan think-tank, told DW.

Three painful topics were on the table at the summit for discussion between Zelenskyy and EU leaders: US relations with Russia, Starlink ― and money.

Zelenskyy's visit to Brussels comes at a time when he needs European support more than ever. That's because his relationship with the US is worsening. Worries are growing in the EU and Ukraine that the US is growing more sympathetic to Russia.

President Trump told US news channel Newsmax: "I think I find Zelenskyy to be more difficult to deal with than [Russian President Vladimir] Putin."

Trump struck a deal to buy Russian diesel on October 12, which signifies a step back from sanctions placed on Russia and a blow for Ukraine.

When Zelenskyy ordered Ukrainian forces to conduct fresh strikes on Russia's oil refineries, Trump labelled the Ukrainian leader's decision as "a disgrace."

At the press conference at the summit on Friday, Zelenskyy told reporters that he knows that US-built missiles "are being sent to the Middle East, so it is no secret that we are not a priority."

He is asking Europe instead to supply the military power Ukraine needs to get through the winter.

Since the beginning of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, the US has been the biggest military donor to Ukraine. But the relationship between the two countries has become more difficult since the start of Donald Trump's second term in the White House.

Ukraine uses Starlink, a satellite Internet service developed by tech billionaire Elon Musk. The country also uses Starshield, the military-grade version, for battlefield communications, mid-range strikes on Russian-occupied territory and interceptor drones, though not for long-range strikes in Russia.

At the summit, Zelenskyy spoke of his "deep and unpleasant" surprise upon finding out that Ukraine was experiencing disruptions to the systems. He said this has hobbled Ukraine's ability to defend itself.

Both Elon Musk and the White House say they are not responsible for the slowdown.

The EU's foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas told the press at the summit before the talks began: "Starlink is really necessary for Ukraine and unfortunately in [the] short term Europe can't replace this capability."

Prokopenko said that this was the reason "why Ukraine's most credible medium-term solution here is to continue relying on the US. And the EU is critical in this context in terms of backing Ukraine's requests for the US administration to keep those technologies on offer" for Kyiv.

Speaking to journalists at the summit, Zelenskyy said the speed of Starlink had still not been fully restored but had improved. He said Ukraine is cooperating with various countries, including France, to search for a partial solution.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Zelenskyy urged EU leaders Friday to keep backing Kyiv financially as well, asking for nearly $80 billion (€70 billion) more next year.

"This is a realistic amount and I ask you to find this support," Zelenskyy said. "It will help us hold Russia back."

The EU gave Kyiv an approximately $100 billion (€90 billion) loan last year, making the EU Ukraine's biggest international backer. But the Ukrainian government is saying it needs more.

"The war is becoming objectively more expensive, and the Ukrainian economy is increasingly affected by the Russian strikes, leading to a drastic decline in tax and customs revenues," Prokopenko said. "So the needs will continue growing."

So will Ukraine get what it needs? Closing the summit, President of the European Council Antonio Costa said that Ukraine "remains a priority" and asked the European Commission to come up with a proposal to pull together more funds for the country in 2027.

Essentially, it looks as though the EU will try to find a way to meet Ukraine's cash demands ― though it is not yet clear how.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen promised the EU will "continue to lead" but urged international partners to step up as well.

Zelenskyy will leave Brussels without concrete promises or numbers, but with renewed commitments for support from Europe.

The Ukrainian president concluded his press conference with an emotional statement: "We will keep living and fighting with dignity."

#983. Thousands protest Czech government’s public media overhaul after rushed vote

Sign up now: Get ST's newsletters delivered to your inbox

People attend a protest against government plans to change the funding system for public television and radio at the Old Town Square in Prague, Czech Republic, on Oct 25.

PRAGUE - Thousands protested in Prague on Oct 25 after government lawmakers gave initial backing to public media funding changes in a rare overnight vote despite criticism the overhaul will damage media independence.

The proposal’s first reading was unexpectedly brought to the lower house floor outside the planned order of proceedings on Oct 23.

Opponents and media advocacy groups have objected to fast-tracking the legislation, which will abolish household fees that currently fund Czech public television and radio stations.

The populist government of billionaire Prime Minister Andrej Babis, backed by the far-right SPD party, has frequently clashed with public and private media.

It wants to move funding for Czech Television and Czech Radio to the state budget, which critics say will leave broadcasters vulnerable to political pressure.

Babis says it is a matter of funding transparency and not an attack on independence.

Smaller protests first broke out on Oct 23 at the Bill’s unexpected introduction. Speaker Tomio Okamura of the SPD limited debate and scheduled a vote for 4.36am local time on Oct 24.

The Bill is now at the committee stage before a later vote.

A woman holds a placard reading 'We won't give up the media' during the protest at Old Town Square in Prague.

“Mr Babis ... Mr Okamura, nobody in this country believes that your intention was pure,” Mikulas Minar, a protest leader, said on Oct 25, criticising the overnight vote.

“(This protest) is a clear message to this government: you have really gone too far this time,” he told protesters who had filled Prague’s historic Old Town Square, amid chants of “Resignation” and “We’ve had enough”.

Czech Television is the country’s most-watched broadcaster across major age groups. Public media are among the most trusted news sources in the country, according to a 2025 Reuters Institute survey.

The proposal would cut funding for Czech Television and Czech Radio by about 15%, possibly as early as 2027.

Opposition parties have compared the funding changes with reforms in Hungary under former Prime Minister Viktor Orban, who oversaw a major expansion of pro-government media.

On Oct 23, the European Broadcasting Union, along with 15 other groups including other public broadcasters as well as Reporters Without Borders, called for more debate and the removal of any measures threatening the broadcasters’ financial sustainability.

President Petr Pavel also called for more expert scrutiny.

“The Czech Republic is among the few countries in central and eastern Europe where the system of public service and private media works very well,” he said on X on Oct 24. REUTERS

Luke Littler’s hopes of completing the set of major tournaments ended for another year as Ross Smith won the European Championship in Germany.

Littler is vying to become just the second player after Michael van Gerwen to win all major televised events and the tournament in Dortmund is the only missing piece.

And that remains the case as the 19-year-old was well below par in a shock quarter-final defeat to Krzysztof Ratajski in what is one of the worst results of his fledgling career.

He posted on Instagram: “Played well in the lead up to today, but just didn’t click for me earlier.

“Thank you for all the support this weekend. The wait for this one goes on.”

Smith was able to take advantage of Littler’s newfound vulnerability, with an 11-8 victory over home favourite Martin Schindler.

Littler seemed unbeatable when he won the World Matchplay in July with a record average to make it five major tournaments from five this year.

This time last month, Littler was going for a clean sweep of major titles in 2026 and he seemed untouchable, but he has lost his cloak of invincibility.

He lost in the quarter-finals of the World Series of Darts, the first round of the World Grand Prix and now exited in the last eight in Dortmund.

And that could give hope to the rest of the tour that Littler’s untouchable spell at the top events is over.

Littler’s attention will now turn to his Netflix show where he will take on 24 ‘amateur’ players in a one-off leg with a £501,000 prize on the line.

The show has attracted controversy this week after the line-up includes Fallon Sherrock, who has reached the third round of the World Championship, and World Darts Federation number one Mitchell Lawrie.

Smith claimed a second major title in six weeks by backing up his victory at the World Series of Darts Finals in September.

He was the top seed, based on his performances on the European Tour throughout the course of 2026, and lived up to the billing with a fine weekend of action.

The 37-year-old overcame Luke Woodhouse in the quarter-final before then seeing off Gerwyn Price in the last four.

He was then too strong for Schindler, earning a hard-fought victory in the final, silencing the partisan Westfalenhalle crowd with a second European Championship crown.

“It’s absolutely amazing, I was a bit sweaty going into the end with Martin, he wouldn’t let up,” Smith, who has gone up to number six in the world, said.

“To have this trophy in my hand and win another major, I am absolutely over the moon. Drained, but I’m buzzing.

“I don’t expect anything, I just play the game in front of me, every game I play. I don’t really know what to say.

“I am buzzing to have won another major.”

Still, it was quite the weekend for Schindler, who created history in Dortmund by becoming the first German to reach the final of a major event.

#990. Venezuela opposition leader Maria Corina Machado returns home after months in exile

Sign up now: Get ST's newsletters delivered to your inbox

Opposition leader Maria Corina Machado after returning to the country following nearly a year abroad, in Lara, Venezuela, on Oct 25.

CARACAS – Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado returned to Caracas in a surprise move that could pose the biggest test yet to acting President Delcy Rodriguez’s political opening and the Trump administration’s strategy for a post-Maduro Venezuela.

“I’m here, with you,” Machado posted on X on Oct 25, confirming her return after months abroad.

She gave no details on how she entered Venezuela, but her party shared photos and videos of her arriving at a church in Lara state, where emotional supporters embraced her and said “she will be the next president of Venezuela”.

Machado’s team earlier thanked US President Donald Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio for their support, signalling an effort to underscore her ties with Washington even as her return risks complicating the administration’s Venezuela strategy.

Trump, speaking to reporters as he left the White House, said he did not know about Machado’s return. Other US officials, including her long-time ally, Representative Maria Elvira Salazar of Florida, celebrated the move, with Salazar calling it “the beginning of a new chapter”.

Rubio said Machado’s return is the “direct result of the US-supported reconciliation talks”.

“The United States expects the freedoms of all sectors of Venezuelan politics to continue to be respected,” Rubio said on X.

“Likewise, we expect all political actors to support these talks which represent the best chance Venezuela has had in 30 years to peacefully achieve not just a free and fair election, but also an enduring democracy.”

The move confronts Rodriguez with a difficult choice over how much political space to give her most formidable rival.

Her government has allowed politicians, activists and journalists who spent years in exile to return, including some of Machado’s closest allies.

Allowing Machado to organise and campaign freely would mark the most consequential expansion yet of that opening.

Detaining her or restricting her activities, meanwhile, could put pressure on Washington to respond.

Machado’s ability to mobilise supporters “adds a new layer of complexity” for the interim government, said David Smilde, a sociology professor and Venezuela expert at Tulane University in New Orleans.

“The big absent voice so far this year has been the voice of the Venezuelan people,” Smilde said.

Machado’s return, he added, could spur greater public mobilisation and demands for a return to democracy.

An official from Venezuela’s Information Ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Signs of Machado’s impact quickly emerged. Her party called on supporters to gather in Caracas later on Oct 25 to welcome her as she made her way from western Venezuela towards the capital in a caravan escorted by motorcycles.

People gathered along the route, singing the national anthem, chanting and reaching out to touch Machado as she greeted them from the window of the sport utility vehicle carrying her.

In Caracas, supporters carrying Venezuelan flags gathered in Altamira, an area in the city’s east long associated with the opposition.

Some chanted “the leader has arrived”, while passing drivers honked their horns amid music and the blare of vuvuzelas.

Machado had a 61% positive rating in the latest AtlasIntel survey for Bloomberg News. The same poll showed her leading Rodriguez 52% to 19% in a hypothetical presidential election.

Washington has prioritised economic stability and rebuilding Venezuela’s oil industry alongside a gradual political transition, while relying on Rodriguez to maintain order and negotiate changes to the country’s political institutions.

The approach has culminated in a major energy agreement giving the US access to as much as 65 billion barrels of Venezuela’s crude reserves.

The political process has largely advanced without Machado. US-backed talks between Rodriguez’s government and a faction of the opposition ended their latest round this week with agreements to begin reviewing laws governing political disqualifications, political parties and public demonstrations, among other measures.

Opposition negotiator Dinorah Figuera also met Rodriguez at the Miraflores presidential palace following the talks, a striking image of engagement between the government and some of its political opponents even as Machado remained outside the process.

Figuera celebrated Machado’s return in a social post, saying the opposition will continue “without interruption in the conversation process until achieving a real and sustainable democracy in Venezuela”.

Machado had been signalling that her return was imminent. In a recent interview with the New York Times, she suggested she intended to mobilise Venezuelans ahead of eventual elections.

She has also criticised parts of Washington’s transition strategy, including the energy deal with businessman Alejandro Betancourt, potentially complicating an agreement that has become central to the administration’s plans for Venezuela.

The timing may also be significant. She has returned less than two weeks before US midterm elections that could shift control of Congress and subject the administration’s Venezuela policy to greater scrutiny.

Machado’s arrival follows fresh opposition protests in several Venezuelan cities demanding a presidential election date.

The authorities briefly detained at least seven people and blocked a route ahead of demonstrations in Caracas, testing the limits of the government’s political opening.

Machado went into hiding shortly after the disputed 2024 presidential election, saying she feared for her life as Nicolas Maduro’s government targeted opposition leaders.

She left Venezuela in late 2025 in a clandestine operation to collect her Nobel Peace Prize. BLOOMBERG

#991. An existential threat to THC drinks pits Willie Nelson against Mitch McConnell

The $1.5-billion hemp drink market pioneered by legendary stoners like Cheech & Chong and Willie Nelson is facing an existential crisis, unless lawmakers in Washington strike a deal overturning legislation poised to make the psychoactive-infused seltzers and sodas illegal in the coming weeks.

The beverages — a favorite of everyone from alcohol-averse Gen-Zers to boomers who sip THC-infused cocktails before bedtime — exploded in popularity, exploiting a loophole in an agriculture bill originally drafted by Sen. Mitch McConnell (R-Ky.) that legalized hemp for commercial purposes. The powerful lawmaker has since said that was a mistake that has left children at risk, and tucked a provision outlawing the beverages into subsequent legislation. But that’s put him at odds with other Republican lawmakers — and even potentially the White House — who worry that the new restrictions will hurt the hemp industry. They also know they’re risking the wrath of constituents used to grabbing THC and CBD products at breweries, restaurants and gas stations across the country.

Caught in the middle is a nascent but quickly growing industry that says that if lawmakers can’t strike some sort of deal before the Dec. 11 deadline, their companies will face an extinction-level event.

JuneShine Inc., which produces Willie’s Remedy, an assortment of “social tonics” featuring the country music icon, would consider shutting down the line if lawmakers fail to act, company co-founder Greg Serrao said in an interview. That’s despite the spirits, sodas and gummies being “wildly profitable,” projected to bring in roughly $200 million in sales this year — up from $30 million when the company launched last year.

Brandon Harshbarger, who runs a commercial holding company for the comedy duo Cheech Marin and Tommy Chong, says 80% of his company’s business is THC products, like their High & Dry Seltzers and High Teas. Sales would be cut in half without congressional intervention, he estimates, which is reported to be roughly $100 million annually.

“It’s just crazy that we’ve been living in this world where, in theory, something that has been so robust and so positive from our perspective as a business, and so well received by the broad public” could be shut down, Harshbarger said.

Ironically, it was McConnell who opened the door to the new industry, when he helped push a provision in the 2018 farm bill that legalized the cultivation of industrial hemp.

The idea was that the plant — which is the same species as marijuana, but harvested with lower levels of THC, the chemical responsible for users’ high — could be a boon for farmers in his home state of Kentucky. Hemp grows fast and produces durable fibers that can make rope, cloth and paper that is longer-lasting.

But the law included a significant omission. While it defined hemp as having less than 0.3% of a certain type of THC, called delta-9, producers found that beverages could fly under that threshold and still get consumers high. They also extracted other, milder types of THC, as well as CBD, a non-intoxicating compound that some people believe can help with sleep or anxiety issues. Clinical evidence remains limited.

In the ensuing years, entrepreneurs seized on the new rule to create high-inducing, sometimes high-potency drinks, edibles and smokable flower available in grocery, liquor and convenience stores. Beyond greater retail access, hemp’s legal status allows companies to advertise, operate across state lines, ship directly to customers and be taxed like normal corporations — none of which is available to cannabis operators.

While some states moved independently to impose restrictions, the industry flourished. But McConnell, realizing his error, tucked language limiting the overall THC content of hemp products into a fiscal year 2026 appropriations bill over the objections of his more libertarian fellow Kentuckian, Rand Paul, who warned it would destroy the hemp industry. The law also said synthetic cannabinoids no longer qualify as hemp.

President Trump signed the bill into law, but has subsequently posted to social media that Congress should pass legislation “to ensure that Americans can continue to access the full-spectrum CBD products they have come to rely on, and that help them, while preserving Congress’s intent to restrict the sale of products that pose Health risks.”

McConnell said his legislation would preserve the industrial hemp uses he originally envisioned while protecting kids from intoxicating hemp products. And a spokesperson for his office said the Kentucky lawmaker remains firmly opposed to an extended delay, which he believes would continue to expose children to unregulated, intoxicating hemp-derived THC products that are packaged similarly to well-known candy and snacks. “Children end up being the unknowingly consumers of these poisonous products and being sent to the hospital at an alarming rate,” McConnell said in a speech last November.

Closing the federal loophole would not restrict sales of marijuana in states like California and New York, which have legalized recreational sales of the drug.

The industry won a temporary reprieve with a massive lobbying effort — aided by the convenience store lobby, which doesn’t want to lose a lucrative business — that pushed new restrictions back from Nov. 12 to Dec. 11. But that doesn’t leave much time for a deal to be struck.

Sens. Amy Klobuchar, a Minnesota Democrat, and Tim Sheehy, a Montana Republican, are drafting a bill that would provide the industry a bridge until full regulation is implemented. It would limit sale of THC products to those over 21 years old but also raise the amount of the psychoactive compound permitted in harvested plants.

A White House spokesperson, asked if the president supported the draft legislation, pointed to his original social media post but did not weigh in further. But there is still an array of groups seeking to remove the products from shelves, including competitors for sales of intoxicating products like cannabis and alcohol interests, who typically face tougher regulations.

“The hemp industry’s business model was a loophole, and loopholes close,” said Kevin Sabet, who leads Smart Approaches to Marijuana, a political organization that opposes marijuana legalization and sales. “That should be a warning to any industry betting its future on profiting from addiction at the expense of kids and vulnerable people. Our advice to these companies is simple: spend less time lobbying for another delay and more time planning for life after Dec. 11.”

Other detractors point to the proliferation of synthetic hemp-derived products that appeal to children and often carry high THC content. The Senate only narrowly approved the one-month reprieve, and actual legislation is likely to face stiff opposition from lawmakers like Sen. Ted Budd (R-N.C.), who has said the hemp beverages lure in children at gas stations.

Hemp proponents say a proper regulatory framework will eliminate the majority of those products.

“The good operators want regulation,” Cheech & Chong’s Harshbarger said, adding that is the best way to protect consumer safety.

Getting it right could prove important for politicians, who face constituents both concerned about safety — and protective of a favorite way to unwind.

Over 58% of THC drink users are 45 years old or more, according to one survey conducted by beverage brand Crescent Canna. More than half of respondents said the drinks help them unwind or get to sleep, while three out of four report having decreased or eliminated alcohol consumption outright because of canned cannabis. Elder voters historically are far more likely to vote, which means the elimination of a favorite beverage could cause political headaches.

Absent regulatory clarity, the infrastructure around hemp has already begun to contract.

Before the proposed ban passing last year, FundCanna, which offers credit in the often opaque world of cannabis financing, had a loan book comprising 15% of hemp. In the ensuing months the financier has dialed back its exposure to around 1%, according to Chief Executive Officer Adam Stettner.

“Just from a standpoint of assessing risk, we began reducing our exposure by declining repeat business and not taking on new clients,” following the original hemp definition change last November, Stettner said in an interview. “I don’t want to be bridge financing where the bridge doesn’t lead to a place that you can identify and so we were in a position where we had to say no,” he added.

Edibles.com, an e-commerce platform and subsidiary of Edible Arrangements International Inc. that began selling THC products last year, was informed by one supplier three months ago that the latest shipment would be its last as they wind down their hemp business, the company’s president, Thomas Winstanley, said in an interview.

“We haven’t run into supply restrictions yet, but we know that they are coming and we are starting to have those conversations,” Winstanley said. “It’s really hard to build a brand new business, it’s really hard to build one in a very restrictive category and it’s even harder to do so when the government can’t figure out how to deal with your business and you might have an extinction threat,” he said.

Crescent Canna has already moved to lay off its entire sales force of 19 people in June, Chief Executive Officer Joe Gerrity said in an interview. Last year, the company sold more than 9.5 million cans, according to Gerrity.

“Our sales team is around the country and their goal is to grow accounts, to add more accounts, and at a certain point you can’t invest in the future of this industry right now,” Gerrity said in an interview.

Crescent Canna’s distributors have been making fewer, smaller orders. One important partner in Louisiana has already informed the company that its most recent purchase will likely be the last substantial one they make until they get clarity from Washington.

Some companies are launching promotions to move the product ahead of the December deadline. On Oct. 1, THC-infused beverage brand Wynk sent out an email to customers with the subject line “Last Call Coming for Wynk Nationwide.” Similarly, Pamos has been offering customers buy one, get 80% off promotions. Cheech & Chong launched a buy now, pay later option closer to the ban date so consumers can stock up with larger purchases.

“We’re fond in our country to say ‘existential threats’ — that’s this for hemp companies,” Terry Mendez, chief executive officer of SHF Holdings Inc., said in an interview.

#994. Hijab ban at schools in Azerbaijan: What's behind the rare wave of protests?

Girls wearing headscarves have been turned away from schools in Azerbaijan, triggering unusual protests involving children. The government rules do not mention hijabs. Why are schools enforcing unwritten rules?

A dispute over Islamic headscarves in Azerbaijani schools has triggered protests at home and an unusual exchange of criticism between politicians in Azerbaijan and Turkey, two countries whose leaders routinely describe their relationship as that of "one nation, two states". The row has raised questions about religious freedom, sovereignty and the limits of Turkish and Iranian influence in the south Caucasian country.

The unprecedented protests have been taking place across Azerbaijan for a nearly week. Children have demonstrated against the headscarf ban introduced at schools. Among those rallying outside of schools are girls who wear Islamic headscarves; others, including boys, have joined classmates in solidarity.

Rallies in general are rare in a country where police routinely disperse any public protests. But demonstrations involving children are unprecedented in Azerbaijan. As the videos showing the protests started spreading on social media, access to Instagram and TikTok was disrupted in the country, indicating how seriously the authorities are taking the issue. Internet monitors documented blocks; the authorities have not explained their cause.

The dispute follows a series of legal changes. On July 7, Azerbaijan amended its general education law, reinforcing the principle of secular education and requiring pupils and teachers to comply with dress codes. On September 21, the government adopted Resolution No. 309, tightening school uniform rules.

The resolution prohibits additional clothing that disrupts the standard uniform or conflicts with secular education. It does not explicitly mention the hijab ― a Muslim headscarf covering the hair and neck ― or instruct schools to exclude pupils wearing one. But some school administrators have interpreted the rule as applying to hijabs and turned girls covering their heads away. The regulation gives each school's pedagogical council responsibility for resolving compliance issues.

A separate decision on October 6 set dress requirements for teachers. Reports followed of women wearing headscarves being prevented from teaching.

Azerbaijan is a predominantly Muslim country, but Article 18 of its constitution separates religion from the state and requires state education to be secular. Articles 42 and 48 protect the right to education and freedom of conscience.

Supporters of the schools' actions say the same dress rules should apply to all pupils. Critics argue that excluding girls because of religious clothing violates their rights. The dispute cuts across conventional political divisions: some government critics support the restrictions, while some non-religious Azerbaijanis oppose them. School headscarf restrictions also prompted protests in 2010 and subsequent years.

A Baku literature teacher with 40 years of experience, said that girls wearing headscarves were not admitted to classes at the teacher's school. Some removed their scarves; others went home or wanted to study at home. The teacher, who didn't want to be identified by name and provided only the initials M.C., supported enforcing the uniform rules, arguing that children were too young to make decisions about religious dress.

A parent identified as D.A. told DW this was not a nationwide hijab ban, but a matter of school uniforms. Another parent who opposed the restrictions withdrew an interview before publication.

Facebook user Sarraf Cabbarov from Baku posted on his social media account that his daughter Sevil, a primary school teacher in Azerbaijan's capital, was dismissed for refusing to remove her headscarf. He also published a school order issuing her a written warning under the new dress regulations.

On October 12, the Interior Ministry said 37 people had been detained in connection with the protests. According to the ministry's statement, the group had confronted school staff, damaged property and attempted to obstruct school activities and traffic. A criminal case was opened under Article 233, concerning disruption of public order. The ministry did not identify those detained or say whether they included children.

Artist and activist Ilkin Huseynov went missing after launching a project linking volunteer tutors with pupils affected by the restrictions. Local media later reported, citing people close to him, that he had been given 30 days of administrative detention for allegedly disobeying police orders.

Some observers linked the introduction of the new rules for school uniform to the attempts by the Azerbaijani government to counter the influence of neighboring Iran and the growing strength of religious groups within the country. This interpretation is, in essence, echoed by government officials as well, although they stop short of explicitly naming Iran.

Fazil Mustafa, who chairs the Committee for Public Associations and Religious Institutions at Azerbaijan's parliament, said the authorities were concerned about religious groups influenced from abroad and defended the school rules. Allahshukur Pashazade, head of the Caucasus Muslims Office, also warned of outside interference but called for a peaceful solution. The alleged foreign involvement has not been independently established.

Amnesty International condemned the exclusion of girls wearing hijabs and called for the release of anyone detained solely for protesting peacefully.

The controversy has also drawn criticism in Turkey, Azerbaijan's close ally. Protesters gathered outside Azerbaijan's consulate in Istanbul on October 3. Oktay Saral, an adviser to Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, criticized the restrictions,saying it's unacceptable to deny education to students wearing headscarves. Azerbaijan's ruling New Azerbaijan Party replied that close relations did not justify interference in its internal affairs.

For affected families, the immediate question remains whether children can attend school without removing their headscarves.

#996. A new state on the way? More Illinois counties could vote to leave Chicago behind

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

More than 30 counties have already approved the non-binding measure to leave Illinois

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Momentum is building in Illinois to form a new state, with more counties ready to vote on leaving because of Chicago’s influence.

Eleven counties are set to vote on non-binding referenda this year to secede from Cook County. If all 11 vote to leave they would join 33 counties that have already approved similar measures.

Cook County is home to Chicago, but people in the state and nation have criticized it for its crime rate, cost of living, Democratic leadership and oversized influence on state politics.

Loret Newlin, director of Illinois Separation, said Illinois leadership does not take concerns from other parts of the state into consideration.

“This is our lived experience. We are ignored. We are not taken into consideration when they’re making a lot of the laws that hurt us,” she told NBC Chicago.

Iroquois County, just 70 miles south of Cook County, is one of 33 counties that have voted to leave the state. About 73 percent of its voters backed the non-binding proposal.

The state’s 8th most populous county, Madison County, also joined the movement.

“Having Madison and Iroquois on the map, we are no longer rural only and we are not southern only,” Newlin told NBC Chicago. “Now with adding several counties on the western side, that’s equally far north as Iroquois, that’s shoring up that we’re not just for southern Illinois anymore.”

Madison County approved the vote in 2024 and one of the organizers said it’s more than just a symbolic measure.

“I think this movement has a lot more teeth to it than the governor has given it credit for. He's kind of pooh-poohing us and not taking us very seriously,” Dave Stopher, who helped get the measure before voters in Madison County said to NPR. “We're hoping that this sends a very distinct and clear message to Springfield and to Cook County.”

Newlin said the votes are the first step to creating a new state. The group’s plan is based on Article IV of the U.S. Constitution, which was used to create West Virginia during the Civil War.

The state’s General Assembly would have to approve the counties leaving the state, then the U.S. Congress would need to approve the new state.

Gov. JB Pritzker has previously referred to the movement as a “stunt.”

If the 11 counties approve the measure this year, it would bring the total to 44 of the state’s 102 counties that want to leave. Newlin said other counties have also asked her about getting the measure to their voters.
