#1071. Alarming fraud trend puts small-town mosque with industry and foreign govt ties in focus: ‘Our motherland now’

Fox News Digital spoke to Ohio Republican state Rep. Michelle Teska about the need for her legislation cracking down on non-English speaking truck drivers.

This article is Part 2 of a Fox News Digital exclusive series investigating trucking fraud, public safety, and assimilation concerns in southwest Ohio. You can read Part 1 here.

MAINEVILLE, OHIO — A mosque rising amid rural homes and farmland in southwest Ohio has become a focal point in the community’s growing concerns over an influx of foreign-owned trucking companies and trucking fraud, with a Fox News Digital review revealing significant financial ties between the mosque, trucking companies and the government of Uzbekistan.

Roughly one mile north of the main intersection in Maineville, a small Warren County village with about 1,400 residents, sits the Islamic Center of Maineville, which has been under construction for the past four years following its approval by Hamilton Township in April 2022.

Fox News Digital found that the mosque received substantial donations from trucking companies that government records show were cited for serious safety and compliance violations, while the mosque’s own Telegram channel displayed associations with people identified as current or former Uzbek officials.

For years, the Islamic Center of Maineville has posted on Telegram to its 3,600 members, courting donations, acknowledging partnerships with trucking companies, and even sharing screenshots of donations from local trucking companies, owned by Uzbeks, totaling hundreds of thousands of dollars.

HOW AN UZBEK TRUCK DRIVER’S FATAL CRASH EXPOSED TROUBLING FRAUD TREND IN MIDDLE AMERICA: ‘CHAMELEON CARRIERS’

A mosque rising amid rural homes and farmland in southwest Ohio has become a focal point of community concerns over an influx of foreign-owned trucking companies after a Fox News Digital review found significant financial ties to the industry and the government of Uzbekistan. (Fox News Digital)

Buraq Limited, a Springboro trucking company associated with Rukhshona Sultonova, donated at least $28,000 to the Islamic Center across 28 gifts, according to Telegram screenshots reviewed by Fox News Digital.

A review of the company’s records found dozens of reported violations, including multiple English-proficiency violations, four ELD (electronic logging device) violations, three invalid-CDL violations, four expired medical cards and four hours-of-service violations.

Premier Trucking Group Inc., owned by Sam Avazov, has received over 100 total violations, including for unsafe driving and invalid CDLs. In September, the Islamic Center posted a screenshot of a $1,000 donation from Premier Trucking Group, which has donated at least $25,000 to the mosque.

OUT OF CONTROL, UNQUALIFIED ILLEGAL ALIEN TRUCKERS ENDANGERING KIDS ON US ROADS, INSIDER WARNS: ‘JUST MADNESS’

The Islamic Center of Maineville currently being constructed in southwest Ohio. (Fox News Digital)

Foko Logistics LLC, owned by Abubakr Olimov and based in Hilliard, donated $20,000 in a single gift to the mosque, and had 52 violations across 37 inspections in FMCSA’s current 24-month record. The company had vehicle-maintenance violations involving damaged brake hoses, an inoperable tractor-protection valve and severely underinflated tires. Ten of its 24 vehicle inspections resulted in an out-of-service designation, a rate of 41.7%.

Maca Transportation and Services LLC, based in Dayton and owned by Muminkhuja Kholkhujaev, donated at least $7,000 across eight gifts. FMCSA’s records show 120 violations across 72 inspections, including an English-proficiency failure and multiple false or incomplete hours-of-service records. The company also had serious brake, tire, and other vehicle-maintenance violations, with 14 of 36 vehicle inspections resulting in an out-of-service designation, or 38.9%.

One trucking company that gave $150,000 to the mosque and helped organize the overall fundraising effort , Phoenix Cargo, told Fox News Digital the mosque approached the company multiple times asking for donations but said the $150,000 figure the company ultimately donated "represents only a fraction of the mosque's total construction budget" and that "Phoenix Cargo is not even among the project's top 100 donors."

Phoenix Cargo has been cited hundreds of times for safety violations, including English proficiency, ELD tampering, and unsafe driving violations.

Fox News Digital reached out to the mosque for comment but did not receive a response. Earlier this month, the Islamic Center said it is "committed to operating responsibly and in accordance with applicable law."

"The fundraising for the Islamic Center concerns me because a large percentage of the Uzbek truck companies that donate have been repeatedly cited for the same kinds of serious inspection violations," Nodawolf, an online researcher who lives in the area and has been documenting alleged trucking fraud in southwest Ohio for months and was granted anonymity due to death threats he's received, said. "Those violations suggest a pattern of non-compliance with our laws and regulations among the donors, which is troubling given the community’s concentration in the freight industry in Maineville."

Fox News Digital also asked the mosque if an administrator for their Telegram channel with the name "Bek A" is Bekhzod Asrarov, an Uzbek truck driver living in Maineville who authorities say struck and killed 21-year-old Ohio soccer player Tobias "Toby" Forsythe earlier this year. Asrarov was unable to communicate effectively in English at the scene, according to authorities, and has been accused of removing and concealing his dashcam after the crash.

ICE LAUNCHES CDL FRAUD TIPLINE AS DHS HIGHLIGHTS DEADLY CRASHES INVOLVING ILLEGAL IMMIGRANTS

The death of college soccer player Tobias "Toby" Forsythe, who was allegedly struck and killed by truck driver Bekhzod Asrarov (pictured) in Ohio, has fueled debate over commercial trucking safety. (Madison County Sheriff's Office ; Kevin Carter/Getty Images)

The Islamic Center’s website says it does "not solicit donations from any foreign government, organization, association, partnership or individual or any agent thereof" and that "any such attempt" should be reported to the mosque immediately. However, the organization's Telegram account suggests close ties with the government of Uzbekistan, specifically when it comes to trucking companies.

Hamkor Uz Cincinnati Association is a nonprofit organization established in 2020 to unite Uzbeks in the Cincinnati area and support community projects, including the construction of religious and cultural centers. Hamilton Township records identify Hamkor as the owner of the roughly 6.7-acre property where the Islamic Center of Maineville is being built.

Telegram screenshots reviewed by Fox News Digital show the organization’s ties to former Uzbek government officials. One image shows the Mason office of Erkinbay Abdulla, with an accompanying message describing him as a former Uzbek official who "creates the trucking companies."

Another screenshot contains a community statement attributed to Sukhrob Norbekov, whom an accompanying message identifies as another former Uzbek official who represents the mosque. The material places officials linked to Uzbekistan alongside an organization involved in the mosque project and individuals involved in creating local trucking companies.

Current Uzbek officials also appear to be involved with the mosque and local trucking industry via the central Asian nation’s Ministry of Digital Technologies, according to photos posted on the mosque’s Telegram.

The screenshots show a list of a six-member Uzbek delegation that traveled to the United States in April 2025, including Ambassador Furqat Sidiqov, regional government officials, and three officials from the Ministry of Digital Technologies. Separate posts invite entrepreneurs and truck-company managers to an April 19 IT conference hosted by Hamkor Uz Cincinnati at a banquet hall in Loveland, Ohio.

TRUMP ADMIN INVESTIGATING 75 TRUCK DRIVER SCHOOLS FOR FRAUD, HELPING NON-CITIZENS GET LICENSES

A sign outside the Islamic Center of Maineville which is currently being constructed. (Fox News Digital)

Additionally, a review of the Hamkor Uz Telegram channel, with current and former Uzbek government officials as administrators, showed advertisements for local trucking companies, removable truck signs, English courses for truck driving school, and legal counseling. Other posts include the owner of the mosque providing guidance on how to understand "Shariah compliant banking" and a post on "speaking English with the police" and how to "learn on the road."

Nodawolf said the ties to the government of Uzbekistan are troubling to him "because these Uzbek trucking companies appear to be tightly organized, with patterns that look almost like a shared blueprint."

"Given the documented safety and compliance problems in many of these companies, it’s reasonable to ask whether gaps in U.S. regulations are being systematically exploited," he added.

Several locals who spoke to Fox News Digital said they have expressed their concerns about the rise in Uzbek trucking companies and potential safety gaps that could come along with it to their elected officials but have largely been ignored.

"They're scared, I think they recognize that they could be called names, they can recognize they could be called out for, you know, like, Islamophobic or racist or things, but it's not that at all," a resident from nearby Middletown, Ohio, which has also experienced an influx of foreign-owned trucking companies, who posts information about trucking companies online under the name GHOSTOPSUZ, told Fox News Digital.

One lawmaker who has taken action against trucking fraud is Ohio Republican state Rep. Michelle Teska, who represents most of Warren County, including Maineville, and has introduced legislation to strengthen commercial-driver licensing requirements, including a measure requiring driver examinations to be administered in English, which she told Fox News Digital addresses the "low-hanging fruit of the problem."

"I did some research and basically found out that you can get your driver's license and your CDL license in the state of Ohio and you can have that test in 10 different languages," Teska said. "So that, to me, common sense says that's insanity."

Teska says she has seen the problem "firsthand" while driving around her district, calling it "rampant."

"This past weekend, I was at an event in Warren County and I was at an event that is right across the street from the BMV and I was just kind of observing a gentleman pulling in a semi truck cab into the parking lot on a Saturday at the BMV taking up four spaces, clearly had no idea how to drive the truck," Teska explained. "So I walked over to the BMV and spoke to this person and kind of confronted him and said, hey, do you speak English? He replied, no, I don't speak English. Asked him where he was from. He was from Uzbekistan. So it was crazy because I was watching it all take place live."

Authorities in Warren County have been ramping up their presence in the trucking industry and on the roads in recent weeks, including a crackdown over the last week.

"The Hamilton Township Police Department actively monitors traffic safety concerns within our jurisdiction and works with our public safety partners to address violations and unsafe driving behaviors when identified," a spokesperson for Hamilton Township said. "In fact, our officers recently participated in a targeted traffic enforcement initiative focused on commercial motor vehicles, working alongside partner agencies to identify safety violations and improve roadway safety. We will continue to enforce applicable laws and take appropriate action when circumstances warrant."

Warren County Prosecutor David Fornshell stressed there is nothing inherently wrong with mosque fundraising and he has not received any information that any laws have been broken. He told Fox News Digital, however, that clearly "there’s something going on" within the Uzbek community in southwest Ohio that "warrants at least awareness on the part of law enforcement."

"It's disproportionate to what we see with any other immigrant community," Fornshell said.

Since 2021, Fornshell said the area has seen an "influx of cases involving Uzbeks" that has prompted the need to hire more court interpreters and city employees who speak the language, particularly in the lower courts that deal with traffic offenses.

"I would say hardly a week goes by where we don't have some felony case involving an Uzbek, it's pretty frequent at this point," Fornshell said.

Census data from 2024 shows that roughly 1,500 people born in Uzbekistan live in Greater Cincinnati, while about 3,800 Uzbekistan-born residents live across Ohio. Uzbek community leaders say the actual population is significantly higher, estimating that roughly 4,000 Uzbek families live in southern Ohio, including U.S.-born children.

"This is our motherland now, from now on," Hamkor Uz board member Nodirjon Ernazarov told the Cincinnati Enquirer through a translator last week in a story highlighting the Uzbek population’s efforts to become part of the community. The article explains that the influx of Uzbeks was driven, in part, by the area’s proximity to the trucking industry.

"Uzbek people are very hardworking people," Ernazarov added. "So this mosque is (being built) by the help of all Uzbeks."

The article does not mention that Ernazarov also owns a trucking company, Ray Cargo Corp., which has donated tens of thousands of dollars to the mosque and has been cited for numerous safety violations, including unsafe driving and driver fitness.

Fox News Digital reached out to every trucking company mentioned in the article for comment.

#1074. Thousands of German gamblers could sue for their money back

German gamblers may finally be able to beat the house, thanks to new court rulings in the EU and in Germany. The decisions could help gambling addicts — but the legal road might be difficult.

A German court has followed the European Court of Justice in finding that gamblers can seek compensation from gambling companies if they lost money when online casinos and fruit machines were illegal in Germany.

The verdicts could have major consequences for gambling addicts, as thousands of people could potentially bring civil lawsuits against gambling companies.

A series of court decisions at regional, federal, and European level have found in favor of gamblers in the last year, beginning with the Higher Regional Court Stuttgart in September 2025, which agreed with a plaintiff in the state of Baden-Württemberg who sued the Malta-based online betting company Tipico Games.

The plaintiff lost around €10,000 ($11,200) between 2020 and 2022, but because online gambling was prohibited in Germany until 2021, the court found that operators had therefore received the winnings without legal basis and must return them.

Tipico Games then appealed to the Federal Court of Justice (BGH), the highest civil and criminal court in Germany. In an initial verbal hearing in mid-September this year, the court followed the principle of the plaintiffs' case on one key point: That gamblers have the right to claim back losses if the companies did not have a license in Germany at the time the losses were incurred. But a final decision on the case is only expected to be made in January 2027.

Online casinos and fruit machines were banned in Germany from 2008 to 2021, but several gambling operators were active in the country because they had gaming licenses in other EU countries.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In April this year, the European Court of Justice ruled that EU law does not preclude a member state from "prohibiting certain services," or from "attaching civil-law consequences to that prohibition." In other words, even if a gambling company has a legitimate license in one member state, that doesn't override national gambling laws elsewhere.

Thomas Dünchheim, a business lawyer at global law firm Greenberg Traurig who specializes in gambling law, said law firms were now gathering clients — sometimes trawling the internet with the help of AI tools — to prepare massive collective lawsuits. Dünchheim himself has people who have lost tens of thousands of euros come to him seeking representation.

"The pendulum is swinging more and more towards the consumer. It's a bit like in America — we're seeing a mass phenomenon like the Dieselgate lawsuits against VW," he told DW. "And there are lawyers who will collect all these little cases, bundle them, and then maybe even drive it forward with the help of a legal financing firm. It's a good business for all involved, and the ones that will have to pay are the gambling firms who operated unlawful gambling in Germany."

The decisions could bring a measure of help for addicts, as online gambling can be particularly dangerous for people with addiction issues. According to Tobias Hayer, a psychologist at the Institute for Public Health and Nursing Research at Bremen University, that comes down to four main features of online gambling: Anonymity and the consequent lack of social control, 24/7 accessibility, the frictionless nature of cashless transactions, and the high frequency of games played.

"These court verdicts are not surprising at all," Hayer told DW, but he added that he had an ambivalent attitude to them. "On the one hand I can imagine that this will be a huge relief to many gamblers who had an addiction problem. On the other hand, if these people suddenly get a lot of money in their hands, but they haven't worked through their problems, then of course there's a danger of recidivism."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

But Dünchheim suggested that the gamblers may not have such an easy ride when making their claims. It's true that German law has now concluded that if the gambling contract that the player makes with the company turns out to be unlawful in the country where they live, the player can claim their losses back. But only if the player themselves "did not act illegally," as Dünchheim put it.

"You also have to say: Many of these players deliberately went to games in this gray zone because the winnings are potentially bigger," he said. "Because the companies don't pay taxes."

"Then the defense team of the gambling company will of course say: 'You took part in an illegal game yourself, so you were acting illegally.' And this question of interpretation is not simple," he added. "It's a very interesting intellectual question, but it's also existential for the gambling companies."

The Tipico case is perhaps particularly interesting in the German context because, although the company is based in Malta, it was founded in 2004 by a group of German lawyers. The company is a big employer, with several thousand employees worldwide, and has been a sponsor of more than one top German football club. Tipico has also said that it has rigorous consumer protection measures in place to identify and prevent dangerous betting behavior.

But there was some legal ambiguity about its online operations in Germany up until 2021.

"They always had lawyers who could attest that what they are doing conforms to European law, because it is permitted in a European Union member state," said Dünchheim. "But that is a false assumption, as it has now been established that a gambling permit in another EU state doesn't apply in Germany, because unlike other areas, gambling law isn't harmonized across the bloc."

"Tipico was started by two businessmen and grew big in a gray zone," as Dünchheim put it. "They had professional lobbying firms on board and they hired experienced lawyers, they had private equity firms on board. But of course they are carrying a huge financial risk."

#1078. Conventional wisdom whiffed on Freddy Peralta, and the World Series proves it

This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here.

See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred

In retrospect, conventional wisdom might not be all that wise. Just check out this postseason.

The Atlanta Braves should have started Chris Sale in Game 2 of the division series against the Dodgers. They didn’t. They won.

The Braves then had an edge with Sale starting Game 3. They didn’t. They lost that game, and they were eliminated in the next game.

The Milwaukee Brewers should have considered trading rookie pitcher Logan Henderson in a package for Tarik Skubal, a win-now proposition for a team that has dominated the regular season but had not appeared in the World Series in 44 years. They didn’t. Skubal and the Dodgers missed the World Series, and Henderson started Game 2 for the Brewers on Saturday, helping them move within two victories from their first championship.

That brings us to Freddy Peralta, who starts Game 3 for the Tampa Bay Rays on Monday. Peralta was one of the top pitchers in the majors for the Brewers last year, and he has been one of the top pitchers in the majors since the Rays acquired him from the New York Mets three months ago, but in between he performed so poorly for the Mets that he cannot really explain why.

“Sometimes I ask the same question myself,” Peralta said.

A small-market World Series matchup is not easing tensions between MLB team owners and the players’ union on the issue of the salary cap.

So poorly that, when the league’s website ranked the most impactful trades at the deadline, the Peralta deal did not make the top 10, behind trades for six other starting pitchers: Skubal, Casey Mize and Robbie Ray to the San Diego Padres, Kevin Gausman and Clay Holmes to the Chicago Cubs, and Jose Soriano to the Toronto Blue Jays.

For the Mets, Peralta put up a 4.99 ERA and a negative WAR. For the Rays, he put up an 0.79 ERA in his last six starts of the regular season and a 1.07 ERA so far in the postseason, honored as American League Championship Series MVP.

“I feel like he’s kind of come back to being Freddy Peralta with us,” Rays manager Kevin Cash said.

Peralta went 17-6 with a 2.70 earned-run average for Milwaukee last year, leading the National League in victories and posting 5.5 WAR, third behind Cristopher Sanchez of the Philadelphia Phillies and Cy Young winner Paul Skenes of the Pittsburgh Pirates.

If you wonder why the Brewers would trade Peralta, well, you don’t know the Brewers.

Peralta was approaching free agency, and the Brewers routinely trade All-Star pitchers like that for prospects: Corbin Burnes, Josh Hader, Devin Williams.

This is how the Brewers restock: The Burnes trade brought two pieces of this World Series team, pitcher DL Hall and infielder Joey Ortiz. The Hader trade brought Game 3 starter Robert Gasser and journeyman outfielder Estuery Ruiz, and within a subsequent three-team trade, the Brewers swiped All-Star catcher William Contreras for Ruiz.

The Mets wanted Peralta for what they considered an inevitable playoff run, with the largest Opening Day payroll of any major league team, the Dodgers included. The Mets finished in last place, and Peralta’s ERA exceeded 6.00 in each of the two months preceding the trade deadline.

“I was feeling bad,” Peralta said, “because I couldn’t do anything.”

The adjustments the Mets asked him to make, he said, were “a little different” than the ones that reversed the course of his season with the Rays.

Brewers World Series pitcher Logan Henderson grew up cheering for the Astros, but he reluctantly concedes their cheating scandal alters the 2017 title.

The Rays let him pitch from the stretch, as he had in Milwaukee. They modified his delivery, including having him start it from the third-base side of the pitching rubber. His fastball got faster: 94 mph with the Mets, hitting 97 mph in the playoffs.

“We see that he’s in his element, man,” Brewers manager Pat Murphy said. “That’s Fastball Freddy.”

In Milwaukee, it’s all love for Peralta. The fans even cheered his bullpen session there before Game 1.

He’ll start Game 3 in Tampa Bay and, after that, who knows, but he would be lined up to start a potential Game 7 in Milwaukee.

“I know how special it is to pitch on this mound here in Milwaukee,” Peralta said. “I would like to pitch here during the postseason.”

He would have liked to pitch in New York during the postseason too.

“They had a lot of big expectations for me, the fans too, in New York,” he said. “They were waiting for something great from me.”

Conventional wisdom can boomerang. The conventional wisdom on Peralta’s free agency in the spring: he should make more in free agency than any pitcher besides Skubal; in the summer: this is a bad year to take into free agency; in the fall: he should make more in free agency than any pitcher besides Skubal.

But, given what happened in New York, what were the realistic expectations in Tampa Bay?

“I was able to go to a new team that probably needed me for …” Peralta said, his voice trailing off.

“Crazy,” he said. “For the World Series, yeah.”

#1086. Netanyahu rebuked for plan to use crypto to bypass economic sanctions

Sign up now: Get ST's newsletters delivered to your inbox

FILE PHOTO: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu speaks at the JNS (Jerusalem News Syndicate) International Policy Summit in Jerusalem, June 21, 2026. REUTERS/Ronen Zvulun/File Photo

JERUSALEM, Oct 25 - Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who faces re-election this week, is drawing criticism from economists and political rivals after suggesting Israel could use cryptocurrency to help shield its economy from potential international sanctions.

In an interview with Israel's Channel 10 on Friday, Netanyahu said he was preparing for a scenario in which broader sanctions were imposed on Israel.

Last month, Britain, France and Canada said they would block imports from Israeli settlements in the West Bank in what was the latest in a series of actions targeting Israel's settlement policy, underscoring its growing diplomatic isolation among some of its traditional allies.

"There could be sanctions, and sanctions on banks so you need to set up a bypass economy," Netanyahu said. "You know, there are currencies that can bypass (sanctions). We are also working on that."

Asked whether he was referring to cryptocurrency, Netanyahu replied: "Very true, very true," adding that blockchain technology was another possibility.

The comments drew a rare rebuke by the Bank of Israel, which said crypto currencies cannot serve as a route to bypass sanctions and that political leaders should focus on policy that would render such measures unnecessary.

"The right course for Israel's economy is to preserve our economic relations with our main trading partners, and to focus on preventing sanctions and their negative impact on the economy," it said.

Netanyahu on Sunday continued to defend his record, urging voters to back him and saying he and US President Donald Trump had two years left to work together to topple Iran's rulers.

On Sunday, more than 100 economists, including former Bank of Israel officials, ex-central bank governor Jacob Frenkel and several Nobel laureates, signed a letter expressing alarm over Netanyahu's proposal. They said it would lead to higher unemployment, a fall in foreign investment and the collapse of Israel's economic standing in the world.

"As we have seen in countries that have suffered similar sanctions, such as South Africa, Iran, and Russia, the living standards of Israeli citizens would plummet dramatically, and the state's ability to finance its security and defend itself against its enemies would be severely damaged," the letter read.

"Netanyahu is knowingly leading the State of Israel toward boycott and international economic isolation, and all he has to offer the Israeli economy is a puzzling solution, one accepted in criminal organizations, that will not help in the slightest."

Netanyahu's main rival in Tuesday's election, Gadi Eisenkot, called the crypto plan "madness" and said he feared that the "BibiCoin policy" would drive companies abroad and undermine national security.

Opposition leader Yair Lapid said: "Netanyahu has gone off the rails ... He promises the citizens of Israel before these elections that they'll be standing in line for an hour and a half for bread, like in Russia and Iran."

Opinion polls point to a potential stalemate in the election with neither Netanyahu's ruling coalition nor an opposition alliance securing a governing majority in parliament. REUTERS

#1087. Germany news: Train station alcohol ban comes into force

Consuming alcohol is no longer permitted at train stations in Germany, to improve the lot of travelers and staff alike. Coalition talks are restarting in Berlin, and an inmate is loose in Essen.

Below, you can read our roundup of headlines across Germany from Thursday, October 15.

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click hereto add DW as a Preferred Source on Google

Lawmakers from Germany's Left Party turned their backs on a far-right AfD politician after he questioned the historical consensus that Germany had committed genocide in what is now Namibia. The protest came during a heated debate over reparations for descendants of the victims.

Germany's government acknowledged the genocide in 2021, but parliament has yet to pass its own formal recognition resolution. A formal apology by Germany's president is also still pending. A proposed deal with Namibia includes €1.1 billion in development aid over 30 years, but no legally binding reparations. The agreement remains unsigned and controversial among descendants of the victims.

Germany and France reached a provisional agreement on Thursday that backs a scaling down of European emissions rules for new cars largely in line with the wishes of German carmakers, according to a draft document seen by news agencies.

The provisional agreement centers on a European Commission proposal last year backing off on banning new internal combustion engines by 2035, the new deal instead calls for a 90% drop in CO2 emissions from 2021 levels.

The remaining 10% was to be covered by compensatory measures like low-carbon ​steel and alternative fuels.

Now, the new agreement would scrap those measures, calling for the 10% to be compensated by manufacturers.

Europe's car industry, led by Germany, has been struggling in recent years amid the switch to electric vehicles and competition from China. This has led the EU to come up with ways to increase competitiveness while still maintaining pledges to reduce emissions. Germany and France have disagreed on how to do this.

The draft agreement still needs official confirmation. Then it faces approval by Germany's governing coalition led by the Christian Democrats (CDU), who have pushed for more watered-down emissions regulations than their Social Democratic Party (SPD) partners.

Then Germany and France will still need to convince other EU members and the European Parliament for the agreement to take effect.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The Bundestag has lifted immunity of a center-left Social Democrat (SPD) lawmaker, seemingly as part of a corruption probe pertaining to a tender for a hospital site in the northern city of Hanover.

Adis Ahmetovic, 33, had his immunity lifted so as to authorize searches requested by investigators.

He is one of three SPD politicians from the Hanover area under investigation in connection with the site in Lehrte, near Hanover.

The Hanover Public Prosecutor's Office said Ahmetovic's Bundestag office and three apartments were searched on Wednesday after his immunity was lifted.

The case came to fairly considerable prominence earlier in the year, because one of these politicians is Steffen Krach.

Krach was the lead SPD candidate for last month's state election in Berlin, and news of him being under investigation surfaced at the height of the campaign.

This may well have helped the Left Party and the Greens to fare better than predicted in the poll, while the SPD slumped to 12% — by far the party's worst ever result in the capital.

Alcohol bans came into force at all German train stations when the clock struck midnight and Thursday began.

All the roughly 5,700 stations across Germany, including the train platforms themselves, are now booze-free zones.

Pubs, restaurants and other such hospitality businesses at train stations are exceptions to the rule, though, and can still serve alcohol. Consumption of alcohol will also remain legal on many trains, with long distance ones still serving beers and other tipples at their on-board bistros.

Rail operator Deutsche Bahn says the change aims to make train stations safer and cleaner, and more pleasant places to spend time waiting for a (who knows, perhaps delayed) train.

Various misdemeanors and incidents had prompted discussions on alcohol at stations over the years, but two this year in particular brought the issues into sharp focus.

A 26-year-old security staff member for Deutsche Bahn was beaten and kicked by a drunken passenger when trying to check their ticket. During the struggle the train door buckled and opened, and the Bahn employee fell from the train, suffering severe injuries. Earlier in the year, a train conductor was killed when attacked by a man without a valid ticket.

The new rules are part of DB's house rules, rather than being criminal law — meaning that at least in the first instance it is a matter for Bahn security staff to enforce rather than police.

"The alcohol consumption ban applies at stations every day, also on days with major events," Bahn spokeswoman Anja Bröder said when asked about often beer-fueled train usage days, like when football fans flock to Bundesliga games.

Around 40 stations piloted the project for some time prior to its implementation, including some of the largest like Cologne, Munich, Hamburg and Berlin. DB says it has had positive experiences with the early experiments, reporting more peaceful stations with less litter and travelers and employees saying they preferred the atmosphere.

A federal group dedicated to helping the homeless has criticized the measure, however, saying that for homeless people with addiction illnesses, train stations often served as "important, weatherproof and comparatively safe places" to shelter. A spokeswoman also told the Rheinische Post newspaper that if they were driven from sites like train stations, it would be harder for social workers to locate them.

German television's most famous orange mouse, WDR's eponymous star of the long running "Sendung mit der Maus" (Show with the mouse), stands in statue waving to whoever walks by the station's headquarters in Cologne.

And after a torrid few years for the celebrity rodent — in which he was kidnapped one year and set on fire by unknown assailants the next — now the mouse has been joined by its partners in crime the elephant and the duck, as was the case as the long-running show evolved.

"Life is always much better with friends," WDR Director General Katrin Vernau said at Thursday's unveiling. "Together the mouse, duck and elephant stand for a children's program that has conveyed knowledge for decades explaining the world and encouraging children to ask questions."

The children's show "Die Sendung mit der Maus" has been on WDR on Sunday mornings since 1971.

The show has various educational and entertainment elements and has had an array of presenters over the years, but the animated shorts featuring the mouse that separate the segments are probably the best known parts.

These short segments of perhaps 30 seconds of 2D animation never involve the mouse, or its accomplices the duck and the elephant who joined later, speaking.

Typically they interact and try to solve some kind of problem, often seeking a reward, by experimentation and trial and error.

Police in Essen continued their search for a 34-year-old prisoner and the two men who violently freed him during a doctor's visit the previous day.

Officers searched parts of the city center, with the help of tracking dogs trying to catch the fugitives' scent.

Two men are thought to have attacked and tied up the prison officers accompanying the inmate on his medical visit, before the three of them split up and fled the scene. Police warned at the time that it "could not be ruled out" that they might be armed.

The 34-year-old was in the JVA Essen prison on drugs and assault convictions.

Potato prospects this year are poor after the prolonged hot and dry weather in the summer, according to the government's statistics office Destatis.

"The 2026 potato harvest will be considerably more meager than the previous year, according to forecasts, which will have consequences for the prices of potatoes at various economic levels," Destatis wrote.

In September, Destatis said, potatoes were 11.3% more expensive than in the same month in the previous years. For frozen produce like chips/fries, the difference was less pronounced at 4.7%.

But these figures vastly outstripped both overall year-on-year inflation for September, 3.35%, and particularly the rate of inflation for food and drink products, 0.4%.

Destatis estimated that the 2026 harvest would be almost exactly one-quarter smaller than the previous year — partly because of fewer hectares being used to grow spuds but in larger part because of reduced average yields on the farmed soil in use.

Forecasts predict a yield of around 38.9 metric tons per hectare this year, compared to 46 tons per hectare in 2025.

A court in Hamburg has sentenced two men convicted of planning attacks in Germany on behalf of Iran's secret service.

One was given an eight-and-a-half-year prison sentence, while the other was ordered to spend four-and-a-half years behind bars on charges of espionage and attempted murder.

Among others, they were accused of plotting to attack Josef Schuster, the president of the Central Council of Jews in Germany and Volker Beck, a Green party politician and president of the German-Israeli society. Beck hailed the verdict online.

Choo-choo! All aboard the October 15 German rail news express, stopping wherever and whenever the conductor asks politely.

Ansbach train station in northwestern Bavaria, west of Nuremberg, has been named the finest in all the land.

The "Pro Rail Alliance" travel organization's special jury named Ansbach the Bahnhof des Jahres 2026, saying that after a renovation process lasting several years, it now "receives travelers in a light and friendly atmosphere."

They praised its well-lit waiting area, easy accessibilty by car, bike or bus, and ample storage for bicycles. They also noted its practical connection to the wider public transport network.

"Ansbach's bus station can be found right outside the train station building, and so can be reached with the greatest possible ease," the jury wrote.

If you're looking for a reason — other than the now alcohol-free train station, that is — to visit the town of roughly 40,000 people, you'll find it on the historic Castle Road from Heidelberg to Bayreuth. It's near the Frankenhöhe National Park, is home to the Ansbach Residence medieval castle complex, the picturesque Ansbach Court Gardens, an 18th century synagogue, and is also the site of the crypts of the Margrave noble family of Franconia.

The government's planned changes to emergency service response have cleared the lower house of parliament, the Bundestag.

One opposition party, the Greens, also supported the grand coalition's proposals, which are similar to plans that were under discussion in the previous government before it was cut short by early elections in 2025.

Health Minister Carsten Linnemann says the changes aim to ensure that patients receive care quicker, and in the right place.

Its main goal is to help ease the burden for paramedics and emergency first responders, by trying to prevent unncecessary calls to the 112 emergency hotline when a different service might be more appropriate.

Perhaps the main pillar of the plan is to directly network the emergency ambulance phone line 112, with the out-of-hours emergency doctor helpline 116 117 that is designed for less life-or-death medical cases.

Linnemann said the reforms were long overdue and that the reality was still that too many people did not really know who they were supposed to call when, and if in doubt would just call 112.

The reform package also envisages setting up integrated emergency centers, known by the German acronym INZ, that will be open around the clock and will bring doctors and hospital staff and other emergency responders together at one site.

Special emergency centers for children and adolescents will also be set up.

Alla hopp! Another day, another digest of the main news morsels on the menu in fair Deutschland, delectable and perhaps disgusting alike. Thanks for stopping by, Planet Earth.

If you're waiting for a train and frustrated by the delay — hardly an unthinkable scenario in modern Germany — on no account crack open a beer to wile away the time. Starting this Thursday, booze is banned at all of the country's train stations. It's part of a bid to improve behavior, fight littering and in extreme cases protect travelers and staff alike.

Various reform plans should start the parliamentary reading process in the Bundestag, after the Cabinet signed off on them in a Wednesday meeting. These include hikes to tobacco taxes, emergency service reforms, and changes to the federal law on support in education.

The Bundestag will also vote, in what's probably a formality, on extending the military peacekeeping deployments in the Red Sea and in South Sudan into 2027.

Left-leaning coalition negotiations are set to restart in Berlin after hitting a big bump in the road earlier this week.

Essen police are still searching for a prisoner who was violently freed from custody yesterday by two accomplices during a doctor's visit.

And the government stats office is warning of a meager potato harvest and increased prices after the scorching, dry summer.

We'll endeavor to keep you abreast of these stories and whatever else breaks as the day develops.

#1088. Swingers diner launches in Silver Lake with a takeout window that's open til 3 a.m.

This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here.

One of L.A.’s favorite late-night haunts just landed in Silver Lake, bringing milkshakes, burgers and omelets to the building that formerly housed All Day Baby at the corner of Sunset Boulevard and Descanso Drive.

Swingers, the nostalgic diner that has served as a community hub and appeared in media such as “Knocked Up” and “Insecure,” made its way across town to its new location. Owner Stephanie Wilson quietly launched takeout from a window along one side of the building, slinging tuna melts, meatloaf and more until 3 a.m.

In December she plans to unveil Swingers’ new Silver Lake dining room (plus jukebox and photo booth), flipping what was once Lien Ta and the late Jonathan Whitener’s lauded diner All Day Baby — and more recently smash-burger spot Heavy Handed — back into her own kind of diner.

“I never get tired of this place, it feels like home,” Wilson said. “This is a new project, and it’ll have a new energy, but we’re still going to keep the same vibe of course. It’s exciting to be working on something new.”

In 1993 Swingers launched at the base of the Beverly Laurel Motor Hotel at the edge of the Fairfax District and Beverly Grove. With its 1960s exterior and vintage “coffee shop” signage, it quickly became a “hipster coffee shop” hangout serving sandwiches and all-day breakfast to the city’s glorious cast of characters. The plaid booths, counter-seat stools and general Americana comprise a funky-chic hideaway that has become an iconic late-night destination for generations of Angelenos.

“In the booth behind you, eating scrambled-egg burritos, is the band headlining the Roxy tonight; behind them, by the Day-Glo cows, a couple of aspiring screenwriters are working on a draft,” late L.A. Times Food critic Jonathan Gold wrote in a 1993 review. “Over there in the corner, the skank in the ripped T-shirt: That’s a zillionaire record tycoon, looking doleful as he eats a low-fat muffin. If you can conceive of all the types of dudes who might possibly be conducting business breakfast at 3:30 in the afternoon, you will have pegged the clientele to a tee.”

Swingers, which previously also operated a diner in Santa Monica, nearly closed permanently in 2020 due to the COVID-19 pandemic. Then Wilson, a longtime general manager, pooled the funds to purchase the business, reopened in late 2020 and kept it running.

Swing Shift: Jonathan Gold reviews Swingers

Since then, it has maintained its eclectic clientele at all hours and has served as a communal gathering space through some of the city’s ups and downs. In 2023 it became a central hub for organizing during the WGA strikes, with picketers convening at the big booths and patio tables almost daily — and with Drew Carey often picking up the tab.

More recently, Wilson decided to expand to Silver Lake after she saw many of her customers moving east.

“Now and again we’ll see an old face and we’ll say, ‘Where have you been? We missed you!’” she said. “And they say, ‘We’ve moved to Silver Lake,’ ‘We’ve moved to Echo Park,’ and so I thought,’We should go check out the Eastside, and it really feels like a perfect fit for our little diner.’”

Wilson wants to honor the late Whitener — who died in 2024 and whose cooking became an L.A. culinary staple at All Day Baby and Here’s Looking at You — with a dish or other form of memorial, and said she is currently in discussions with his friends and former colleagues to determine how best to pay homage.

Currently the Swingers menus are more or less identical across both locations, though Wilson expects to introduce unique daily specials at each.

The Hollywood writers strike affects a culinary ecosystem dependent on catering, private events and business lunches. Some restaurants face big losses, but many are still rallying behind the strike and sending food to picket lines.

She envisions guests walking across retro-inspired terrazzo floors, tucking into omelets and Cobb salads at tables along a freshly placed mosaic tile wall or wood paneling, and picking out slices of pie from the bakery case she plans on installing soon.

For now the little takeout window is serving from 6 p.m. to 3 a.m., with breakfast and lunch to come once doors fully open.

Swingers is now open for takeout at 3200 Sunset Blvd., Los Angeles.

#1090. Iran’s oil lifeline is drying up. The biggest pain may fall on ordinary citizens

Iran sanctions expert Miad Maleki explains what could happen if Tehran's crude revenues fall to zero — and why the economic pain may hit ordinary Iranians before the regime's military.

Iran is approaching a financial reckoning as a U.S. naval blockade threatens to wipe out its seaborne crude oil revenues by mid-December — but the economic pain may fall more heavily on ordinary Iranians than on the military Washington is trying to constrain.

Iran’s trackable floating oil inventory outside the U.S. blockade zone has fallen to zero, according to energy intelligence firm Kpler, which projects that Tehran's crude revenues could dry up by the middle of December as outstanding payments are settled.

But the loss of oil revenue would not necessarily translate into an immediate military funding crisis. Tehran could shield military spending while cutting civilian programs, allowing inflation to erode purchasing power and drawing on alternative revenue sources.

BESSENT SAYS IRAN WILL HAVE 'NOTHING LEFT TO TRADE' WITHIN TWO WEEKS AS OIL LIFELINE DRIES UP

Export oil pipelines are seen at an oil facility on Kharg Island, on the shore of the Gulf, Feb. 23, 2016. (Str/AFP Via Getty Images)

That complicates Washington's pressure campaign: The blockade may deprive Tehran of one of its biggest sources of cash without immediately starving the military and Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps of the money they need to operate.

Oil directly accounts for roughly 30% of Iran's government budget, according to Gregory Brew, a senior Iran and energy analyst at Eurasia Group, and Miad Maleki, an Iran sanctions and financial expert at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies.

Iran entered the year expecting to export about 1.7 million barrels per day at roughly $54 per barrel, Brew said. Actual exports have fallen short of that target, though higher oil prices allowed Tehran to build some financial cushion.

Maleki estimated that oil and refined petroleum products account for between 50% and 60% of regime revenue when indirect income is included.

Still, the December deadline is not a date on which Iran suddenly runs out of money.

Daily life continues in Tehran, capital of Iran, amid ongoing tensions between Iran and the United States, under the impact of US sanctions, on September 14, 2026. ( )

"The December timeline is more of a cash flow kind of disruption, and not really a collapse state," Maleki told Fox News Digital.

Tehran has so far allowed inflation and the weakening rial to absorb some of the pressure rather than abruptly stopping government salaries or allowing widespread shortages to develop.

"The purchasing power of Iranians incrementally declines," Maleki said.

Losing a revenue stream that covers roughly 30% of the government budget would nevertheless force increasingly difficult choices. Tehran can cut spending, borrow more or run larger deficits. Deeper cuts could hit subsidies, pensions and other government programs, while deficit spending risks fueling already high inflation.

"There's already expectations that government spending next year is going to be greatly reduced," Brew said . "A bigger chunk of the budget is likely going to be met through borrowing and deficit spending, which is of course going to add to inflation."

IRAN LOSES KEY ECONOMIC LIFELINE IN MIDDLE EAST THAT TRUMP'S SANCTIONS COULDN'T REACH AS DEADLOCK PERSISTS

Military spending, however, could prove more resistant.

"There is a broad expectation that non-military spending is going to be slashed significantly, while military spending is going to be maintained and might even increase because of the overall war footing that the Iranian regime has been put on," Brew said.

Iran is already spending resources to rebuild missile production facilities and other military infrastructure, expand underground facilities and repair damage to its nuclear program, Brew said.

Iran's armed forces also have a direct connection to the country's oil trade.

US TARGETS CHINESE REFINERY IN SWEEPING IRAN OIL CRACKDOWN, SANCTIONS ‘SHADOW FLEET’ TANKERS

The Treasury Department said last year that Tehran was allocating roughly 200,000 barrels of crude per day to its armed forces, with the value of planned allocations expected to exceed $10 billion annually. Military organizations can sell allocated oil abroad and use the proceeds themselves.

Maleki said those sales have helped finance equipment, chemicals and weapons components and support Iran-backed groups including Hezbollah and Hamas.

The IRGC also draws revenue from smuggling, black-market commerce and sanctions-evasion networks outside the formal state budget. Brew said its economic influence has expanded as sanctions have squeezed Iran's private economy.

A boat floats as commercial vessels appear anchored in the Strait of Hormuz off Bandar Abbas, Iran, Tuesday, Oct. 13, 2026. (Razieh Poudat/ISNA via AP)

"If the IRGC is the single most important institution in the country, and if it largely benefits from sanctions and blockades and various forms of U.S. economic pressure, then there's a world in which it benefits from this new environment rather than being squeezed like the overall government budget," Brew said.

Iran's oil squeeze has been months in the making.

Tehran held roughly 135 million barrels of crude in floating storage before the war began in February, providing a stockpile it could continue selling after U.S. forces restricted new exports. That offshore inventory has now been exhausted.

U.S. Central Command estimates the blockade has already denied Tehran at least $25 billion in oil revenue.

Buyers of Iranian crude typically settle payments one to two months after delivery, creating the lag between the disappearance of Iran's floating inventory and Kpler's projected revenue cutoff in December.

Even if that projection broadly holds, however, Iran is unlikely to stop earning money from hydrocarbons altogether.

Smaller quantities of oil can still move overland by truck and rail and across the Caspian Sea, while refined petroleum and petrochemical products can travel through routes outside the seaborne crude trade targeted by the blockade.

"While the amount of Iranian oil that can be tracked has fallen to zero, it's unlikely Iran's oil exports completely fall to nothing," Brew said. "The amount will likely be fairly small, but it won't be completely zeroed."

Both experts said an agreement with Washington allowing Iranian tankers to resume leaving the Persian Gulf could reverse the trajectory . Without a deal or relaxation of the blockade, the financial pressure is expected to build into next year.

The bigger test may arrive in March, when Iran begins its new fiscal year and must reconcile its spending plans with dramatically lower oil income.

"There's going to be a fiscal squeeze, and there's going to be pressure around the release of the new budget," Brew said. "There's going to be economic unrest, potentially even economic turmoil as the government rolls out spending cuts."

By then, Tehran could have gone months without its traditional seaborne crude income, forcing the regime to decide how much of the financial squeeze it is willing to pass on to its population while preserving spending elsewhere.

#1094. Serbia election: Main players, voter concerns and what is at stake

Sign up now: Get ST's newsletters delivered to your inbox

Oct 25 - Serbia is holding parliamentary elections on Sunday, in which a popular student movement is seeking to end the rule of longtime leader Aleksandar Vucic.

Here are the main players, issues and stakes in the vote.

WHO ARE THE MAJOR PLAYERS AND WHAT DO THEY STAND FOR?

Aleksandar Vucic – United Serbia: The Serbian Progressive Party (SNS)-led electoral list is campaigning on economic growth, higher wages and pensions, infrastructure investment and political stability. SNS leader Milos Vucevic has pledged 4% economic growth in 2027. Vucic, who resigned as president on September 27, is running to become prime minister.

Students Win: Emerging from protests over the November 2024 Novi Sad railway station canopy collapse that killed 16 people, the anti-corruption movement has campaigned for accountability and transparent public procurement. The Democratic Party and Kreni Promeni movement have backed it rather than fielding their own lists.

Socialist Party of Serbia (SPS) – Ivica Dacic – Factor of Stability: A longstanding ally of the SNS, the pro-Russian SPS leads a coalition with Unified Serbia, the Social Democratic Party of Serbia and the Greens of Serbia. It campaigns on social justice, workers' rights and welfare, political stability, and national interests.

European Serbia: A pro-European opposition alliance led by Marinika Tepic and Zdravko Ponos, bringing together the Party of Freedom and Justice, Serbia Centre, and the Solidarity, Self-Defence and Liberation movement. It advocates closer European integration, sanctions against Russia and democratic reforms.

WHAT ARE PARTY LISTS AND HOW DO THEY WORK?

Political parties, party coalitions, movements and other groups can submit party lists, or electoral lists comprising no more than 250 candidates.

The election commission has approved a total of 18 lists.

On election day, voters vote for one electoral list on the ballot, rather than individual candidates.

Corruption and government accountability have dominated the campaign since the Novi Sad disaster. Protesters accuse Vucic and his allies of corruption, controlling the media and mistreating demonstrators, allegations the authorities deny.

Living standards, economic development and the fairness of the electoral process are also campaign issues.

HOW WILL A VICTORY OR LOSS FOR VUCIC IMPACT SERBIA AT HOME AND ABROAD?

A victory allowing Vucic to become prime minister would extend his political leadership and could preserve Serbia's balancing act between its ambition to join the European Union and maintain Belgrade's close ties with Russia and China.

A defeat could pave the way for sweeping domestic reforms, including stronger institutions and measures against corruption. REUTERS

#1097. How I learned to stop worrying and love the culatello

See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred

When I met Scott Lem — a hobbyist charcutier, or meat curer — at his small, makeshift prep space in South Pasadena last week, I had about a million questions for him.

I was there to help break down a pig leg, which we would then salt and turn into culatello and fiocco, two Italian cured meats. Before we could even pick up our knives, I started grilling him on every step of the process.

What salt percentages do you use? Do you have to cure it in plastic bags? How do you control the humidity during drying?

Truth is, I’ve wanted to cure meat at home for a long time, but I’ve always been too intimidated to take the plunge.

Sign up to get a taste of Los Angeles — and the world — in your own home and in your inbox every Friday

Why? Well, I think I’ve never totally understood what’s going on when you preserve meat — the levers to pull, the variables to control and how to control them, the safety.

Preservation was really my entry point into cooking (“The Art of Fermentation” by Sandor Katz was one of the first cookbooks I ever owned), though my first at-home fermentation experiments were hit or miss.

I turned apple scraps into apple cider vinegar (a fly got in and left a school of revolting little wrigglers swimming through my brew), attempted mead (used bread yeast instead of wine yeast and it exploded) and made kimchi out of cauliflower and then used that to inoculate cream for cultured butter (tasted like pizza, kind of awesome). I made gravlax, hot sauce, ginger bugs, bad mustard, mushy pickles.

I fell in love with the fermentation process and soon my kitchen was cluttered with bubbling, odorous jars. When it worked, it was magical.

More than just the magic, I was chasing this romantic vision of myself as the type of person that always has something unique, delicious and homemade tucked away, ready to be shared with guests.

Early in my preservation journey, I met someone just like that.

Some close friends and I were staying at an acquaintance’s old stone house in a small, forgotten village in northern Italy. One night, we made dinner for our host, and as we sat down to eat he ducked down to the cellar and returned with a gallon of local wine, a hunk of mite-infested cheese from a neighbor, and a mysterious, thick, milky-white block wrapped loosely in parchment.

It was lardo — cured pork fat — which I’d never had before. He sliced it transparently thin and told me to stick out my tongue. Never one to say no to a new friend’s request, I obliged, and he gently laid a slice in my mouth. It melted immediately into pure, porky, salty, Hitchcock-zoom-inducing richness. That might have been the moment I became determined to cure my own meat.

That was 10 years ago, and though it’s long been at the top of my culinary bucket list, I still haven’t done it.

This is the year that I overcome my fears.

Enter Scott Lem. Lem is mostly self-taught and has made a variety of salumi, forcemeats and cured whole muscles, which he shares at occasional Lem Party pop-ups, which he started with Cynthia Wong, his wife and business partner.

I asked Lem to explain the whole process to me. He did so very patiently.

For whole muscle curing, Lem butchers the meat, rubs it with 2% salt and 0.25% curing salt (nitrate for long-curing meats, nitrite for shorter curing) by weight, then vacuum seals it and puts it in his fridge for a couple weeks to a month to allow the salt to penetrate evenly through the muscle. Then he cases the meat (often in what can only be called a “beef bung”), dunks the whole thing into a mold solution and allows it to air dry at room temperature for a day. Then, he dries the meat, hanging it in a refrigerator he rigged to control the temperature (aiming for 45 to 50 degrees Fahrenheit) and humidity (aiming for 75% to 80%) until it has lost 35% to 40% of its weight, which might take four to six months. Then it’s often vacuum sealed again to allow the remaining moisture content to balance throughout the entire piece of meat. Finally, it’s ready to eat.

When I’d finished interrogating Lem, I felt like I was finally starting to understand the principles of meat curing — the variables, the levers, the safety.

Basically, you’re trying to get enough salt into the meat so that it’s protected from bad bacteria. The curing salt (which contains nitrates) helps to prevent botulism, and the mold on the outside helps draw out moisture and outcompete other unwanted surface bacteria. The drying process and humidity slowly reduces the water content of the muscle, which aids in preservation, as excess water would make it more likely to spoil.

After we’d finished breaking down the pig leg (Lem let me do this part — I did … OK), then salting and bagging the culatello and fiocco, Lem and Wong invited me to sit down for a meal.

Lem cut thin slices off a couple finished culatelli, some fiocco and some coppa. The meat — truly — was incredible. Among the finest cured meats I’ve had in recent memory.

As we ate together, I realized I’d found myself in another one of those beautiful moments where someone had welcomed me into their space and shared their work and pride and homemade creation with me.

I learned a lot from Lem. Am I going to buy a whole pig’s leg next week? Probably not. But maybe I’ll buy a coppa. Or it might be more appropriate to start with a nice big chunk of lardo.

If you’re curious about fermentation, kimchi is a great place to start. It’s fun to make, highly customizable and — of course — very tasty. This version by Haejung Kim is made with Napa cabbage and is very similar to how I’ve made it at home. Get the recipe. Cook time: 2 hours 30 minutes. Makes 3 quarts.

Cody Reiss is the cooking editor for Los Angeles Times Food, making videos focused on fundamental cooking techniques, philosophies and principles. Previously, he has worked as a cook in the Chez Panisse Café, as a private chef and a travel and food writer. Reiss has eaten his way through 46 states and over 30 countries, and is on a constant search for the best bean and cheese burrito in town.

#1100. Brazil's elections matter for the planet. This is why

Brazil is heading back to the polls, but the impact could be felt worldwide. With the Amazon vital to the health of the planet, the election could help shape its future.

Few national elections carry as much environmental weight as Brazil's presidential race. And this one is being watched from far beyond the country's boundaries.

Home to the largest section of the Amazon rainforest, Brazil is guardian of a carbon sink of vital importance, making the country's conservation policies globally relevant.

Environmentalists have already voiced alarm at Flávio Bolsonaro — son of right-wing former president Jair Bolsonaro — coming out 2% ahead of incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in the first round of elections.

"It's going to be a second coming of Bolsonaro, therefore a more radical Bolsonaro," said Claudio Angelo, international policy coordinator at Climate Observatory, a network of Brazilian NGOs.

"At the risk of sounding alarmist, I would say Lula's re-election is the only thing standing between us and the end of the Amazon."

The Amazon rainforest stores huge amounts of the carbon dioxide (CO2) released into the atmosphere from the burning of fossil fuels. As a result, it helps regulate the Earth's climate.

For decades, the tropical forest has acted as one of nature's most powerful defenses against climate change. But it has also suffered from widespread deforestation.

During Jair Bolsonaro's presidency, from 2019 until 2023, environmental agencies were weakened and enforcement efforts curtailed, meaning tropical forest was cleared at unprecedented rates.

"The environment agenda was disregarded and the level of control the government had on pollution overall, but specifically on deforestation, was reversed," said Claudio Forner, head of climate policy at Berlin-based think tank Climate Analytics.

Over Bolsonaro's four-year term, an estimated 45,586km2 of the Amazon was destroyed, an area bigger than the size of Denmark. And the forest is not as resilient as it once was, with scientists warning that parts of it are now emitting more carbon than they absorb.

Lula came to office with a message of protection for the Amazon. Besides calling for an end to deforestation by 2030, he increased monitoring of the forest and strengthened Brazil's environmental enforcement agency IBAMA.

Deforestation has plummeted under his leadership, with 2026 set to be its lowest level in a decade. That represents a 41% drop overall compared to Jair Bolsonaro's tenure.

Experts have already criticized Flávio Bolsonaro's record on forest protection. As a senator in 2019, he authored draft legislation that could have stark impacts for the Amazon. While landowners are currently required to preserve 80% of their property for the growth of native plants, the bill would allow them to use their holdings as they please.

"The signal from the president will say 'now you can deforest' or 'it's harder to deforest,'" said Ana Yang, director of the Environment and Society Center at London-based think tank Chatham House.

"The moment that you decrease enforcement capability, deforestation grows," she told DW.

Bolsonaro has also pledged to end illegal deforestation by 2029, a year before Lula. But Claudio Angelo is critical of that message.

"He will end illegal deforestation not by enforcing the law, but by making it legal," he said.

More generally, environmental experts fear Bolsonaro might dismantle many of the protections strengthened under the current president.

"Unfortunately, climate change has become a partisan issue, so rather than offering a solution from their perspective, the right pictures climate change as an invented problem...that regulation goes against economic growth or it goes against competitiveness, that it's the aim of the left to control the means of production," Forner said.

In an interview with Brazilian media in August, Bolsonaro said he regarded extreme weather events to be cyclical and did not believe they were solely linked to human influence.

A Bolsonaro win is likely to see Brazil move away from its position as a climate leader, a role the country embraced last year as it hosted the COP30 climate conference in the Amazonian city of Belem.

But even a Lula victory would not represent a straightforward climate success story, say experts. While the current administration has overseen significant reductions in deforestation, it has also backed plans to expand oil production.

Angelo said the decision to allow exploratory drilling was a "betrayal" of Lula's mandate but added that the president's overall record on climate had been "quite impressive".

"Lula is the world's worst climate leader, except for all the others," he told DW.

The current president will face a runoff election with Bolsonaro on October 25. But while experts say the outcome could determine the fate of the Amazon and the wider efforts to curb global warming, for many Brazilians climate is not high on their list of priorities.

"Ultimately what people care about is access to education, sanitation and health," said Yang. A road built through the Amazon to access those services, while criticized from outside Brazil for destroying parts of the rainforest, would be desirable to voters, she added.

"They don't have time to care. Not because they don't want to. They care about their own survival," she said.

#1103. Suspected ‘racist terrorist’ shooter put in French police psychiatric unit

Sign up now: Get ST's newsletters delivered to your inbox

French President Emmanuel Macron meeting rescue forces at the town hall following a shooting in Trappes, near Paris, on Oct 23.

PARIS – A man suspected of a gun attack in the Paris suburbs that killed one person and wounded five has left custody and been placed in a psychiatric unit for observation, French anti-terror prosecutors said on Oct 25.

The 39-year-old suspect, partly identified as Kevin T, was arrested on Oct 23 in possession of a submachine gun and tear-gas grenades in his car, shortly after the victims were shot as a vehicle drove through the working-class town of Trappes and neighbouring La Verriere.

President Emmanuel Macron had branded the shooting a “racist terrorist attack”, as most of the victims were from foreign backgrounds.

The French National Anti-Terrorism Prosecutor’s Office (PNAT), which is handling the case, on Oct 24 extended the suspect’s time in detention to pursue its interrogation.

But a day later, the PNAT said: “After a psychiatric examination of Kevin T carried out in the evening (of Saturday), his custody has been lifted.”

It said that, in line with conclusions from a psychiatric expert, he “was transferred to the police psychiatric unit to be subjected to a psychiatric observation period likely to last 48 hours”.

That observation period “should allow us to evaluate whether his state of psychiatric health is compatible with pursuing interrogation sessions”.

The PNAT added that traces of cannabis and cocaine were found in the suspect’s blood.

Police have searched his home in the town of Plaisir outside of Paris.

According to a source close to the investigation on Oct 24, they found a Bible, a Quran and a copy of Adolf Hitler’s Mein Kampf.

The person killed in the Oct 23 shooting was a 26-year-old man of Congolese origin, Pengo Bossio Wangi.

One of those wounded was a 12-year-old girl who was hit by bullets eight times. She remains in a critical condition.

The shooting comes at a moment of deep divisions in France, which is heading for elections in six months with far-right candidate Marine le Pen leading in the polls.

Political and social tensions boiled over a week ago into riots that have marred the country’s image ahead of the vote to choose Macron’s successor. AFP

#1106. A new food hall brings Japan's most coveted restaurants — and bowling — to Ventura

This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here.

See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred

Silken udon noodles crowned with crispy chicken tempura. Yuzu-kosho karaage that’s marinated so thoroughly it requires no sauce. Ramen that ranges from tonkotsu to Sapporo miso and niboshi (made with dried sardines). These are just a few of the options at YUU Japanese Food Hall, which brings some of Japan’s most coveted restaurants stateside for the first time.

The food court, which opened Saturday with 14 vendors in a Round1 bowling and arcade center in Ventura’s Pacific View shopping mall, is three years in the making. According to Round One Entertainment executive vice president and chief operating officer Hirotoshi Takahashi, restaurant owners and chefs were meticulous about ingredient sourcing and how the food is served, ensuring that each dish is as close as possible to the version you’ll find at the original locations in Japan.

New equipment was installed in order to achieve specific textures and flavors, such as a filtration system that produces soft, low-mineral water similar to what you’ll find in Japan. Although some ingredients are procured locally, many are imported directly from Japan.

“We can’t say that it’s 100% [the same] because of the difference in ingredients,” Takahashi said, “but we are confident that it’s well over 80%.”

From tiny omakase bars to neo-Neapolitan pizzerias and world-renowned coffee roasters, these are the Tokyo restaurants, bars and teahouses that we willfully lose ourselves in.

For example, at its 23-seat Tokyo restaurant, Tonkatsu Keita uses Roppaku Kurobuta, known as the Wagyu of pork, for its juicy, golden-crusted tonkatsu. Unable to source the same pigs in America, the Ventura stall opted to use heritage black pork instead.

Okonomiyaki Hana stands out for the light, tempura-like batter on its cabbage pancakes, and Curry bitSOMA cooks each ingredient separately before layering them in deeply flavorful curry dishes. Onigiri Gorichan serves delicate Koshihikari rice balls stuffed with salmon flakes, pickled plums or Spam and egg.

Not all stalls are focused on Japanese cuisine. Kyoto-based Pizzeria Da Naghino offers crackly edged Neapolitan pies and Gelateria Il Brigante, from the coastal city of Kamakura, serves scratch-made Sicilian gelato.

Orders are placed at self-service kiosks, allowing guests to mix and match items from various vendors without the hassle of separate checks. When the food is ready, the order number appears on a screen above the kiosks as well as on individual screens at each corresponding stall. Food is picked up directly at each stall.

The current generation of omakase chefs in Los Angeles are returning to the essence of the cuisine. A trip to Tokyo confirms what’s been driving their pursuit for excellence.

A wraparound bar anchors the massive food hall, with mounted TVs playing live sports. A full cocktail menu is available, including premium sake and drink specials such as $3.99 Bud Light and wine all day.

Upstairs is the Round 1bowling alley and arcade, with karaoke, rows of claw machines and other games imported from Japan. Billiards and ping pong tables will soon be added. Takahashi said the goal for the food hall and activity center is to become an all-day destination that will attract locals as well as day trippers from Los Angeles and the Central Coast.

YUU Japanese Food Hall plans to open in Escondido later this year with a fresh slate of concepts, including Shaved Ice Housekibaco, serving kakigori with ice that is slowly frozen over 72 hours, and Takoyaki Do-Raku Wanaka, a takoyaki shop founded in Osaka in 1986.

“It’s exciting that we’ve been able to bring so many Japanese restaurants to the United States,” Takahashi said. “It’s a long time coming.”

YUU Japanese Food Hall and Round1 Bowling and Arcade are at 3295 E. Main St., Suite 2, Ventura, and open daily from 10 a.m. to 2 a.m.

The Obama Presidential Center's projected price tag has surpassed $1 billion, nearly triple its original $350 million estimate, according to previous Fox News Digital reporting. Subcontractors have alleged they are owed millions for their work, while taxpayers have been saddled with hundreds of millions of dollars in associated public infrastructure costs separate from the center's construction budget.

Obama's criticism extended beyond the presidential residence to Trump's handling of the conflict with Iran, which the former president blamed for higher energy costs.

"Most importantly, he decided to start an unnecessary war that nobody asked for and nobody voted for," Obama said.

He also defended the nuclear agreement negotiated during his presidency.

The agreement offered Tehran sanctions relief in exchange for nuclear restrictions and international inspections. Inspectors reported some Iranian compliance before the U.S. withdrawal, although Iran subsequently expanded uranium enrichment beyond the deal's proposed limits.
