#1112. Why Chinese tech brands are outpacing Western rivals from EVs to robot vacuums

From action cameras and smartphones to EVs and robot vacuums, Chinese brands are gaining ground worldwide, despite privacy and security concerns. What's driving their rise, and can European rivals keep up?

Do you remember the days when GoPro was synonymous with action cameras?

At its peak in 2015, the US company reigned supreme with around 6.6 million units sold that year and a market share of over 70%. Today, the pioneer is fighting for survival.

GoPro's biggest rivals, DJI and Insta360, entered the action camera market in 2019 and 2021, respectively. Today, they account for more than 90% of global smart handheld camera sales.

Alexander Hannemann, who regularly uses action cameras to film his motorcycle rides, says he switched from GoPro to Insta360 around two years ago.

"The quality is much better than a GoPro, even when I'm speeding up and going into corners at like 80 kilometers per hour," he told DW.

GoPro's case is not an exception. Since around 2010, many Chinese brands have not only caught up but surpassed once-dominant Western rivals across the consumer technology industry, from smart TVs to robot vacuums.

Gone are the days when "Made in China" stood for cheap, mass-produced products.

"China is still making affordable products today," says Chris Pereira, a Canadian entrepreneur and author with over 20 years of experience in China. "But the products are also high quality."

This combination has led to well over half of new consumer tech products globally coming from Chinese suppliers, Pereira adds.

BYD, Xpeng and other Chinese car manufactures sold almost two-thirds of all electric cars last year, surpassing incumbents like Tesla. In robot vacuums, Chinese brands dominate the global market, leaving former pioneer US company iRobot struggling to compete.

So why do Chinese companies increasingly outperform their Western rivals?

Pereira, whose consultancy iMpact helps Chinese companies gain traction overseas, attributes China's success to fierce domestic competition in cities like Shenzhen, Hangzhou and Shanghai; highly integrated supply chains and a can-do business culture that allows companies to innovate; and respond to problems quickly.

Other key reasons for China's competitive edge include unparalleled industrial automation, the strategic use of AI in manufacturing, responsiveness from regulators as well as relatively cheap labor, which together leads to significantly lower production costs and much faster innovation cycles than in the world's most advanced economies.

Joey Cheng, who moved to the US for his PhD studies over 20 years ago, is familiar with both the American consumer and the Chinese producer sides.

While his startup is based in the US, almost all the manufacturing is done in Shenzhen, where a large share of the world's hardware and consumer electronics are made.

"The supply chain in Shenzhen is basically inevitable for cost cutting and quick product development," Cheng says. "Especially as a startup you must get the product out quickly, or you'll get blown out of the water."

Although consumers are flocking to Chinese companies, some reservations persist.

A recent poll found that more than 90% of Europeans do not trust Chinese technology companies with their data, while about 80% distrust US firms. Germans expressed the highest level of mistrust.

Nadine, a German travel blogger who uses DJI and Insta360 products, says she wouldn't use any Asian products at home.

"My home robot vacuum is from a German company for precisely this reason: So the data remains compliant with German regulations. After all, manufacturers can connect directly to the camera," she said, referring to camera and audio hacking incidents involving robot vacuums.

Still, Pereira says that Chinese companies expanding abroad have to pay a "trust premium."

"This trust deficit means that they need to be extra competitive in terms of product and price in order for the market to choose them," he says, adding that the gap can be narrowed by a presence in overseas markets like BYD's first European passenger-car plant, expected to open in Hungary later this year.

Chinese companies say they comply with EU data protection rules. However, domestic security laws in the US and China can require firms to hand over data to authorities, and German officials note limited oversight of whether data is transferred from European servers abroad.

In addition to privacy concerns, Chinese consumer tech firms have come under scrutiny over espionage and other risks, most recently regarding connected devices like EVs.

In light of security concerns, trade deficits and China's overall dominance, the US and several other Western countries have hit Chinese imports and companies with tariffs, blacklists and strict requirements. In late July, the Trump administration banned the import of humanoid robots manufactured outside the US.

A representative of Chinese robot maker Primebot told DW that all Chinese consumer tech companies are feeling the effects.

"We might seek cooperation with a local US company. Another potential solution is building a factory there," he said.

European countries and the EU are also weighing more tariffs against Chinese companies.

Chris Pereira foresees that the tariffs will accelerate two trends among Chinese companies: Moving more manufacturing overseas and an increasing focus on challenging top-tier Western brands with premium goods.

"Chinese officials and companies recognize that manufacturing needs to be localized to a certain degree. One reason is to assuage the challenges of exporting, another is to create trust locally," Pereira sums up.

"The other trend is that once duties wipe out the price advantage at the bottom, the margin left is at the top, so Chinese brands are increasingly competing directly with established Western names, where trust matters most."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

As China's dominance keeps growing, Western companies are scrambling to find ways to stay competitive.

Kaz Merchant, who works for a UK-based company that imports and exports IT hardware, says smaller companies, in particular, must carve out a geographic niche.

"They need to have their own unique selling point for a certain product, which China might not have for that region. Or they need to partner with a Chinese company," he says.

To Pereira, a key issue Europe needs to solve is regulators' responsiveness.

"Chinese regulators tell you very clearly and quickly what you can do. That speed helps companies iterate and succeed overseas," Pereira says.

"If you're waiting weeks for a response, you're going to lose business."

#1113. What’s It Like Inside a Data Center?

Northern Virginia is laden with structures that house data for Fortune 500 companies. I went inside just one of those monstrosities that bothers its neighbors.

Northern Virginia is laden with structures that house data for Fortune 500 companies. I went inside just one of those monstrosities that bothers its neighbors.

The sun was beating down as I made my way through a quiet community in Ashburn, Virginia. The roads were wide and lined with cars; there was a nice central playground with no one playing in it; the houses seemed monstrously large; and there were ample trees dotting the clean-cut lawns of the neighborhood.

In so many ways, it felt like your typical US suburb, until you looked past the thick wall of trees that defined its boundaries. The white walls of a large facility peeked out from above the deep green foliage. It ran on in the distance, the large houses making it impossible to see its full extent. Towering above it a little farther away were the high-voltage transmission lines that fed it with electricity. The trees acted like a shield, allowing those who lived in the community not to think about what stood on their doorstep and the growing demands that came from the surrounding industrial expansion. I’m talking, of course, about hyperscale data centers.

No location on the entire planet has more data centers than Virginia. The state holds more than 13 percent of global hyperscale capacity—double that of Beijing, which comes in second. There were nearly 600 data centers within the state’s boundaries in 2025, about 150 of which were hyperscale—the monstrously large variety that have become much more common since the advent of generative AI—and most of them were clustered in an area in the north of the state around Ashburn, which has since been dubbed “Data Center Alley.”

Data centers are unavoidable in Northern Virginia. When I sat on a bench next to a neighborhood lake, a hyperscale data center owned by Microsoft stared back at me from the opposite bank. As I drove through industrial parks, they were dotted throughout. When I pulled into a shopping area to grab a bite to eat, facilities that powered Amazon Web Services loomed behind the strip mall. I could even feel their influence in the street names: Cloud Plaza, Performance Circle, and, worst of all, Growth Mindset Lane. We can thank Microsoft for that one.

In short, they were everywhere when I visited in 2025, and following them wherever they set down were the high-voltage power lines needed to keep them running. Data centers were remaking the fabric of a whole region; there seemed to be no end in sight for their expansion. They had become a major industry, and neither worries over local resource demands nor growing concern from residents seemed able to stop the ambitions of some of the most powerful companies on the planet.

It’s hard to generalize about the data centers themselves. They come in many shapes and sizes, operate at various scales—from rooms in a nondescript building to entire parks of warehouse-sized facilities crammed with thousands of servers apiece—and seem to be getting bigger with every passing year. Some of them exist to serve the companies operating them; others exist as places where many different groups can rent space for servers of their own. Certain facilities are cooled with air-conditioning, while others depend more on water-based cooling, and even the way those systems are implemented can differ. I guess what I’m trying to say is that one description of a data center will never cover the gamut: There is some standardization, but there is also a lot of room for operators to put their own stamp on how their facility or network of locations is going to work.

The interiors of some Google data centers have clusters of brightly colored tubes running throughout them—echoing the primary colors present in the company’s branding—while the average Microsoft or Amazon facility might appear more utilitarian. Digital Realty is one of the largest data-center operators in the world. The company has two major lines of business: It builds entire facilities that then get leased to other companies, including the major cloud providers, but it also offers colocation services. Those are facilities where Digital Realty runs the data center, renting space in racks to other companies that they can then fill with their own servers. I stopped to walk the length of one of its facilities in Northern Virginia. The simplest way to describe it is to say that it looks like a massive box. The company’s logo was visible near the upper portion of the building, and it had some different shades of gray and blue across its exterior.

The data center seemed quiet that weekend afternoon, though even on a weekday there weren’t likely to be many people there. Data centers don’t need many employees to keep them clean, secure, and running; the bulk of the jobs they provide are created in the construction phase and mostly disappear once that’s over. The parking lot at the front of the building was surrounded by a large black fence that went around the entire property. I wasn’t trying to get in, but I did wonder if there was a security officer behind a desk somewhere inside the building peering at me through the video feed of one of the facility’s many security cameras. Data centers are notoriously well-guarded, to keep their data safe and to assuage the worries of their clients.

There wasn’t much to see as I walked along the fence, the spikes at the top of each pole warning me not to try anything rash. It took nearly five minutes to walk from one end of the building to the other, and this wasn’t even one of the bigger ones I’d seen that day. At the far end, a little beyond the fence, I walked onto a wooden platform where I could make out a serene pond obscured by tall trees and plants. The chirps and trills of birds and insects were just barely audible over the buzz of the air-conditioning system on the facility’s roof. The pond appeared impossible to access as its lifeless neighbor encroached upon it.

When I pulled into an outdoor shopping mall, I parked across from the shell of a structure that was soon to become a data center. Some tech companies will take over an existing facility and convert it into a data center, but most end up being built from scratch on vast tracts of newly cleared land. Towering outer walls of concrete reached far above even the retail stores that surrounded me. Each one was held up with steel braces as they waited for the installation of roof trusses that would be used to bind the various pieces together. After that, it would all be sealed against the elements with some utilitarian exterior cladding, then fitted with the cabling, temperature-regulation systems, power backups, and everything else needed to get thousands of servers running and wired to the Internet.

It’s not always easy to know when a data center is slated for a community before it starts rising out of the ground—or, when residents do get that information, who is actually behind it. Consider Lowell Charter Township, which sits about 20 miles outside Grand Rapids, Michigan. In 2025, its residents learned that a new data center was planned for their area, and they saw their local leaders moving fast to rezone the land and get any barriers out of the way to make it happen. Yet no one would reveal which company would ultimately run the facility.

The public was not happy, and near the end of the year so many angry residents crowded into a planning-commission meeting that officials were forced to put the project on ice. It was only then that Microsoft finally came out from behind the curtain to reveal itself as the proprietor.

Situations like this are not uncommon, though they rarely end in the outcome that the residents of Lowell achieved. Major tech firms use shell companies to hide their involvement in data-center projects until it’s too late for locals to stop them, just as Google did in The Dalles, Oregon, when it used the name “Design LLC.” Amazon has gone by “Razor5 LLC” in Indiana, and Meta deployed “Sidecat LLC” in Ohio and “Degas LLC” in Wisconsin.

Tech companies need a lot of data centers to fuel their ambitions. They do not need nearly as many offices where engineers create the products that justify the need for data centers. When I saw that shell of a data center in Virginia, I was also seeing the phase in which it would provide the most employment. During construction, a data-center project tends to employ over 1,000 people—even more for the monstrously large hyperscale facilities—but once they’re done, the employment numbers tend to drop into the dozens. These are not high-paying engineering jobs: Many of the workers are doing security, cleaning, or conducting maintenance on the systems. Is that really worth hundreds of thousands, if not millions, of dollars per job in tax breaks and incentives? A growing number of Virginians didn’t think so.

The rush to build out data centers in response to the generative-AI boom has led to a renewed rush for land, this time led by the companies competing in the AI race or trying to profit from powering it. With time of the essence, access to electricity has become one of the defining metrics of a site’s viability. Companies can’t wait years for capacity to be built or grid connections to be made. In some cases, that competitive pressure has led companies to bypass some of the demands they typically make of local governments—as was the case when xAI, Elon Musk’s AI company, did not demand property-tax abatements from Memphis, Tennessee. Musk wanted the data center up and running as quickly as possible. But the construction boom has also lifted some surprising companies along with it. Construction firms clearly benefit from all the additional projects they get hired to complete, while electricity companies and computer-hardware manufacturers find there’s a much greater demand for what they’re selling.

Communities like the one I visited in Virginia were feeling the brunt of the AI boom. As the data centers got closer, some property owners even started begging government officials to rezone their land for industrial use so they could sell and move away from it all. In Northern Virginia, the signs of that opposition are increasingly common. I spotted large banners hanging from gazebos along a central stretch of road in Loudoun County, warning that towering high-voltage transmission lines would slash the values of people’s homes. “Who pays? Loudoun families,” the banners read. “Who profits? Data centers and Dominion”—the local electricity provider and utility.

Residents also have to deal with tremors through their homes during the construction period, followed by the incessant hum of air-conditioning units once the center is up and running. Some people have to contend with the bright lights that stay on all night to illuminate the exterior of the facilities. It’s easy to dismiss some of these concerns as typical NIMBY complaints, but most Virginians were not initially opposed to data centers. For a long time, there wasn’t much of a concerted campaign to stop data centers at all. That only began to change as they started encroaching on communities and people experienced the tangible impacts in their lives.

In early 2026, a cold snap hit many parts of the United States. Once the grid was stressed, data centers in Virginia were given permission to run fully on their diesel generators, with little regard for the air-quality impacts of burning all that fuel. They did not have to “reduce their consumption, take some of the AI offline,” said Chris Miller, the president of the Piedmont Environmental Council. Instead, the decision was made “to expose the general public to an increased level of public-health hazard” from the burning of all that diesel fuel. It’s no wonder that as data-center construction ramped up in 2024 and ’25, opposition began growing around it.

Between 2024, when I’d first spoken to Miller, and early 2026, when we reconnected, there had been what he described as a night-and-day shift. People were feeling the effects of data centers near their communities, and they were also getting confirmation that what they were feeling was real. Over that time, a lot more data became available on the facilities’ water use and electricity demands, and media reports shed further light on how they were contributing to higher electricity prices in places like Virginia. People were finally waking up to what was going on around them.

When you’re stuck on the outside of a data center, it’s easy to imagine the interior as sinister: ominous, towering black boxes filled with servers whose small lights and indicators give off an eerie glow in the dimmed light of a chilly server room. But the truth is that they’re typically quite mundane and utilitarian spaces. In bigger facilities, the floors can be concrete, but many others have elevated floors covered with removable tiles, while fluorescent lights keep things well lit—at least when humans are inside. Miles of cables running overhead and down into the racks enable rapid data transfer and the servers’ ultimate connection to the wider Internet.

There’s no question that the sensitive data held inside must be protected, and the extent of the effort to do so must be visible to clients. But it’s not a form of theater that ends at the door. Stringent security practices are present throughout the facility, beginning with the people who are allowed through the door. I had a hard time getting inside a major data center: The most recognizable companies rejected my requests, if they responded to them at all. Several of the experts I spoke with told me that’s typical. Since the generative-AI boom has increased the scrutiny placed on data centers, getting inside their walls has become much more difficult.

When I finally visited a data center for a tour, the extent of the security measures struck me more than anything else. Security officials already had my name when I arrived at the gate. Once I got through the door, I needed to check in and hand over my passport before I could go any further. No photos were allowed. As we made our way through the facility, it became clear that you couldn’t simply walk through any of the doors. Each one of them had its own digital lock, meaning the executive escorting me had to tap us into room after room as he explained how the different parts of the facility worked.

When you enter the server room of a data center, the warm air produced by all of the computer hardware envelops you, but far more striking is the incessant metallic hum that feels like an auditory assault—the product of all the servers and whirring fans in the room. Rows of tall lockers (called “racks”) fill the facility, each containing dozens of long, thin servers. Depending on the size of the data center, there can be hundreds, thousands, or hundreds of thousands of servers throughout the building. The server racks stand seven feet high, with bundles of colored cables connecting to the hardware and running along the back of each rack. When the servers are cooled with air-conditioning, you can feel the difference in the heat they produce simply by standing on either side of a rack.

Standing inside a data center, I couldn’t help but think of the vast network of supply chains that make them possible. The Internet has extended to touch every corner of the world, but so too do the trade routes whose finished goods eventually sit within the facility’s racks. The many thousands of servers overwhelmingly arrive from factories in Asia, with supply chains that snake out to mines across the world where the minerals and metals essential for their production originate.

The Internet can seem like an immaterial thing when we log on to social-media platforms or do Google searches that send us to any number of websites. But structuring data centers as real-estate-investment vehicles required defining and treating the network in a wholly different way. It’s an important element of the business of the Internet that often gets ignored, but it has significant implications for the Web itself. Those corporate structures shape the incentives that drive the companies ultimately building out the foundations of the digital world.

Paris Marx is the author of Hyperscale: The Ambition and Excess of Big Tech's Data Empires. He hosts the Tech Won’t Save Us podcast and writes the Disconnect newsletter.

A teenager was arrested after a boy died in a fatal collision following a police pursuit, Avon and Somerset Police has said.

The boy who died at the scene was a passenger in a white Nissan Juke which was in a collision with a black Audi S3 in south Bristol just after 4am on Sunday morning.

Avon and Somerset Police said it happened on the A37 Wells Road at its junction with Airport Road and Wootton Park.

The force said: “It followed a short police pursuit involving an unmarked police vehicle and the white Nissan Juke.

“Sadly, one person – a teenage boy who was a passenger in the white Nissan Juke – died at the scene.”

Two other teenage children from the Nissan were taken to hospital with injuries not thought to be life-threatening, along with the man driving the Audi.

“Officers later arrested a 17-year-old boy at a residential property on suspicion of causing death by dangerous driving,” police said.

“This young person was taken to hospital for assessment and discharged. He remains in police custody.

“Specialist officers have traced and informed the family of the boy who died and offered them support.”

A mandatory referral has been made to the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) as a death following police contact, and Avon and Somerset’s Professional Standards Unit has been informed.

The road was closed for collision investigation and vehicle recovery and reopened just after 4pm on Sunday.

A detective inspector from the force major crime investigation unit is currently leading the inquiry into the collision, pending any decision by the IOPC.

Two Utah residents who hiked Mt. Shasta in Northern California were rescued after they became stranded during a perilous 36-hour journey through freezing conditions.

The Siskiyou County Sheriff’s Office received a distress call around 10:20 p.m. Monday from a 19-year-old man and a 20-year-old woman, both from Salt Lake City, who were in the Avalanche Gulch area, about 11,000 feet above sea level, according to a news release from the office.

The hikers, who had planned only for a daylong hike, said they were cold and unable to finish their descent of the towering volcano.

At the time of their call, temperatures hovered around 15 degrees, and the pair lacked adequate clothing, food or water to safely endure the night, according to the Sheriff’s Office.

Authorities advised the hikers to continue descending the mountain to maintain their body heat. By 2 a.m., the hikers called authorities again to say they had arrived at Helen Lake (about 10,400 feet above sea level). Not long after, their phones died.

The hikers made it to Horse Camp, a popular staging area, but couldn’t find the trail and traveled down a steep, dry river canyon. They continued walking for several more miles until they were stranded between 30- to 50-foot-tall cliffsides.

The Sheriff’s Office, along with the California Highway Patrol and search-and-rescue volunteers, began searching for the hikers at dawn Tuesday. Around 4 p.m., a search party heard shouting in the Cascade Gulch area, about 1,000 feet from the McBride Springs Trail.

The hikers climbed out of the gulch with help from authorities, according to officials. After hiking for 36 hours, neither was injured.

Authorities warned against hiking this route this time of year because of deteriorating conditions and the onset of winter weather.

“This ordeal is also an important reminder for anyone hiking, climbing, or hunting to prepare for worst case scenarios, such as an unintentional overnight stay, inclement weather, or an injury,” the Sheriff’s Office said in a news release. “With winter conditions returning, it is imperative to research your route ahead of time and only choose objectives that are safe for the season, as a simple mistake can turn deadly in the Siskiyou County high country.”

#1116. Second Amendment fight moves beyond guns with Supreme Court poised for big ruling

National Association for Gun Rights President Dudley Brown says the AR-15 ban before the Supreme Court could shape challenges to restrictions on automatic knives, body armor, magazines and other defensive equipment.

Two federal court rulings Wednesday extending Second Amendment protections to switchblade knives and body armor have fueled optimism among gun-rights advocates ahead of a major Supreme Court showdown over bans on AR-15-style rifles.

The Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals ruled that a federal law restricting the interstate commerce of switchblade knives violated the Second Amendment, while a federal judge in the Western District of New York struck down New York’s restrictions on personal body armor. In both cases, the courts determined that switchblades and body armor qualify as constitutionally protected "arms."

The twin rulings come as the Supreme Court prepares to hear oral arguments in Viramontes v. Cook County, a case that could determine whether AR-15-style rifles qualify as "arms" protected by the Second Amendment.

National Association for Gun Rights President Dudley Brown, whose organization filed an amicus brief in Viramontes, said a Supreme Court ruling against AR-15 bans could influence future legal challenges to restrictions on ammunition magazines, automatic knives, body armor and other defensive equipment.

"The interesting thing about both of these cases is that they’re both going to be really decided by the U.S. Supreme Court in the Viramontes decision," Brown told Fox News Digital.

National Association for Gun Rights President Dudley Brown hold a switchblade as he describes the Fifth Circuit ruling that knives are protected under the Second Amendment (Fox News Digital | Elaine Mallon)

SUPREME COURT UNANIMOUSLY LIMITS USE OF GUN LAW USED TO PROSECUTE HUNTER BIDEN

The recent rulings rely on two major Supreme Court decisions defining the scope of the Second Amendment: District of Columbia v. Heller and New York State Rifle & Pistol Association v. Bruen — both of which will play a key role in the Supreme Court’s review of AR-15-style rifle bans.

In its 2008 decision in Heller, the Supreme Court established that the Second Amendment protects an individual right to possess firearms for lawful purposes, including self-defense. The Court also ruled that the amendment protects weapons in lawful common use while acknowledging a longstanding tradition of restricting "dangerous and unusual" weapons.

Heller recognized that the term "arms" encompasses both offensive weapons and defensive armor. The decision did not address switchblades or body armor directly but the recent rulings relied on its broader understanding of what may qualify as an arm.

The decisions also reveal how Bruen ’s text-and-history test could shape the Supreme Court’s review of bans on AR-15-style rifles.

Under Bruen, courts first determine whether the Second Amendment’s text covers the weapon or conduct at issue. Because both courts answered that question affirmatively, the burden shifted to the governments to show that the restrictions were consistent with the nation’s historical tradition of arms regulation.

George Lyon, a Second Amendment attorney, said the governments in both cases failed to identify sufficiently similar historical laws justifying the modern restrictions.

AR-15 style rifles are displayed for sale at Blue Ridge Arsenal in Chantilly, Va., on Jan. 9, 2015. (Samuel Corum/Anadolu Agency/Getty Images)

ATF SUSPENDS FEDERAL REGISTRATION AND APPROVAL RULES FOR CERTAIN FIREARMS

"Once what you want to do is shown to come within the text of the Second Amendment, the presumption is that the regulation is unconstitutional," Lyon said.

The Fifth Circuit found that switchblades are commonly used "arms" protected by the Second Amendment, citing their historical use for defense and everyday purposes. It then ruled that the government had failed to identify a sufficient historical tradition for the Federal Switchblade Act’s specific restrictions on interstate commerce, which regulated switchblades in a way that differed from historical laws.

In the New York ruling, the state argued that body armor was a tactical accessory to a firearm rather than an "arm" protected by the Second Amendment. The judge rejected that argument, finding that body armor falls within the historical definition of arms recognized in Heller. The court then concluded that New York had not shown a sufficient historical tradition supporting its civilian purchase ban.

That reasoning could become important in Viramontes, where the Supreme Court is being asked to decide whether AR-15-style rifles fall within the definition of protected arms recognized in Heller.

The U.S. Supreme Court cleared the way for the Trump administration to continue third-country deportations while the justices consider a legal challenge to the policy. (Getty Images)

GUN RIGHTS GROUPS CAPITALIZE AFTER JUDGE REVERSES DECADES-OLD RESTRICTIONS: 'MONUMENTAL'

The case arises from a challenge to Cook County’s assault-weapons ban. The Seventh Circuit concluded that AR-15-style rifles were comparable to machine guns and therefore fell outside the category of arms protected by the Second Amendment. The Supreme Court’s decision could resolve whether that reasoning is consistent with Heller and Bruen.

Lyon said the Seventh Circuit improperly treated AR-15-style rifles as comparable to machine guns.

"The current case at the Supreme Court, Viramontes, will address that because the Seventh Circuit had taken the position that because AR-15s are ‘like machine guns,’ they don’t constitute an arm as defined under Heller," Lyon said. "That was just totally wrong in my view."

Justin Davis, director of public affairs for the National Rifle Association, said the dispute over AR-15-style rifles is part of a broader legal fight over what qualifies as an "arm" under the Second Amendment.

"There’s a major discussion going on in the courts about what is and what aren’t arms," Davis said.

Davis pointed to litigation involving suppressors, ammunition magazines, stun guns, pepper spray and other equipment used for self-defense.

"They talk about how the Second Amendment only applied to muskets because that’s what existed at the time of the Founders, but we don’t apply the First Amendment only to newspapers, books or speech in public forums," Davis said. "Social media, texting and phones didn’t exist at that time, either."

"The world evolves, but the core fundamental rights never change," Davis continued.

Elaine Mallon is a writer for Fox News Digital and Fox Business covering national politics.

#1118. Beirut's $13 chicken sandwich becomes symbol of Lebanon divide

Sign up now: Get ST's newsletters delivered to your inbox

BEIRUT, Oct 25 - Seven years after Lebanon’s devastating financial meltdown, a debate over a chicken sandwich has exposed an increasingly stark divide between those who can still spend freely and those struggling to get by.

A trendy health restaurant wanted to offer its calorie-conscious customers a healthier take on the beloved Levantine wrap known as the shish taouk. So, The Glow Paradise launched the “Chic Taouk”, pricing it at around $13 — nearly double what an un-chic chicken sandwich typically goes for in Beirut.

The pricy pun proved hard to swallow, with outraged critics accusing the restaurant of overcharging in a country where many households struggle to afford basic necessities.

Yet while the debate raged on social media, customers kept buying. The Glow Paradise sold more than 20,000 Chic Taouk sandwiches in just 11 days, according to managing partner Hrag Jeghalian, who described the online exchanges as "natural marketing".

The contrasting reactions touched a nerve in Lebanon, where years of financial turmoil, political dysfunction and conflict have reshaped the country's social landscape, hollowing out much of the middle class while leaving a smaller group of consumers able to sustain an affluent lifestyle.

DEBATE PULLS FOCUS AWAY FROM URGENT CRISES

Sami Nader, an economist at the Saint Joseph University of Beirut, said the throngs at The Glow Paradise belied another reality.

“So you see people in the restaurant, but what you don't see is that 22 restaurants closed last month,” Nader told Reuters.

Lebanon’s Instagram-active community was split between those accusing the restaurant of theft and others saying the sandwich was intended for those who could afford it.

Some questioned whether the dispute itself reflected misplaced priorities in a country grappling with urgent crises, from Israel’s occupation of large swaths of the country’s south to the endemic electricity and water crises.

Lebanon’s 2019 financial collapse was prompted by decades of corruption and profligate spending by the ruling elite, and several rounds of conflict since then have worsened the country’s economic outlook.

GDP has declined by nearly 40% since 2019 and inflation is expected to rise to 17.5% due to rising global energy and shipping prices eating away at people’s purchasing power, according to the World Bank. The figure is more than quadruple the global headline inflation rate flagged by the International Monetary Fund in July.

Four in five households in Lebanon struggle to afford basic necessities, the UN children’s agency said in September.

The country’s middle class has “disappeared,” Nader said, dismantled by a series of crises including the collapse of the financial system in 2019, the 2020 Beirut Port explosion and two wars in under two years.

Monthly bills from private generator operators, which provide electricity to many homes and businesses during outages on Lebanon's failing national grid, jumped by nearly 20% in August 2026 alone, bringing rates nearly 60% higher than they were in February of this year, according to the kilowatt-hour prices set by Lebanon’s energy ministry.

For many, that means paying for 24/7 electricity now costs several hundred dollars a month, in a country where the minimum wage is set at $400.

“Everything has become expensive, and people can’t keep up,” said Fouad Fakhreddine, a 53-year-old restaurant worker from nearby Hamra. “We are now getting paid, then getting in debt over that just to get by.”

The years of economic instability, he said, have produced “a class that is living, and a class that is not dead and waiting to die from the unbearable situation it is in.” REUTERS

#1120. What Are Democrats Prepared to Do if Trump Rigs the Election?

In this week’s Elie v. U.S, our justice correspondent challenges Democrats’ lack of a plan if Trump steals the midterms. Plus: the most racist, and honest, AI add ever.

California Gov. Gavin Newsom speaks while campaigning for New Hampshire Democratic Senate candidate, U.S. Rep. Chris Pappas.

During a speech in New Hampshire, governor of California and presidential hopeful Gavin Newsom warned that Donald Trump is trying to rig the midterm elections. “Trump is not screwing around,” he said. “We know what he’s doing right now. He’s doing it all across the country.” Newsom was referring, in part, to a Department of Justice lawsuit aimed at purging voter rolls in California, a baseless effort targeting 20,000 people Trump says, without evidence, are not citizens.

One might be inclined to chalk up Newsom’s talk to his own campaigning. He was speaking in New Hampshire, after all, not California, and “orange man bad” is going to be a popular applause line at Democratic rallies for the rest of my natural life.

But here are two chilling-ass sentences from a recent article by Washington Post national security expert Noah Robertson:

A small group of U.S. national security officials has been discreetly advising state governments and congressional lawmakers on how to prepare for the possibility that the Trump administration will attempt to interfere in November’s midterm elections, according to people involved in the effort.

The group includes about 10 current and former officials with experience in the Defense Department, some of whom have previously focused on countering authoritarianism abroad.

When you’ve got experts on authoritarianism trying to advise state governments on how to counteract Trump’s efforts to mess with the election, you know you’ve got a very serious problem.

I don’t think I have to convince most people reading this that Trump’s threats to manipulate the election are very real. I’ve been saying it; most of the people you read or watch have been saying it; it’s all over social media. Indeed, almost nobody paying attention to this election thinks it will be on the up-and-up.

The question is, what are we supposed to do about it? And to that, the answers seem scarce to nonexistent. In the WaPo article, Robertson says the secret national security group is trying to “raise awareness” among lawmakers and “harden election protocols” among state boards of election. But most people are already really freaking aware of the threat. And I don’t know how you can harden a voting machine to prevent Trump’s goons from just stealing it, which they might try to do.

I guess I just can’t think of many historical examples of when an authoritarian regime has tried to steal an election and been stopped. What I can think of are situations where an authoritarian regime tried to steal an election, was successful at stealing it, and then, later, that illegitimate regime was overthrown by the people.

But even that situation is rare. Most of the time, the party that steals the election is rewarded with power, even when everybody knows the election was rigged.

Let me put it like this: What do you think the most likely reaction will be should Trump successfully steal the thing we all know he is trying to steal? Will people say, “To the streets! We are going to stop these illegitimate congresspeople from taking their seats in Washington, and we will not go home until new elections are called”? Or will people say, “Ah, well, nevertheless, we should do an autopsy of our poor midterm messaging so we can win the 2028 election”?

We know what Trump is prepared to do. But the operative question is: What is Gavin Newsom prepared to do?

Vivek Ramaswamy might be the worst human being running for public office this cycle. I don’t say that lightly (I’m well aware that Ken Paxton exists), but Ramaswamy’s latest attack ad is honestly the most despicable thing I’ve seen done during a campaign since Trump mocked a reporter for his disability in 2015.

Ramaswamy is running for governor of Ohio against Democrat Amy Acton. Acton has talked about her rough start in life: She grew up poor, was abused by her mother, sexually assaulted by her mother’s husband, and eventually removed from her mother’s custody after that same mother’s husband was charged and indicted for rape. She was 12 at the time.

Ramaswamy’s campaign decided to find the estranged, abusive mom and put her in an ad in which she called Acton a “liar.” Neither Ramaswamy nor Acton’s mother provided any evidence to dispute Acton’s story, much of which is backed up by court records. But Ramaswamy, who is apparently bound by no standard of accuracy or decency, decided to hand the woman a mic anyway.

Acton’s brother, Philip Stearns, corroborated Acton’s story and slammed Ramaswamy in a statement: “It’s not surprising that Vivek Ramaswamy has stooped to such a despicable low as to attempt to turn the sexual abuse Amy endured at twelve years old from our birth mother’s husband into a political talking point.… After he was arrested and Amy and I were removed from their custody, our birth mother stayed married to Amy’s rapist until he died. This desperate, disgusting attack reveals exactly who Vivek Ramaswamy is at his core—a pathetic excuse for a man who is willing to hurt anyone as long as it gets him what he wants.”

Ramaswamy has doubled down on the ad, vowing to keep it running. He said that Acton “has no vision other than to complain about what someone did to her.” In this moment, Ramaswamy has gone from denying that his opponent was raped to mocking her for being raped when she was 12 and talking about it.

I honestly have no words for what Ramaswamy is doing—and I’m supposed to come up with words for a living. It’s disgusting, and it’s disgusting to a degree that I think people who vote for him after this are disgusting too. This is beyond a political question, or a policy question. If you can vote for a person who uses their opponents’ abuser against them, you are a bad person, full stop. There’s no coming back from that. There’s no “Actually I was economically aggrieved.” If an ad like this “works” on you, you are just as terrible as the guy who thought it would work. Either you have a core sense of decency or you don’t.

The Supreme Court granted cert in another case this week, this one aimed at affirmative action—or whatever is left of it. Having largely succeeded at taking opportunities away from college students, the GOP justices have moved on to… fifth graders. I wrote about this latest legal attack.

Microsoft Copilot released a new ad to try to get people to use its AI “assistant,” and, hoo boy, it’s a doozy. The amazing thing about the ad is that the people who made it were actually honest about what AI is all about and how white folks are likely to use it.

The ad features a white guy named “Kyle” who works in a generic corporate office. It opens with him looking enviously at a Black coworker, “Daniel,” who is being praised by his colleagues for his forecast model, which the ad calls “honestly beautiful.” Distressed by all the props Daniel is getting, Kyle starts typing into Copilot; in a blink-and-you’ll-miss-it scroll, we see Kyle typing in “analyze Daniel’s forecast model,” which I suppose is the white, chatbot euphemism for “plagiarize Daniel’s forecast model.” Kyle also asks Copilot to make his model “beautiful.” Smash cut to the next day: All the coworkers are gathered around Kyle—including the only female employee in the frame, who is using a lint roller on Kyle’s suit. Daniel looks on in defeat while the voice-over says, “Kyle is not competitive. It’s not even a contest.”

Suffice it to say that I hate every fucking second of this ad. Like, the kind of hate that makes you reflexively grit your teeth and ball your hand into a fist as if you’re about to get into a fight with your computer screen. The ad has so many levels of gross. There’s the implicit white grievance against the high-performing Black coworker, without which the rest of the ad doesn’t even make sense. There’s the implicit acknowledgement of white male mediocrity; again, the ad doesn’t even make sense unless we all assume that Kyle is not able to produce work on the level that Daniel does. There’s the willingness to do anything to come out on top, even to the point of plagiarizing. And there’s the deep sexism of reducing a woman colleague to a lint cleaner, literally grooming the white male who cheated his way to victory. It’s all so amazingly awful.

It’s also… the most honest thing these people have ever said about AI. The point of AI is not to enhance your own work like the tech-bro mafia keeps insisting. The point of AI is to steal somebody else’s work, potentially everybody else’s work, and pass it off as your own. What the other guy (who happens to be Black) did with talent and hard work, you can do in a day with AI and no skill but metastasizing jealousy. The ad is promoting the fact that AI allows you to be the worst version of yourself.

The mind reels when you think about how many people at Microsoft must have seen and approved this ad before it went live. Then again, sometimes the most dangerous thing a corporation can do is tell the truth.

Before the project can move forward, Volkswagen's supervisory board must grant final approval for the investment

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

The top executive at German carmaker Audi defended on Sunday a proposed $4 billion investment in a new facility in the United States, following an announcement made by President Donald Trump during his campaign for the upcoming November midterm elections.

Audi Chief Executive Gernot Doellner appeared alongside Trump during a campaign event in Perry, close to Macon in central Georgia, on Saturday.

At the event, Trump stated that Audi, a brand under the Volkswagen Group, intends to construct a manufacturing facility in Georgia capable of producing 200,000 SUVs each year.

"This decision was preceded by many months of careful planning and intense negotiations," Doellner informed reporters on Sunday. "If the American president invites you, you accept the invitation. That is what respect for the office and for the country in which we invest demands."

Before the project can move forward, Volkswagen's supervisory board must grant final approval for the investment.

The state of Georgia features closely contested races for its governor and the U.S. Senate.

Trump is seeking to demonstrate that his trade tariffs on foreign automobiles are strengthening the American economy and encouraging domestic manufacturing.

In Germany, those same trade tariffs have heightened strain across European industrial sectors while escalating tensions between Volkswagen executives and labor representatives concerned about potential plant closures and layoffs.

Audi previously stated that Trump's tariffs on automobiles, steel, aluminum, and components cost the business approximately €1.2 billion ($1.4 billion) over the past year, as all of its cars sold in the American market are currently imported from Mexico or Europe.

Opponents of the trade policies argue that the tariffs have likewise harmed the domestic economy in the US by raising vehicle prices for consumers and delaying investment plans across the auto industry.

A spokesperson for Germany's IG Metall union remarked that Doellner's choice to appear alongside Trump amidst the political campaign was "hard to understand.”

"Trump has never failed to make it clear what he is after: he wants to weaken our domestic economy, particularly the automotive sector," the spokesperson said.

Christiane Benner, head of the IG Metall union and Volkswagen's deputy supervisory board chair, noted that establishing a US manufacturing footprint was "right and necessary" to enhance the company's competitive standing. "However, firm prospects for workers at all sites, particularly those here in Germany, must be clearly defined and set out," she said.

Doellner refrained from disclosing full terms of the US investment agreement, declining to confirm whether the deal incorporates tariff relief for the automaker.

Olaf Lies, state premier of Lower Saxony—the German state holding Volkswagen's second-largest ownership stake—remarked that expanding operations in the United States presents a positive prospect only if German employees benefit as well.

"Growth in America must secure jobs and value creation here and must not displace them," he said.

According to Audi, the proposed manufacturing complex will generate around 4,500 jobs. Construction work is slated to begin next year, with vehicle production anticipated to start in the early 2030s.

The facility is expected to produce Audi's Q7, Q8, and Q9 SUV models, according to a US official who spoke to Reuters.

The US official added that Audi further intends to manufacture 25,000 vehicles annually in neighboring South Carolina, with a portion of those models—currently produced in Europe—earmarked for export.

Those additional vehicles are set to be manufactured at a $2 billion facility for Scout Motors, VW's off-road vehicle brand, which is under construction in Blythewood, near Columbia, the state capital, the official stated.

"We regard the region as a key market for profitable growth," Volkswagen CEO Oliver Blume said. "A potential Audi plant in the US would create further conditions for this."

During Saturday's campaign rally, a gold Audi displaying manufacturer license plates was parked outside the event location.

#1122. Sky-high LADWP bills light up social media

This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here.

See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred

Social media and online forums are aflame over higher than usual Los Angeles Department of Water and Power bills, with some customers noting recent charges hundreds of dollars over what they paid in previous billing cycles and years.

Residents are posting bills they call “outrageous,” “insane” and “extremely crazy” as charges for summer use continue to hit mailboxes. Canter’s Deli made headlines when its owners received a $35,700 bill, up almost $11,000 from four months earlier.

Recent increases in sewer and trash fees, plus steadily rising water rates and higher summer water use are partly to blame. But Angelenos’ ire has been especially directed at electricity bills as the extra AC needed during triple-digit heat waves landed people in the utility’s higher-cost tiers, which also have been rising.

Aggressive and impactful reporting on climate change, the environment, health and science.

More than 24,000 people have signed a petition calling for the city to investigate the bills and adjust the tiers. It was started by a San Fernando Valley man who received a $2,115 electric bill for his 2,500-square-foot home that he said he kept at 74 degrees between the months of August and September.

Electric bill sticker shock is common for customers of investor-owned utilities, but less so for municipally owned utilities such as DWP.

Denise Grab, clean-energy project director at UCLA’s Emmett Institute on Climate Change and the Environment, said that over the past three years, Southern California Edison‘s rate for the typical household using 500 kWh per month has risen about 4% while DWP’s has gone up 45%. But Edison still charges about 20% more than DWP.

“They’re closer than they were last year,” when she published a report comparing the two utilities, Grab said. She also expects Edison rates to rise further when wildfire liability from the Eaton fire hits.

DWP says its recent high bills are driven by spiking power use during the record-breaking summer heat, especially for air conditioning, not by rate increases.

Most of its residential customers are in a three-tier price structure that changes seasonally. As people consume more power, they are bumped into Tier 2, where electricity is more expensive, with the highest rates in Tier 3, which is only in effect from June through September. The pricing is designed to encourage people to use less electricity and cover the costs of providing power, DWP said. The utility adjusts the rates based on its costs before billing customers.

“This year was especially difficult,” said Joe Ramallo, chief customer officer at DWP. “It was so much hotter this summer than the prior.”

The city’s independent ratepayer advocate, Timothy O’Connor, agreed that high temperatures were a big driver of the skyrocketing bills, with more people moving into Tier 2 and Tier 3. But he added that rates have also been rising, with sharper increases in recent years as the utility catches up on infrastructure spending at a time when costs have gone up across the board.

DWP controlled its increases pretty well from 2015 to 2023, he said. “Rates were going up, but they indexed really close to inflation.” This year and last, however, rates have gone up “well in excess of inflation,” O’Connor said.

From January 2025 to this October, Tier 1 rates went from 22 cents per kilowatt hour to 27 cents, a 23% increase in a year and a half.

“This spending is core to keeping this utility operational,” O’Connor said, noting it has gone for valuable things like upgrading big transmission lines as well as the more local distribution lines, plus climate initiatives such as switching a coal plant in Utah to run on natural gas, with plans to convert it to hydrogen. Unfortunately the spending comes as climate change drives increasingly extreme heat waves and higher electricity use. “It’s probably only going to get worse,” he said.

A new California law legalizes the plug-in solar panels that are becoming popular in other states and in Europe.

Ramallo said most DWP customers stay within the first two tiers and don’t hit Tier 3, even during heat waves.

There is a lot people can do to control their electricity use in the heat, he said. The utility recommends setting air conditioners to 78 degrees, closing curtains during peak sun hours and using fans to circulate the air. DWP also has payment options to smooth out higher and lower bills, assistance for those who have difficulty paying, and energy efficiency incentives, such as rebates for attic insulation and more efficient equipment, including pool pumps.

Ramallo said Micah Reed, who started the online petition, used six times the power of the median customer, and the utility has offered him an energy efficiency audit, but Reed hasn’t taken them up on it. (“I asked them if they’re going to make that available to every LADWP resident and they have not replied,” said Reed.)

O’Connor said he’d like to see the utility allow more people into the low-income bill assistance program and reduce payments to customers with solar, which he said raise bills for customers across the board. He’d also like to see the utility update its rate structure to better price power based on the times of day when it’s most in demand.

“If we can get policies in place that accurately price energy and reward people based on when they use energy, that would help,” he said. He noted that such rate reform, and boosting assistance to low-income customers in Los Angeles, is made difficult by Proposition 26, which limits the utility’s ability to charge for anything other than the direct cost of providing power.

Reed’s online petition has attracted the attention of city Controller Kenneth Mejia, who said last week that he would investigate.

“The Controller’s Office has received thousands of requests from frustrated Angelenos who are outraged by their unusually high LADWP bills,” Mejia said in a statement. “We are specifically interested in understanding why certain rates have increased, how the Tier structure can trigger significant cost increases, and what more can be done to assist customers with these higher bills during peak seasons.”

On Monday, City Council member and mayoral candidate Nithya Raman held a news conference with Mejia at which she called out the electricity rate increases under Mayor Karen Bass’ tenure and rules that allow the utility to raise rates without City Council review.

“The public deserves transparency about the costs that they are experiencing,” she said, promising that DWP will have to justify its rates in City Council meetings if she is elected.

Bass’ campaign said Raman herself voted to increase sewer and trash fees in 2025.

“Meanwhile, under Mayor Bass, a comprehensive suite of financial assistance, energy efficiency and water conservation programs, specifically designed to support Angelenos with affordability, has been implemented,” spokesperson Alex Stack said.

Experts say the increases are likely to keep coming. A recent presentation of DWP’s long-term power plan modeled rates for electricity reaching 71.1 cents per kWh by 2044.

As for this season, residents probably have another big charge coming, as many have not yet received their September bills reflecting the state’s highest electricity use in four years, and there was another major heat wave in October.

#1125. Manchester City, the UAE and the UK's OM in a political tangle

Nearly 20 years after arriving in England, Manchester City's UAE owners could exit amid cheating charges. That would pose a challenge for a city — and prime minister — closely tied to Abu Dhabi.

Defiance was the word that stood out as Manchester City returned home for the first time since they were found guilty of 114 financial charges by the Premier League in a case that's made headlines around the world.

City showed a measure of it on the pitch, even as they lost 4-2 to holders, Qatari-owned Paris Saint-Germain, in the Champions League group stages on Wednesday.

Among the home fanbase at the Etihad Stadium, DW found universal support for City's Abu Dhabi owners — headed by Sheikh Mansour, who is also UAE's vice president and deputy prime minister.

"I'm all in with the ownership now," said local fan Matt. "If we end up back in League Two [fourth tier], so be it. We've got 15 years of memories we wouldn't have otherwise and to me it's just an accounting line on a spreadsheet really."

The stadium name itself is a reminder of the takeover that changed this club, and its part of Manchester, in 2008. The national airline of the UAE, Etihad's inflated sponsorship of City is among the key planks of the case against them, while many buildings and businesses around the stadium bear the brand. It's a stadium that's also seen plenty of success of late.

"We've seen things other fans will never see," added fellow City fan Josh. "I think people have got to consider how many people this club has given great memories to, how many people's lives have been changed by it, myself included....you've got to be grateful for that."

Though many in sky blue shared those sentiments, most outside the club now view the trophies won in the relevant period as tarnished. On top of that, critics point to City's reticence in providing evidence in their case, the long-documented human rights abuses in UAE and the often dismissive tone with which the owners have dealt with being found guilty of charges they have now appealed.

But those City fans appear to have one powerful ally in British Prime Minister Andy Burnham. Though he has since sought to tone down his position on Mansour and co. somewhat, the former mayor of Greater Manchester said he "would be really concerned to lose them," after the verdict was announced in late September. "They've been such a huge partner in the building of modern Manchester," he added.

While Burnham has since denied being close to City's ownership, even as City were playing on Wednesday, The Guardian reported a club representative was invited on a government-backed trade delegation to India this week by Burnham's successor as Manchester mayor, Bev Craig.

Earlier the same day, Burnham was forced to confirm he had two additional dinners with the club chair, Khaldoon Al Mubarak, at the Etihad Stadium, having previously declared those only as matchday hospitality. It has become a serious domestic issue for the man who replaced Keir Starmer in July.

What is clear is that Burnham welcomed Abu Dhabi investment during his time in charge of the northwestern city. This came mainly in the form of residential and commercial buildings as well as libraries and sports centers, all popping up in previously run-down areas in and around the stadium.

Georgina Blakeley, a Professor at the University of Huddersfield who wrote a book called "The regeneration of east Manchester," told DW that UAE investment has transformed swathes of the city.

"One of the prime drivers for building this partnership with the Abu Dhabi United Group [a private equity arm of the state mostly concerned with the football club] was that at that point in time, 2014, there was no other private investor willing to invest at the scale that the council wanted. And to do so in a way that created a build-to-rent market," she said.

The UAE investment in Manchester, accelerated by the Manchester Life Partnership with the city's council signed in 2014, has been a key defense for the City owners and fans when faced with sportswashing allegations in the past. And while Blakeley believes councils in the UK are often forced to seek foreign investment, there has been some pushback on how east Manchester has changed.

"A lot of people would be critical of some of the developments in [the districts of] Ancoats and New Islington and say that it's gentrified the area and there are some tensions between newer populations coming in and living in the more expensive flats and those already there. I think there's some truth to it. But I also think there's some truth to the fact that people forget really, really quickly that if you go back to just the 1990s, Ancoats was a no-go area," she said.

While profit for both council and state have certainly been a driver of the partnership, Blakeley thinks that forging greater links to the community could be something City's owners see "as a beneficial side effect."

After 18 years in the club and city, the UAE are deeply embedded in this part of Manchester. With political ties between the UK and UAE now reportedly strained as a result of the charges, there are suggestions that City's owners will try to sell the club. They may also be forced to do so, with sanctions still to be decided pending City's appeal.

There is no such trouble at PSG, who look capable of winning a third straight Champions League powered by their own Gulf-State coffers.

What is clear is that state-owned football clubs can become successful fast in a free market, as the Premier League was when the UAE owners arrived. Deep pockets, strong contacts at the top tables of the sport and canny strategies to integrate with the local area can be a heady mix.

It's certainly one that's proved intoxicating to City's fans, who brush off secret second contracts, sham sponsorship and unreliable witnesses with a loyalty built on success, community and investment. Judging by the mood in Manchester on Wednesday, no sanctions are going to change that.

#1126. Explainer-How Ukraine's strikes on Russian energy sites deepened the rift with Trump

Sign up now: Get ST's newsletters delivered to your inbox

WASHINGTON, Oct 25 - Relations between US President Donald Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy took a sharp downward turn in recent weeks, with each leader openly criticizing the other. The two have long had a testy relationship, but Trump's frustration over Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy infrastructure triggered a crisis that Kyiv's supporters fear could threaten vital US support going forward.

WHAT IS THE HISTORY OF TRUMP-ZELENSKIY TENSIONS?

Trump has been skeptical of US involvement in Ukraine ever since his first term when, shortly after taking office in early 2017, he was asked to provide lethal aid to Ukraine and approved the sale of Javelin missiles to Kyiv.

“Everyone around him wanted him to do it, and they pushed him hard and he eventually signed off on selling them Javelins, very reluctantly,” said a former senior Trump administration official, who spoke on condition of anonymity. “He didn’t consider it a core US interest. It was a European issue.”

Trump's first major encounter with Zelenskiy came in a July 2019 phone call in which the Republican president asked the Ukrainian leader to investigate his Democratic rival Joe Biden and his son Hunter, in exchange for military support Congress had authorized.

That episode led to Trump's first impeachment. Biden beat Trump in the 2020 presidential election.

Trump also has fostered a relationship with Russian President Vladimir Putin that runs against the norms of US foreign policy but echoes his warm ties with authoritarian leaders Xi Jinping of China and North Korea's leader Kim Jong Un.

“Trump has always wanted better relations with Russia,” the former official said.

WHAT DEEPENED THE RIFT BETWEEN THE TWO LEADERS?

Trump's current frustration centers on Kyiv's attacks on Russian diesel infrastructure.

Diesel prices have hit record highs since the US and Israel launched a war against Iran in February, and global energy costs spiked. US lawmakers in Trump's Republican party face voter anger over inflation ahead of the November 3 midterm elections.

On September 13, Trump began publicly calling on Ukraine to stop targeting diesel infrastructure. The following week, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Washington was also concerned that Ukraine had hit US-linked oil shipments.

Ukraine has refused to halt the strikes, saying its long-range drone campaign is its only viable response to nearly five years of Russian bombardment. Moscow was forced in July to ban diesel exports as part of a raft of measures to address domestic fuel shortages.

Angered by Zelenskiy’s defiance, Trump on October 9 announced a deal to buy diesel from Moscow, issuing a temporary general license that allows Russian diesel to reach the global market. He also waived sanctions on Russia authorized by a bill he signed into law in September.

Suriya Jayanti, a former US official who runs a power sector company in Ukraine, said Russia’s strikes on Ukraine’s power grid have increased, despite Trump unilaterally announcing an energy ceasefire on October 11.

"It is clear to everyone in Kyiv that the goal is not actually an energy ceasefire, but it is really just an effort to hobble Ukraine and give Russia a decisive advantage," said Jayanti, who is also a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council think tank.

HAS THE US THREATENED TO CUT OFF SUPPORT TO UKRAINE?

Zelenskiy has said Ukrainian military officials had been threatened by US counterparts, who said continuing the energy strikes would lead the US to cut off intelligence sharing. A US official familiar with the situation disputed Kyiv's account.

Speaking on condition of anonymity, the US official said there has been no increase in pressure on Ukraine.

“We don't have to pressure Zelenskiy. If he wants to make a deal he'll make a deal. I think Putin is putting a ton of pressure on him and he (Zelenskiy) is putting some pressure on Russia but Russia doesn't seem to be minding it as much even though they are getting hit."

On Thursday, Trump said he had asked SpaceX CEO Elon Musk to restore Ukraine’s access to the company's Starlink satellite system. Starlink's disruption temporarily hampered Kyiv's military drone operations and spurred fears that Kyiv would be left defenseless against Russia's attacks going into the winter.

WHAT IS THE STATUS OF MOSCOW-KYIV PEACE TALKS?

Peace efforts have continued but so far have not yielded tangible results.

At talks in Oslo on October 20, Ukraine presented new proposals, and Trump’s son-in-law and envoy Jared Kushner repeated Trump's demand that Ukraine stop attacking Russian diesel refineries.

The next day, envoy Witkoff – a close friend of Trump's - met Putin in St. Petersburg. Putin agreed to release detained American Stephen Hubbard in what the two countries called a goodwill gesture.

Zelenskiy said on Friday that negotiators from Ukraine, Russia and the US would meet in Abu Dhabi in the first half of November, a possible precursor to a meeting of the three countries’ leaders. The last US-mediated peace talks took place in February. REUTERS

Sacha Baron Cohen comedy character Ali G left Noel Gallagher red-faced as he dragged him out of his seat at the cinema on Saturday night.

The Oasis legend, 59, felt the wrath of his character at a screening of Sacha's new mockumentary, Ali G: Who Iz I?, which released on Friday.

Noel came face to face with the character and was mocked for his 'sad' Oasis reunion as he sat down to watch the movie alongside his partner Nina Johnson.

In a video shared on the official Instagram account for Ali G, he shouted at Noel: 'Iz you got a ticket? Get up! Get up, get up,' before pulling him out of his chair.

Standing opposite Noel, Ali G quipped: 'Oh, you look like what's his name? One of them Oasis twins, innit. It's Nigel Gallagher, innit?

'50-year-old white man, trying to make a comeback after 20 years, so sad!'

Ali G later pointed to Noel's girlfriend Nina and said: 'Is this your girlfriend? Is this your girlfriend?'

Sacha Baron Cohen comedy character Ali G left Noel Gallagher red-faced as he dragged him out of his seat at the cinema on Saturday night (source: Ali G/ Instagram)

The Oasis legend, 59, felt the wrath of his character at a screening of Sacha's new mockumentary, Ali G: Who Iz I?, which released on Friday (source: Ali G/ Instagram)

When Noel confirmed she was, Ali said: 'Not anymore she ain't. Hello sweetness, what's your name?'

Sacha's alter ego later left Noel and his girlfriend Nina to relax while he addressed the whole audience before the film began rolling.

The film has polarised viewers, earning a 50 per cent 'rotten' critics rating on reviews aggregator site Rotten Tomatoes.

Ali G: Who Iz I? charts the wannabe gangster's life 'since the world went to crap' as he prepares to welcome his first child with girlfriend Julie, played by Morgana Robinson, 44.

There have been calls to boycott the film over claims that Ali G is offensive for perpetuating stereotypes, with Baron Cohen revealing his life was threatened.

Yet the actor has been praised for 'pushing comedy to its limits', with The Times' Ed Potton awarding the film four stars and noting: 'The plot of the film is shamelessly flimsy and not all of the gags land, but when they do they are hilarious.'

Nick Schager of The Daily Beast also praised the film with a 'fresh' rating on Rotten Tomatoes, penning: 'Despite its inherent limitations and more than a handful of easy-target gags, it’s always mildly amusing and, on a couple of memorable occasions, legitimately laugh-out-loud funny.'

Noel came face to face with the character and was mocked for his 'sad' Oasis reunion as he sat down to watch the movie alongside his partner Nina Johnson (source: Ali G/ Instagram)

Ali G: Who Iz I? has been praised for 'pushing comedy to its limits' but not everyone is a fan as Sacha Baron Cohen's mockumentary on cancel culture receives mixed reviews

Another 'fresh' rating came from The Hollywood Reporter's Frank Scheck, who noted: 'Cohen is so naturally funny and quick with improvisation that there are plenty of laughs along the way.

'And while much of the material is offensive, that’s really the point. But the humour starts to drag with the feature-length running time.'

Not won over by Ali G was The Guardian's Peter Bradshaw, who awarded the film two stars, saying: 'If you liked Sacha Baron Cohen’s Ali G the first time around, you’ll like this less; if you disliked it, you’ll dislike this more; if you suspected it was racist, you’ll be more emboldened to say so – especially as Baron Cohen has dreamed up a whole new character apparently to pre-empt and mock precisely that objection.'

Two stars was also the verdict of Empire's Helen O’Hara, who noted: 'He has a few gently funny scenes – a polite and remarkably chill estate agent is a welcome antidote to all the weirdness and bombast – but too much of the first and second act feel like they’re treading water and, importantly, not always punching up.'

The same rating came from Tim Robey of The Telegraph, who mused: 'A couple of decades since Baron Cohen’s career-launching rude boy was last at large, he has contrived a comeback that delivers only scattered laughs and stray bursts of inspiration; the whole thing has the feel of a strained stunt.'

On the fence with a three star review was Time Out's Phil de Semlyen, who wrote: 'The results of this second Ali G movie are as scattergun as you might expect from Staines’s thinly sketched white-boy wannabe rapper.'

Three stars also came from The Financial Times' Danny Leigh, who said: 'Baron Cohen has long prized his own fearlessness.

'Here, he seems weirdly jumpy – speaking up for humanist harmony in character, as if hopeful it will make a difference.'

The polarising reviews for Ali G: Who Iz I? follow calls for the mockumentary to be banned in UK cinemas, with a sinister campaign being launched amid claims the film and character are 'enforcing racist stereotypes', with the Daily Mail exposing how AI was used as a part of the campaign.

However, Baron Cohen has insisted that Ali G being 'outdated and problematic' is precisely why he believes it is time to reprise the role.

The British star has expressed concern about growing political polarisation and the normalisation of extreme views, arguing that the prejudices his characters expose have been amplified by social media and, increasingly, AI.

Speaking to The Hollywood Reporter about his decision to revive Ali G, he explained: 'Because I'm terrified of where our society is headed, and the way I can comment on that is through my comedy.

'I wanted to show the extremism on both sides of the political spectrum and the danger of virtuous violence. And obviously we wanted to make the funniest film that's ever been made.'

Baron Cohen also touched on the importance of making 'dangerous' films because of the rise of AI and the 'lies spread by social media'.

The final scene in the upcoming film is a continuous shot filmed across 12 different locations, which includes gunfire, a medical procedure, drones and explosions.

The new film charts Ali G's life 'since the world went to crap' as he prepares to welcome his first child with girlfriend Julie, played by Morgana Robinson, 44

He recalled being told by one of the 'great stuntmen' working on the film that he would be hospitalised due to the intense climate while filming.

But Baron Cohen insisted that it needed to be done, telling the publication: 'These really are the hardest movies to make, but I suppose I made it because I’m scared of this world of conspiracies and lies that are spread by social media and now by AI.

'If we don’t have these shared facts, then democracies crumble and we can’t have a tolerant society. And to make people laugh is therapy.'

In a recent interview, he said the character is 'designed to expose prejudice'.

Baron Cohen wrote for Time magazine: 'The fact that Ali G is outdated and problematic is the very reason I resurrected him.

'All the prejudices my characters are designed to expose haven't just lingered –they've metastasised.

'They're fuelled by the greatest propaganda machine in history – social media – and now by its monstrous child, AI.'

He claimed that in 2026 'ignorance reigns and truth is inverted'.

Criticism for the Amazon MGM film has been widespread.

A day after the trailer's release in August, NewsCord, a UK news comparison and media monitoring platform, started a campaign urging cinemas around the world to refuse to screen the film.

The campaign group have said they emailed 15 major chains globally with the request on behalf of those who register.

At the time, NewsCord had reached a total of 44,946, with an explanation for the campaign reading: 'On 11 January 2000 the Guardian reported the verdict of Black British comedians under the headline "Comics find Ali G is an alibi for racism"...

'Jeanette Winterson: "I don't know what the difference is between him and the Black and White Minstrels".'

A defiant Baron Cohen also addressed the growing backlash, writing on X: 'In an age where a comedian's career can be ended by a single un-PC joke, I thought I'd play it safe and bring this guy back.'
