#1172. The full truth about JFK Jr and Carolyn Bessette's plane wreck is finally revealed: The heartbreaking details redacted from the report… and how close officials came to calling off the search

By CAPTAIN RUSS WEBSTER FOR THE DAILY MAIL

Published: 20:39 GMT, 25 October 2026 | Updated: 23:09 GMT, 25 October 2026

As darkness fell on the night of July 16, 1999, John F Kennedy Jr climbed into the cockpit of his Piper Saratoga II.

The avid flyer was taking his wife of nearly three years, Carolyn Bessette, to his cousin's wedding in the Massachusetts village of Hyannis Port, dropping off Carolyn's sister Lauren in Martha's Vineyard on the way.

About an hour after taking off from the Essex Country Airport in New Jersey, tragedy struck, with Kennedy, 38, becoming disoriented, losing control of the plane and plummeting downwards in what experts call a 'graveyard spiral.'

The crash, just seven and a quarter miles off the southwest tip of Martha's Vineyard, killed Kennedy, Carolyn, 33, and Lauren, 34, on impact, the wreckage settling 116 feet beneath the surface on the ocean floor.

Captain W Russell 'Russ' Webster was one of the first on the scene after getting word of the Kennedy heir's missing plane. Because the crash happened in his area of responsibility as Coast Guard Commander of Group Woods Hole on the western edge of Cape Cod, Webster served as Incident Commander for Operations of the grueling five-day mission – the largest search-and-rescue operation for private citizens in a small-aircraft crash in US history.

Twenty-seven years later, his full account of those days is detailed through The Last Flight: The Untold Story of the Search for JFK Jr and the Race Against the Atlantic, written with his historian wife Theresa Mitchell Webster.

In this exclusive excerpt, he describes how the Coast Guard, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), and the Navy worked together to find the plane wreck site. Then began the seemingly impossible search for its passengers.

Amid talks of calling off the operation, they were finally found, with rescuers undertaking the heartbreaking and extremely delicate mission to recover the three victims, and respectfully bury them at sea.

JFK Jr and his wife Carolyn were killed instantly in the crash

Wreckage of the single-engine Saratoga settled 116 feet beneath the surface on the ocean floor

Senator Ted Kennedy, in a red-and-white-striped short-sleeved polo shirt and a life jacket, watches intently as the divers descend, his face inscrutable.

His adamant request is that Navy divers raise John, Carolyn, and Lauren at the same time – that way his nephew isn't perceived as receiving special treatment, even in death.

Once at the wreck, the divers are on a strict timetable. Walking the Atlantic floor stirs up silt, further compromising low visibility. But sunrays filtering through the 116-foot water column provide a bit of natural light as they descend into the Atlantic.

JFK Jr is on his side on the ocean floor near his wrecked Saratoga.

The divers, with care and reverence, lift his remains and bring him to where the body bags are stowed on the Navy's salvage basket.

It is then that they discover that Kennedy's legs are missing – or that's what they report up the chain, according to retired Navy diver Josh Benjamins.

Whatever the circumstance, the divers still must do their job.

There is little light 116 feet below the surface, and divers can hardly see. But skilled as they are, they undo the tape affixing the rolled-up body bags to the basket. Next, they unroll one of the bags, laying it flat on the seafloor. The zipper extends the full length of the bag and is carefully opened.

Finally, once the top of the bag is opened, Kennedy is lowered into it. The bag is lifted and secured at four points.

It's time to recover the Bessette sisters.

Together, the divers walk through rising sandy silt, again with limited light, toward the fuselage to retrieve Carolyn and Lauren.

Both women's bodies are intact but badly damaged and horribly so. (Later, a witness at the autopsies, Frank Ciaccio of the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB), would only say that Carolyn and Lauren 'were not facially recognizable.')

The impact of the crash forced the backs of their seats to fold in forward over them.

Ted Kennedy aboard the USS Grasp on Wednesday morning, July 21, 1999, being briefed by Lieutenant Commander Eric Anderson

The wreckage of JFK Jr's plane was pulled from the water

The rescue team fought the tides and the weather to recover the beloved son of a slain president and his passengers (photographed: John and Carolyn in January 1997)

The divers pry the seats back, slowly, then cut the seat belts. They can't tell which sister is which except by hair color. Lauren is a brunette, Carolyn an unmistakable blonde.

In a high-impact collision, this is not an unexpected outcome. Out of respect for the Kennedy and Bessette families, we leave further descriptions unsaid.

The first sister is lifted from her seat and, using a fireman's shoulder carry, her diver exits the fuselage, slowly and with great care, and walks toward the salvage basket.

He returns to the basket and, together with another diver, retrieves the second sister and places her into a body bag.

It's zipped, slowly, methodically. Both sisters are finally secured, together at last.

But before the basket reaches the surface, the Navy's Jeff Pauls informs Senator Kennedy about the suspected condition of his nephew's remains.

The uncertainty unsettles all. Will the other half of his body – if the impact had indeed cut JFK Jr in half – rise on its own?

Then the dive team and the basket holding the deceased ascend into daylight. All three victims are together in the salvage basket, just as Senator Kennedy had insisted. For the first time in days, JFK Jr, Carolyn, and Lauren are above the waterline.

It will be a few hours before a second dive team descends to attempt to raise the fuselage and engine.

In Pocasset, north of Woods Hole, the afternoon slides into early evening.

Three men – and only those three – are in a small, cream-tiled room at the aging Barnstable County Hospital, site of the medical examiner's office.

There, a pathologist, a Massachusetts State Police photographer, and Frank Ciaccio of the NTSB are present for the autopsies.

The medical examiner is methodical in his work during the four-hour autopsy procedures. There is very little talking; they discuss only what is essential.

Captain Webster coordinates the exit strategy meeting with Rear Admiral Richard M Larrabee (hand on chin), NTSB Chairman Jim Hall, and NTSB Managing Director Pete Goelz (leaning on table)

Deep sea Navy divers prepare to descend 116 feet to the Atlantic floor to retrieve the remains of John, Carolyn, and Lauren

As Coast Guard Commander of Group Woods Hole on the western edge of Cape Cod, Webster (left) served as Incident Commander for Operations

'There is no other extenuating conversation going on in the room, compared to other cases that I have worked on,' remembers Ciaccio. 'In all my years of doing autopsies and everything, this was probably one of the most solemn I was ever a part of.'

It is determined that John, Carolyn, and Lauren were killed instantly from numerous traumatic injuries when the Saratoga slammed into the Atlantic.

Toxicology tests on JFK Jr reveal no alcohol or drug use.

'You never want to make these things personal,' adds Ciaccio. 'But I think what made this very difficult for a lot of us is what we knew of the person. The two others in the room told me afterward they visualized this little boy saluting his father, the president, when he had died. It was very solemn. We knew what our job was.'

The question of the condition of Kennedy's body has been answered yet remains controversial.

The story I was told at the time of the tragedy was that JFK Jr's legs were folded up into his chest cavity, and this was revealed during the medical examiner's autopsy.

Others concur. 'The report I received was that he had been jammed up, so that he was basically compressed from the impact. But everything was there. It was just mashed together,' says the USS Grasp's commanding officer, Eric Anderson. [Grasp was the Navy rescue and salvage ship that led recovery operations.]

The NTSB's forensic anthropologist, Frank Ciaccio, as noted before, witnessed the autopsies: 'I will tell you 100 percent that [the report that Kennedy's legs were missing] is false. His legs were not severed.

'His legs were in fact fragile and hanging on by tendons and muscles. But they were not amputated at all.'

This account differs from that of Navy diver Josh Benjamins.

Benjamins is one of two divers on the second plunge a few hours after the three deceased were respectfully recovered.

According to Benjamins, he and his diving partner are briefed by the master diver during the safety check process. The two are tasked with retrieving the plane wreckage and the engine. Unofficially, however, they are to undertake 'a quick search for the legs.'

A flag flies at half staff at the Kennedy Compound in Hyannis Port on July 19, 1999

The public mourned the deaths, creating a makeshift shrine outside their apartment building in New York

Family members embrace at the burial service

Benjamins says the first set of divers did a quick check but didn't see any body parts.

Benjamins and his partner descend. They first search for human limbs. Finding none, the divers set to work hoisting the fuselage and, minutes later, the engine.

Benjamins insists, even after all these years, that what he had heard that day was that '[Kennedy's] torso up was all they had' before he was placed in the body bag.

'They both [the divers below] had actual physical hands on him, and they both had done multiple body jobs before. They went on record saying, "We know for sure that only his upper half was recovered,"' Benjamins will recall.

From Tuesday through Thursday, Navy divers continue to recover items at the wreck site, Benjamins recalls. This is to be the Navy's last plunge in recovery efforts.

Always in pairs, this last set of divers goes for the larger remnants first: bits of wreckage like parts of the wings. When big items are placed in the salvage basket, the divers reach for smaller things, digging through sand and silt in the low light. They come up with watch bands and CDs and hats.

Something else is discovered: a chunk of scalp tightly wrapped around an air diving hose. Benjamins, then a mere 23 years old, is manning the communications microphone when word of the discovery reaches him.

'Hey, Topside, we have this substantial size scalp with long blonde hair wrapped around our umbilical [the communications hose that acted like a lifeline to above]. What do we do?'

Benjamins recalls turning to a senior diver and relaying the message.

'No, you didn't,' is the reply – in other words, no, you didn't see anything of the kind.

The divers untangle the tissue and convey the locks to the currents.

'So, in all our wisdom mindset, [we thought] what was the difference? They did a ceremony, they put them at sea, let them go to sea.'

The last physical part of Carolyn remaining on Earth had its own burial at sea the same day her ashes were conveyed to the nearby depths.

Taken from The Last Flight by Captain W Russell 'Russ' Webster and Theresa Mitchell Webster. Copyright © 2026 by William Russell Webster and Theresa Mitchell Webster. Used by permission of Harper Select, an imprint of HarperCollins Focus, LLC.

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

The renewed fighting in Yemen has shattered a UN-brokered truce that had largely held since 2022

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Saudi Arabia reported that two terminals at its primary airport reopened on Sunday, despite threats from Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis to continue targeting the hub, which they branded a "military target".

Operations at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh were suspended on October 10 after a Houthi-claimed assault left 13 people dead, marking the kingdom’s deadliest attack in over a decade.

Riyadh stated that it intercepted another barrage of drones and missiles on Sunday as hostilities with the militant group continued unabated.

Houthi forces claimed responsibility for targeting the aviation hub along with additional locations across the kingdom, including Jazan and Khamis Mushait.

It remains unconfirmed whether these actions corresponded to the strikes Saudi Arabia claimed to have blocked.

This conflict has become an increasingly destabilizing element in the US-Israeli offensive against Iran, turning American ally Saudi Arabia into a pressure point in the wider war.

Following the kingdom's declaration of a partial resumption of operations, Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree declared the hub would "never be safe" and urged airlines, airport staff and travelers not to use it.

Late on Saturday, the airport announced Terminal 1 would be designated for domestic flights and Terminal 2 for international flights operated by national carriers starting Sunday.

Despite the announcement, flight tracking data from Flightradar24 showed little traffic at the airport on Sunday.

The Saudi-led coalition said earlier this month that the Houthis had carried out 20 attacks on the airport between October 1 and 11.

Saudi civil defense stated on Sunday that shrapnel from two intercepted Houthi ballistic missiles over Khamis Mushait and Ahad Rafidah injured two people and damaged residential buildings and vehicles.

Civil defense authorities earlier issued emergency alerts for Riyadh and the cities of Abha, Khamis Mushait, Jazan and Najran on Sunday, before saying minutes later that the danger had passed.

The coalition reported two drones and a ballistic missile launched toward Riyadh, alongside a cruise missile aimed at Khamis Mushait. It subsequently stated it intercepted 10 ballistic missiles fired toward southern Saudi Arabia.

The Houthis stated they attacked the airport and Saudi oil facilities on Saturday. Kingdom authorities did not comment directly on the Houthi statements.

Saudi Arabia has intensified its strikes against the Houthis after the group seized strategic territory along the Red Sea coast last month, closing in on the Bab el-Mandeb Strait – a global maritime chokepoint and shipping route for Gulf oil producers on the opposite side of the Arabian Peninsula to the Strait of Hormuz.

The renewed fighting in Yemen has shattered a UN-brokered truce that had largely held since 2022. Saudi Arabia intervened in Yemen's civil war in 2015 at the head of a coalition supporting the internationally recognized government, after the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa a year earlier.

#1175. How the death of two CIA agents in northern Mexico led to a treason case

This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here.

MEXICO CITY — The deaths of two CIA agents in April following an operation to dismantle a drug lab in northern Mexico have led to the unusual federal charge of “treason” against a former Chihuahua state attorney general. He is also accused in state court of “illegal exercise of public office.”

The defendant, César Jáuregui, is being held in pretrial detention at a maximum-security prison for allegedly authorizing the agents’ participation in the operation. President Claudia Sheinbaum said her administration neither authorized it nor was informed of it.

The deaths of the U.S. officials in an opposition-led state fueled speculation about the scope of the Trump administration’s actions on Mexican soil. It also called into question Sheinbaum’s strong defense of national sovereignty and her refusal to arrest a former governor from her own party accused of drug trafficking by the United States.

According to Héctor Villasana, one of Jáuregui’s defense attorneys, the prosecution’s argument is that an “exemplary punishment” against his client was necessary to prevent a situation in which “the United States could carry out an action similar to the one it undertook in Venezuela when it removed President [Nicolás] Maduro.”

According to sources familiar with the operation, the raid of a clandestine drug lab involved four CIA agents, raising questions about the scope of the agency’s activity in Mexico.

The U.S. State Department told the Associated Press that it is aware and watching Jáuregui’s case but didn’t make a link between the case and the CIA deaths.

These are some key points on how a traffic accident in the mountains of Chihuahua led to a charge of treason — a crime Mexico has not successfully brought to trial in decades despite one recent attempt.

On April 19, the Chihuahua Attorney General’s Office reported the dismantling of a synthetic drug lab in the municipality of Morelos, in the mountains of that state. On the way back, a vehicle in the convoy veered off the road and fell into a ravine. Two state agents and two Americans were killed.

The Federal Security Cabinet reported the dismantling of laboratories there during a joint operation by the state prosecutor’s office and the army but did not provide details.

The operation ended without any arrests because the criminals fled.

According to the federal prosecutor’s office, Jáuregui endangered national security for allegedly authorizing the participation of U.S. agents in the field operation, a decision that only the federal government can make. Experts say it is a political decision ahead of the 2027 Mexican midterm elections.

The crime could carry from 5 to 40 years in prison and is very difficult to prove.

Carlos Pérez Ricart, a professor at the Mexican university CIDE and author of the book “A Hundred Years of Spies and Drugs,” said that even if the case is ultimately dismissed, its public impact is huge.

Revelations about the presence of CIA agents at a drug raid are causing an uproar in Mexico

Trump has repeatedly said Mexico isn’t doing enough against the cartels. The Mexican political debate centers on whether Sheinbaum’s Morena party is properly defending national sovereignty or whether there is a “narco-government,” as opponents of the National Action Party (PAN) that rules Chihuahua claim.

All this debate “sends a very bad signal to Washington” because Mexico is talking about a treason case while the discussion should center on “more or better” collaboration with the U.S., Pérez Ricart said.

Samuel González, a former chief prosecutor for organized crime and an analyst, said that Jáuregui may have failed to fulfill his obligations by not informing the federal government or by allowing the foreign agents to carry weapons in violation of the law — as Sheinbaum confirmed Thursday. But “even if that were the case, it would not constitute treason,” a wartime crime.

Luis Villegas, the former prosecutor’s defense coordinator, said it was unacceptable for the federal prosecution to compare the presence of the agents to a foreign “invasion.”

Villegas said that the two Americans who died were officials providing training related to intelligence and drones. U.S. Ambassador Ronald Johnson stated that they were “embassy personnel.” The AP later confirmed that they were CIA agents.

According to Jáuregui’s defense team, the federal prosecutor’s office said the agents were close to the person who led the operation, the Chihuahua investigations chief who was one of two deceased Mexicans.

The day of the operation there were two other U.S. agents in the convoy traveling in another vehicle, who were later expelled from the country. The president said none of them had permission to operate in Mexico and that the military was unaware of the foreigners’ presence.

The next day, Sheinbaum said she was unaware of the operation. Jáuregui clarified that the Americans had joined the group after the operation.

The presence of U.S. agencies in Mexico has been a constant for decades, although former President Andrés Manuel López Obrador (2018–2024) limited their activities, and Sheinbaum amended the Constitution to prohibit field operations without the express authorization and cooperation of the Mexican government. The law does not allow members of U.S. agencies to be armed.

Pérez Ricart, the professor, said that, beyond official relations, there have always been anti-drug agents involved in operations of this kind, “often without the federal government’s knowledge.”

“These actions happen, have happened and will continue to happen because they are based on U.S. trust with state or local officials and facilitate ongoing collaboration,” he said.

“However, since there are no clear rules, they can lead to abuses.”

#1177. Trump officials warn decades-long decline among American men could carry national security consequences

Adm. Brian Christine tells Fox News Digital how the Trump administration is tackling declining testosterone levels among American men and addressing broader concerns about men's health and military readiness.

The Trump administration is targeting testosterone deficiency as a potential threat to military readiness, rolling out new screening guidelines for male service members amid growing concerns about the health of American men and the shrinking pool of young people qualified to serve.

"There is absolutely national defense readiness ramifications for [low testosterone]," Adm. Brian Christine, a senior Department of Health and Human Services official, told Fox News Digital in an interview.

Christine also pointed to broader health challenges facing the military's recruiting pool, warning that 77% of Americans ages 17 to 24 do not qualify for service without a waiver, with obesity, chronic disease and other barriers contributing to the problem.

THE REAL REASON BEHIND HEGSETH'S VIRAL MILITARY TESTOSTERONE SCREENING ORDER

Among young men, he said, more than 70% are ineligible, while only about 3% of young Americans express interest in serving.

The warning comes as the Trump administration places a renewed emphasis on military readiness, with Christine helping shape an initiative that led the Pentagon to issue testosterone deficiency screening guidelines for male service members ages 30 and older in September.

Senior military leaders listen as U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth speaks at Marine Corps Base Quantico Sept. 30, 2025, in Quantico, Va. (robynmac)

Trump entered his second term with an aggressive approach to rebuilding the American military, tightening fitness requirements, axing DEI policies, overhauling weapons acquisition, building up recruitment and refocusing the force on combat readiness and lethality.

Christine, a urologist who spent more than 35 years specializing in men's health, said testosterone levels have been declining for decades, raising concerns about the long-term health of American men and the physical demands placed on those serving in uniform.

"I think it's incredibly important, incredibly timely," Christine said of the screening guidance.

Under the Pentagon's guidelines, male service members ages 30 and older undergo mandatory screening for testosterone deficiency, beginning with an assessment of symptoms and risk factors, with further testing and potential treatment available when medically appropriate.

'WOKE' MILITARY ACADEMIES TARGETED IN NEW BLUEPRINT FOR SWEEPING WARFIGHTING OVERHAUL

President Donald Trump speaks during a visit with Michigan Air National Guard troops April 29, 2025, at Selfridge Air National Guard Base in Michigan. (Scott Olson/Getty Images)

"We're not forcing testosterone on anybody," Christine said. "But what we are doing is screening, taking those men who are symptomatic and have low numbers and offering them a pathway forward."

The HHS official pointed to obesity and chronic disease as established factors associated with low testosterone, while raising concerns that environmental exposures, including microplastics and other toxins, could also be contributing to the decline, a possibility researchers are still investigating.

"In the mid-1970s, the average testosterone level for men in this country ... was well over 650. Now it's approaching 350," Christine said.

POPULAR WEIGHT LOSS DRUGS LINKED TO UNEXPECTED MALE FERTILITY BENEFIT

National Institutes of Health Director Jay Bhattacharya echoed those concerns in a separate interview with Fox News Digital, warning that some testosterone deficiency may be going undiagnosed even as medical guidelines stress that a diagnosis requires both symptoms and consistently low hormone levels.

"It's interesting because if you look at the epidemiological trends, testosterone levels in the American male population have been declining over the last decades. And, again, we don't know why. We don't have an answer," Bhattacharya said.

Bhattacharya said researchers must determine not only why testosterone levels are declining, but also what medical guidance should follow for men diagnosed with a deficiency.

"There are under-diagnosed testosterone deficiencies," he said.

"The question of what to do about it, how to prevent it, that's at the top of my mind."

LONGER LIVES, WORSE HEALTH? SCIENTISTS UNCOVER TROUBLING TREND ACROSS GENERATIONS

Pete Hegseth led a record-breaking push-up charge at Navy's football game Oct. 4, 2025. (Department of War)

The NIH director also pointed to declining sperm counts as another area requiring further scientific investigation, suggesting that environmental exposures could be contributing to broader reproductive health concerns.

"But even more importantly, what are the factors, probably environmental factors, that have led to the decline in sperm counts, for instance? We need an answer to those questions," Bhattacharya said.

Bhattacharya said the NIH is investing in research to better understand the potential causes of those trends and determine how doctors should advise American men.

Christine said that testosterone is about more than muscle growth or physical appearance, arguing that hormone levels play an important role in men's overall health.

DEMS ROASTED FOR COMPARING HEGSETH'S TESTOSTERONE INITIATIVE TO 'GENDER-AFFIRMING CARE'

President Donald Trump, center, salutes passing troops during a parade to honor the Army's 250th anniversary, coinciding with Trump's 79th birthday June 14, 2025, in Washington. (Doug Mills/The New York Times via AP, Pool)

"Testosterone levels in men are absolutely related to their overall well-being, to their lifespan, to their health span and to their wellness," Christine said.

He also noted that men with low testosterone tend to experience higher rates of anxiety and depression.

The administration is also developing separate hormonal health guidance for female service members, which the Defense Health Agency said would follow the September guidelines issued for male troops, with women's health specialists contributing to the recommendations, Christine said.

Christine said the goal is ensuring that service members are equipped to perform their duties while addressing broader health challenges affecting American men.

"If we truly want our men who are in uniform to be at their best," Christine said, the focus must be on their ability to function and perform their jobs.

Ashley J. DiMella reports on politics for Fox News Digital.

The clarification establishes an absolute prohibition on transferring polling station turnout data to political entities.

Speaking on Channel 14, Netanyahu said, "This supposed rivalry between us is all nonsense," attacking Channel 12 and saying, "I keep looking for the times when they report the truth. It almost never happens."

Yashar party chairman Gadi Eisenkot warned that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu would do whatever it takes to remain in power, urging voters not to take political change for granted at the party's final campaign rally Sunday.

"Anyone who thinks change is guaranteed is mistaken and misleading," he said. "Until the polling stations close on Tuesday, each and every one of us must act knowing that change is in danger. The responsibility for making it happen rests with each and every one of us."

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu warned his voters that if the opposition wins the upcoming election on Tuesday, Israel will "give citizenship to hundreds of thousands of Palestinians."

Speaking on the pro-government Channel 14, Netanyahu said Israel will make the move if the opposition bloc led by election frontrunner Gadi Eisenkot (Yashar) wins the election, adding that it would be "the end of the Jewish state."

The petition, filed by the Adalah Legal Center for Arab Minority Rights in Israel and the Joint List, followed announcements by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud party and far-right Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich's Religious Zionism party that they would deploy some 2,000 election observers in Arab communities, as well as a police directive allowing licensed gun owners to carry their weapons at polling stations.

Joint List chairman Yousef Jabareen said the court "has once again demonstrated that it is neither willing nor able to protect the rights of the Arab public from persecution by the racist right-wing government," adding that Netanyahu "is panicking over the rising voter turnout among Arab citizens."

The son of former Prime Minister Menachem Begin – who founded Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud party and signed Israel's peace treaty with Egypt – urged Likud party members to vote Netanyahu out of office.

"Ten or fifteen years ago, I served in a government headed by Benjamin Netanyahu," former lawmaker Avinadav Begin said. "It was a good government that benefited all Israeli citizens. #1179. Do non-German nationals commit more crimes than Germans?

People without German passports appear more frequently in German police crime statistics than German nationals. A new study explains why.

Every year, when the Federal Criminal Police Office publishes the police crime statistics, the Alternative for Germany (AfD) — a party that is, in part, right-wing extremist — pays particularly close attention. They are looking for crimes committed by refugees, migrants and foreigners living in Germany.

But studies by media scholars show that 95% of the AfD's press releases focus on non-German suspects, while crimes involving German suspects are almost completely ignored.

However, the common narrative of the AfD — that non-Germans are inherently much more violent — is simply not true.

In a new research paper, Susann Prätor, a sociologist, criminologist and professor at the Lower Saxony Police Academy, has taken a very close look at crime data in Germany, together with her colleagues from the University of Zurich and the Lower Saxony Criminological Research Institute.

She looked not only at officially reported crime — that is, all offenses that appeared in police crime statistics — but also at unreported crime: These are all offenses that are not reported or detected, and therefore do not appear in any official statistics but are identified through representative surveys.

"According to police crime statistics, people who do not have German citizenship commit crimes more frequently than German citizens. However, studies into unreported cases show that non-German nationals are twice as likely to be reported. Differences between the two groups are also evident in crimes that go unreported, but they are significantly less pronounced," Prätor told DW.

Crimes committed by foreign nationals are therefore twice as likely to appear in police crime statistics as crimes committed by Germans.

These statistics record all reported cases and do not specify whether the allegations prove to be true.

When the statistics are adjusted for the bias in the reporting of crimes, foreigners are no longer 2.6 times more likely to commit crimes than Germans, but only 1.7 times more likely. This figure is also consistent with the results of studies on unreported juvenile violent crime. According to these studies, foreign youths are about 1.6 times as likely to commit violent crimes as German youths.

Other factors affecting crime include age and gender. Young men make up a larger proportion of the foreign-born population, and young men are the group most prone to criminal behavior across all societies.

According to Prätor, "categories such as being young, male, poorly educated and having a history of violence are factors that increase the likelihood of violent behavior. A certain concept of masculinity also plays a role, wherever that may come from. But we do not see culture as a factor, contrary to the prejudice that masculinity and violence play a greater role in other cultures."

Prätor points to a survey on attitudes toward violence. According to the survey, 5% of German youths view violence positively. Among those without a German passport, the figure is 10%.

The criminologist has identified a crucial factor: "Family upbringing plays an important role in shaping attitudes toward violence, because these attitudes are formed in the home. If I experience violence in my own home, I will have a different relationship to violence than if I hadn't experienced it," said Prätor.

Germany is, however, on the right track, says Prätor, even if it doesn't always feel that way. "Fifty or sixty years ago, parental violence was much more common in child-rearing than it is today. Acts of violence committed by young people are also far less frequent than they were in the 1990s or the early 2000s."

Prätor emphasizes that it is important to bring objectivity to the debate. A good illustration of this is a look at police records of serious violent crimes — such as aggravated assault, manslaughter, or murder. "Of every 100 German citizens, 0.2% commit violent crimes; among non-German nationals, the figure is 0.6%."

However, Prätor points out that "more than 99% of the people living here in Germany — whether of German or non-German origin — the overwhelming majority in this country do not commit any serious violent crimes at all."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Prätor also trains prospective police officers. She wants to send the message to policymakers that they should place greater emphasis on the positive aspects of migration. She argues that the debate on immigration is far too negative, largely due to an overly narrow focus on police crime statistics. The vast majority of non-Germans integrate exceptionally well, she says.

She wants the government to invest more money in prevention.

"By starting as early as possible with children and adolescents: strengthening social skills as early as preschool, building on that in school and responding when incidents of violence do occur. It's also important to invest in infrastructure and recreational activities in certain regions. After all, a key factor in youth violence — regardless of background — is that young people lack a meaningful daily structure," she said.

This article was originally written in German.

#1180. The Decades-Long Battle Within the Democratic Party Establishment Between the Heirs of Dean Acheson and Franklin Roosevelt

The calamitous history of America’s wars of choice.

As Trump’s disastrous war against Iran continues to grind on, it might benefit the incoming class of Democratic policymakers who seem poised to take over not just the House but possibly the Senate to reflect on the calamitous history of Washington’s wars of choice. The first such war was President Harry Truman’s, in Korea, begun by North Korean forces in June 1950. As Nation contributing editor James W. Carden shows in The Great Betrayal: How the Democrats Became the Party of War, Truman and his hawkish secretary of state, Dean Acheson, steered the party in a direction not intended by Truman’s predecessor, Franklin D. Roosevelt. Truman and Acheson’s embrace of the burgeoning national security state and their adoption of the paranoiac anti-communism that heretofore had been characteristic of the American right led them headlong into an unnecessary war of choice in Korea. Korea set the precedent for Vietnam, for Iraq, and for Iran—it was the first of many wars waged in the absence of constitutional authorization on the flimsiest of pretexts.

The invasion of South Korea by North Korea’s Kim Il Sung provided Washington’s Cold War planners with just the story they needed at just the right time. As President Harry Truman reached the midpoint of his first elected term, he surprised some of his Defense and State Department planners by not immediately accepting his national security staff’s more hawkish recommendations. “We were sweating over it,” one Truman adviser admitted later, “then thank god Korea came along.”

The idea that South Korea represented a core US national security interest was a novel one. In fact, there was, in the years and months leading up to the conflict, broad agreement among US policymakers that it represented no such thing. At Yalta, a four-power trusteeship was created to oversee the former Japanese colony. In April 1948, Truman and the Joint Chiefs of Staff (JCS) admitted that Korea was “of little strategic value to the United States.” In a speech on January 12, 1950, Acheson famously left both Korea and Formosa (Taiwan) outside the boundaries of the US defense perimeter in East Asia. North Korea launched its attack on June 24, and even then the Joint Chiefs of Staff warned that it would be “militarily unsound” for Washington to commit large forces “in an area of slight strategic importance.”

But once the war was joined, Truman made the ever-dubious historical parallel with Neville Chamberlain’s decision to “appease” Hitler at Munich. “The free nations have learned the fateful lesson of the 1930’s. That lesson is that aggression must be met firmly. Appeasement leads only to further aggression and ultimately to war,” declared Truman on July 19. Truman later claimed that upon learning of North Korea’s invasion, he “remembered how each time that the democracies failed to act, it had encouraged the aggressors to keep going ahead. Communism was acting in Korea just as Hitler, Mussolini and the Japanese had acted ten, fifteen and twenty years earlier.”

“If this was allowed to go unchallenged,” he continued, “it would mean a third world war, just as similar incidents had brought on a second world war.” In his seminal study on the “Origins of the Cold War,” the realist scholar Hans Morgenthau noted, “The misinterpretation of the North Korean aggression as part of a grand design at world conquest originating in and controlled by Moscow resulted in a drastic militarization of the cold war.” Indeed, Truman and Acheson viewed Asia solely through the prism of the Cold War. Not surprisingly, Acheson blamed the Russians for starting the war, but there is no evidence the project originated with Stalin.

Dean Rusk, an Acheson protégé then serving as assistant secretary of state for the Far East, blithely dismissed China as a puppet of the Soviets. China, in Rusk’s view, was merely a “colonial Russian government, a Slavic Manchukuo on a large-scale.” Acheson also thought he saw Moscow’s hand behind Ho Chi Minh’s insurgency in Vietnam. Acheson worried that Ho might establish a “communist-dominated, Moscow-oriented” regime. For Acheson and his disciples like Rusk, Moscow’s was the not-so-hidden hand behind every problem everywhere.

Paranoia is a poor substitute for strategy, but driven by their fears of a monolithic communist movement, Truman and Acheson provided $15 million to France to bolster its efforts against Ho’s insurgency. Truman also created a US Military Assistance Advisory Group, Indochina, to provide material support and advisers to the French forces fighting the Viet Minh. On October 9, Army Brigadier General Francis G. Brink arrived in Saigon with a contingent of 65 American troops—the first of many more to come. As a recent, and sympathetic, Acheson biographer admits, Acheson “was in the vanguard in leading the United States into Indochina’s Big Muddy.” As with many of his Cold War policies, Truman’s intervention in Vietnam was diametrically opposed to the intentions of his predecessor.

At the Tehran Conference, Roosevelt said the Allies should not fight to restore Vietnam to the French—in his view, after 100 years of French colonialism, the Vietnamese were worse off than ever. In Bohlen’s judgment, Roosevelt’s views on Vietnam reflected the president’s “strong dislike of colonialism,” which Roosevelt frequently expressed. Yet by the time Truman and Acheson left office, Washington was funding nearly half of France’s costs in Vietnam. Ultimately, these decisions set in motion a war that would eventually kill upwards of 3.5 million Vietnamese and 58,000 American soldiers, sailors, and airmen.

By 1952, Truman was a deeply unpopular and polarizing figure, so much so that he was defeated in the New Hampshire primary by a margin of 11 points (55 percent to 44 percent) by Tennessee Senator Estes Kefauver. By the end of March, he had abandoned his bid for reelection. Truman left office with a 32 percent approval rating, the second-lowest approval rating for a departing president after Richard Nixon, who had sunk to 24 percent in 1974. Yet in the three-quarters of a century since leaving office, Truman’s reputation has witnessed a remarkable turnaround. By the time the new century dawned, Truman’s decision to drop the atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki; his headlong rush into a Cold War with the Soviet Union; and his unconstitutional war of choice in Korea were all treated as acts of statesmanship by both popular historians and the Democratic elite. In September 2000, President Bill Clinton presided over a ceremony naming the headquarters of the State Department in honor of Truman. “Thanks, in no small measure to President Truman, we have won the Cold War,” said Clinton.

Truman’s stock has only risen further in the quarter-century since Clinton spoke those words. A Siena College survey released in 2022 ranked Truman as the seventh-greatest president. The 2024 Presidential Greatness Project at the University of Houston ranked Truman as the sixth-greatest. There are precious few dissenters from the pro-Truman consensus. Among the most astringent was the novelist and critic Gore Vidal, who noted, “The inexorable beatification of Harry Truman is now an important aspect of our evolving imperial system.”

But it was Acheson who lent an intellectual sheen and respectability to Truman’s parochialism. It was he, not Truman, who, as the main driver behind institutions like NATO and programs like the ERA, spawned generations of imitators among the Democratic foreign policy cognoscenti. Kennedy’s secretary of state, Dean Rusk, learned at his knee; Clinton’s secretary of state, Madeleine Albright, said Acheson was her model. Republicans also now line up to praise him. Henry Kissinger observed in 2006—and perhaps with not a little envy—that “Accolades for him have become bipartisan.” Later in life, working to defeat congressional opposition to President Nixon’s anti-ballistic missile program, Acheson served as an early mentor to the young neoconservative operatives Paul Wolfowitz, Richard Perle, and Edward Luttwak. Acheson spent his years out of office crafting one of the most enduring and pernicious of Cold War myths: that of Roosevelt’s credulousness in the face of Stalin. Acheson succeeded in selling the story that the Cold War was unavoidable, and the course he and Truman chose could not have been otherwise. Yet others, like Harriman, who knew the Soviets, Stalin, and Roosevelt far better than Acheson, thought otherwise. “FDR was basically right in thinking he could make progress by personal relations with Stalin,” said Harriman some years later. Harriman, like Bohlen, was at Tehran and Yalta and remembered that “Stalin was very much impressed with Roosevelt; you could almost say he was in awe of Roosevelt.” “I don’t know what would have happened if FDR had lived,” said Harriman toward the end of his long, eventful life. “I only know things would not have been the same.”

The militarization of the Cold War that took place under Truman and Acheson was a conscious choice. But it was not a choice with which everyone agreed; and so began a decades-long battle within the Democratic Party establishment between the heirs of Acheson and the heirs of Roosevelt.

James W. Carden is a contributing writer for foreign affairs at The Nation. He served as a policy adviser to the Special Representative for Intergovernmental Affairs and the Office of Russia Affairs at the US State Department.

#1183. DAILY MAIL COMMENT: No one voted for a return to this toxic Brexit psychodrama

Published: 23:00 GMT, 25 October 2026 | Updated: 23:09 GMT, 25 October 2026

Andy Burnham called yesterday for ‘an honest discussion’ about the merits of a return to allowing free movement of people between Britain and countries of the European Union.

Perhaps the PM should start by being honest about his own intentions. In June, he specifically told the mainly Eurosceptic voters of Makerfield that he would not re-run the old Brexit arguments.

‘I’m not proposing the UK considers rejoining the EU,’ he said. ‘I respect the decision that was made at the referendum, and it’s going to undermine everything I’ve said about strengthening democracy if we don’t respect that vote.’

It got him elected, but what a difference a few months makes in his morally flexible world. Shamelessly flouting that Makerfield pledge, he is already dragging this country back towards Brussels. He even says we may go ‘all the way’ and apply to rejoin.

Not only has Mr Burnham deceived the people of Makerfield, he is also making a mockery of Labour’s 2024 manifesto, which expressly rejected a return to free movement, the single market or customs union. Hardly the way to start an honest debate.

But then Remainers are used to churning out falsehoods. They love to complain about the notorious Leave campaign bus slogan claiming Britain sent £350,000 a week to the EU. And they had a point. After the UK rebate and other benefits were taken off, it turned out to be merely £252,000 a week. But compared with the mendacity and outrageous scaremongering of the Remain campaign, this was a minor sin.

In June, Andy Burnham told the mainly Eurosceptic voters of Makerfield that he was 'not proposing the UK considers rejoining the EU'

Treasury forecasts before the 2016 vote predicted that Brexit would bring economic catastrophe – a GDP fall of up to 6 per cent, as many as 820,000 more unemployed, a drop in real wages of 3-4 per cent, and house prices plummeting by up to 18 per cent. It was all tosh.

In the event, jobs and vacancies soared, wages and GDP continued to rise, while house prices, far from collapsing, remained buoyant in the years after the referendum.

Spurred into life by Mr Burnham’s double-dealing remarks, Remainers are at it again, spewing out spurious figures purporting to show how disastrous Brexit has been. Yet more humbug.

They don’t mention that going back would mean cancelling the many trade deals made with other countries since Brexit and relinquishing control of our trade policy.

Or that it could mean state investment in steel and other domestic industries becoming illegal and that AI and other technical developments could be hampered by EU regulation.

Nor the net £9.2billion a year we no longer pay in membership fees. As our rebate would not be renewed, that figure would be substantially higher if we went back in. Would we be allowed back anyway, and if so, would we have to join the single currency? Would there be a fresh entry fee, would we have to join the border-free Schengen zone?

If Mr Burnham really wants to rake over dead coals, he must take account of the demonstrable cons of shackling ourselves once more to the ailing EU, as well as the imagined pros.

Vanishingly few people want to go through the Brexit psychodrama again – including another toxic debate over free movement. It can only bring more rancour and division.

Four months ago Mr Burnham claimed he respected the referendum result, while clearly plotting to overturn it all along. Is that his idea of honesty?

#1186. A fire devastates the Eagle's Nest retreat built for Hitler in Germany. A suspect is detained

This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here.

BERLIN — A fire swept through the mountaintop retreat built for Adolf Hitler and known as the Eagle’s Nest as emergency services struggled to tackle the blaze in snow and wind, and a man was arrested on suspicion of arson, authorities said.

Emergency services in the Berchtesgaden district, in the Bavarian Alps in Germany’s southeastern corner, were alerted to the fire by an alarm at about 9:15 p.m. Friday. Firefighters and police rushed to the scene — located at the end of a narrow road that winds up the mountain, in part through a series of tunnels — and could see the flames as they approached.

They stopped and arrested a man on a motorcycle driving the other way down the road.

Prosecutors said Saturday that the 33-year-old suspect, a German citizen who has ties to the Berchtesgaden area but doesn’t currently live there, was questioned. They said he showed signs of mental illness and he was being sent to a psychiatric facility, but they also would look into the possibility of a political motive in view of the building’s history. Police said there were no indications that anyone else was involved.

Rain that turned into the season’s first significant snow, accompanied by strong wind, complicated the already difficult task of tackling the blaze, and firefighters had to pull out overnight after several hours, officials said. No one was injured in the fire, and firefighters hoped to finish their work Saturday though they weren’t able to enter the building because of a danger of falling material.

The building, known in German as the Kehlsteinhaus, is located on a cliff 6,017 feet above sea level. It is reachable by an elevator built inside the rock from the end of the mountain road, which is closed to public traffic but used during the day by buses for visitors.

It has been operated as a restaurant since 1952 and contains an exhibition on its history. Hitler rarely used the Kehlsteinhaus — unlike the Berghof residence, also in the Berchtesgaden area, the ruins of which were demolished in 1952.

The Obersalzberg Documentation Center, farther down the mountain, is home to the area’s main historical exhibition and was unaffected by the fire.

Officials indicated that the Eagle’s Nest would be restored, though details were sketchy about how exactly that would be done.

“We’re not going to leave a ruin there,” Bavaria’s interior minister, Joachim Herrmann, told reporters in Berchtesgaden. But what the site will look like in the future will be a matter for discussions with local officials, historians, preservationists and others.

“I think we will be able to find a sensible solution,” Herrmann added. Bavaria’s state government owns the building.

The minister stressed that “it is important that we continue to do the work of remembrance.”

The measure in question, the Office of the Inspector General law, creates an independent statewide watchdog that oversees inspectors general, investigates alleged fraud across state programs, establishes fraud prevention standards and improves coordination and data sharing.

However, Heidi Heino, the Republican candidate for Minnesota’s 36th Senate District, told Fox News Digital her test against the Feeding Our Future scheme and other past fraud cases found the law lacks extra safeguards when potential risks emerge.

"When I stress tested against Feeding Our Future and some of the other fraud schemes that we had in Minnesota, it would have found the fraud eventually, but it's way after the money was already gone, and we would still be stuck trying to claw it back," Heino said.

"Business does a lot with a little," she said. "Government does the opposite. They do a little with a lot of resources."

Heino also argued Feeding Our Future should not have been allowed to address complaints against itself.

"We had 30 complaints to the Minnesota Department of Education regarding the fraud, and they are mostly overlooked, or Feeding Our Future had to go correct itself and that was a huge gap there," she said.

She proposed immediately freezing payments, conducting a full review and triggering an outside audit.

"The OIG has good bones, but it needs teeth," she said.

Without independent audits, Heino said Minnesota will not be able to uncover fraud-related gaps, saying the additional oversight would save more money than it costs.

"We get a lot of pushback saying this is going to be expensive, but is it?" she said. "It will be less expensive to have an independent audit than it is going to be to have all the fraud and lose taxpayer dollars to fraudulent activities."

Those same issues apply to current state programs like Minnesota’s Paid Leave program, according to Heino.

"However, we need to rein it in and have more investigation before we start sending out the checks, especially with paid family leave," she said. "They pay out before they have the doctor's note certifying that this is actually true and they have verified it."

She acknowledged that the law is a "great first step" toward addressing the problem but said it does not go far enough to protect taxpayers and prevent future fraud.

As a mother, grandmother and taxpayer, Heino said she is fed up with how leaders in her home state have handled fraud, adding the problem has gotten so bad that Minnesota has become the "laughing stock of the nation," and people no longer want to say they are from the state.

"We need to funnel those resources to the people that actually need them and keep people committing fraud from taking our money and running away with it, buying luxury condos or homes and then funneling it out of the country," she said.

Fox News Digital reached out to Walz's office and the Minnesota Department of Education for comment.

"We have not slowed down. There is no sense in which the fraud has been stopped in Minnesota," Bill Glahn, a policy fellow at the Center of the American Experiment, told Fox News Digital in August, making the case that the fraud situation in the state has not been properly addressed.

Kiera McDonald is a Production Assistant for Fox News Digital.

#1189. FIFPRO report highlights growing pains in women's football

Expected global revenue of over $1 billion and new faces at the U17 World Cup show women's football is booming, but a recent report also highlights need for better structures globally.

At first glance, women's football is healthier than ever. A recent report by FIFPRO, football's global players' union, said worldwide revenue is expected to reach over $1bn (€894m) in 2027. The World Cup in Brazil, a first in South America, will be the last with 32 teams and is expected to be the most watched and biggest revenue-generating women's tournament ever.

The good news continues with the U17 Women's World Cup in Morocco, where the tournament is being held every year for five straight years. Germany, France, Spain, Brazil, the United States and defending champions North Korea are all at the 2026 edition of a competition whose reputation continues to grow.

"You can just see where the game is going, which is so exciting," US head coach Ciara Crinion told FIFA. "The level has just gone up. We have to continue to stay with that and compete as well. [The U-17 Women's World Cup] almost feels like that first stepping stone in a major tournament for young players, and now you see how serious it is taken."

Puerto Rico, Australia and Argentina are making their debuts. For Puerto Rico, qualification is historic, as no football team in the men's or women's game has ever reached a World Cup tournament before.

"We've embraced this idea of being Puerto Rico's first team to qualify for a World Cup," head coach Andres Mirabelli told FIFA. Alongside national development plans, player recruitment was aided by a diaspora of nearly four million in the United States, perhaps the strongest place for women's football in the world. According to FIFPRO, the regional football average salary in North America is $5,940 (€5,547) per month, which is far higher than any other continent.

But even for the handful of players who make it out of these youth tournaments to a professional career, creating a living out of the beautiful game remains a real challenge. The aforementioned FIFPRO report details that many professional female players across the world barely earn minimum wage, with some even falling below it.

The report, which sourced its data from player surveys across the world, found that only 66% of professional players are paid for 12 months a year. The global average salary is $2,600 (€2,300) a month, but the range varies drastically across the world. In Eastern Europe, for example, that average is $880 per month. In Africa, it is $432, but in North America it is just under $6,000.

"I think what you also find in the women's game is the gaps are not just between the top five leagues and the rest. There is a gap there, but even within leagues themselves [there is one]," FIFPRO head of research and strategy for women's football Frankie Brown told DW.

"In some of the other leagues you're dealing with teams that are operating professionally, so will be paying their players on a reasonable wage, and playing in the same league as them you'll have players that are on amateur contracts and not being paid at all."

With economic and job security an issue for many, the report reveals that psychological stress factors are now the second main reason many consider leaving football.

"This is one of the most concerning parts of the report," Alex Culvin, the director of women's football at FIFPRO, said in a statement.

"Of the 49% of women’s football players considering leaving the sport early, 46% cited their mental health as the reason. In interviews, players say the sport's growth brings new pressures — including extra workload and social media abuse — but that clubs do not have the necessary safeguards in place to support these changes. We want clubs and national associations to provide mandatory mental health support focused on wellbeing, which is independent of sporting performance objectives."

FIFPRO's report is asking FIFA to set a so-called floor for the women's game so that minimum standards in key areas such as contracts, pensions and health can be enforced. Perhaps inspiration can be taken from the labor deal the WNBA agreed in 2026. It was long-negotiated deal that ultimately sent a message to female athletes everywhere to push for better pay, conditions and a greater share of the revenue they help generate.

"It is positive that average salaries are increasing for some players and that more are earning a satisfactory wage, but it’s important to note that there is a huge disparity in pay across regions," said Culvin.

"There is also an imbalance in conditions, not only across the globe but also within regions; in Europe, for example, the difference in standards between the east and west is enormous. This is a gulf we need to work hard to narrow; the growth in the most advanced markets must not be completely isolated from the rest of the industry.

With high hopes for the 2027 World Cup in Brazil and recent moves to increase professional football domestically, Germany is aiming to become an example for structural improvement in women's football. Hosting the Euros in 2029 certainly gives them an incentive to improve standards.

While salaries are in the upper tier — in the 2023-24 season, a women's Bundesliga player earned an average base salary of around €48,000 per year — the process of structural development in the country is still in its infancy. A new German football association rule shows that even basic professional structures are still being established. Only since the 2025–26 season have teams in the Women's Bundesliga been required to employ assistant coaches, goalkeeper coaches and athletic coaches on a full-time, professional basis.

"The facilities and the staff members," Nicole Anyomi told DW, were a factor in her making a recent move to London City Lionesses. "We have 30-plus staff members here whereas in Frankfurt we had like seven or eight. You can learn from each person and there is something new to learn every day. I think that's how you develop as a player faster."

Ultimately, the faster the game grows, the greater need to close the gaps.

"Despite playing on different continents, players are connected by their precarity," Culvin said. "The redistribution systems in women's football need to be more effective, touching more players and supporting a more sustainable ecosystem."

#1190. Tom Hayden’s Legacy and the New American Left

Standing in front of protesters on a misty day in Seattle, a 59-year-old Tom Hayden spoke into a bullhorn, declaring his hope. “I never thought the time would come that a new generation of activists would part the waters, the waters in which your idealism is supposed to be drowned.” The venerable activist, cofounder of Students for a Democratic Society (SDS), had spent almost two decades in the California State Legislature. But like other progressive legislators, he, too, was stymied by the conservative politics of the late 20th century. Earlier that day, tens of thousands of people—a historic coalition of union members, environmental activists, and anarchists—overwhelmed city officials and shut down the World Trade Organization (WTO) Ministerial Conference on November 30, 1999. It was the first major blow against the Clinton-era free-trade consensus.

The crowd repeated Hayden’s words through the “people’s mic” method and mirrored the then–state Senator’s visible giddiness toward the end of his remarks. “You have slowed the machinery of destruction down. But it can’t be about slowing the rate of destruction. It has to be about speeding the rate of creation of a new world, a better place.” Decades after he organized the landmark anti-war protests at the 1968 Democratic National Convention, Hayden was inspired by what he witnessed in Seattle. He could once again imagine a left that could win.

Tom Hayden passed away 10 years ago, on October 23, 2016, just weeks before Trump’s unexpected victory. As a result, his worst fears of an authoritarian right’s limiting the gains of the 1960s came true. Still, his life has become an even more relevant case study for those trying to figure out the most effective way to resist the current administration’s assault on democracy. As a lifelong insider-outsider, a Freedom Rider who later advised presidential candidates, Hayden was a passionate proponent of both radical direct action and electoral campaigns. Whether in the streets of American cities fighting back against ICE or in the offices of activist politicians like Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez or Mayor Zohran Mamdani, today’s progressives are finding creative ways to build on the work of Hayden’s generation. As memory of the Vietnam War era fades, a reexamination of ecumenical organizers like him will strengthen our understanding of the links between the victories and defeats of the past and today’s attempts to build a better democracy.

Born in 1939, Thomas Emmet Hayden was a product of middle-class America. Coming of age as the American left was decimated during the Red Scare, he did not consider himself political until he learned about the sit-in movement in 1960. He was first arrested as a Freedom Rider in Albany, Georgia, on December 10, 1961, the moment he began work on the first draft of SDS’s manifesto, the Port Huron Statement. Completed by Hayden and other founders of the organization the following June, the document promoted participatory democracy, offered a powerful rebuke of the era’s Cold War consensus, and soon became required reading for organizers for decades to come. What began as a modest network of student leaders would grow dramatically following the expansion of the war in Vietnam, with approximately 100,000 members at its peak in the late 1960s.

Hayden became one of the leading figures of the New Left, a figure whom many reporters treated as an entry point to a new age of radicalism. Together with other SDS leaders, he helped establish community organizing projects in several cities, traveled to Vietnam, where he once facilitated the release of three American POWs, and was put on trial for conspiracy to riot as part of the Chicago Eight. Over time, the times increasingly radicalized Hayden, who vacillated between calling for “Two, Three, Many Columbias” and clinging to his battered but lingering hope for mainstream politicians like Robert F. Kennedy during his presidential campaign.

However, Hayden’s work stretched far beyond the 1960s. Like other New Left leaders, he is often tied to a narrative of decline about the New Left’s rise and fall, centered on the well-documented implosion of SDS in 1969. The truth is that Hayden’s life tells a far more complicated and representative story of the decade’s activism, its ongoing influence on today’s progressives, and the porous relationship between radicals and reformers in America.

Unlike some high-profile leaders of his era, Hayden remained dedicated to movement work. Instead of burning out, he gradually shifted toward more conventional tactics in the early 1970s. Together with his then-wife Jane Fonda, he led the Indochina Peace Campaign, which helped sustain the anti-war movement’s political power and cut off funding for the Vietnam War. Following an insurgent Senate campaign, he and Fonda established the Campaign for Economic Democracy in California in 1977. By the early 1980s, CED had become a statewide organization that helped pass rent control initiatives and elect dozens of local and statewide officials. Hayden won a State Assembly seat in Santa Monica in 1982, serving a decade as a state representative, then another eight years as a state senator. Despite Republican governors’ limiting him for most of his time in Sacramento, Hayden still championed environmental reforms, including the Safe Drinking Water and Toxic Enforcement Act of 1986, and pushed for peace among street gangs in Los Angeles.

After he was termed out of the State Legislature, Hayden taught classes on social movements, joined The Nation as an editorial board member, and once again became a fixture at anti-war rallies and other meetings in progressive spaces. During his brief stint as a fellow at Harvard’s Institute of Politics, he led a series of workshops, “Activism Now!: Students, Sweatshops and Globalization,” that culminated in a trip where four students were arrested while documenting planned protests against the Free Trade Area of the Americas. After Occupy Wall Street, Hayden was in regular contact with new movement figures such as Debt Collective cofounder Astra Taylor after the two appeared on a panel together in 2014. “Good luck to Strike Debt. As your generation’s prospects decline and a new Dark Age rises, I do think you have a window of glory ahead though,” he wrote to Taylor. It was one of many interactions where Hayden cheered on a new generation shaped by the WTO protests, the post-9/11 wars, and the 2008 financial collapse.

In his final years, Hayden tried to situate the Obama presidency within a longer history of protest that contributed to his 2008 victory. He encouraged progressives to celebrate the best elements of the 44th president’s foreign policy (Cuba, Iran) while remaining critical of the war in Afghanistan and the administration’s tepid domestic agenda. He drew links between the Black Lives Matter movement and his work in Newark and lauded the lobbying efforts of the Dreamers. In 2016, Hayden infuriated many progressives when he backed Hillary Clinton over Bernie Sanders just days before the New York primary. He saw it as a pragmatic choice, rooted in fears of a Trump administration and the future of the Supreme Court. Those fears were legitimate and have proven prescient, but his endorsement underestimated the Sanders campaign’s potential impact.

If he were alive, he would celebrate that 2016 was a real turning point for the American left, when countless young organizers began to seriously engage in electoral politics. While he never would have predicted that the Democratic Socialists of America would become the post-2016 left’s primary beneficiary (even though he spoke at their annual convention in 2013), he would praise its electoral work, especially in cities like New York City, Chicago, and Los Angeles.

Much as he felt witnessing the Battle of Seattle in 1999, Hayden would have been ecstatic to see how a broad cross section of ordinary people has stood up to masked ICE agents occupying American cities over the past two years. The Minneapolis protests and general strike were, in many ways, the model many others from the 1960s generation had dreamed of for decades. The former community organizer would have been moved by how Minnesotans courageously faced down the president and won.

It is, in fact, a new dark age, but it has also benefited from those who built on the work of figures like Tom Hayden. He recognized the long battle but was also often driven by his desire to take urgent action to confront injustice. His story reflects that of many from his era who spent decades searching for different channels for progressives to win political power. Hayden had a searching mind, open to experimentation and adapting to history. Throughout it all, he thought that radical grassroots movements could merge with conventional politics to create a new democracy.

Michael Koncewicz is a historian and Associate Director of NYU's Institute for Public Knowledge. He is currently working on a biography of Tom Hayden.

#1193. I'm a Leo in love with a Virgo, but the sex is nonexistent. What gives?

This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here.

This story is part of Image’s October Pleasure issue, which luxuriates in the personal pleasures of stylists, buyers, poets, designers and more.

My partner is a Leo and I’m a Virgo. We are deeper in love and more connected than ever, but the sex is kind of nonexistent. What gives?

Isn’t it agonizing when most of your stars align with a lover’s — but not all? We’re victims of a battle-scarred dating landscape filled with minefields: option paralysis, transactional relationship attitudes, ghosting and all of the other infuriating and disheartening things that make a lot of us want to give up. I commend you for reaching out, because that in and of itself is an indicator that you’ve found something special with your beloved. It’s beautiful that you’re doing your best to harmonize what you already have, instead of discarding it for the next shiny thing.

Leo and Virgo are adjacent signs. Adjacent signs, coming one after the other, are an interesting combination because they are so different, but encapsulate certain similarities due to their proximity in the zodiac. It’s possible that the both of you enjoy being leaders in your own capacities — Leo is known for their directness and presence, while Virgo can express some of the same traits in their work life and ability to hold it all together. It’s no surprise that you’ve found kindred spirits in each other.

Finding lost jewels in paper recreationsLingering on L.A.’s sexy sidewalksStaying in uniform with Thom BrowneLuxuriating in the personal with fashion buyersSearching for a mattress that feels like nothingToasting our 2026 Image Makers in ChinatownConsidering all forms of pleasure with Gabi Abrão

I’ve said this before in our corner of the digital world, and I’ll say it again: Sex with a partner is like a Venn diagram. You and your partner come together with all the intricacies and idiosyncrasies of your respective sexualities, and you find the sweet spot where your desires overlap. You might be feeling like that intersection is smaller than you would like, but it doesn’t mean that it doesn’t exist. Plenty of couples take more time than others to find a rhythm in their sex life, whether that’s frequency, pace or incorporation of fantasies. There are infinite possibilities when it comes to finding what works with another human being.

Step one: Address your sexual discrepancies honestly and openly with your partner, with love. Many couples, when faced with a less-than-ideal sex life, can feel like they’re “failing” at their relationship (ahem, Virgo) or that it’s some horrible harbinger of relationship collapse to come. The reality is that for all couples, sex ebbs and flows. If you spend enough time with someone, there are bound to be periods of fruition and aliveness as much as there are periods of fallow and stagnancy. It’s normal. Other couples also might have great sex lives, but struggle connecting in the deeper ways that the two of you have already handled beautifully. In communicating your unmet needs and any fears you may have about the future of the relationship, you can open a portal to a more profound understanding of each other.

We’ve found the ultimate talisman of Virgoan vigor: a dutiful pebble grinder.

And since we’re talking about astrology, it’s a common misconception that Sun signs are the be-all, end-all of synastry (a.k.a. relationship compatibility). It’s really the Moon, Venus and Mars that matter most when it comes to whether a connection has staying power, or room for sustainable improvement. Delve into your and your partner’s astrological signatures in a more nuanced way, and you’ll find clues to how to move forward. For example: Someone with their Mars in Libra needs romance, beauty and peace to feel turned on, whereas a Mars in Aries person could delight more in the spontaneity of energetic play. Your partner’s Mars sign is like a cheat code for you to find out what gets them there sexually.

If all else fails, there’s no shame in bringing this to a sex therapist or couples counselor. Depending on how locked in you’re feeling with your partner, it could be a worthy investment in the future you’re building together on your already-amazing foundation of connection. And remember: Sex is best when it feels comfortable, safe and joyous for all parties involved. Try not to get too in your head about the performance of it all, or assume sex alone is the ultimate litmus test for a healthy, long-lasting relationship. Know yourself, understand as much as you can about your loved ones and the rest will follow.

#1196. California must respond to DOJ's emergency request over ballots mailed to alleged noncitizens, court rules

The 9th Circuit ordered California to respond to an emergency Justice Department request seeking to set aside ballots tied to roughly 20,000 suspected noncitizens ahead of the midterm elections.

A federal appeals court ordered California to respond by noon Saturday to the Trump administration's emergency request involving roughly 20,000 mail-in ballots sent to people the Justice Department suspects are noncitizens ahead of the midterm elections.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit issued the order late Friday after the DOJ filed an emergency request earlier in the day seeking a ruling by Saturday.

The Justice Department sought emergency relief from the appeals court after U.S. District Judge David Carter did not rule by a deadline previously requested by the department.

The DOJ is asking California election officials to set aside ballots associated with individuals on its list while their eligibility is reviewed, rather than allowing the ballots to be processed alongside other votes.

DOJ GIVES CALIFORNIA 48 HOURS TO REVIEW LIST OF POSSIBLE NONCITIZENS ON VOTER ROLLS

California Gov. Gavin Newsom speaks about the Election Rigging Response Act at a News conference at the Democracy Center, Japanese American National Museum Aug. 14, 2025, in Los Angeles.  (Mario Tama/Getty Images)

In its emergency filing, the DOJ emphasized the urgency of its request.

"This is an emergency," the filing, submitted by Attorney General Todd Blanche and First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli, stated.

"Every minute of processing that occurs without segregating the ballots of suspected non-eligible voters causes untraceable disenfranchisement and dilution of the votes of United States citizens," the filing continued.

Despite the Ninth Circuit's order, a hearing before Judge Carter remains scheduled for Tuesday, according to Fox News' Matt Finn. It remains unclear whether the appeals court will rule before that hearing.

BLANCHE WON'T RULE OUT DOJ BLOCKING ELECTION CERTIFICATION IN 'DOOMSDAY' SCENARIO

Bill Essayli, the first assistant U.S. attorney for the Central District of California, appears at a news conference at the Spring Street Courthouse Aug. 13, 2026. (Allen J. Schaben/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images)

Essayli previously told Fox News Digital that federal investigators have evidence showing the 20,000 individuals received mail-in ballots in October.

His office sued California last week seeking a court order to prevent ballots returned by those individuals from being counted.

"We're not asking California to take any drastic steps other than to sequester the ballots from the suspected noncitizens," Essayli said in an interview Wednesday. "We believe it's at a minimum of 20,000. That's the floor."

Essayli also clashed with California Gov. Gavin Newsom on social media this week over the state's safeguards against noncitizen voting.

Essayli accused California of allowing noncitizens onto its voter rolls because of what he described as inadequate citizenship verification procedures, while Newsom defended the integrity of the state's elections and maintained that California was following the law.

‘RAW MATERIAL FOR ELECTION FRAUD’: EXPERT FLAGS VOTER-ROLL PROBLEMS FAR BEYOND ONE STATE

An official vote-by-mail ballot, mailed to a Southern California resident ahead of the general election, Oct. 17, 2026, in Los Angeles. (Jay L Clendenin/Getty Images)

California election officials have rejected the Justice Department's demands.

In court filings, they argued that county election offices lack both the authority and access to federal records needed to verify voters' citizenship status.

They also said separating ballots associated with people on the DOJ's list would be impossible in cases where the ballots have already been processed.

California officials say that once a mail-in ballot's signature has been verified, the ballot is separated from its identifying envelope and processed with other ballots.

According to court records, officials have already processed 331,000 ballots in Los Angeles County alone.

Friday's escalation comes after Essayli's office initially filed the suit Oct. 15, roughly two weeks after California began mailing ballots.

Fox News Digital's James Cirrone contributed to this report.
